BrainChip Lança Sequora: IA de Ponta Que Além de Reconhecer, Também Entende e Responde
AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 14 de outubro de 2026
LAGUNA HILLS, Califórnia, Oct. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — BrainChip Holdings Ltd. (ASX: BRN, OTCQX: BRCHF, ADR: BCHPY), líder global em IA neuromórfica de ultrabaixo consumo de energia, totalmente digital e baseada em eventos, anunciou hoje o lançamento da BrainChip Sequora Core IP, um núcleo de IP de processador que executa IA generativa, incluindo grandes modelos de linguagem (LLMs), diretamente em dispositivos de borda alimentados por bateria.
O próximo passo no roteiro de IA de borda da BrainChip, Sequora, utiliza os pontos fortes da plataforma Akida da empresa. Sua eficiência vem da estrutura do modelo: um design de espaço de estados mantém o uso da memória fixo, independentemente da duração do fluxo de dados ou da conversa. Por isso, a Sequora escala de modelos com alguns milhões até 3 bilhões de parâmetros. Dispositivos que antes só conseguiam reconhecer um sinal agora podem entender, explicar e responder com os níveis de potência que os clientes esperam da BrainChip.
“Nossos clientes comerciais e aeroespaciais/de defesa estão incorporando a IA em muitos dos sistemas de borda de última geração que oferecem processamento e tomada de decisões em tempo real em ambientes congestionados e disputados, com o mínimo de impacto em termos de tamanho, peso e consumo de energia”, afirmou Frank Ferrante, CEO da ForwardEdge ASIC. “A Sequora coloca a IA generativa em um núcleo de IP de baixo consumo de energia que atende a muitas das demandas dos chips personalizados que desenvolvemos. Ele proporciona um caminho para adicionar inteligência no dispositivo a ASICs de borda de missão crítica.”
O que a Sequora faz
A Sequora elimina o gargalo de memória e energia que impedia a IA generativa de ser usada em dispositivos alimentados por bateria, como fones de ouvido e nós de sensores. Em conjunto com a Akida, ela reúne duas cargas de trabalho em uma única solução: A Akida processa dados de sensores em tempo real vibração, áudio, radar, dados IQ brutos de radiofrequência (RF) e sinais biológicos enquanto a Sequora executa IA generativa e sequencial, incluindo LLMs no dispositivo, interação de voz para voz e agentes de IA.
Mercados de assistentes de voz, wearables para consumidores aeroespacial e defesa, radares automotivos e industriais, IoT industrial e dispositivos médicos e biomédicos precisam de inferência convencional e inferência generativa no mesmo produto.
“A borda é onde a IA se torna útil na infraestrutura cotidiana, desde os medidores de serviços públicos até os sistemas de mobilidade”, disse Jay Kim, CEO da edgeAI Inc. “A BrainChip percebeu cedo que a eficiência decidiria quem venceria na borda. Agora, eles estão aplicando esse mesmo raciocínio à IA generativa, proporcionando recursos de linguagem e raciocínio para dispositivos que funcionam com uma bateria pequena.”

YIBIN, China, Oct. 15, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — The 2026 World Power Battery Conference recently convened in Yibin, China, where Yibin-based automaker KAIYI presented flagship X7 Hybrid, showcasing its capabilities and applications of hybrid battery technology. With X7 Hybrid’s expansion into Central and South America, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Eastern Europe, it unlocks greater outdoor freedom for consumers.
Advanced Battery Technology, Anchored in Safety and Stability
The X7 Hybrid features the KAIYI Super Hybrid system, coordinating an engine and dual electric motors. The drive motor delivers 150 kW peak power and 310 N·m peak torque. With a quad-core dual-control MCU, the system reaches 98.5% maximum mechanical efficiency for smoother, quieter, more efficient driving.
Building on this powertrain, the X7 Hybrid incorporates an onboard 18.67 kWh high-energy lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, which supports 105 km of NEDC all-electric range. Whats more, a 30%80% SOC charge takes only 30 minutes, further enabling effortless daily all-electric commuting. IP68-rated dust and water resistance and full-time intelligent thermal management ensure reliable operationfrom desert heat to humid rainforestswhile LFP chemistry delivers lasting stability and capacity retention.
6.6 kW V2L Output Unlocks Outdoor Power in Every Scenario
More than the vehicles driving core, the battery serves as a mobile energy station. The X7 Hybrids 6.6 kW vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability channels energy from the traction battery beyond the vehicle to power external equipment. It can power induction cooktops and projectors at campsites, sound and lighting systems at outdoor gatherings, and charge drones and camera gear. By way of illustration, the 18.67 kWh battery can theoretically sustain a 1.5 kW appliance for more than 12 hours.
Moreover, enabled by the KAIYI Super Hybrid system, when the battery runs low, the engine can generate electricity to replenish it and sustain the external power supplytruly bringing the comforts of home to the great outdoors.
X7 Plus Hybrid Battery Upgrade Delivers Greater Ease for Outdoor Power
Under KAIYIs global product roadmap, the all-new X7 Plus Hybrid is scheduled to make its debut in 2027. Its battery capacity will rise to 27.2 kWh, and the vehicle will retain 6.6 kW V2L output. As the X7 lineup continues to evolve, KAIYI will offer global customers more outdoor travel options and help them enjoy a greener, more convenient, and more enriching outdoor lifestyle.

Por Laís Adriana*
São Paulo, 13/10/2026 – O presidente do Banco do Japão (BoJ), Kazuo Ueda, afirmou nesta terça-feira que a inflação subjacente do país está próxima de 2% e que é importante estabilizar os preços nesse nível, ao participar de sessão na Câmara dos Representantes.
Segundo a Reuters, várias fontes disseram que o banco central japonês confirmará que a inflação atingiu a meta em sua próxima reunião. Ueda também disse monitorar pressões inflacionárias da guerra no Oriente Médio, emissões de dívidas relacionadas à inteligência artificial, políticas fiscais de cada país e indicadores econômicos positivos, principalmente nos Estados Unidos. Na visão do presidente do BoJ, tudo isso está contribuindo para a escalada de rendimentos soberanos globalmente, que é monitorada “cuidadosamente” pelo BoJ.
Já a primeira-ministra do Japão, Sanae Takaichi, ressaltou que mantém comunicação próxima com os Estados Unidos para assegurar um comportamento ordenado do mercado cambial. De acordo com o jornal The Financial Express, Takaichi disse ainda que este é o momento de implementar urgentemente uma política fiscal “responsável e proativa”.
Já a ministra das Finanças japonesa, Satsuki Katayama, confirmou que assumirá o papel de chefe do Comitê de Desenvolvimento Conjunto do Banco Mundial e do Fundo Monetário Internacional (FMI), de acordo com o Kyodo News. Será a primeira vez que uma pessoa japonesa comanda o comitê desde sua criação, em 1974, e o mandato terá duração de dois anos. A decisão deve ser formalmente anunciada pelas instituições após uma reunião na quinta-feira.

Marvell, Microsoft e Oracle anunciaram nesta terça-feira, 13, um esforço alinhado ao Open Compute Project (OCP) com o objetivo de padronizar um módulo de segurança de hardware integrado para infraestrutura de nuvem e data centers.
Em comunicado conjunto, as empresas apontaram que a missão é definir especificações abertas para um módulo voltado ao gerenciamento do ciclo de vida de chaves criptográficas diretamente no nível do servidor. As chaves são usadas para proteger dados privados e sensíveis em armazenamento, em trânsito e os dados só podem ser lidos uma vez que sejam descriptografados com sua chave associada.
Assim, a abordagem deve reduzir a latência, melhorar a escalabilidade e fortalecer a postura de segurança das cargas de trabalho em nuvem, projetam as empresas.
“À medida que a IA transforma a cibersegurança e a tecnologia quântica remodela a criptografia, proteger as chaves e credenciais no coração da nossa infraestrutura digital nunca foi tão importante”, disse Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO e technical fellow do Microsoft Azure.
O OCP é uma comunidade colaborativa focada em redesenhar tecnologia de hardware para apoiar de forma eficiente as crescentes demandas de infraestrutura de computação.

Brasil encara Argentina em segundo amistoso antes do Mundial Feminino
Após vencer o primeiro confronto, seleções voltam a campo na Arena de Pernambuco em preparação para a Copa do Mundo de 2027
A Seleção Brasileira Feminina enfrenta a Argentina nesta terça-feira (13), às 20h30 (de Brasília), na Arena de Pernambuco, em Recife. O amistoso é o segundo confronto entre as equipes e serve como preparação para a Copa do Mundo Feminina de 2027, que será disputada no Brasil.
No primeiro duelo, realizado no último sábado (10) no Beira-Rio, em Porto Alegre, a equipe brasileira venceu por 3 a 1.
Luany, Geyse e Angelina marcaram os gols do Brasil, enquanto Maricel Pereyra descontou para a Argentina.
Para a partida desta terça-feira (13), o técnico Arthur Elias terá que lidar com desfalques importantes. A volante Angelina, uma das artilheiras do último jogo, fraturou o nariz durante o confronto e foi cortada da convocação.
A lateral Bruninha também está fora, após romper o ligamento cruzado anterior (LCA) do joelho direito, necessitando de cirurgia.
Reforços e possível escalação
Em contrapartida, a Seleção Brasileira terá o retorno de três atletas que cumpriram suspensão no primeiro amistoso: a zagueira Tarciane e as atacantes Kerolin e Bia Zaneratto. O próprio técnico Arthur Elias também estará de volta à área técnica, após cumprir suspensão no último sábado.
Com essas opções, Arthur Elias pode promover mudanças na escalação e dar minutos a jogadoras que não atuaram ou tiveram pouca oportunidade no confronto anterior. Uma possível formação do Brasil inclui Lorena; Isabela, Mariza, Tarciane e Raíssa Bahia; Duda Sampaio, Maiara e Kerolin; Tainá Maranhão, Bia Zaneratto (Jhonson) e Geyse.
Histórico do confronto e próximos jogos
Brasil e Argentina já se enfrentaram 22 vezes na história do futebol feminino, considerando o primeiro amistoso deste mês.
Os dados do Fifa Data Centre mostram a superioridade brasileira, com 19 vitórias, um empate e apenas duas derrotas contra as rivais.
Este duelo será o último compromisso da Seleção Brasileira em território nacional em 2026. A equipe de Arthur Elias já tem agendados dois amistosos contra o Japão na próxima Data Fifa: em 29 de novembro, em Hiroshima, e em 5 de dezembro, em Okayama.

artigo.texto: Gil Torquato, Abranet: É difícil pensar na regulamentação do Redata ainda este ano Para o presidente da Abranet, a renovação do Congresso Nacional e a própria eleição presidencial deve provocar um delay. "É ruim, mas é o momento que estamos vivendo". Ele também defendeu o adiamento da Reforma Tributária. O presidente da Associação Brasileira de Internet (Abranet), Gil Torquato, defendeu ao participar de um painel na Futurecom 2026 que a regulação da Inteligência Artificial tem de ser “o mais cirúrgica possível e cobrir setores específicos para não inibir a inovação”. Segundo ele, quanto menos regulação será melhor para a IA, uma vez que é necessário estimular e não inibir o mercado. Em entrevista, Gil Torquato disse que as regulamentações têm de dar respaldo e segurança jurídica para assegurar os investimentos. Sinalizou ainda que uma agência para IA tem de ajudar nas diretrizes, mas não teria de ter uma visão punitiva. Gil Torquato é descrente da possibilidade de o Marco Legal de IA ser aprovado ainda este ano. “Houve uma renovação do Congresso e o tema tem de ser mais discutido”, pontuou. O presidente da Abranet falou também sobre o Redata. Ele também acha difícil ter a regulamentação ainda este ano – ela está com o poder executivo – diante das eleições presidenciais. “O Redata é muito importante, gostaria que saísse, mas acho que teremos um delay”, admite. E ao ser questionado sobre a Reforma Tributária, Gil Torquato lembrou que as empresas não estão preparadas e o próprio governo está atrasado. Ele defendeu o adiamento da vigência do novo regime. “É um tema sensível. Afeta todas as empresas e é preciso rediscutir as alíquotas”. Assista a íntegra da entrevista com o presidente da Abranet, Gil Torquato.

artigo.texto: A expansão dos data centers voltados à inteligência artificial e o uso da fibra e dos lasers nos drones, em especial na guerra da Ucrânia, provocou uma busca acima da demanda de componentes e uma crise igual a vivida na pandemia da covid no supply chain, revela o CEO da PadTec, Carlos Raimar. A empresa, multinacional brasileira que tem como objetivo dar vida a conexões de alta capacidade, está negociando com os seus fornecedores. “A fotônica está entrando nos data centers. São dezenas e dezenas de semanas de espera. Tem de se programar por um a dois anos à frente com nossos fornecedores. E, infelizmente, não há cenário dessa crise terminar tão cedo. O que temos de fazer é tentar desenvolver fornecedores e tecnologia local”, observa o CEO da PadTec, em entrevista à CDTV, do portal Convergência Digital. No mercado brasileiro, a PadTec está abrindo uma unidade fabril em Manaus. E a escolha está ligada aos custos e à segurança de manter os benefícios até 2070. A empresa tem uma fábrica em Campinas e uma sala limpa, dentro do CPQD, também em Campinas. “A Lei de Informática vai até 2029 e não sabemos que irá acontecer com ela. Nossos planos são de longo prazo. E Manaus tem acordos com Zonas Francas da América Latina, o que expande muito o nosso mercado”, observa o executivo. A unidade em Manaus vai produzir toda a linha de valor agregado, mas não produzirá amplificadores, que são muito sensíveis e exigem uma mão de obra muito especializada. Raimar diz que na América Latina, o ano foi de expansão. Mas no Brasil, o cenário foi de aperto. “Muitos projetos engavetados e redes estão no limite. Acredito que no ano que vem, os investimentos voltem”. Um dos recados da PadTec é que a empresa está indo além da fotônica e quer ser a fornecedora de infraestrutura crítica digital. “Nós preparamos o barco para avançarmos muito. E vamos crescer no mercado de cabos submarinos. Estamos negociando contratos maiores”, detalha. Sobre o Redata, Raimar diz que vai beneficiar porque data centers virão para o Brasil e há uma ‘certa’ proteção à indústria nacional. Mas ele diz que a indústria terá de ser criativa para fazer soluções de cloud e inteligência artificial para o ambiente digital. Uma situação incomoda muito: o mercado dos Estados Unidos perdido para o tarifaço. “O mercado americano ficou impossível com o tarifaço e investimos muito na homologação e nos testes para atender a demanda local. Hoje o que vendemos é o que nossos concorrentes não entregam”. Assistam a íntegra da entrevista com o CEO da PadTec, Carlos Raimar.

artigo.texto:
Energy infrastructure AI platform Karman (formerly known as Utilidata) has partnered with French industrial group Legrand to integrate Karman into its data center power distribution product lines.
According to the companies, this will include Legrand's intelligent AC rack PDUs and DC power shelves, which it claims are designed for high-density AI data centers.
Karman’s platform utilizes AI to provide real-time visibility for grid operators and data center firms. It works by identifying and managing distributed energy resources, which it claims enhances resiliency and offsets the need for future infrastructure investments. The platform can integrate with smart meters, providing AI solutions for utility companies and their customers.
The company developed the platform using a custom version of the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, which it claims provides 100 times the processing power of other meter-based solutions. The platform can connect to millions of endpoints and coordinate them to monitor and react to real-time conditions.
According to the partners, the deployment could allow Legrand’s data center customers to power more compute and generate 50 percent or more AI tokens using the same provisioned power.
"By partnering with Karman, Legrand continues to demonstrate its technological leadership and innovation by delivering additional value to data center operators,” said Swen Anderson, CTO of Legrand's data, power, and control division.
“We’re providing data centers with the tools to unlock stranded power and deliver measurable competitive advantages and increased revenue.”
“Power continues to be the primary limiting factor to data center capacity expansion. Yet, a large portion of provisioned power in data centers goes untapped,” added Josh Brumberger, CEO of Karman. “This partnership with Legrand changes that. By embedding Karman into Legrand’s power distribution products, data center operators can now utilize that power to expand capacity immediately, while reducing the price per GPU hour.”
Karman was rebranded earlier this month, formerly operating under the name Utilidata.
In June, the firm raised $60.3 million in Series C funding to scale its platform, led by Renown Capital Partners, with participation from Quanta, Nvidia, and existing investor Keyframe Capital.

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Why AI Data Center Cooling Needs to Get Smarter AI is pushing data center cooling to its limits, so the real advantage comes from integrating smart sensing, motor control, and power management into a single responsive, failure-anticipating system. The job of a data center cooling system is simple in concept: absorb heat where it isn’t wanted and move it where it can be released safely. AI is making that job much harder, pushing rack power past 100 kW, with some AI clusters expected to exceed 1 megawatt within the next few years. Operators racing to add AI capacity must deploy quickly while protecting uptime, managing energy use, and safeguarding valuable hardware. There is no single way to cool an AI data center. The right architecture depends on rack power, workloads, and facility requirements. Engineers typically reserve the most advanced liquid cooling for AI racks, while other approaches serve standard workloads and facilities without existing water infrastructure. Liquid cooling is becoming increasingly important, but this mix of approaches adds complexity: mitigating leak risk, supporting multiple architectures at once, and ensuring that cooling responds precisely as thermal demands change. Moving heat more efficiently is no longer enough. The next step is to make cooling systems more intelligent through real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. Together, these technologies can make cooling more responsive, reduce energy consumption, and maximize uptime while laying the foundation for AI-enabled predictive maintenance. Why Smarter Control Matters Consider what happens when a liquid-cooled rack develops a leak. Many of today’s rack installations use on-off valves that stop the coolant when a sensor detects a leak, shutting down the entire rack until technicians can locate and fix the leak source. With a whole rack at stake, detection must be reliable. Yet the most common leak sensors, moisture-sensitive resistive ropes, can be limited in both accuracy and response time. A more intelligent approach could detect leaks faster and control coolant flow at the server-tray level, helping keep unaffected parts of the rack running. That points to three capabilities working together: real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. Real-Time Motor Control Keeps Coolant Moving Inside the coolant distribution unit (CDU), pumps and fans form the mechanical heart of the cooling loop. Reliability is the top priority. Depending on the CDU placement, a single pump failure can take an entire rack – or worse, an entire row – of AI computing equipment offline. Real-time motor control helps keep that system stable. Microcontrollers process sensor data and adjust performance accordingly, while motor drivers run pumps and fans efficiently. Motor control also extends to the server tray. Valves at the CDU typically open or close, but linear valves at the tray level can regulate coolant flow much more precisely. As power density inside the tray continues to rise, that level of precision becomes more important. Precision Flow Sensing Tracks Coolant at the Tray Precise flow control requires precise flow measurement, so linear valves at the tray work alongside accurate flow sensors. Together, they enable more granular control of GPU and CPU die temperatures. How the sensor is installed matters, too. Conventional flow sensors are inserted into the coolant line, creating an additional potential leak point. Non-invasive ultrasonic sensing can avoid that risk while also making installation easier and faster. Moisture-sensitive resistive ropes are still commonly used for leak detection. Still, concerns about accuracy and response time are pushing engineers to evaluate alternatives such as humidity sensors, capacitive sensors, and negative-pressure CDU designs. Flow readings also contribute to a broader operating picture. Combined with temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors, they can help detect changes that any single sensor might miss. High-Efficiency Power Management Keeps Cooling Lean The pumps and fans cooling AI racks consume power themselves, so their efficiency matters. Power management and motor control meet in the pump drive, where gallium nitride (GaN) power devices can improve overall pump-system efficiency by up to 2% compared with traditional silicon while enabling a smaller form factor. In server trays that still combine air and liquid cooling, fans remain critical, and many are shifting from 12 V to 48 V to reduce power consumption and improve efficiency. Power delivery is evolving as well. CDU pumps already operate on input voltages ranging from 48 V DC to 380 V AC. As 800 V high-voltage DC (HVDC) distribution gains traction in parts of the industry, operators will need pumps designed to support it. Edge AI Lays the Groundwork for Predictive Maintenance Sensing can also become predictive. Edge AI can process data from a cooling system’s full sensor array, an approach known as “sensor fusion,” enabling faster response times and lower latency. That matters for leak detection, which remains a bottleneck for reliable liquid cooling. Sensor fusion can improve detection speed and accuracy. It also opens the door to predictive maintenance for pumps and other critical mechanical components. Combined with tray-level flow control, edge AI and sensor fusion point toward cooling systems that sense changing conditions, anticipate problems, and adjust automatically. Building Intelligence into Every Architecture No single cooling design fits every AI data center, and mixed architectures are likely to serve the industry for years. But every architecture, from rear-door heat exchangers to immersion tanks, shares many of the same building blocks: sensors to measure conditions; motor control to drive pumps, fans, and valves; power management to supply them

artigo.texto: How Chiplets Could Transform Server Design – And Data Centers Chiplets are reshaping CPU design, enabling data centers to do more without increasing space or power consumption. Since the advent of microprocessors more than 50 years ago, CPUs have typically been built as single pieces of silicon. As a result, servers and the data centers that house them have largely been designed around that model. However, that is beginning to change. The growing adoption of chiplets – small modular dies that can be combined in a single processor package – is giving chipmakers a new way to build CPUs. By improving manufacturing flexibility and enabling more specialized processor designs, chiplets could reshape not just server architecture but also how data centers approach compute density, power efficiency, and infrastructure planning. What Are Chiplets? A chiplet is a small integrated circuit designed to perform a specific function within a larger processing package. Depending on the design, chiplets may handle compute, input/output (I/O), cache, memory connectivity, or workload-specific acceleration, such as AI acceleration. When combined, chiplets can provide the same overall capabilities as a traditional CPU. The key difference is that, instead of manufacturing a processor as one large monolithic die, chipmakers can build it from multiple smaller dies assembled in a single package. The chiplet concept has existed for decades, and related multi-die approaches are not entirely new. But adoption accelerated in the late 2010s as chipmakers sought more efficient ways to improve processor performance, manage manufacturing complexity, and scale designs across different workloads. The Benefits of Chiplets A chiplet-based approach to CPU design offers several potential advantages. Reduced manufacturing costs. Smaller dies are often easier to manufacture with higher yields than a single large, complex die. If a single die has a defect, the loss is usually less significant than losing an entire monolithic processor. It can also be easier to engineer and optimize a smaller die for a specific function than to design one large chip that must handle multiple functions at once. Design freedom. By separating functions such as compute and I/O into different dies, chipmakers can tailor processor designs more efficiently for different types of workloads and product segments. Potentially higher compute density. In some cases, chiplets allow chipmakers to pack more processing capability into a single processor package, helping to enable more powerful servers without necessarily increasing physical server size. Supply chain flexibility. Because smaller dies are often easier and faster to manufacture than very large monolithic chips, chiplet-based designs may reduce some production constraints. That said, they do not eliminate supply chain risk altogether, because advanced packaging and integration can create bottlenecks on their own. In short, chiplets can make it easier for chipmakers to scale processor designs, improve yields, and optimize hardware for growing demand. What Do Chiplets Mean for Data Centers? Although chiplets directly affect processor design, their impact could extend well beyond the chip itself. One important implication is the potential for increased compute density inside data centers. If chiplets allow server vendors to deliver more processing power within a single server platform, operators may be able to support heavier workloads without expanding physical footprints at the same pace. Historically, higher compute density has often meant higher power draw and greater cooling requirements. Chiplets do not automatically solve that problem. However, if they enable more efficient processor designs or better performance per watt, they could help offset some of the infrastructure strain that typically comes with denser compute environments. A key result of greater chiplet adoption, then, could be data centers that support higher IT loads without requiring proportionally more space or power. In that scenario, existing facilities could become more valuable because operators would be able to do more with the infrastructure they already have. Chiplets may also help reduce the risk of server procurement delays by giving manufacturers more flexibility in how processors are designed and produced. This does not remove supply chain challenges altogether, but it could make sourcing CPUs and servers somewhat easier over time. In the longer term, chiplets could also encourage more specialized server designs. As chipmakers gain flexibility to mix and match dies optimized for different functions, server platforms may become increasingly tailored for workloads such as AI, analytics, storage, or high-performance computing. That would give data center operators more options, but it could also make infrastructure planning more workload-specific than it is today. A Shift Worth Watching Chiplets are no longer a futuristic concept. They are already becoming an important part of modern processor design, especially as chipmakers look for new ways to improve performance and efficiency. For data centers, the biggest impact may not come from chiplets themselves, but from the servers they enable. If chiplet-based designs continue to improve compute density, efficiency, and workload specialization, they could play a major role in shaping the next generation of data center infrastructure.

artigo.texto: AI Data Center Land Buying Hits $6B as Power Premiums Rise US data center land spending hit roughly $6 billion in the first half of 2026, as power access now drives land value and pricing more than location alone. US purchases of land for future data centers reached about $6 billion in the first half of 2026, up 79% from a year earlier, according to Avison Young. The spending reflects demand for large AI campuses, as hyperscalers, neocloud providers, energy-first developers and investors compete to secure sites for new computing capacity, according to the Q2 2026 Data Center Market report. For data center operators, the stakes are both operational and financial. Delayed power can push back capacity delivery, complicate customer commitments and leave expensive buildings waiting to enter service. “The biggest thing right now is speed to power,” John Andril, manager of market intelligence at Avison Young, told TechTarget in an interview. In Northern Virginia, entitled land without power can sell for roughly $4 million an acre, compared with at least $6 million an acre for powered land, Andril said. Entitlements, infrastructure and other site characteristics also affect prices, so the comparison does not isolate the value of electricity alone. “The premium is increasingly payment for uncertainty removed, not just for megawatts nearby,” said Neil Osnato, an industry analyst who has examined data center land transactions. Committed Power Drives Land Value An Altus Group analysis of 80 verified data center land transactions in August found committed utility load was the strongest predictor of land pricing. Sites associated with 230-kilovolt or 500-kV infrastructure traded at roughly 2.4 times the pricing of sites associated with 138-kV or lower infrastructure, according to the analysis. Transmission access can reduce the upgrades required to serve a project. In some cases, existing infrastructure can also shorten the regulatory process and save about a year, Andril said. However, proximity to a transmission line doesn’t guarantee that a utility can deliver the required capacity on schedule. “If you don’t have power until the early to mid-2030s, you’re probably not going to get a lot of interest,” Andril said. Andril said a genuinely power-ready property generally needs electrical infrastructure deliverable within about 18 months, roughly matching the time needed to prepare a building for its initial load. Developers also need clarity on the equipment required for a substation and who will fund and build it. For campus planning, developers generally use about 0.5 to 1 acre per megawatt as a rule of thumb, Andril said, although land-constrained markets can support higher densities. A large project, therefore, requires both enough land and a credible plan for delivering its electricity. A Texas Deal Puts a Value on Power A transaction involving Plug Power and Stream Data Centers illustrates how power capacity can affect a project’s economics. Plug agreed to sell its Graham, Texas, project to Stream for $50 million, with up to $26.5 million in additional consideration tied to the electrical load capacity ultimately established for the project. The agreement used a 164-megawatt (MW) reference capacity. Plug had an interconnection request with Oncor and had deposited $6.5 million with the utility to secure a requested 164 MW of load. It also posted a $7.75 million letter of credit under the ERCOT Batch Zero agreement. The project includes about 66 acres, development rights and grid-interconnection assets. The transaction was later restructured. Stream acquired high-voltage electrical infrastructure for $40 million in August, while the land and remaining interconnection assets remained subject to closing conditions. The original agreement shouldn’t be described as a completed $76.5 million land sale. Its significance is that additional consideration depended on the capacity ultimately established, putting a price on the uncertainty surrounding the project’s power supply. Northern Virginia Shows the Stakes Loudoun County records show SDC Twin Creeks Parent LLC, a data center developer, paid $615.05 million for 97.15 acres in November 2025, or about $6.33 million an acre. The property is part of the Twin Creeks data center development in Leesburg, Va. Dominion Energy separately paid $45 million for about 14 acres associated with the development. The transactions don’t isolate electricity’s contribution to the land prices. Entitlements, development rights, site assembly and market conditions also influence valuations. They illustrate the scale of investment in data center sites in one of the country’s most competitive markets. Andril said the effect can be pronounced in lower-cost markets, too. Land that might sell for roughly $10,000 an acre without a viable data center power path can become worth six figures per acre after developers establish the infrastructure and utility relationships needed for a large project. They must prepare for large new loads without spending billions of dollars on projects that never materialize. Developers, meanwhile, want confidence in power delivery before committing substantial capital to a site. Andril described the problem as a “chicken-and-egg” situation. Letters of credit, take-or-pay agreements and stricter interconnection-queue requirements can help utilities separate serious projects from speculative requests. Andril said established developers and end users can support those measures because removing speculative projects makes legitimate demand easier to evaluate. Onsite generation offers another option. Developers can use it to support initial operations while waiting for utility infrastructure, Andril said. Whether that approach makes financial sense depends on generation costs and the project’s economics. For data center operators, those factors belong in site selection

artigo.texto: Data Center Developers Face Tighter Margins as Construction Costs Rise JLL says strong AI demand is not enough to protect projects lacking power certainty, anchor tenants, and credible delivery timelines. Data center developers may be able to pass higher construction costs on to tenants, but only when projects have power access, committed customers, and a credible path to delivery, according to JLL. In its Global Construction Costs Index 2026, the real estate services firm said annual construction cost escalation of 3% to 6% has become the new baseline, up from the 2% to 3% range common before 2020. JLL also forecasts another 3.1% to 4.2% increase in global tender prices in 2027, including 3.2% to 4.2% in North America. Those forecasts apply to construction broadly rather than the data center sector alone. The JLL report notes that rising rents and asset values have helped data center projects absorb some of that inflation. However, Matthew Giddings, executive director of technical services with JLL’s Data Centers and Critical Environments team, said stronger market fundamentals do not automatically protect individual projects. “The economics break down when costs outpace contracted revenue or power delays postpone income while financing costs continue to accumulate,” Giddings told Data Center Knowledge. “Higher asset values alone cannot close that gap.” That risk is most acute for speculative campuses without anchor tenants, projects with uncertain power delivery, and developments tied to fixed-rent agreements that leave little room to absorb construction escalation. Older facilities being repositioned for AI workloads may also face difficult economics if upgrades become too extensive. “Strong demand supports the market, but it does not make every project viable,” Giddings said. Developers should reassess projects when rising capital costs erode expected returns, utility schedules slip beyond committed occupancy dates, or tenant demand no longer supports planned capacity, he said. Reduced power availability and delays in anchor-tenant commitments are also signs that a project may need to be reworked. One way to manage that risk is through phased construction. By aligning spending with confirmed electricity supply and customer demand, developers can limit the amount of capital they commit before fundamentals are in place. Skilled Trades Constrain Delivery Labor constraints are adding to the pressure. Giddings said the electrical and mechanical trades are creating the greatest cost and schedule challenges, particularly electricians, high-voltage specialists, pipefitters, and advanced cooling technicians. “Controls, commissioning, and startup teams have also become critical bottlenecks, as their availability often determines when a completed facility can be placed into service,” he noted. Competition for utility and substation construction crews is also intensifying, adding risks that extend beyond the data center site itself. To reduce exposure, Giddings recommended that developers bring in trade partners early and test project schedules against real workforce availability rather than assumed labor capacity. He also pointed to standardized designs, off-site prefabrication, and phased construction as ways to reduce peak labor requirements. In remote markets, developers may need to offer housing, transportation, and travel incentives to attract workers. In the longer term, investment in trade schools, apprenticeships, and union training facilities could help support future construction phases while expanding local employment opportunities, he said. Buy Early Without Freezing the Design Procurement strategy is becoming just as important. Long lead times for critical equipment have pushed many developers to place orders earlier, but doing so can create problems if tenant requirements shift, particularly as AI infrastructure continues to evolve. “The key is to secure manufacturing capacity early without freezing every design decision,” Giddings said. He said developers should reserve production slots for transformers, switchgear, generators, and cooling equipment while negotiating flexibility to modify specifications before fabrication begins. Orders should advance in line with validated tenant requirements and clear decision deadlines. That approach is especially important as operators try to account for shifting rack densities and growing interest in liquid cooling. Modular power and cooling systems, built-in expansion capacity, and design provisions for liquid cooling can help facilities adapt without undermining the overall project. “Early procurement protects the schedule, while flexible design protects the long-term value of the asset,” Giddings said. Retrofitting older facilities can offer another path to faster delivery and lower upfront costs, particularly when a site already has available power, sufficient structural capacity, and infrastructure that can be reused. However, those advantages can disappear quickly if a building requires major mechanical upgrades, higher electrical distribution capacity, heavier floor loading, or large-scale liquid-cooling retrofits. “The economics ultimately depend on how much existing infrastructure can be retained while still meeting current and future performance requirements,” Giddings said.

artigo.texto: Brazil’s Data Center Growth Pushes Beyond São Paulo Brazil’s data center growth is spreading beyond São Paulo to Rio, Fortaleza, and the south, but power grid delays and lengthy permitting will decide which markets actually succeed. Brazil’s data center market is beginning to expand beyond its longtime base in São Paulo as hyperscale and AI-driven projects draw attention to Rio de Janeiro, Fortaleza, and southern Brazil. The shift reflects growing demand for capacity, but it also highlights a harder question for developers: whether Brazil’s energy and connectivity advantages can be translated into sites with dependable power and workable construction timelines. São Paulo still accounts for 76% of Brazil’s live data center capacity, according to DC Byte’s August market analysis. The city continues to benefit from its concentration of customers, network density, and established operator presence. That ecosystem gives the market a depth that emerging regions cannot quickly replicate. However, São Paulo faces a shrinking supply of powered land and slow transmission upgrades. At the same time, newly enacted federal tax incentives could improve project economics in other parts of the country, even as environmental licensing and electricity infrastructure remain potential constraints. São Paulo’s advantage comes from more than scale alone. The market combines demand from Brazil’s largest metropolitan economy with dense fiber connectivity and access to international networks, reinforcing its position as the country’s primary cloud and interconnection hub. Operators including Ascenty, Elea, and Scala have built substantial footprints in Brazil. DC Byte also points to investments by Microsoft and Equinix as evidence of growing international interest. Gomez said the maturity of that ecosystem remains central to Brazil’s appeal. Investors can enter a market with established customers and infrastructure while also pursuing opportunities in less developed locations. “At the same time, Brazil is beginning to see greater investment in facilities designed to support AI workloads, reflecting the global shift toward high-density computing and next-generation digital infrastructure,” he said. This leaves Brazil serving two overlapping tracks of demand: continued growth in cloud and enterprise capacity, and the development of larger, higher-density facilities designed for AI and other intensive computing workloads. Brazil’s access to renewable electricity strengthens the country’s long-term investment case, but generation does not necessarily mean a site can be connected on schedule. Gomez identified the pace of electrical infrastructure development as the market’s main challenge. Generation, transmission, and broader grid expansion all take time, making delivery schedules for new substations and transmission capacity critical for developers. Bruno Porto, manager for industrial, logistics, and data centers in Brazil at real estate services firm JLL, told Data Center Knowledge that some locations will require transmission reinforcement before additional data center load can be supported. “Environmental licensing in Brazil is also critical, with this phase alone potentially taking up to 18 months depending on the region and the scale of the project,” Porto noted. Those factors can stretch project timelines even where land, capital, and customer demand are available. For developers looking outside São Paulo, the key question is not just whether a market looks attractive on paper, but whether permits and power delivery can align with construction schedules. artigo.texto: Could the Societal Value of Workloads Shape Data Center Policy? As opposition to data center expansion grows, policymakers may eventually look beyond power and water consumption to ask whether the digital services those facilities support justify their environmental and infrastructure costs. Data centers are facing increasing scrutiny, and, in some cases, regulation, over their energy and resource usage, especially amid public opposition to rapid expansion in some regions. Much of that scrutiny still focuses on data centers as energy- and resource-intensive buildings rather than on the workloads they ultimately support. But as the largely AI-driven build-out of new facilities comes under greater pressure, questions are also being raised about the societal value of the services data centers provide relative to their environmental and infrastructure costs. That is still more of an emerging policy question than an immediate regulatory reality. Today, most regulation and public criticism remain centered on the physical footprint of data centers – power demand, water use, land consumption, and grid impact – rather than the digital services running inside them. But discussions at Informa’s recent Data Center Europe event in Vienna, which ran Oct. 13-15, suggested that the distinction may become hard to maintain over time. Could Some Workloads Be Seen as More Valuable Than Others? Data centers, and the internet more widely, support a broad range of workloads and services, from enterprise and business applications to social media, video streaming, generative AI chatbots, agents, and other AI services. According to Sandvine’s 2024 Global Internet Phenomena Report, video streaming, social media, and related applications from companies including Meta, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Netflix account for about 65% of total internet volume. Some digital services are already facing greater scrutiny in their own right. Social media regulation, including Australia’s move to ban access for under-16s, illustrates how governments are becoming more willing to intervene directly in digital activity when broader social concerns are at stake. That does not amount to data center workload regulation, but it does show how the societal impact of online services is increasingly part of the policy debate. AI is likely to sharpen that debate further. Estimates of AI’s contribution to total data center footprint vary, but Goldman Sachs has projected that AI’s share of the overall data center market will double to 30% over the next two years, taking share from conventional and cloud workloads. At the same time, although data center opposition groups – particularly in the US – have largely focused on the environment and physical footprint of new facilities, there is also concern – often driven by a lack of transparency – about the services those facilities host and enable – most obviously, AI. “The AI boom is being sold as inevitable progress, but the real question is not whether artificial intelligence can do useful things in theory. It is who owns it, who profits from it, what it is mostly being used for…,” environmental group Greenpeace said in a recent publication. In response, data center operators and the wider industry have pointed to the broad range of services that data centers provide beyond AI, and on which many aspects of society depend, from banking to healthcare. In a recent blog post, AWS CEO Matt Garman made that case directly, writing: “Today, virtually everything we do each day—shopping, banking, stock trading, ride hailing, booking travel, receiving healthcare, streaming entertainment, as well as critical research in everything from preventing and curing disease to finding ways to use less energy and natural resources – is digitally driven and enabled by data centers, which manage the computing, storage, and access necessary for these activities.” Still, the question remains whether all workloads should be treated equally if policymakers decide how to allocate scarce power, approve grid connections, or weigh the local impact of new projects. Healthcare research, for example, may be seen differently from gambling, social media, or some speculative AI use cases. To date, however, there have been no significant attempts to reflect those distinctions directly in regulation, for instance, through lighter treatment or faster approvals for facilities that support a higher proportion of socially valuable workloads. In practice, that would be highly challenging. Cloud and colocation environments support multiple workload types, often in the same facility, and digital infrastructure is far too complex for neat categorization. Even so, some broader distinctions are possible, particularly if governments begin to place greater emphasis on sovereignty, critical services, flexibility, or public benefit. What Industry Leaders in Vienna Said Responding to a question from Data Center Knowledge at the Informa Data Center Europe event this week, a panel of industry experts acknowledged that greater scrutiny around workloads, services, and their wider societal value could emerge in the future. Branko Jovanović, CTO for data centers at ADVANT d.o.o. and president of the IT infrastructure and data center section of the ICT Association of Slovenia, suggested there are already early signs of that shift. “There is maybe a case which is already under supervision,” Jovanović said, pointing to recent amendments to grid connection rules in Finland that would prioritize smaller data centers under 1 MW. artigo.texto: Reliability Standards for AI Data Centers, Crypto Miners Move Closer to Adoption The proposed rules must still be approved by NERC’s board and federal regulators. As written, they would apply to computational loads of 50 MW or more connected at voltage levels of at least 100 kV. This article was originally published on Utility Dive. North American Electric Reliability Corp. stakeholders approved new reliability standards for AI data centers, crypto mining facilities and other computational loads – an important step toward finalization, the grid watchdog said Thursday. The standards now head to the NERC Board of Trustees for a vote, and, if adopted, will be filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for final approval. The proposed standards build on insights and research related to a Level 3 alert NERC issued in May after several incidents where data centers unexpectedly dropped load or oscillated demand rapidly, threatening the stability of regional grids. The alert included seven actions grid entities “must implement to address immediate risks posed by computational loads” while permanent rules are created, NERC said. The new standards aim to “establish requirements to support the reliable integration of large computational loads into the bulk power system,” the reliability organization said in a statement. Electricity demand is increasing after decades of stagnant growth, with data centers, in particular, driving load projections. Summer peak demand across the bulk power system is forecast to grow by 224 GW over the next 10 years, a 24% increase from 2025 peak demand, NERC said in January. “These loads are reshaping the demand profile and exposing reliability gaps in both operational and planning time horizons,” NERC said on its standards development project site. Multiple standards for computational loads were developed as part of NERC Project 2026-02, including requirements around interconnection studies and modeling; operational data and communications; and load protection coordination and disturbance monitoring. Among other requirements, the standards establish modeling data, verification, and reporting procedures “for development of planning horizon cases necessary to support analysis of the reliability of the interconnected transmission system.” They are designed to ensure transmission operators, balancing authorities and reliability coordinators have computational load site data needed “to plan, monitor, and assess the reliable operation” of the bulk power system, and to establish communication capabilities “with predefined communications protocols to ensure prompt action to prevent or mitigate occurrences that adversely impact the reliability of the Bulk Power System.” The standards would apply to computational loads greater than or equal to 50 MW, connected at voltage levels greater than or equal to 100 kV. NERC’s board is expected to consider the new standards in the fourth quarter, based on development timelines in the proposals.

artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. artigo.texto: A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira, 13 de outubro, o requerimento de urgência do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que propõe retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias como reserva de capacidade. Com a decisão, a proposta poderá ser votada diretamente pelo plenário, sem precisar passar pelas comissões. O requerimento de urgência foi apresentado pelo deputado Danilo Forte (PP-CE). Já o projeto é de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). O PL revoga o parágrafo 6º do artigo 3º-A da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determina que os custos das contratações de reserva de capacidade com baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Com a revogação, passaria a valer para as baterias a regra geral da lei, que prevê o rateio dos custos da reserva de capacidade entre os consumidores, assim como acontece copm as demais tecnologias contratadas nessa modalidade. Apoio das associações A aprovação da urgência ocorre após seis associações do setor elétrico divulgarem, em 7 de outubro, uma nota conjunta em defesa do projeto. As entidades argumentam que a regra atual estabelece tratamento diferente para as baterias em relação às demais tecnologias contratadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade. O posicionamento foi assinado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica), Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape), Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv), Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) e Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). Segundo as entidades, a cobrança exclusiva dos geradores pode elevar os custos da energia elétrica para os consumidores, uma vez que os valores podem ser repassados às tarifas no mercado regulado e aos preços dos contratos no mercado livre. As associações também argumentam que os sistemas de armazenamento podem reduzir outros custos do setor elétrico. artigo.texto: Um grupo de 32 entidades e nove frentes parlamentares pediu ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva que acelere a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em setembro. Em carta aberta, os signatários defendem que as regras permitam o uso de diferentes fontes de energia, incluindo gás natural e nuclear, no suprimento dos empreendimentos beneficiados. A Lei nº 15.504, sancionada em 15 de setembro de 2026, estabelece incentivos tributários para a instalação, modernização e ampliação de data centers no Brasil. Entre os benefícios estão a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins e Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) na aquisição de equipamentos e componentes, além do Imposto de Importação para produtos sem equivalente nacional. Para acessar os incentivos, os empreendimentos deverão atender à totalidade de sua demanda de eletricidade por meio de contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A legislação, no entanto, deixou para a regulamentação a definição dos critérios de atendimento dessa exigência. Na carta, as entidades defendem uma abordagem tecnologicamente neutra no Redata, que considere hidrelétricas, solares, eólicas, biomassa, biogás, biometano, energia nuclear e gás natural. Segundo os signatários, as regras devem considerar a necessidade de fornecimento firme e contínuo de energia e evitar a transferência de custos associados aos data centers para os demais consumidores do sistema elétrico. O documento reconhece a existência de divergências técnicas no governo, mas propõe que o decreto seja publicado com os parâmetros essenciais do regime, deixando questões ainda não consensuadas para regulamentação posterior, inclusive mediante consulta pública. As entidades também pedem que a lista de equipamentos beneficiados pelos incentivos tributários não seja excessivamente restritiva e solicitam ao governo federal apoio para acelerar as discussões sobre o ICMS no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz). A regulamentação é cobrada cerca de um mês após a sanção da lei, que estabelece prazo até 31 de dezembro de 2026 para os benefícios fiscais relativos ao PIS/Pasep, à Cofins e ao IPI. Entre os signatários estão a Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas (Abraget), a Associação Brasileira de Energia Nuclear (Aben), a Associação Brasileira de Distribuidores de Energia Elétrica (Abradee), a Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado (Abegás), o Instituto Brasileiro de Petróleo, Gás e Biocombustíveis (IBP) e a Associação Brasileira dos Grandes Consumidores de Energia e Consumidores Livres (Abrace Energia).

artigo.texto: A falta de definição sobre a aplicação de incentivos tributários aos projetos de armazenamento de energia pode elevar os custos de financiamento e comprometer a competitividade dos leilões de baterias previstos para dezembro de 2026. O alerta é da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), que defende o esclarecimento das regras do Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento da Infraestrutura (Reidi) antes dos certames, para evitar que os custos adicionais sejam repassados aos consumidores por meio dos encargos setoriais. Em ofício encaminhado em 13 de outubro ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) e ao Ministério da Fazenda, a associação pediu ajustes no Decreto nº 6.144/2007 para viabilizar o acesso dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia (SAE) ao regime especial. A Lei nº 15.269/2025 incluiu esses empreendimentos no Reidi e estabeleceu um limite de R$ 1 bilhão por exercício para a renúncia fiscal, condicionado à previsão na Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA). A regulamentação, porém, ainda não foi atualizada. Os leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) para armazenamento estão previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Para a Absae, a definição antecipada das regras tributárias é necessária para que os participantes considerem o benefício na formação dos preços dos lances. A entidade também defende que os editais esclareçam como o Reidi será aplicado aos projetos, já que a aprovação pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) está prevista para até 27 de outubro. Se não houver tempo para concluir os ajustes regulatórios até essa data, a associação considera que a publicação do decreto antes dos leilões ainda poderá oferecer mais segurança aos investidores, já que, sem uma definição, os participantes podem adotar premissas tributárias diferentes, incluir margens de segurança nos cálculos ou exigir maior remuneração para investir nos projetos. Essa incerteza, segundo a entidade, pode prejudicar a comparação entre as propostas e a eficiência econômica dos certames. Impacto financeiro de R$ 36,4 milhões em projetos de 2 GW Para demonstrar os possíveis efeitos da ausência do benefício, a associação considerou um investimento de R$ 5 mil/kW, com base no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE) 2035, e uma contratação hipotética de 2 GW. Nesse cenário, o investimento total seria de R$ 10 bilhões. Considerando, apenas para fins ilustrativos, uma alíquota de referência de 9,21% para a CBS em 2027, a Absae estima que o tributo poderia representar cerca de R$ 921 milhões sobre essa base. O valor efetivamente sujeito à tributação e elegível ao Reidi dependerá da composição dos investimentos de cada projeto. A associação também adotou um prazo aproximado de 105 dias para a recuperação dos valores e uma taxa Selic de 13,75% ao ano. Com essas premissas, estimou um custo financeiro de aproximadamente R$ 36,4 milhões durante o período. A Absae ressalta que os valores são ilustrativos e que o impacto decorre da necessidade de antecipar recursos enquanto os créditos tributários não são recuperados. Mesmo com o ressarcimento posterior, o custo de financiar esse intervalo pode afetar a rentabilidade e a estrutura econômica dos empreendimentos. Incentivo reduz necessidade de financiamento dos projetos Com base nesse contexto, a Absae pede esclarecimentos sobre a aplicação do benefício diante da exceção prevista na Lei Complementar nº 224/2025 para incentivos sujeitos a limite quantitativo global e a habilitação ou autorização administrativa prévia. Outro pedido é o reconhecimento de que a exclusão da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS) e do Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS) da formação da receita fixa prevista nos editais não afasta nem torna desnecessária a aplicação do Reidi. O enquadramento no regime permite suspender a incidência de PIS/Pasep e Cofins sobre a aquisição de bens e a contratação de serviços destinados à implantação de projetos de infraestrutura. Entretanto, a partir de 1º de janeiro de 2027, está prevista a extinção dessas contribuições e a introdução da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS) e do Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS), conforme a Emenda Constitucional nº 132/2023 e a Lei Complementar nº 214/2025, posteriormente alterada pela Lei Complementar nº 227/2026. A Absae argumenta que a exclusão da CBS e do IBS da formação da receita fixa dos contratos não elimina a importância do Reidi. Pelas minutas dos editais, a receita fixa deverá contemplar os custos necessários à implantação e à prestação do serviço de armazenamento, com exceção desses dois tributos. A regra busca evitar que a incerteza sobre suas alíquotas afete os preços dos lances. O ponto central, segundo a associação, é o intervalo entre o pagamento dos tributos e a recuperação dos valores. Sem o Reidi, os investidores podem precisar utilizar recursos próprios ou contratar financiamento para pagar os tributos incidentes sobre os investimentos e aguardar a posterior recuperação por meio de créditos, compensação ou ressarcimento. Esse intervalo é especialmente relevante para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, que exigem investimentos elevados antes do início da receita fixa contratada. A aquisição de baterias, inversores, sistemas de conversão e outros equipamentos ocorre durante a implantação, enquanto os pagamentos previstos nos contratos começam posteriormente. Por isso, a entidade avalia que a possibilidade de recuperar créditos tributários não elimina o custo financeiro da antecipação dos recursos. A aplicação do Reidi reduziria a necessidade de capital de giro e poderia favorecer a competitividade dos projetos. URBANA — As data centers continue to be a hot-button issue locally and nationally, the Champaign County Board is moving forward with two pieces of legislation to address some of the concerns that have been raised by members of the public.
The board voted at its Tuesday committee-of-the-whole meeting to send forward two items to the next regular meeting: An ordinance prohibiting nondisclosure agreements, and a resolution prohibiting the county from negotiating property-tax incentives for hyperscale data-center developments.
County Director of Administration Michelle Jett said that the ordinance on NDAs came about after the public signaled its “distaste” for such contracts and most of the board expressed “shock that an elected official would enter into a nondisclosure agreement.”
“It seemed like a very logical thing for you all to make that statement publicly to the residents of Champaign County that that’s not the kind of mentality that you all have and that you would not be engaging in nondisclosure agreements,” she concluded.
As currently drafted, the ordinance would prohibit county board members and county employees from entering into NDAs regarding county business — in any situation, not just instances where data-center developers are involved.
Board member John Farney, who is in favor of the ban, asked if the language should be tweaked since there are some instances where information about legal settlements cannot be shared.
Jett said that she would discuss the language with Champaign County State’s Attorney Julia Rietz and provide more information to the county board at its next meeting.
“NDAs are the absolute wrong way to go,” said board member Brett Peugh. “I would suggest that each of us goes to every municipality in our district and ask them to pass their own prohibition on NDAs. We’ve already seen what one rogue town can do.”
He also advised board members to encourage school districts to pass their own bans against tax incentives for data centers.
Farney noted that “any government entity” can negotiate with a potential developer regardless of whether or not it has home-rule authority.
“You’re the one that’s setting your levy,” he said. “You can abate taxes. You can come up with other agreements. … This resolution we’re voting on tonight, it only covers the county portion of the tax bill. That’s why we have to get every other entity to do their own.”

One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency.

artigo.texto: Você sabe carregar seu celular corretamente? Confira dicas para preservar a vida útil da bateria Conectar primeiro o carregador ou o celular? Onde deixar o aparelho? Usar o celular durante a carga tem problema? Veja alguns cuidados básicos Por O Globo Atualizado Há hábitos diários que repetimos sem nem nos dar conta. E, com certeza, carregar o celular é um deles. Tem quem demore até a bateria ficar no vermelho, outros preferem se precaver e, na primeiro oportunidade, dar aquela carga a mais por garantia. Apesar da duração das baterias poder variar entre as marcas e modelos, há alguns protocolos que merecem ser respeitados para prolongar na vida útil do aparelho, segundo especialistas. - Você é um dos 83 milhões de brasileiros endividados? Ferramenta do GLOBO ajuda a organizar suas contas; confira - Fim da escala 6x1: você trabalha mais ou menos do que a média no Brasil? E no mundo? Confira Pequenos cuidados podem ajudar a evitar, por exemplo, microdescargas causadas por flutuações de tensão. Aquela "escorregada" vez ou outra não compromete o aparelho, o problema está na recorrência de maus hábitos, em que, sucessivamente, vai mitigando o funcionamento. Mesmo nessa tarefa simples de carregar o celular, a ordem impacta no aparelho. Idealmente, você deve primeiro conectar o carregador à tomada, e só então conectar o cabo ao celular, dando início à recarga. Isso acontece porque o circuito interno precisa de alguns instantes para estabilizar o fluxo de energia. Na hora de desconectá-lo deve ser feito o caminho inverso, à fim de proteger os componentes, primeiro desconectando o celular do cabo do carregador, e só depois retirá-lo da tomada. Às vezes pode ser difícil ficar longe do celular, deixando-o recarregar sem uso. Responder uma notificação rápida, até vai, mas ações como jogar videogames ou assistir a vídeos em alta resolução geram um aumento de temperatura que afeta sua vida útil. Outro risco é tensionar ou dobrar o cabo durante esse manuseio, o que pode causar fissuras e rupturas comprometendo o carregamento e até estragando-o. Também está diretamente relacionado à temperatura do aparelho a superfície em que ele é mantido apoiado durante o carregamento. Materiais que ajudem a dissipar o calor, pois facilita o resfriamento durante o processo, dispondo o celular sobre móveis, como mesa ou escrivaninha, ou pedra, como mármore ou granito. Isto deve ser combinado a uma área bem ventilada e uma superfície seca. Deixar o aparelho sobre cobertores, travesseiros ou plástico deve ser evitado. O recomendado é escolher ambientes com pouca umidade, por isso, é importante evitar cômodos como banheiros e cozinhas, ainda para evitar risco de choque elétrico. Deixar o celular no chão também não é uma boa opção devido às chances de entrada de sujeira na porta de carregamento. Outros fatores que merecem atenção é o uso de carregadores de baixa qualidade, que causa tensões instáveis que danificam tanto a bateria quanto seus circuitos internos. O uso do acessório original ou de um certificado pelo fabricante garante a transferência segura de energia para o equipamento. E deixar o dispositivo conectado à tomada durante a noite é desnecessário para baterias modernas.

Whether you're developing renewable energy, BESS or hybrid projects, this webinar offered key insights for obtaining requisite approvals and preparing for financing. Summary As data centers become more complex and AI-driven workloads place new demands on power, cooling, and facility infrastructure, operators need better ways to connect operational data across traditionally siloed systems. Achieving that visibility, however, doesn’t require replacing the infrastructure already in place. This webinar brings together RoviSys, Inductive Automation, and Advantech to explore a practical approach to bridging physical infrastructure with modern Data Center Infrastructure Management (DCIM) environments. Using a real-world, edge-to-enterprise architecture, the discussion will follow how data moves from industrial devices and facility equipment, through edge computing and connectivity, into an operational software layer where it can be normalized, contextualized, visualized, and shared with higher-level monitoring systems. Attendees will learn how industrial edge hardware, Ignition, and systems integration work together to address common challenges such as diverse communication protocols, legacy equipment, fragmented data, and multi-facility scalability. Rather than focusing on rip-and-replace modernization, the session will demonstrate how organizations can build on existing infrastructure to improve operational visibility, create a reliable flow of facility data, and establish a scalable foundation for increasingly connected and AI-driven data center operations.

artigo.texto: The Nozu Project adds to Trina Storage's growing track record in Japan's utility-scale energy storage market. As deployment of grid-scale battery storage expands in the country, Trina Storage has established local capabilities to support projects from system configuration and technical consultation through delivery coordination and after-sales service. Through its team in Japan, Trina Storage works closely with customers and project partners to address local technical and project requirements, providing support throughout the project lifecycle. This local capability is complemented by Trina Storage's global experience in battery cell technology, system integration and utility-scale energy storage deployment. Dr. Leo Zhao, Head of Energy Storage (APAC), Trina Storage, said, "We are pleased to support Japan's growing renewable energy portfolio through the AEJ Nozu Battery Energy Storage System project. With Trinasolar's longstanding experience in solar and Trina Storage's growing presence in utility-scale energy storage, we see significant opportunities to support Japan's evolving energy needs. For Nozu and other projects in Japan, our focus is on combining advanced technology with strong local capabilities." Trina Storage is also supplying a 160MWh utility-scale BESS project in the Kyushu region, adding to its growing project track record in Japan. In September, it also signed an MoU with AMP-lify for approximately 1GWh of grid-connected BESS projects in Japan, featuring the latest Elementa 3 series. The MoU agreement, together with projects like Nozu, reflects Trina Storage's continued expansion in Japan as demand for utility-scale energy storage grows.
