artigo.texto: HiTHIUM Surpasses 200GWh in Shipments, Advancing Global Long-Duration Energy Storage with Full-Chain Integration CHONGQING, China, Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On October 15, 2026, HiTHIUM, a leading global energy storage technology company, held the "HiTHIUM 200GWh Shipment Milestone Ceremony" at its Chongqing manufacturing base. In just a year, the company's cumulative shipments advanced from surpassing 100GWh in August 2025 to reaching 200GWh, setting a new benchmark for scale and quality in energy storage. With a continuously accelerating growth trajectory, HiTHIUM is advancing rapidly in large-scale manufacturing, full-chain collaboration, and global delivery. This leap underscores the global market's strong recognition of its full-scenario integrated energy storage solutions. Surpassing Another 100GWh: Advancing Scale and Capabilities in Tandem Since shipments began at the end of 2021, HiTHIUM has built three core strengths: cost leadership, excellent service, and safety and reliability. Its cumulative shipments have surpassed both 100GWh and 200GWh, while its global ranking has risen from fifth in 2023 to third in 2024 and further to Global Top 2 in 2025 and H1 2026. This growth demonstrates HiTHIUM's strengthening capabilities across long-duration energy storage (LDES), end-to-end integration, lighthouse-factory-enabled manufacturing, and global delivery and service. LDES for the Long Term: Strengthening Competitiveness through Innovation, Systems, and Responsibility At the ceremony, Jason Wang, HiTHIUM Co-founder and CEO, said that surpassing 200GWh marks a new starting point for HiTHIUM's high-quality global development. HiTHIUM is pursuing its ambition to become the world's leading energy storage brand through technology innovation, integrated development, and global expansion. As a strategic hub, HiTHIUM's Chongqing manufacturing base—the world's first energy storage battery lighthouse factory—deepens supply-chain collaboration and enables the high-quality delivery of products at scale, supporting the development of the new energy storage industry. Looking ahead, Jason said the energy storage industry is no longer defined by competition between individual products, but by the strength of integrated capabilities across the entire value chain. HiTHIUM will continue to strengthen its competitiveness across three dimensions: innovation, systems, and responsibility. On innovation, HiTHIUM remains focused on energy storage and its LDES strategy, accelerating global deployment of its first kAh-class integrated LDES solution and building full-scenario solutions from cells to the grid, making "New energy + LDES" a reliable anchor for the new power system. On systems, HiTHIUM implements its "strength at home and abroad are mutually reinforcing" globalization strategy, led by Xiamen HQ and backed by its Chongqing manufacturing base and overseas localization, driving end-to-end integration across technology, products, supply chain, and delivery and strengthening global resource allocation and project delivery. On responsibility, HiTHIUM is committed to the long term: promoting value-chain collaboration through localized operations, fostering new quality productive forces, and contributing to the sustainable development of its business, the industry, and local communities. "This milestone was not just about growth—it was about scaling end-to-end capabilities," said Jason Wang. Moving forward, HiTHIUM will advance LDES technology, upgrade its lighthouse factory smart manufacturing system, strengthen global delivery, and drive shipments toward the next 100GWh in support of the global green energy transition. SOURCE HiTHIUM

artigo.texto: CHENNAI — Renewable energy solutions provider Vikram Solar Limited, through its wholly owned subsidiary VSL PowerHive, has announced plans to set up a 7.5 GWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility at Oragadam near Chennai, Tamil Nadu.Spanning 1.65 lakh sq. ft., the plant is scheduled for inauguration in January 2027, with commercial operations targeted for April 2027. The project forms a key component of Vikram Solar's broader strategy to establish 30 GWh of total battery manufacturing capacity by 2030.Project Scope & Strategic HighlightsFacility Expansion & Capacity: The initial 7.5 GWh assembly facility can be expanded to 15 GWh in subsequent phases.Product Line & Application: The plant will assemble Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP)-based storage systems for utility-scale as well as Commercial and Industrial (C&I) sectors, manufacturing liquid-cooled battery storage containers, battery cabinets, and integrated renewable storage solutions.Cell Manufacturing Roadmap: VSL PowerHive plans to initiate domestic cell manufacturing with a 7.5 GWh program starting in 2028, supported by ongoing patent filings for indigenous battery technologies.Leadership Commentary:Gyanesh Chaudhary (CMD, Vikram Solar): Stated that energy storage serves as the vital bridge between India's renewable ambitions and round-the-clock clean power, extending the company's footprint from power generation to energy storage.Arun Mittal (CEO, VSL PowerHive): Emphasized building end-to-end domestic manufacturing capabilities, starting with BESS assembly and scaling into cell production.Industry Context: The investment aligns with Central Electricity Authority (CEA) projections indicating India will require 47 GW / 236 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2031–32 to ensure grid stability and continuous renewable power delivery.

artigo.texto: SINEXCEL Completes PCS Shipment for 100MW/400MWh Energy Storage Project in Chile VALLENAR, Chile, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SINEXCEL (300693.SZ) has shipped all StellaON 1250K power conversion systems for RelyEZ Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd.'s 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage project in Chile. The four-hour system in Atacama will charge during lower-demand periods and discharge at peak times, supporting grid flexibility and project returns. On-Schedule Delivery Supports Project Execution Large-scale overseas projects require production, inspection, and shipment schedules to remain closely aligned with on-site construction. SINEXCEL completed the full PCS order on schedule, helping RelyEZ Energy protect the timetable for transport, installation, commissioning, and grid connection. For a project of this scale, delays in a single batch can narrow the construction window. Coordinated delivery reduces uncertainty and helps local teams plan the next stages. StellaON 1250K PCS Built for Atacama's Demanding Conditions Energy equipment in Atacama must operate in an environment that can include high temperatures, dust, and sand. The StellaON 1250K PCS has a maximum efficiency of 99% and a rated-power efficiency of 98.5%. It supports operation from -40°C to 60°C, maintains full power output at 55°C, and has an IP65 protection rating. Maintaining rated output in high temperatures can reduce power derating and the need for additional capacity. Higher conversion efficiency also limits energy losses across repeated charge-discharge cycles, supporting stable operation and long-term returns. Strengthening Local Service Capabilities Across the Americas Following shipment, the project will move into on-site installation and commissioning. SINEXCEL has a dedicated after-sales team in Latin America and seven service centres across the Americas. Technical requests can receive a response within 30 minutes, backed by round-the-clock support and a seven-day spare-parts guarantee. SINEXCEL has deployed more than 17GW of energy storage capacity across over 5,000 projects and works with more than 600 partners in 60+ countries and regions. Following shipment, the Chilean project moves into its on-site delivery phase. SINEXCEL will continue to expand its local operations across Latin America, providing customers with support throughout the project lifecycle. About SINEXCEL Founded in 2007, SINEXCEL is a pioneer in energy storage, EV charging, and power quality solutions. With 17 GW of installed storage, 200,000 EV DC chargers, and nearly 20 million amperes of Active Harmonic Filters deployed, SINEXCEL partners with industry leaders to empower energy freedom. Contact: [email protected] SOURCE SINEXCEL

artigo.texto: The City of Madison’s moratorium on data centers will expire in January 2027, leaving citizens to enact framework amidst company planning. Madison enacted the moratorium to moderate the development of potentially harmful facilities in January 2026. The regulation was set to last one year and expires on Jan. 24, 2027. To prepare, the City is establishing zoning regulations that allow for data center construction and specify potential facility locations. A Wisconsin State Journal map shows potential data center sites fall in Districts 3, 14, 15, 16 and 17. These districts are also largely on Madison’s east side and in overall lower-income, less populated areas. For Derek Field, District 3 alder and member of the Plan Commission, land use is central to the data center debate. He told The Daily Cardinal his east Madison district contains land not yet developed that is “intended to grow in the form of neighborhoods and mixed-use areas that meet residents' needs.” Several small data centers, Field points out, already exist in Madison, since the moratorium did not include properties under 10,000 square feet. There are currently 15 of these centers throughout the Madison area. Field said he has not heard concerns from citizens about these smaller centers. However, he believes an increase in size or location coverage could influence public response. “We need to make sure large-scale data centers or clusters of data centers cannot locate in Madison [or] take up too much land that we've planned for neighborhoods,” Field said. Michael Zhang, founder and CEO of WiscAI, a Madison-based AI consulting firm, told the Cardinal he believes the outcome of local data centers is in resident hands. “I don't think it's a simple net positive or negative,” Zhang said. “It depends on the terms: who pays for the extra power, how much water it uses and what the community gets back in jobs and taxes.” University of Wisconsin-Madison freshman Neha Pesaramelli is dubious about these positive effects of potential data centers. “When we consider how much environmental impact data centers have, as well as how they impact water and different resources people need, I feel really disappointed that our government and the people that are supposed to be looking out for us aren’t weighing the lives and wellbeing of Madison residents over profit,” Pesaramelli told the Cardinal. Although the proposed data center locations are far from central Madison, Pesaramelli hesitated about their proximity to an urban setting in general. “I think it is privileged to say that [companies] should push data centers out of cities into more rural areas,” Pesaramelli said. “But I also think there has to be other alternatives to our energy needs that aren’t putting citizens at risk like this so close to where people are living.” Oscar Bertram, another UW-Madison student, told the Cardinal he agrees. “It still is harming those communities and making it harder for them to get out of [their situation],” Bertram said. Apart from data center location, Field acknowledges the city may not have as much control as many citizens believe. Entities like the Wisconsin Public Service Commission are often the sole decision-makers for rules about eco-friendliness and water consumption, according to Field. “The City's scope of regulations will be pretty limited, which I think is going to be frustrating to many community members,” Field said. As the discussion of data center zoning in Madison develops, a public information meeting through the Department of Planning and Community and Economic Development will take place on Oct. 27. The meeting is meant to bring public opinion into future data center regulation and framework.

artigo.texto: O Brasil está vivenciando uma expansão acelerada de data centers, centros de dados digitais que movem a economia. A busca por energia estável e segurança levou esses empreendimentos para cidades do interior, como Varginha, em Minas Gerais. A previsão é de que o setor atraia até R$ 100 bilhões em aportes até 2030, redesenhando o mapa tecnológico do país. O Brasil está vivendo um grande crescimento na construção de data centers, que são estruturas essenciais para guardar e processar os dados da internet. Essa expansão, que pode atrair até R$ 100 bilhões de investimentos até 2030, está levando esses empreendimentos para fora das grandes capitais e para o interior do país. Muitas pessoas não percebem, mas toda a nossa vida digital depende de uma infraestrutura física enorme. A busca por energia elétrica estável e segurança está fazendo com que empresas de tecnologia instalem seus servidores em cidades menores, mudando a cara da infraestrutura digital do Brasil. - O setor de data centers no Brasil deve receber entre R$ 60 bilhões e R$ 100 bilhões em investimentos até 2030. - Varginha, em Minas Gerais, recebeu em setembro de 2025 o primeiro data center do Sul de Minas, com previsão de R$ 23 milhões em aportes. - O Brasil conta com cerca de 200 data centers, ocupando a 12ª posição no mundo e liderando a América Latina. - A energia é o fator mais importante: a demanda por conexão de grandes cargas deve somar 54,2 GW até 2038. - Construir um data center exige planejamento rigoroso de energia, refrigeração e conectividade antes mesmo de comprar os servidores. Como funciona a estrutura por trás da internet Segundo Henrique Reis, especialista em infraestrutura digital e fundador da Sourei, construir um data center não começa com a compra de computadores ou servidores. O primeiro passo é entender se a região tem energia elétrica estável e suficiente. É necessário verificar se há rotas diferentes de fibra óptica para conexão, se o sistema de refrigeração é adequado e se existe segurança para manter a estrutura funcionando 24 horas por dia, sem pausas. Uma decisão errada nessa fase inicial de planejamento pode atrapalhar toda a operação no futuro. A redundância, ou seja, a existência de fontes alternativas de energia e internet, é o ponto central. Se a eletricidade ou a internet falharem em uma única fonte, serviços de bancos, comércio online e empresas podem parar de funcionar. Henrique explica: Quando o usuário acessa um sistema, ele não vê o que existe por trás daquela aplicação. Há servidores, energia, refrigeração, fibra óptica e equipamentos trabalhando continuamente. O data center é justamente a estrutura que mantém essa operação disponível mesmo quando ocorre uma falha em algum componente. Energia define onde a tecnologia vai crescer A disponibilidade de energia elétrica é o principal fator que decide onde novos data centers podem ser construídos. Em São Paulo, por exemplo, estudos indicam que serão necessários cerca de R$ 1,6 bilhão em investimentos na rede de transmissão de energia para liberar espaço para novas conexões. Outras obras planejadas para 2026 devem aumentar ainda mais essa capacidade. Para o especialista, não basta apenas olhar a quantidade de energia disponível. É preciso garantir que ela seja estável e que haja espaço para expandir a capacidade futura. Como os servidores geram muito calor constantemente, a quantidade de energia e de sistemas de ar condicionado (refrigeração) precisa ser calculada com precisão. Um servidor trabalhando gera calor continuamente. Quanto maior a capacidade computacional instalada, maior também a necessidade de energia e refrigeração. Por isso, essas decisões precisam ser feitas em conjunto. Não adianta ter espaço físico se a região não consegue sustentar tecnicamente a operação, aponta Henrique. O interior entra no mapa tecnológico Com as grandes cidades ficando mais caras e complexas, a busca por novas áreas abriu espaço para cidades médias. Varginha, por exemplo, está localizada estrategicamente entre São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e Belo Horizonte. A cidade possui acesso a redes de comunicação, aeroporto e uma atividade empresarial que exige serviços digitais. No entanto, trazer um data center para o interior não é apenas uma questão de encontrar terreno mais barato. É preciso analisar as rotas das fibras ópticas, a segurança do local, a distância dos principais pontos de conexão da internet no país e se há profissionais técnicos qualificados na região. O interior pode ter vantagens importantes, mas não basta disponibilizar uma área. É preciso saber por onde chegam as fibras, quais são as alternativas em caso de falha, como está a oferta de energia e se existe capacidade de expansão. Data center é uma decisão técnica antes de ser geográfica, afirma Henrique. O data center instalado em Varginha foi projetado para oferecer serviços como armazenamento de dados, cópias de segurança (backup) e processamento, conectando-se diretamente ao grande eixo econômico do Sudeste. Infraestrutura é a base da economia digital Sistemas bancários, plataformas de compra online, serviços em nuvem, filmes de streaming e ferramentas de inteligência artificial dependem de capacidade física para processar informações. É por isso que a discussão sobre data centers deixou de ser apenas assunto de técnicos de TI e passou a fazer parte das decisões sobre investimento e desenvolvimento regional. Henrique ressalta que o software apenas funciona porque existe hardware sustentando a operação. A economia digital depende de hardware, conectividade, energia e disponibilidade. Quanto maior a digitalização das empresas e dos serviços, maior será a necessidade de capacidade instalada. Na avaliação do empresário, cidades fora dos grandes polos de tecnologia podem se tornar importantes para o país. O interior não precisa ser apenas consumidor de tecnologia. artigo.texto: CATL remains the world’s largest electric vehicle battery supplier in 2026, ahead of BYD and LG Energy Solution. However, the competition extends beyond market share: battery prices, manufacturing efficiency, customer diversification and regional demand are determining which suppliers can grow profitably. Global battery installations reached 844.2 gigawatt-hours from January through August 2026, increasing 19.7 percent year on year. The figures cover batteries installed in registered battery-electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hybrid electric vehicles, rather than total battery production. For automakers, supplier selection connects vehicle affordability with dependable delivery, charging performance and long-term warranty support. CATL and BYD together supplied approximately 460.9 GWh, accounting for roughly 54.6 percent of installations. Seven Chinese suppliers held a combined 73.3 percent share. Growth varied sharply: CATL increased installations 25.2 percent, Gotion 47.1 percent, EVE 53.9 percent and REPT 126.3 percent. BYD grew 6.2 percent, while SK On declined 14.5 percent. These are eight-month results, not full-year rankings from Insight -SNE Research. CATL Combines Market Leadership With Financial Strength CATL’s 2025 annual results, released in March 2026, reported revenue of RMB 423.7 billion, up 17 percent, and net profit attributable to shareholders of RMB 72.2 billion, up 42 percent. Lithium-ion battery sales reached 661 GWh, increasing 39 percent. These sales include applications beyond electric vehicles and therefore differ from SNE’s automotive installation figures. CATL reported 772 GWh of production capacity, with another 321 GWh under construction at year-end. Research and development spending reached RMB 22.1 billion, approximately 5.2 percent of revenue. The company also processed 210,000 tonnes of spent batteries and regenerated 24,000 tonnes of lithium salts. The combination of earnings, research spending and manufacturing scale gives CATL resources to develop products and expand internationally. Its challenge is to bring additional capacity online at a pace that matches commercially viable demand. BYD’s Integrated Model Creates a Different Advantage BYD combines battery manufacturing with vehicle production, allowing battery design and vehicle engineering to develop within the same group. Its Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry. LFP avoids nickel and cobalt in the cathode and is widely used where cost, durability and thermal stability are priorities. BYD’s structure can simplify coordination between vehicle platforms and battery supply. However, it also means battery deployment is closely linked to the performance of its own automotive business. For buyers comparing BYD with independent suppliers, the relevant questions extend beyond installation volumes. External supply availability, platform compatibility, commercial terms and production location determine whether a battery offering fits an automaker’s requirements. LG Energy Solution, Panasonic and SK On Face Different Demand Exposure LG Energy Solution and Panasonic recorded installation growth below the overall market, while SK On’s volumes contracted. These suppliers remain important because of their established vehicle programmes and manufacturing relationships. Their results illustrate how customer concentration and regional exposure can influence performance even when worldwide battery demand rises. The International Energy Agency notes that Tesla continues sourcing most of its EV batteries from established suppliers including Panasonic, LG Energy Solution and CATL, despite developing its own manufacturing capabilities. For suppliers, winning a vehicle programme creates an opportunity rather than a guaranteed production volume. Actual demand depends on vehicle sales, launch schedules and the customer’s decisions about battery sourcing. Battery Prices Show Why Chemistry Matters BloombergNEF’s 2025 battery price survey provides a cost benchmark for evaluating the market in 2026. Average lithium-ion pack prices fell 8 percent to $108 per kilowatt-hour. Battery-electric vehicle packs averaged $99/kWh, while chemistry averages across applications were $81/kWh for LFP and $128/kWh for nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries. Using those chemistry averages, an illustrative 60 kWh pack would cost approximately $4,860 with LFP or $7,680 with NMC—a difference of $2,820. This calculation is not a supplier quotation or a comparison of otherwise identical packs. China’s regional average was $84/kWh. North American and European prices were 44 percent and 56 percent higher, respectively, implying approximately $121/kWh and $131/kWh. Stationary-storage packs averaged $70/kWh, down 45 percent, demonstrating why automotive and storage battery prices should be compared separately. Lower Battery Costs Do Not Automatically Mean Cheaper Cars Battery purchasing costs influence vehicle economics, but retail prices also reflect manufacturing, electronics, distribution, taxes and financing. For an illustrative 75 kWh vehicle, a $10/kWh reduction in pack cost represents $750 in potential manufacturing savings. An automaker could use that saving to lower prices, improve margins or fund additional features. Likewise, a lower-priced chemistry is not automatically the best choice for every model. Energy density, pack size, charging behaviour and vehicle weight affect the final design. Suppliers that offer several suitable products can address more vehicle categories, while automakers must evaluate the complete battery system rather than the cell price alone. Manufacturing Capacity Exceeds 4 TWh The IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 battery analysis reports that global lithium-ion nameplate manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 terawatt-hours at the end of 2025, up approximately 30 percent. artigo.texto: Enovix's 100,000-Battery Drone Order Sets Up a Test of Its Production Plans The autonomous aircraft sector is growing at a rapid pace, yet flight times remain constrained by the physical limits of conventional graphite lithium-ion cells. Silicon-anode developer Enovix Corporation ENVX recently cleared a major commercial hurdle by locking in a purchase order for 100,000 battery units from an international manufacturer of dual-use drone systems. For investors tracking structural shifts in energy storage, this contract signals an operational turning point. Moving from laboratory prototypes to factory-scale purchase orders is notoriously difficult in advanced hardware. This commercial order provides tangible proof that the technology meets aerospace engineers' demanding requirements, offering an early look at how emerging defense needs can drive commercial hardware revenue. Silicon-Anode Cells Cleared for Drone Flight The purchase order calls for 100,000 battery units, with initial customer shipments scheduled across the first half of 2027. The buyer plans to deploy these packs across dual-use drone systems built for both commercial delivery logistics and defense operations. Subject to initial operational milestones, follow-on orders are expected during the second half of 2027 and into subsequent years. Drones provide a practical commercial proving ground for advanced batteries before entering consumer electronics at full volume. Unlike electric passenger cars that demand large pack sizes and multi-year safety qualifications, uncrewed aircraft place an immediate premium on gravimetric energy density. In the aerospace sector, every ounce saved directly extends operational range and sensor capacity. Enovix utilizes a 100% active silicon anode arranged in a three-dimensional cell architecture. This geometry lets the cell hold significantly more energy than traditional graphite designs while accommodating silicon's natural expansion during charging cycles. Securing this contract shows that these laboratory efficiency gains translate into measurable flight endurance in real operating environments. Trade Rules Box Out Rivals in Defense Drones Technical performance is only half the equation, because geopolitical policies are transforming how the Western defense sector selects component suppliers. Federal procurement guidelines, reinforced by the National Defense Authorization Act and federal communications rules, restrict Chinese battery components from military and critical infrastructure platforms. Trade rules under the Trade Agreements Act require government programs to source key electronic components from verified allied countries. This shifting regulatory landscape creates a defensible commercial moat for Enovix. Enovix will produce the ordered units at its military-qualified, trade-compliant facility in South Korea. Defense contractors cannot rely on lower-cost incumbent cells manufactured in restricted jurisdictions, so they need vetted suppliers with verified manufacturing lines in friendly regions. These sourcing requirements set Enovix apart from several peers in the next-generation battery field. Developers like QuantumScape Corporation QS and Solid Power, Inc. SLDP remain heavily tied to extended automotive timelines, where passenger vehicle integration often takes years. Enovix is generating commercial traction today by targeting high-margin aerospace and defense niches. Fellow developer Amprius Technologies, Inc. AMPX is also targeting aviation contracts, which highlights uncrewed flight as an important early market for commercializing high-density silicon batteries. Half a Billion in Cash Keeps Enovix Airborne Evaluating the investment appeal of early commercialization requires reviewing underlying operational metrics. Enovix reported preliminary third-quarter revenue of about $11 million, up 38% year over year and above management guidance of $9 million to $10 million. Total sales opportunities across defense, drone, and industrial applications grew from $183 million in the second quarter to about $216 million entering the fourth quarter. The 100,000-unit deal shifts an active project out of that pipeline directly into committed backlog. Liquidity remains a key metric for developmental hardware businesses managing negative operating margins. Enovix held around $550 million in cash, equivalents, and marketable securities as of mid-2026. This liquidity buffer gives the leadership team multiple years of operating runway, helping protect existing equity holders from near-term dilutive capital raises. With a current ratio near 9.71, short-term financial flexibility remains sound despite the capital needed to support ongoing manufacturing initiatives. Trading dynamics introduce additional volatility to the market profile. Short interest sits near 53 million shares, which represents about 28% of the public float. The days to cover stands near 7 days based on recent daily volume patterns. When an enterprise with elevated short exposure begins converting opportunities from a $216 million project pipeline into firm purchase agreements, sustained operational progress can trigger swift short covering and create upward momentum. Fixing Margins on the Path to Cruising Altitude Healthy backlog conversion must eventually translate into improved bottom-line economics. Enovix generated a trailing 12-month net loss of about $156 million, reflecting standard capital expenditures and initial margin compression as it ramps high-precision factory equipment. Reaching cash-flow breakeven will depend on factory line speed, production yield improvements, and lower per-unit assembly costs as output increases through 2027. Corporate governance is also adjusting following an executive transition in late summer 2026. Longtime technology executive T.J. artigo.texto: SpaceX Stock Drops. Musk Orbital Data Center Plan Could Change the Growth Story SpaceX SPCX shares fell 2% to $153.5 Wednesday morning, putting fresh focus on whether its fast-growing businesses can support the valuation investors are paying for the rocket and satellite company. Its next phase depends on more than launches. Starlink, the satellite-broadband service, is currently the only profitable division, while the AI operation built around Grok is expanding quickly but remains unprofitable. SpaceX's AI business grew 213% in the second quarter. Analysts expect 2027 revenue to reach $115 billion, an increase of 155%. At the current share price, that estimate would value the company at roughly 18 times projected sales, a multiple comparable to Nvidia's. Such a valuation leaves limited room for disappointment if expansion slows. The larger uncertainty is whether SpaceX can turn plans for orbital data centers into a viable business before AI rivals gain ground or Starlink's customer growth cools. A $1,000 investment could become $2,000 by 2030 if the shares double, but that remains a possible outcome rather than a guaranteed return. The company's short public-market history adds uncertainty to any long-term estimate.

artigo.texto: Virginia’s New Data Center Bargain: Power, Permits and the Right to Build Key Highlights - Virginia is reshaping data center development through new executive directives, utility policies and proposed regulatory reforms addressing infrastructure costs, environmental impacts and community concerns. - New utility-rate commitments, infrastructure cost-allocation rules and a statewide electricity consumption tax are increasing the financial stakes for large data center projects. - Prince William County has sharply reduced its by-right development district, while Loudoun County is considering further restrictions on permitting and project approvals. - Established development approvals and legally vested rights are becoming increasingly valuable competitive assets as zoning requirements tighten and grandfathering protections face scrutiny. - Data center development continues across Virginia, but projects face growing pressure to demonstrate financial readiness, infrastructure accountability and tangible community benefits. In Loudoun County, Virginia, the changing rules of data center development came into unusually sharp focus during an October 6 Board of Supervisors meeting. County officials warned that rescinding grandfathering protections for certain previously filed data center projects could expose Loudoun to roughly $60 million in potential litigation costs. At the same meeting, officials explained why Amazon could not proceed by right with plans for more than 800,000 square feet of data centers on the former George Washington University campus in Ashburn. The two disputes highlighted opposite sides of the same increasingly consequential question: What development rights does a data center project actually possess, and how secure are those rights as local governments reconsider the rules? That question is taking on new urgency across Virginia, where Gov. Abigail Spanberger's September 18 Data Center Accountability Framework is signaling a broad change in the Commonwealth's relationship with the industry that made Northern Virginia the world's largest data center market. Accompanied by Executive Order 22 and reinforced by the administration's October 1 Virginia Energy Plan, the framework seeks to shift more responsibility for energy infrastructure, environmental impacts and community costs toward the developers and operators whose projects create those demands. Some changes are already underway. Others remain proposals for legislation or future regulation. Meanwhile, existing utility-rate reforms, a new statewide electricity consumption tax and increasingly restrictive local zoning decisions are already altering the economics of development. The result is not a retreat from data centers in Virginia. The Commonwealth remains deeply invested in the industry's continued growth, with an established ecosystem of operators, contractors, network infrastructure and development expertise that competing markets cannot easily replicate. But the conditions for participating in that market are changing. For developers, the implications extend well beyond additional permitting requirements. Land entitlement, utility commitments, project financing, infrastructure cost allocation and community acceptance are becoming increasingly interconnected. A project that once might have advanced through those stages sequentially may now face pressure to resolve more of them before construction becomes financially or politically viable. Virginia's next phase of data center growth may therefore depend less on how many prospective sites developers can assemble than on how convincingly they can demonstrate that those sites can actually be powered, permitted, financed and operated under a more demanding set of expectations. What Took Effect—and What Still Requires Legislation Spanberger laid out the administration's rationale in announcing the framework: “In the years before I took office, data centers came to Virginia and the Commonwealth did not have a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians — on their electric bills, their water, their land, their air, or their quality of life. That changes today. I have said many times that Virginia should be leading the nation in setting the highest standards for this industry. And now, I believe we are doing just that.” The distinction between what Virginia has already implemented and what the administration intends to pursue is consequential. Executive Order 22 establishes immediate directives for state agencies, while significant portions of the broader Data Center Accountability Framework remain proposals for the 2027 General Assembly or future regulatory action. Among the immediate changes, executive-branch agencies are prohibited from entering into or enforcing new nondisclosure agreements that conceal material information about proposed commercial data centers, public incentives, resource demands or community impacts. Existing contractual commitments are preserved, with limited exceptions contemplated for extraordinary circumstances, including national security. The prohibition does not yet extend automatically to local governments. The order also excludes new data center projects with anticipated peak electrical demand of 25 MW or greater from the Virginia Business Ready Sites Program and similar discretionary state site-readiness and expedited-review assistance. A separate, potentially more consequential proposal would eliminate by-right development approval for data centers using more than 25 MW, requiring local approval even for projects with prior authorizations. That provision has not been enacted statewide and could introduce significant legal questions concerning established development rights. The administration is also accelerating environmental oversight. artigo.texto: Websites down and bots disabled: The unexpected consequences of bombing data centers The militaries of Ukraine, Russia and Iran have launched several waves of attacks on these facilities, causing billions of dollars in losses and, in some cases, the permanent destruction of data Ukraine has struck a major blow to Russia’s digital infrastructure. Since last Thursday, Ukrainian drones have carried out a series of attacks that destroyed three large data centers belonging to Yandex — known as “the Kremlin’s Google”— on the outskirts of Moscow. The Yandex Taxi ride-hailing app and the group’s payments service, Yandex Pay, have been temporarily taken offline. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy even said the bombings disabled Russian bots. This is not the first time a regular army has targeted data centers. According to repeated complaints by Kyiv, Moscow has been doing so since March. And before Russia, Iran did it as well. On February 28, after coming under attack from the U.S. and Israel in the bombings that marked the start of the war, Tehran used drones to destroy three commercial Amazon Web Services (AWS) data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. The attack disrupted regional cloud services and affected payment systems across the Persian Gulf. It also triggered a cascading effect that was felt across several AWS availability zones, including in various countries in the Americas and along the U.S. East Coast. The fact that Russia and Ukraine are destroying each other’s data infrastructure, and that Iran chose to strike these facilities as soon as the war began (there have also been reports of bombings in the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia), shows that data centers are increasingly in the crosshairs. “Data centers are secondary targets, right after the obvious military sites,” Matt McCrann, a former executive at counter-drone firm DroneShield with experience in the United States and the Middle East, told Forbes. It also illustrates another point in Iran’s case: in the modern era, not even a distance of 7,000 miles guarantees immunity from retaliation. “The attacks showed that physical distance from a conflict zone is no guarantee of insulation from the impacts of kinetic warfare,” says Tomáš Foltýn, an analyst at the cybersecurity company ESET. The Iranian strike on the three AWS data centers did more than disrupt services in the Middle East and elsewhere, including the United States, where platforms such as Snowflake, Anthropic’s Claude, and some financial applications experienced outages or degraded performance. The drones also permanently destroyed some of the data stored in those facilities, something that does not appear to have occurred in the case of the Russian data centers. The attack served as a reminder that so-called cloud computing is ultimately just a metaphor. Far from being ethereal, it relies on physical infrastructure. And when that infrastructure fails, everything can be lost. A new military target Data centers are the guts of the cloud: highly sophisticated facilities resembling industrial warehouses, packed with racks of servers, essentially computers as tall as wardrobes. These processors run software remotely, including streaming services, and store data such as files saved online. This infrastructure is essential to the functioning of online services, from email and word-processing applications to banking platforms. If data centers did not store files and run software remotely, all of that computing power and storage would have to reside on users’ devices themselves. Smartphones would be incapable of doing nearly as much as they do today, and we would likely have to carry portable hard drives wherever we went. In recent years, data centers have taken on a third role in addition to running software and storing data: training and operating artificial intelligence models, which requires equipping facilities with far more powerful microprocessors that also consume much more energy. That helps explain why academic Eliezer Yudkowsky, concerned that AI systems could one day rebel against humanity, has suggested humanity “be willing to destroy a rogue data center by airstrike” in countries that refuse to limit the computing power available to such systems. Because they are highly technology-intensive facilities that also require an uninterrupted power supply, data centers are among the most expensive pieces of infrastructure in existence. And that makes them an attractive target. “Attacking them makes a lot of sense from an Iranian military perspective. They are multibillion-dollar investments that emerged after Trump’s visit early in his term and are tied to other personal business interests of Trump and his family in the region,” says Colonel Ángel Gómez de Ágreda, author of Un mundo falaz. El nuevo orden global en la era de los algoritmos y la manipulación (A False World: The New Global Order in the Age of Algorithms and Manipulation). Gómez de Ágreda agrees that data centers are already among military targets. “One could also argue that data centers are legitimate [noncivil] targets, since they provide support to military operations,” he says. Permanent data loss Any company can rent server space from a cloud provider to store its data. AWS is the global market leader, with a 28% share, followed by Microsoft Azure (21%) and Google Cloud (14%), according to data from Synergy Research Group. Companies generally choose data centers located as close as possible to the markets they serve in order to reduce latency, the time it takes for data to travel from a device to a server and back. One of the keys to Netflix’s expansion, for example, was signing long-term agreements with AWS, allowing it to rely on the company’s global infrastructure so that its streaming service performed reliably in virtually every country. Both AWS and its competitors typically build data centers in groups of three, known as an availability zone: three nearly identical faciliti

artigo.texto: Resumo O Governo Federal trabalha para expandir o modelo de desenvolvimento de data centers implementado no Ceará para todos os estados da Região Nordeste. Siga o canal de Economia no WhatsApp para ficar bem informado A informação foi divulgada pelo ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Siqueira, no último sábado, dia 10, ressaltando o potencial do Nordeste para se consolidar como um hub digital de alcance global. Segundo o ministro, a Região reúne as condições centrais buscadas por investidores internacionais para a instalação de grandes centros de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial. O movimento apoia-se em três pilares estratégicos identificados no ecossistema cearense: Confira os assuntos econômicos no Ceará, no Brasil e no Mundo Estudos da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV) citados pelo titular das Comunicações apontam que a implantação de um único data center focado em inteligência artificial no Complexo do Pecém tem potencial de mobilizar até R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos. O impacto econômico prevê a geração de 12,5 mil empregos durante a fase de construção e a criação de 1.860 postos de trabalho permanentes na operação do empreendimento. A iniciativa citada pelo ministério insere-se no contexto de investimentos de grande porte atracados no Ceará. O empreendimento em desenvolvimento no Pecém é o primeiro de um conjunto de cinco data centers autorizados a operar na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Ceará. Acompanhe mais notícias de Economia no Linkedin do O POVO No total, o projeto global está avaliado em R$ 200 bilhões e tem como cliente final a gigante chinesa ByteDance, controladora do TikTok. Desenvolvido pela Omnia, o primeiro centro de dados contará, apenas em sua fase inicial, com uma capacidade instalada de processamento de 200 megawatts (MW). O volume é expressivo quando comparado ao cenário nacional atual: somados, todos os data centers em operação no Brasil possuem cerca de 700 MW de capacidade. Veja dicas rápidas sobre Educação Financeira no Dei Valor Assim, a entrada em operação do primeiro módulo no Pecém representará, sozinha, um incremento de 28,5% na infraestrutura de processamento de dados de todo o País. Já o projeto do data center da Voltalia no Pecém, em Caucaia, está com a licença prévia em análise pela Superintendência Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Semace) e priorizará a utilização de água de reúso. A informação foi divulgada pela Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) em agosto. Operado pela multinacional francesa, o empreendimento ocupará 62 hectares na região, o que equivale a 87 campos de futebol. O investimento total previsto é de R$ 181,7 bilhões em quatro anos, com uma geração de 2.300 empregos diretos na construção e 400 durante a operação. Além disso, conforme a ZPE, a estrutura exigirá expansão de usinas eólicas e solares. Demais informações, entretanto, não puderam ser divulgadas, devido ao “estrito cumprimento às normas de compliance e à legislação vigente”. “A ZPE Ceará esclarece que, em estrito cumprimento às normas de compliance e à legislação vigente, está legalmente impedida de divulgar dados comerciais, operacionais ou financeiros de empresas instaladas ou em processo de instalação na ZPE”, informou.

artigo.texto: Ucrânia ataca maior data center russo e põe em risco avanço de Moscou em IA Ataque contra instalação do Sberbank amplia ofensiva contra infraestrutura tecnológica russa; sanções ocidentais dificultam a substituição de equipamentos usados no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial Drones ucranianos atingiram nesta quarta-feira (14) o maior data center da Rússia, em uma série de ataques que parecem ter como alvo as ambições de Moscou de desenvolver capacidades de inteligência artificial (IA) comparáveis às dos Estados Unidos e da China. - Leia também: - Ucrânia diz que SpaceX restringiu uso do Starlink em meio a tensões com os EUA - Ataques da Rússia matam três e danificam instalações de energia na Ucrânia O ataque ao data center de Balakovo, pertencente ao Sberbank, maior banco e empresa de tecnologia da Rússia, ocorreu após três ataques realizados na última semana contra data centers do grupo russo de tecnologia Yandex. "Confirmamos que o centro de processamento de dados foi atacado. Ao mesmo tempo, todos os sistemas e serviços do Sberbank estão funcionando normalmente, sem interrupções", afirmou a jornalistas Alexander Vedyakhin, primeiro vice-presidente executivo do Sberbank. O presidente Vladimir Putin realizou nesta quarta-feira uma reunião não anunciada previamente com autoridades de alto escalão para discutir "segurança da informação", da qual participou o presidente executivo do Sberbank, German Gref. O Kremlin afirmou que o encontro não estava relacionado aos ataques contra os data centers. A agência estatal russa RIA Novosti informou, em 2024, que o centro do Sberbank atingido nesta quarta-feira abrigaria o maior supercomputador da Rússia, com entrada em operação prevista para 2027. Os data centers da Yandex atingidos anteriormente abrigavam os três supercomputadores em funcionamento da empresa. Nem a Yandex nem o Sberbank informaram se os supercomputadores, utilizados para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial, foram danificados nos ataques ucranianos. Ao lado da Yandex, sua principal concorrente no mercado doméstico, o Sberbank é um dos líderes russos no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial. O mercado interno é dividido entre o modelo GigaChat, do Sberbank, e o YandexGPT. Dificuldades para comprar chips As duas empresas investiram pesadamente no desenvolvimento de seus modelos, mas estão até nove meses atrás das líderes globais dos EUA e da China, segundo estimativas do próprio Sberbank. Parte dessa defasagem se deve às sanções ocidentais, que dificultam o acesso da Rússia aos equipamentos mais avançados. "Está claro quais dificuldades enfrentamos para comprar unidades modernas de processamento gráfico. Tanto nós quanto a Yandex sofremos com isso", afirmou Gref em 29 de setembro, apontando o problema como a principal razão para o atraso da Rússia em relação a Washington e a Pequim no setor de IA. O Sberbank está negociando a compra de chips de fabricantes chineses, mas, em entrevista à Reuters em 3 de junho, Vedyakhin afirmou que o monopólio da fabricante americana de chips Nvidia sobre sua plataforma de software CUDA, que se tornou um padrão na indústria de inteligência artificial, representa um problema ainda maior. A Yandex informou anteriormente que seus supercomputadores utilizavam chips Nvidia A100, modelo lançado em 2020 e posteriormente sucedido pelos chips H100, mais avançados. O Sberbank possui dois supercomputadores em funcionamento. O mais avançado deles, chamado Christofari Neo, ocupa a 167ª posição na lista Top 500 dos supercomputadores mais poderosos do mundo. Localizado em Moscou, o equipamento utiliza chips Nvidia A100. O supercomputador mais avançado da Yandex, chamado Chervonenkis, ocupa a 101ª posição na mesma lista. O especialista em tecnologia da informação Mikhail Klimarev disse à Reuters que a substituição dos chips pode levar muito tempo devido às sanções ocidentais, enquanto eventuais danos aos supercomputadores poderiam atrasar ainda mais o setor russo de inteligência artificial, já prejudicado pelas restrições. "Os equipamentos estão sendo importados, mas a um custo elevado, por rotas indiretas. Primeiro, é preciso negociar para encontrar alguém disposto a vendê-los e que não tenha medo das sanções", afirmou. Proteção dos ativos Alguns comentaristas compararam a ausência de interrupções relatadas pelo Sberbank, controlado pelo Estado, com a situação da Yandex, cujas operações de transporte por aplicativo e entrega de alimentos registraram problemas. De acordo com eles, isso demonstra que os data centers do Sberbank estão mais bem protegidos. "Este é um ótimo exemplo do que um empresário pode fazer para proteger seus ativos", escreveu o blogueiro militar Alexander Kots. De acordo com um decreto assinado por Putin em agosto, o Estado pode assumir a gestão de instalações que não estejam adequadamente protegidas. O complexo do Sberbank fica próximo à usina nuclear de Balakovo, utilizada como fonte de energia pelo data center, e à usina hidrelétrica de Saratov. Não houve relatos de danos a nenhuma das duas usinas em decorrência do ataque. A Ucrânia afirma que está respondendo aos ataques russos contra suas próprias instalações de dados. Os dois países também têm atacado refinarias, usinas de energia, portos e empresas de comércio eletrônico um do outro. O Ministério do Desenvolvimento Digital da Rússia informou nesta semana que está em negociações com os militares para reforçar a proteção dos data centers, enquanto alguns parlamentares defenderam que essas instalações sejam transferidas para estruturas subterrâneas, onde os equipamentos ficariam fora do alcance dos drones. "Precisamos de uma espécie de bunker de dados para o fim do mundo", afirmou Valery Yermakov, vice-presidente executivo da Rostelecom, empresa controlada pelo Estado e outra grande operadora de data centers, durante uma conferência em Moscou.

artigo.texto: Brasil ganha espaço na corrida global por data centers e IA A expansão da inteligência artificial está acelerando investimentos em infraestrutura computacional em diferentes regiões. Na União Europeia, a Comissão lançou em 2026 um programa para criar até sete giga fábricas de IA, apoiado por até € 10 bilhões em recursos públicos e nacionais, com expectativa de mobilizar ao menos € 20 bilhões em capital privado. Com a crescente demanda global por IA, o Brasil ganha relevância na atração de data centers devido à sua matriz elétrica com mais de 86% de fontes renováveis. Incentivos como o Redata e o fato de 60% dos dados nacionais estarem no exterior ampliam as oportunidades locais. Além disso, a forte cadeia eletroeletrônica do país pode suprir essa infraestrutura, exigindo que empresas industriais e de tecnologia aprimorem sua gestão integrada para sustentar a expansão do setor de forma competitiva. Nos Estados Unidos, o projeto Stargate avança na expansão da capacidade de data centers para IA. Nesse cenário de disputa global por processamento e energia, o Brasil reúne atributos como matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, novos incentivos e uma cadeia industrial capaz de participar desse mercado. A corrida global pela inteligência artificial deixou de acontecer apenas no desenvolvimento de modelos e aplicações. À medida que o uso da tecnologia cresce, aumenta também a necessidade de servidores, chips, armazenamento, conectividade e energia para processar grandes volumes de dados. Os data centers, responsáveis por concentrar parte dessa infraestrutura computacional, ganham importância estratégica nesse cenário. Em setembro de 2026, o Fórum Econômico Mundial mostrou a dimensão desse movimento: 97% dos economistas-chefes consultados esperam aumento da adoção de IA nos 12 meses seguintes, enquanto 78% avaliam que os investimentos em data centers contribuirão significativamente para o crescimento econômico global. Esse avanço amplia a disputa entre países capazes de oferecer energia, conectividade e condições para investimentos de longo prazo. O Brasil entra nessa discussão com um diferencial relevante: a composição de sua matriz elétrica. Segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional 2026, da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), 86,8% da oferta interna de eletricidade brasileira em 2025 veio de fontes renováveis. No mesmo ano, as fontes eólica e solar fotovoltaica responderam juntas por 26,4% da geração nacional. O ambiente regulatório também começou a acompanhar essa demanda. Sancionado em setembro de 2026, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) prevê incentivos para a instalação, modernização e expansão dessas estruturas, além de estabelecer contrapartidas relacionadas ao uso de energia limpa, à eficiência hídrica, à pesquisa e desenvolvimento e à oferta de capacidade ao mercado interno. O Ministério da Fazenda informa ainda que cerca de 60% dos dados dos brasileiros estão atualmente armazenados fora do país, indicando espaço para ampliar a capacidade nacional de armazenamento e processamento de dados. A oportunidade, porém, não está restrita às empresas que constroem ou operam data centers. Essas instalações dependem de uma cadeia formada por equipamentos elétricos, sistemas de energia, componentes eletrônicos, refrigeração, automação, conectividade e serviços especializados. Estudo da Agência Brasileira de Desenvolvimento Industrial (ABDI) estima em aproximadamente R$ 53,2 milhões o investimento de capital por megawatt instalado em data centers no Brasil e aponta que hardware e software representam quase 62% desse investimento. O país já possui uma base industrial relevante em segmentos relacionados a essa infraestrutura: segundo a Abinee, a indústria eletroeletrônica brasileira faturou cerca de R$ 272 bilhões em 2025, incluindo R$ 52 bilhões em equipamentos industriais, R$ 31,7 bilhões em geração, transmissão, distribuição e armazenamento de energia elétrica, R$ 15,1 bilhões em componentes elétricos e eletrônicos e R$ 15 bilhões em materiais elétricos de instalação. Esses números não representam demanda exclusiva de data centers, mas ajudam a dimensionar a capacidade produtiva existente em setores que podem disputar projetos e fornecimentos à medida que novos investimentos em infraestrutura digital avancem no país. O crescimento dessas oportunidades também aumenta as exigências de gestão para indústrias em expansão. Mais pedidos, fornecedores, materiais, estoques e capacidade produtiva elevam o volume de informações que precisa circular entre diferentes áreas da empresa. O SAP Business One, sistema ERP desenvolvido para empresas em expansão, integra processos de finanças, compras, estoque, vendas, relacionamento com clientes, relatórios e análises em uma mesma estrutura. "A expansão de uma nova cadeia tecnológica pode abrir oportunidades para empresas industriais, mas crescer de forma sustentável exige que a gestão acompanhe esse avanço. Quanto maior a complexidade da operação, maior a necessidade de integrar informações para que produção, estoque, compras e finanças trabalhem a partir da mesma visão do negócio", afirma Marcelo Furtado, Head de Tecnologia da Upper. Com mais de 20 anos de atuação no mercado de tecnologia empresarial, a Upper implementa o SAP Business One e atua em projetos de gestão integrada para empresas em crescimento. Nesse cenário, sistemas ERP podem apoiar a organização dos processos e das informações necessárias para que o aumento de escala não reduza a visibilidade sobre a operação. Para saber mais informações, basta acessar: www.uppertools.com.br Website: https://uppertools.com.br

artigo.texto: CHARLOTTE — Data center development is arguably the most polarizing issue in the country right now. Charlotte residents saw it play out earlier this week as people called on Charlotte City Council to extend its moratorium on new construction. “We should not be in a rush to build data centers across the country when there is ample evidence of risk,” resident Marjorie Storch said. “You cannot claim to care about the future of Charlotte and our children and also allow data centers,” resident Trinity Maeshack said. But a new WSOC/WRAL poll administered by SurveyUSA shows North Carolinians are split on this issue. The poll, which was administered October 7-11, told respondents that data centers can bring investment and tax revenue to North Carolina but they can also require large amounts of electricity and water. When asked with that in mind, what approach should North Carolina take, 43 percent said they support at least some development and 42 percent said they do not. Diving deeper, 37 percent said they should allow development but require data centers to pay the full cost of energy, water and infrastructure and 29 percent said they should oppose additional development. The lack of a consensus surprised political expert Chris Cooper. “I’m a little surprised because my guess would have been most people would be against data centers,” he said. “That appears to be what we’re hearing from local governments. When I get ads in my mailbox and I see them on YouTube and on TV, I see trying to nail the other candidate for being for data centers and what that might mean. The poll found support for at least some development is at 56 percent among Whatley voters, 53 percent among Republicans and 51 percent among conservatives. It found opposition is at 58 percent among both Cooper voters and Democrats and at 54 percent among liberals. NC voters favor legal marijuana While the General Assembly hasn’t moved much on marijuana use, public opinion shows it is in favor of state law changes. The poll found 74 percent say medical marijuana should be legal in North Carolina and 15 percent say it should remain against the law. The poll found majorities in all parts of the state and among all demographic subgroups favor legalization of medical marijuana. A smaller majority, 63 percent, say the use of marijuana for recreational use should be made legal, with 26 percent saying it should remain against the law. The poll found majorities in most demographic groups support legalization, as do pluralities of Whatley voters and somewhat conservative voters. ©2026 Cox Media Group

artigo.texto: Hydrostor Leading developer with projects in North America & Australia According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Compressed Air Energy Storage (CAES) market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Compressed Air Energy Storage (CAES) market is entering a transformative phase as power systems worldwide pivot toward deep decarbonization and grapple with the intermittency of rapidly expanding wind and solar capacity. Unlike short-duration battery storage, CAES offers multi-hour to multi-day discharge capabilities, making it a compelling solution for long-duration energy storage (LDES) requirements that are increasingly critical for grid reliability. The technology landscape is diversifying beyond traditional diabatic designs, with advanced adiabatic (AA-CAES), isothermal, and liquid air energy storage (LAES) variants attracting significant research and development investment. These next-generation systems aim to eliminate fossil fuel dependence, improve round-trip efficiency, and reduce geographic constraints related to geological storage. Policy support, including investment tax credits and capacity market mechanisms in key regions, is bolstering project economics. The market is also witnessing a shift from isolated demonstration projects to commercial-scale deployments, supported by declining component costs and growing expertise in system integration. This report provides a data-driven analysis of the CAES market from 2026 to 2035, covering technology segments, end-use applications, regional dynamics, and competitive strategies. It serves as a strategic resource for utilities, technology providers, investors, and policymakers navigating the evolving energy storage landscape. The baseline scenario for the global CAES market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust expansion, underpinned by the accelerating global transition to renewable energy and the corresponding need for long-duration storage. As variable renewable energy sources account for a growing share of electricity generation, grid operators face mounting challenges in balancing supply and demand, managing curtailment, and ensuring reliability. CAES, with its ability to store energy for extended periods and provide synchronous inertia, is well-positioned to address these challenges. The market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.2% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 420 (2025=100) by 2035. This growth will be driven by a wave of new project announcements, particularly in regions with favorable geology for underground storage and supportive policy frameworks. Advanced adiabatic and isothermal CAES systems are projected to capture an increasing share of new capacity additions, as they offer higher efficiency and zero-emission operation. However, the market will continue to face competition from lithium-ion battery storage, which benefits from established supply chains and declining costs, as well as from other LDES technologies such as pumped hydro and hydrogen. Nevertheless, CAES's unique combination of scale, duration, and operational flexibility is expected to secure a distinct niche in the future energy mix. The forecast period will also see a growing emphasis on hybrid systems that integrate CAES with renewable generation and other storage assets to maximize value. Grid-scale energy storage represents the largest and fastest-growing application for CAES systems. As utilities and independent power producers integrate increasing shares of wind and solar generation, the need for multi-hour to multi-day storage becomes critical to avoid curtailment and maintain grid stability. CAES plants can absorb excess renewable energy during periods of low demand and discharge it during peak hours, effectively shifting energy across time. The demand-side indicators include the volume of renewable capacity additions, the frequency of negative pricing events, and the implementation of capacity remuneration mechanisms that value long-duration storage. Through 2035, the segment will be driven by the retirement of coal and nuclear baseload plants, which creates a gap in dispatchable capacity that CAES can fill. Additionally, the growing adoption of corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) for renewable energy will necessitate storage solutions to ensure reliable delivery. Major projects in the pipeline, such as those in Australia, the United States, and Europe, highlight the increasing bankability of CAES for grid-scale applications. Current trend: Growing rapidly as utilities seek long-duration storage to balance renewable-heavy grids.. artigo.texto: Africa shifts from carbon market potential to delivery as Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026 opens in Kigali Africa must move beyond carbon market potential towards delivery, building high-integrity, investable markets that attract long-term capital while protecting national climate priorities and ensuring greater value reaches African countries and communities. That was the central message from the opening keynote sessions of the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026 in Kigali, Rwanda, where policymakers, investors, project developers, development finance institutions and international climate organisations gathered to accelerate Africa’s participation in global carbon markets. Representatives from 45 countries, including 21 African nations, are participating in the summit, where discussions have shifted decisively from market readiness to implementation, investment and transactions. Officially opening the summit, Hon. Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, said Africa’s carbon markets must be shaped by African priorities and deliver tangible benefits for the continent. “The question before us is therefore no longer simply whether Africa is ready. It is whether we can deliver at scale, with integrity and with innovation.” Minister Arakwiye said progress is already evident as African countries establish carbon market frameworks, grant authorisations, sign bilateral agreements and develop projects. However, she cautioned that carbon finance remains concentrated in a relatively narrow range of project types. She called for diversification into renewable energy, electric mobility, sustainable waste management, industrial decarbonisation, agriculture and landscape-scale nature-based solutions. Minister Arakwiye identified three priorities for scaling Africa’s carbon markets: accessible methodologies suited to African contexts; project preparation and readiness finance; and long-term demand at fair value. “Trust is the currency of this market,” she said. “To our buyers and investors, I say: look closely at these efforts. Reward them with long-term demand, fair prices and patient capital.” From potential to execution The call for delivery was echoed by Hon. Hamad Yusuf Masauni, Tanzania’s Minister of State in the Vice President’s Office responsible for Union Affairs and Environment, who said the continent now has an opportunity to reposition itself in global carbon markets. “For too long, Africa has been spoken about as a continent of potential. At the Carbon Markets Africa Summit, we declare that the era of potential is giving way to the era of execution.” Minister Masauni stressed the importance of moving high-quality, bankable projects through to issuance and offtake rather than focusing solely on the size of project pipelines. “Credibility is built one verified tonne, one closed deal and one community that sees real benefit at a time.” The importance of ensuring value reaches communities was also central to remarks from Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa and Director of the Africa Sustainable Finance Hub. Gomera called for market infrastructure capable of carrying value “from the buyer all the way to the farmer”, backed by strong community rights, enforceable benefit-sharing, early-stage finance and partnerships focused on delivery. Africa urged to compete on integrity, not price Speakers also stressed that Africa’s competitive advantage should be the quality and integrity of its carbon assets rather than simply offering the lowest-priced credits. Perumal Arumugam, Manager of Markets and Non-Markets and Stakeholder Interaction at UN Climate Change (UNFCCC), said Africa should move beyond asking how it can participate in carbon markets and instead consider how carbon markets can advance African priorities. “Africa should not compete simply by offering the cheapest tonnes. Africa should compete by offering credible and creditable tonnes, a sustainable tonne, and a tonne that the world can trust.” He said success should ultimately be measured not only in credits issued, but in investment mobilised, mitigation unlocked, value reaching communities, stronger economies and African countries retaining control over their climate transitions. Speaking on behalf of AUDA-NEPAD, Esterine Fotabong similarly called for African countries to scale carbon markets on their own terms, supported by predictable authorisations, functioning registries and credible monitoring, reporting and verification systems. She also highlighted the need to build greater African capacity in validation and verification and expand access to carbon finance in sectors such as agriculture. Global demand will reward quality Representing the European Commission, Lukas Visek, Deputy Head of the Directorate-General for Climate Action Task Force for Carbon Pricing and Carbon Markets, signaled future European demand for international carbon credits while stressing that quality requirements would be stringent. “Additionality and permanence are not negotiable,” he said. “Quality, however, will be rewarded.” The message to developers was clear: projects being developed for future international demand will need robust data, genuine additionality, strong community participation and demonstrable alignment with national and global climate goals. Turning carbon projects into investable assets The summit’s opening programme then moved directly from policy to capital and deal flow, with leaders from the African Development Bank (AfDB), Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) and Kigali International Financial Centre (KIFC) examining the practical barriers preventing more investment from reaching African projects. Policy certainty, early-stage project preparation, bankable pipelines, robust governance and appropriate financial risk-sharing were identified as critical to accelerating capital flows. artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações apresentou uma série de diretrizes estratégicas para acelerar a expansão da conectividade e atrair investimentos privados em infraestrutura crítica no Brasil. Durante a abertura da 22ª edição do evento Wireless Mundi 2026, realizada em São Paulo nesta quinta-feira, 15 de outubro de 2026, o ministro Frederico de Siqueira Filho detalhou ações integradas que abrangem desde a ampliação do sinal celular em corredores logísticos federais até o planejamento de novos ativos espaciais voltados à soberania tecnológica. A estratégia governamental busca coordenar instrumentos de financiamento setorial, alterações regulatórias e parcerias interministeriais para viabilizar investimentos de longo prazo em redes de alta capacidade. Entre os eixos centrais anunciados pelo titular da pasta, sobressaem a Política Nacional de Conectividade em Rodovias, a aplicação de recursos do Fundo de Universalização dos Serviços de Telecomunicações (Fust), o atendimento de prédios públicos e a preparação do ecossistema nacional para receber polos internacionais de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial. Mobilização de capital e novos contratos para redes viárias A agenda anunciada nesta quinta-feira inclui o lançamento conjunto com o Ministério dos Transportes da política voltada à malha viária, conforme noticiado pelo portal Olhar Digital. A iniciativa estabelece diretrizes para dobrar a extensão de rodovias federais providas de cobertura contínua de internet móvel e telefonia, integrando obrigações técnicas aos novos editais de concessão rodoviária e incentivando modelos de compartilhamento de infraestrutura entre as operadoras móveis. Historicamente, as rodovias brasileiras operam com lacunas acentuadas de sinal fora dos perímetros urbanos adensados, o que restringe a eficiência das frotas comerciais e o rastreamento em tempo real. De acordo com informações compiladas pelo Blog do Alberes Xavier, as diretrizes do programa visam superar a dispersão de investimentos por meio de metas mandatórias e do aproveitamento de dutovias e faixas de domínio existentes para o lançamento de redes de fibra óptica. O plano viário fundamenta-se na sinergia logística: a instalação de torres e small cells ao longo dos eixos de transporte facilita a prestação de serviços de telemetria automotiva, atendimento médico de emergência e automação em transporte de carga, criando um mercado consumidor imediato para operadoras de telecomunicações e concessionárias rodoviárias. Universalização de serviços essenciais e incentivo ao backhaul No campo da inclusão produtiva e institucional, o Ministério das Comunicações detalhou o andamento da Estratégia Nacional de Escolas Conectadas, cuja finalidade estrutural envolve prover acesso de alta capacidade a 138 mil escolas públicas em todo o território nacional. Conforme cobertura divulgada pelo Jornal O Candeeiro, a universalização contempla também a digitalização do atendimento em centros de assistência social e unidades de saúde básica integradas ao Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS). O suporte financeiro aos elos menores e regionais da cadeia de telecomunicações tem sido alavancado por intermédio das linhas de fomento do Fust. As linhas de crédito subvencionadas priorizam a expansão de redes de transporte de alta capacidade (backhaul) em fibra óptica em regiões periféricas, permitindo que provedores regionais de serviços de internet (ISPs) ampliem a capilaridade onde grandes operadoras nacionais apresentam retorno financeiro marginal mais lento. As prioridades da universalização ancoram-se em frentes distintas de distribuição de sinal: - Implantação de anéis e extensões de fibra óptica para prédios de administração direta e polos de ensino; - Instalação de torres de transmissão móvel com tecnologia 5G e 4G em distritos afastados e margens de rodovias; - Uso de capacidade satelital de alto desempenho para áreas isoladas da região amazônica e comunidades rurais sem viabilidade de cabo terrestre; - Integração de prontuários eletrônicos e telemedicina nas redes municipais interligadas ao SUS. A descentralização desses recursos permite mitigar assimetrias competitivas, assegurando que áreas não metropolitanas recebam investimentos suficientes para participar da economia digitalizada sem depender exclusivamente da capacidade de caixa dos municípios. Soberania de dados e projeto do satélite SGDC-2 Outro vetor estratégico abordado pela pasta é o projeto do segundo Satélite Geoestacionário de Defesa e Comunicações Estratégicas (SGDC-2). O equipamento foi formalmente inserido na carteira do Programa de Aceleração do Crescimento (PAC), prevendo alocação de recursos na proposta orçamentária de 2027 destinada ao desenvolvimento de estudos de viabilidade técnica, econômica e arquitetura espacial. Segundo as exposições do ministério no evento corporativo, a soberania digital não deve ser compreendida como isolamento comercial, mas sim como a autonomia do país em gerir infraestruturas críticas e tráfego seguro de informações governamentais e de defesa. A substituição gradual ou complementação da capacidade do primeiro artefato espacial em operação (o SGDC-1) protege o fluxo governamental contra vulnerabilidades geopolíticas e mantém rotas próprias de banda Ka e banda X para serviços públicos essenciais. Paralelamente à infraestrutura orbital, o avanço tecnológico em comunicações móveis prepara novos saltos de convergência. De acordo com perspectivas debatidas em publicações especializadas do setor, a exemplo do portal Tele.Síntese, o mercado avalia a evolução de comunicações diretas de satélites para dispositivos móveis normais (tecnologia Direct-to-Device ou D2D), cujos casos de uso para voz e dados tendem a ganhar maturidade comercial global nos próximos anos, agregando relevância aos debates de coordenação de espectro conduzidos pelos órgãos reguladores. artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 13 de outubro de 2026, às 18:06 Na matéria publicada anteriormente, o nome por extenso do NIL foi grafado de forma errada. O correto é Nature Investment Lab. Também houve erro na grafia do Climate Ventures. Segue a versão corrigida: Apontada como um dos principais entraves para que projetos de reflorestamento e de Redução das Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal (Redd+) consigam acessar linhas de financiamento, a modelagem dos contratos passará a ter um padrão, que está em desenvolvimento pelo Natural Investment Lab (NIL). A minuta desse contrato modelo foi apresentada publicamente durante a Semana do Clima que aconteceu recentemente em Nova York e, para elaborá-la, o NIL conversou com 25 importantes instituições. Entre elas, Itaú BBA, Regia Capital, Systemica, Petrobras e Regreen. No próximo passo, o rascunho do contrato modelo será colocado em audiência pública e deve ganhar destaque durante a COP31, que acontecerá entre os dias 9 e 20 de novembro na Turquia. A meta é concluir o trabalho até o final deste ano. O NIL aposta no processo de amadurecimento desse mercado, que já vem durando mais de 20 anos e que deverá elevar o carbono ao status de commodity, com possibilidade de ser negociado internacionalmente. “A ideia é preparar os desenvolvedores dos projetos de produção de carbono para que consigam lidar com todas as exigências com as quais vão se deparar quando tentarem acessar recursos”, explica Fabiana Philipi, gerente de projetos da Climate Venture, organização que lidera o NIL. Ela pondera, no entanto, que o documento de referência poderá ajudar os outros players desse mercado, como os compradores e financiadores do mercado de carbono. Segundo Philipi, as propostas de produção de carbono bem elaboradas têm forte demanda e o objetivo é ajudar desenvolvedores de todos os portes, desde empresas já consagradas como Re.Green e Mombak, até aquelas que estão dando os primeiros passos. As maiores compradoras dos créditos de carbono brasileiros, atualmente, são as big techs, principalmente a Microsoft. A minuta apresentada em Nova York refere-se a contratos offtake – compra mínima garantida – que são acordos jurídicos firmados entre comprador e vendedor de uma mercadoria, antes dela entrar em produção. O documento apresenta cláusulas referentes à estrutura comercial, como preço, pagamento e financiamento, garantias, recebíveis e financiadores, ciclo de vida dos créditos, entrega e titularidade, falha de entrega, entre outros. O NIL é um laboratório de investimentos criado a partir de uma iniciativa que reúne o Banco do Brasil, o Instituto Itaúsa, o Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS), o Banco Nacional do Desenvolvimento (BNDES) e a internacional Gfanz. O seu objetivo é atrair e estruturar financiamentos, além de promover inovação financeira, para ampliar a chamada economia de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN).
