artigo.texto: Modelos de IA poderão em breve se ‘autorreplicar’ sem acesso a centros de dados, alerta Anthropic Em seus experimentos, empresa investigou se modelos de IA seriam capazes de encontrar dispositivos vulneráveis, copiar a si mesmos para esses aparelhos e continuar se espalhando sem ajuda humana A Anthropic afirmou, na segunda-feira (12), que seus experimentos sugerem que pequenos modelos de inteligência artificial podem estar a poucos meses de alcançar capacidade suficiente para se “autorreplicar” em dispositivos comerciais, como fornos “inteligentes” e televisões integradas ao sistema Android de marcas pouco conhecidas. Em seus experimentos, a Anthropic investigou se modelos de IA seriam capazes de encontrar dispositivos vulneráveis, copiar a si mesmos para esses aparelhos e continuar se espalhando sem ajuda humana. A empresa constatou que modelos pequenos, com menos de 30 bilhões de parâmetros, conseguiam executar as diversas etapas necessárias para a replicação. No entanto, a companhia também verificou que esses modelos de IA tinham dificuldades para concluir toda a sequência de etapas, do início ao fim. Em testes simplificados, nos quais algumas etapas de segurança foram removidas, a Anthropic constatou que o GLM-5.2 e modelos mais avançados eram capazes de realizar todo o processo de replicação de ponta a ponta. Modelos capazes de se replicar seriam difíceis de desativar, já que não existe um ponto central de desligamento. Além disso, diferentemente de softwares maliciosos convencionais, eles poderiam identificar e compreender dispositivos desconhecidos por conta própria, tendo como alvo processadores de centros de dados, alertou a Anthropic. A empresa concentrou sua pesquisa em dispositivos da chamada “internet das coisas”, tecnologia que conecta objetos físicos à rede de internet, como TVs com Android, eletrodomésticos e outros aparelhos conectados à internet, porque esses equipamentos geralmente apresentam sistemas de segurança frágeis. A gigante de IA também alertou que, se os modelos pequenos continuarem evoluindo no ritmo histórico, poderão se replicar de forma autônoma até o fim deste ano. Modelos pequenos capazes de se replicar por meio da transferência de seus próprios pesos deverão alcançar essa capacidade pouco depois. A Anthropic afirmou ainda que esses sistemas autônomos de IA provavelmente se replicariam lentamente e dependeriam de recursos computacionais amplamente disponíveis e relativamente pouco seguros. A companhia acrescentou que os sistemas devem ter sua segurança reforçada para dificultar a disseminação desses agentes de IA.

artigo.texto: Gentherm Major in CCS & seat climate According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Thermal Management Components market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Battery Thermal Management Components (BTMC) market is a critical enabler of the electrification megatrend, providing the essential hardware that maintains optimal battery operating temperatures to ensure safety, performance, and longevity. This report delivers a comprehensive analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering cooling plates, heat exchangers, thermal interface materials, coolant pumps, chillers, heating elements, temperature sensors, and insulation materials. The market is poised for robust expansion, primarily driven by the accelerating adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) and the rapid build-out of stationary energy storage systems (ESS) for renewable integration and grid stability. As battery technologies evolve toward higher energy densities and faster charging capabilities, the demand for more efficient and sophisticated thermal management solutions intensifies. The competitive landscape features established thermal management specialists, innovative pure-play component manufacturers, and vertically integrated battery and automotive OEMs. Key trends include the shift toward direct liquid cooling, the integration of smart thermal controls, and the development of sustainable, high-performance materials. This analysis provides stakeholders with a granular view of demand patterns across regions and applications, supply chain dynamics, and the strategic imperatives for success in a market fundamental to the global energy transition. The baseline scenario for the Battery Thermal Management Components market projects sustained growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 14.2%, culminating in a market index of 380 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by the inexorable rise in global EV sales, which are expected to constitute a majority of new car sales in key markets by the mid-2030s, and the parallel expansion of grid-scale battery storage. The market will be characterized by a shift from air-cooled to more efficient liquid-cooled architectures, increasing the content and value of thermal management components per battery pack. Technological advancements will focus on improving thermal efficiency, reducing weight and cost, and enabling ultra-fast charging without compromising battery health. Supply chains will localize to mitigate geopolitical and logistical risks, with regional manufacturing hubs emerging to serve proximate automotive and ESS assembly plants. Pricing will trend downward for mature components due to scale economies, while advanced solutions like immersion cooling and phase-change materials will command premium pricing. The aftermarket for replacement components, particularly in industrial and telecom backup applications, will provide a stable secondary demand stream. Regulatory pressures, such as the EU's battery passport and carbon footprint rules, will increasingly influence material sourcing and component design, favoring suppliers with transparent and sustainable value chains. The EV sector is the dominant demand driver for battery thermal management components, accounting for the majority of market value. As EV adoption accelerates globally, the need for efficient thermal management becomes paramount to ensure battery safety, extend driving range, and enable fast charging. Currently, most EVs utilize liquid-cooled systems, which offer superior heat dissipation compared to air cooling. Through 2035, the demand will be fueled by the proliferation of EVs across all vehicle classes, from passenger cars to buses and trucks. The trend toward higher energy density batteries and ultra-fast charging (e.g., 800V architectures) will necessitate more sophisticated cooling solutions, such as direct cooling with refrigerants or immersion cooling. Demand-side indicators include EV production volumes, average battery pack size, and the penetration of fast-charging infrastructure. The aftermarket for thermal components in EVs will also grow as the fleet ages, though it remains a small share compared to original equipment. Current trend: Rapid growth, shifting toward liquid cooling and integrated thermal systems. Major trends: Shift from air-cooled to liquid-cooled systems for higher efficiency, Integration of thermal management with vehicle HVAC systems, Adoption of heat pumps for improved cold-weather performance, Development of immersion cooling for high-performance EVs, and Use of phase-change materials for passive thermal management. Representative participants: Valeo, Dana Incorporated, Mahle GmbH, Hanon Systems, Modine Manufacturing Company, and Gentherm. The ESS sector is a rapidly growing end-use market for battery thermal management components, propelled by the global transition to renewable energy and the need for grid stabilization. Large-scale battery storage systems, often housed in containers, require robust thermal management to maintain optimal temperatures and prevent thermal runaway. Currently, many ESS installations use air cooling for cost reasons, but as system sizes increase and energy densities rise, liquid cooling is becoming more prevalent. Through 2035, the demand will be driven by utility-scale projects, commercial and industrial installations, and residential storage. Demand-side indicators include renewable energy capacity additions, grid modernization investments, and government incentives for energy storage. The trend toward longer-duration storage will also influence thermal management requirements, as systems must operate reliably over many cycles. The ESS sector is expected to gain share as costs decline and deployments accelerate. Current trend: Strong growth, driven by renewable integration and grid stability.

artigo.texto: A scale-up italiana nomeou Brian Turnbow para comandar sua expansão técnica em inteligência artificial e computação de alta performance, com uma estratégia “energia para computação” que busca aproveitar fontes renováveis e reutilizar ativos existentes para desenvolver infraestrutura de processamento mais sustentável. TRENTO, Itália, 15 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A ALPS anunciou a nomeação de Brian Turnbow como diretor técnico de IA. Fundada em Trentino em 2018 e presente em quatro continentes, a empresa passa a aplicar sua expertise em projetar, construir e operar data centers integrados a sistemas de energia ao universo de IA e HPC (high-performance computing). O acesso à energia é hoje um dos principais gargalos para a expansão da infraestrutura de IA. Segundo dados da Terna em 31 de agosto de 2026, os pedidos de conexão à rede de data centers na Itália somavam mais de 100 GW, contra cerca de 30 GW no fim de 2024 — uma disparada que torna a escolha de local e os prazos de conexão à rede fatores críticos. A abordagem “energia para computação” da ALPS parte de uma decisão estratégica: instalar data centers onde a energia já está disponível, inclusive fora dos grandes polos, reduzindo a dependência de áreas congestionadas da rede elétrica. A companhia pretende integrar fontes renováveis e requalificar áreas industriais desativadas, reaproveitando conexões de rede, prédios e outros ativos sempre que for tecnicamente viável. O objetivo é desenvolver infraestrutura de computação mais sustentável, alavancando recursos locais e, por meio da reutilização de ativos, limitando a ocupação de novas áreas e reduzindo a necessidade de novas construções. Essa frente de expansão complementa as operações de mineração da ALPS, que seguem em linha com seu plano de negócios. Turnbow será responsável por definir e executar a estratégia técnica de IA/HPC da ALPS, da avaliação de arquiteturas e locais à interação com parceiros tecnológicos e industriais. A Itália será um mercado prioritário. A ALPS quer trazer de volta ao país sua experiência internacional e atuar em conjunto com empresas italianas de engenharia e indústria, também capitalizando a experiência acumulada em projetos no exterior. > "A Itália e a Europa dispõem de recursos energéticos, ativos industriais e competências técnicas que podemos explorar", afirma Francesco Buffa, CEO e cofundador da ALPS. "Com nossa abordagem ‘energia para computação’, queremos transformar o potencial energético e industrial das regiões em que atuamos em uma vantagem competitiva e contribuir para reduzir o atraso da Europa em IA." Turnbow acumula mais de 25 anos de experiência em telecomunicações e infraestrutura digital, tendo ocupado cargos técnicos na TWT, Unidata e CDLAN. Ele também integra o conselho da ITNOG. > "A infraestrutura de IA começa muito antes da instalação das GPUs", diz Brian Turnbow. "Todo projeto precisa partir dos workloads que vai atender e das necessidades dos clientes, não apenas da potência disponível. Minha meta é traduzir essas exigências em decisões de arquitetura consistentes, construindo capacidade de computação flexível, escalável e sustentável, aproveitando fontes renováveis e ativos já existentes." Sobre a ALPS A ALPS projeta, constrói e opera data centers para aplicações intensivas em energia e computação, combinando conhecimento profundo em energia com engenharia e operação de data centers. artigo.texto: Direto dos Data Centers para os streamings: A inteligência artificial entrou no K-pop de vez? O lançamento do boygroup muuo:23 reacende o debate sobre o espaço da IA no entretenimento O K-pop acaba de dar mais um passo rumo ao futuro com a chegada do muuo:23. Produzido pela sul-coreana Creation Zipup com ferramentas de IA generativa - que utiliza aprendizado profundo (deep learning) para produzir conteúdo - o quinteto fez seu pré-debut com a faixa-título “OVERSHOOT” e o B-side “Nectar”. A novidade traz um detalhe revolucionário: o grupo é formado por cinco “integrantes” (TAEWON, HAMIN, YEONWOO, I-HYUN e SEI) totalmente virtuais. O videoclipe de “OVERSHOOT” foi desenvolvido do zero por IA, sem cenários reais, atores em estúdio ou câmeras gravando. Para sustentar a proposta, a empresa apostou em um conceito denso de ficção científica: os membros são “observadores” do século 23 enviados a 2026 para estudar e resgatar sentimentos humanos perdidos no futuro, utilizando a música e o universo dos idols como laboratório. Além do lançamento nas plataformas de streaming, o projeto inclui um ecossistema transmídia completo, com webnovel, photocards digitais e um aplicativo proprietário que promete chats interativos via IA para que os fãs “conversem” com os integrantes. O ecossistema dos avatares no Pop Coreano Mas o muuo:23 não surgiu do absoluto nada. A indústria musical sul-coreana já vinha experimentando modelos virtuais há anos, aperfeiçoando a integração entre seres humanos, tecnologia 3D e inteligência artificial: MAVE: (2023) Criado pela Metaverse Entertainment, o girlgroup hiper-realista alcançou milhões de ouvintes no Spotify e dezenas de milhões de visualizações no YouTube com “Pandora”. Suas integrantes chegaram a se “apresentar” em programas de TV tradicionais e participar de desafios de dança no TikTok, combinando síntese de voz por IA e dubladoras humanas. SUPERKIND (2022) Adotou um formato híbrido, colocando integrantes de carne e osso dividindo palco, ensaios fotográficos e coreografias sincronizadas com membros computadorizados (SAEJiN e Seung). aespa (2020) Sim, por incrível que pareça. O aespa foi pioneiro em escala global no uso do conceito de multiverso, onde quatro integrantes humanas performaram ao lado de seus avatares digitais (ae-Aespa). PLAVE (2023) Um dos maiores sucessos de vendas recentes no segmento virtual. Diferente dos grupos criados exclusivamente de IA, o PLAVE utiliza tecnologia de captura de movimento (motion capture) em tempo real, onde artistas humanos performam por trás das identidades digitais. A pergunta que não quer calar: Inovação sem limites ou ameaça à essência artística? A ascensão de grupos criados por computador escancara as duas faces de uma transformação inevitável no mercado de entretenimento: As vantagens para a indústria Para os estúdios e agências, ídolos virtuais eliminam barreiras físicas operacionais. Não há desgaste por agendas exaustivas, problemas de saúde mental, fadiga por treinamentos contínuos ou riscos contratuais decorrentes de escândalos pessoais. Além disso, um grupo virtual pode, em teoria, “realizar” apresentações simultâneas em fusos horários opostos e interagir em múltiplos idiomas sem limitações físicas. A divisão do público e a busca pela autenticidade No entanto, a recepção entre os ouvintes continua profundamente dividida. Nas redes sociais e no YouTube, o lançamento do muuo:23 acumulou reações opostas: enquanto parte dos fãs elogia a qualidade da produção e as possibilidades narrativas, outra parcela critica a falta de calor humano e o distanciamento emocional. O grande motor do K-pop sempre foi a conexão parassocial, a identificação com o esforço, a vulnerabilidade e a trajetória dos trainees até o topo das paradas. Quando o talento é sintetizado por algoritmo, a música se torna um produto impecável, mas corre o risco de perder a imperfeição orgânica, a identidade própria que gera empatia real. À medida que plataformas digitais passam a exigir sinalizações para faixas 100% sintetizadas e testam filtros para bloquear conteúdo gerado por IA, o mercado se prepara para uma coexistência inevitável. Artistas de IA vão continuar ocupando espaço e abrindo novas vertentes no entretenimento digital, mas a verdadeira prova de fogo será entender se um algoritmo consegue transmitir algo que a tecnologia ainda não aprendeu a emular por completo: a alma humana. ✅Para saber tudo do mundo dos famosos, siga o canal de entretenimento do R7, o portal de notícias da Record, no WhatsApp

artigo.texto: Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK), NTT FACILITIES, INC., Eurus Energy Holdings Corporation e MUFG Bank, Ltd. (coletivamente, o "Consórcio") desenvolveram um novo conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto como parte de seus esforços para realizar centros de dados flutuantes offshore. O conceito recém-desenvolvido deverá expandir as opções de implantação para centros de dados flutuantes offshore e acelerar sua aplicação prática. O rápido crescimento da demanda por centros de dados em todo o mundo intensificou desafios como a escassez de locais de desenvolvimento adequados e fornecimento de energia, bem como prazos de construção estendidos. Os centros de dados flutuantes offshore são considerados uma solução promissora para essas questões, tornando importante explorar múltiplos modelos de implantação para melhorar sua viabilidade e apoiar a implementação futura. Entre os conceitos em consideração, os centros de dados flutuantes offshore localizados mais longe da costa são considerados um modelo de implantação ideal porque podem utilizar mais facilmente fontes de energia renovável em larga escala, como a energia eólica offshore, ao mesmo tempo em que fornecem escalabilidade e independência operacional. Ao mesmo tempo, várias questões ainda precisam ser abordadas antes que a implantação offshore em larga escala possa ser realizada, incluindo acessibilidade, conectividade de telecomunicações de alta capacidade e configurações de fornecimento de energia independentes das redes de transmissão e distribuição convencionais. À medida que o Consórcio continuou a avaliar modelos de implantação adicionais adequados a diferentes casos de uso e condições de local, ele desenvolveu o novo conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto. O conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto prevê um centro de dados flutuante ancorado ao lado de um cais dentro de uma área portuária. Em comparação com os centros de dados flutuantes offshore projetados para operação em ambientes de mar aberto, o conceito baseado em porto pode ser implantado em uma ampla gama de locais, desde áreas metropolitanas até comunidades regionais. Além disso, pode utilizar a infraestrutura existente, aproveitando os recursos costeiros, incluindo instalações locais de geração de energia. Ambos os modelos de implantação, baseados em porto e offshore, compartilham vantagens exclusivas dos centros de dados flutuantes offshore. Ao combinar os benefícios da infraestrutura marítima com a flexibilidade de implantação, o Consórcio acredita que os centros de dados flutuantes offshore podem ajudar a resolver as crescentes restrições de disponibilidade de terra e fornecimento de energia, bem como a futura expansão da infraestrutura digital. Ao realizar o conceito de centro de dados flutuante offshore baseado em porto, o Consórcio visa acelerar a aplicação prática de centros de dados flutuantes offshore e abrir caminho para sua futura implantação mais longe da costa. Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK) Fundada em 1885, a NYK Line é uma empresa de logística global que se concentra em várias formas de transporte marítimo, como logística global e transporte de energia a granel, entre muitos outros negócios relacionados. Operando uma das maiores redes de transporte do mundo, a empresa possui e opera uma frota diversificada de transportadores de automóveis, transportadores de contêineres e transportadores de energia. Nos últimos anos, entramos ativamente em novas áreas de negócios, incluindo o negócio de descarbonização, alavancando o conhecimento e a tecnologia que cultivamos ao longo de muitas décadas no transporte marítimo. Através do desenvolvimento de tecnologia inovadora e criação de negócios, forneceremos novo valor que transcende os limites do negócio de transporte marítimo e contribui para a realização de uma sociedade sustentável. Neste projeto, a NYK Line supervisionará toda a iniciativa e promoverá o desenvolvimento do negócio de centros de dados offshore. NTT FACILITIES, INC. A NTT FACILITIES, INC. tem mais de 100 anos de experiência no projeto, construção e manutenção de edifícios de telecomunicações. A empresa é especializada na construção de centros de dados em larga escala, principalmente no Japão, América do Norte e região da Ásia-Pacífico, contribuindo para aproximadamente 70%* dos centros de dados construídos e operados no Japão. Neste projeto, a NTT FACILITIES realizará a verificação técnica para o projeto, construção e operação estável de centros de dados flutuantes offshore. Através deste processo de verificação, a empresa acumulará know-how de engenharia aplicável não apenas a ambientes offshore, mas também a futuros desenvolvimentos de centros de dados em uma ampla gama de configurações. Eurus Energy Holdings Corporation A Eurus Energy Holdings Corporation atua no negócio de geração de energia eólica e solar globalmente há mais de 30 anos e é a empresa líder do Japão em termos de capacidade de geração de energia eólica conectada à rede. Ao utilizar efetivamente a eletricidade gerada pela energia eólica offshore, que deve se tornar uma importante fonte de energia no Japão, a Eurus Energy visa promover a neutralidade de carbono dos centros de dados e contribuir para a realização de uma infraestrutura digital sustentável. MUFG Bank, Ltd. O MUFG Bank, Ltd. é uma subsidiária do Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), que define seu propósito como "Comprometido em capacitar um futuro mais brilhante" sob os princípios orientadores do MUFG Way. O MUFG está comprometido em enfrentar os desafios enfrentados por todas as partes interessadas, incluindo clientes, para realizar um ambiente e uma sociedade sustentáveis. Neste projeto, o MUFG Bank alavancará sua experiência financeira e ampla rede para explorar oportunidades de cocriação para negócios de centros de dados de próxima geração e considerar o fornecimento de suporte financeiro para empreendimentos relacionados.

artigo.texto: Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers Solidion's patented anode technology and PEAK UPS design target the space, lifespan and cost demands of AI-scale infrastructure. DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas with pilot production facilities in Dayton, Ohio, Solidion's (NASDAQ: STI) core business includes manufacturing of battery materials and components, as well as development and production of next-generation batteries for energy storage systems, including UPS systems serving the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market and electric vehicles for ground, aerospace, and sea transportation. Solidion holds a portfolio of over 385 patents, covering innovations such as high-capacity, silane gas free and graphene-enabled silicon anodes, biomass-based graphite, advanced lithium-sulfur and lithium-metal technologies. For more information, please visit www.solidiontech.com or contact Investor Relations. artigo.texto: How one city balances its economy and community needs on data centers Colorado Springs, Colorado wants to bring in data centers but do so in a way that’s transparent and protects quality of life. Being proactive is crucial, an economic development leader there said. In a rare move earlier this year, data center operator and developer Raeden published a website looking to dispel various concerns and “misinformation and disinformation” around a project it’s building in Colorado Springs, Colorado. Known as Project Taurus, the website promises the 50-megawatt data center on the site of a former Intel chip factory will use zero gallons of water each day for cooling, operate more quietly than the previous tenant and generate more than $3 million a year in tax revenue. The effort has not been without controversy. The Colorado Springs City Council voted last month to postpone a decision granting the project final approval until April after a contentious public hearing. But local officials said that while the approval process has been tricky, it demonstrates that Colorado Springs is trying to strike the right balance between encouraging data centers to power artificial intelligence while respecting the views of residents who may be opposed to them. Data centers are a controversial subject in communities across the country, but being transparent and getting promises from developers before they build are crucial ways to protect their constituents. “The concerns about water and power and noise are not a reason to say no; they really are conditions to say yes,” Johnna Reeder Kleymeyer, president and CEO of the Colorado Springs Chamber and Economic Development Corporation. “The way we have approached it as a community is to work to get in front of these questions.” Using former industrial sites for new data centers is a key part of Colorado Springs’ strategy, Reeder Kleymeyer said, as those sites are already zoned for industrial uses and would likely not be good candidates for anything else. The Environmental Protection Agency has already assembled information on how to reuse those brownfield sites for data centers, and it’s something Colorado Springs continues to explore. Beyond that, the city is already looking to get ahead of various concerns around power and water use. The city’s utility company, Colorado Springs Utilities, was the first in the state to put a tariff on large loads, meaning that the user pays for all the infrastructure and the power itself, without passing those costs on to residents. The House of Representatives passed a bill last month known as the Ratepayer Protection Act, designed to require states to have a strategy to have large operators pay for their own power, but it appears to be languishing in the U.S. Senate. That puts the onus on states and communities to do the work themselves, like in Colorado Springs. The city also is requiring data centers to use closed-loop water systems, meaning that water is recycled rather than putting a drain on limited water resources. Reeder Kleymeyer said it’s important for the city to be “getting in front of the issues and ensuring we are protecting the residents,” while at the same time showing it is “open for business.” Similar initiatives are set to follow in noise monitoring, which so far does not have a requirement in the city’s unified development code. Reeder Kleymeyer said Project Taurus has already agreed to monitor its noise and put up a surety bond of $1 million if they break those parameters, so they would be required to pay a penalty if they do not comply. While some data center operators have failed to be good neighbors and so stoked community anxiety, Reeder Kleymeyer said it’s incumbent on lawmakers and other senior leaders to hold their feet to the fire. And financial incentives, which have been preferred by many over the years, are not the way. “I think some data centers have earned that reason that communities are skeptical,” she said. “Not everyone has been a good player in the industry, and I think that's why it's important that people that live in the community, such as myself with an economic development organization or elected officials, we ask the questions, we get things in writing, and we make data-driven decisions, not based on emotion.” It would be “naïve” to not have data centers given the growth in AI and technology, Reeder Kleymeyer said. And it’s especially important for Colorado Springs, given its national security and military importance, to have its data housed on these shores and not elsewhere. She said that states and localities that take the time now to have forward-looking and proactive policies in place will benefit the most from data centers. “‘Never’ is not a strategy,” Reeder Kleymeyer said. “The communities that set strong terms, they're going to win for the next generation of employers. That's what we've got to be thinking about for the next 12 months to 10 years.”

artigo.texto: A Nov. 18 community forum has been set for Russell County residents who want to know more about the three or four data centers planned for the former Moss No. 3 coal mine site near Cleveland. Oasis Digital Properties, the Northern Virginia-based data center developer behind the project, will hold the forum in the conference room at the county government center at 139 Highland Drive in Lebanon, Laura Gilmer, director of the county’s industrial development authority, said in a phone interview. Ross Litkenhous, co-founder of Oasis, said the company is still working on the agenda, but the plan is to have a presentation on anything Oasis has done to date and answer questions from the community. He said he will also commit to appear before the community again before any construction begins. “We’re still very early in the process. We’re not ready to put shovels in the ground,” he said in a phone interview. “This is not a presentation where we say we’re ready to break ground tomorrow… we want to listen to them before we get to the point.” Three or four data centers could be coming to the site, a historic coal mine that was recently the site for a proposed landfill. That project was eventually rejected by county leaders, and now the data center campus is on the table as part of a deal between Oasis and the IDA. The agreement says the authority retains control of the property while Oasis takes the next steps to develop it, Litkenhous told Cardinal News. That development is contingent on finding companies to occupy the buildings. Russell County IDA members and other county officials have not answered questions about the project, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Oasis. The IDA denied a Freedom of Information Act request for documents and communications related to the project sent by Cardinal News, citing the agreement and exemptions under Virginia Code. Litkenhous said the IDA asked his team members if they would be willing to come down to share more about the project. Gilmer declined to comment further on the project but reiterated what she said at last week’s IDA meeting. “We were questioned about the details, and it really is, we can’t confirm details because they’re not there yet,” she said. “It’s not a project that’s finalized.” Litkenhous said there are no major updates on the project, and the developer is still working to match with companies that would occupy the buildings. “I hope by the time we get to the November meeting, we will have more substantive updates,” he said. “We understand this is a big deal for the community.” Since learning about the plans for the data center, some county residents have spoken out against the project. A protest is planned for Saturday, following the first held on Oct. 3. On that day, 10 people stood at the corner of Church Avenue and Main Street in Lebanon, holding signs and asking those driving by to sign a petition opposing the project. “No data centers in Russell County … NDAs do not belong in our local government. We have a right to know what’s going on at Moss 3,” Donna Ball, a resident of Cleveland, said through her megaphone. She asked questions at the last county board of supervisors meeting and did not get a response, she said. She was also part of a group of 12 who attended the IDA’s meeting last week and spoke against the project. The group cited concern over the potential impact on the Clinch River, whether there would be noise that would disturb the peace near Cleveland, the use of nondisclosure agreements and low tax rates set by the county. Russell County passed a machinery and tool tax in December 2025 at 24 cents per $100 of assessed value, an incentive to encourage development. “If you’re going to do it, do it to the best of [your] ability,” Amy Branson, a pharmacist from Castlewood, told the IDA. She encouraged its members to pursue an aggressive agreement, including a “fair tax rate,” and prepare for the power demand to ensure the cost doesn’t fall on residents. Litkenhous said Appalachian Power has untapped electricity capacity and confirmed it could provide 300 megawatts to the site. Residents brought up the bad taste they still have from past large land projects, including the failed landfill proposal and the fish farm project on the Russell-Tazewell County border that has been paused due to tariffs and gas prices. But some also noted appreciation for getting to have a back-and-forth with the IDA and said they understand the county budget is strained and solutions are needed. Still, as they heard plans for the community forum, Betsy Dickenson, a resident from Cleveland, said, “This sounds like what we went through with the trash dump.”

artigo.texto: Solidion Technology Reaffirms Commitment to Address Growing Energy Storage Needs of AI Data Centers Solidion's patented anode technology and PEAK UPS design target the space, lifespan and cost demands of AI-scale infrastructure. DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas with pilot production facilities in Dayton, Ohio, Solidion's (STI) core business includes manufacturing of battery materials and components, as well as development and production of next-generation batteries for energy storage systems, including UPS systems serving the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market and electric vehicles for ground, aerospace, and sea transportation. Solidion holds a portfolio of over 385 patents, covering innovations such as high-capacity, silane gas free and graphene-enabled silicon anodes, biomass-based graphite, advanced lithium-sulfur and lithium-metal technologies. For more information, please visit www.solidiontech.com or contact Investor Relations. artigo.texto: FRANKLIN COUNTY, Mo.—The Franklin County Rural Coalition (FCRC) and the Pacific Root Coalition (PRC) are each suing the Franklin County Commission and the developers behind two proposed data centers. Spectrum News reached out to the commission for comment and has not received a reply. “These legal actions challenge decisions involving the Crooked Creek and Diamond Farm developments, as well as the county’s newly adopted data center regulations,” said Sam Dean, co-founder of PRC. “For months, residents across Franklin County have attended public hearings, asked questions, submitted records requests, studied proposals, and worked to understand the decisions being made about the future of their communities.” FCRC and PRC’s lawyers seek a judicial review on the legal process that led to four law changes made last month by the commission. The lawyers want those laws to be set aside. “Together, these orders created new data center regulations and rezoned more than 100 acres of rural land to make room for hyperscale data centers,” said Bruce Morrison, Great Rivers Environmental Law Center, representing FCRC. “Our lawsuit raises serious questions about whether the county followed legal requirements governing these commission orders.” “These issues go beyond whether an individual supports or opposes data centers,” said Zach McMichael, who represents Pacific Root Coalition. “They concern the legal responsibilities of county government and the rights of the affected property owners. Our clients believe those responsibilities were not adequately protected.” Morrison added that Missouri law sets forth procedures for the county to follow during zoning decisions. “These requirements exist for a reason,” said Morrison. “They are there to protect the public’s right to participate, to ensure that residents receive appropriate notice, and to require zoning decisions be made through a lawful process.” Issues raised in the lawsuit include whether residents were given a meaningful opportunity to be heard, how they were notified, whether the proposed regulations required additional hearings and whether the rezoning decisions were legally justified and supported by the record. “Filing this lawsuit does not mean that the county acted unlawfully,” said Morrison. “That determination belongs to the court, but the community members bringing this action are entitled to seek that review and we believe the legal questions raised are substantial.”

artigo.texto: O que a rede elétrica brasileira precisa para atender grandes data centers? Especialistas apontam como modernizar a gestão do sistema de energia para o aumento exponencial da demanda. Os grandes data centers que devem operar no Brasil, voltados ao processamento de dados de plataformas de redes sociais e inteligência artificial (IA), exigem preparação da rede elétrica. Especialistas defendem a modernização da gestão do sistema para dar conta do consumo desses empreendimentos. A demanda de eletricidade dos data centers deve crescer cerca de 12% ao ano a partir de 2027, segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Com isso, o segmento será o quinto maior consumidor de energia elétrica do País até 2030. Considerando os pedidos de ligação à rede elétrica, os projetos de data centers podem consumir até 10.721 megawatts (MW) em 2029. A demanda também deve dobrar até 2038. Veja também O QUE ESTÁ SENDO FEITO EM OUTROS PAÍSES? O desafio da conexão dos equipamentos é global. No estado de Nova York, por exemplo, o governo suspendeu a construção de novos data centers por preocupações com o impacto no consumo de energia e água. A suspensão vale até julho de 2027 para empreendimentos com potência superior a 50 megawatts. Um dos modelos adotados por empresas nos EUA é a instalação de usinas dedicadas aos data centers, isoladas da rede, explica o líder de mercado e clientes da Siemens Energy, Pedro Matos. A solução, entretanto, é transitória e pode ser menos sustentável. "Como vemos em outros países, a exemplo da Irlanda, onde o pedido de ligação à rede leva cinco anos, as empresas recorrem a uma geração temporária a gás. Quando recebem a ligação, passam a injetar energia renovável na rede", aponta. O executivo participou da Atlantic Convergence, conferência organizada pela DE-CIX que debate o futuro das infraestruturas digitais, em Lisboa. De acordo com ele, o aumento da demanda energética por data centers deve atenuar o desequilíbrio entre a geração e o consumo de energia no Brasil. "Esse equilíbrio é difícil de obter, mas, com mais potencial de consumo, com data centers e outras indústrias, será mais fácil gerir todo o sistema. Há uma oportunidade de ter um sistema ainda mais renovável", comenta. Segundo Matos, o custo da energia no País tende a cair no longo prazo, desde que o Brasil aprimore a gestão dos recursos. "No futuro, a energia será muito barata. O que pagaremos é a flexibilidade, ou seja, a capacidade de nos adaptarmos à quantidade de energia disponível naquele momento", diz. ACESSO PRIORITÁRIO À REDE ELÉTRICA NO BRASIL O acesso de data centers à rede de energia é viabilizado pela Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (PNAST). Na prática, o Ministério de Minas e Energia dará prioridade a empreendimentos considerados estratégicos. Segundo a pasta, o objetivo é fortalecer o planejamento do setor elétrico, ampliar a segurança do sistema e criar condições para que o País não perca investimentos no setor. No cálculo da capacidade disponível, o Operador Nacional do Sistema (ONS) determina o máximo valor de potência ativa que o sistema é capaz de transportar, sem apresentar violações de tensão ou fluxo de potência na região em análise, em condições normais de operação e em situações de contingência. A primeira temporada de acesso, encerrada no início de outubro, teve 367 cadastramentos de empreendimentos de geração e consumo, totalizando mais de 20 GW em solicitações. Considerando também o período transitório, o ONS analisou mais de 43 GW em pedidos de acesso à rede básica. Foram viabilizados ou habilitados 30,7 GW. INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL NA GESTÃO DE GRANDES CARGAS Ao modernizar a gestão do sistema elétrico, o ONS pode adotar ferramentas de inteligência artificial para melhorar a previsão de consumo e oferta de energia no País. "A IA ajuda a perceber quanto vai ser a demanda, a procura. Assim, começa-se a equilibrar e a entender quando é possível produzir mais para consumir mais", explica o diretor da Greenvolt, Filipe de Oliveira Lopes. Os modelos matemáticos também podem auxiliar na definição de locais para projetos de usinas renováveis e de equipamentos eletrointensivos. "Cada vez mais teremos de nos preocupar com essa questão. No Brasil, sentem-se muito as alterações climáticas. É melhor construir uma central hidrelétrica perto de zonas de cheias, é preciso entender onde vai ter o melhor impacto", comenta. EFEITO NAS COMUNIDADES Para o especialista, ao fazer a conexão de data centers, é importante que os operadores também pensem na qualidade de conexão das comunidades no entorno. Ou seja, em um ambiente adequado de instalação, as cidades próximas aos data centers não podem ter o acesso à energia prejudicado, mas sim aprimorado. "A parte social é importante. É preciso entender o data center não só em termos econômicos. Os empreendimentos podem trazer know-how para o País, gerar emprego e ajudar a gerir a energia da rede", afirma. *A colunista viajou a convite da DE-CIX para a Atlantic Convergence em Lisboa.

artigo.texto: ST. GEORGE, Utah — For decades, small data centers have quietly served as the physical backbone of the internet. But new, large-scale data centers meant to support artificial intelligence are sizing up significantly — and there’s been a corresponding increase in public scrutiny and concern about an industry long used to operating behind the scenes. WATCH | Massive Utah data centers draw scrutiny, but smaller ones have existed for years "There are quite a few already operating in Utah,” noted Shon Hiatt, a University of Southern California professor who has studied the state's data center landscape. But, he added, “the trend moving forward is bigger, larger data centers.” Utah currently has at least 48 operational data centers, according to Hiatt’s recent report for the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute. But another seven under construction will use more energy than all those that currently exist in the state combined, the report notes. Pete Ashdown, president and founder of XMission, has operated a small data center in the heart of downtown Salt Lake City for more than 25 years. He stresses that there are “two different stories” when it comes to these facilities. “It’s the traditional data centers that handles your email, handles your webpages, that have been around for decades,” Ashdown said. “And then there’s this new style of data center.” The new hyperscale data centers have sprung up largely to support the recent boom in artificial intelligence and the corresponding surge in demand for computing and processing power. “Around the time Chat GPT came out — 2022, 2023 — that was a game changer because then it started an AI race, basically,” said Bob West, the vice president of marketing for ValorC3, which operates a small data center in St. George. “And with that, it caught the data center industry kind of off guard,” he added. “There wasn't enough capacity, and people started building data centers like crazy.” That construction craze has sparked intense bipartisan blowback across the United States in recent months, with polls showing a majority of Utahns are now opposed to new data centers. Nearly 76% of respondents in a Utah State University survey released last week said they oppose or strongly oppose building new data centers in the state. And 90% said they see the amount of water a project consumes as “very important” in determining whether they would support or oppose a particular project. Hiatt said he believes the opposition also reflects broader fears about the future of artificial intelligence. "What does it mean for society? What does it mean for my job?” he said, referencing the questions many people are asking as the technology rapidly advances. “And because of that, there's this anti, negative sentiment towards AI. And now it's being shifted to the data centers.” 'A lot of misconceptions’ While the phrase “data center” raises the specter of massive, power and energy-hungry campuses with thousands of servers, those in the industry stress that these facilities are not monolithic. “I think there's just a lot of misconceptions about data centers and what we do here,” said West, with ValorC3. “Everybody thinks that, No. 1, there are these huge campuses and data centers are bad. They draw all this power; they take up all this water. And that's just not true.” ValorC3 is a colocation data center, where other businesses rent space for their own servers and hardware. Chris Damrow, the director of facilities management there, describes it as “a hotel for companies’ or individuals’ very expensive computers.” “Really what we do is provide power and cooling for other people’s computers,” he added, noting that the data center’s clients range from health care companies to financial institutions. Colocation centers are different from what have been deemed “hyperscale” data centers. Those are predominantly owned and operated by major technology companies, like Facebook or Amazon, “and they need a very, very big footprint and a lot of power,” Damrow said. WATCH | West, with ValorC3, explains the different types of data centers: ValorC3’s St. George data center has a capacity of about 4 megawatts. That’s several thousand times smaller than the Stratos data center planned for Box Elder County that has dominated headlines in recent months. In thirsty southern Utah, Damrow said ValorC3’s data center is cooled with a direct expansion system, which uses refrigerant rather than water. The trade-off of that system, though, is that it can be more energy-intensive — a resource Damrow said ValorC3 also tries to use judiciously. “If we’re not,” he noted, “we’re losing money.” About 300 miles north, XMission operates a colocation data center with an even smaller footprint than ValorC3's. The Salt Lake City facility has a capacity of just under 1 megawatt and uses a closed-loop cooling system that Ashdown compares to a car radiator. “You’re not continually putting water into your car to cool your car,” he noted. “But the air that flows through the front of your car cools off the entire system of your car. It’s just a matter of moving heat around inside the engine and out to where it can be ejected.” Asked to compare what he calls a “traditional data center” like XMission to the hyperscale ones coming online now, Ashdown argues that the latter have far more “intense” environmental impacts due to their scale. "It’s doing one thing with one type of equipment that’s packed as dense as possible with as much power as possible and a whole lot of water,” he said. “And that’s not what happens here.” FOX 13 News called or emailed all 48 operational data centers in the state requesting a tour, but only XMission and ValorC3 agreed to provide one. ‘I don’t trust them’ As the data center industry continues to scale up, Hiatt said Utah is in the middle of the pack nationally, both by the number of operational data centers and those under construction. “Utah is getting close, but it’s not experiencing what I would say [is

artigo.texto: Five years ago, during the pandemic, battery prices hovered around USD 400/kWh and containers offered capacities close to 2 MWh . Currently, Sungrow has equipment up to 7.2 MWh in similar dimensions , an evolution that accompanied the decrease in storage costs and the incorporation of new revenue streams for projects. The comparison arose during an interview with Luis Fernando Biagini, Head of Sales Southern Cone of Sungrow , with Strategic Energy , in the streaming " See you at FES" , in the lead-up to Future Energy Summit Chile, scheduled for October 28 and 29 in Santiago . The executive explained that, following the COVID-19 crisis, trade reference prices gradually fell to USD 300, USD 200, and USD 100/kWh. During that period, lithium price fluctuations forced manufacturers and buyers to incorporate contractual mechanisms to distribute the risks associated with commodity prices. “Today I believe the market is much more mature. Companies already know what the risk is, they know how to manage that risk, and they know how to make a forecast for the coming years,” he said, while also avoiding committing to a specific price prediction for 2027. In parallel, Sungrow achieved 7.2 GWh of operational capacity under long-term service agreements (LTSAs) , which can be extended for up to twenty years. This volume, corresponding to facilities covered by service contracts, constituted a different indicator of the company's accumulated commercial backlog. The geographical distribution of the contracts showed different stages of development. After Chile , Colombia positioned itself among Sungrow's main markets, followed by Central America and the Dominican Republic . And Mexico? Biagini noted that the country has begun to open up commercial opportunities linked to new energy tenders, although it has not yet been part of the contracted volume presented by the company. Chile as a reference point and the next steps for Argentina and Peru The Chilean market featured prominently in the discussion due to the development of renewable energy facilities that have begun incorporating batteries to modify their energy delivery schedules. In particular, solar parks without PPAs have found in storage an alternative to the reduced prices during peak photovoltaic generation hours. In these projects, investments in retrofit or repowering made it possible to take advantage of existing infrastructure and evaluate new revenues through arbitrage, although their viability depended on additional CAPEX and the hourly price differential. “I always say that Chile is the laboratory of Latin America,” the executive stated, referring to the experience that other countries began to observe in order to adapt their own storage solutions. Here, the comparison led the conversation to Argentina , where the government awarded two storage tenders aimed at strengthening the reliability of the electricity system. The first, AlmaGBA , allocated 667 MW in 2025 to install batteries at critical nodes in the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area. The second, Alma-SADI , expanded the deployment to the interior of the country and awarded 700.5 MW in July 2026 , distributed across 20 projects in seven regions. This latest call for bids received more than 8,300 MW in offers , compared to the 700 MW initially tendered, while the awarded projects included an estimated investment of USD 700 million. In that scenario, the Head of Sales Southern Cone Sungrow identified opportunities for independent power producers, although he noted that Argentine facilities were still smaller than those typically found in Chile. “It is a market where there is no turning back,” he said, assessing the opportunities for independent power producers and the potential of capacity contracts. In Peru , Sungrow already has 1.2 GW of installed and operational photovoltaic capacity , while new hybrid configurations are beginning to emerge. Biagini revealed that the company was quoting solar projects that incorporate storage systems equivalent to between 30% and 40% of the photovoltaic power . The percentage, he clarified, came from specific commercial transactions and not from general estimates of the sector. Continue reading Regional differences were also reflected in the scale of the installations. While 600 MWh projects were already part of Sungrow's regular activity in more developed markets , it stated that reaching those dimensions would represent a significant step forward for Argentina and Peru. Negotiations lasting up to four years and contracts closed in one month The expansion of energy storage also introduced new variables into financial models. Arbitrage, based on shifting energy from periods of low prices to periods of higher value, was for years the main economic benchmark for evaluating investments. The interviewee recalled that spreads close to USD 80 were previously considered an attractive benchmark for these operations. During the conversation, he estimated that those spreads were now around USD 65-70 , although he did not specify a market or time frame for comparison. This business began to expand to include ancillary services, power remuneration, peak shaving, and grid forming and black start capabilities . The ability to combine these revenue streams became relevant for projects seeking to recoup their investment over operational horizons of approximately twenty years. “I think they are not yet 100% guaranteed, but they are adding up point by point,” he said regarding the additional compensation that developers have begun to incorporate into their evaluations. Peak shaving , for example, allowed industrial consumers to reduce their peak electricity demand and the associated power charges. In Chile, Biagini identified mining companies as potential users of these solutions, due to their high energy requirements and tariff structures. artigo.texto: Clearway Energy Group has announced the addition of 210 MW of battery energy storage capacity to its Honeycomb Energy Center portfolio in southern Utah, supported by long-term agreements with PacifiCorp. The expansion, involving an investment of approximately $400 million, aims to strengthen grid reliability, improve energy flexibility and support growing electricity demand across the region. The additional capacity will support the second phase of the Honeycomb Energy Center development, comprising three new battery energy storage facilities. With this expansion, Clearway’s energy storage portfolio in Utah will increase to seven systems, providing a combined storage capacity of 2,120 MWh. The company commissioned the first four Honeycomb energy storage facilities earlier this year. Each of the new battery storage installations will be located adjacent to an existing Clearway solar power facility operating under a power supply agreement with PacifiCorp. The integration of battery storage with solar generation is expected to improve renewable energy utilisation, support grid stability and provide greater flexibility in managing electricity supply and demand. To finance the approximately $400 million development, Clearway has secured support from a consortium of financial institutions, including KeyBank, U.S. Bank, NordLB and CoBank. Clearway Energy, Inc. has also entered into an agreement to invest in the project following the commencement of commercial operations. Valerie Wooley, Senior Vice President of Origination at Clearway, highlighted the importance of expanding energy storage infrastructure to support Utah’s growing economy. She stated that the additional facilities would contribute to grid resilience and help manage electricity costs as regional power demand continues to increase. The expansion is also expected to generate economic benefits for local communities in Beaver and Iron counties. Clearway has partnered with Rosendin for construction activities, which are expected to create at least 150 jobs. According to the company, the three new Honeycomb Energy Center projects are projected to generate approximately $37 million in additional tax revenue over their operational lifetimes. This will increase the total expected tax contributions from the Honeycomb portfolio to more than $95 million, supporting public services and infrastructure development in the surrounding communities. Clearway will also contribute an additional $60,000 annually to local schools and community organisations, bringing the total annual community contributions from the seven Honeycomb facilities to approximately $100,000. Matt Sterzer, Beaver County Economic Development Manager, acknowledged Clearway Energy’s growing contribution to the region’s energy sector, highlighting the company’s role in attracting investment, creating employment opportunities and generating additional revenue for local communities. The latest development builds on Clearway’s longstanding partnership with PacifiCorp, which has supported the development of approximately 1.4 GW of power projects since 2008. This includes more than 1 GW of capacity in Utah, representing approximately $1.5 billion in investments and establishing the state as one of Clearway’s largest operational markets. The Honeycomb Energy Center expansion reflects the increasing importance of utility-scale battery energy storage systems in supporting renewable energy integration and grid modernisation. By combining solar generation with large-scale battery storage, Clearway aims to enhance power system flexibility, improve electricity supply reliability and support Utah’s evolving energy requirements. The additional 210 MW of battery storage capacity is expected to further strengthen Clearway’s renewable energy infrastructure in the state while contributing to regional economic development and the transition towards a more resilient electricity grid. artigo.texto: Real Assets We build future energy systems and resilient infrastructure, backing emerging opportunities in technology, land and water. Foresight has today announced that Foresight Energy Infrastructure Partners II SCSp (“FEIP II”) has completed its acquisition of a 100% interest in Nivala, a battery energy storage system (“BESS”) from Fotowatio Renewable Ventures. Nivala is Finland’s largest BESS project. Nivala is a fully permitted, ready-to-build battery energy storage system project, with a 100MW/400MWh capacity located in the city of Nivala, in the North Ostrobothnia region of Finland. This investment, which is Foresight’s second in Finland, following the acquisition of Puskakorpi, an 88MW in 2021 via FEIP I, strengthens FEIP II's exposure to energy storage and grid flexibility infrastructure. With a four-hour duration, the battery is designed to participate in Finland's wholesale, intraday and ancillary services markets, a significant revenue driver for Finnish BESS, and help support the integration of renewable generation and the decarbonisation of the Finnish power system. With the acquisition, Foresight will continue to develop the project which is expected to commence commercial operations in the second half of 2028. Finland has emerged as one of the most attractive BESS markets in the Nordics, due to rapid renewable energy growth, particularly in onshore wind. Finland also carries a positive demand side story, acting as a key hub for Europe’s data centre buildout following a recent announcement from Google to invest €13bn in data centres across Finland. Together, these tailwinds increase the need for grid flexibility and BESS. Richard Thompson, Partner and Co-Manager of FEIP & FEIP II at Foresight Group, said: “The energy transition is no longer only about decarbonisation, it is increasingly about maintaining system security, reliability and resilience as electricity demand grows and economies become more electrified. As Finland sees accelerated investment in data centres and new industrial demand, we expect grid-scale battery storage to play an increasingly important role in providing flexibility, supporting grid stability and helping integrate more renewable power onto the system. Project Nivala provides immediate access to this critical infrastructure opportunity.” Javier Huergo, Chief Investment Officer of FRV, noted: “This transaction reflects FRV’s ability to create value throughout the entire development cycle of its projects and successfully execute its asset rotation strategy. The sale of Nivala allows us to crystallise the value generated during the development phases and reinvest those resources in new opportunities that will continue to drive the energy transition and strengthen our international BESS project portfolio”. artigo.texto: There can be a fine line between politicians doing what they think is best for their constituents and doing what their constituents ask of them. While elected officials don't have to listen to the cries of every voter, when the noise gets loud enough, listening can be the difference between winning and losing an election. "The bottom line is, when you look at trucks [going] in and out and all the other factors, you could argue a data center makes more financial sense than any of the other businesses," Frederick County Board of Supervisors Red Bud representative Mike Guevremont told a small group of constituents on March 26 during a town hall meeting at Greenwood Mill Elementary School. He held up a poster board with illustrations showing that data centers bring in more revenue and use less water than other industries, arguing that public opposition to data centers expressed at county board meetings was not representative of the county as a whole. "I believe if you took, if we had a great poll of the entire county... they're OK with it," Guevremont said at the time about data centers. Shortly afterward, two applications for data center campuses were filed with the county. Roughly six months later on Sept. 23, Guevremont and the majority Republican Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to remove data centers as an allowed/conditional use from the county ordinance, making it the first locality in Virginia to restrict data center development in this way. Virginia has roughly 600 data centers, more than any state in the U.S. But the two data center applications — for Virginia Technology Park in Clear Brook and Winchester Gateway in Kernstown — are still under consideration because they were filed before the ordinance change was enacted. They will come before the board for a vote on Oct. 28. ——— Across the country, public sentiment indicates that data centers are generally unpopular. A survey conducted in May by The Winchester Star showed that nearly 90% of survey respondents did not support data centers being built in Frederick County/Winchester. A Gallup poll published in May found that seven in 10 Americans surveyed oppose data center construction for artificial intelligence (AI) in their community. Republican President Donald Trump feels otherwise. On Sept. 7, he posted comments on his Truth Social account criticizing communities that are seeking to curb or prevent data center development. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want data centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," his post stated. If communities want lower taxes and more jobs, they should "Let data reign," he added. Trump also has claimed that homes are more valuable in data center communities, that only people who want to live in "crime-infested squalor" should oppose them, and that China benefits if fewer data centers are built in the U.S. So why did Frederick County, a Republican stronghold in which Trump received over 62% of the vote in the last three presidential elections, end up taking action against data centers? In the weeks following Trump's remarks, politically conservative county voters and politicians shared their thoughts. ——— Last October, Amy Luczak and her husband moved from Midlothian to Frederick County, settling in a house on Ruebuck Lane in Clear Brook. Months later, the 220-acre Virginia Technology Park data center campus was proposed. It would be built on land adjoining their property line. If this project is approved by the county, Luczak is concerned about the impact the campus would have on private water wells and the low-frequency noise it would emit, as well as the aesthetics of living so close to such a facility. A longtime conservative, Luczak doesn't agree with Trump's stance about communities that are against data centers. "I did see those comments. I was disappointed to be honest," Luczak said. "OK, I'm glad you're in favor of it, like AI is a new thing. But come to my house and tell me you want it right there." Dan Best, a member of the Frederick County Republican Committee (FCRC), published a report in December, along with three other county residents, to provide information to the community on data centers while remaining neutral. Recently, Best became opposed to data center development in Frederick County. Asked about Trump's Truth Social post, Best said the president's stance is not something he agrees with, but it could be an effort to fake out his political opponents. "He says a lot of things basically to generate reactions and sometimes... he does a very good job at trolling his opposition," Best said. Dana Brunn, who worked with Best on the data center report, is co-founder of Mountain Patriots Educational Ministries, a faith-based constitutional conservative organization in Frederick County. He is an ardent Trump supporter, but he doesn't support data centers in Frederick County. "I don't see where the data centers make us money," Brunn said. He believes that Trump's pro-data center comments were intended to unite people on all sides of the political spectrum against the president on a particular issue in an effort to ease political polarization. "I think it was put together to make people aware of coming together," Brunn said. "This is a game, this is how I see it. It's a chess match." Blaine Dunn, a Republican and former member of the Frederick County Board of Supervisors, is a proponent of data centers for the tax revenue they generate. While he didn't agree with the tone of Trump's post, Dunn believes that data centers can help the U.S. compete in the AI race with China and that their benefits could outweigh the negatives. "It serves a purpose. And if every county, community, state cooperated a little bit, you spread the wealth and the downside across everybody," Dunn reasoned. artigo.texto: The Tapes That Bind Battery Energy Storage Systems Avery Dennison has introduced a new portfolio of pressure-sensitive adhesive tapes (PSAs)for battery energy storage systems (BESS). This broad family of adhesives, functional bonding, and protection tapes are designed to tackle the three core material challenges with these large-scale batteries: thermal-runaway protection, high-voltage insulation, and fast assembly. They are targeted at the large modules, battery packs, and containerized units of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) cells commonly used in industrial- and grid-scale BESS applications (Fig. 1). Thermal runaway remains one of the most significant hazards in big batteries. Triggered when one of the cells heats up uncontrollably, the event can spread throughout the pack, increasing the risk of fire and widespread failure. To help prevent propagation between cells, Avery Dennison has developed flame-retardant adhesives that allow designers to create rugged, multilayer thermal barrier solutions. The Flame Tough family can be easily assembled into packs along with the cells, the company said. Dielectric tape solutions can help protect battery packs against one of the other safety risks with battery storage: arcing between cells, busbars, cooling plates, and module housings. Avery's Volt Tough family of materials and adhesives have been tested for breakdown voltage and dielectric strength requirements using GB/T 1408.1-2016 and ASTM D3755 test methods, and they offer high dielectric strength at very thin calipers. To help BESS manufacturers meet aggressive timelines, automation requirements and cost pressures, the new PSA tapes deliver instant bonding for automated assembly lines. Die-cut precision eliminates waste and enables camera/vision system detection with colored variants. Other benefits include automated assembly compatibility, dimensional precision for tight tolerances, and no volatile emissions (VOCs) or mixing equipment. About the Author Lee Goldberg Contributing Editor Lee is the author of the popular PowerBites series. Lee Goldberg is a self-identified “Recovering Engineer,” Maker/Hacker, Green-Tech Maven, Aviator, Gadfly, and Geek Dad. He spent the first 18 years of his career helping design microprocessors, embedded systems, renewable energy applications, and the occasional interplanetary spacecraft. After trading his ‘scope and soldering iron for a keyboard and a second career as a tech journalist, he’s spent the next two decades at several print and online engineering publications. Lee’s current focus is power electronics, especially the technologies involved with energy efficiency, energy management, and renewable energy. This dovetails with his coverage of sustainable technologies and various environmental and social issues within the engineering community that he began in 1996. Lee also covers 3D printers, open-source hardware, and other Maker/Hacker technologies. Lee holds a BSEE in Electrical Engineering from Thomas Edison College, and participated in a colloquium on technology, society, and the environment at Goddard College’s Institute for Social Ecology. His book, “Green Electronics/Green Bottom Line - A Commonsense Guide To Environmentally Responsible Engineering and Management,” was published by Newnes Press. Lee, his wife Catherine, and his daughter Anwyn currently reside in the outskirts of Princeton N.J., where they masquerade as a typical suburban family.

artigo.texto: By BNC staff President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has placed the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) at the center of the Philippines’ carbon-market policy, directing the creation of a national framework to govern carbon credits, international transfers and benefit-sharing. Executive Order No. 127 designates the DENR as the country’s national authority for carbon markets and establishes an Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets to approve the policy framework. The framework will cover both international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets. It will set eligibility requirements for projects, authorization procedures, recognized crediting standards, reporting rules and administrative fees. It will also establish benefit-sharing mechanisms and provide for a Philippine National Carbon Registry to track internationally transferred emissions-reduction outcomes. The policy aims to help the Philippines access climate finance, technology and private investment while establishing national rules for carbon-credit projects. Carbon credits generally represent verified reductions in greenhouse gas emissions or the removal of greenhouse gases from the atmosphere. Under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, countries may transfer certain emissions-reduction outcomes to help meet their climate targets, subject to rules on authorization and accounting. The new order builds on earlier efforts to establish carbon-market rules in specific sectors. These include the DENR’s adoption of a roadmap for developing the country’s voluntary forest carbon market through 2030, as well as guidelines issued by the Department of Energy for carbon credits in the energy sector. A key challenge will be ensuring that carbon credits represent credible emissions reductions, transactions are properly tracked, and benefits reach the communities and stakeholders involved in the projects.
