artigo.texto: As battery fires have occurred consecutively in electric vehicles and data centers, industry demand for "non-flammable batteries" is growing. Consequently, all-solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid electrolyte of lithium-ion batteries with a solid one, are drawing attention. The currently used liquid electrolytes are highly flammable and are cited as the primary cause of fires. While solid electrolytes can significantly reduce this risk, the problem is not solved by the electrolyte alone. This is because cathode materials, which determine battery performance, do not match well with solid electrolytes. If existing cathode materials are used as-is in all-solid-state batteries, their lifespan rapidly decreases with repeated charging and discharging cycles. To solve this problem, Kim Woon-hyuk's research team at Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST) EnerJi Gong-hak-gwa (Prof.) developed a cathode material design technology tailored for all-solid-state batteries. Professor Kim explained, "The method involves creating the outermost surface of cathode particles with nano-sized crystals to block microcracks, which are the cause of lifespan degradation," adding, "A key feature is that it can be applied without significantly modifying existing cathode production equipment." Professor Kim's research team will directly introduce this technology at the "2026 K-Premier Deep Tech Festa" (Registration: https://vvd.bz/buvX) to be held on the 29th at COEX in Seoul. Professor Kim's Ji Do (Prof.) is Professor Sun Yang-gook of Hanyang University. In 2022, Professor Sun transferred approximately 40 cathode material patents to LG Chem, which is considered the largest technology transfer by a domestic university in history. The transfer amount is known to be 25 billion won. Professor Kim is expanding this research into cathode materials for all-solid-state batteries. Cathode materials expand and contract in volume with each charge and discharge cycle. When this process repeats, microcracks form in the particles. Professor Kim stated, "Due to microcracks, lifespan decreases; a battery that initially lasted 10 hours can only last 8 hours after two years." In lithium-ion batteries, even if cracks form, the liquid electrolyte seeps into the gaps, allowing lithium to continue moving. However, solid electrolytes and solid cathode materials do not move relative to each other and cannot fill the gaps. Professor Kim said, "Since both the electrolyte and the cathode material are solid, once a part breaks, that portion becomes unusable capacity," adding, "Using general cathode materials leads to much more severe lifespan degradation in all-solid-state batteries." The research team began its study based on the hypothesis that composing the surface of cathode particles with small nano-sized crystals would disperse the stress caused by volume changes. Experimental results confirmed actual performance improvements. Professor Kim stated, "If you change the electrolyte, you must create a new cathode material to match it," adding, "We obtained results showing that a structure where the outer surface of spherical cathode particles is composed of nano-crystals is suitable for all-solid-state batteries." All-solid-state batteries are more expensive than lithium-ion batteries due to the high cost of solid electrolytes. The research team plans to prioritize markets where safety is more important than price. Their first target is the BBU (Battery Backup Unit) in AI (Artificial Intelligence) data centers. A BBU is a small battery that supplies power when a server experiences a power outage. Professor Kim said, "If a fire breaks out in a BBU, all expensive GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) burn," adding, "We must target markets where there are customers who can afford the high price." He further noted, "Humanoid robots are also used in households, so they are an area where fires absolutely cannot occur," and cited drones and the defense sector as other target markets. Commercialization preparations have progressed to the prototype stage. The research team is conducting process verification with a goal of reaching Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6-7. Professor Kim stated, "No matter how good a technology is, if it is difficult to implement, companies hesitate to adopt it," adding, "We are focusing on creating entirely different cathode materials by adding just a little of our technology to existing equipment." He continued, "Battery material companies such as L&F, EcoPro BM, POSCO Future M, and LG Chem can license this technology and supply it to cell manufacturers," noting, "If applied to electric vehicles, Hyundai Motor, OEM companies that manufacture drones, or companies that make BBUs could find this technology extremely useful." Professor Kim expects this technology will also contribute to the competitiveness of the domestic battery material supply chain. Most of the precursors, which are raw materials for domestic cathode materials, are dependent on China. He emphasized, "Secondary batteries are directly linked to energy security," adding, "Korea must secure a super-gap in next-generation cathode materials to avoid ceding the market to China and to preemptively capture the North American and European markets." - Date: October 29, 2026 (Thu) at 1:00 PM - Location: Hall B PLUS STAGE, COEX, Seoul Samsung-dong - Participants: Companies considering technology transfer, joint research, or new businesses; family companies of government-funded research institutes; investment firms - Fee: Free (Pre-registration required) - Hosts: Ministry of Science and ICT, KAIST, GIST, DGIST, UNIST, MoneyToday Unicorn Factory - Sponsors: Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI), Commercialization Promotion Agency for Small and Medium Technology (COMPA) - Application: https://vvd.bz/buvX [MoneyToday startup media platform Unicorn Factory]

artigo.texto: In Partnership with Greenworks Greenworks is looking to shake up the power tool industry with their new 24V Pro lineup by delivering professional-grade performance and quality at surprisingly low prices. Designing the tools to achieve that goal is only part of the equation, though. The power source is the other. In this article, I’m taking a deeper dive into Greenworks’ battery design and technology. Along the way, we’ll explore its advantages and compare it to other popular battery systems so you can see how it stacks up. Is 24V Really Better Than 20V? Greenworks claims its PowerAll 24V batteries deliver 20% more power and 35% more runtime than 20V systems, but is that just marketing hype? To find out, let’s take a closer look at how the packs are built and what that means for the tools they power. 20V vs 24V Batteries A 20V battery is built with sets of 5 lithium cells that use series connections. Each one of those cells contributes 4.0 volts to the pack. 5 cells x 4.0 volts = 20 volts. Greenworks 24V batteries use sets of 6 lithium cells instead of 5. The extra cell is what boosts it to 24 volts (6 cells x 4.0 volts = 24 volts). More importantly, it offers very real performance enhancements. At a basic level, a 6-cell battery system has 20% more cells than a 5-cell battery system. In other words, there’s 20% more energy stored in a 24V battery. That’s why Greenworks can accurately claim there’s 20% more power available. But Greenworks also claims up to 35% more runtime. How do you get that if there’s only 20% more energy? The answer is energy efficiency. For comparison, think about the fuel economy of a car. According to the US Department of Energy, a typical midsize car at 55 MPH gets 45 Miles-Per-Gallon. At 75 MPH, that efficiency drops to 32 MPG. You’ll get to your destination faster, but you’ll have to use more fuel to get there. If the engine is working harder, it is working less efficiently. It’s similar for power tool batteries. The more power you drive through a battery, the less efficient it becomes. By having just one extra cell in each row, Greenworks 24V batteries can last up to 35% longer, thanks to the efficiency boost of running lower current through the cells. A Quick Note About 18V and 20V Batteries 18V and 20V battery systems actually have the same voltage. When an 18V battery is fully charged, it measures at 20V, which is why those systems are often labeled “20V max”. At its stable, or nominal, voltage, they measure 18 volts. So, when we compare 20V batteries, we’re also talking about 18V batteries. READ 20V Max vs 18V: Setting the Record Straight Opening Up the Throttle with Advanced Technology Electrical resistance is also the key player in unlocking the benefits of advanced battery technology. Think of electrical resistance as a restriction, kind of like pinching a hose. The lower the resistance, the easier it is for the water to flow. The same principle applies to energy in power tool batteries. If you lower the electrical resistance, energy flows more easily and efficiently. One of the major sources of electrical resistance in a battery is where the lithium cell connects to the pack. Greenworks uses what’s known as “tabless” connection technology in its High Power batteries. Those tabless connections greatly reduce the electrical resistance so the energy can flow more easily. Easier energy flow reduces the amount of heat that builds up in the pack, especially at high power levels. This allows Greenworks High Power batteries to safely handle more voltage and charge up to 35% faster than standard batteries. Since the energy transfer is more efficient, you also get additional runtime advantages on top of what the extra cell alone provides. High Power batteries help you get the maximum performance from your Greenworks PowerAll 24V Pro power tools, with higher power and longer runtimes. READ Power Tool Tech: Pouch Cell vs Tabless Cell Batteries More Than a Tool Battery Smartphones, tablets, and laptops have become essential parts of the job for professional tradesmen. You might be taking client calls, checking emails, ordering supplies, or a host of other tasks throughout the day. To help you keep your tech charged, Greenworks PowerAll 24V batteries have a bi-directional USB-C port to charge the devices you need. Beyond the jobsite, Greenworks 24V batteries power more than 200 cordless products. There are plenty of power tools, including the new Pro line that targets the needs of tradesmen. There are also lawn care tools, lights, speakers, and lifestyle products. Greenworks designed all of their 24V batteries to work in every Greenworks 24V product, so one battery system can cover all your cordless needs. Ready to see how the Greenworks PowerAll 24V battery system fits into your life? Visit your local Walmart or shop online to have tools, batteries, and accessories delivered, with delivery times under an hour in some locations.

artigo.texto: Em Vinhedo (SP), a EBM Engenharia realiza projeto na modalidade turnkey de um data center de inteligência artificial (IA) para a Ascenty, com capacidade de 20 MW. A primeira fase do empreendimento, com 10 MW, está sendo entregue em setembro, e a outra etapa, com mais 10 MW, será finalizada em dezembro. Eduardo Menossi, cofundador e CEO da EBM Engenharia, explica que a empresa é responsável desde o detalhamento do projeto até a construção, além de fornecimento de equipamentos e comissionamento. Ele afirma que nesse mercado, pouco importa o metro quadrado do empreendimento – o de Vinhedo tem inicialmente cerca de 5 mil m² de área construída. “Cada vez mais os data centers estarão menores de tamanho e maiores em capacidade, que é o que realmente importa num empreendimento desse tipo”, ressalta. Quando a EBM entrou no site para realizar o projeto, em fevereiro desse ano, já existia uma estrutura feita de pré-moldado com apenas um andar. “A gente fez o segundo shell (o primeiro shell é a estrutura pré-moldada de concreto), totalmente metálico”, destaca Eduardo. Shell se refere à estrutura básica incluindo pilares, vigas, paredes e cobertura. A montagem eletromecânica é feita simultaneamente à colocação da segunda camada de shell. “Shell metálico é uma solução tradicional e visa facilitar a montagem interna, para dar velocidade e qualidade à obra”, ressalta o executivo. A estrutura metálica faz o fechamento das diferentes áreas do data center. O CEO da EBM conta que o data center em construção não tem piso elevado e o insuflamento (sistema que distribui o ar condicionado) será feito pelas laterais do empreendimento. O rack (estrutura metálica usada para fixar os servidores do data center) é apoiado direto no piso. De acordo com Eduardo, o piso tem 6 t/m³ de capacidade. PÉ-DIREITO ELEVADO Ele conta que o empreendimento tem pé-direito elevado, com 12 m de altura. O motivo desta altura é para posicionar os racks e passar as redes de fibra e de alimentação elétrica, e para oferecer espaço interno para garantir a circulação adequada de ar frio. O projeto interno de um data center, segundo Eduardo, varia, mas neste de Vinhedo constam salas elétricas, central de ar condicionado (refrigeração), distribuição elétrica para cada rack através do busway (condutores elétricos), além do próprio rack com os servidores (data hall). “Tem projeto que a sala elétrica está fora do prédio”, cita. A eletricidade do empreendimento chega pela distribuidora ou é alimentada a diesel – uma área externa do site da Ascenty produz energia gerada a diesel. TROCA DE CALOR A refrigeração faz a troca de calor nas salas de equipamentos. “O ar-condicionado é item relevante porque ele impacta diretamente na eficiência do data center. Não que a parte elétrica não fosse importante, mas é que a parte de ar-condicionado deve ser desenvolvida especificamente para atender cada projeto”, afirma. O executivo lembra que é preciso levar em consideração o local que está se construindo o data center, incluindo a altitude e temperatura média externa. “Isso muda a eficiência da troca de calor. Por isso que o item ar-condicionado requer um conceito personalizado”, diz. A refrigeração no empreendimento da Ascenty é feita por um circuito de água gelada fechada. De acordo com Eduardo, isso evita consumo externo de água. Eduardo Menossi ressalta o prazo recorde de entrega da obra. “Trabalhamos desde o início em três turnos para conseguir entregar no prazo. Este foi o maior desafio”, pontua. O processo de comissionamento deste tipo de empreendimento, segundo o executivo, se divide entre a verificação dos sistemas de ar condicionado e dos elétricos, e do chamado comissionamento a quente, no qual se simula por 24 horas a operação com potência máxima da carga dos equipamentos. “Para o nosso grupo, este projeto foi muito relevante porque nós conseguimos implementar todas as soluções do grupo EBM. Iniciamos com a parte de design e engenharia, utilizamos a solução de produtos do grupo que se chama IDS (equipamentos de energia) e da Trusted Data (infraestrutura para data center)”, explica Eduardo. A EBM tem 16 anos e está em nove países. A empresa já construiu pelo menos 35 data centers. Sua atuação até bem pouco tempo era voltada somente para data centers de nuvem (cloud) para operar serviços de internet. “Quando a gente atuava na parte de cloud, eram data centers com até 6 MW. Este é de 20 MW, o que é bastante relevante”, comenta. “E os desafios só vão aumentar. A gente já está olhando projeto com entrega de 40 MW. O mercado promete capacidades cada vez maiores”, complementa. ASCENTY INVESTIRÁ R$ 6 BI EM 4 DATA CENTERS NO PAÍS Com novos contratos, a Ascenty, joint venture formada pela Digital Realty e Brookfield Infrastructure, anunciou no primeiro semestre investimentos de R$ 6 bilhões para o desenvolvimento de quatro novos data centers no Brasil voltados para inteligência artificial (IA). A empresa já possui 21 data centers em operação no país e a projeção é de possuir um total de 40 centros nos próximos anos. Segundo a Ascenty, os contratos fechados exigem entregas de data centers até o fim de 2027. Os investimentos serão assegurados por meio de instituições privadas. O aporte anunciado representa acréscimo até o ano que vem de 150 MW de capacidade computacional, um incremento de 40% sobre toda a capacidade construída pela companhia. Os data centers serão construídos em Sumaré e Vinhedo, na região metropolitana de Campinas (SP). O principal deles ficará em Sumaré – cidade onde a empresa já tem operação – e a Ascenty informa que ele será o primeiro concebido desde o início para aplicações de inteligência artificial. Este empreendimento, que será o primeiro a ser finalizado dos quatro anunciados, terá 90 MW de capacidade inicial, com previsão de expansão adicional de mais 90 MW. artigo.texto: China's lithium battery exports jump 36% in first three quarters; overseas plant construction and services become new competitive focus China's lithium battery exports maintained strong momentum through the first three quarters. Data released by the General Administration of Customs on October 14 showed that China's lithium battery exports grew 36.4% year-on-year in the first three quarters. More noteworthy is the structural shift: while exports to the United States declined, other markets are rapidly filling the gap, and the way Chinese battery companies participate in overseas markets is evolving from pure product supply to heavier models involving joint-venture plant construction and long-term operational services. According to customs data compiled by the Power Battery Applications Branch, lithium battery exports to the United States fell 24% in the first eight months, but exports to markets outside the U.S. grew approximately 53% on a comparable basis. This means the U.S. market shortfall has been fully offset by Europe, Asia, and other emerging markets, signaling a shift in the overseas focus of China's battery industry. Market share reshuffle: CATL gains as South Korean rivals retreat The sharp divergence in regional demand has directly redrawn the competitive landscape of the overseas power battery market. According to SNE Research, CATL's share of the non-China power battery market rose from 29% to 33.7% in the first eight months of this year, with European business maintaining growth and Asian installations increasing rapidly. In contrast, LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI—dragged down by weakening North American demand—saw their combined overseas share plunge from 37.9% to 26.8%. It should be noted that SNE Research's overseas installation figures include both batteries shipped with complete vehicles and batteries produced through overseas localization, which differs from customs export statistics. But both point to the same trend: Chinese battery companies are systematically strengthening their presence in overseas markets. BYD's domestic and overseas performance presents a stark contrast. In the first eight months, its global power battery share slipped from 17.1% to 15.1%, but its overseas share climbed from 8.2% to 11%. With domestic auto sales under pressure, vehicle operations in Europe, Asia, and South America continue to drive battery installation growth. BYD's own-brand vehicles remain the most important vehicle for expanding its overseas battery share. The second tier is catching up just as rapidly. In the first eight months, Gotion High-tech's overseas power battery share doubled to 4%, with overseas installations already surpassing Samsung SDI. EVE Energy rose from 0.9% to 2.1%, and SVOLT Energy Technology and CALB also increased their shares. Both CALB and EVE Energy entered the top ten in overseas power battery installations. Heavier cooperation models: from selling products to joint investment Independent battery makers expanding their overseas automaker client base are also being pushed to adapt to diversified technology roadmaps. Sunwoda has been supplying hybrid batteries in volume to Renault and Nissan, while CALB provides stable supply for Toyota and Mazda global models. Although the share of pure electric models in Europe is rising, conventional hybrids still account for the largest proportion, and international automakers' battery procurement is not following a single product route. The deepening of cooperation is even more pronounced. Volkswagen and Gotion High-tech have advanced to the joint-investment stage. Volkswagen wants to increase lithium iron phosphate (LFP) supply for mainstream-priced models and has pointed out that Europe lacks relevant scale production capacity. Under the announced arrangement, Gotion plans to invest approximately €1.1 billion (approximately $1.2 billion) for a 49% stake in a Spanish joint-venture plant, with the agreement still pending approval. For such partnerships, Chinese battery makers need to bring not only products and manufacturing technology, but also real capital to build local supply chains. The energy storage business has opened another window for overseas expansion for a different group of companies. Data released by InfoLink shows that the top five overseas energy storage cell shippers in the first half of this year were CATL, EVE Energy, BYD, Hithium, and Great Power. Surging overseas residential storage demand lifted EVE Energy and Great Power in the rankings; in the global small-scale storage cell market, EVE Energy, Great Power, and Rept Battero together hold more than 60% share. Hithium's strength is concentrated in large-scale storage projects, ranking second globally in utility-scale storage cell shipments. Services and capacity: the twin tests of overseas expansion Repeat purchases by power plant developers are generating continuous order flows for suppliers. BYD's customer Grenergy again procured energy storage systems in March this year for a new project in Chile, with a batch of equipment already shipped from China. CATL's customer ContourGlobal made a single procurement covering three countries—the United Kingdom, Greece, and Chile—with the cooperation scope extending to degradation management and end-of-life battery recycling. artigo.texto: Vattenfall has entered into a tolling agreement with Royal Vopak to obtain access to battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity in the Netherlands. Under the terms of the deal, Vattenfall will secure 100MW/400MW-hours (MWh) from a planned BESS near Meeden in Groningen province. The total project, developed and managed by Vopak, will have a capacity of 150MW and is expected to begin commercial operations in the second quarter of 2028. The agreement aims to support the balancing of fluctuations between electricity supply and demand as the Dutch power system incorporates increasing amounts of renewable energy. Battery storage enables the absorption of surplus electricity from renewable sources during periods of high production and can return power to the grid when demand rises or renewable output drops. According to Vattenfall, the secured BESS capacity will contribute to greater flexibility in its operations and aligns with the company’s objective to contract at least 1.5GW of BESS capacity across its core markets. Vattenfall wholesale energy head Erik Suichies said: “As the energy system becomes increasingly renewable, flexibility plays a crucial role in maintaining balance between supply and demand. Battery storage helps make better use of renewable electricity and contributes to a more reliable and efficient energy system. “We are pleased to partner with Vopak and support the development of large-scale energy storage in the Netherlands.” For Vopak, the deal represents a further step in its business expansion into electrical energy storage. Vopak battery energy storage solutions business development vice-president Jarno Veldhoven said: “With our aim to provide reliable and affordable battery systems to our customers we are excited to have Vattenfall as a long-term partner.” The partnership brings together Vattenfall and Vopak, both established players in the Dutch energy sector, and combines large-scale storage infrastructure with market expertise in flexibility optimisation. The companies aim to enhance the resilience of the Dutch electricity grid and support the integration of renewable energy sources. In July 2026, Vopak completed the acquisition of a 79% controlling interest in Green Energy Storage, a Netherlands-based developer specialising in BESS.

artigo.texto: Planning commission weighs future of data centers in New Orleans The City Planning Commission has been tasked with recommending guidelines for data center creation in the city. Planning commission weighs future of data centers in New Orleans The City Planning Commission has been tasked with recommending guidelines for data center creation in the city. The New Orleans Planning Commission failed to approve a recommendation for data center creation guidelines Tuesday. Planning staff were tasked with creating definitions for data centers and making a recommendation for which, if any, should be allowed in New Orleans. The planning staff's recommendation was to prohibit large and hyperscale data centers, and allow small and medium data centers in certain parts of the city, with certain restrictions. According to their definitions, small data centers must be no greater than 20,000 sq. ft. and consume no more than 5 megawatts of power. Medium data centers must be no greater than 100,000 sq. ft. and consume no more than 20 megawatts of power. Large and hyperscale data centers are greater than 100,000 sq. ft. and consume greater than 20 megawatts of power. Planning commissioners decided the recommendation was not ready to go to City Council. They voted against approving the recommendation, and are now asking City Council to extend the moratorium on new data center creation. City Council approved a one-year moratorium back in January, in order to give the planning staff time to make a recommendation and come up with definitions. In the meantime, the commission is asking the planning staff to make amendments to the recommendation. They want to change the definitions for small and medium data centers. They are suggesting a small data center be reduced from 20,000 sq. ft. to 10,000 sq. ft. and the maximum usage be reduced from 5 megawatts to 3 megawatts. They also want the maximum size for a medium data center to be reduced from 100,000 sq. ft. to 50,000 sq. ft. and the maximum energy usage to be reduced from 20 megawatts to 15 megawatts. Their other suggestion is to increase the buffer between homes and data centers from 500 ft. to 1000 ft. The decision came after several people spoke against the recommendation during public comment, and a small group gathered outside City Hall ahead of the vote. The demonstration was led by members of the Party for Socialism and Liberation. They believe no type of data center should be allowed in New Orleans. They cited quality of life and environmental concerns, and said any new data center would put a strain on utilities. According to the planning staff report, it was found that many small data centers already exist in New Orleans. There are at least four operating in the downtown area. The report also says the biggest concern with new data centers is their impact on water and power usage. The item to approve a recommendation was originally on the agenda for the commission's August 25 meeting, and was deferred multiple times.

artigo.texto: Agricultural equipment has relied on diesel engines and hydraulic systems for decades, but battery-powered machinery is beginning to appear on farms across North America. This shift affects not only how equipment operates but also how farmers maintain their fleets, what skills repair technicians need, and which components fail most often. Understanding these changes helps farm operators make informed decisions about equipment purchases and maintenance planning. The Maintenance Advantage of Electric Drive Systems Electric motors contain fewer moving parts than internal combustion engines. A typical diesel tractor engine has pistons, valves, camshafts, fuel injectors, and turbochargers that require regular service intervals. Electric motors eliminate these components entirely, reducing the number of maintenance tasks. Oil changes, filter replacements, and cooling system flushes remain necessary for tractors with diesel engines, but electric alternatives require none of these services for their drive systems. This reduction in maintenance tasks does not mean electric equipment is maintenance-free. Battery packs require thermal management systems to prevent overheating, and these systems need inspection. Electrical connections must be kept clean and tight to prevent resistance that can cause heat buildup. The regenerative braking systems common in electric farm equipment need periodic checks to ensure they capture energy efficiently during deceleration. Battery Management and Replacement Costs Lithium-ion batteries degrade over time regardless of use patterns, though heavy discharge cycles accelerate this process. Most agricultural battery packs are designed to retain 70 to 80 percent of their original capacity after several thousand charge cycles. For equipment that operates daily during planting and harvest seasons, this translates to several years of service before capacity loss becomes noticeable. Replacement costs for battery packs remain the largest concern for farmers considering electric equipment. Unlike engine rebuilds, which can extend the life of diesel tractors at moderate expense, battery replacement often represents a significant portion of the equipment’s original value. Farmers must factor this eventual cost into their total ownership calculations. Some manufacturers offer battery leasing programs to spread this expense over time, though these arrangements add ongoing costs that traditional equipment does not carry. Impact on Hay and Forage Operations Hay production equipment has particularly demanding duty cycles. Balers, mowers, and rakes operate for extended periods during narrow weather windows when conditions are right for cutting and baling. Battery capacity becomes a limiting factor during these intensive work periods. A diesel-powered baler can refuel in minutes and continue working, while battery-powered alternatives require charging time that can interrupt operations during critical harvest windows. For farmers managing hay operations across Tennessee, Kentucky, and Illinois, this operational reality shapes equipment decisions. Traditional repair services remain essential for maintaining the diesel-powered fleets that most operations depend on. Facilities offering tractor repair services and agricultural equipment maintenance understand that new holland hay equipment and similar conventional machinery will continue to dominate hay production for the foreseeable future, particularly in regions where charging infrastructure is limited and work schedules are dictated by weather patterns rather than planned intervals. Training Requirements for Technicians Repair shops that have serviced diesel equipment for decades now face the need to train technicians in high-voltage electrical systems. Working on battery packs rated at 400 volts or higher requires specific safety protocols that differ fundamentally from mechanical repairs. Technicians must understand battery management systems, power electronics, and diagnostic software that reads error codes from electronic control units rather than mechanical symptoms. This training gap affects rural areas more severely than urban regions. Agricultural equipment dealers in smaller communities may struggle to justify the cost of certification programs and specialized diagnostic tools when only a handful of electric machines operate in their service area. The result is a transitional period where farmers with electric equipment may face longer wait times for repairs or need to transport machines to distant service centers with qualified technicians. Safety Considerations in Farm Equipment Electrification Electric farm equipment introduces new safety concerns alongside its operational benefits. High-voltage systems remain energized even when the equipment is turned off, creating shock hazards during maintenance or after accidents. Battery fires, though rare, burn intensely and require specialized extinguishing methods that differ from diesel fuel fires. Farmers and technicians accustomed to conventional machinery safety protocols must learn additional precautions specific to electrical systems. The silent operation of electric motors also creates situational awareness challenges. Diesel engines announce their presence with noise and exhaust, alerting nearby workers to moving equipment. Electric tractors and implements operate quietly enough that workers may not notice approaching machinery, particularly in noisy environments like grain handling facilities or livestock barns. This characteristic requires deliberate changes to farm safety practices and communication protocols among crew members. Expanding resources for green transformation At the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance-Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized that, in addition to resources from the State budget, capital markets, and money markets, developing new market mechanisms is crucial in mobilizing resources for green transformation. According to the Deputy Governor, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This provides businesses with additional motivation and resources to continue investing in the transition process, instead of relying primarily on bank credit. In recent years, the banking sector has gradually improved its policy framework, promoting green credit and managing environmental and social risks in lending activities. Capital flows are directed towards areas that bring environmental benefits, especially sustainable agriculture , green energy, and projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Data from the State Bank of Vietnam shows that by the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856 trillion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, green credit maintained an average growth rate of over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; green energy accounts for nearly 28%. Notably, outstanding loans that have undergone environmental and social risk assessment reached over VND 6.2 million trillion, equivalent to more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy. However, according to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, the important thing for green credit is not only that the capital is disbursed to projects identified as green, but also that the results of energy saving, emission reduction, and environmental protection achieved by borrowers can be verified. From this perspective, green credit and carbon markets have a mutually supportive relationship. Credit provides resources for businesses to innovate technologically, improve energy efficiency, and thus generate emission reductions. Conversely, when carbon markets operate effectively, the recorded and commercialized emission reductions can generate additional revenue, improve cash flow, support debt repayment capacity, and enhance credit quality. Speaking at the conference, Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-in-Chief of the Finance-Investment Newspaper, argued that if the carbon exchange is the infrastructure of the market, then credit policy, the banking system, and the capital market are the driving forces for the green transition process. According to Mr. Pham Van Hoanh, a market that wants to develop sustainably needs not only an exchange, commodities, and trading regulations, but also liquidity, data, verification mechanisms, trust between buyers and sellers, and a sufficiently strong financial ecosystem. The crucial issue is how to gradually make carbon value a reliable factor in financial decisions, helping capital flow to the right, effective projects. Unblocking bottlenecks Despite the significant potential of the carbon market, translating emission reduction results into actual cash flow still faces considerable challenges. A project's ability to reduce emissions does not automatically guarantee carbon credits, buyers, or a sufficiently stable revenue stream for banks to consider granting credit. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, analyzed that the capital needs for emission reduction projects often arise right from the preparation and implementation phases. Meanwhile, carbon credits can only be generated after emission reduction results are measured, reported, verified, and all related procedures are completed. The time gap between investment needs and the time when carbon revenue is generated is a challenge for both businesses and credit institutions. For agriculture and forestry, the dispersed nature of production makes the cost of measuring and verifying emission reduction results relatively high. If each producer has to carry out the entire process themselves, economic efficiency is difficult to guarantee. Meanwhile, linkages through cooperatives, raw material areas, or production chains require clear data governance mechanisms and benefit sharing. Based on this practice, Agribank proposes a "two-tiered cash flow" assessment principle. In this principle, cash flow from core production and business activities remains the foundation for debt repayment; carbon revenue is only considered as a supplementary source, depending on the level of legal, technical, and commercial certainty. From an international perspective, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, noted that the carbon market provides economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides the capital for investments. Of this, the capital needed for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, and for emission reduction is approximately US$114 billion. artigo.texto: South Korea is set to launch the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) next year, a platform for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits. The initiative will utilize blockchain technology to record core data, aiming to enhance the credibility of carbon credits. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il announced the finalized “Detailed Implementation Plan for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)” after a meeting of economy-related ministers. The GVCM will facilitate the issuance and trading of carbon credits derived from international greenhouse gas reduction projects. Credits will be categorized into two types: GVCM A, usable for both regulatory compliance and voluntary environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities when host countries authorize transfers, and GVCM NA, restricted to voluntary ESG purposes. The government plans to sign letters of intent with potential participating countries at COP31 next month and is in discussions with the World Bank and Green Climate Fund to convert existing project credits. Blockchain Integration for Enhanced Credibility A key feature of the GVCM is the integration of blockchain technology for data management. Core information, including project operators, reduction volumes, unique identification numbers, and methodologies, will be recorded on the blockchain. Other data will be stored in traditional databases. This selective application of blockchain aims to balance management efficiency with data integrity and stability. Initially, credits will be issued in electronic form and traded on South Korea’s voluntary carbon market exchange. The government is considering parallel issuance in digital asset form in the future, contingent on trading volumes, the evolving digital asset legislation, and market confidence. The market’s name change from “Global Voluntary Carbon Market” to “Global Verified Carbon Market” reflects its expanded scope to include regulatory markets. Dual-Track Credit System and Governance The GVCM’s dual-track credit system differentiates based on host country authorization. GVCM A credits, with host country approval, can satisfy regulatory requirements such as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement or the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), as well as voluntary ESG activities. GVCM NA credits, lacking such authorization, are limited to voluntary corporate environmental initiatives but can be upgraded to GVCM A if corresponding adjustment approval is later granted. The government is also exploring links between the GVCM and South Korea’s domestic emissions trading scheme, provided that credibility standards, Paris Agreement Article 6 requirements, and domestic legal conditions are met. The issuing body will comprise a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is currently serving as the interim secretariat. Governance structures are designed to ensure direct participation from developing countries, allowing them to influence operational processes and gain experience in carbon market management. The project sectors will align with participating countries’ development needs and South Korea’s technological strengths, encompassing areas like mangrove restoration, agricultural waste treatment, methane capture, and energy efficiency improvements. The anticipated growth of the international carbon credit market, projected by MSCI to reach $45 billion, $250 billion by 2050, underscores the significance of standardized and credible market criteria. The GVCM aims to address current controversies surrounding credit credibility and actual reduction effectiveness by establishing clear international market criteria. The government plans to leverage networks such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable (APCMR) to secure participating countries. Full-scale operations are expected to commence after the establishment of the issuing body next year and the specification of project structures. The GVCM initiative aligns with the broader trend of major financial institutions exploring blockchain for core operations, as detailed in reports on how major financial institutions move core operations onto blockchain networks. This move also echoes the strategic planning seen in projects like the CENTEL Blockchain Roadmap, which pairs CNT participation with network plans, as highlighted in CENTEL Blockchain Roadmap Pairs CNT Participation With Network Plans. The involvement of entities like the World Bank and Green Climate Fund in such initiatives reflects a growing institutional interest in blockchain-based solutions for global challenges, similar to how Chainlink Co-Founder presented blockchain finance at a major banking conference. Frequently asked questions - What is the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)? The GVCM is a platform South Korea will launch next year for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits, utilizing blockchain for enhanced credibility. - How will blockchain be used in the GVCM? Blockchain technology will be applied to record core data, such as project operators and reduction methodologies, to ensure the credibility and stability of carbon credits. - What are the two categories of GVCM credits? Credits are divided into GVCM A, usable for regulatory compliance and ESG activities, and GVCM NA, limited to voluntary ESG purposes, based on host country transfer authorization. - Who will be involved in the GVCM's issuing body? The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat, with plans for developing countries to participate directly. - When will the GVCM fully launch? The GVCM will fully launch starting next year, with plans to sign letters of intent at COP31 next month and establish the issuing body in the coming year.

artigo.texto: Dell shares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout. Hewlett-Packard Enterprise, Oracle and Super Micro all joined in the downward slide. In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE and NetApp, "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing." Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled. However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerning revenue figures out of OpenAI and more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloud CoreWeave plunged 15%, wiping out its gains for 2026. The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers. "There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time." The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue. Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress over the weekend on a new chip structure. Micron is down 11% for the week, while South Korea's SK Hynix has tumbled 13% in U.S. trading and Western Digital has dropped more than 8%. artigo.texto: Nightpeak Energy has completed the 150MW Bocanova 2 battery storage facility in south-east Texas, US, raising the total storage capacity at the Bocanova site to 300MW. The company also announced the successful financial close for the facility, noting that it went into commercial service on 17 September. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. Bocanova 2 aims to provide additional flexibility to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas electricity grid amid rising demand, particularly as data centres and other large energy consumers expand operations in the state. Located in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area, Bocanova 2 follows Bocanova 1, an earlier 150MW battery storage project at the same site. According to Nightpeak Energy, Bocanova 1 commenced commercial operation in August 2025. The combined projects form part of the company’s ongoing battery storage development in a region recognised for its fast-growing power demand. Bocanova 2 is equipped with Tesla’s Megapack 2 XL lithium-ion battery systems. It operates under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty. The financing structure included a tax equity bridge loan and a construction-to-term loan provided by MUFG Bank, while U.S. Bank supplied traditional tax equity for the project. Nightpeak Energy co-founder and CEO/chief development officer Paris Hays said: “We are seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand. “Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change. “With 300MW now operating at Bocanova, we are putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country.” Nightpeak Energy was founded in 2022. Since then, the company has developed and acquired more than 1GW of operating and de-risked capacity, including battery storage, gas-fired generation and powered land development. The company continues to develop additional flexible generation and large-load projects as part of efforts to address growing power needs in the US.

artigo.texto: Julio Friedman, chief scientist at Carbon Direct, warned a captive audience to “proceed with caution” regarding space-based data centers (SBDCs) during a talk at the Press Building on Monday. The event, hosted by the Precourt Institute of Energy, summarized an upcoming report about the dangers of space-based data centers. Friedman spoke alongside David Sandalow, inaugural fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, and Roger Aines, the former energy program chief scientist at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The trio, along with a few other scientists, has spent the last few months researching the scientific and social implications of sending data centers into space. Sending data centers into space doesn’t actually mean sending a large megaton computer into orbit. According to Sandalow, a single SBDC will consist of “approximately 10,000 satellites, orbiting in a constellation.” These satellites would all communicate with each other to avoid collisions and operate as a singular, large data center. They would orbit along the terminator — the line that separates dusk and dawn — and “as a result, have access to 24/7 solar power,” as Sandalow explained. The swarms of satellites would have to be in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) to stay close enough to devices on Earth and avoid lag. Scientists are developing SBDCs to address the rising need for compute, the processing power required to run large AI models. By 2030, “700 large launches a year are going to be required to put roughly 10% of projected global AI compute in space,” Sandalow said. This year, SpaceX has launched under 120 rockets. All three presenters warned that innovation and development without extensive testing would lead to several problems. “The American Astronomical Society says that with the larger climate of these constellations, you will see more satellites than stars in a nice sky, particularly [at] dawn and dusk,” Sandalow said. “There is a very significant risk of cascading collisions [that] might render portion[s] of the lower orbit unusable for communication satellites or other types of uses in use.” Sandalow also warned that a sudden increase in rocket launches and landings could re-threaten the ozone layer, which has recovered tremendously under the Montreal Protocol, an international treaty that phased out ozone-depleting substances like chlorofluorocarbons. “Aluminum oxides and the soot are particularly bad because those create surfaces for the surface chemistry that destroys the ozone,” Friedman said, detailing the effects of two emittants released by rocket launches. Sandalow also emphasized the importance of energy, as it’s “at the core of so many aspects of human life,” he said in an interview with The Daily. “[I’ve] seen students paying very close attention to global warming threats, because I think that’s going to make a huge difference in our ability to solve this problem.” Arpita Kalra, director of marketing and engagement at the Precourt Institute of Energy, said the institute hosts these events to expose students to diverse perspectives. “We organize a lot of these seminars, and most of our seminars are open to the public,” Kalra said. The Precourt Institute of Energy organizes roughly 200 events a year, according to Kalra. Cheng Ma, a visiting political science and anthropology researcher from Berlin, said he found the event “quite interesting.” He attended the talk to stay informed on conversations concerning data center development. “We still talk about different [geopolitical] boundaries[except] now it’s space,” he said, describing space as a new frontier in international development. Sandalow emphasized the importance of staying informed, especially for students. “[Energy] is a multigenerational problem. So we need the younger generation really focused on this issue,” he said.

artigo.texto: Johannes Linder, Director, System Design & Innovation at BELECTRIC, a member of the Elevion Group, shared ideas on optimizing system designs for PV-plus-storage hybrid power plants, particularly in Germany, at the TaiyangNews Solar Power Plants & Storage Conference 2026. His presentation focused on hybrid system design optimization for engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firms and investors. Linder shared a German co-located PV + battery energy storage system (BESS) system design case study with a 1:1 PV + BESS AC-coupled configuration as a reference project. In 2024, BELECTRIC simulated the project and found that a 58 MW BESS size corresponds to the project's highest Net Present Value (NPV). NPV, which indicates how much value a project is expected to add to a business in current monetary terms, is considered a key performance indicator (KPI) for optimization. Back then, the company could adjust BESS and PV size by optimizing the ratio of fixed-tilt and tracker-based systems within a given land area to get maximum BESS revenues. Linder argued that although these optimization types still apply to grey BESS, which charges itself from either PV or the grid, Germany has changed a few frameworks. These include regulations backed by grid oversizing, such as flexible grid connection agreements (FCAs), grid connection restrictions for grey BESSs, right balancing between the grid operator's acceptance and project profitability, and a focus on green BESS. Green BESS allows only renewable energy to charge it. From an investor's perspective, the company follows optimized system design in three stages: 1) Set the project frameworks; 2) Define technology and design parameters; and 3) Check sensitivities/critical assumptions. However, Linder noted that these procedures make hourly battery simulation challenging, with many possibilities and scenarios. The company has adopted a ‘practical’ four-step approach to address challenges. They are: pre-selection of PV system designs, BESS optimization for pre-selected designs, PV + BESS market value analysis and clustering, and simulation of all relevant scenarios. In a nutshell, this clustering of market value analysis reduces the need to handle too many simulations. Linder shared a case study for a PV + green BESS hybrid plant system design with an AC-coupled system architecture, no grid restrictions, and within 33 ha of land in Central Germany, following these steps. The simulation results showed that the optimized BESS size is 40% of PV MWp with a corresponding backup duration of 4 hours. For PV + BESS optimization, a 45 MWp PV array mounted on a fixed mounting structure with a 3P module mounting architecture at a 10° inclination angle showed the highest NPV and ranked first. In comparison, modules mounted on trackers, those installed along the east-west (E-W) direction, and those mounted vertically relative to flat land ranked at 178, 782, and 3,005, respectively.

artigo.texto: Na manhã de 14 de outubro de 2026, o jornal Finanças e Investimentos, em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã, organizou o seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde" em Hanói . Em seu discurso de abertura no workshop, o Sr. Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-Chefe do Jornal de Finanças e Investimentos, afirmou que, na busca pelo objetivo de crescimento verde e pelo compromisso com emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Vietnã está gradualmente aprimorando instrumentos políticos e mecanismos de mercado para mobilizar recursos para o processo de transição verde. O lançamento do mercado doméstico de carbono em 29 de junho de 2026 não apenas marca a formação de um novo mercado, mas também exige a consolidação de um ecossistema financeiro para garantir seu desenvolvimento eficiente e sustentável. Se as bolsas de carbono são a infraestrutura do mercado, então a política de crédito, o sistema bancário e o mercado de capitais são as forças motrizes por trás da transição verde. Dentro desse ecossistema, a política de crédito desempenha um papel fundamental na canalização de recursos financeiros, apoiando empresas e indivíduos a investirem em atividades de redução de emissões e conectando os objetivos de desenvolvimento sustentável aos fluxos de capital da economia . Em outras palavras, a transformação verde deve, em última análise, se traduzir em investimentos concretos: investimentos em tecnologias mais limpas, uso mais eficiente de energia, mudanças nos processos de produção, desenvolvimento da agricultura de baixa emissão, proteção e desenvolvimento florestal, tratamento de resíduos, desenvolvimento de energias renováveis e construção de cadeias de suprimentos mais sustentáveis… E para que esses projetos sejam implementados na prática, é necessário um sistema financeiro capaz de identificar, valorizar, alocar e gerenciar fluxos de capital verde. O arcabouço legal para o mercado de carbono do Vietnã foi estabelecido pela Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020 e detalhado por meio de diversos documentos. Mais recentemente, incluem-se o Decreto 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado interno de carbono, e o Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado internacional de resultados de redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. Ao mesmo tempo, o Vietnã também adquiriu experiência na comercialização dos resultados da redução de emissões no mercado internacional. Em março de 2024, o Vietnã recebeu, pela primeira vez, US$ 51,5 milhões do Banco Mundial, referentes a 10,3 milhões de toneladas de resultados comprovados de redução de emissões no âmbito do Programa de Redução de Emissões da Região Centro-Norte. Segundo o editor-chefe do jornal Finanças e Investimentos, a negociação de cotas de emissão no sistema de negociação, que será implementada a partir de 29 de junho de 2026, não se trata apenas da formação de um novo mercado. Mais importante ainda, ela cria uma nova abordagem para a avaliação econômica das atividades de redução de emissões. No entanto, também precisamos reconhecer, de forma realista, que a formação de um novo mercado de carbono é apenas o começo. Um mercado sustentável precisa de mais do que apenas uma bolsa de valores, commodities e regulamentações comerciais. Ele também requer liquidez, dados, mecanismos de verificação, confiança entre compradores e vendedores e um ecossistema financeiro robusto para dar suporte aos participantes do mercado. Ao mesmo tempo, essa jornada rumo à sustentabilidade ainda levanta muitas questões que precisam de respostas de todas as partes. Quais gargalos precisam ser abordados no arcabouço legal do mercado de carbono e nos mecanismos financeiros desse mercado? Como o capital verde pode fluir para os projetos certos? Como os bancos podem avaliar as oportunidades e os riscos de um projeto verde? Como as empresas podem demonstrar a eficácia de sua transformação e atrair capital não apenas de bancos, mas também se conectar mais estreitamente com fontes de capital de médio e longo prazo do mercado de capitais? E como o valor do carbono pode se tornar gradualmente um fator confiável nas decisões financeiras das partes interessadas relevantes? O editor-chefe do jornal Finanças e Investimentos enfatizou que, para responder a essas perguntas, o jornal está organizando o seminário de hoje com o tema "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando os Fluxos de Capital Verde". Quando as empresas percebem os benefícios econômicos da redução das emissões, os bancos e as instituições do mercado de capitais conseguem gerir os fluxos de capital de forma eficaz, os investidores percebem o valor e os produtores beneficiam proporcionalmente, então o mercado de carbono cria verdadeiramente um novo impulso para a economia. Com esse espírito em mente, o jornal Finance and Investment espera que a conferência se torne um fórum substancial para que agências reguladoras, bancos, empresas, especialistas e organizações troquem ideias, forneçam feedback e busquem soluções viáveis.

artigo.texto: Planning for development is notoriously local in Pennsylvania, but one of the largest and most contentious building proposals in the region is now heading into a county-run public input process. Springdale Borough is one of around two dozen municipalities in Allegheny County that do not have ordinances establishing their jurisdiction over subdivision and land use decisions. Instead, the county carries out the process. Over the next two weeks, Allegheny County Economic Development’s (ACED) Planning Division will hold public meetings as part of this process for the proposed development of a data center campus, which has drawn opposition from residents of the borough and the surrounding community due to concerns over noise, air pollution and transparency from the developer Allegheny DC Propco LLC. The first meeting, which will be held virtually tonight, has even drawn a watch party organized by Save Allegheny Valley Environment (SAVE). SAVE Treasurer Marty Garrigan said that group has been educating residents on the process dictated by the county’s SALDO, or Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance. For Garrigan, the preferred outcome would be a denial. “We’re hopeful. In the worst case scenario, they would approve this with conditions. But that’s a scary thought, too,” he said. Anna Jewart, who serves as land use counsel for Allegheny DC Propco LLC, which recently rebranded as Dynamo DC, said that the SALDO process for major developments can be broken down into three steps: zoning approval at the local level, approval of the preliminary land development plan and final approval of the plan. The developer is on the second step. The ACED Planning Division has 90 days from its Oct. 28 meeting at Springdale Borough Municipal Building to issue its decision, she said. The county will accept written comments through Nov. 30. A preliminary approval would not allow Allegheny DC Propco to start building any structures or complete any grading work, she said. But because the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development Standards now require local approvals to be complete before data center developers apply for Department of Environmental Protection permits, Jewart said an approved preliminary plan would allow Allegheny DC Propco to apply for those. “This is a big hurdle. And it takes a lot of work, a lot of engineering. But there is much more that has to be done still,” she said. One application, dozens of issues Last December, Allegheny DC Propco received approval from Springdale Borough Council to build the data center complex as a conditional use. The borough also granted the developer six variances. Lessons of Springdale: Towns must prepare if they want any say over data centers At the municipal level, the preliminary plan submitted as part of the SALDO process typically provides a broad overview of what’s being proposed, said Brigitte Meyer, a staff attorney for the environmental advocacy organization PennFuture. But that also depends on the town’s zoning ordinance and the level of detail it requires. The county’s SALDO requires preliminary applications to include a range of documents, including a description of the project and its purpose and maps of the development’s proposed location and surrounding developments. Depending on a site’s conditions, a developer might also have to submit reports that assess soil contamination, landslide proneness and subsidence risk. Allegheny DC Propco’s preliminary plan proposes transforming 47 acres of the former Cheswick Generating Station site into a data center campus that would include power generators, utility yards and stormwater facilities to support its operations. In response to the 182-page application, ACED’s Planning Division asked for correction of several inconsistencies. Some of those issues include: - Certification from the Allegheny County Health Department that it was notified about the proposal, as required, wasn’t included in the application. Notification to the Health Department would also trigger air pollution requirements for the facility, according to the county’s review. - Several concerns surrounding the application’s treatment of the St. Mark’s Lutheran Church cemetery, which sits to the west of the proposed data center campus. The review notes that there’s a call to move earth in proximity to existing headstones there, and a proposal to relocate access to the cemetery would require building a bridge. - Despite the plan showing that parts of the site are contaminated with methylnaphthalene and arsenic, the application did not signal that any remediation had been done. Two consultants — Mackin Engineers and Consultants and GFT Infrastructure, Inc. — also conducted reviews of the plan on behalf of the county and borough. Similar to the county’s internal review, the third parties took issue with missing or incomplete information throughout the plan. Jewart, counsel for the developer, said that the length of the county’s review was not surprising for a plan of this size. She also said that it’s standard for these reviews to include several reminders to obtain certain permits, some of which she said the developer cannot apply for at this time due to the state’s GRID Standards. Allegheny DC Propco has submitted a letter in response to the county’s review, she said, and plans to submit an updated plan ahead of the Oct. 28 meeting. In June, county Sustainability Director Brittany Prischak said the county is working on a model data center development ordinance that municipalities can adopt, but that the county was still figuring out its role in the evolving space. Harrisburg also has a role. According to the state’s data center permit tracker, the developer already has state water obstruction and encroachment permits, but still has to submit permit applications related to erosion control and brownfield cleanups. Mia Hollie is the economic development and housing reporter for Pittsburgh’s Public Source. She can be reached at mia@publicsou

artigo.texto: New BYD Act 8: everything we know The new 7-seater electric SUV, which made its debut at the Paris Motor Show, sits at the top of the brand’s European range. It is set to arrive on European markets in 2027 Key points BYD unveiled the new Atto 8 – a seven-seater electric SUV that will sit at the top of the Chinese brand’s range – in a world premiere at the Paris Motor Show. Measuring 5.04 metres in length, 1.99 metres in width and 1.76 metres in height, the new Atto 8 features a three-row seating layout, complemented by a 270-litre boot capacity that expands to 1,960 litres when the second and third rows are folded down. The exterior design stands out for its Matrix LED headlights, slim daytime running lights and all-new light clusters, whilst the spoiler and aerodynamic features improve the car’s aerodynamic efficiency. There are two versions of the new SUV, both powered by the same second-generation 115 kWh Blade Battery. BYD Act 8: high-tech interiors Inside, the 2.39 m² panoramic roof, the 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster, the 26-inch head-up display and the 15.6-inch central touchscreen with Google Built-in immediately catch the eye. The seats in the first two rows are heated, ventilated and feature a massage function, whilst those in the third row have adjustable headrests. Three-zone climate control and leather upholstery come as standard. The standard equipment is rounded off by a 50 W on-board wireless charging pad and several USB Type-C ports. BYD Act 8: available engines The entry-level version of the BYD Atto 8 is the rear-wheel-drive Design model, which features a single 340 kW electric motor – equivalent to 462 cv – with a maximum torque of 365 Nm. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 8 seconds. The 115 kWh battery delivers a range of 653 km, the highest in the range. At the top of the range is the Excellence AWD. A second motor on the front axle is added to the rear motor to provide all-wheel drive. Power rises to 570 kW, equivalent to 775 cv, whilst torque reaches 775 Nm and acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h takes 4.6 seconds. The battery capacity remains unchanged at 115 kWh, but the combined range stands at 602 km – a result attributable to the presence of the second motor and the all-wheel drive system. BYD Atto 8: battery and charging Both versions feature the second-generation 115 kWh Blade Battery. This is the same technology that the Chinese brand uses in its flagship models, characterised by a high level of safety and remarkable energy density. New to the European market is the introduction of Flash Charging technology: for the first time on a BYD car sold in Europe, the battery can go from 10 per cent to 97 per cent in just 9 minutes. This places the new Atto 8 amongst the models with the fastest charging times in its segment. The combination of such a generous battery, two clearly differentiated power levels and ultra-fast charging makes the Atto 8 one of the most technically innovative new models amongst the seven-seater electric SUVs currently on the market.

artigo.texto: On the morning of October 14, 2026, the Finance and Investment Newspaper, in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam, organized the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" in Hanoi . In his opening remarks at the workshop, Mr. Pham Van Hoanh, Editor-in-Chief of the Finance and Investment Newspaper, stated that, in pursuing the goal of green growth and a commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050, Vietnam is gradually perfecting policy tools and market mechanisms to mobilize resources for the green transition process. The launch of the domestic carbon market on June 29, 2026, not only marks the formation of a new market but also necessitates the completion of a financial ecosystem to ensure its efficient and sustainable development. If carbon exchanges are the infrastructure of the market, then credit policy, the banking system, and the capital market are the driving forces behind the green transition. Within this ecosystem, credit policy plays a leading role in channeling financial resources, supporting businesses and individuals to invest in emission reduction activities, and connecting sustainable development goals with the capital flows of the economy . In other words, green transformation ultimately must be translated into concrete investments: investments in cleaner technologies, more efficient energy use, changes in production processes, development of low-emission agriculture , forest protection and development, waste treatment, development of renewable energy, and building more sustainable supply chains… And for these projects to be implemented in practice, a financial system capable of identifying, valuing, allocating, and managing green capital flows is needed. The legal framework for Vietnam's carbon market is established by the 2020 Environmental Protection Law and further elaborated through various documents. Most recently, these include Decree 29/2026/ND-CP regulating the domestic carbon exchange; and Decree 112/2026/ND-CP regulating the international exchange of greenhouse gas emission reduction results and carbon credits. At the same time, Vietnam has also gained experience in commercializing emission reduction results on the international market. In March 2024, Vietnam received $51.5 million from the World Bank for the first time for 10.3 million tons of verified emission reduction results in the North Central Region Emission Reduction Program. According to the Editor-in-Chief of the Finance and Investment Newspaper, the trading of emission quotas on the trading system, which will be implemented from June 29, 2026, is not just the formation of a new market. More importantly, it creates a new approach to the economic value of emission reduction activities. However, we also need to realistically recognize that the formation of a new carbon market is only the beginning. A sustainable market needs more than just an exchange, commodities, and trading regulations. It also requires liquidity, data, verification mechanisms, trust between buyers and sellers, and a robust financial ecosystem to support market participants. At the same time, this green journey still raises many questions that need answers from all parties. What bottlenecks need to be addressed in the legal framework for the carbon market and the financial mechanisms for this market? How can green capital flow to the right projects? How can banks assess the opportunities and risks of a green project? How can businesses demonstrate the effectiveness of their transformation and attract capital not only from banks but also connect more closely with medium- and long-term capital sources from the capital market? And how can carbon value gradually become a reliable factor in the financial decisions of relevant stakeholders? The Editor-in-Chief of the Finance and Investment Newspaper emphasized that, to answer these questions, the Finance and Investment Newspaper is organizing today's seminar with the theme "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows". When businesses see the economic benefits of reducing emissions, banks and capital market institutions can manage capital flows effectively, investors can see value, and producers benefit proportionally, then the carbon market truly creates a new impetus for the economy. With that spirit in mind, the Finance and Investment Newspaper hopes that the conference will become a substantive forum for regulatory agencies, banks, businesses, experts, and organizations to exchange ideas, provide feedback, and seek feasible solutions.
