artigo.texto: Professor da Universidade Estadual da Califórnia em Fullerton compara a expansão digital à infraestrutura de óleo e gás. Quando um data center chega a uma cidade, a promessa costuma aparecer na forma de arrecadação, aluguel de terrenos e obras de infraestrutura. O impacto mais persistente, porém, pode ficar longe dos usuários que utilizam serviços de nuvem, videoconferências e plataformas digitais. Uma pesquisa conduzida por David Adams, professor associado de Administração Pública da California State University, Fullerton, nos Estados Unidos, aponta que a expansão desses complexos segue uma lógica semelhante à do setor de petróleo e gás: o benefício se espalha, enquanto parte importante do custo permanece no território onde a instalação funciona. A análise foi apresentada em entrevista publicada em 12 de outubro de 2026 e reúne estudos do professor sobre energia, água, infraestrutura e atuação do poder público. Segundo a California State University, Fullerton, havia cerca de 7.000 edifícios de data centers em operação, propostos ou em construção nos Estados Unidos em 1º de setembro de 2026, com aproximadamente 2.100 unidades operando em cerca de 1.400 locais. O lugar escolhido depende de cabos e eletricidade Os data centers são estruturas que concentram servidores responsáveis por armazenar, processar e distribuir dados. Para funcionar, precisam de conexão rápida com redes de fibra óptica e fornecimento contínuo de energia. Por isso, o levantamento de Adams identificou uma tendência de localização próxima às rotas de cabos já existentes e às áreas com oferta energética considerada mais conveniente. Essa escolha produz efeitos diferentes dos gerados por uma fábrica tradicional. O empreendimento pode recolher impostos sem necessariamente criar uma grande demanda por moradias, escolas, transporte coletivo ou contratação permanente de trabalhadores. Para municípios e condados, a combinação parece vantajosa: entra uma nova fonte de receita, mas a população não cresce na mesma proporção. O problema aparece quando a análise considera o ciclo completo da instalação. Um campus de grande porte pode consumir eletricidade equivalente à de uma cidade pequena. Além disso, muitos equipamentos precisam ser resfriados continuamente, o que pode ampliar a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos, especialmente em regiões sujeitas a secas. A água economizada pode reaparecer na usina O sistema de resfriamento cria uma escolha difícil. Quando o operador utiliza ar para reduzir o consumo direto de água, a instalação tende a demandar mais eletricidade. Se essa energia for produzida em uma usina que também utiliza água, parte do consumo apenas muda de lugar dentro da cadeia de fornecimento. Esse deslocamento torna o impacto menos visível para a comunidade. A água pode não ser retirada diretamente pelo data center, mas ainda ser necessária na produção da energia que mantém os servidores ligados. A consequência é uma disputa por recursos que envolve empresas, concessionárias, governos locais, órgãos reguladores e moradores. A comparação com o petróleo e gás se estende ao risco de abandono. Adams avalia que a evolução tecnológica pode tornar determinados complexos pouco úteis ou economicamente inviáveis, deixando uma infraestrutura de grande porte sem função. O paralelo é feito com poços abandonados e órfãos, cuja manutenção e recuperação podem acabar recaindo sobre o poder público. O caso do Arizona expõe a divisão de responsabilidades Um episódio em Tucson, no Arizona, mostra como a aprovação pode atravessar várias instituições. Um empreendimento associado à Amazon Web Services adquiriu terras no condado, mas encontrou resistência da cidade para obter acesso à água. O projeto foi redesenhado para utilizar resfriamento a ar e, depois, buscou autorização para a conexão elétrica junto à Arizona Corporation Commission, reguladora estadual do setor de energia. Enquanto moradores participaram de manifestações e o conselho municipal rejeitou o projeto, a comissão estadual aprovou o acordo de fornecimento de energia. Como o condado já havia negociado o terreno, as decisões tomadas por diferentes órgãos produziram um resultado que contrariava a posição expressa no município. A situação, segundo Adams, deixa o público diante de uma dúvida prática: qual governo tem, de fato, poder para interromper ou alterar a instalação? O pesquisador afirma que um único empreendimento pode envolver até 15 governos, com participação de estados, municípios, condados, distritos especiais e comissões reguladoras. A fragmentação dificulta a fiscalização e pode fazer com que moradores procurem a instituição errada para apresentar reclamações sobre água, energia, zoneamento ou impactos ambientais. O que a experiência pode ensinar à Amazônia O debate também interessa aos estados amazônicos, onde a expansão da infraestrutura digital convive com rios estratégicos, sistemas elétricos ainda desiguais e municípios com capacidade administrativa variada. Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Pará, Rondônia, Roraima e Tocantins podem enfrentar discussões semelhantes caso novos complexos de processamento de dados sejam planejados na região. A principal lição é que a autorização não deveria considerar apenas a área ocupada ou a arrecadação esperada. É necessário avaliar a origem da energia, a disponibilidade hídrica durante períodos de estiagem, a capacidade das redes de transmissão, o destino dos equipamentos ao fim da vida útil e quem pagará por eventuais reforços na infraestrutura. Na Amazônia, essa análise ganha peso porque o custo ambiental pode atingir comunidades que não são as principais beneficiárias dos serviços digitais. Uma instalação pode atender usuários de várias partes do país e do mundo, enquanto a demanda por água, eletricidade, estradas e terrenos se concentra em um município específico. artigo.texto: China monthly power battery installations 2024 2025 2026 - China's EV battery installations rose 14.7% year-on-year in September, with growth slowing for the second consecutive month. - LFP battery installations rose 19.9% year-on-year, accounting for 85.5% of the total, while ternary battery installations fell 10.9%. China's EV battery installations reached a fresh high for the year for the second consecutive month in September, but annual growth slowed further, with lithium iron phosphate batteries continuing to drive most of the increase. Domestic EV battery installations totaled 87.2 GWh in September, up 14.7% year-on-year and 10.4% from August, according to data released Thursday by the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance (CABIA). The figure surpassed August's 79.0 GWh to set a new monthly high for the year, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. However, annual growth slowed from 33.5% in July and 26.3% in August to its lowest level since April. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery installations reached 74.5 GWh in September, up 19.9% year-on-year and 10.3% month-on-month, also marking a high for the year. China monthly power battery installations: Ternary vs LFP LFP Ternary LFP batteries accounted for 85.5% of total installations, slightly below August's record 85.6%, ending a run of 3 consecutive months of record market share. Ternary battery installations totaled 12.3 GWh in September, down 10.9% year-on-year but up 11.7% month-on-month, ending 3 consecutive months of sequential declines. Their share edged up to 14.1% from 14.0% in August, but remained well below the year-earlier level. In the first 9 months of the year, domestic EV battery installations totaled 576.3 GWh, up 16.7% year-on-year, slightly slower than the 17.0% growth recorded in the first 8 months. LFP battery installations reached 477.2 GWh over the period, up 18.5% year-on-year and accounting for 82.8% of the total. Ternary battery installations totaled 97.9 GWh, up 7.3%, with a 17.0% share. CABIA said growth in installations during the first 3 quarters was supported by the expansion of commercial new energy vehicles (NEVs) and higher battery capacity per NEV, with battery-electric trucks and special-purpose vehicles making significant contributions. Alongside the increase in installations, combined production of power and energy storage batteries reached 237.8 GWh in September, up 57.3% year-on-year and 0.3% month-on-month. China monthly battery production China monthly battery production: Ternary vs LFP LFP Ternary Combined sales of the 2 battery categories totaled 222.7 GWh, up 52.0% year-on-year but down 0.2% from August. Sales growth for energy storage batteries continued to significantly outpace that of power batteries. Power battery sales reached 149.2 GWh, up 35.0% year-on-year, while energy storage battery sales rose 104.4% to 73.5 GWh, accounting for 33.0% of total sales. Combined exports of power and energy storage batteries totaled 44.0 GWh in September, up 64.5% year-on-year and 3.7% month-on-month, equivalent to 19.7% of sales. China monthly power battery and energy storage battery exports 2024 2025 2026 Power battery exports reached 28.4 GWh, up 60.9% year-on-year and 14.9% month-on-month. Energy storage battery exports totaled 15.6 GWh, up 71.4% year-on-year but down 11.9% from August. China monthly power battery exports 2024 2025 2026 China monthly battery exports: Ternary vs LFP LFP Ternary China monthly energy storage battery exports 2024 2025 2026 In the first 9 months, combined exports of the 2 categories reached 302.9 GWh, up 51.6% year-on-year. Power battery exports rose 54.7% to 199.7 GWh, while energy storage battery exports increased 45.9% to 103.2 GWh. CABIA said power battery exports grew faster than energy storage battery exports in the first 3 quarters, mainly driven by rising vehicle exports and automakers' overseas factories gradually starting production. The 7 Chinese companies in the top 10 held a combined 73.3% share of the global EV battery market.

artigo.texto: Los Angeles plans floating solar and iron-flow battery system on Encino Reservoir to generate and store electricity Los Angeles is pushing its green shift forward by deploying floating solar on a reservoir. The United States is actively pursuing its national climate goals to meet rising energy demands more sustainably. However, urban regions with the highest consumption and emissions struggle to raise renewable capacity. Ultimately, unused municipal reservoirs and floating photovoltaics can unlock local energy resilience, meeting rising demands more sustainably. Spatial limitations are a major bottleneck, which is why developers are turning to floatovoltaics. Will Los Angeles’ latest approved project serve as a vital blueprint for other cities? How U.S. cities struggle to progress in the clean transition The United States currently ranks 19th in the global renewable energy transition. Domestically, clean power generation accounts for 30% of total electricity supply. Despite this, the nation is still far from reaching its national climate mandates. This is because urban centers have concentrated, dense populations, industrial hubs, commercial infrastructure, and heavy transit networks. Cities’ extreme density accounts for more than 70 percent of global energy-related carbon emissions. In the U.S., electricity consumption and building operations drive roughly 40 percent of national greenhouse gas output. As industrial and transport electrification and AI data center infrastructure expand, power consumption will continue to surge. Consequently, energy demand is rising much faster than new power generation capacity can be added. This leads to a growing supply gap, threatening the stability of regional grids. To bridge this gap, rapid deployment of utility-scale renewable energy sources is key. Unfortunately, urban planners face significant spatial and economic hurdles. Structural obstacles faced in cities trying to go green Solar power has become a core pillar in America’s renewable energy shift, with capacity reaching major milestones in recent years. Currently, the nation’s total operational solar capacity is 299.4 gigawatts. However, this generation is highly concentrated in specific regions, and cities still face challenges raising solar production. Traditional utility-scale photovoltaic facilities require vast open land, roughly 5 to 10 acres per megawatt. Densely built urban regions cannot provide this footprint. Furthermore, U.S. permitting bottlenecks slow solar growth. This is because developments must navigate overcrowded grid distribution, complex zoning laws, and historic preservation rules. Additionally, limited undeveloped real estate in cities commands a premium market price. These high land acquisition costs make urban ground-mounted photovoltaic projects uneconomical. As a result, urban planners are forced to turn to dual-use infrastructure like floatovoltaics to generate localized clean power. In Los Angeles, a floating solar pilot project has been approved after the LADWP filed a formal Notice of Determination. The floatovoltaics project on the Encino Reservoir California’s solar-and-storage portfolio is set to increase, with the San Fernando Valley region of Los Angeles leading in innovation. A new floating solar project will be constructed directly on the Encino Reservoir. LADWP owns and manages the 960-acre site, which means private land acquisition was completely bypassed. The project will comprise a 5-megawatt floatovoltaic array covering 10 acres of the reservoir surface. There will also be a 30-kilowatt mounted solar system spanning 4,000 square feet on adjacent land. A 5-megawatt iron-flow battery system will ensure long-duration energy storage. Meanwhile, on-site transformers, inverters, and switchgear will be connected directly to an existing distribution line. The project achieved fast-tracked approval Regulatory review was quickly completed by filing a Mitigated Negative Declaration under CEQA. This bypassed a lengthy Environmental Impact Report. Environmental evaluations confirmed no significant ecological impact. By bypassing standard zoning delays, construction can proceed rapidly. With the environmental clearance completed, LADWP can proceed to procurement and development. The goal is to operationalize this project as a core clean energy pilot. The combined deployment of floating solar and local battery storage creates a vital blueprint for other urban regions nationwide. Ultimately, unused municipal reservoirs and floating photovoltaics can unlock local energy resilience, meeting rising demands more sustainably. Anke Maree is a writer with a clear and engaging editorial style. Her work focuses on making complex topics accessible, informative, and relevant for readers across different areas of interest.

artigo.texto: Uma proposta de data centers estimada em US$ 9 bilhões é apresentada para o Brasil, com foco nas vantagens do Nordeste. A discussão envolve energia, conectividade, água e empregos, mas a fonte não identifica responsáveis, município, cronograma ou documentos que permitam confirmar o investimento e suas condições concretas de execução. Um projeto de data centers avaliado em US$ 9 bilhões é apresentado como possibilidade de ampliar a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial no Brasil. A proposta coloca em discussão o aproveitamento de energia renovável no Nordeste, mas deixa sem números definidos o consumo de água e os empregos permanentes. As informações aparecem em vídeo do canal Dax Experiments, publicado em 9 de outubro de 2026. A apresentação descreve um complexo ainda em planejamento, sem identificar as empresas responsáveis, a localização exata ou a documentação que sustentaria o valor anunciado. US$ 9 bilhões aparecem como estimativa, sem detalhamento do investimento O montante de US$ 9 bilhões é associado pela fonte a uma cidade de servidores voltada à inteligência artificial. Não há discriminação dos gastos com terrenos, construção, equipamentos, transmissão elétrica ou conexão. - Triciclo elétrico leva duas caixas de compras e ainda sobra espaço, mas o dono mantém uma restrição quando o assunto é transportar o filho - Geólogo aposentado de 78 anos cria seis lagos em terreno onde a horta morreu por falta de água e transforma a rotina da propriedade - Rocha vulcânica abundante no Brasil pode virar vergalhão para concreto, mas o desafio de substituir o aço vai muito além de evitar ferrugem - Casa que consome 200 kWh por mês pode precisar de seis baterias de lítio no exemplo apresentado, mas sair da rede exige mais cuidados A ausência desses detalhes impede tratar o valor como dinheiro já aplicado ou financiamento confirmado. O relato tampouco apresenta etapas contratadas, licenças ou datas para início da operação. Cidade de servidores significa um complexo industrial A expressão cidade de data centers descreve um agrupamento de prédios com infraestrutura digital. O conjunto imaginado reúne servidores, sistemas de resfriamento, acessos e instalações elétricas. Esses espaços processam informações e sustentam serviços usados longe de suas instalações. A localização das máquinas, por si só, não define quem contratará a capacidade disponível ou onde ficará a maior parte dos benefícios econômicos. Inteligência artificial exige processamento durante treinamento e uso O treinamento de modelos utiliza processadores especializados para realizar grandes volumes de cálculos. Depois dessa etapa, os sistemas continuam trabalhando para responder às solicitações dos usuários. A geração dessas respostas é chamada de inferência. Em aplicações com muitos acessos simultâneos, ela mantém uma demanda contínua por processamento e ajuda a explicar o interesse em ampliar a infraestrutura. Energia renovável é uma das vantagens atribuídas ao Nordeste A fonte relaciona a atração de data centers à presença de geração eólica e solar no Nordeste. A lógica apresentada é aproximar um consumidor de funcionamento contínuo das áreas produtoras de energia. O argumento inclui o aproveitamento de momentos em que a geração precisa ser limitada pelo sistema elétrico. Essa possibilidade, porém, não comprova que o empreendimento teria abastecimento garantido, conexão disponível ou contratos suficientes para funcionar. Cabos submarinos ajudam a explicar o destaque de Fortaleza Fortaleza, no Ceará, aparece na apresentação como um ponto relevante de chegada de cabos submarinos. Essas conexões integram a infraestrutura que permite transportar dados entre o Brasil e outros continentes. A combinação de conectividade e oferta elétrica é apresentada como uma vantagem regional. A menção à capital cearense, entretanto, não identifica o município onde o complexo de US$ 9 bilhões seria instalado. Resfriamento coloca o consumo de água entre as principais dúvidas Os servidores liberam calor durante o funcionamento e precisam de refrigeração. A apresentação descreve alternativas que utilizam ar, circulação de líquido e evaporação, com diferentes exigências de operação. O consumo de água depende da solução escolhida e das condições do empreendimento. A fonte não informa qual tecnologia seria adotada, de onde viria o abastecimento ou qual volume seria necessário. Terrenos e redes de transmissão também afetam o entorno A implantação de grandes instalações exige acesso, espaço e ligação à infraestrutura elétrica. Essas necessidades podem alterar o uso do território e envolver áreas próximas de comunidades e atividades agrícolas. O relato defende diálogo e transparência sobre esses impactos, mas não identifica comunidades atingidas nem apresenta estudos específicos do projeto. Assim, os conflitos são discutidos como riscos a avaliar, sem comprovação de um caso concreto nessa proposta. Empregos da construção não equivalem às vagas permanentes A fase de obras pode demandar profissionais de construção civil, montagem elétrica, instalação de equipamentos e logística. Esses empregos estão ligados à implantação e não necessariamente continuam depois da entrega. A operação dos data centers é descrita como automatizada e dependente de equipes especializadas. Sem estimativas separadas por etapa, não é possível quantificar os empregos duradouros nem a parcela que poderia ser ocupada por trabalhadores locais. Formação profissional e fornecedores locais entram na discussão dos benefícios A apresentação aponta capacitação, pesquisa e participação de fornecedores regionais como caminhos para ampliar o retorno econômico no entorno. Essas medidas aproximariam o investimento das atividades e necessidades locais. A instalação no Brasil também é associada à possibilidade de ampliar a capacidade de processamento em território nacional. Esse benefício potencial não esclarece, sozinho, quem controlaria os equipamentos, os serviços ou os dados processados. A distrib

artigo.texto: A infraestrutura de nuvem da Yandex, uma das maiores empresas de tecnologia da Rússia, enfrenta uma grave crise após ataques com drones danificarem três de seus data centers. Os incidentes, registrados em outubro de 2026, provocaram interrupções operacionais e instabilidade em serviços de armazenamento, computação e inteligência artificial, levantando preocupações sobre a capacidade da empresa de manter suas operações durante emergências físicas. As instalações atingidas ficam em Sasovo, Kaluga e Vladimir. Entre os serviços afetados estão componentes do Yandex Cloud, o armazenamento compatível com S3, o Kubernetes e o Yandex Disk. Clientes também relataram falhas em requisições, dificuldades para baixar arquivos e respostas HTTP de erro. Diante do cenário, a empresa recomendou que os clientes recorressem a seus planos de recuperação de desastres enquanto a infraestrutura permanecesse instável. O episódio expõe uma fragilidade importante da computação em nuvem: embora os serviços pareçam funcionar de maneira virtual e distribuída, eles dependem de instalações físicas que podem ser danificadas. Para empresas que hospedam aplicações críticas, a crise reforça a necessidade de manter backups independentes, redundância geográfica e planos de continuidade operacional. Ataques com drones interrompem operações em três data centers da Yandex A sequência de ataques atingiu três instalações importantes da Yandex em poucos dias, reduzindo a capacidade disponível para executar aplicações e atender às solicitações dos clientes. A empresa, frequentemente comparada ao Google pelo conjunto de serviços digitais que oferece na Rússia, opera plataformas de busca, armazenamento, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. A interrupção simultânea de diferentes instalações representa um desafio maior do que a falha isolada de um servidor. Quando um data center inteiro deixa de operar, milhares de componentes podem ficar indisponíveis, incluindo servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de rede. A recuperação também depende das condições físicas do local e da possibilidade de transferir as cargas de trabalho para outras instalações. Sasovo, Kaluga e Vladimir foram atingidas em sequência Os incidentes foram registrados em três localidades russas durante outubro de 2026. Em Sasovo, na região de Riazan, um ataque ocorrido na noite de 7 para 8 de outubro provocou danos graves e levou ao desligamento da instalação. O local abriga parte da infraestrutura de computação utilizada pela Yandex, inclusive em atividades relacionadas à inteligência artificial. Em Kaluga, outro ataque, registrado em 9 de outubro, danificou módulos do data center e comprometeu parte de sua capacidade operacional. Embora a interrupção tenha sido parcial, a perda de recursos contribuiu para aumentar a pressão sobre a infraestrutura restante. Já em Vladimir, um ataque em 11 de outubro levou à suspensão das operações da instalação. A sequência dos incidentes reduziu a margem disponível para redistribuir serviços e manter a capacidade habitual da plataforma. Os episódios também levantaram preocupações sobre a concentração de recursos computacionais em instalações sujeitas a riscos físicos. Mesmo quando uma empresa mantém vários data centers, a redundância pode ser insuficiente se os locais compartilharem dependências ou se a capacidade remanescente não suportar a demanda. Yandex Cloud entra em modo de operação de emergência Durante a crise, a Yandex reconheceu dificuldades operacionais e orientou clientes a utilizar seus planos alternativos de recuperação de desastres, conhecidos pela sigla DR, de Disaster Recovery. Esse tipo de recomendação indica que a recuperação pode exigir mais do que uma manutenção convencional. A perda de instalações inteiras demanda avaliar equipamentos, reconstruir capacidade computacional, verificar a integridade dos dados e restabelecer as dependências necessárias para os serviços voltarem a funcionar. A ausência de uma previsão definitiva para a recuperação integral também dificulta o planejamento das empresas afetadas. Sem uma estimativa confiável, administradores precisam decidir se aguardam a normalização, transferem aplicações ou ativam ambientes alternativos. O cenário demonstra por que planos de contingência devem prever interrupções prolongadas, em vez de considerar apenas falhas temporárias de rede ou indisponibilidade de componentes individuais. Kubernetes, S3 e APIs enfrentam instabilidade A crise atingiu diferentes componentes do Yandex Cloud, plataforma utilizada para hospedar aplicações, armazenar dados e executar cargas de trabalho empresariais. Entre os serviços citados nos relatos sobre a interrupção estão Kubernetes, Object Storage compatível com S3, Container Registry, Console, APIs, IAM e serviços de bancos de dados. Também foram relatados problemas em componentes relacionados à inteligência artificial, incluindo o AI Studio. Os efeitos variam conforme o serviço e suas dependências. O Kubernetes, por exemplo, pode reiniciar contêineres e redistribuir aplicações entre nós disponíveis, mas não consegue compensar automaticamente a perda de toda uma instalação quando faltam capacidade computacional, armazenamento ou componentes essenciais do plano de controle. O armazenamento compatível com S3 também merece atenção. Muitas aplicações utilizam esse tipo de serviço para guardar documentos, arquivos de usuários, registros e cópias de segurança. Se as operações de leitura e gravação falham, o problema pode se propagar para sistemas que dependem desses dados. Da mesma forma, a instabilidade nas APIs e no IAM pode prejudicar a autenticação, o gerenciamento de recursos e a execução de operações automatizadas. Assim, uma interrupção física pode afetar tanto os usuários finais quanto as equipes responsáveis pela administração da infraestrutura. artigo.texto: I am writing today to address an integral piece of our local and national discourse: the debate over data centers. I am writing to challenge a recent letter I read in the local newspaper: “Nobody wants a data center in their backyard” (Sept. 8, Morgan Hill Times and Gilroy Dispatch). I respect the author’s perspective; many residents do not want data centers in their community, as there are negative externalities associated, such as water and power usage and the unsightliness of the power facilities associated with it. However, I believe that when it comes to such a contentious issue, we must tread carefully and treat the subject with the nuance it deserves. This article quickly served to attack the character of those in favor of data centers saying “the people who want the data centers are the same ones who never want them in their own neighborhood.” I, for one, can unequivocally refute this—I would love for more data centers to be built in San Martin, where I live, and Gilroy, where I was born and went to elementary school. Data centers are an opportunity to employ both blue collar and white collar workers—something that Gilroy would gladly take more of. Counties which host data centers experience a rise in local employment, total wages, median household income, business growth, construction revenue and tax revenue. I would love this for the South Valley, where I grew up, and in which not a single family member of mine worked, because of the lower wages compared to the rest of the Bay Area. The article continues to poke at Gilroy Mayor Greg Bozzo, and in reference to why he was allowing the data centers to be built, said he was “looking forward to an early and comfortable retirement.” The insinuation that Bozzo is looking out for his personal interest is a blatant attack on his character. As for how this got passed through without input from other stakeholders, the approved facility is more than a half mile away from the nearest residential area. The data center is being built in an area inhabited by the 145 Gilroy Outlets and other big box retailers and businesses. While I agree community input should be vital in a project like this, it is understandable that the Gilroy City Council would approve a project like this in an area which has hundreds of neighboring businesses, and no housing in close proximity. There are 107 data centers currently operating in Santa Clara County, and I contend this is a great thing. Data centers store data such as personal photos and database information for businesses. They stream media, like movies and TV shows into our homes. They help with cybersecurity, which protects local and corporate businesses from data breaches. They power online services, such as social media, online banking and the online print of the Morgan Hill Times, Gilroy Dispatch and Hollister Free Lance. They make our modern lives possible. When it comes to data centers, there are many issues that will arise. Seeing them in the community we live in and love can be difficult. It can seem that big tech companies and powers outside our control are dictating how our communities change. I am writing to say that these are entirely valid criticisms, but there are positive changes that come along with their construction, and they can serve to better our lives and the generations in the South Valley after us. Ellis Richardson San Martin

artigo.texto: MESA – “The noise and the pollution is happening now,” Ana Marshall said. “I lost count how many times I had to take my kid (to the doctor) for sinus infections this year.” Marshall, her husband and son live 150 feet from the Menlo Digital data center being built in Ahwatukee. Since April 2026, she has sent about 10 noise complaints to the City of Phoenix regarding construction of the center. Each one has been acknowledged but none has been resolved, she said. Dust from construction, noise pollution, excessive water use, health concerns, strains on the power grid, dropping property values and increasing temperatures are worries voiced by people in the Ahwatukee Community Alliance, a nonprofit organization that opposes the Menlo Digital data center. On Aug. 31, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes called for a statewide pause in the approval and construction of future data centers. She hosted a town hall meeting Wednesday, Oct. 14, to address the fears of Arizonans. Many attendees were concerned residents who live in Ahwatukee and members of the community alliance. Several speakers shared their experiences with living so close to a data center being constructed – many saying it’s not what they planned for when they moved to Ahwatukee. “There’s been instances where we measure 110 decibels inside my son’s bedroom,” Marshall said. “I’m not talking in the afternoon. I’m talking early.” Compared to an everyday noise, 110 decibels is equivalent to being front row at a rock concert or standing arm’s length from an operating chainsaw. Lisa Everett, an attendee at the town hall, mentioned that data centers are usually built in industrial areas and expressed concern that misinformation is spreading about them. “A data center uses less water than a subdivision in the same area,” Everett said. “I understand the frustration. I understand it’s new, but I’m asking you: Is this just a fashionable thing to be against data centers? Are we really going to have honest conversations?” Located at East Thistle Landing Drive near a residential neighborhood, the Menlo Digital project is scheduled to open in the first quarter of 2027, according to U.S. Data Centers. The project will include five buildings on 38 acres of land. It is expected to use 257 megawatts of power, according to U.S. Data Centers. This isn’t the only data center already in the works. U.S. Data Centers, a project that tracks data centers across the US, says Phoenix is the second-largest data center hub in the United States and Arizona is home to 182 data centers. Sixteen of those data centers are under construction and 53 are in the planning stages. According to U.S. Data Centers, the top users of data centers in Arizona are Arizona Public Service, with 11 sites, and Salt River Project with 10 sites. Other planned data centers include locations in Buckeye, Page, Tucson and more. The Buckeye Technology Park data center, owned by Tract, is set to take up 2,069 acres and be equipped to use 1,800 megawatts of power. The largest operational data center in Arizona is Compass Datacenters, located in Goodyear, and takes up 200 acres and 212 megawatts of power. In June, Gov. Katie Hobbs signed a three-year suspension of data center tax credits, prohibiting the Arizona Commerce Authority from accepting applications for exemption from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2029. Mayes called for full disclosure by companies who make agreements with cities. “Data center development and operations should be transparent without unnecessary secrecy. Again, I’m concerned by data center developers asking local officials to ever enter into non-disclosure agreements, which limit the ability of local governments and the public to discuss the project with their constituents,” Mayes said. “There should be no nuisance. No business has the right to use its facilities in ways that disturb the well-being of citizens, the functions of local governments or the state.” According to a 2026 study by Arizona State University, heat pollution from data centers can increase residential neighborhood temperatures by 4 degrees Fahrenheit. Mayes said the centers put stress on local water supplies and can produce 94 decibels of noise, which is comparable to a factory floor with machinery. “It’s just so much noise,” said Annette Poleon, Marshall’s neighbor. “The other day, I realized I wasn’t hearing the noise. And what I think has happened is it’s become white noise to me now, which is worse because you don’t recognize the damage that’s occurring.” She said bright lights from construction disrupt her sleep, shining into her bedroom window early in the morning. She said she feels “very anxious for someone who is about to retire in what she thought was her forever home.” Tanja Kotowski, an Ahwatukee resident who spoke at the town hall, said her biggest concern is her health. “I told my doctor about the data center and how it’s going to be outfitted, the fact that it’s a hyperscale, 257-megawatt facility,” Kotowski said. “Do you know what he told me? He said, ‘You need to move. You need to move.’ My doctor said that.” While the town hall meeting was to address the entirety of data centers in Arizona, Mayes said she planned to visit Ahwatukee. “In Arizona, it is a tradition that any large development project gives back to the community it inevitably impacts, whether this is through taxes, fees, assessments, or even water storage credits,” Mayes said. “We must ensure that communities that host data centers and that choose to host data centers, indeed, all Arizonans benefit from their development.” According to a Congressional Research Service report on data center energy consumption published in May, a data center is a physical facility that houses and runs large computer systems. It usually holds multiple computer servers, data storage and network equipment that provide information technology infrastructure services for companies to manage large amounts of data. artigo.texto: Know Data centers prohibited under St. Pete’s city code According to Planning Director Derek Kilborn, data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. Standalone data centers, including large-scale facilities used to power artificial intelligence, are prohibited under St. Petersburg’s existing zoning regulations, according to a new memorandum from the city’s planning director. In an Oct. 9 memo to Mayor Ken Welch, Planning Director Derek Kilborn clarified how the facilities are classified under the city’s land development code. He concluded that data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. The determination comes as local governments across Pinellas County consider how to regulate the rapidly expanding industry amid concerns about electricity consumption, water resources and land availability. St. Petersburg’s zoning code contains a matrix identifying permitted land uses. Data centers are not included, and city regulations presume that uses not specifically listed are prohibited. Kilborn also examined whether data centers could qualify as similar to other permitted uses, including utility infrastructure, but found no sufficient justification. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Senate Bill 484, which recognizes the infrastructure and environmental challenges of large utility users, like data centers, last May. However, DeSantis preserved local authority over land use regulation in the same bill, which took effect July 1. Under the new law, a large-scale data center is defined as a facility with an anticipated monthly peak electrical demand of at least 50 megawatts at a single location. St. Petersburg’s determination applies to standalone data centers regardless of whether they meet that threshold. The memo follows similar actions elsewhere in Pinellas County. Pinellas Park approved a one-year moratorium on data center development in August. Additionally, in September, county commissioners adopted a resolution restricting large standalone facilities in unincorporated areas. Unlike those actions, St. Petersburg’s memorandum simply clarifies that standalone data centers are already prohibited under existing regulations, and presumably no further action is needed to overhaul the law. It was not indicated whether the city has received any recent data center development proposals, or whether officials are considering changes to the zoning code.

artigo.texto: Quang Ngai promove o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal. Com quase 826.000 hectares de floresta, Quang Ngai tem amplo espaço para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono, mas precisa concluir a coleta de dados, desenvolver projetos-piloto e atender aos padrões relevantes. Existe um grande potencial, mas é preciso atingir os padrões exigidos. Em entrevista ao jornal Indústria e Comércio, o Sr. Nguyen Van Nam, chefe do Departamento de Proteção Florestal da província de Quang Ngai , afirmou que a região possui atualmente 825.851,24 hectares de floresta, incluindo 603.996,71 hectares de floresta natural e 221.854,53 hectares de floresta plantada. A vasta área e a diversidade de tipos e condições florestais fornecem à província uma base sólida para pesquisar e implementar programas de redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolver créditos de carbono florestal. Segundo cálculos do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal, as florestas da província de Quang Ngai absorvem e armazenam aproximadamente 2 milhões de toneladas de carbono anualmente, o equivalente a 2 milhões de créditos de carbono. Atualmente, a província está implementando o Programa de Redução de Emissões para as regiões Centro-Sul e Planalto Central, no âmbito da iniciativa LEAF (Aliança de Liderança para a Redução de Emissões por meio do Financiamento Florestal Aprimorado), e a previsão é de que sejam alocados 1,13 milhão de créditos de carbono. Esses números demonstram o significativo potencial de Quang Ngai para acessar mecanismos financeiros vinculados à redução de emissões. No entanto, a quantidade estimada de carbono absorvida e armazenada anualmente não significa que toda ela tenha se tornado créditos reconhecidos e negociáveis. Para transformar esse potencial em valor econômico , a localidade precisa atender aos requisitos relativos aos métodos de cálculo, padrões aplicáveis, avaliação de resultados e procedimentos de concessão de créditos, conforme estipulado pela regulamentação. De acordo com o plano de implementação, Quang Ngai concentra-se em duas vertentes para o desenvolvimento do carbono florestal. A primeira é a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa por meio da gestão e proteção florestal sustentável, da limitação de incêndios florestais e do manejo adequado da vegetação rasteira durante o reflorestamento. Essas atividades contribuem para a proteção dos recursos florestais e também fornecem uma base para considerar a conversão dos resultados da redução de emissões em créditos de carbono. Por meio disso, as localidades podem acessar o apoio de organizações não governamentais e empresas internacionais. Você também pode gostar A segunda abordagem consiste em desenvolver projetos-piloto de carbono florestal de acordo com normas nacionais ou internacionais, com foco em florestas naturais e florestas recém-plantadas. Os resultados dos projetos serão avaliados e submetidos à autoridade competente para consideração e reconhecimento antes de participarem da negociação no mercado nacional de carbono. A implementação dessas duas abordagens ajuda a vincular a proteção florestal às metas de redução de emissões e a mobilizar recursos financeiros. No entanto, a eficácia depende não apenas da área florestal ou das emissões de carbono estimadas, mas também da capacidade de demonstrar resultados de redução de emissões, manter a qualidade da floresta e atender aos padrões de cada programa e projeto. Melhorar gradualmente as condições de concessão de crédito. Uma das condições essenciais para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal é o estabelecimento de um sistema de dados suficientemente confiável sobre a área, o estado e as características de cada tipo de floresta. Isso constitui a base para determinar os estoques de carbono, monitorar as mudanças nos recursos florestais e avaliar os resultados da implementação do projeto. Segundo informações, o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente da província de Quang Ngai está realizando um inventário e levantamento florestal, conforme orientação do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente e do Comitê Popular Provincial. Os resultados do inventário devem ser publicados em 2027. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Van Nam, os dados de levantamento e inventário florestal são a base para determinar os estoques de carbono. "A coleta completa desses dados é, portanto, crucial no processo de elaboração e implementação do projeto, além de auxiliar as localidades a avaliarem com mais precisão o potencial de cada área", afirmou o Sr. Nam. Além disso, Quang Ngai também está coordenando com o Instituto de Ciências Florestais do Vietnã para promover a construção de projetos-piloto de carbono florestal na Dak To Forestry Company Limited, na Kon Ray Forestry Company Limited e no Conselho de Gestão Florestal de Proteção de Dak Ha. As áreas piloto são selecionadas com base no tamanho da área florestal, na extensão da floresta e no nível de diversidade de tipos e condições florestais. O Sr. Nguyen Van Nam afirmou que os critérios para a seleção das áreas do projeto piloto incluem uma grande área de floresta e extensão de terra florestal; uma variedade de tipos florestais dentro do povoamento florestal, como florestas latifoliadas perenes, florestas de coníferas e florestas plantadas; e uma condição florestal rica, incluindo florestas ricas, medianamente ricas, pobres e severamente degradadas. artigo.texto: Canada Is Missing A Massive Battery Storage Opportunity October 15, 2026 | Electrification, Canada Katye Altieri says battery deployment is outpacing government plans as falling costs strengthen the case for solar, storage and domestic energy security Canada is giving battery storage too little attention as falling costs and rapid global deployment reshape electricity markets, according to Ember researcher Katye Altieri. In an interview with Energi Media, Altieri said the research organization found no official Canadian national storage target in its assessment of plans for 2030. Its tracker instead relies on an older Canadian energy scenario. “It’s a missed opportunity from a government perspective,” she said, adding that Canadians also stand to benefit from cleaner, affordable and reliable electricity. Batteries Outrun Government Planning Ember’s report finds that combined national storage targets have nearly tripled since COP29, reaching 822 gigawatts. They still fall well short of the international pledge to reach 1,500 GW by 2030. Actual construction is moving faster than those national commitments require. Global storage additions reached 118 GW in 2025, including 108 GW of batteries. Annual battery additions increased seventeenfold over five years. Altieri said batteries moved from roughly ten gigawatts of annual installations to more than one hundred in four years, compared with nine years for solar. China and the European Union account for about eighty per cent of the combined 2030 targets Ember tracks. Other markets, including the United States, are installing batteries without comparable national targets. Solar And Storage Strengthen Energy Security Batteries allow electricity generated during sunny hours to serve demand later in the day, reducing curtailment and improving the usefulness of solar generation. Altieri pointed to California’s success shifting daytime solar electricity into the evening. She also challenged the assumption that Canada’s climate leaves little room for these technologies, noting successful applications in Nordic countries. Energy security has become a central motivation for renewable investment, she said. Countries can use domestic solar and wind resources to reduce exposure to volatile imported fuel prices and geopolitical disruptions. Equipment imports still involve global supply chains. However, buying generating equipment differs from continuously importing the fuel needed to operate an electricity system. Planning Must Follow The Economics Lithium-ion batteries remain dominant despite growing interest in sodium-ion and other technologies. Altieri said substantial cost declines are already supporting deployment with commercially available equipment. The challenge is increasingly how to integrate storage with generation, transmission and changing demand. “The economics for storage are fantastic, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s being installed in the right places,” she said. National targets can help governments coordinate investment, identify locations where batteries offer the greatest value, and give investors clearer signals. The report makes a case for clearer direction while acknowledging that market forces already drive construction. Canada Faces A Different Electricity Future Altieri cautioned against assuming that Canada’s historical electricity strengths will automatically meet future needs. Expanding the system requires decisions about new resources, infrastructure and technologies. Past reliance on established sources does not settle those choices. She also suggested that pressure for change can come from households seeking affordable solar and battery systems, better grid access and regulations that enable adoption. For Canada, the issue is whether planning recognizes the technologies changing electricity economics elsewhere. Altieri argues storage deserves a much larger role in that discussion as governments prepare for growing demand and a more electrified economy.

artigo.texto: NDSU forum tackles data centers, AI FARGO, N.D. (Valley News Live) - Dozens of people attended a forum at NDSU’s Memorial Union Wednesday night looking for answers about artificial intelligence and data centers. Applied Digital is building a data center in Harwood, with another proposed in Harmony Township by Geronimo Power. Students weigh in on AI’s role Michael Nelson, a student at NDSU, said he has been interested in data center infrastructure for the last couple of years. “I’ve been interested in data center kind of infrastructure the last couple of years. North Dakota is a big component to that. I just think it’s beneficial for everybody to kind of learn a little bit more. Whatever side you’re on of it, I think learning about the issue is highly valuable,” Nelson said. Will electric bills go up? Experts say there is not a one-size-fits-all answer to whether the data centers will lead to higher electric bills. Officials at Cass County Electric Cooperative said they don’t want to interrupt service because of data centers. Paul Matthys, President and CEO of Cass County Electric Cooperative, said the cooperative has large investments to make in generation for its members. “If we can take some of the revenue from those large data loads and help pay for some of the costs that we will have to incur, to build new power generation for our legacy load, that will help drive down pressure on rates,” Matthys said. AI’s growing presence While discussion around data centers continues, AI continues to become more popular. Robert Mayo, a Research Specialist at the Challey Institute for Global Innovation and Growth, said AI systems can function as tutors. “Those systems can function as very effective user-friendly tutors. It’s also been bad because it allows students to basically plagiarize sometimes in a way they shouldn’t,” Mayo said. AI is impacting NDSU students’ everyday lives. “It’s kind of a double-edged sword. You can become dependent on it obviously to some degree, just like I think everybody does. But if you use it the right way, you can create study sets for yourself,” Nelson said. Cooperative says it must adapt quickly As data centers multiply, Cass County Electric Cooperative says it has to adapt just as fast. “We have to evaluate, make decisions and ensure that we’re not taking any unnecessary risks for the cooperative or our members,” Matthys said. artigo.texto: A re-engineered lead-acid battery system aimed at helping businesses cut power bills is now operating in Geelong, with its developer seeking to make energy storage cheaper and easier to install. New Zealand energy storage company ArcActive has switched on the pilot at Deakin’s new Renewable Grid-Connected Battery Testing Facility at its Waurn Ponds campus, with support from Origin Energy. Related article: Partnership to accelerate Allegro Energy’s flow battery tech ArcActive aims to make battery storage cheaper and easier to install, allowing more businesses to store solar electricity for later use and buy less power when prices are high. Its system builds on lead-acid technology already used to support critical infrastructure, including telecommunications, hospitals, and data centres. ArcActive has redesigned the batteries’ internal structure, using a fabric framework to support the material that stores and releases energy. The design aims to extend cycling life while preserving low cost, making lead-acid more attractive for everyday energy storage. The pilot operates within Deakin’s renewable energy microgrid, which provides electricity generation and storage for operational use. ArcActive CEO Stuart McKenzie said the pilot was a step forward in making battery storage accessible to more businesses. “The cost of installing a battery goes beyond the battery itself. Businesses also need to account for engineering work, approvals, insurance and safety measures. If they don’t know what their site will need or how much it will cost, they can be reluctant to invest.” McKenzie said using lead-acid technology offered a familiar starting point. “It is a technology that engineers, approval authorities and insurers already know. There are established pathways for approving and insuring these installations, which is an important starting point when you want to put batteries alongside businesses and occupied buildings.” ArcActive is targeting commercial and industrial businesses that could benefit from storage but face costs and complexity that can prevent projects from proceeding. Related article: Sicona acquires US firm and New Orleans battery facility “We want businesses to be able to deploy storage through a more standardised, repeatable process, with greater confidence about the cost, the approval requirements and the financial return,” McKenzie said.

artigo.texto: Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with members of the government via videoconference in Moscow on June 23, 2026. | Gavriil Grigorov/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Ukraine’s strikes on data centers inside Russia aimed to disrupt military planning and communication services. There were also reports of another kind of disruption: to customers waiting for their dinner from food-delivery apps. Kyiv’s drone strikes on three Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir saw delays and interruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex's cloud infrastructure, including e-commerce, digital payment platforms and apps of food delivery and car services. Ukrainian drones on Wednesday targeted a major Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region, though a senior company executive said it hadn’t affected operations. After the strikes on Russian data centers, Kyiv noted that Moscow has already repeatedly targeted its digital infrastructure. “Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that two can play this game,” a senior official familiar with the operation told POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. Advertisement The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy. The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill. Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia. “To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov. Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences. “These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO. Advertisement When servers become targets Data centers have entered the crosshairs of other recent armed conflicts. During the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran earlier this year, drone strikes hit three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. Since data centers can serve civilian and military purposes simultaneously, the legal status of targeting them is far from straightforward. Kubo Mačák, an expert on international humanitarian law, said a data center must meet two conditions to qualify as a military objective under the Geneva Conventions: it must make an effective contribution to military operations and destroying it must offer a “definite military advantage.” A delivery robot from Russian tech giant Yandex moves through Moscow. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images “If you know that they are storing military intelligence or that they're using the data center to power military artificial intelligence tools,” Mačák said, there could be grounds to consider it a military objective. Following the most recent strikes of the Yandex data centers, users on social media platform X reported a sudden drop in automated bot activity, including from accounts associated with pro-Russian, pro-Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narratives. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on the reports to boast that the strikes had made social media less toxic, even as independent researchers and national research institutes found no evidence they specifically disrupted any Russian disinformation campaigns. Advertisement Mačák said that even if a data center is being used to “let's say, run some trolls or these bot farms to interfere with elections abroad … that would not be sufficient.” In other words, hosting propaganda bots does not, by itself, make a data center a lawful military target. The dual-use quandary has often focused on the targeting of energy infrastructure, which has been frequent in the Russia-Ukraine war. On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for rising fuel prices. He has since called for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, although the existence of any ceasefire agreement remains disputed. As data centers become increasingly central to national economies, they will become more consequential targets. A senior NATO official granted anonymity to discuss the matter told POLITICO that data centers are already considered potential targets and that the alliance is factoring their vulnerability into its planning. NATO allies recognize that their data centers could come under attack in a conflict, the official said: “We would get it in a fight.” Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: BYD Energy Storage showcased its MC-Cube-XT and BYD Haohan BESS at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 The former product features 12 cube-type cabinets in a 7,550 × 2,438 × 2,896 mm container frame, while the latter combines 4 cubes on a common base frame The company also displayed its Battery-Box HVB/HVE/HVM+ storage, and Power-Box residential hybrid inverters BYD Energy Storage, the energy storage arm of well-known Chinese car maker BYD, showcased its latest product lineup at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 for utility and residential customers. The company displayed its MC-Cube-XT and BYD Haohan utility battery energy storage systems (BESS), both built around long, thin, and blade-shaped battery packs. Traditional BESS accommodates multiple battery stacks within a 20- or 40-ft container. Instead, the displayed products combine multiple cabinet-based storage sections within a container frame. MC-Cube-XT consists of 12 cube-type cabinets and features 1,980 Ah blade-type batteries, for a total storage capacity of 6,437 kWh. It measures 7,550 × 2,438 × 2,896 mm (W × D × H). In comparison, BYD Haohan uses 4 cubes with a higher battery capacity (2,710 Ah) for a total storage capacity of 14,568 kWh. The company says its size is comparable to a standard 20 ft container. The two BESS systems have a rated full-load DC power output of 1,608 kW and 1,820 kW, respectively. BYD also showcased its GC Flux series bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) station at its booth. The above products can be charged or discharged from or to the grid via this PCS, offering a maximum rated capacity of 7,000 kW. The company specifies a maximum conversion efficiency of 99% and an overload capacity of up to 300% for 10 seconds. For residential applications, the company introduced its Battery-Box HVB/HVE/HVM+ storage and Power-Box hybrid inverters (3-phase) at the show.

artigo.texto: Publicado em 14 de outubro de 2026 A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) participou da primeira edição do Data Center World Brasil, realizada entre 6 e 8 de outubro em São Paulo. O evento reuniu líderes dos setores de data centers, infraestrutura digital, cloud computing e inteligência artificial para debater os principais desafios e oportunidades da transformação digital. A EPE foi representada pelo Consultor Técnico Daniel José Tavares de Souza no painel “Expansão na Era da IA: Decisões que Definem Bilhões em Investimentos”. Entre os principais debates esteve o papel estratégico da energia para a expansão da infraestrutura digital. Em sua participação, Daniel destacou que conectividade, profissionais qualificados e investimentos financeiros não são suficientes para viabilizar um projeto de Data Center sem a disponibilidade de energia e de margem de conexão. A transmissão e a geração de energia aparecem como pontos fundamentais para acompanhar o crescimento acelerado do setor. O principal desafio apresentado pela EPE está na diferença entre os cronogramas de implantação. Um grande data center pode começar a operar em dois ou três anos. Já uma obra de transmissão exige pelo menos cinco anos de execução, considerando a complexidade de construção de linhas de transmissão e subestações, além dos processos de licenciamento ambiental. Quando são incluídos os estudos e o planejamento, o intervalo entre a decisão de expansão e a entrada em operação da infraestrutura pode alcançar sete anos. “Enquanto isso, os data centers estão entrando”, observou Daniel. Apenas para o estado de São Paulo, já foram recomendados mais de R$ 7 bilhões de investimentos em obras de transmissão para viabilizar margem de conexão para cerca de 7 GW no total. Além de São Paulo, também foi recomendado pela EPE um montante de R$ 5,7 bilhões em obras de transmissão na região Nordeste, com o intuito de viabilizar margem de conexão de 4 GW para grandes cargas. Por fim, foi reforçada a mensagem de que a EPE mantém a interlocução com grandes players de data centers e segue acompanhando os processos de acesso, como a PNAST, para identificar os locais de maior procura e avaliar a probabilidade de concretização dos empreendimentos, que são importantes insumos para os estudos realizados pela EPE. 14/10/2026 - A EPE publica o Roadmap para Fortalecimento da Resiliência do Setor Elétrico Brasileiro em Resposta às Mudanças Climáticas, estudo que consolida uma avaliação sistêmica dos potenciais impactos das mudanças do clima sobre o sistema elétrico brasileiro e propõe estratégias e medidas para ampliar sua capacidade de adaptação. 14/10/2026 - A EPE, o ONS e a CCEE realizarão online, no dia 21 de outubro, das 9h às 12h30, o Workshop sobre os Processos de Previsão de Carga, voltado aos representantes dos agentes do setor elétrico. O evento será transmitido pela plataforma Webex. 13/10/2026 - A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) publica o Informe Técnico “Iluminação Pública como Vetor de Transformação Digital e Eficiência Energética nas Cidades”, que apresenta um panorama do setor no Brasil e propõe caminhos para ampliar a eficiência, a qualidade dos serviços e a integração da iluminação pública ao planejamento urbano e energético. 13/10/2026 - Pela primeira vez, a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) disponibiliza em inglês o Informe de Monitoramento sobre a Política de Exploração e Produção (E&P) de Petróleo e Gás, edição de 2026, e seu respectivo Fact Sheet. 09/10/2026 - Estudo sobre fungibilidade e precificação de certificados de descarbonização, selecionado entre os três melhores trabalhos da ROG.e na categoria Diversificação Energética e Soluções de Baixo Carbono, ajuda a entender o que o mercado de biometano pode aprender com a experiência do CBIO

artigo.texto: Andhra Pradesh has issued a tender for 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of standalone BESS with four-hour storage duration Winning bidders will sign 12-year BESPAs with state discoms Projects need to be set up across three locations under a build-own-operate model Andhra Pradesh has launched a call for the deployment of 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity at selected project locations across the state. As the bid coordinator, the Andhra Pradesh Power Coordination Committee (APPCC) may procure up to 25% additional BESS capacity for each project under a green shoe option, amounting to 125 MW/500 MWh each for Projects 1 and 3, and 50 MW/200 MWh for Project 2. The tender documents state that the additional capacity will be included in the contracted capacity if allocated. To be set up under a build-own-operate (BOO) model, the capacity will be established at three locations. Of the total, 500 MW/2,000 MWh will be located at Dr. M.V. Ramana Reddy Rayalaseema Thermal Power Plant (RTPP). Another 250 MW/1,000 MWh will come up at the Talaricheruvu RE Project, and 500 MW/2,000 MWh at the NP Kunta RE Project. The entire 1,250 MW translates into 4-hour storage capacity. Bidders are required to design the BESS under Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreements (BESPAs), ensuring the system can charge and discharge at a C-rate of 0.25. It must also be capable of being charged and discharged in blocks of either 50 MW/200 MWh or 100 MW/400 MWh, alone or in combination up to the total rate capacity specified for each location. Interested BESS developers are invited to submit bids for the grid-connected projects, each of which will be tendered, evaluated, and awarded separately, with tariffs determined independently. No viability gap funding (VGF) is available for these projects. APPCC has launched the call on behalf of AP discoms, namely Andhra Pradesh Central Power Distribution Corporation Limited (APCPDCL), Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APEPDCL), and Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APSPDCL). State discoms will enter into a 12-year BESPA with the winning bidders to secure energy storage facilities on an on-demand basis. APPCC issued the tender on October 7, 2026. It will accept bids till November 23, 2026. Details of the tender are available on the APEPDCL website. Under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, Andhra Pradesh targets 25 GWh of BESS and 22 GW of pumped storage hydropower capacity by 2029 to accommodate growing renewable energy capacity. It also aims to add 78.5 GW of solar and 35 GW of wind capacity between 2024 and 2029.

artigo.texto: Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a battery factory near Austin, Texas, to supply its planned network of solar-powered plants for data centers. The 150,000-square-foot facility is designed for 10 gigawatt-hours of battery production, with full output targeted within two to three years. Co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced the project Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco. The startup is developing solar and battery systems to deliver continuous electricity at $100 per megawatt-hour, using daytime generation to power customers and store energy for use after sunset. “That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” Longmier said. Solar and batteries target continuous power Ambrosia emerged from stealth in June with a plan to build power plants serving data centers. Longmier and co-founder Sara Spangelo chose solar paired with batteries because they considered it the cheapest option and the fastest to deploy. The pair previously founded satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX. Their power plant design assigns solar generation two jobs during daylight hours: supplying the data center and charging batteries. Stored electricity then supports operations at night and during cloudy conditions. The approach requires substantially more solar generating capacity than the continuous power supplied to the customer. Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, according to Longmier. More from Energy See All That project pairs 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of battery storage. The intended output is 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a target uptime of 99.3%. Pilot passes 100 days of operation Sections of Ambrosia’s first pilot-scale power plant have operated continuously for more than 100 days, Longmier said. The pilot is capable of generating 200 kilowatts of electricity around the clock. The commercial project represents a substantial increase in scale from that demonstration, while retaining the same basic combination of solar generation and battery storage. Longmier said Ambrosia can remain profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour despite the additional solar panels and batteries needed to maintain supply beyond daylight hours. At that price, the company aims to compete with natural gas turbines, which many hyperscalers are planning to use to supply their data centers. The cost claim remains the company’s assessment, alongside its stated targets for commercial output and uptime. Simpler battery packs lower costs The company buys battery cells and assembles its own packs rather than manufacturing the cells themselves. “We buy existing cells and we make our own pack in-house, and it has the fewest parts by a factor of about 100 compared to any other competitor we’ve seen,” Longmier said. “We’ve been able to get to about 1.3x the cost of the bare cell compared to about a 5- or 7x for most stationary storage systems,” he added. To reach its pricing target, Ambrosia has focused on simplifying equipment, including solar mounts and battery packs. Reducing component counts and manufacturing more equipment in a factory has helped lower costs compared with purchasing from outside suppliers, according to Longmier. Ambrosia’s next challenge is to carry those manufacturing savings into commercial operation while meeting its targets for electricity costs and uptime.

artigo.texto: NYK-Led Consortium Develops Floating Data Center Concept for Ports A Japanese consortium led by shipping giant NYK Line has developed a new port-based floating data center concept designed to accelerate the commercialization of offshore data centers while addressing growing constraints on land availability, electrical power and construction timelines. The consortium, comprising Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK), NTT FACILITIES, Eurus Energy Holdings and MUFG Bank, envisions floating data centers moored alongside existing port quays, leveraging established shoreside infrastructure and local energy resources. Unlike floating data centers positioned farther offshore, which could directly utilize large-scale renewable energy sources such as offshore wind, the port-based model offers easier access, established telecommunications connectivity and more conventional power supply arrangements. The approach could enable deployment in locations ranging from major metropolitan ports to smaller regional harbors, potentially opening new opportunities for port authorities seeking to diversify waterfront infrastructure and services. The consortium sees the port-based concept as an intermediate step toward more ambitious offshore installations, where accessibility, telecommunications connectivity and independent power supply systems remain significant technical challenges. Under the initiative, NYK will oversee project development and business strategy. NTT FACILITIES will handle technical verification of data center design, construction and operations, while Eurus Energy will explore renewable power integration, particularly offshore wind. MUFG Bank will evaluate financing opportunities and potential business partnerships. The companies believe floating data centers could provide an alternative to conventional land-based facilities as global demand for digital infrastructure continues to expand. No construction timetable, project location, investment value or computing capacity was disclosed.

artigo.texto: Before it was fully contained, the Hawk Fire that started in August in Reno, Nevada, burned 15,085 acres, destroyed 48 homes and other structures, claimed the life of one person, and forced the evacuation of 42,000 residents. The cause of the wildfire remains under investigation. The Hawk Fire is one of thousands of wildfires that have burned across the United States this year, but a photo of that particular fire caught my attention for one reason. There's no vegetation. It is not burning in forest land but is burning in a desert environment with little fuel on the ground. Granted, Reno sits in an arid, dry region and wildfires are not uncommon. Wildfires are burning with a greater intensity than ever before and are much more difficult to control because the effects of climate change greatly exacerbate these already existing dry conditions. Wildfire seasons are much longer and not just contained to the western part of the country. Extreme weather events are occurring daily throughout the world. Just look at the record flooding that has hammered many parts of West Virginia in recent years. Severe weather events dominate our daily news cycle. The problem is here now We can no longer speak of climate change as a phenomena that will impact our lives in the future. We are in a climate crisis now and it is clearly the number one environmental issue facing mankind today. Water temperatures in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean, where El Niño is measured, have been at record levels for more than three months straight. El Niño’s effects are already evident worldwide. The pattern has contributed to more frequent heat domes, persistent temperature records in Peru, deadly storms in Chile, destructive hurricanes in Hawaii, floods across the United States and the Atlantic hurricane season’s record calm so far. Ocean temperatures in the central Pacific are on a record trajectory. They’re projected to reach an average peak of around 4.1 degrees Celsius above average in December — about a degree higher than a record-breaking El Niño in 2015 — leading to catastrophic weather events this fall and winter. A new UN Environment Programme report released in early September warns that global warming is likely to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold within the next few years. Even if governments fulfill their current pledges, temperatures will peak at 1.8 degrees Celsius, with some models indicating a rise above 2degrees. Every fraction of a degree above 1.5 degrees Celsius heightens the risks of extreme weather, heat waves, floods, and dangerous climate tipping points. The current crisis can be compared to leaning back in a chair: for a while, nothing happens, but eventually the chair tips over. Our climate is now at that tipping point. Action is needed There is only one way out of this crisis: end fossil fuel use as quickly as possible so global temperatures can decline. There is no alternative. It is frustrating to watch West Virginia’s political leaders fall short of the skills and vision needed to lead the state in the 21st century. Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s commitment to attracting data centers to the state is predicated on the false premise that it will benefit the state economically by increasing coal and natural gas production. Even the most backward countries across the globe are moving away from that insane idea. On Sept. 14, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the repeal of most of the Biden administration's greenhouse gas requirements for U.S. power plants and West Virginia’s politicians responded like lemmings. Attorney General J.B. McCuskey praised the move in a news release. Gov. Morrisey said, “Today marks an important victory for reliable, affordable American energy after years of fighting federal efforts to shut down West Virginia’s coal and natural gas industries.” The state’s entire congressional delegation fully supported the move as well. West Virginia suffers Is there no hope for West Virginia? The state’s current political leadership lacks the skills required to hold office. Their backward views on climate change are deeply reactionary, willfully ignorant, and betray a profound lack of understanding of the issue.” Unfortunately, I believe their views also accurately reflect those of the majority of the citizens of the State. We must phase out coal and natural gas from our energy portfolio now! I fear West Virginia’s political system is incapable of producing leaders intelligent enough to guide the state in the direction it must go.

artigo.texto: DALLAS, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solidion Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: STI) ("Solidion Technology" or "the Company"), an advanced battery technology solutions provider, today reaffirmed its commitment to address energy storage for artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, centered on its PEAK Series uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. As AI workloads increase the power density of data centers, operators face growing pressure on the systems that keep facilities running during grid disruptions. Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) batteries take up floor space that could otherwise hold AI servers and additional computing equipment, and they require periodic replacement. Solidion's approach is built around its PEAK Series, a UPS battery system built for AI data centers using its proprietary 5500 silicon-carbon anode cell, designed for AI data center environments and well positioned to address these evolving requirements. The Company's strategy focuses on three priorities: - Energy density and space efficiency: Based on Company testing, PEAK is designed to reduce UPS footprint by up to 30%, freeing floor space for servers. - Reliability and longevity: The 5500 cell is designed to last up to three times longer than conventional backup systems, reducing replacement cycles and maintenance. Solidion is focused on advancing technologies intended to support demanding data center operating environments. - Materials-level innovation: Solidion's portfolio of +385 patents covering silicon anodes, graphene and next generation battery chemistries, together with its pilot production facility in Dayton, Ohio, gives the Company a U.S. based foundation for developing data center energy storage. "AI infrastructure represents a compelling market for advanced energy storage," said Jaymes Winters, Chairman and CEO of Solidion. "Our focus is on translating our technology into practical commercial solutions that address real customer demand. We are not betting on which chips win; we are focused on supplying something every data center needs." Solidion intends to continue pursuing opportunities to apply its battery technologies directly to end users. About Solidion Technology, Inc. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas with pilot production facilities in Dayton, Ohio, Solidion's (NASDAQ: STI) core business includes manufacturing of battery materials and components, as well as development and production of next-generation batteries for energy storage systems, including UPS systems serving the artificial intelligence (AI) data center market and electric vehicles for ground, aerospace, and sea transportation. Solidion holds a portfolio of over 385 patents, covering innovations such as high-capacity, silane gas free and graphene-enabled silicon anodes, biomass-based graphite, advanced lithium-sulfur and lithium-metal technologies. For more information, please visit www.solidiontech.com or contact Investor Relations.
