artigo.texto: O agricultor para o trator na beira do terreno O agricultor para o trator na beira do terreno e aponta para a faixa de terra que ainda carrega o cheiro de cultivo. À frente dele, o mesmo solo deve receber torres de servidores, salas técnicas e a infraestrutura de refrigeração do que autoridades e investidores descrevem como o maior data center da Europa. A frase que se repete entre vizinhos é direta: claro que isso nos preocupa. O medo não é abstrato. Fala de água, de ruído, de calor residual, de paisagem alterada e de um ritmo de obra que transforma o cotidiano de comunas até então ligadas à agricultura e ao deslocamento pendular em direção a Paris. Seine-et-Marne é um departamento da região Île-de-France, a leste da capital francesa, marcado por planícies cultivadas, pequenas cidades e eixos rodoviários que ligam o leste parisiense ao interior do país. É nesse tecido misto de campo e periferia metropolitana É nesse tecido misto de campo e periferia metropolitana que o projeto de um grande hub de dados ganhou contorno público e dividiu a opinião local. A narrativa oficial enfatiza ganhos financeiros para o território, atração de empresas de tecnologia e um destaque internacional capaz de aproximar a área da imagem de um Silicon Valley à francesa. A contrapartida, segundo moradores e associações ambientais, é um custo que não cabe só em planilha de emprego e imposto, e que se mede em litros, decibéis e hectares que deixam de respirar como campo aberto. Como um data center de escala continental consome água, energia e silêncio Data centers concentram milhares de servidores que processam, armazenam e redistribuem informação para nuvem, streaming, comércio eletrônico, inteligência artificial e serviços públicos digitais. Cada rack consome eletricidade de forma contínua. Processadores geram calor. O calor precisa ser retirado para evitar falha de equipamento e perda de dados. Em muitos projetos, a refrigeração combina ar forçado, circuitos de água gelada, torres de resfriamento e, em desenhos mais recentes, sistemas de imersão ou free cooling quando o clima externo permite baixar a temperatura sem chillers pesados. O resultado prático para o entorno é demanda elétrica elevada O resultado prático para o entorno é demanda elétrica elevada, possível captação ou circulação intensa de água, emissão de ruído de ventiladores e geradores de backup, além de volumetria industrial que rompe a escala de vilarejos e zonas agrícolas. No recorte de Seine-et-Marne, a tensão nasce exatamente do choque de escalas. De um lado, o discurso de modernização territorial: o complexo seria âncora de uma nova economia digital, com canteiros de obra, contratos de manutenção, segurança patrimonial e serviços auxiliares. De outro, a percepção de quem vive ao lado do perímetro de implantação e calcula o que sobra quando a obra termina e as máquinas passam a operar vinte e quatro horas por dia. Moradores descrevem inquietação com o consumo de recursos, com o trânsito de caminhões na fase de construção e com a irreversibilidade de ocupar hectares que hoje ainda funcionam como campo produtivo ou margem de biodiversidade. Associações ambientais reforçam o alerta sobre pressão hídrica e energética em um país que já convive com verões mais quentes, restrições sazonais de água em bacias sensíveis e debate permanente sobre a matriz elétrica. A França opera majoritariamente com energia nuclear de base, o que em tese reduz a pegada de carbono direta da eletricidade em comparação com redes a carvão. Isso não elimina a discussão local nem a conta de quem divide o mesmo aquífero e a mesma subestação. Um data center de grande porte desloca megawatts de demanda para um ponto específico da rede, exige reforço de linhas, subestações e, em muitos casos, contratos de fornecimento prioritário. Quando a refrigeração depende de água, o volume anual pode rivalizar com o de pequenas indústrias intensivas. Mesmo projetos que anunciam circuitos fechados ou reúso precisam de reposição por evaporação e de rejeição térmica para a atmosfera ou para corpos d’água. Para quem cultiva ou depende de poços e cursos d’água próximos, a pergunta deixa de ser tecnológica e vira de prioridade: quem fica com a água em ano seco, o servidor ou a lavoura. Empregos, impostos e o cartão de visita de um Silicon Valley no leste parisiense O argumento econômico a favor do empreendimento segue uma lógica familiar em disputas de infraestrutura pesada. Empregos na construção civil, depois postos técnicos permanentes, aumento de base tributária municipal e departamental, efeito de arrasto sobre hotéis, restaurantes e serviços de apoio. Há ainda o capital simbólico: sediar o maior data center do continente funciona como cartão de visita para atrair outras empresas de nuvem, cabos, cibersegurança e pesquisa aplicada. Em regiões que buscam diversificar além da agricultura e do turismo de passagem, esse pacote pesa nas reuniões de câmara e nos discursos de desenvolvimento territorial. O risco apontado por críticos é o de trocar O risco apontado por críticos é o de trocar um ativo paisagístico e hídrico de longo prazo por uma monocultura de infraestrutura digital cujo valor agregado local pode se concentrar em poucos operadores e em cadeias de suprimento externas. Moradores ouvidos no debate público local não rejeitam tecnologia por princípio. O que aparece com frequência é a sensação de assimetria de informação. Projetos dessa magnitude chegam com estudos de impacto, audiências e mapas de zoneamento que poucos leigos conseguem decifrar por completo. Termos como PUE, indicador de eficiência no uso de energia, free cooling, redundância N+1 e corredores quentes e frios circulam em reuniões técnicas, enquanto na mesa da cozinha a conversa gira em torno de barulho noturno, iluminação perene, valor do imóvel e futuro da escola do vilarejo se o perfil demográfico mudar com a chegada de mão de obra temporária. artigo.texto: LOWELL — The Lowell residents who attended the city’s second meeting on data centers were virtually unanimous in their feedback to restrict future growth of the facilities in every district in the city. “The only way to protect our community from the environmental impacts that we know are caused by these data centers, particularly when these data centers are put in environmental justice neighborhoods, is to prohibit them … ,” the participants at Table No. 4 said during their presentation. The community engagement event was hosted on Oct. 7, by the Department of Planning and Development at the Senior Center on Broadway Street in the Acre neighborhood. Residents give city planners feedback More than 50 participants broke into a dozen small groups to discuss DPD’s two zoning options for consideration by the City Council for regulating data centers in the city, part of an overhaul of Lowell’s outdated zoning code. Option 1 is restricting future data center growth to 15 megawatts with climate-friendly infrastructure. Option 2 is that data centers are prohibited in every district. Lowell is currently home to a 352,000-square-foot data center in the city’s Sacred Heart neighborhood. Markley Lowell LLC operates the state-of-the-art data-storage and cloud-computing colocation data center that rents secure space to more than 500 clients to run their own technology. Its systems power and provide routing to a wide variety of private companies, state and local governments, internet companies and universities, including UMass Lowell. The privately owned company has faced some local headwinds, driven in part by consistent neighborhood opposition, as well as a national angst over the unchecked growth of hyperscale projects that are the backbone of the artificial intelligence revolution. Residents in the economic justice neighborhood have consistently testified to noise and air quality concerns, ongoing and disruptive construction projects and violations of approved permitting. “We say these are the rules in place, you can build your data center,” the moderator for Table No. 1 said. “Who’s going to enforce those rules? What are we going to do to make sure that they’re following them? And if they’re not, what is going to happen? Because we’ve seen it in other places where they come in, they say, ‘This is what we’re going to do,’ and then they far exceed that and it harms the community and the damage has already been done.” Markley Lowell only data center operating in Lowell Markley Lowell was not on DPD’s data center zoning agenda, but its shadow loomed over the residents’ workshopped conversations. When the Markley Group purchased the derelict and long-vacant former Prince Pasta plant in Lowell for $4 million in 2015, Lowell welcomed the high-tech center with a $77 million tax break. Over the past 10 years, the company embarked on a dramatic renovation and expansion, with founder and CEO Jeff Markley claiming to have invested at least $650 million in the site and related developments to date. The company’s power profile has expanded from seven to 23 diesel-powered backup generators, 16 chillers and two water towers to secure its growing energy needs. And despite significant pushback from both residents and the City Council, the company has continued to expand its footprint in Lowell. Both Markley Lowell and Jeff Markley have purchased multiple properties in and around its existing facility at 1 Markley Way. City lacks zoning on data centers The City Council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium March 10 to allow the city to develop zoning around data centers in Lowell. Under the city’s existing zoning, the data center company is not required to divulge its long-term development plans for any of its new sites. But the parcels either contain or are colocated to generators of the scale needed to power data centers, perhaps even artificial intelligence. The company’s website recently added “Now available for your generative AI workloads.” DPD Deputy Director Camilo Espitia reminded participants that Markley’s current projects are “locked in.” “Whichever option we go with today is irrelevant to where Markley stands today,” he said. “They are grandfathered in and that business will keep operating. This is intended for any other land that has not been touched by data centers or that hasn’t been subdivided in the future for any other type of developer including Markley themselves.” At the end of the almost two-hour session, Assistant City Manager and DPD Director Yovani Baez-Rose thanked the community for their feedback. “We appreciate the fact that you’re taking time out of your personal lives to sort of help us frame what our community is going to look like moving forward,” she said. In late October to early November, DPD will present the data center ordinance to the City Council Zoning Subcommittee, followed by a final draft of the zoning ordinance to the council in early to mid-December. A Planning Board public hearing will be held in January, and the council will hold a public hearing and hold a vote later that month.

artigo.texto: Data center development divides candidates and communities Pennsylvania governor and representative races are both taking strong stances Data center development divides candidates and communities Pennsylvania governor and representative races are both taking strong stances Data center development has become a major topic in western Pennsylvania this fall, with residents and officials debating regulations and community concerns as elections approach. Kristin Kanthak, an associate professor of political science at the University of Pittsburgh, said, "One of the big issues of this election, it seems, is artificial intelligence. For example, we've seen the governor candidates come down on different sides of that issue, and parties are really trying to figure out where they sit on that." More than a dozen data center sites have been proposed or explored in western Pennsylvania, and the state is aware of at least 100 proposals across Pennsylvania, most of which are still in the early stages. Shapiro, Garrity Stances Gov. Josh Shapiro has issued an executive order requiring developers to meet stricter commitments before the state reviews their permit applications. "You've got to generate your own power, and the developers and the tech companies have to pay for it. You've got to protect our air and water, and most importantly, you have to earn the support of the local community first," Shapiro said. State Treasurer Stacy Garrity, Shapiro’s challenger, has called for a temporary pause on data center development to allow municipalities time to update their zoning regulations. "I heard the same thing. They're not against data centers, but they want time to get their zoning updated," Garrity said. What Local Officials are Saying Local officials, who make zoning decisions, are staying in office as regular elections for Pennsylvania’s local offices are held in odd-numbered years. Some state representative and congressional races also feature candidates representing municipalities involved in data center development. In Elizabeth Township, where a data center has been proposed, Republican State Rep. Andrew Kuzma is running against Democrat Dylan Altemara. Kuzma addressed the issue at a recent town hall, saying, "I am a state representative, meaning that I represent the people that live here. And if 95% of them are taking a position, I am 100% with them because that is my job as a state representative." Altemara shared a statement at the town hall calling for more transparency in development plans from the township. With just weeks left before the election, many residents are still deciding which candidates will best address their concerns about data center development. Some are advocating for stricter regulations, while others are calling for a complete halt to the projects.

artigo.texto: On October 14 in Hanoi, VIR held a seminar on credit policy and the carbon market, where experts focused on discussing the links between credit policy, the carbon market, and the capital market, with a view to identifying solutions to mobilise financial resources for the green transition. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV), said the Party, state, and government had introduced key policies and guidelines in recent years to promote green growth, energy transition, and a low-carbon economy, supporting Vietnam’s commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. “This transition requires substantial investment in technological innovation, changes to production methods, greater energy efficiency, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction,” Canh said. “Alongside funding from the state budget and capital and money markets, market-based mechanisms, including the carbon market, are needed to mobilise additional resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions.” “By establishing emission allowances, measuring emissions reduction results, and determining transaction prices for emission allowances and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism for converting emissions reduction results into economic value. This gives businesses additional incentives and resources to continue investing in the green transition, rather than relying primarily on bank credit,” he said. The government issued Decree No.29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange in January, establishing the legal framework for the organisation and operation of the market and the trading of GHG emission allowances and carbon credits. The initial pilot market has been established with a scale of more than 511 million tonnes of CO2, equivalent to the emission allowances allocated to facilities in three major emitting industries, including thermal power, iron and steel, and cement for the 2025-2026 period. The pilot phase will run until the end of 2028, before the market transitions to full mandatory operation from 2029. Commercial banks will participate in the market as settlement banks, with BIDV serving as the sole settlement bank during the pilot phase. From the banking sector’s perspective, Canh said it was important to clearly recognise the respective roles of green credit and the carbon market in the green transition. “First, green credit provides capital for investment and technological innovation, creating resources for the development of green industries and sectors and thereby generating emissions reduction results. The emissions reductions achieved by projects financed with bank capital, in turn, provide the foundation and commodities for the development of the carbon market,” Canh stated. “Conversely, an effectively functioning carbon market will enable businesses to generate revenue and maintain stable cash flows from emissions reduction results to support their production and business activities, while improving their credit quality. Businesses will also be better positioned to purchase carbon credits to meet the stringent standards applicable to imports and exports,” he added. Regarding green credit, Canh explained that the key consideration was not merely whether funds had been disbursed to a project classified as green, but also whether the borrowing customer had demonstrated measurable results in energy savings, emissions reduction, and environmental protection. “Measurement, reporting, and verification of emissions reduction results, together with the trading of emission allowances and carbon credits on the carbon market, can provide additional information for monitoring the environmental performance of projects. This, in turn, can help credit institutions assess the effectiveness of capital utilisation and strengthen the management and supervision of green capital flows,” he said. In practice, the banking sector has proactively implemented various measures in recent years to promote green credit and direct capital towards industries and sectors that deliver environmental benefits and reduce GHG emissions. The SBV has gradually refined the policy framework and issued orientations and guidelines on green credit and environmental and social risk management. It has also encouraged credit institutions to develop strategies and internal processes, as well as introduce credit products aligned with green growth objectives. This is particularly important in the context of developing green and low-carbon financing channels. Speaking at the event, Canh said that since green credit was first introduced in 2017, the sector had expanded in both credit scale and the participation of credit institutions. As of the end of June this year, outstanding green credit had exceeded VND 856 trillion, up 9.87 per cent from the end of 2025. Average annual growth exceeded 20 per cent over the 2017-2025 period, with lending concentrated primarily in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, which accounted for more than 31 per cent, and green energy, which accounted for nearly 28 per cent. Outstanding loans that had undergone environmental and social risk assessments exceeded $240 billion, representing more than 31.33 per cent of total outstanding credit across the economy. “This result reflects the banking system’s commitment and efforts to support the green transition of businesses and the economy. When the carbon market operates effectively, emissions reduction results can be converted into financial resources for the businesses themselves. Accordingly, the development of the carbon market can help ease pressure on green credit resources,” said Canh. “Rather than relying predominantly on their own capital, the state budget, or bank credit to finance their transition needs, businesses will have additional opportunities to generate resources from their own emissions reduction results. artigo.texto: Did Ukraine’s strikes on data centers really silence Russian bots? Russia's army of bots is apparently offline. At least, that's according to chatter on social media and even Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Over the past week, Ukrainian drones struck three data centers belonging to Yandex, the tech giant often called "Russia’s Google." The first strike happened on Oct. 8, followed by a second attack on Oct. 9. On Sunday, Oct. 11, a third strike damaged a Yandex data center in the Vladimir region, east of Moscow. The company said operations at that facility were completely suspended and some of its services were unavailable, according to the BBC. The attacks disrupted Yandex services, from its AI chatbot to its smart home devices. Per the BBC, the military strikes were meant to target "places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine." You May Also Like Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelenskyy said "everyone noticed" a drop in Russian bot activity on social media after the strikes. On X, Reddit, and elsewhere, users in several Western countries reported seeing less right-wing activity in their feeds, from pro-GOP accounts in the U.S. to supporters of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Czech member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský also pointed to claims that online support for the AfD had dropped after the strikes. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. The prediction market Polymarket’s X account was among those amplifying the claim. Take that with a grain of salt, though, as the account has a tendency for posting breaking-news-style claims without sources or verification. This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. Much of the buzz traces back to a report from U24 Media, the media arm of United24, a platform run by the Ukrainian government. To its credit, U24’s own report is careful about what the numbers can and can’t prove. It cites an Oct. 12 analysis by The Deep Dive of data from Cloudflare Radar, which monitors internet traffic. According to that analysis, automated web traffic from Yandex’s network fell sharply after Oct. 8 and nearly disappeared by Oct. 11. At one point, it measured just 0.3 percent of the chart’s peak, compared with 88.2 percent at the same hour a week earlier. U24 also cites German tech publication t3n's report of a similar plunge — with bot traffic dropping to about 0.4 percent of the previous week’s level before bouncing back to around 20 percent later in the day on Oct. 11. The catch is that "automated traffic" and "Russian propaganda bots" aren’t the same thing. Automated traffic is any request sent to a website by software rather than a person. Most of it is mundane, e.g., search engine crawlers indexing pages or monitoring tools checking whether sites are up. Because Yandex runs Russia’s biggest search engine, its network constantly sends out crawlers to index the web. Knocking its data centers offline would bring traffic to a halt regardless of whether a single troll account went quiet. As U24 itself notes, the measurements show a sharp drop in automated network activity, but they can’t tell us whether propaganda bots disappeared or whether damaged infrastructure simply stopped producing ordinary automated traffic. The numbers also track how much traffic Yandex’s network sent relative to its peak, not how many social media accounts were active. Mashable has yet to see published evidence tying Russian influence operations on X or Reddit to Yandex’s servers specifically. Many of the claims to that effect are sourced from the same Cloudflare Radar and Deep Dive data reports that we cited here. Influence campaigns can run on infrastructure anywhere, and the accounts posting the content don’t have to live on Yandex’s network at all. It's easy to see why the claim has caught on, as social media platforms are rife with hyper-polarization fueled by ragebait political engagement. However, not all political content online comes from Russian bots. As The Atlantic's Ali Breland writes, operatives based in Eastern European countries like Latvia are paying people to post pro-GOP talking points — $3 for every 1,000 views. That also doesn’t mean the strikes had no effect online. Per U24, the bombings have found a way to rattle Russia’s internet, including widespread outages. Whether it also silenced Russia’s online propaganda machine is a much bigger claim. artigo.texto: By Charlotte Underwood JACKSBORO, TN (WLAF)- County commissioners briefly discussed data centers at Monday’s county commission workshop, saying that the county needed to pursue education regarding data centers. TOP PHOTO: Left to right- Lonnie Weldon, Ralph Davis, Chris Stanley, Suzette Davenport, Johnny Bruce and Beverly Hall. Commissioner Lonnie Weldon brought the topic up at the close of Monday’s workshop, saying he had attended the Tennessee Governor’s Economic Development Conference in Chattanooga. He and several other commissioners attended that conference. “We sat in on one of the meetings on data centers, I don’t know what the commission thinks of data centers or what they know about data centers, but there are multiple kinds of data centers. I think they would be willing to come and speak to the commission about data centers, whether it’s a good thing or a bad thing,” Weldon said, adding that he thought the citizens had a “misconception about data centers” because of all the “bots that have been on the internet, telling how bad they are.” “Not all data centers are bad, they are profitable for the county, but if the commission likes, we could probably get in touch with them and have them come talk to the commission about data centers … there’s a good side, they can also talk to you about what we might want to do to keep data centers from coming here, but its up to the commission if they want to pursue that info,” Weldon said. Commissioner David Greene spoke briefly on the topic as well, saying he felt more education was needed on data centers. “I kind of agree with you on that, there’s good and there’s bad and I was all bad until I went and listened to them talk about that. I just think it’s an opportunity we keep an open mind to. I am not saying we do them or don’t do them, but I think we need to educate ourselves about them, because the one that I was in, they have some that are self-contained units, you fill the water one time basically and it does for several months as they recirculate it – they generate their own power. Good or bad, I don’t know, but the one that I sat in on that talked about it, they said that 75% of the negativity on social media on them was done by bots and those bots are owned by Chinese companies, they are trying to create the negativity about it because they want China to be the leading developer of AI,” Greene said. Weldon said that there were data centers that the county needed to “guard from” since Campbell County “does not have zoning.” “The ones that you hear the most negativity about is the hyper skill data centers that use all the water, and all has the loud noises, that is probably the one that the county needs to guard from, where you hear all the social media about the noise that you hear from it, or all the water that they use or power that they use and take away. The way I take it, this latter one is something the county needs to guard against because we don’t have zoning, that is something that we probably need to look at, but most of these others are self-contained and they are money makers,” Weldon said. Commissioner Chris Stanley, who also attended the conference in Chattanooga said there “were several counties there who were talking about how they were making money off of it, of course, I went into the meeting kind of like David, I thought they were all bad, but it did look like there are several different kinds, I think it would be good to hear both sides, and educate ourselves on it and the biggest thing right now is, and I know zoning is a bad word in the county and we are not trying to say zone your property, and I am not on the planning commission, but they probably need to talk about zoning for data centers and the only places that they can go, because I think right now, there is no zoning, no law against them moving in next door,” Stanley said. (WLAF NEWS PUBLISHED-10/15/2026-6AM)

artigo.texto: (Xinhua/Guo Qi) Fuzhou, 16 out (Xinhua) -- A Conferência Mundial de Armazenamento de Energia 2026 acontece de quarta a sexta-feira na cidade de Ningde, na Província de Fujian, no leste da China, reunindo participantes para discutir tecnologias de ponta, perspectivas para o setor de armazenamento de energia e a posição da China no mercado global de armazenamento de energia. Em 2025, as adições anuais globais de armazenamento em baterias atingiram aproximadamente 307 GWh, sendo que a China respondeu por 56%. A escala de implantação na China tornou-se fundamental para o mercado global de armazenamento e está "ajudando a mudar a economia da eletricidade renovável", disse Ilina Stefanova, chefe da Coalizão para Ação da Agência Internacional de Energia Renovável (IRENA), na cerimônia de abertura. A experiência da China em tecnologia, fabricação, implantação e integração à rede será importante não apenas no âmbito nacional, mas também para a transição energética global, acrescentou ela. À medida que as energias renováveis se tornam uma importante fonte de energia em todo o mundo, o armazenamento está evoluindo de uma instalação de apoio para uma nova infraestrutura essencial para os sistemas de energia. É preciso atender às diversas demandas da rede elétrica e, ao mesmo tempo, melhorar continuamente a confiabilidade e a estabilidade, disse Zeng Yuqun, fundador e presidente da CATL, fabricante líder de baterias da China, com sede na cidade de Ningde. Dados do setor mostram que a China está respondendo a essas demandas. O setor de armazenamento de energia de novo tipo da China alcançou resultados notáveis, disse Xiong Jijun, vice-ministro da Indústria e Informatização, em seu discurso de abertura. A produção de baterias de armazenamento da China ultrapassou 420 GWh no primeiro semestre de 2026, um aumento anual de cerca de 110%. O setor está avançando por diversas vias tecnológicas, com as baterias de lítio desempenhando um papel de liderança ao lado das baterias de íons de sódio e de fluxo. O governo buscará equilibrar desenvolvimento e segurança, fortalecerá a inovação tecnológica, seguirá princípios orientados pela demanda e promoverá um ecossistema industrial global, ao mesmo tempo que se protegerá firmemente contra a competição desenfreada e orientará o setor para que passe da expansão em escala para um crescimento impulsionado pela inovação, acrescentou Xiong. A cidade de Ningde já sediou a conferência três vezes anteriormente, um evento que atraiu representantes de governos, indústrias e da academia de mais de 50 países e regiões. (Xinhua/Guo Qi)

artigo.texto: Brightray Science Inc, a majority-owned subsidiary of BUUU Group Limited, has announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Brightray Veridian Pte. Ltd. has signed a letter of intent (LOI) with an unnamed US-based mission-critical infrastructure partner for a planned 10 MW AI data center project in Indiana, United States. This is, according to a press release, Brightray’s first project LOI signed in the US and an important step toward expanding into the world’s largest data center market. Under the LOI, Brightray will deploy a prefabricated data center solution. The implementation is subject to final agreement on technical specifications, commercial terms, the project schedule, and definitive contract documentation. “Entering the US market is an important step in Brightray’s international development. The US has enormous data center demand, and customers face real pressure to turn their AI investments into usable computing power as quickly as possible. Our entry point is delivery: with Brightray prefabricated data center solution, we move more of the work into the factory and run manufacturing in parallel with on-site works, with the aim of shortening the delivery period for this project to within one year,” said Bin Wang, Brightray founder. By taking this approach, Brightray says it can deliver the 10 MW AI data center within a year. That timeline covers the entire schedule, including design finalization, permitting, international shipping, on-site foundation and ancillary works, installation, and commissioning. “We look forward to working further with our partner on the technical solution and implementation arrangements and to building delivery experience in the US market through this 10MW project. Addressing the power, cooling and space requirements of next-generation AI equipment, we aim to bring the efficiency advantages of our prefabricated data center solution to the project and lay the foundation for the further expansion of our US business,” said Wang. If this agreement is finalized and the project delivered, it could serve as a blueprint for Brightray’s expansion into the US market. Grid capacity constraints, community opposition, and infrastructure bottlenecks can significantly delay data center buildouts in the US market, a problem Brightray looks to want to solve. Despite the constraints, US data center investments have nearly doubled since 2024, according to Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, and demand for AI will only push that growth higher with the US data center market expected to be worth US$ 494.49 billion by 2031.

artigo.texto: ND counties talk about how to handle data centers BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - The North Dakota Association of Counties said that data center construction should be considered on a county-by-county basis. The Association held its annual meeting this week in Bismarck. The group said questions about the size of data centers, proximity to urban and rural areas and potential tax benefits differ between counties. These differences are why it’s necessary for counties to have individualized zoning and planning rules. “There’s obviously people that are highly opposed, but we’re still gathering facts, getting the right information out there,” said Association President Nick Moser. “That’s one great thing about this event, is getting that information and getting the proper information to people is huge.” In Moser’s own county, Cavalier, data centers are not allowed within one mile of town. The noise from data centers only reaches 50 decibels at this distance, according to research. Moser encourages public hearings to ensure the correct information is being given to people. artigo.texto: To the editor: Monticello’s proposed data center has become a focal point in this year’s local election. Data centers are also focal points in elections across the country. A Gallup poll reported by Fox News found that 71% of Americans oppose construction of an AI data center in their local area. This opposition crosses the political spectrum. People oppose data centers for a number of reasons, including concerns about increased electricity costs caused by their large power consumption, noise pollution and use of a finite resource: groundwater. I believe a center of this size would have one main purpose: supporting the expanding use of artificial intelligence. Three members of the Monticello City Council and Mayor Lloyd Hilgart voted to adopt zoning regulations allowing data centers through a conditional-use process. Only Councilmember Charlotte Gabler voted against the ordinance. The data center would increase the city’s property tax revenue. It would also benefit property owners who have sold or will sell land for the project. You have to decide whether this is worth the economic trade-off. This project needs an environmental impact statement, not only the alternative urban areawide review completed by the city. An environmental impact statement would provide a deeper study of the project’s possible consequences. The appointed, rather than elected, Planning Commission has now recommended that the City Council approve the project. Since the data center will not be on the ballot for approval by city voters, our only voice may be at the polls. When you vote Nov. 3, support Hilgart and Councilmember Tracy Hinz only if they change course and oppose final approval of the data center. The City Council has chosen to move this project forward. It is time to stop it before final approval. Mike Beck Monticello

artigo.texto: When the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran earlier this year, Tehran responded by striking energy infrastructure across the Gulf. The result was a severe shock to global energy markets that continues to this day. Less publicized at the time were its strikes on another kind of infrastructure: data centers. Similar attacks have since taken place in Russia and Ukraine, where both sides have been trading tit-for-tat strikes on data centers. Experts say these attacks represent a new front in warfare, in which facilities powering the technology behind many critical industries have become military targets. The AI boom has led to a surge in demand for computing power, data storage and cloud services, making the data centers that provide them a crucial part of modern infrastructure. A mass of data center construction is currently underway in the U.S., and tech companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars a year to meet AI demand. Telecommunications companies, banks, hospitals and energy suppliers all rely on them. “Data centers are now on the critical path for modern digital infrastructure,” Kirk Cameron, founding director of the Institute for Advanced Computing at Virginia Tech, tells TIME. “The loss of key data centers could collapse economies, disrupt public and private transportation with loss of GPS, and affect government essential services for health, emergency dispatch, and power grids.” Military use of AI for targeting and information processing has made data centers crucial to fighting a war. Ukraine uses AI for an array of battlefield functions such as drone targeting, battle planning, and missile analyzing Russian missile attacks. U.S. tech companies such as Palantir now work closely with Ukraine’s military to develop new AI-powered weaponry, taking advantage of the ability to immediately test their technology on the battlefield. The U.S. military also uses Palantir’s Maven system to help identify targets for strikes. “Data centers are competitive advantages in warfare,” Cameron says. “Knocking out capabilities means potentially crippling combat operations for an adversary. It’s also a form of economic warfare and could lead to longer-term competitive challenges for the target.” Where have data centers been attacked? The first wave of attacks on data centers was carried out in March this year by Iran, when it launched strikes on two Amazon facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and another in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby drone strike. Those facilities have been mostly offline ever since; Amazon said on Sept. 15 that it had been “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in those two regions. Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers in late September disrupted television broadcasts and internet access. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it was striking data centers because they “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.” Ukraine’s response began on Oct. 8, and it has since carried out drone strikes on three data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, often called Russia’s version of Google. The first site hit, in Sasovo, houses two of the three supercomputers Yandex uses to develop its AI models, Meduza reported, and the outage disrupted several companies relying on Yandex’s cloud services, including Russian Railways, MegaFon, T-Bank, and several media outlets. Following the first strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the retaliation: "We always respond in kind. You all know that they are hitting and hitting our data centers; we responded to them.” How have tech companies responded? The spate of attacks over the last year has already caused tech companies to rethink how and where they build data centers. The United Arab Emirates is reportedly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project following the Iranian strikes. The original plan envisioned a 10-square-mile campus in Abu Dhabi, to be built in partnership with American tech companies like Oracle, Nvidia, and Cisco. Now the data centers will likely be spread out across the UAE, according to officials who spoke to Reuters. Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, believes that data centers have become a new frontline in warfare—and that may require new strategies. “If you’re Russia and you attack a Microsoft data center, is that an attack on Ukraine? Is that an attack on Microsoft? Is that an attack on a U.S. company and, by extension, the U.S.?” she asks. The U.S. has largely followed a policy that attacks on American companies do not constitute an attack on the United States, but Harding says the government may need to decide on a new approach “that creates deterrence not just to protect life and health, but also data.” And while the threat to data centers in the U.S. may be relatively low compared to the Gulf and Ukraine or Russia, tech companies will also have to think more about the security of their facilities when building, while trying to keep pace with massive demand. “The knock-on effect is that the companies that own the data centers are realizing they can't protect them, and that kind of calls into question the cloud model in general,” Harding says. “They're having to make big adjustments. You could see a time in the future where Amazon starts losing business to Microsoft because Microsoft does a better job of hiding where their data centers are.”

artigo.texto: Marblehead could move to ban data centers under a new zoning bylaw, following a discussion at the Planning Board’s Oct. 13 meeting. Planning Board Chair Marc Liebman raised the possibility of prohibiting data centers in town, citing concerns about their impact on communities and pointing to similar efforts underway in Salem. “There’s all kinds of reasons why data centers create a strain on the communities they’re in,” Liebman said. Data centers are facilities that house computer servers and other equipment used to store, process and distribute digital information. Large facilities, including those supporting artificial intelligence, can consume substantial amounts of electricity and water and require extensive infrastructure. Liebman said several town officials have expressed interest in exploring a prohibition and wanted to gauge the Planning Board’s willingness to pursue one. “There are many people in various parts of town government who wanted to test our appetite for defining data centers and coming up with a bylaw to prevent data centers from existing in Marblehead,” he said. “I fully support that.” The Salem City Council approved a data center ban earlier this month. Liebman said one of the biggest challenges is developing a legal definition of a data center. He proposed working with Select Board members, Planning and Community Development Director Brendan Callahan and town staff to develop draft language for the Planning Board to review at its November meeting. The proposal could then be brought before Town Meeting for consideration. No formal vote was taken, and no specific restrictions or exemptions were proposed. The discussion was preliminary, with the board agreeing to explore the idea further. ADU approvals highlight multigenerational housing needs Earlier in the meeting, the board considered three accessory dwelling unit applications, approving two and continuing a third amid concerns about whether the proposed designs complied with the town’s 900-square-foot limit.

artigo.texto: Data center developer offers residents of Kansas town $1,000 each for 10 years Amid a pronounced public backlash against data center construction in the U.S., one real estate developer is making an offer it hopes will win over one Kansas community: money. Digital Realty is offering every household in De Soto, Kansas, where it plans to build a data center, $1,000 in utility and property tax credits for 10 years. "Digital Realty builds critical infrastructure that enables the modern economy, and we believe we also have a responsibility to help strengthen the communities that make this growth possible," Andy Power, the developer's president and CEO, said in a statement on Wednesday. The offer is part of a $20 million community investment Digital Realty is pledging in De Soto as the company paves the way for a 280-acre data center site. The company said the project, which will eventually cover 1,400 acres, will provide recurring tax revenue, create jobs and deliver other economic benefits to local residents. Digital Realty, a publicly traded company based in Austin, Texas, with a market worth of more than $67 billion, said in a news release that it is working with De Soto to finalize distribution of the $1,000 credits to households. The company, whose clients include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Nvidia, expects to create 250 permanent jobs for local suppliers and contractors once the site is complete. The initial phase of development will also support "thousands of construction jobs over time," Digital Realty said in its news release. A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, citing concerns that the facilities harm the environment, drain local resources and raise utility costs.

artigo.texto: Cadoux (ASX:CCM) reports its premiumHPA material has contributed to a milestone in sustainable battery manufacturing through the European Union-funded SAFELOOP consortium. The consortium completed factory-scale production of 18650 size lithium-ion battery cells incorporating recycled materials at Turkish manufacturer Aspilsan Enerji’s facility during the September quarter. The achievement involved 500kg of battery-grade recycled graphite delivered by consortium member AETC for the pilot manufacturing campaign. The cells are intended for integration into battery modules for an electric bus manufactured by Bozankaya. SAFELOOP focuses on developing direct-recycling technology to recover and restore high-value graphite from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries for reuse in new battery anodes. The initiative aims to reduce reliance on newly mined raw materials while supporting sustainable battery supply chains. Cadoux serves as the sole high-purity alumina materials supplier to the SAFELOOP consortium. The company’s premiumHPA material contributes to ceramic battery coatings and enhanced battery safety applications. Managing Director Roland Hill says the SAFELOOP milestone recycling and manufacturing achievement represents “a meaningful step towards industrial-scale giga-factory circular battery production”, further positioning Cadoux to pursue opportunities for premiumHPA in advanced battery applications. The company notes that the milestone validates the use of recovered materials in commercial battery production. Cadoux is an emerging critical minerals developer, with a focus on high-purity alumina and rare earth minerals. Write to Paula Fabe at Mining.com.au Main image: Cadoux

artigo.texto: The investment firm once helmed by local financier and former Union-Tribune owner “Papa” Doug Manchester is considering building what could be California’s largest AI data center right next door to downtown San Diego, our MacKenzie Elmer reveals. Emails obtained by Elmer show Manchester Financial Group is in talks with the Navy and local power officials about a proposal to build a 400-megawatt data center at the site of the Naval Information Warfare Systems Command near Old Town. The data center would be part of a larger overhaul of the 70-acre site that would include a new headquarters for the command center along with housing, hotels, retail and other amenities. If built, the data center could be the state’s largest. By comparison, a controversial data center proposed in Imperial County would be 330 megawatts. Ted Eldredge, Manchester Financial’s President and CEO, said the data center is just one of several proposals for the naval site and might never get built at all. “No final project has been approved,” company representative Matt Awbrey said in a statement. Elo-Rivera Demands Transparency Around Data Center Costs Since breaking the news about the data center proposal on Thursday, Voice also has learned that the developer engaged in talks with the city’s energy grid builder, San Diego Gas and Electric, and the city’s power buyer, San Diego Community Power, before local elected leaders knew about the project. After learning about the proposal, San Diego City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera said he had some questions for SDG&E. He asked whether the grid has enough capacity to add 400 megawatts of continuous power demand from a data center. SDG&E officials said no matter where the demand is coming from, be it a data center or a new hospital, they will update the grid to meet it. “If we’re being told that customers would absorb that cost, it’s incredibly alarming and SDG&E owes a response to the public about it,” Elo-Rivera said. “The idea that we’d be adding costs so a billionaire could build a data center is something we’d all find offensive.” Midway Rising’s Final Snag During yearslong negotiations over the Midway Rising project, San Diego city officials insisted the developer be required to build 2,000 “net new” affordable homes – meaning the new homes would actually be new, not just homes initially slated for other projects and tacked onto Midway Rising. Our Scott Lewis learned that may not happen. Meaning Midway Rising might not increase its neighborhood’s total supply of affordable housing as much as proponents hoped. The final deal outlining requirements for the project, slated for initial City Council review at a committee hearing Friday, no longer includes the “net new” homes requirement. Instead, the developer would be allowed to absorb affordable housing units initially slated for other projects within a three-mile radius of Midway Rising. In practical terms, that means developers of other projects could pay Midway Rising to build the affordable housing the city otherwise would require the developers to build. The units would still get built. But there would have been even more affordable units in the neighborhood if all developers, including Midway Rising, built their full complement of affordable housing instead of trading them around. Midway Rising representatives said insisting on the “net new” requirement would remove crucial flexibility that often enables developers to build affordable housing without losing money. “It’s important to explore all available tools to expedite…affordable housing,” said Charles Schmid of Chelsea Investment Corp., an affordable housing builder in the Midway Rising partnership.. Mayor Todd Gloria Picks New COO Mayor Todd Gloria on Thursday appointed Bethany Bezak, who currently serves on the mayor’s executive team, to be the city’s new chief operating officer and oversee the city’s day-to-day operations. Bezak has served as chief performance and logistics officer since December 2025, overseeing several city departments, including transportation, purchasing and contracting, and general services. Gloria fired the city’s last COO in February 2025 and filled the role himself. Councilmembers and others pushed multiple times for him to rehire a COO, after what they perceived as management failures. “This was both a budget reduction as well as a desire to be fully accountable for the difficult decisions that are gonna need to be made in order to put the city on a stronger footing,” he told Voice of San Diego on Thursday. Read more about the mayor’s appointment here. Latest State Reports Show Growth, Declines at San Diego Unified New student performance metrics from the state show quite a few bright spots for San Diego Unified — but also some worrying declines. Reporter Jakob McWhinney breaks down how the district fared. The district outperforms other large urban districts: The district’s graduation rate showed a marked increase, likely helped along by officials’ creation of new graduation pathways. The percentage of graduates who qualified as “prepared” under the state’s career and college indicator metric also increased. Good declines: The district’s suspension rate and the number of students who were chronically absent declined. Post-pandemic, chronic absenteeism reached crisis levels for districts across the country. Despite the declines, the district still hasn’t erased the pandemic-era increase. Room for improvement: And while student math performance continued to inch up, performance declined in two important areas – students’ scores on English standardized tests and the percentage of English language learners who were making progress toward proficiency. artigo.texto: Ad spend on data center messaging surges ahead of midterms Spending on ads discussing widely unpopular data centers increased 61% in September, according to Sensor Tower, and messages are even coming to non-political advertising. • 3 min read Data centers aren’t just taking over local communities. They’re invading political ads, too. Last month alone, spending on political ads that discussed data centers increased 61% month over month, according to data compiled for Marketing Brew by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. (The firm analyzed US political ad spend encompassing ads involving data centers in creative text keywords.) Data centers, the construction of which Americans largely oppose, have increasingly factored into political ad campaigns, according to Sensor Tower, as candidates, their advertising teams, and PACs use the controversial political issue to reach voters ahead of the US midterm elections. By leaps and bounds: The number of US political ad campaigns that mentioned data centers has roughly quadrupled since June, according to Sensor Tower. While five campaigns included related messaging in June, that figure increased to around 20 by last month. The political groups that made up significant portions of that spend include: - Shapiro for Pennsylvania, a political action committee supporting the re-election of Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, whose ad spend made up 42% of total national data center–focused messaging (Of Shapiro for Pennsylvania’s total 2026 ad spend, over 50% of it mentioned data centers as of October 2.) - Friends of Byron Donalds PAC, a PAC supporting Republican Rep. Byron Donalds’s candidacy for Florida governor, accounted for 11% of national ads featuring data center–specific messaging as of October 2. - Friends of Sherrod Brown, a PAC working to get former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his Ohio Senate seat in 2024, re-elected, which made up 13% of data center–focused messaging in national ads as of October 2. Marketing Brew informs marketing pros of the latest on brand strategy, social media, and ad tech via our weekday newsletter, virtual events, marketing conferences, and digital guides. By subscribing, you accept our Terms & Privacy Policy. Shapiro for Pennsylvania, Friends of Byron Donalds PAC, and Friends of Sherrod Brown did not respond to requests for comment. Deep dive: Some PACs, like Friends of Sherrod Brown, are using ads featuring data centers to attack opponents: One ad, a 30-second spot titled “Face of Data Centers” spotlights opponent Sen. Jon Husted’s previous associations with data centers. Friends of Sherrod Brown has been focusing the message heavily on YouTube; ad spend allocation from the group on ads mentioning data centers on YouTube increased from 39% in July to 79% in August, Sensor Tower found. Friends of Sherrod Brown’s overall US ad spend mentioning data centers increased 81% MoM in August; In July and August, 38% of the group’s ad spend involved ads discussing data centers. That “could suggest it has become one of the campaign’s primary messaging points as public opinion on data centers sours,” according to Sensor Tower. Zoom out: Overall, ad spend this election cycle is projected to reach $11.6 billion, according to AdImpact, making it the most expensive on record. For non-political advertisers, political spending typically drives up prices and limits inventory. As data centers remain unpopular with the public, the topic is also creeping into non-political advertising. Liquid Death and Garage Beer recently ran an ad campaign asking consumers to send their urine to AI data centers in order to “save humanity.” About the author Jasmine Sheena Jasmine Sheena is a reporter for Marketing Brew writing about adtech, Big Tech, and streaming.

artigo.texto: Project doubles capacity of Bocanova site in one of the country's fastest-growing electricity load centers HOUSTON and OAKLAND, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nightpeak Energy announced today the successful financial close and commercial operation of its 150 MW, two-hour duration Bocanova 2 battery storage project in Southeast Texas. The project reached commercial operation on September 17, doubling the Bocanova site's capacity to 300 MW and adding significant flexibility to the ERCOT grid as data centers and other large loads drive rapid growth in electricity demand. Bocanova 2 is the second phase of Nightpeak's battery storage development in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area. The first 150 MW phase, Bocanova 1, began commercial operation in August 2025. Bocanova 2 uses Tesla's Megapack 2 XL battery storage systems. Operating under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty, the project was financed through a tax equity bridge loan and construction-to-term loan with MUFG Bank. U.S. Bank provided traditional tax equity. Paris Hays, Co-founder and CEO/CDO, Nightpeak Energy, said, "We're seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand. Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change. With 300 MW now operating at Bocanova, we're putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country. We're grateful to the City of Alvin, Brazoria County, and the local community for their support in bringing Bocanova to life." Since its founding in 2022, Nightpeak has developed and acquired a portfolio of over 1 GW of operating and de-risked capacity spanning gas-fired generation, battery storage and powered land development, and continues to advance an additional pipeline of flexible generation and large-load projects to meet growing demand in the U.S. About Nightpeak Energy Nightpeak Energy develops, owns and operates flexible power generation and large-load enablement assets that help meet growing electricity and AI demand while supporting a reliable, lower-carbon electric grid. Applying a technology-agnostic approach across gas-fired generation, energy storage, renewables, and large-load project types, the company combines generation and load into integrated solutions for its customers. Nightpeak is a portfolio investment of Energy Spectrum Partners VIII, LP, which is an infrastructure-focused private equity fund based in Dallas, Texas. artigo.texto: Para analisar a relação entre crédito verde e o mercado de carbono sob a perspectiva de um banco comercial, a Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank , fez uma apresentação no seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finanças e Investimentos em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã, em 14 de outubro. O mercado de carbono abre novas oportunidades para créditos verdes. No contexto internacional, a precificação do carbono tornou-se uma ferramenta econômica cada vez mais importante. O relatório do Banco Mundial "Estado e Tendências da Precificação do Carbono 2026" identifica 87 políticas de precificação direta do carbono em todo o mundo, abrangendo mais de 29% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa; essas ferramentas geram mais de US$ 107 bilhões em receita orçamentária em 2025 e o preço médio direto do carbono é de quase US$ 21/tCO₂e. Esses números não implicam um preço único para todos os créditos, mas demonstram que os custos das emissões estão sendo cada vez mais incorporados às decisões de investimento e negócios. A Sra. Ha afirmou que, para o Agribank, essa questão está diretamente ligada aos seus clientes e áreas de atuação. A agricultura , os agricultores e as áreas rurais são significativamente impactados pelas mudanças climáticas e têm espaço para redução de emissões na produção de arroz, pecuária, silvicultura, energia de biomassa, tratamento de resíduos e economia circular. Portanto, a questão central não é "se o banco comprará e venderá créditos", mas sim "como o banco pode financiar o processo de geração de resultados de redução de emissões e quando o valor do carbono é suficientemente certo para influenciar as decisões de crédito?". O arcabouço legal para o mercado de carbono do Vietnã foi estabelecido pela Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020 e detalhado por meio de diversos documentos. De 2022 até o presente, a lista de empresas obrigadas a realizar inventários de gases de efeito estufa aumentou de 1.912 para 2.441, um aumento de quase 28%. Em 2022, a Decisão 01/2022/QD-TTg listou 1.912 estabelecimentos; em 2024, a Decisão 13/2024/QD-TTg listou 2.166 estabelecimentos, um aumento de 254 estabelecimentos, representando aproximadamente 30% do total das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa; e em 2026, a Decisão 42/2026/QD-TTg listou 2.441 estabelecimentos, um aumento de 275 estabelecimentos. Em relação aos créditos verdes, a Decisão 21/2025/QD-TTg sobre critérios ambientais e a Lista de Classificação Verde fornece uma base para a identificação de projetos verdes, e a Decisão 46/2026/QD-TTg sobre orientações para a determinação de projetos verdes e projetos que atendem aos critérios da economia circular contribui para a criação de novos projetos verdes, desbloqueando capital, expandindo os padrões para a economia circular e os critérios ESG. No entanto, é importante ressaltar que a inclusão de um projeto na lista de classificação verde não significa automaticamente que ele possua créditos de carbono e, inversamente, um projeto com créditos não atende automaticamente às condições para a concessão de créditos. A Decisão 42/2026/QD-TTg, em vigor a partir de 25 de setembro de 2026, atualiza a lista de setores e instalações que devem realizar inventários de gases de efeito estufa, ampliando ainda mais a base de dados para a gestão de emissões. De acordo com dados da HNX, o código de cota VN2025 para o período de conformidade de 2025-2026 possui um volume total de 511.473.846 tCO₂e, alocado a 110 instituições; o primeiro dia de negociação é 29 de junho de 2026 e o último dia de negociação é 24 de dezembro de 2027. Esta é uma transição significativa da estrutura política para a infraestrutura de negociação propriamente dita. No entanto, os dados publicamente disponíveis na HNX mostram que, durante esses dias de negociação, tanto o volume quanto o valor negociado foram zero. Isso não significa que o mercado não tenha potencial, mas sugere que os bancos não devem presumir que já exista um preço de referência estável ou liquidez abundante para usar diretamente na avaliação de pedidos de empréstimo. O Vietnã também possui experiência na comercialização de resultados de redução de emissões no mercado internacional. Em março de 2024, o Vietnã recebeu US$ 51,5 milhões do Banco Mundial por 10,3 milhões de toneladas de resultados comprovados de redução de emissões no âmbito do Programa de Redução de Emissões da Região Centro-Norte. A lição importante não está em dividir US$ 51,5 milhões por 10,3 milhões de toneladas para formar um "preço de referência", mas sim em que os resultados ambientais só se tornam fluxo de caixa quando há uma metodologia clara, dados, verificação, contrato e mecanismo de compartilhamento de benefícios. Proposta para facilitar o fluxo de capital verde vinculado ao mercado de carbono. Segundo representantes do Agribank, em meados de 2026, o total de ativos do Agribank ultrapassará 2,7 trilhões de VND, o capital mobilizado ultrapassará 2,5 trilhões de VND e a carteira de empréstimos para a economia ultrapassará 2 trilhões de VND. Em agosto de 2026, a carteira de empréstimos para agricultura, agricultores e áreas rurais atingirá mais de 1,34 trilhão de VND, representando 64,7% do total de empréstimos. Em 31 de julho de 2026, todo o sistema contará com mais de 58.000 grupos de empréstimo, com mais de 910.000 membros e um total de empréstimos pendentes superior a 216 trilhões de VND. Essa é uma vantagem única para a coleta de dados, a organização do financiamento ao longo da cadeia de valor e a implementação de modelos de redução de emissões em áreas de produção dispersas. Em relação ao crédito verde, até o final de março de 2026, o saldo total de crédito verde do Agribank atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND. Em 2026, o Agribank continuará a implementar um programa de crédito verde de 3 trilhões de VND para client

artigo.texto: The global energy storage market is moving fast. Battery costs have fallen sharply, installations are accelerating, and projects are being built in markets where governments have yet to set a 2030 storage target. So, if the market is already delivering, why do governments still need targets? Because deployment alone does not guarantee that storage will be built at the scale, in the places or on the timelines needed to support the energy transition. Global energy storage additions reached a record 118 GW in 2025, including 108 GW of batteries. Battery additions have increased seventeenfold in five years, and deployment is already outpacing current national targets. Yet, Ember’s latest analysis finds that national 2030 storage targets total just 822 GW across 99 countries and the EU. That is nearly three times the ambition assessed at COP29, but still 45% below the global pledge to reach 1,500 GW by 2030 (see Global Storage Targets Reach 822 GW, 45% Below COP29 Goal). The apparent contradiction is important. The market is moving, but government planning has not caught up. The case for storage is increasingly clear in solar markets. Solar generates most of its electricity during daylight hours, while demand continues into the evening and night. Batteries can store surplus daytime generation and release it when needed, helping reduce curtailment, ease pressure on grids, and make better use of renewable capacity. That is why countries with ambitious solar targets often have ambitious storage targets too. But the relationship is far from universal. Of the world's 20 largest solar markets by installed capacity in 2025, eight still have no storage target for 2030. The lack of a target has not stopped deployment everywhere. The US has installed roughly 52 GW of utility-scale batteries, Germany has around 30 GWh of battery storage installed, and Saudi Arabia has connected a 7.8 GWh project, the world's largest single battery project. These examples show that market forces and grid needs can drive investment without an explicit national target. But they do not mean targets are unnecessary. They show that deployment can move ahead while government planning lags behind. Other markets have made less progress on both targets and installations. Without a clear signal of future ambition, investors may have less certainty about the scale and timing of demand. Where storage development remains limited, the absence of a target can mean a missed opportunity to unlock investment and make better use of existing and planned solar capacity. A national target is not a substitute for a functioning market. Nor does announcing a number guarantee that projects will be built. Targets need to be supported by effective policies, investment frameworks and grid planning. But they can help align these elements. A credible target gives investors a clearer indication of the scale of future deployment governments expect. It can help guide decisions on procurement, grid development, and the coordination of storage with new renewable generation. It can also draw attention to gaps between planned renewable capacity and the flexibility needed to integrate it. The distinction matters because storage is not just about adding up gigawatts. It is about ensuring that the right amount and type of storage is available where and when the power system needs it. A national target should therefore be connected to the country's broader energy plans, including its renewable capacity ambitions and grid requirements. The global picture also shows how concentrated the recent increase in ambition has been. China raised its 2030 storage target to 460 GW in its 15th Five-Year Plan, while the EU set its first bloc-wide target at 200 GW in June 2026. Together, they account for more than 80% of national storage targets worldwide. This is significant progress, but it is not evidence of a broad-based shift in government planning. Most other major solar markets have not substantially increased their storage ambition since COP29. The stakes will rise as electrification expands. More electricity use across transport, buildings and industry can reduce dependence on fossil fuels, but only if power systems can supply that electricity reliably and increasingly from clean sources. The Global Electrification Pledge being advanced ahead of COP31 aims to raise electricity's share of final energy demand from around 20% to 35% by 2035. Delivering on that ambition will require more than electrifying end uses. It will also require sufficient renewable generation, grid infrastructure and storage to meet demand when it occurs. The storage market has already demonstrated that it can scale rapidly. Ember's analysis suggests that even if annual battery additions grow much more slowly than they have since 2020, the world could still reach the 1,500 GW pledge by 2030. Falling battery costs are helping make that possible. The challenge now is to translate this momentum into reliable power systems. Governments do not need to dictate every investment decision or set targets just to have them. They do need credible plans that give markets direction and ensure deployment meets system needs. Storage is booming, which is reason enough to raise ambition, not abandon it. This matters even more as the world enters the Age of Power, with electricity taking on a growing role across all sectors. Targets can help turn a fast-growing market into a more coordinated build-out of the flexibility needed for a renewables-powered, increasingly electrified world.

artigo.texto: Desbloquear fluxos de capital verde através dos mercados de crédito e de carbono. Juntamente com a expansão do crédito verde, espera-se que o mercado de carbono crie recursos financeiros adicionais, reduzindo a pressão de capital sobre as empresas em processo de transformação verde. O saldo devedor em crédito verde ultrapassou 856 trilhões de VND. O crédito verde está em expansão, contribuindo para o fluxo de capital para setores que apoiam a transformação verde. No entanto, a necessidade de investimentos de grande porte e longo prazo exige o desenvolvimento de canais adicionais de mobilização de capital, incluindo o mercado de carbono. Em seu discurso no seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", organizado pelo jornal Finanças e Investimentos em 14 de outubro, o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, afirmou que, no processo de alcançar a meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050, a demanda por capital para inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa está aumentando. Embora outros canais de mobilização de capital verde estejam se desenvolvendo, o crédito verde continua a desempenhar um papel crucial na transição para um modelo de crescimento de baixo carbono. Segundo o vice-governador, o setor bancário tem implementado proativamente diversas soluções para promover o crédito verde, direcionando fluxos de capital para indústrias e setores que trazem benefícios ambientais e reduzem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Paralelamente, o Banco Central do Vietnã está aprimorando gradualmente o arcabouço político, emitindo diretrizes e instruções sobre crédito verde e gestão de riscos ambientais e sociais, e incentivando as instituições de crédito a desenvolverem estratégias, processos internos e produtos de crédito alinhados às metas de crescimento verde. Os resultados da implementação mostram que a escala do crédito verde se expandiu. No final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. Durante o período de 2017 a 2025, a taxa média de crescimento foi superior a 20% ao ano. Os empréstimos em aberto concentram-se principalmente nos setores de agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade, representando mais de 31%; o setor de energia verde representa quase 28%. Além disso, os empréstimos avaliados quanto aos riscos ambientais e sociais ultrapassaram 6,2 milhões de VND, representando mais de 31,33% do total de empréstimos em aberto em toda a economia . De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, esses resultados demonstram o compromisso do sistema bancário em apoiar a transformação verde dos negócios e da economia. De fato, no Banco de Desenvolvimento Agrícola e Rural ( Agribank ), o crédito verde está sendo implementado em conjunto com os setores de produção e grupos de clientes que necessitam de transformação. Até o final de março de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde do banco atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND. Em 2026, o Agribank continuará a implementar um programa de crédito verde de 3 trilhões de VND para clientes individuais e um programa de 50 trilhões de VND para financiar a agricultura limpa e de alta tecnologia. Você também pode gostar Um programa notável é o programa de empréstimos que vincula produção, processamento e consumo no âmbito do Projeto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável para 1 milhão de hectares de arroz de alta qualidade e baixa emissão no Delta do Mekong, com um valor mínimo de 30 trilhões de VND. A Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank, acredita que a agricultura, os agricultores e as áreas rurais são significativamente impactados pelas mudanças climáticas e que há espaço para redução de emissões em setores como o cultivo de arroz, a pecuária, a silvicultura, a energia de biomassa e o tratamento de resíduos. Portanto, a questão não se resume apenas a fornecer capital para atividades produtivas, mas também a financiar o processo de criação de resultados mensuráveis e verificáveis de redução de emissões. O crédito é um canal crucial para o fluxo de capital; no entanto, o Sr. Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, acredita que o crédito bancário por si só não consegue suprir todas as necessidades de capital para a transformação verde. Estima-se que o Vietnã necessite de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Desse total, a necessidade de adaptação e aumento da resiliência é de aproximadamente US$ 254 bilhões, enquanto a redução de emissões requer cerca de US$ 114 bilhões. Somente o setor elétrico necessita de aproximadamente US$ 136 bilhões em investimentos para o desenvolvimento da geração e transmissão de energia entre 2026 e 2030. O Sr. Bui Minh Giap afirmou: "Os bancos são um canal importante para o fluxo de capital, mas não podem, sozinhos, atender às necessidades de capital de longo prazo para financiamento verde e financiamento de conversão." Portanto, é necessário combinar crédito com títulos verdes, títulos de conversão, capital próprio, financiamento misto, garantias e mecanismos de compartilhamento de risco. Cada tipo de risco precisa ser alocado a partes com capacidade de gestão adequada. O mercado de carbono precisa gerar valor econômico real. Juntamente com os créditos verdes, espera-se que o mercado de carbono desbloqueie mais recursos para as empresas, convertendo os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico.
