artigo.texto: Unlocking green capital flows through credit and carbon markets. Along with the expansion of green credit, the carbon market is expected to create additional financial resources, reducing the capital pressure on businesses undergoing green transformation. Outstanding green credit reached over 856,000 billion VND. Green credit is expanding, contributing to the flow of capital into sectors supporting green transformation. However, the need for large and long-term investments necessitates the development of additional capital mobilization channels, including the carbon market. Speaking at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, in the process of achieving the goal of net zero emissions by 2050, the demand for capital for technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is increasing. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role in the transition to a low-carbon growth model. According to the Deputy Governor, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Along with this, the State Bank of Vietnam is gradually perfecting the policy framework, issuing guidelines and instructions on green credit and environmental and social risk management; and encouraging credit institutions to develop strategies, internal processes, and credit products that align with green growth goals. The implementation results show that the scale of green credit has expanded. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. During the period 2017-2025, the average growth rate was over 20% per year. Outstanding loans are mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; the green energy sector accounts for nearly 28%. In addition, loans assessed for environmental and social risks reached over 6.2 million billion VND, accounting for more than 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy . According to Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Canh, these results demonstrate the banking system's commitment to supporting the green transformation of businesses and the economy. In fact, at the Agricultural and Rural Development Bank ( Agribank ), green credit is being implemented in conjunction with production sectors and customer groups with a need for transformation. By the end of March 2026, the bank's outstanding green credit balance reached nearly VND 30,000 billion. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a VND 3,000 billion green credit program for individual customers and a VND 50,000 billion program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture. You may also like One notable program is the lending program linking production, processing, and consumption under the Sustainable Development Project for 1 million hectares of high-quality, low-emission rice in the Mekong Delta, with a minimum scale of 30,000 billion VND. Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank, believes that agriculture, farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in sectors such as rice cultivation, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, and waste treatment. Therefore, the issue is not only about providing capital for production activities, but also about financing the process of creating measurable and verifiable emission reduction results. Credit is a crucial channel for capital flow; however, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, believes that bank credit alone cannot meet the entire capital needs for green transformation. It is estimated that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the need for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, while emission reduction requires about US$114 billion. The electricity sector alone needs approximately US$136 billion in investment for power generation and transmission development between 2026 and 2030. Mr. Bui Minh Giap affirmed: "Banks are an important channel for capital flow, but they cannot alone meet the long-term capital needs for green financing and conversion financing." Therefore, it is necessary to combine credit with green bonds, conversion bonds, equity capital, mixed financing, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms. Each type of risk needs to be allocated to parties with appropriate management capabilities. The carbon market needs to create real economic value. Along with green credit, the carbon market is expected to unlock more resources for businesses by converting emission reduction results into economic value. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, by establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the market creates incentives for businesses to proactively invest in green transformation. The Deputy Governor argued that when the carbon market operates effectively, the results of emission reductions can become a source of financing for businesses themselves. This would give businesses the ability to generate additional resources from their emission reductions, helping to reduce pressure on equity capital, the budget, and bank credit. artigo.texto: O governo federal trabalha para regulamentar o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) até o final de 2026. A expectativa foi confirmada pelo ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, que afirmou, durante a Futurecom 2026, que o Executivo está articulando com outros ministérios para acelerar o processo após as eleições. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Entidades pedem ao Confaz redução de ICMS para equipamentos de data centers “O mais difícil era aprovar o Redata no Congresso Nacional – na Câmara e no Senado – e isso aconteceu. A questão da regulamentação agora são ajustes finos”, disse o ministro, ao comentar a possibilidade de implementação do regime ainda neste ano. Segundo Siqueira Filho, a infraestrutura digital já foi equacionada nas discussões, enquanto a questão energética permanece em debate. “Então, a expectativa é que sim, a gente consiga resolver até o final do ano”, afirmou. O ministro disse que o Ministério das Comunicações mantém conversas com outras áreas do governo para viabilizar a regulamentação. Entre os interlocutores citados estão os ministérios responsáveis pelo comércio e pela energia, além da Casa Civil. A intenção é acelerar as tratativas no período posterior às eleições. Reforma tributária e benefícios para investidores A regulamentação do Redata ocorre em meio às discussões sobre os efeitos da reforma tributária, cuja implementação começa em janeiro de 2027. A mudança no sistema tributário levanta dúvidas sobre a efetividade de parte dos incentivos previstos no regime especial para investimentos em data centers. Questionado sobre o risco de o Redata perder relevância diante das mudanças tributárias, Siqueira Filho afirmou que a discussão deve se concentrar nos benefícios efetivamente oferecidos aos investidores. “O que vale no final do dia é o tema de qual é o benefício que toda essa solução vai trazer para o investidor”, declarou. Para o ministro, é necessário avaliar como os incentivos disponíveis, seja por meio do Redata ou da reforma tributária, afetam as empresas que pretendem investir no país e ampliar a infraestrutura digital brasileira. Siqueira Filho também afirmou que o governo trabalha para viabilizar a regulamentação dentro do curto prazo. O ministro confirmou que há articulações em andamento para que projetos usufruam dos benefícios do Redata ainda em 2026, mas não anunciou projetos específicos nem detalhou um cronograma de implementação. artigo.texto: To analyze the relationship between green credit and the carbon market from a commercial bank's perspective, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank , delivered a presentation at the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" organized by the Finance and Investment Newspaper in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam on October 14th. The carbon market opens up new opportunities for green credit. In the international context, carbon pricing has become an increasingly important economic tool. The World Bank's State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2026 report identifies 87 direct carbon pricing policies worldwide, covering more than 29% of global greenhouse gas emissions; these tools generate over $107 billion in budget revenue in 2025 and the average direct carbon price is nearly $21/tCO₂e. These figures do not imply a single price for all credits, but they demonstrate that emission costs are increasingly being internalized into investment and business decisions. Ms. Ha stated that, for Agribank, this issue is directly linked to its customers and operating areas. Agriculture , farmers, and rural areas are both significantly impacted by climate change and have room for emission reduction in rice production, livestock farming, forestry, biomass energy, waste treatment, and the circular economy. Therefore, the central question is not "whether the bank will buy and sell credits," but rather "how can the bank finance the process of generating emission reduction results, and when is the carbon value sufficiently certain to influence credit decisions?" The legal framework for Vietnam's carbon market is established by the 2020 Environmental Protection Law and further elaborated through various documents. From 2022 to the present, the list of businesses required to conduct greenhouse gas inventories has increased from 1,912 to 2,441, a nearly 28% increase. In 2022, Decision 01/2022/QD-TTg listed 1,912 establishments; in 2024, Decision 13/2024/QD-TTg listed 2,166 establishments, an increase of 254 establishments, accounting for approximately 30% of the total national greenhouse gas emissions; and in 2026, Decision 42/2026/QD-TTg listed 2,441 establishments, an increase of 275 establishments. Regarding green credit, Decision 21/2025/QD-TTg on environmental criteria and the Green Classification List provides a basis for identifying green projects, and Decision 46/2026/QD-TTg on guidance for determining green projects and projects meeting circular criteria contributes to creating new green projects, unlocking capital, expanding standards for the circular economy and ESG criteria. However, it is important to emphasize that a project on the green classification list does not automatically mean it has carbon credits, and conversely, a project with credits does not automatically meet the conditions for granting credit. Decision 42/2026/QD-TTg, effective from September 25, 2026, updates the list of sectors and facilities that must conduct greenhouse gas inventories, further expanding the data base for emission management. According to HNX data, the VN2025 quota code for the 2025-2026 compliance period has a total volume of 511,473,846 tCO₂e, allocated to 110 institutions; the first trading day is June 29, 2026, and the last trading day is December 24, 2027. This is a significant transition from the policy framework to the actual trading infrastructure. However, publicly available data at HNX shows that during these trading days, both trading volume and value were zero. This doesn't mean the market lacks potential, but it suggests that banks shouldn't assume a stable reference price or deep liquidity already exists to use directly in loan application assessments. Vietnam also has experience commercializing emission reduction results on the international market. In March 2024, Vietnam received US$51.5 million from the World Bank for 10.3 million tons of verified emission reduction results in the North Central Region Emission Reduction Program. The important lesson is not in dividing US$51.5 million by 10.3 million tons to form a "benchmark price," but in that environmental results only become a cash flow when there is a clear methodology, data, verification, contract, and benefit-sharing mechanism. By August 2026, outstanding loans for agriculture, farmers, and rural areas will reach over VND 1.34 trillion, accounting for 64.7% of total outstanding loans. By July 31, 2026, the entire system will have over 58,000 loan groups with more than 910,000 members and total outstanding loans exceeding VND 216,000 billion. This is a unique advantage for gathering data, organizing financing along the value chain, and bringing emission reduction models to dispersed production areas. Regarding green credit, by the end of March 2026, Agribank's total outstanding green credit reached nearly 30,000 billion VND. In 2026, Agribank will continue to implement a 3,000 billion VND green credit program for individual customers and a 50,000 billion VND program to finance clean, high-tech agriculture. This platform is particularly suitable for testing how to manage data, cash flow, and carbon benefits in an organized production chain. artigo.texto: Northfield council moves away from data center ban, toward tiered regulation After more than two hours of public comment and council discussion, the Northfield City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday night to reduce the required setback between data-processing facilities and parks or trails from roughly three-quarters of a mile to 200 feet. But the setback change was only part of the story. In a separate motion, the council also directed staff to explore a tiered regulatory framework for data-processing facilities as part of the upcoming Land Development Code update, looking beyond just power consumption to include water use and other emerging concerns. The change to the setback had been in the works since 2024, when the city passed an ordinance regulating data-processing facilities. That ordinance required a 3,950-foot setback from any existing or planned park, trail, or recreational feature. It also required a 200-foot setback from residential structures. Community Development Director Scott Wopata acknowledged the moment was about more than one number. “This one’s going to be hard,” he said. “In any example I look at around Minnesota or the Midwest or nationally, there aren’t a lot of examples where communities have figured out a way to have this conversation and learn from each other and to empathetically see things from different perspectives. There’s a lot of negative examples of how elected officials and staff members in different cities have signed NDAs, dismissed the public, not listened to public concerns.” Wopata framed the night as an effort to rebuild public trust after a year of conversations that started long before any application existed. “In 2024, we put a moratorium on all data-center development so that we could develop policies before we had a project application,” Wopata said. “That is what we did. We have been following those best practices.” The city’s regulations include 17 performance standards covering noise, water use, glare, vibrations and more. They also require a conditional use permit triggered by any water use. “If we read anywhere anything about data centers, [there] is a very well documented track of negative externalities,” Wopata said. “There are water quality issues. There’s water quantity issues. There are stories of communities losing water pressure. There’s stories of communities where residents have seen significant spikes in their utility bills because the data centers moved in and this corporate development has happened.” But he also drew a distinction between prohibition and regulation. “Regulating is often a more strategic and sophisticated and just successful approach than prohibition,” Wopata said, listing alcohol and cannabis prohibition as negative examples from history. “Bringing something into the light and regulating it can often help ameliorate some of the biggest harmful negative externalities.” City Planner Mathias Hughey explained the rationale for the change. The 3,950-foot setback made every industrial parcel in the city undevelopable, and it was originally drafted without a clear rationale. “This is still much more restrictive than other industrial uses,” Hughey said. Hughey said the planning commission had separately recommended that data-processing facilities be prohibited outright and that staff research a tiered regulatory framework. Because that recommendation was not part of the published public hearing notice, the council had to proceed with the setback item as written. Competing priorities More than a dozen residents spoke during public comment, most urging the council to keep the moratorium or reject the setback change. One Northfielder, Trisha Brunk, even led the room through a song. Councilor Kathleen Holmes acknowledged the volume of opposition in the room but said the council has to weigh competing priorities. “While there is a high number of people who have spoken out against data centers, we, those of us decision makers, policymakers up here, have to hold many priorities,” she said. “And while we have heard the thoughts, the feedback, the opinions on data centers, I would say probably all of us here more often and more frequently hear ‘Lower our taxes.’ … I take this as the belief that the path forward is through regulation and not prohibition.” Councilor Jessica Peterson White said she saw parallels to hog feedlot debates from the early 2000s. “But when we were talking about hog feedlots, the scale was a really important part of the conversation,” she said. “I don’t have a clear sense myself of what scale of data center or other types of development is where we should set a regulation, but I believe that the regulations that we have make it vanishingly unlikely that we will get a hyperscale data center, and that seems good.” She also addressed the equity dimension. “There is a history in this country of affluent white communities sort of offshoring their industrial needs to communities that don’t have the same resources, don’t have the same organizing power, and those industrial uses are then underregulated and create issues for poorer and less white communities,” she said. “And I hope we don’t play a role in that.” No one is saying ‘Let’s build a huge data center’ Councilor Davin Sokup said he was voting yes despite his own uncertainty. “But I just really want to highlight that what we’re considering here tonight, I think, in my opinion, does show an openness to having a data center in Northfield,” he said. “I’m not willing to say that it couldn’t possibly be that in the future.” Councilor Chad Beumer said he understood the distrust but believed the city’s regulations were already strong. “I don’t think there’s a single person artigo.texto: Vattenfall has awarded Fluence Energy a contract to supply and support a large-scale battery energy storage facility at the Brunsbüttel site, currently the location of a decommissioned nuclear power plant in Germany. The agreement includes both the delivery of the storage system and long-term service for the facility, which will have a capacity exceeding 1GW-hour (GWh) and an output of 254MW. The project is expected to become operational by the end of 2028. Once completed, the Brunsbüttel project will be among the largest battery energy storage system (BESS) installations in Germany and represents Vattenfall's most substantial battery commitment so far. The facility will be built using Fluence's Gridstack Pro 5000 platform, which incorporates battery systems and associated power conversion equipment. It also includes an energy management system designed to enhance grid resilience and support renewable energy integration. Fluence is responsible for providing a turnkey solution covering engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning, along with ongoing long-term service to help maintain performance over the facility's lifespan. The four-hour BESS is designed to respond to fluctuations in electricity supply and demand as Germany experiences increasing amounts of wind and solar generation and growing price volatility. Vattenfall solar and batteries head Claus Wattendrup said: "Projects like this battery storage facility play an important role in strengthening the resilience of the energy system and enabling the continued integration of renewable power generation. "Together with Fluence as our long-term partner, we are creating a flexible asset that can respond to changing electricity market needs for many years to come. "The project will further strengthen our portfolio of flexibility solutions and support the transition away from fossil fuels." The company reached a final investment decision last month to build the Brunsbüttel BESS facility. Construction is set to begin in 2027, with grid connection planned to the 50Hz, 380kV transmission network by late 2028. The new installation will nearly double Vattenfall's existing battery storage portfolio. "Vattenfall selects Fluence for 1GWh Brunsbüttel battery storage project" was originally created and published by Power Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: San Jose leaders consider new rules for data centers amid several proposals San Jose city leaders are holding a community meeting Thursday evening to discuss new regulations for data centers in the future. According to the city, there are currently 11 applications for data centers under review. "Within the last 10 years, we had like Google warehouses coming through here, we had distribution centers," Marcos Espinoza, the president of Alviso in Action, told CBS News Bay Area. Alviso, a district of roughly 2,000 residents in the northern part of San Jose, has a few large-energy use projects brewing in its backyard. "This is not just something that can be swept under the rug," Espinoza said. A Microsoft data center is under construction about a mile away from his home. "Anxious to see once it's built, what impact it will be, that's causing noise pollution, air pollution," he said. Espinoza has been living in the area for about 20 years. As the head of Alviso in Action, he informs the community of the environmental impacts of projects like these. "Just the location, it's right next to a river, Coyote Creek," he said. "That river is the one that actually caused the flooding in Alviso back in 1983. So, they say that with the data center is not a flood zone, but it's right next to the river." He said there are rumors of a data center coming to the intersection of North 1st Street and Anderson Alley, right by the Top Golf site. The city said that developer had not filed an application as of now. "This is the worrying site, because we're so close to residential units here, we got the library over there," Espinoza said. San Jose officials said they are continuing to finalize rules for newly adopted data center projects. "California already has a lot of requirements, we're building on top of those requirements," Manuel Pineda, San Jose deputy city manager, told CBS News Bay Area. "Noise has been a significant component. We are doing two key things. One is, we're requiring sound barriers as part of the equipment around the data centers. And two, we're implementing a noise monitoring program as well to make sure that they're staying within the standards and requirements." Pineda said the city is working to ensure that these centers only use recycled water or low water-cooling technology. Generators must also now be EPA Tier 4, which is the strictest emission standards. "Regarding the generators, the district has an enforcement requirement, we can actually enforce this as well. We have yearly reporting requirements as well for noise, for sewage, we have yearly reporting requirements for energy use and water use. And we have different mechanisms to make sure that projects are in compliance. And if they're not in compliance, we can bring them back in compliance. That can be, they have to pay penalties, or they have to build additional projects to make sure they meet the requirements," he added. The regulations would impact more than just data centers. Google's project in Alviso, technically a research facility on paper, could still draw 250 megawatts at capacity. "They also do other things functionally, as well as have different backup generators. The key thing for us is whether you are a data center or a research and development facility over 20 megawatts, all the standards apply to both projects equally," Pineda said. As for Espinoza, he said he is relieved the city is gathering feedback from the community. "Maybe we can adjust some of these developments from their concerns," he said. But he said he and residents in Alviso feel defeated. "We're trying to live here for generations, you know, start families here, continue this as such an amazing community, but is that going to be possible with these data centers?" he said. "Families been here so long. This is somewhere that families, especially my family have decided that it's somewhere we call home." City officials said the goal is to come before council by December with the finalized policy. The tentative ordinance second reading is scheduled for December 15, and the law would go into effect 30 days after the second reading.

artigo.texto: The US is set to have access to about 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium over the next decade following a new agreement to produce the critical mineral using advanced lithium extraction technology. The GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) and refining technology was developed by Energy Exploration Technologies (EnergyX). The Texas-based firm specializes in lithium extraction and critical mineral production. On Monday, October 12, EnergyX announced that it signed a binding, 10-year, take-or-pay agreement with Singaporean global commodity trader Trafigura to supply lithium from two major projects in Texas and Chile. The supply will support electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and other industries that depend on battery materials. The company said commercial production is scheduled to start in 2028. “Offtake agreements are among the most important steps in taking a lithium project from development to production,” Teague Egan, EnergyX founder and CEO, disclosed. A new extraction method The US produces about 6,600 US tons (6,000 metric tons) of lithium annually. This accounts for less than one percent of the global production. Moreover, it relies on net imports for more than 50 percent of the lithium it consumes. To address this, EnergyX came up with the GET-Lit direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology. More from Energy See All Backed by more than 150 patents, the approach extracts lithium from mineral-rich brines and refines it into materials suitable for batteries. The novel process works by separating lithium directly from liquid brines. EnergyX has already tested the method in labs, pilot facilities, and demonstration plants in the US and Chile. In April 2026, it commissioned its Project Lonestar lithium production plant in Texas, which is the largest DLE lithium production plant in the country. At the same time, the company is also working on another major lithium project in Chile called Black Giant. It has a planned annual production capacity of around 57,871 US tons (52,500 metric tons). The two projects will produce different lithium products. Black Giant will supply lithium carbonate, while Project Lonestar will produce lithium hydroxide. Both materials are essential for rechargeable batteries used in EVs and energy storage systems. Commercial operations Under the agreement, Trafigura will buy 110,000 US tons (100,000 metric tons) of battery-grade lithium products over the next decade. The deal covers 66 percent of the planned first-phase output from Project Black Giant, as well as 30 percent from Project Lonestar. Meanwhile, EnergyX is also talking to other potential buyers to secure customers for 80 percent of its planned production. At current lithium prices of about USD 18,100 per US ton (roughly USD 20,000 per metric ton), the deal could generate over USD 2 billion in revenue over its lifetime. “A long-term purchase commitment from a counterparty of Trafigura’s scale and credit quality shows that the market wants EnergyX’s product,” Egan stressed in a press release. “It also gives lenders and investors the revenue visibility they need before committing capital to commercial construction.” EnergyX has also secured financial support for its expansion plans. This includes a USD 225 million investment from energy company Eni for Project Black Giant and a USD 690 million letter of intent from the US Export-Import Bank for potential debt financing. “We are pleased to support EnergyX as it develops its lithium projects in Chile and the US,” Daniel von Arx, Trafigura’s head of battery metals, stated. He added that long-term deals are important for starting production and securing reliable supplies of critical minerals.

artigo.texto: A China intensificou as sanções contra os principais emissores que não cumprirem o prazo para devolver suas cotas de emissão de carbono. Segundo o correspondente da Agência de Notícias do Vietnã em Pequim, as regulamentações revisadas sobre o comércio de emissões de carbono, anunciadas recentemente pelo Ministério da Ecologia e Meio Ambiente da China, estipulam multas iniciais que variam de 1 milhão de yuans (equivalente a US$ 149.429) a 5 milhões de yuans. Caso a infração persista dentro do prazo estipulado, a entidade infratora estará sujeita a uma multa adicional equivalente a 5 a 10 vezes o preço médio de mercado da quota de emissão de carbono. Além disso, as autoridades ambientais poderão exigir que a entidade infratora suspenda a produção até que as medidas corretivas sejam concluídas. O comércio de carbono é um mecanismo para a compra e venda de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa entre entidades designadas. A China lançou programas-piloto de comércio de carbono em outubro de 2011 em sete regiões, incluindo a província de Hubei, Pequim e Xangai. O mercado nacional de negociação de carbono da China começou a operar oficialmente em julho de 2021, inicialmente aplicado ao setor de geração de energia a carvão. Por meio desse mecanismo, as usinas termelétricas recebem cotas de emissão de carbono correspondentes à sua produção de eletricidade. Após cada ciclo de negociação, os operadores podem vender as quotas restantes após cumprirem os requisitos de emissão. Por outro lado, aqueles que excederem os limites de emissão alocados devem adquirir quotas adicionais para cumprirem a regulamentação. Até 2025, espera-se que o mercado de negociação de carbono da China se expanda ainda mais para as indústrias de aço, cimento e fundição de alumínio.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The Chicago commuter rail system, Metra, and rail vehicle manufacturer Stadler debuted a battery-electric train at the American Public Transportation Association conference and expo in Chicago last week. - Metra has ordered eight of the train sets, which are expected to enter passenger service by 2028, according to a news release. Each train set will consist of four cars with a seating capacity of about 200, a Stadler spokesperson told Smart Cities Dive. - Metra will be able to deploy the battery-powered trains without adding infrastructure along the right-of-way. Metra plans to introduce the train sets along a route between two stations on the Beverly Branch of the Rock Island Line, a distance of 16.4 miles. Dive Insight: Commuter rail operators are exploring battery-electric trains and locomotives. Caltrain, a commuter rail line that serves the San Francisco Peninsula, electrified 51 miles of its route with overhead catenary wire and will add battery-electric trains to run beyond the wired portion of the route. The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority is planning to replace diesel-powered trains with battery power on the Fairmount Commuter Rail Line, which serves an environmental justice community. The New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority ordered 13 battery-electric passenger locomotives to serve trains on its Metro-North lines, marking the first use of the technology in North America. A portion of the Metra train set was on display at the expo. The trains, which will be manufactured in Salt Lake City, are capable of speeds up to 90 mph but will be restricted to 79 mph in use, the spokesperson said. The batteries have a range of about 50 miles, he said, which allows the train to make three runs between the LaSalle Street and Blue Island stations. The trains can be recharged at the terminal stations, the spokesperson said. “These new trainsets are coming at a perfect time,” Northern Illinois Transit Authority Chairman Tom Kotarac said in a statement. “We are excited about the potential for these new trainsets to help increase service and improve regional connectivity, while at the same time reducing regional pollution and noise.” The train set will be on display at the LaSalle Street Station in Chicago today and tomorrow.

artigo.texto: Under the draft regulations, facilities drawing 20 megawatts or more would be barred from using drinking water in open cooling systems, required to run on 100% clean power, and limited to 25 hours a year for backup generator testing. The proposed policies follow weeks of community outreach in which city residents expressed many of the same anxieties over data centers that have been growing nationwide. While the projects promise millions of dollars in revenue for cities that welcome them, they also bring massive energy and water demands alongside quality-of-life concerns like noise pollution. The new draft regulations target large data centers and other tech facilities drawing massive amounts of electricity and water. To cut down on environmental harm, facilities would be banned from using drinking water in open cooling systems, which continuously lose water rather than recirculating it. Sites would also need built-in sound barriers, shielded lights that point downward to prevent neighborhood glare, and mandatory annual city checkups on their power, water, and sewer usage to ensure they stay within legal limits. The proposals also set new expectations for developers and neighbors. Companies would be required to comply with state "prevailing wage and skilled and trained workforce requirements" and notify residents within a 1,500-foot radius of a proposed site. The city is also weighing new developer fees to fund local affordable housing and strengthen the power grid, while ensuring tax dollars from equipment sales remain in San Jose. "The standards are intended to mitigate potential impacts related to energy consumption and sourcing, water use, air quality, backup power generators, and other environmental factors, and to outline a clear and consistent process for community notification and engagement," the city said in a statement. City officials emphasize that the proposals are only a first draft and that residents can still help shape them during a special community forum next Thursday, Oct. 15, from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at San Jose City Hall Council Chambers and online via Zoom. Following Thursday's meeting, staff will present the final draft standards and accompanying ordinances to the Planning Commission on Nov. 18. The proposals are expected to reach the City Council on Dec. 8, with a second and final vote set for Dec. 15. San Jose's push for local oversight echoes a statewide effort to rein in data centers driven by the artificial intelligence boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven bills aimed at protecting electric customers from paying for grid upgrades needed for data centers, forcing transparency on water usage, and curbing environmental exemptions for these facilities. While other Bay Area cities have enacted temporary bans on data centers — prompted by pushback from communities concerned about environmental, health, and quality-of-life impacts — San Jose has taken a different route. Mayor Matt Mahan said the city is opting for a more tailored approach that addresses community concerns item by item through specific regulations. "We have found a middle path. We have not defaulted to unfettered capitalism, nor have we put our head in the sand and tried to ban change," Mahan said. "And I believe we have an opportunity and a responsibility to regulate technological change to make it work for people." The city projects multimillion-dollar deficits over the next two years — though smaller than the $50 million shortfall it grappled with this year due to stagnant revenues and rising costs. With each data center projected to generate between $3 million and $7 million annually, the city is relying on these developments to help secure its financial future. City officials said public feedback gathered across multiple outreach events directly shaped the proposed rules, pointing to generator limits and environmental monitoring as community-driven additions. "There were a lot of concerns that we heard that we weren't aware of," said Deputy City Manager Manuel Pineda, highlighting public input on noise and sewer impacts. "We're setting up some pretty robust programs to monitor those... and address any issues that come up through our process." Mahan emphasized the process is not finished and encouraged the community to continue weighing in. "We have two months and at least three large public meetings to go," Mahan said. "This is very much an iterative process with the community. So we're continuing to listen. I hope that community members will take time to review the standards and let us know what isn't clear or seems lacking so that we can continue to improve." ©2026 Silicon Valley, Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

artigo.texto: Microsoft is planning to build fewer data centers at its sprawling complex in Mount Pleasant. In January, the Mount Pleasant Village Board approved the site plan for the company to build nine data centers as part of an expansion of its plans in the village. The company is now amending that down to seven data center buildings. “We continue to refine the design and layout of our expansion parcels in the Village of Mount Pleasant,” a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement. “The changes in no way reflect a reduction in our ambition, they have been made to ensure faster development, allowing us to access this increased capacity quicker. We will continue to evolve our design and keep the community updated prior to beginning any vertical construction.” Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. While there are fewer buildings in the updated plan, the total square footage of building space is greater. The updated plan has over 5.8 million-square-feet of building space, up from the just over 5.2-million-square feet in the plan approved by village officials earlier this year. “There’s two fewer buildings than the last site plan you saw, but they are actually slightly larger in square footage,” said Samuel Schultz, the community development director for the village. On Wednesday, the Mount Pleasant Plan Commission unanimously approved the amended site plan. The village board is expected to vote on it later this month. As part of the updated plan, Microsoft plans to build an office and storage building, a guardhouse and two substations at the site. Sean Ryan, a spokesperson for the village, said the 5.8 million-square-feet figure includes the data center buildings, as well as the offices and guard houses. It does not include the two utility substations, he said. Schultz said Microsoft’s plans could continue to change. He said the square footage for the site, “will likely fluctuate, maybe up, maybe down, over time.” The estimated taxable value per acre is also decreasing under the updated plan, down from around $10 million in the original plan, to around $7.7 million in the amended plan. Ryan said compared to earlier this year, “planners are using a more conservative estimate now for what the possible future value of the buildings would be.” “And this is just a more careful way to approach this exercise and know that in the end, if these buildings are built, it would result in a net positive in terms of the financials for the community,” Ryan said. “It would show that even under these more careful conservative predictions of the future taxes that these buildings would generate, the potential property tax revenue still far exceeds the cost of service,” he added. The plan commission approved the updated site plan with more than a dozen conditions Wednesday. Village Trustee Nancy Washburn, a member of the plan commission, made a motion to add a condition for Microsoft to look to add “noise protection” to a portion of the site. In June, Microsoft announced its first data center facility in Mount Pleasant, known as “Fairwater,” was operational. Construction on Microsoft’s second data center in the village is expected to be completed in 2028. Microsoft was sued in July due to noise complaints from residents who live nearby. Some people who live near the development have also complained about construction noise and dust, light pollution, traffic and a changing rural landscape. The company also plans to build a data center project on around 240 acres in Kenosha about 8 miles away from the tech giant’s campus in Racine County. artigo.texto: Na manhã de 14 de outubro, o jornal Finanças e Investimentos organizou um seminário intitulado "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde". Em sua apresentação, o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã (SBV), Nguyen Ngoc Canh, enfatizou a relação complementar entre o crédito verde e o mercado de carbono na mobilização de recursos para o processo de transformação dos negócios e da economia . Converter os resultados da redução de emissões em recursos financeiros. Segundo o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh, para cumprir o compromisso assumido pelo Vietnã na COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Partido, o Estado e o Governo emitiram diversas diretrizes e políticas para promover o crescimento verde, a transição energética e o desenvolvimento de uma economia de baixo carbono. Esse processo exige recursos significativos para inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Portanto, além do orçamento estatal e do capital mobilizado nos mercados de capitais e monetário, outros mecanismos de mercado precisam ser desenvolvidos para complementar os recursos e criar incentivos econômicos para que as empresas reduzam proativamente as emissões. Ao estabelecer cotas, mensurar os resultados da redução de emissões e definir preços de transação para cotas e créditos de carbono, o mercado de carbono cria um mecanismo para converter os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico. Isso proporciona às empresas mais incentivos e recursos para continuarem investindo na transformação verde. Em 29 de janeiro de 2026, o Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta o mercado interno de carbono, criando um arcabouço legal para a organização e operação do mercado e negociação de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono. O mercado interno de carbono iniciou suas operações em 29 de junho de 2026. O mercado piloto foi inicialmente estabelecido com mais de 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente em quotas de emissão alocadas a instalações nos três setores de energia térmica, ferro e aço e cimento durante o período de 2025–2026. A fase piloto durará até o final de 2028, antes da transição para a operação totalmente obrigatória a partir de 2029. Bancos comerciais participam como bancos liquidadores; durante a fase piloto, o BIDV é o único banco liquidador no mercado. Do ponto de vista do setor bancário, o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh acredita que o papel de cada instrumento no processo de transição verde precisa ser claramente compreendido. O crédito verde fornece capital para investimentos, inovação tecnológica e desenvolvimento de indústrias e setores verdes, gerando, assim, resultados de redução de emissões. Esses resultados formam a base para a criação de bens no mercado de carbono. Por outro lado, um mercado de carbono que funcione de forma eficiente pode complementar as receitas das empresas através da redução das emissões, apoiar a produção e as operações comerciais e contribuir para a melhoria da qualidade do crédito bancário. “Quando o mercado de carbono funciona de forma eficaz, as reduções de emissões resultantes podem ser convertidas em recursos financeiros para as próprias empresas. Consequentemente, o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono pode contribuir para reduzir a pressão sobre o financiamento de crédito verde”, afirmou o vice-governador. Em vez de dependerem principalmente de capital próprio, orçamentos ou crédito bancário, as empresas têm a capacidade adicional de mobilizar recursos a partir dos resultados de sua própria transformação. A longo prazo, esse mecanismo contribui para a diversificação das fontes de financiamento e facilita uma alocação mais eficiente do capital de crédito. No entanto, para o crédito verde, o requisito vai além do simples desembolso de fundos para um projeto identificado como verde; inclui também a verificação da economia de energia, da redução de emissões e dos resultados de proteção ambiental. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados da redução de emissões, juntamente com a negociação no mercado de carbono, podem fornecer informações adicionais para que as instituições de crédito monitorem a eficácia ambiental dos projetos, avaliem a eficiência do capital e aprimorem a supervisão dos fluxos de capital verde. Segundo Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, estima-se que o país necessite de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Desse total, o capital necessário para adaptação e aumento da resiliência é de aproximadamente US$ 254 bilhões, e para redução de emissões, de aproximadamente US$ 114 bilhões. Especificamente para o setor elétrico, o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado estima um investimento de US$ 136 bilhões para o desenvolvimento da infraestrutura de geração e transmissão de energia durante o período de 2026 a 2030. Segundo o Sr. Giap, as necessidades imediatas de capital concentrar-se-ão em energia limpa, na rede elétrica e na poupança de energia; seguidas pela produção industrial, transportes, agricultura e tratamento de resíduos. A procura é enorme, mas o capital só será desembolsado quando os projetos forem considerados eficazes, capazes de amortizar a dívida e quando os resultados da redução das emissões forem verificáveis. O mercado de carbono oferece incentivos econômicos para a redução de emissões, enquanto o crédito fornece capital para que as empresas façam os investimentos necessários. Essas duas ferramentas só são eficazes quando as instituições de crédito têm capacidade para avaliar o desempenho ambiental, as atividades de transição, o fluxo de caixa dos créditos de carbono e a capacidade de pagamento de cada projeto. artigo.texto: On the morning of October 14th, the Finance and Investment Newspaper organized a seminar titled "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows." Speaking at the seminar, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized the complementary relationship between green credit and the carbon market in mobilizing resources for the transformation process of businesses and the economy . Converting emission reduction results into financial resources. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, in fulfilling Vietnam's commitment at COP26 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the Party, State, and Government have issued numerous guidelines and policies to promote green growth, energy transition, and the development of a low-carbon economy. This process requires significant resources for technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Therefore, in addition to the state budget and capital mobilized from the capital and money markets, other market mechanisms need to be developed to supplement resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions. By establishing quotas, measuring emission reduction results, and forming transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This gives businesses more incentive and resources to continue investing in green transformation. On January 29, 2026, the Government issued Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP regulating the domestic carbon exchange, creating a legal framework for organizing and operating the market and trading greenhouse gas emission quotas and carbon credits. The domestic carbon market commenced operation on June 29, 2026. The pilot market was initially established with over 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent to emission quotas allocated to facilities in the three sectors of thermal power, iron and steel, and cement during the 2025–2026 period. The pilot phase will last until the end of 2028, before transitioning to full mandatory operation from 2029. Commercial banks participate as settlement banks; during the pilot phase, BIDV is the sole settlement bank in the market. From the perspective of the banking sector, Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh believes that the role of each tool in the green transition process needs to be clearly understood. Green credit provides capital for investment, technological innovation, and the development of green industries and sectors, thereby creating emission reduction results. These results form the basis for the creation of carbon market goods. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market can supplement businesses' revenue through emission reductions, support production and business operations, and contribute to improving the quality of bank credit. “When the carbon market operates effectively, the resulting emissions reductions can be converted into financial resources for businesses themselves. Accordingly, the development of the carbon market can contribute to reducing pressure on green credit financing,” the Deputy Governor said. Instead of relying primarily on equity, budgets, or bank credit, businesses have the added ability to mobilize resources from the results of their own transformation. In the long term, this mechanism contributes to diversifying financing sources and facilitates more efficient allocation of credit capital. However, for green credit, the requirement goes beyond simply disbursing funds for a project identified as green; it also includes verifying energy savings, emission reductions, and environmental protection results. Measurement, reporting, and assessment of emission reduction results, along with trading on the carbon market, can provide additional information for credit institutions to monitor the environmental effectiveness of projects, evaluate capital efficiency, and enhance oversight of green capital flows. According to Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, Vietnam is estimated to need approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Of this, the capital needed for adaptation and resilience enhancement is approximately US$254 billion, and for emission reduction is approximately US$114 billion. Specifically for the electricity sector, the revised Power Development Plan VIII estimates a US$136 billion investment needed for power generation and transmission infrastructure development during the 2026-2030 period. According to Mr. Giap, the immediate capital needs will focus on clean energy, the power grid, and energy saving; followed by industrial production, transportation, agriculture , and waste treatment. The demand is huge, but capital will only be disbursed when projects are assessed as effective, capable of repaying the debt, and when the emission reduction results are verifiable. The carbon market provides economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides capital for businesses to make necessary investments. These two tools are only effective when credit institutions have the capacity to assess the green performance, transition activities, cash flow from carbon credits, and repayment capacity of each project. Facilitating capital flow while controlling risks. Over the years, the banking sector has implemented numerous solutions to promote green credit, directing capital towards industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits. The State Bank of Vietnam has gradually perfected the policy framework, issued guidelines and instructions on green credit, environmental and social risk management; and encouraged credit institutions to develop strategies, internal processes, and products consistent with green growth goals. artigo.texto: FISHKILL – Governor Kathy Hochul and U.S. Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan last Tuesday toured Fishkill Farms, a family-owned, multigenerational farm in East Fishkill, Dutchess County and held a roundtable discussion with several local farmers, advocates and businesses to discuss the impacts of hyperscale data centers. Today’s discussion highlighted New York’s nation-leading moratorium on hyperscale data center construction, which is helping to protect local communities amid concerns over water and land use, energy costs, and proposed data center development, including in East Fishkill. New York State is experiencing an unprecedented surge in proposals for data center development driven by artificial intelligence and other computing operations that could require massive amounts of energy and water to run and cool thousands of computer servers. This summer, Governor Hochul signed an Executive Order hitting pause on new hyperscale data center development. This action has temporarily paused discretionary State environmental permits for up to one year in order to build a regulatory framework that will protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities across the state. By pausing discretionary state environmental permits for new hyperscale data center construction for up to one year and imposing strict new rules that hold data center developers accountable and ensure benefits for local residents, Governor Hochul’s moratorium is addressing the ongoing concerns being raised by communities statewide. “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind,” Governor Hochul said. “I enacted a nation-leading data center moratorium to protect our communities and hold developers accountable because I believe New Yorkers deserve a say in the decisions that affect their future. I’m proud to stand with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan as we deliver a government that’s committed to fighting for working families across New York.” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “Across the country, Silicon Valley billionaires are trying to impose data centers on communities that don’t want them. Today, Governor Hochul, Representative Ryan, and I heard directly from Hudson Valley farmers on the impacts these data centers have on the farming communities in New York State. In July, Governor Hochul took action to protect farmers and working New Yorkers by instituting a one-year moratorium on data center construction. New York is once again showing Americans what is possible when we put working people at the center of our agenda.” Representative Pat Ryan said, “I’m so proud that here in the Hudson Valley we’re standing together and fighting back against these data center projects. We’re not going to let anyone — especially not a bunch of billionaire tech oligarchs — come in here and poison our water, drive up our utility bills, and build this powerful technology that even they acknowledge could have devastating impacts for humankind. This is a fight that transcends so many of the divides in our country right now because we’re all united in putting our community ahead of corporate profits. From our town boards, to the Governor’s nation-leading moratorium, to urgently needed action at the federal level, we’re going to continue our fight to ensure that we the people are the ones to decide what happens in our lives and in our communities.” State Senator Michelle Hinchey said, “Tech companies are racing to profit off the AI boom, building data centers wherever they can and leaving communities to bear the costs through increased pressure on water supplies, energy infrastructure, and utility bills. New York is responding the right way — with Governor Hochul’s nation-leading moratorium, which is critical to giving the state time to understand the risks involved and, above all, protect ratepayers from higher bills and our natural resources from depletion. New York has an opportunity to lead in responsible innovation, and I thank Governor Hochul for her leadership and Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez for bringing this fight to the federal level.” State Senator Kristen Gonzalez said, “Across New York State, communities are struggling with the impacts of unchecked data center development from demands on our natural resources to strains on our energy grid. On my New York Fights AI Data Centers Statewide Tour, I visited 13 proposed or existing data centers and met with communities, just like East Fishkill, fighting to protect their air, water, and land. I want to thank the Governor for her first-in-the-nation moratorium on the largest data centers and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for her work introducing federal data center legislation.” In the absence of guidance from the federal government, Governor Hochul has taken action to regulate AI by signing and championing the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act. Starting in November, New York will direct large frontier AI developers to register with the State and prepare for compliance with strict requirements on transparency, safety, and incident reporting as prescribed by the RAISE Act. Those strict standards require large frontier AI developers to report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. Beginning in January 2027, AI companies will be required to comply with those strict standards and provide regular reporting to the state’s new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust (DIGIT) established within the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS).

artigo.texto: With the midterm elections less than a month away, the U.S. economy is top of mind for many voters. But one topic that’s not too far behind is artificial intelligence, which — for better or for worse — has a massive and complex effect on both the economy and the stock market. Concerns around AI are widespread, with economic, ethical and existential issues making headlines in recent months. But data centers — and their effect on nearby communities — remain one of the loudest issues surrounding the AI boom. People across the country are pushing back against new data center projects in their neighborhoods, citing concerns about surging electricity bills, strained water supplies and a lower quality of life, including potential health impacts. In fact, nearly 75% of U.S. voters don’t support the idea of a new data center popping up near their communities, according to a recent poll from Embold Research, WTOP News reports. Thanks for subscribing! The money news that actually matters. By signing up, you accept Moneywise Terms of Use, Subscription Agreement, and Privacy Policy. “The data center story fits in with the economic anxiety story because people are very concerned that some of the deals that are being offered to data center developers involve processes that will end up with people paying higher bills for their utilities,” Stephen Farnsworth, a political science professor at the University of Mary Washington, told WTOP News. “The concern, above all, is one of economic anxiety, and the data center story is part of that.” One of the loudest voices that’s pushing back against data centers is environmental activist Erin Brockovich, who says that, in many communities, data centers are being “shoved down their throat.” “There’s a lot of secrecy and NDAs at a very proposal stage,” Brockovich said on an episode of The Jim Acosta Show. In some cases, Brockovich claims, the data centers are presented to residents as warehouses rather than as the increasingly unpopular resource-gobbling facilities. What’s the problem with data centers? AI has infiltrated nearly every aspect of our digital lives, from streaming services to business platforms to popular chat tools like Claude and ChatGPT. Those tools work by processing massive amounts of data on real-life servers — and that requires data centers. However, data centers have received some high-profile backlash. Shark Tank star Kevin O’Leary got his fair share over his proposed $100 billion data center in Utah, which would cover 10,000 acres. While O’Leary claimed detractors had ties to China, protestors say that’s not true. “The only foreign operative here is a Canadian wealthy person trying to ruin our state,” Utah-based political strategist Gabi Finlayson told Business Insider, referring to O’Leary’s Canadian citizenship. Brockovich noted to Acosta that “those three elder council men in Utah, they had the power to put a pause and to say we aren’t going to zone or permit anything — that’s their authority — until we have further studies on their impact.” The pushback comes largely down to resources. Data centers require massive amounts of fresh water, electricity and land. There are currently over 4,700 data centers in the U.S., and a large data center can consume up to five million gallons of water per day, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute (EESI). That is about the same amount of water used by an entire town of up to 50,000 people. The strain on the power grid is just as significant. According to the EESI, utilities received requests for more than 700 gigawatts of power connections from data centers in 2025 alone, nearly double U.S. electricity consumption in 2023. To meet that demand, utilities are investing heavily in new infrastructure and passing those costs on to consumers. In communities where data centers have been built, wholesale electricity prices have jumped as much as 267% over the past five years. In Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox appears to be listening to residents, as he issued a framework on May 29 establishing “a higher bar for data center development in Utah,” which includes principles protecting utility customers and water resources. The average homeowner who implements audit recommendations saves around $685 annually — and at an average audit cost of $437, that can pay for itself in around seven months. Many utility companies offer free or subsidized audits, so check with your provider before paying out of pocket. Look into community solar programs You don’t need rooftop panels to benefit from solar energy. Community solar programs let you subscribe to a share of a local solar farm and receive credits on your regular utility bill. Typical savings range from 5% to 15% annually, making it a practical option if you can’t install solar panels yourself. Lock in fixed-rate electricity plans where available Some states, such as Texas, Ohio and Pennsylvania, allow you to lock in your electricity rate with a fixed-rate plan. artigo.texto: Four-hour battery storage is now less expensive than open-cycle gas turbines in 43 markets across the globe, according to the latest global report on levelized cost of electricity by Wood Mackenzie. One of the leading global research, analytics, and consultancy firms, Wood Mackenzie has modeled open-cycle gas turbines and four-hour battery energy storage systems (BESS) in 43 countries. It compared the LCOE of four-hour BESS and the gas peaking plants that are used to meet peak demand. With a growing share of renewables, gas power plants increasingly shift from baseload generation to providing flexibility and grid balancing. In the Middle East and Africa, where utility-scale solar already leads at USD 37 per MWh, four-hour storage is forecast to fall a further 33% to USD 80 per MWh by 2035, displacing gas peaking on cost across every gas market in the region, the analysis reads. China remains the global storage cost benchmark, at more than 55% below the rest of Asia Pacific average, illustrating how manufacturing scale is redrawing the global cost map. “This economic shift is decisive and widening. Gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are driving up peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing continues to push storage costs down,” Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie, said. He noted a similar transformation has already reshaped baseload economics. Single-axis tracker solar is now the lowest-cost new-build technology in 43 of 48 modeled markets, with onshore wind leading in five. In the most competitive markets, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, solar LCOE is on track to fall below USD 20 per MWh by 2033, according to the update. The Wood Mackenzie reports cover the regions of Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia Pacific and the Middle East and Africa. China leads the world on grid-scale storage costs China leads the world on grid-scale storage costs, with a benchmark LCOE more than 55% below the rest of Asia Pacific average of USD 134 per MWh. This is driven by domestic supply chain integration and manufacturing at scale. Competitive Chinese supply is expected to pull the rest of Asia Pacific average down to USD 92/MWh by 2036, Wood Mackenzie stressed. Battery storage turnkey capex rose about 2% in Europe Solar PV retains its position as the cheapest power technology in Europe, with fixed-tilt LCOE forecast to fall 22% by 2060 as capital costs decline and technology improves, despite a 14% capex increase in 2026 driven by higher PV module costs. Battery storage turnkey capex rose about 2%, the first increase in three years, as battery cell prices rebounded around 10% from their 2025 low on stronger demand and higher lithium prices. Capex is forecasted to fall 12% by 2031, before the pace moderates as lithium prices roughly double in 2029 when oversupply clears and demand outgrows new mine and refining capacity, according to the analysis.

artigo.texto: Speaking at the seminar on credit policy and the carbon market organised by VIR on October 14, Bui Minh Giap, chief economist at the Asian Development Bank in Vietnam, said that Vietnam was estimated to need approximately $368 billion in additional investment by 2040 for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emissions reduction, equivalent to 6.8 per cent of GDP annually. Of this amount, $254 billion would be required for climate change adaptation and resilience enhancement, while approximately $114 billion would be needed for emissions reduction. In the power sector alone, the revised Power Development Plan VIII estimates that $136 billion in investment will be required for power generation and grid development during the 2026-2030 period. “The financing needs are substantial, but funding will only be disbursed when projects are assessed as effective, capable of generating sufficient cash flow to service debt, and supported by verifiable emissions reduction data,” said Giap. “The carbon market creates economic incentives for emissions reduction, while credit provides the capital businesses need to make the necessary investments.” According to Giap, these two instruments can effectively complement each other only when credit institutions have the capacity to assess customers’ green and transition activities, cash flows from carbon credits, and the debt repayment capacity of individual projects. “An emissions reduction project may generate energy savings, reduce the cost of purchasing emission allowances, or generate revenue from carbon credits. For projects expected to sell carbon credits, credit institutions need to assess the likelihood of credit issuance, actual volumes, buyers, selling prices, verification costs, and the timing of payments. Long-term offtake agreements can reduce market risk, but they do not guarantee that a business will generate the credits or deliver the contracted volumes,” he explained. Giap said that credit institutions should tailor financing packages to the specific characteristics of each project. Such support could include assistance with application preparation, technical due diligence, and the arrangement of appropriate financing amounts, tenors, and interest rates. Accordingly, financing portfolios should cover both green activities, those that already meet environmental criteria and transition activities, which do not yet meet green criteria but have feasible emissions reduction plans with clearly defined targets and timelines, as well as verifiable outcomes. Giap shared that international experience showed there was no single model suitable for every country. Some central banks provide direct funding support, while others focus on risk supervision, maintaining data systems, and strengthening the capacity of credit institutions. “I believe the lesson for Vietnam is that investment support must be combined with risk management. First, the country needs to strengthen its criteria, data, and assessment capabilities; it can then pilot funding support for eligible loans. Regardless of the instruments used, credit institutions must conduct their own assessments and remain accountable for loan quality,” said Giap. “I would emphasise that banks are an important channel for channelling capital, but they cannot meet the long-term financing needs of green and transition finance on their own,” he added. “Credit must be combined with green bonds, transition bonds, equity capital, blended finance, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms. Each type of risk should be allocated to the parties best positioned to manage it.” Vietnam's domestic carbon exchange began pilot operations in June, establishing the basic infrastructure for trading emission allowances and eligible carbon credits. The exchange can connect buyers and sellers, but it cannot itself generate high-quality carbon credits or create demand for them. The market therefore needs to develop both its credit supply and its institutional framework. On the supply side, Giap said it was necessary to develop high-quality carbon credits that reflect actual emissions reductions or removals, are calculated and independently verified, avoid double counting, and account for the risks of reversal or emissions leakage to other locations. Project documentation should be standardised, and smaller projects should be aggregated to reduce participation costs while maintaining credit quality. On the institutional side, regulations need to clearly define ownership rights, the rights to have credits issued and sell them, revenue-sharing arrangements, procedures for credit registration, issuance, transfer, and use, as well as the responsibilities of each party in the event of disputes, according to Giap. The registry system must be capable of tracking each credit throughout its lifecycle. “To unlock green capital flows, I believe Vietnam needs to develop its institutional framework alongside the carbon market and green finance. Policy quality and effective coordination among regulators, credit institutions, and market participants will directly affect the scale and cost of financing, as well as access to capital,” Giap stated. According to Giap, the essential foundations include, first and foremost, a standardised set of criteria for green and transition activities, followed by a reliable emissions database, well-prepared projects, and appropriate risk allocation mechanisms. “Responsibilities for drafting regulations, managing and supervising the system, and operating it must be clearly delineated. Inter-agency and interbank coordination should be strengthened, while credit institutions’ capacity to assess green and transition credit should be enhanced. A comprehensive institutional framework will help the market operate with greater confidence, lower transaction costs, and better direct capital towards viable projects,” he said. artigo.texto: Data center ordinance dominates Harmony mayoral forum HARMONY, Minn. (KTTC) — Voters in Harmony packed the community center Tuesday evening to question their mayoral candidates and hear how each one plans to tackle local issues. The forum hosted by the Filmore County League of Women Voters featured candidates current Mayor Steve Donney, Kerry Kingsley, owner of Kingsley Mercantile, and Harmony Public Library assistant Sue Olinger. During the hour-long forum, the candidates covered a wide range of topics, answering questions on everything from election security in Fillmore County to how to maintain strong emergency services in small towns. The issue that drew the most attention was the city’s current data center ordinance. Candidates were pressed on where they stand, where they’re getting their information, potential incentives from developers, and what, if anything, might make them change their position. One candidate said she hopes to bring the town back together. “And with my volunteer service, I am working all the time on bringing more and more to the seniors of the community. I’m hoping that I can bring positive change and eliminate some of the current division,” Olinger said. KTTC offered each candidate a chance to interview. Mayor Steve Donney had to attend a city council meeting, and Kerry Kingsley declined. Harmony’s current data center ordinance is set to go in front of the planning and zoning committee at a special meeting on October 28 with a public hearing.
