artigo.texto: Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections (Indiana Capital Chronicle) - In the course of a single election cycle, the backlash against data centers has grown from an issue at local planning commission and city council meetings to become a flashpoint in state and federal races across the country. Candidates who once touted data centers as an economic boon have backtracked, and voters in at least three dozen cities, counties and townships will consider ballot measures in November that could ban data centers in their communities. Analysts say the opposition to data centers has come from Republican and Democratic voters alike. READ ORIGINAL REPORT HERE: Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections “The people are speaking, and they’re speaking in one voice in opposition to this infrastructure,” said Tatishe Nteta, provost professor of political science at UMass Amherst. “It is not something that people desire in any shape, form or fashion. This potentially could be the issue that gives you the status of a former member of a city council or a former member of Congress.” Last month, UMass Amherst published a poll, directed by Nteta, showing that only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an artificial intelligence data center in their local community. The poll found that 65% of respondents oppose the construction of such facilities. Local and national activists have a long list of grievances against data centers, which tech companies are aggressively building to provide the computing power for artificial intelligence platforms. The rapid buildout of data centers is expected to strain the electrical grid and drive up energy costs, some forecasts show. Opponents are also concerned about the facilities’ pollution, water use, noise, and conversion of farmland and other open spaces. Many developers are also building private, “behind-the-meter” natural gas plants to power their data centers, increasing concerns about emissions and public health. Some activists also object to the artificial intelligence technologies the sites will power, which threaten to disrupt the economy, replace workers, erode critical thinking skills and mental health and even — according to some tech executives — potentially kill all humans. “For so many years, Ohio rolled out the red carpet to become a tech hub,” said Nick Owens, an attorney with Conserve Ohio, a campaign seeking to block data center development. “Unfortunately, what we’ve become is a tech dump.” Anger at both parties Activists across the country have lashed out at elected officials from both parties who have offered state and local tax breaks to entice data center developers. They’ve also called out local officials for negotiating deals behind closed doors and signing non-disclosure agreements with large tech companies. “The politicians are chasing the grassroots; they aren’t leading on the issue,” said Anthony Elmo, public education defender with Good Jobs First, a policy group that tracks government subsidies related to economic development. “(Politicians) who were very pro-data center a year ago are now coming out against them due to political factors.” Tech companies have launched their own political efforts to respond to the backlash. Industry leaders argue that artificial intelligence is key to the nation’s economic competitiveness. They note that the data center boom has created many construction jobs and increased property tax revenue in communities desperate for more money. Leading the Future, a tech-backed Super PAC, has invested in federal and state campaigns in support of both Republican and Democratic candidates who support artificial intelligence. Josh Vlasto, the group’s co-leader, argued that the narrative around data centers has conflated the industry at large with its worst offenders — speculative projects that disregarded local opposition and failed to meet environmental standards. “(Voters) want the jobs in their communities, they want the revenue, but they want the risks and downsides mitigated and addressed,” he said. “There is backlash in communities that don’t want them, but if you look to the states that are building and doing it right, these data centers are being welcomed and generating a massive amount of revenue. If this is done correctly, I could see this issue turning drastically in a different direction.” An investigation earlier this year linked Leading the Future with a news website that used AI bots posing as journalists to solicit quotes for stories that promoted industry talking points. Another investigation found that a dark-money group tied to Leading the Future paid lifestyle influencers to promote artificial intelligence by highlighting the threat of competition from Chinese AI. The Data Center Coalition, a membership association for tech companies, did not respond to a Stateline interview request. Amazon, Google and OpenAI — industry leaders that have pushed for data center construction — did not respond to Stateline inquiries. Think Big, an associated PAC of Leading the Future that supports Democratic candidates, did not respond to an interview request. ‘People coming together’ Across the United States, data centers currently use about 49 gigawatts of electricity, according to the website US Data Center Map. New projects planned or under construction total nearly 350 gigawatts — roughly a quarter of the country’s current electrical generation capacity. While data centers have long powered our online infrastructure, many of the “hyperscale” facilities being built to support artificial intelligence are much larger and use vastly more power. Ohio has become the political epicenter of the data center backlash. Like many states, Ohio agreed to sales tax exemptions for data centers in the 2010s in order to secure investment from tech companies. artigo.texto: Claudio Descalzi, CEO of Italian energy giant Eni said on October 15 that EU should suspend its carbon emissions trading system (ETS), arguing that it is burdening the bloc’s industrial sector as companies face the effects of the wars in Ukraine and Iran. “The emissions trading system should be suspended until a solution is reached to the Russia-Ukraine war and the Gulf war, because it is an extremely costly levy for our industrial sector,” Descalzi said, according to Reuters. The ETS is the EU’s flagship carbon-pricing mechanism, launched in 2005. It operates on a “cap-and-trade” principle in which the EU sets a limit on emissions from sectors including electricity and heat generation, energy-intensive manufacturing, aviation and maritime transport. This cap is reduced over time to encourage companies to lower their emissions. Under the EU ETS, covered industrial facilities, including refineries, must hold emissions allowances to cover their greenhouse gas emissions, exposing them to carbon-price fluctuations. For oil and gas companies, carbon-related costs add to the financial pressure at a time when geopolitical conflicts in the Gulf and the Russia–Ukraine war are disrupting energy supplies and raising operating expenses. The EU leaders is currently gathering in Brussels to discuss on European competitiveness, high energy prices, and proposed reforms to the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

Nebraska independent candidate Dan Osborn, in his second run for U.S. Senate, has made a habit this cycle of creating digital ads that are only slightly less over the top than the Oscar-winning film Everything Everywhere All at Once. The latest, set up as a mock ad for his opponent Sen. Pete Ricketts, praises him for welcoming racks of computers to Nebraska’s open spaces, “finally delivering the tax relief for Google and their hardworking air conditioners that struggling Nebraska families have cried out for.” Then Ricketts zaps pure energy from his hands to summon data centers onto farm fields. It’s something to see. But if you excuse the Green Lantern–style pyrotechnics, the facts in the ad are all true. If anything, Ricketts has been an even more aggressive booster of data centers than the spot makes him out to be. Obviously, data centers are one of the critical contested issues in the midterms, with Republicans now scrambling to hide their past support. But Ricketts’s record on data centers highlights a particular vision for economic development, notably prevalent in red states, that is indistinguishable from corporate welfare. Three pictures from Ricketts’s time as governor display his approach to data centers; in all of them, he is literally dressed as someone building the giant server warehouses himself. In 2017, Ricketts picked up a shovel to announce a planned Facebook data center on 146 acres near Papillion, Nebraska. He personally recruited Facebook to Papillion, part of a planned “data center hub” in the region that he nicknamed “Silicon Prairie.” During a facility tour the following year, Ricketts appeared in a bunch of photos in a hard hat and neon construction vest. And in 2019, Ricketts donned a Google hard hat at the groundbreaking of a $600 million data center in Papillion, which he hoped would “rival the data centers over in Iowa.” That facility was later expanded for another $750 million. Asked why all this activity was happening, Ricketts said that “the number one reason these technology companies are coming to Nebraska is our people.” If by “people” he meant “tax breaks for giant tech companies,” he was right. The ImagiNE Nebraska Act was a typical economic development bill in that it handed out corporate tax breaks to entice companies to locate in the state. Ricketts signed the law in 2017. Central to these were property tax abatements: From January 2021 until an executive order paused any incentives to data centers in July 2026, tech firms received $519 million in property tax exemptions from the Ricketts law. Data centers got another $317 million in tax credits, sales tax exemptions, and direct refunds from the law. About $311 million of this total went to the Facebook facility in Papillion specifically. All these numbers came from the office of the state’s current Republican governor, Jim Pillen. So when Osborn’s ad points out that “Pete delivered $836 million for data centers,” that’s simply a tallying up of data center tax breaks from the ImagiNE Nebraska Act, which were so egregious that the Republican governor who succeeded Ricketts had to stop them. Submitting your email signs you up for The Daily Prospect, our weekday morning newsletter. This tendency to funnel money to corporations to earn their support didn’t end in the governor’s mansion. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) is littered with this kind of corporate tax breaks, all justified as spurs to investment. The law, for example, made permanent the 100 percent bonus depreciation, which allows companies to immediately expense investment in materials. This is particularly useful for data centers, which are just big hunks of servers and wires and air conditioners. Microsoft has already saved up to $12 billion in taxes from this provision, according to its annual report, with billions more going to the likes of Facebook, Amazon, and Google. This giant giveaway is also cited in Osborn’s mock ad, which states that “As senator, Pete voted on a permanent measure to let developers write off critical data center infrastructure.” Beyond bonus depreciation, the Prospect has reported that six companies tied to the data center build-out received $83 billion in tax breaks from OBBBA provisions last year. None of this is a mistake or an oversight: It’s the considered way that Republicans think the economy should work. Corporations get billions of dollars for the privilege of investing, and that’s the only way to create good-paying jobs. This logic even holds in the case of data centers, where jobs after construction are scarce. In the 2019 Google announcement, Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE), who is retiring, boasted that the project was already bringing in 30 jobs. 30! The per-job spending on this type of economic development is astronomical. Bacon also touted, in a way that no politician would today, that the data centers around Papillion “use more power than the entire city of Lincoln.” Ricketts has used the typical Republican line that data centers are “a community decision,” and that cities should negotiate favorable deals for themselves in exchange for allowing development. But when he was governor, in a uniquely powerful position to negotiate with these companies, he didn’t extract anything. The money transfer all went in one direction, from Nebraska’s treasury to Google and Facebook. Big Tech has returned the favor to Ricketts for the billions it has received by kicking back a relative pittance in campaign contributions. The corporate PACs for Google and Meta (Facebook’s parent company) have given $20,000 and $2,500 to Ricketts’ campaign, respectively. artigo.texto: PRESIDENT Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. directed the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to draft a national carbon market policy framework to mobilize green investments, in line with the Philippines’ international climate commitments. Under Executive Order (EO) No. 127, signed on Oct. 13, the DENR was given 30 days to set up the operational guidelines, subject to approval by a newly created inter-agency body. At a news briefing, Palace Press Officer Clarissa A. Castro said the policy framework aims to establish national standards for trading carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as well as voluntary carbon markets. “The order aims to support the Philippines’ commitments under the Paris Agreement, attract funding and investment for climate programs, and open opportunities for environmental projects,” Ms. Castro said. “The executive order establishes a framework for the carbon market and does not impose a new carbon tax,” she added. The EO creates the inter-agency committee on carbon markets, comprising the Climate Change Commission as chair, and Department of Finance as vice-chair. According to the directive, establishing transparent rules for credit issuance, registry tracking, and benefit-sharing will allow environmental projects — such as reforestation, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, and waste management — to generate critical climate finance. Once drafted, the DENR will submit the framework to the committee, which will also be given 30 days to review and approve the guidelines to ensure full operational transparency across all carbon crediting activities. The EO will take effect immediately upon its publication in the Official Gazette or in a newspaper of general circulation. — Erika Mae P. Sinaking

artigo.texto: Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek has directed environmental regulators to temporarily stop issuing pollution permits to data centers, which would effectively pause most data center development in Oregon until next summer. Amazon — which has more than a dozen hyperscale data centers in Morrow and Umatilla Counties — said it was disappointed by the directive, with an executive at the company saying Kotek’s move could cost Oregon thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in planned investment. Data centers have played a growing role in the race for governor, with both Kotek, a Democrat, and her opponent Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan, saying they favor a moratorium on the high-tech developments. Both candidates have attacked one another for not doing more to crack down. Related: Amazon, data centers and the race for Oregon governor Kotek directed Oregon Department of Environmental Quality Director Leah Feldon to pause all air and water pollution permits for new or expanding data centers until July. The governor sent the directive in a letter to Feldon Friday, in response to an update on the agency’s air pollution permitting process. Kotek also told the agency to stop processing applications from cities and counties seeking to renew or modify wastewater permits to accommodate data centers. “This time limited pause will provide an opportunity for me to evaluate and digest recommendations forthcoming from the Advisory Committee, and to provide space for policy and/or regulatory reforms that may be considered in the upcoming 2027 session of the Legislature with my support,” Kotek wrote. The letter was obtained and shared widely by Oregon Rural Action, a grassroots nonprofit that advocates for social justice and environmental sustainability in Eastern Oregon. OPB obtained Kotek and Feldon’s interchange from Kotek’s office. “What this pause means is that everything — assuming it is implemented the way we think it will be — data center development will pause until the legislature has a chance to act over the course of the first half of next year,” said Kaleb Lay, Rural Action’s director of policy and research. The environmental permitting freeze would expand a previous moratorium that paused data center development on state-owned land. Without air or water pollution permits, most large data centers known as “hyperscalers” wouldn’t be able to build in Oregon, whether on public or private land. “This directive was issued abruptly, without meaningful stakeholder engagement of the workers, businesses, and municipalities it will affect,” said Shannon Kellogg, vice president of Amazon Web Services Public Policy for the Americas, in a statement. “Amazon has been a committed partner in Oregon for over 15 years, and we will continue to advocate for policies that protect communities and support responsible growth. Lay, with Oregon Rural Action, hopes the pause gives Oregon policymakers time to implement new laws regulating data centers, from the immense amount of water and electricity they consume to issues involving transparency and nondisclosure agreements. Pausing permits is not enough, Lay said. “What needs to happen at the Legislature, we need new laws to protect all of Oregon from these massive corporations.” Oregon’s next legislative session convenes in January. Lawmakers are expecting a wide range of bill proposals, particularly in response to policy directives from Kotek’s Data Center Advisory Committee.

artigo.texto: Americans are increasingly concerned about AI and data centers, and the impact of computing on climate change. A September poll by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago found that 53% are extremely or very concerned about the environmental impacts of AI—and that the majority of both Democrats and Republicans support policies including requiring data centers to use clean energy and pay for grid upgrades. We asked leading expert Andrew Chien to answer commonly asked questions about data centers. Chien is the William Eckhardt Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science at UChicago. Before joining the University in 2011, he served for five years as the vice president of research at Intel Corporation. Since 2015, he and his research team have studied how to make computing more sustainable and grid-friendly. What is a data center? In the simplest terms, a data center is a room or building that’s full of computers. This can be a single room, a little building on the corner, or a few floors of a skyscraper, all the way up to huge, multi-acre complexes. What do data centers do? When people ask this, I explain by saying, “Data centers are where the Internet lives.” All the cloud computing and the data we use—your pictures, your social media and now AI chatbots—those are all supported by data centers. How has AI changed the need for data centers? The difference now is that AI-based services require massive amounts of power. When you used to type something into Google, it would search a copy of the internet. Now, when you ask a chatbot or an AI agent something, it literally performs a supercomputer-class numerical computation in order to figure out how to tell you that stuff. (It’s approximately a teraflop. That’s not quite the supercomputer of today—it’s a supercomputer of a few years ago—but it’s a gigantic amount of computation.) We also pioneered an approach we call “Middlebox.” The idea is to build a little energy station next to the data center. This means the data center itself gets highly reliable power (and doesn’t have to be flexible about when it runs computations). The combined data center + power station can also now actually reduce peak loads overall on the grid, in addition to supporting renewable energy by increasing consumption when there is excess energy from wind or solar. Remarkably, we did a study on this and showed that in the majority of cases, the data center companies would actually make money from doing this, because they can get better prices for energy and they don’t get charged extra for drawing power during peak usage times. So technically and economically, it’s absolutely clear that this is the right thing to do. All the technology is there. But the companies are not taking these steps. In fact, several of them are bringing lawsuits against attempts to regulate them. Are data centers good for a community? One thing to keep in mind is that data centers don’t employ a lot of people, relative to say, an automotive factory, or even a store of similar square footage. Once the initial construction is done, communities often see very little positive economic impact. One of the problems is that large data center companies have been pursuing aggressive business tactics. But they do so at the cost of alienating the local community and causing a backlash. For example, a common tactic is to come into a small town or county and tell the mayor, “We want to build a data center,” and the first thing they do is make the mayor sign a non-disclosure agreement about the discussions. When the deal is done, then the citizens hear about it—often with surprise and dismay. Worse, some of these deals carry NDAs into their operating stage—where the concessions or permits granted may not be known for many years—or ever. I think it’s a good idea to ban companies requesting or public officials signing such NDAs and require all such deals to be shared openly. This would decrease the information and power asymmetry, and force the data center companies to compete for community support! “If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody.” —Prof. Andrew A. Chien What do you think more people should know about data centers? Data centers don’t have to be built next door. With the modern fiber-optic internet, communication can travel across the country in less than 15 milliseconds. So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them. They can be anywhere in the USA and serve AI to the entire population, businesses, etc. How do you recommend we solve the problem? National and state government needs to organize infrastructure for data centers. Coordinated regulation is needed because the companies are so powerful. It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure. If it’s zoned properly, it will reduce the impact on local community. Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years. They have plenty of profit. If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody. I think sometimes people feel that governments can’t force companies to change. But I don’t really believe that’s true. When I was at Intel, my experience was that if public policy changes, the companies change. The auto companies complied with the Inflation reduction act quickly. American tech companies comply with European policies in order to sell there. We should expect that companies will fight every step of the way to get more profit, but I still believe people can win that battle in the U.S. to reach a balanced solution where we can have the AI computing power we need, but the communities that host data centers get valuable training, community contribution,

artigo.texto: India Earmarks ₹60 Billion for GEC-III Battery Storage ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: The Union Cabinet has approved ₹60 billion (~$631.11 million) in viability gap funding (VGF) to support 50 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) under the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III (GEC-III) program. - Why it matters: This initiative provides critical financial support for large-scale storage integration, directly addressing the intermittency challenges faced by solar and wind developers. - Watch: Upcoming guidelines on VGF disbursement and the specific tender timelines for the 50 GWh capacity allocation. Background and Context The integration of intermittent renewable energy into the national grid remains a primary challenge for India’s ambitious clean energy targets. To address this, the Union Cabinet has officially earmarked ₹60 billion (~$631.11 million) in viability gap funding (VGF) to accelerate the deployment of battery energy storage systems (BESS). This allocation is a cornerstone of the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III (GEC-III) program, which aims to facilitate the evacuation of 135 GW of renewable energy capacity. Key Details The GEC-III program is designed to provide the necessary infrastructure to manage the massive influx of solar and wind power. By dedicating ₹60 billion specifically for 50 GWh of BESS, the government is signaling a shift toward making renewable energy dispatchable. This VGF mechanism is intended to bridge the cost gap for developers, making large-scale battery projects economically viable in a market where storage costs have historically been a barrier to entry. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and renewable energy developers, this funding announcement represents a significant market opportunity. The 50 GWh target creates a massive pipeline for BESS procurement, engineering, and construction services. Developers who have previously struggled with the financial feasibility of storage-integrated projects can now leverage the VGF to improve project IRR. Furthermore, the GEC-III framework provides a clearer roadmap for grid connectivity, reducing the risk of curtailment for future large-scale solar and wind farms. What Happens Next The industry now awaits the detailed operational guidelines from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) regarding the application process for the VGF. Stakeholders should monitor upcoming tender documents that will outline the technical specifications and eligibility criteria for the 50 GWh capacity. As India continues to scale its renewable energy sector, the successful implementation of this BESS program will be pivotal in maintaining grid stability and meeting the country’s net-zero commitments.

artigo.texto: Denver working group on data centers says they're off to promising start, "it exceeded my expectations" Denver's working group on data centers has officially begun meeting with the goal of creating policy recommendations for the city. The group, diversely composed of community members and experts in a multitude of industries, was created after the city council approved a moratorium to pause the construction of data centers in Denver. "This is an opportunity to be a part of democracy in action to help set the rules that we haven't had for these kinds of developments, and to make sure we're protecting Denver's resources and putting Denverites first," said Mark Orrs, who's on the working group. Orrs is an associate professor at Colorado School of Mines, and he's bringing his expertise to the table. "My training is in sustainable development, and I teach responsible engineering, specifically engineering for social and environmental responsibility," he explained. And one of the core questions at the center of the conversation is whether 'sustainable' and 'data centers' can exist in the same sentence. "There are new kinds of technologies coming out every day that might make them more sustainable," Orrs said. "But to date, what we've seen is a lot of unsustainable development in this area." Orrs is one of 26 individuals with diverse backgrounds chosen to participate from more than 250 applicants. But with honor comes enormous responsibility. "We know that others are looking to us, and to see how we decide to proceed, and that they will follow," said Orrs. "We are and have been the tip of the spear on this discussion," said Councilman Darrell Watson. "We are one of the first large municipalities to do a moratorium. We're one of maybe one that are building a working group with this very extensive application process." Watson represents District 9, where the controversial CoreSite facility in Globeville was recently built, which became the catalyst for the moratorium. "I think we have a unique process, and I do believe we're going to come up with a commonsense approach to regulating data centers," said Watson. For now, the working group is just getting started and met for the first time last week. "I thought it went about as well as I could have expected," said Orrs. "In fact, I said it exceeded my expectations." The next working group meeting will be on October 29, and although they are slated to meet through May, Watson says they'll continue to meet as long as necessary for the city council to create legislation.

artigo.texto: GIGante. A espanhola Aena assumiu a gestão do Galeão usando um trocadilho para mostrar o tamanho de suas ambições para o aeroporto do Rio de Janeiro. Os planos para o terminal passam por dezenas de novos voos em rotas internacionais e domésticas, além de projetos imobiliários incluindo um hotel, galpões, um hangar da Gol e até um centro de testes da BYD. Só essas iniciativas já totalizam R$ 1 bilhão em investimentos das empresas responsáveis nos próximos três anos, disse Santiago Yus, o CEO da Aena Brasil. Segundo ele, o aeroporto deve fechar este ano com 19,4 milhões de passageiros, comparado a 17,5 milhões em 2025, e ainda há muito espaço para crescimento diante de uma capacidade total estimada em até 37 milhões de passageiros/ano. “O Galeão é um aeroporto estratégico para o Rio de Janeiro e o Brasil,” Yus disse ao apresentar a estratégia para o terminal, que a Aena passou a administrar no último dia 6. Maior operador aeroportuário do mundo em número de passageiros, o grupo espanhol arrematou a concessão do Galeão num leilão realizado pelo Governo Federal em março, com uma proposta de outorga de R$ 2,9 bilhões. Após uma fase de transição junto aos antigos concessionários, a Vinci Compass e a Changi, a Aena chegou anunciando novas rotas e aumentos na frequência de voos para 30 destinos ao longo dos próximos meses. Ainda em outubro, a American Airlines começa a operar sete voos semanais para Nova York e amplia de sete para nove os embarques para Miami. A Air Canadá inicia três voos semanais para Toronto, e a Air France adiciona um voo para Paris aos dez já realizados. Em novembro, a JetSMART lançará três voos semanais para Assunção, e a Delta, três para Nova York; a Lufthansa passará a voar diariamente para Frankfurt, e a TAP vai adicionar um voo por semana para Lisboa e Porto. A partir de dezembro são previstas novas rotas para Toronto, Montreal, Dallas, Salta, Lima, Assunção e Mendoza, além de aumentos de frequência para Atlanta, Lisboa e Cidade do Panamá. Em janeiro, a Aerolíneas Argentinas começará a voar para Rosario, enquanto Latam, SKY e JetSMART vão quase dobrar a oferta de voos para Santiago, com esta última aumentando também os embarques para Córdoba. No plano doméstico, são previstos incrementos na frequência de voos da Latam, Azul e principalmente da Gol para diversas cidades nos próximos meses. No front dos projetos imobiliários, a Aena anunciou que a operadora bUP vai investir R$ 90 milhões em um novo hotel, com bandeira internacional ainda a ser definida. O empreendimento terá ao menos 232 quartos, podendo chegar a 426. O Galeão também receberá um centro de pesquisa e desenvolvimento e experimentação da BYD com capex de R$ 300 milhões, ocupando 184 mil m² e com previsão de criar 1,2 mil empregos. Estão previstos ainda um hangar de manutenção da Gol de mais de R$ 100 milhões; além de investimentos da Hire Capital em uma nova área de galpões industriais de R$ 430 milhões e uma expansão de galpão logístico de R$ 54 milhões. A Aena nomeou como novo diretor do Galeão seu executivo Felipe Cavalcanti, um ex-coordenador da Infraero que já foi responsável pela gestão do terminal entre 2018 e 2019, quando estava na RIOGaleão, a antiga concessionária. Com 46 aeroportos e 2 heliportos na Espanha, a Aena administra 35 terminais em outros países. No Brasil são 18, incluindo Congonhas. Os investimentos no País já somam R$ 15 bilhões quando incluída a outorga do Galeão.

artigo.texto: HELLENiQ ENERGY has commissioned a 100 MW/200 MWh BESS in Thessaloniki, Greece The facility uses LFP batteries and is designed to reduce renewable energy curtailment and improve grid flexibility The company is developing another 50 MW/200 MWh battery project in Florina HELLENiQ ENERGY has commissioned a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), calling it one among the largest battery storage projects in Greece and Southeast Europe. Built at Thessaloniki, Greece, with an investment of approximately €50 million, it is developed by HELLENiQ Renewables, a subsidiary of HELLENiQ ENERGY as its maiden storage facility. The facility will store surplus renewable electricity and release it when demand increases. It will provide flexibility and balancing services to Greece’s national electricity transmission system, helping reduce renewable energy curtailment and improve grid reliability. The project is supported under Greece’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan, “Greece 2.0,” funded by the European Union’s NextGenerationEU program. The facility covers approximately 100,000 square meters and comprises three battery storage systems using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology with liquid cooling. HELLENiQ ENERGY said the battery system is expected to complete at least one full charge-discharge cycle daily, with its 200 MWh storage capacity. The 56 battery containers will provide enough energy to fully charge around 3,000 electric vehicles (EV). It includes a new 33/150 kV step-up substation and an underground high-voltage transmission line extending about 5 km to the Thessaloniki Extra-High Voltage Centre. The project was selected under the first competitive tender conducted by Greece’s Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY) for energy storage systems. The company is also developing a second battery storage project in Florina, Greece, with a planned capacity of 50 MW/200 MWh. Construction is expected to be completed in the near future. Its overall renewable energy and storage project portfolio under development exceeds 6 GW, including more than 1 GW of storage projects under development across Greece, Romania, Cyprus, and Bulgaria. Greece’s solar association HELAPCO calls energy storage the third pillar of Greek energy market going forward that will support the first two pillars of large commercial projects, and self-consumption. It estimates that more than 6 GW of battery storage capacity could be available by 2030, although around 8 GW may be needed to manage renewable energy curtailment in the country, exceeding the NECP target of 4.33 GW. HELAPCO also forecasts the country’s cumulative solar PV capacity to reach 20 GW by 2030 in its most likely scenario, with potential to rise to 27 GW, up from 13 GW interconnected as of May 2026.

artigo.texto: N.A.N. Silox GreenMet Pvt. Ltd., the joint venture between N.A.N. GreenMet and Belgium’s Silox Group, has appointed Vijay Pasupathy as Chief Executive Officer as the company receives Consent to Establish (CTE) and moves forward with groundbreaking for its ₹1,400 crore lithium-ion battery recycling and critical metals facility at Naidupeta, Andhra Pradesh. The company has also earmarked additional investment beyond the initial ₹1,400 crore outlay to accelerate its downstream expansion into precursor cathode active material (pCAM) and cathode active material (CAM) manufacturing, actively pursuing global technology partnerships. Vijay brings over two decades of industrial leadership across strategy and operations, having previously served as Executive Vice President at Epsilon Advanced Materials, alongside senior roles at Orbia and EY. He will lead N.A.N. Silox GreenMet through plant execution at Naidupeta and drove the company’s expansion into engineered cathode materials. To execute the industrial buildout, N.A.N. Silox GreenMet has assembled a high-caliber leadership team, appointing Rakesh Patel as Chief Operating Officer, Harish Aich as Chief Technology Officer, M. Sri Rama Krishna Murthy as Deputy CFO, Partha Reddy as Chief Supply Chain Officer, and Alisha Abbas as Head of HR. The team brings deep domain expertise across metallurgy, mineral processing, and large-scale plant execution from Hindalco, Shell, ExxonMobil, Adani’s Kutch Copper, and Hyundai. Bridging the Midstream Battery Gap in India The Naidupeta facility will feature an ultimate capacity of 40,000 tonnes per annum (TPA) of shredding and 20,000 TPA of hydrometallurgical processing, deployed in phases. The plant’s hydrometallurgical technology will produce high-purity, battery-grade salts designed directly as feedstock for downstream pCAM and CAM synthesis. By linking battery recycling directly with cathode material manufacturing, the company aims to establish domestic capabilities to process recovered critical metals into cell-ready materials, reducing India’s reliance on imported East Asian cathode supplies. India’s battery ecosystem is scaling rapidly at the cell manufacturing level, but the country remains heavily dependent on overseas supply chains for processed cathode materials. With Consent to Establish secured and groundbreaking underway at Naidupeta, N.A.N. Silox GreenMet is focused on executing its lithium-ion battery recycling and hydrometallurgical facility while pursuing global technology partnerships to expand into domestic pCAM and CAM manufacturing. This expansion aims to strengthen India’s battery manufacturing value chain by enabling recovered critical metals to be processed into high-value battery materials within the country. Naivedya Agarwal, Director and Co-founder, N.A.N. GreenMet, said: “We are delighted to welcome Vijay as CEO alongside a heavily experienced operational leadership team at this pivotal stage. With groundbreaking underway at Naidupeta, our downstream pCAM and CAM expansion will ensure that critical minerals recovered in India are processed further and reused to build new batteries domestically.” Jean-Christophe Bogaert, Chairman, Silox Group, said: “With Vijay and the new leadership team on board, Silox’s advanced hydrometallurgical technology transitions into large-scale industrial execution in India. Our expertise in high-purity metal extraction will be central as we build out the Naidupeta facility and advance discussions on pCAM and CAM technology partnerships.”

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – What was meant to be a stop on the campaign tour for Arizona’s attorney general deep in the heart of Mesa became a one-topic free-for-all instead on Wednesday night. The city of about 500,000 people, near Phoenix, is where Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes came to lay out her vision for data center development. But most of the town hall at the Eagle Community Center was spent talking about a particular 38-acre tract of land in the southern fringes of the Phoenix city limits. As The Center Square covered on Wednesday morning, Mayes’ calls for a data center moratorium have been met by raised eyebrows and criticism from business officials, including executives from the state and Phoenix area chambers of commerce. One such criticism has come from the campaign of Mayes' opponent in the Nov. 3 general election, Republican State Senate President Warren Petersen of Gilbert. His campaign manager, Chad LeBeau, said there's a lack of consistency regarding data center development in Arizona. “Kris Mayes has spent years trying to get data centers to come to Arizona," LeBeau said in an email to The Center Square. "Now that she's on the ballot, she wants a total halt, a position even Governor [Katie] Hobbs rejects. Mayes doesn't have a policy; she has a poll. When the winds shift, she flips.” Regardless, that opposition couldn’t beat back the mood in the East Valley on Wednesday night, with dozens of attendees taking to the microphone to discuss the hot-button subject, forcing Mayes’ staff to cut the meeting at 7 p.m., two hours after it began. The 150 or so attendees in the 180-seat gym at the Eagle Community Center were red-hot and bothered by the Menlo Digital data center development in Ahwatukee, a bedroom community that’s technically part of Phoenix, albeit on the southern side of South Mountain. As the crowd settled in for the two-hour town hall, with attendees passing time by knitting or scrolling their phones between questions, Mayes admitted what Phoenix Chamber CEO Danny Seiden and others said — that she has no legal authority to issue a data center moratorium on her own. Instead, the former member of the Arizona Corporation Commission called on that body, as well as the Arizona Legislature and fellow Democrat, Hobbs, to do the work needed to “press time out” on the industry. “I am limited to the tools that I have as your attorney general, which is the bully pulpit and nuisance law,” Hobbs told the crowd Wednesday. More than half of the people in attendance raised their hands when Mayes asked if they came to discuss the Menlo development. One such attendee was Tina Charon, who has lived in Phoenix for more than 30 years, spending her career as a project manager for a semiconductor manufacturing firm. Charon told The Center Square that the development in her backyard has disturbed her quality of life, spurring her to join a neighborhood activism group called the Ahwatukee Community Alliance. Charon said she hoped her state's attorney general would fight the very industry that Charon worked for, helping her sleep better at night. "We're all hoping that she can intervene and do anything to help reduce the nuisance in our lives," Charon told The Center Square. "This is going to impact thousands of homes of people who were there well before that data center was even a dream. So I'm hoping she'll help in some way." Mayes cited her past work on the ACC as a reason why she will seek to use the state’s nuisance law. That law applies to everything from being “injurious to, indecent, offensive to the senses” to selling, offering to sell, transferring or disseminating items deemed to be offensive within 2,000 feet of any public or private school, public park or residential neighborhood. “One of the things that has alarmed me the most, which is that it seems very obvious to me, and this is one of the reasons that we formally intervened in opposition to the Arizona Public Service and Tucson Electric Power rate increases," Mayes said at the town hall. “We were in opposition to those proposed rate increases in front of the Arizona Corporation Commission, because we are opposing a 14% APS rate increase and a 13% TEP rate increase because I believe it's unnecessary, unjust, and is being fueled by data centers, at least in part.” In her post-town hall press scrum, Mayes addressed what she’d like to see from the data center and AI industries at large, to satisfy her concerns. Chief among them is having residents have more of a say in where and when such facilities are built, with Mayes pitching the idea of having a neighborhood, town or entire city voting on data center development before they can break ground on them. “You have to ask yourself, 'Why would you drop an industrial-scale, hyper-scaled AI data center in the middle of Ahwatukee?' ” Mayes told reporters. “And so, number one, pick the right place. I'm not flatly against data centers. Maybe there is a place in the middle of almost nowhere Arizona where these things would be appropriate, where maybe a community would want one. “But it is very obvious that they are choosing locations that were designed for a lower scale, lower level commercial operation, and then they are somehow flipping that into this gigantic industrial facility that can give off constant noise and pollution and possibly even constant air pollution if they're using diesel generators to power them at any time, and so there's a lot to be investigated here," she said.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual event Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media Lithium-ion batteries could do so much for AI data centers and the power grid. They’re cheaper than the fossil-gas turbines that tech giants are building at gigawatt scale for their “AI factories.” They can cushion the cost of building out grid infrastructure and power plants just to serve data centers’ peak energy demands. And they’re much cleaner than the diesel backup generators almost all data centers rely on. So why haven’t on-site batteries taken off yet with the computing crowd? It comes down to costs and benefits. Data center developers and operators often see fossil fuels as more reliable for 24/7 power. And industry watchers say the companies are leery of adding batteries unless they see a clear payback — or if they simply can’t do without them. Data centers have in fact relied for decades on a type of battery known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. It’s essentially a bank of batteries — most of them old-fashioned lead-acid chemistries — that connects to servers and other computing gear to keep them running smoothly in case utility power flickers or fails. Much like backup generators, they don’t do anything useful except during emergencies. With the right technological fixes, however, lithium-ion batteries that sit between the grid and the data center complex could perform this task, and solve a host of other problems. Specifically, they could serve as shock absorbers to prevent the kind of power disruptions, caused by data centers dropping off the grid unexpectedly, that are emerging as a major threat to grid stability. That’s the idea behind startup ON.Energy’s new AI UPS. According to CEO and cofounder Alan Cooper, it’s the result of roughly a half-decade of technology development, aimed at delivering what he described as “the new standard for connecting the data center to the grid.” The trick has been to prove that these centralized systems are capable of performing the critical tasks they need to. Earlier this year, ON.Energy concluded trials at the nation’s premiere grid testing facility showing that its technology works. Now, with a 5-gigawatt order from major AI data center developer Crusoe, ON.Energy is preparing to put this centralized UPS system to the test at commercial scale. “The grid sees a battery that’s always charging, and the load sees a battery that’s always outputting perfect quality power,” Cooper said. “In an oversimplified way, it smashes together BESS” — the industry term of art for grid-scale battery energy storage systems — “and UPS into a single asset.” ON.Energy isn’t the only company building batteries for this purpose, said Shahil Shah, chief engineer at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Shah is in charge of the grid simulator lab that tested the AI UPS system at multi-megawatt configurations. He’s also overseeing tests of a similar battery system from Prevalon Energy, and some others he said he can’t name yet. Besides providing UPS services, these technologies aim to solve a growing problem created by the rapid buildout of data centers, Shah said. “Many power system operators are coming up with requirements to make sure that the data center loads — the large loads — don’t negatively impact the reliability of the grid.” Data centers are uniquely challenging for utilities and grid operators to manage for a couple of reasons. First, their appetite for power can rise and fall dramatically, depending on how much computing they’re doing at any moment. And those changes can happen really fast, Shah said — “say, from 5% to 100% in a few milliseconds. You’re hammering the grid if you do that.” Second, data centers’ sensitivity to fluctuations in grid power quality can trigger them to disconnect from the grid and switch to UPS and backup generators at a moment’s notice, leading to massive unexpected drops in power demand that threaten to throw grid balances out of whack. Grid operator PJM Interconnection has recorded a handful of such multi-gigawatt drop-offs in recent years, including one in July where nearly 4 gigawatts of data center load in Virginia disconnected. Utilities and grid operators like PJM need to carefully balance supply and demand to avoid voltage and frequency fluctuations that can, in the worst case, lead to region-wide grid collapses. Many grid operators require big solar and wind farms to configure their systems to avoid tripping offline in response to grid voltage disturbances. Now data centers have become large enough to represent similar trip-off risks. The North American Electric Reliability Corp., which oversees the U.S. and Canadian electric systems, has targeted large “computational loads” for new requirements on this front, and Texas utility regulators instituted similar requirements this year. ON.Energy’s AI UPS is designed to handle those kinds of power isolation services, Cooper said. “Our double-conversion technology, which we’ve patented, is basically the process of fully electrically decoupling the load from the power generation source,” he said. “We’re using the fastest-response, best-in-class inverters in the market.” That technological sophistication adds up to a relatively simple solution for the utilities and grid operators, he said. “We’re basically a really predictable utility-scale battery that just sits and takes power from the grid.” To be clear, data centers need to be designed ahead of time to use ON.Energy’s AI UPS system, Cooper said. To illustrate the point, he showed me aerial photos of a Crusoe data center campus under construction. The parts of the campus built first include a central building that will house traditional UPS systems, he said. artigo.texto: Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal held a bilateral meeting with European Commission Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union Gerassimos Thomas in New Delhi to discuss India’s carbon market development, the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and technical cooperation. Discussions covered carbon pricing, emissions monitoring, reporting and verification systems, and capacity building. Key Highlights - Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal met EU Director-General Gerassimos Thomas in New Delhi to discuss carbon markets and CBAM. - India highlighted emission intensity reduction targets notified for 490 industrial units under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. - Non-fossil energy sources account for 308 GW of India’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW, according to the Ministry of Power. - India and the EU agreed to continue technical dialogue on carbon pricing, emissions monitoring and verification, and capacity building. New Delhi, Oct 14: Secretary, Ministry of Power, Pankaj Agarwal held a bilateral meeting with Gerassimos Thomas, Director-General for Taxation and Customs Union at the European Commission, in New Delhi to discuss India’s carbon market development, the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and opportunities for enhanced technical cooperation. The meeting focused on strengthening engagement between India and the EU on carbon pricing frameworks, emissions accounting and approaches to managing the climate-related aspects of international trade. During the meeting, Agarwal highlighted India’s progress under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), including the notification of emission intensity reduction targets for 490 industrial units and the development of a domestic carbon market. The scheme is part of India’s efforts to establish a framework for carbon credit trading and encourage industries to reduce the emissions intensity of their operations. The discussions also covered India’s progress in expanding non-fossil energy capacity as part of its broader energy transition. Agarwal noted that non-fossil sources accounted for 308 GW of India’s total installed electricity generation capacity of 558 GW. The expansion of non-fossil capacity is an important element of India’s strategy to diversify its energy mix and advance its climate and sustainability objectives. The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss the relationship between domestic carbon market mechanisms, industrial decarbonisation and international approaches to carbon-related trade measures. The European Commission delegation appreciated India’s progress in developing its carbon market and shared updates on the implementation of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. Both sides expressed willingness to continue technical engagement on the recognition of carbon pricing mechanisms, monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, and capacity building. They agreed to strengthen cooperation and maintain dialogue on carbon markets, CBAM-related methodologies and other areas of mutual interest. The India–EU meeting highlights the growing importance of technical cooperation on carbon pricing, industrial emissions and climate-related trade measures. Continued dialogue on the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme and CBAM methodologies could help both sides improve mutual understanding of their respective frameworks and identify areas for further cooperation.

Members of the Sioux Falls City Council's Regulatory Oversight Committee are meeting several times over the next couple months to put together regulations and ordinances related to data centers. And they want to hear from community members along the way. - Meetings will be held at 6 p.m. on Nov. 9, Nov. 30 and Jan. 4, with the goal to present final recommendations to the full council on Jan. 12. - "We’re trying to make sure that people can understand where we came from and what exactly the guardrails are that we’re putting in place," Councilor James Oppenheimer said. "So this is really an exercise in transparent governance." - There's also an opportunity to share feedback online on the city's website. - It's also unclear if any of these new ordinances or changes would impact the proposed Gemini data center in northeast Sioux Falls. The Sheriff's Office has established a memorial in her honor at the Law Enforcement Center on 4th and Minnesota, for those who wish to pay their respects. artigo.texto: As ações da Enerflex Ltd. (NYSE:EFXT) sobem 5% nas negociações pré-mercado de terça-feira, após a empresa anunciar um contrato para fornecer mais de um gigawatt (GW) de equipamentos de geração de energia a gás natural com baixas emissões para um empreendimento de data center na América do Norte. O contrato amplia a presença da Enerflex no mercado de infraestrutura de energia dedicada para suporte a instalações de inteligência artificial e computação digital. Em conjunto com os projetos anunciados anteriormente, incluindo aproximadamente 450 megawatts (MW) divulgados em 1 de outubro de 2026, o novo acordo aumenta a carteira de projetos de geração de energia a gás natural da empresa para mais de 1,75 GW. As entregas referentes ao atraso estão programadas para se estender até 2028. Enerflex garante importante contrato de geração de energia para data centers O contrato recém-adjudicado está inserido na área de Sistemas de Engenharia da Enerflex e abrange o projeto, a engenharia, a fabricação e a montagem de unidades de geração de energia a gás natural. O equipamento será implantado em um centro de dados em desenvolvimento na América do Norte, fornecendo capacidade dedicada de geração de eletricidade. O projeto utilizará uma configuração “atrás do medidor”, permitindo que a energia seja fornecida diretamente à instalação sem a necessidade de conexão à rede elétrica convencional para o sistema de geração. Esses arranjos podem suportar grandes instalações industriais e de computação que exigem fontes de alimentação de energia substanciais e confiáveis. A Enerflex descreveu o equipamento como uma tecnologia de geração a gás natural com baixas emissões, embora o anúncio não tenha especificado dados de desempenho de emissões nem comparações com sistemas de geração alternativos. A empresa também não divulgou o valor financeiro do contrato, a identidade do cliente ou a localização exata do centro de dados. A carteira de pedidos de geração de energia ultrapassa 1,75 GW A Enerflex afirmou que sua carteira de projetos de geração de energia a gás natural para consumidores finais agora ultrapassa 1,75 GW. O total inclui o contrato mais recente para mais de 1 GW de capacidade e contratos previamente anunciados, incluindo aproximadamente 450 MW divulgados no início de outubro. A carteira de pedidos representa o trabalho contratado que a empresa espera executar nos próximos anos. A previsão é de que as entregas continuem até 2028, fornecendo um cronograma das atividades futuras de fabricação e execução de projetos. O aumento reflete a crescente demanda por infraestrutura dedicada à geração de eletricidade, à medida que os desenvolvedores expandem a capacidade dos data centers. No entanto, a empresa não forneceu uma discriminação detalhada do valor financeiro da carteira de pedidos nem do reconhecimento de receita esperado por ano. O cronograma e a rentabilidade de cada projeto dependerão dos prazos de fabricação, dos custos de execução e dos termos contratuais. A Enerflex planeja investir US$ 100 milhões em sua unidade fabril Para dar suporte à sua crescente carteira de projetos, a Enerflex autorizou um investimento de aproximadamente US$ 100 milhões em suas instalações e capacidades de Sistemas de Engenharia. Desse montante, US$ 15 milhões estão incluídos na previsão de despesas de capital da empresa para 2026. O programa de investimento tem como objetivo fortalecer os recursos de fabricação e operacionais necessários para executar contratos de geração de energia em larga escala. A Enerflex afirmou que os projetos serão entregues por meio de suas operações de fabricação na América do Norte. O investimento planejado surge em um momento em que a empresa expande seu papel no fornecimento de infraestrutura de energia modular para instalações com alto consumo energético. O anúncio não forneceu uma alocação detalhada do investimento restante nem especificou o cronograma para todas as despesas planejadas. A infraestrutura de IA impulsiona a demanda por energia dedicada A Enerflex atribuiu o crescimento de sua carteira de pedidos de geração de energia à demanda decorrente do desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital. Os grandes centros de dados exigem um fornecimento substancial de eletricidade para operar equipamentos de computação, sistemas de rede e infraestrutura de refrigeração. A geração de energia instalada no próprio local de consumo pode fornecer uma fonte alternativa de energia para instalações que buscam capacidade dedicada sem depender de uma conexão convencional à rede elétrica para essa geração. Paul Mahoney, presidente e diretor executivo da Enerflex, destacou a demanda por esses sistemas. “A demanda por energia confiável e de primeira qualidade que não exija conexão à rede elétrica, e que dê suporte ao desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital, continua a crescer”, disse Mahoney. “O nosso sucesso em garantir mais de 1,75 gigawatts em carteira de pedidos destaca as capacidades únicas da Enerflex em fornecer soluções integradas de design, engenharia, fabricação em grande escala e execução de projetos para geração de energia atrás do medidor.” Os comentários destacam o foco da administração no fornecimento de sistemas integrados de geração de energia para grandes projetos de infraestrutura. Os contratos podem gerar receita adicional com serviços A Enerflex afirmou que sua crescente carteira de pedidos de geração de energia pode criar oportunidades que vão além da entrega inicial dos equipamentos. Isso inclui o comissionamento, a instalação e os serviços pós-venda associados às unidades geradoras. A empresa também identificou uma demanda potencial por suporte digital por meio de seu ecossistema de Gestão de Desempenho de Ativos ReliaCore. Os sistemas de gestão de desempenho de ativos podem ajudar os operadores a monitorar equipamentos, avaliar as condições de operação e gerenciar as necessidades de manutenção. artigo.texto: Energia DHL amplia rede global de logística especializada em baterias Companhia reúne mais de 20 instalações e prepara novos centros na Europa para atender aos setores automotivo, industrial e de armazenamento de energia A DHL está ampliando sua rede internacional de logística especializada em baterias, formada atualmente por mais de 20 instalações. A estrutura atende fabricantes de veículos elétricos, empresas industriais e projetos de energia, oferecendo serviços que vão do transporte de componentes e apoio à produção ao armazenamento, reparo e encaminhamento de baterias para reciclagem. A companhia prevê novas unidades na Europa até 2027. A rede reúne operações de três divisões do grupo — DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding e DHL Express — para integrar transporte, armazenagem, procedimentos aduaneiros e serviços pós-venda. Segundo a empresa, os centros especializados também realizam diagnóstico, testes, carregamento, condicionamento e recebimento de equipamentos devolvidos pelos clientes. A expansão acompanha o aumento da utilização de baterias em diferentes atividades. Além dos automóveis elétricos, os equipamentos são empregados em máquinas industriais, operações de mineração e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Alguns conjuntos pesam mais de 50 toneladas, o que exige veículos apropriados, equipamentos para movimentação de cargas pesadas e planejamento específico das entregas. O transporte desses produtos também está sujeito a requisitos de segurança. De acordo com a DHL, a classificação de baterias como mercadorias perigosas e as diferenças entre as regras aplicáveis ao transporte marítimo, aéreo e terrestre impõem cuidados com acondicionamento, documentação e fiscalização aduaneira. “A logística de baterias é fundamentalmente diferente das cadeias de abastecimento tradicionais”, afirmou Francisco Milián, responsável pela área de logística de entrada para a produção da DHL Supply Chain na Europa, Oriente Médio e África. Segundo ele, os clientes demandam serviços em todas as etapas, desde o fornecimento às fábricas até o recondicionamento, as devoluções e a reciclagem. Novas instalações Na Alemanha, a DHL disponibilizou recentemente 13 mil metros quadrados de armazenagem adaptada a baterias na cidade de Halle. Outra instalação está sendo preparada na Hungria, com início das atividades previsto para 2027. Nos Países Baixos, o grupo está construindo um centro em Holtum, com 17 mil metros quadrados para armazenagem e serviços especializados em baterias de alta tensão. A previsão é de que a operação comece no início de 2027. O empreendimento ficará próximo de instalações já utilizadas para atendimento à indústria automotiva, formando um complexo voltado também a sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Segundo a empresa, a concentração de atividades em centros especializados permitirá reunir operações de transporte internacional, liberação aduaneira, distribuição e atendimento após a venda. O serviço é destinado tanto à indústria automotiva quanto a fabricantes de equipamentos, empresas de energia e projetos relacionados a minerais críticos. Transporte de energia A DHL também atua na movimentação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, do inglês Battery Energy Storage Systems. Esses conjuntos armazenam eletricidade para utilização posterior e podem ser empregados em projetos de energia renovável e infraestrutura das redes elétricas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a companhia transportou mais de 1.100 unidades BESS para diferentes mercados. Segundo o grupo, as entregas podem exigir transporte multimodal, içamento de cargas de grande porte e deslocamentos até áreas remotas, além do cumprimento das normas aplicáveis ao manuseio de mercadorias perigosas. O crescimento dessa atividade ocorre paralelamente à instalação de fábricas de baterias em diferentes regiões. A DHL aponta que a concentração de parte da produção na Ásia e a demanda em mercados como o europeu movimentam matérias-primas, produtos químicos, componentes, equipamentos industriais e baterias prontas entre continentes. “A transição energética está criando corredores comerciais e padrões de cadeias de abastecimento inteiramente novos”, afirmou Hendrik Venter, CEO global da DHL Supply Chain. De acordo com o executivo, fabricantes e operadores estão reorganizando suas redes para atender à produção de veículos elétricos, ao armazenamento de energia e aos empreendimentos de fontes renováveis. A logística para o setor de novas energias integra a Strategy 2030, plano de negócios do DHL Group. A área contempla oito segmentos: energia eólica, solar, veículos elétricos e baterias, armazenamento de energia em baterias, carregamento de veículos elétricos, infraestrutura de redes, hidrogênio e combustíveis alternativos.

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Advancing American Freedom Foundation wants Congress to see how much electricity data centers use. It also wants states to reveal how much their data center tax breaks cost. The conservative group made those recommendations in a paper by Kevin Dayaratna. He’s the president of AAFF’s Institute for Statistical Policy Analysis. The paper argues that lawmakers and utilities need better information before deciding data center policy. He said these policies impact state budgets and utility costs. “There is no precise aggregate measure of how much electricity data centers consume,” Dayaratna wrote. He used Ohio as an example of where this would’ve helped. The state projected that its data center sales tax exemption would cost about $136 million in 2025. Its tax department later told reporters it would cost $1.569 billion, according to published reports. That’s more than 11 times the first estimate, the paper says. The department also shared those figures with a news outlet instead of posting them on a state website. Texas had something similar happen. In February 2023, the state projected that its data center exemption would cost $130 million in fiscal year 2025. By January 2025, that estimate ballooned to $1.016 billion. “States should publish these figures and review these exemptions on a fixed schedule,” Dayaratna wrote. The paper also looks at power forecasts changing. In 2022, Georgia Power expected demand to grow by less than 400 megawatts by 2031. A year later, it raised that estimate to 6,600 megawatts. Dayaratna thinks both low and high forecasts hurt customers. Too little power can cause shortages, too much can raise electric bills, he noted. The paper cites projections saying data centers may use 9% to 17% of American electricity by 2030. AAFF wants Congress to make the Energy Information Administration require regular data collection of this information. EIA announced voluntary pilot studies in March. That pilot program covers just 196 companies. “Congress should make this collection broader and more permanent,” Dayaratna wrote. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 includes a reporting requirement. Senators introduced it last month. Section 2114 would make power companies report how much electricity data centers use. Data centers wouldn’t have to file any new reports. AAFF also wants states to let private utilities use separate power grids to serve data centers. The power company and its customers would negotiate prices and finance their own systems. They would still have to follow environmental, siting and safety laws. Dayaratna says this would protect other utility customers from paying for infrastructure upgrades to benefit data centers. The paper says charging data centers higher electric rates could help, but they would still use the same power grid as everyone else. AAFF also wants to make it easier and faster to build power plants and connect them to the grid. It supports using different energy sources without any emissions rules. The group doesn’t want to ban new data center construction, it says. It wants states to fix power supply shortages and make adding more electricity to the grid easier.

artigo.texto: Data Centers and Public Health The rapid growth of AI and other digital services like search engines and cloud storage and computing is driving a major expansion of data center construction across the United States. As rapid expansion continues, it is necessary to account for related health impacts. Data centers can affect communities and their health in a variety of ways, including air pollution from the burning of fossil fuels, water use and pollution, excessive noise and light pollution, and land use and development. New facilities that are powered by fossil fuels can add to existing pollution and health burdens in communities already facing environmental injustices. Data centers are often placed and operated in the same communities already disproportionately impacted by environmental injustices: low-income, rural, immigrant/refugee, Indigenous communities and other communities of color, and other marginalized populations. It’s important to understand how data centers can affect health and the role public health professionals can play to advocate for transparent decisionmaking and protective policies. Latest Updates - Data Centers and Health: Understanding the Impacts and Taking Action AI data centers are expanding rapidly across the U.S., with growing implications for air and water quality, noise, energy costs and public health. This four-part webinar series equips health professionals and advocates with the evidence, messaging and actionable strategies needed to respond. Watch the recordings. - Q&A with NAACP: Addressing the growing environmental harms of AI data centers | Public Health Newswire From rising emissions to local air, water and noise pollution, AI data centers pose growing concerns about environmental justice and health equity. The NAACP has long been on the front lines of environmental justice and is addressing new threats as they arise. This March 2026 Q&A from Public Health Newswire talks with the NAACP to learn how communities and health professionals can respond. Read the article. How a Data Center Can Affect Health Energy, Air Pollution and Climate Health The energy demand created by data centers can drive grid expansion and fossil fuel energy generation, which can worsen air pollution, amplify the effects of climate change and create affordability concerns for households. Impact on Energy Grid In some areas, utility companies may need to expand or upgrade the power grid to meet data centers’ energy demand. Depending on how these upgrades are funded, this can increase energy costs for surrounding communities, contributing to financial stress and mental health impacts. Inadequate energy access can increase the risk of heat- and cold-related illnesses, such as heat stroke and inadequate blood circulation. Long-term socioeconomic implications of financial hardship can include food insecurity, increasing health disparities and chronic stress. Air Quality Data centers that rely on fossil fuels can increase air pollution, contributing to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, neurological disorders and reduced fertility. One high-growth model suggests that data centers may contribute to approximately 600,000 asthma cases in 2028, with an estimated public health cost over $20 billion. Climate Change Added CO₂ from data center operations accelerates climate change, contributing to more severe heat waves, storms and floods, which are all events that endanger both data centers and nearby communities and compound health risks ranging from heat stroke and respiratory illness to trauma and mental health impacts. The water consumption by data centers may exacerbate growing water scarcity caused by climate change and drought. Data centers can release excess heat that may raise temperatures in nearby neighborhoods. Some researchers have documented increased air temperatures up to 4°F, and this heat impact spanned approximately a third of a mile from the data center. Added heat may increase cooling needs and compound heat-health risks for people who are most vulnerable or unable to afford air conditioning. Water Use, Quality and Scarcity Cooling systems can strain local water supplies and raise concerns about water quality, drought and equitable access. The cooling systems used in data centers can strain local water resources and negatively impact water quality. There are also some concerns around incorporation of chemicals like PFAS in the cooling systems. These forever chemicals are long-lasting in the environment and high levels are linked with some cancers. The changes to water supply and quality may increase the risk of waterborne diseases, water scarcity, pollution ingestion and poor maternal outcomes. Noise, Light and Sleep Health Around-the-clock cooling equipment, fans, generators and construction can create disruptive noise, while nighttime lighting can interfere with sleep and daily rhythms. Noise Pollution Cooling systems, back-up diesel generators, fans and other machinery contribute to constant noise production, which can cause chronic sleep disturbance and stress, with the possibility of long-term conditions such as cardiovascular impacts. Noise pollution is of particular concern for children as it can impact cognition and may have lifelong health impacts. Light Pollution Data centers require lighting throughout the night which can disrupt the circadian rhythm of individuals exposed, impacting melatonin production, sleep cycles, mental health, cardiovascular health and overall quality of life. Beyond the Facility: Supply Chains and E-Waste Construction, mineral extraction and electronic waste create health and environmental impacts beyond the data center site. Beyond the direct health impacts of data centers, the processes required to build and maintain the facilities, such as mining rare-earth metals and concrete production, also impact health outcomes.
