artigo.texto: Ask most people what BYD does and they will say electric cars. That is true, and it undersells the company by a wide margin. BYD is a Chinese multinational manufacturing conglomerate that builds rechargeable batteries, stationary energy storage, solar panels, semiconductors, forklifts, and entire monorail systems. The car business is the loudest part. It is not the whole company, and it was not even the first. BYD Company Ltd. operates across electronics, autos, renewable energy, and rail transit. That spread is not an accident of acquisition. It is the result of a battery maker deciding, over three decades, that it could build the things its batteries power, then the things that move those things, then the infrastructure they run on. To understand BYD you have to start before the cars existed. Wang Chuanfu founded BYD to make rechargeable batteries in February 1995, formally registered as Shenzhen BYD Battery Company Ltd. Before that he worked as a vice supervisor at Beijing's Nonferrous Research Institute. He saw an opening as Japanese companies shifted from NiCd toward higher-value nickel-metal hydride and lithium-ion chemistries, and he went after the segment they were leaving behind. The early strategy was labor, not automation. BYD built its business on manual labor rather than the capital-intensive, highly automated processes Japanese rivals used, and that approach, combined with in-house production of key machinery, cut its unit costs to roughly five or six times lower than Japanese competitors. It worked. BYD won an order from Sanyo in 1996 that marked its arrival in the global supply chain, and by July 2002 it had surpassed Sanyo to become the world's leading NiCd battery maker, accounting for 65% of global production. The car business came later. BYD Auto was established in 2003. For a battery company that had just won the NiCd crown, building cars was the logical place to put all those cells. BYD is well known for its Blade Battery, and one sits in every BYD EV. The headline feature is safety: it has passed the nail penetration test, and its compressive strength reaches 445 kN, the equivalent of a 45-ton truck. The warranty runs eight years or longer, covering 310,685 miles and in some cases up to 621,371 miles. BYD does not keep the batteries to itself. It functions as an OEM battery supplier, and FinDreams Battery, its subsidiary, ranked as the world's number-two EV battery producer in 2024, holding 17% of the EV battery market behind CATL. Its customers include rivals. The Toyota bZ3, a China-only sedan co-developed with BYD, runs a BYD Blade Battery underneath, and regulatory filings show Tesla has fitted BYD cells in the Model Y. BYD Energy Storage was founded in 2008 and specializes in energy storage solutions. According to its website, it has rolled out industrial and residential projects in 110 countries. The scale here is genuinely large and often overlooked in all the EV coverage. In 2025, BYD topped global Battery Energy Storage System shipments at more than 60 GWh, displacing Tesla - the first year it held the number one BESS position worldwide. That gave BYD a 13 percent global BESS market share, against Tesla's 10 percent, per Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Tesla shipped 46.7 GWh of storage that year. The grid-scale battery business, in other words, is now another market where BYD leads and Tesla follows. The most surprising corner of BYD is the one where it stopped being a parts supplier and became a civil engineering firm. SkyRail is an advanced monorail; its carriages ride on an elevated single beam that supports and guides them, and BYD built the entire system - vehicles, tracks, stations, and communication systems. The R&D project ran five years, mobilized more than 1,000 engineers, and cost over 600 million euro, with total SkyRail investment exceeding $1 billion. The pitch is cost. SkyRail runs about a fifth of what a subway costs to build, with construction taking as little as two years - one third the time a subway takes, helped by prefabricated track beams. It can move 10,000 to 30,000 passengers per hour in one direction. BYD positions it for cities worried about the financial burden of a subway. It has launched lines in Shenzhen and Sao Paulo, Brazil. The grand plan was bigger: an initial rollout across more than 200 Chinese cities was cut back sharply once Beijing moved to curb local government debt. The vertical integration shows up in the financials. BYD's net profit in 2025 was CNY 32.62 billion, roughly $4.72 billion, and it earned 1.25 times more net profit than Tesla while pulling in 1.23 times the revenue. It sold 2.81 times as many vehicles. That volume comes at a lower price per car - a domestic average selling price around CNY 141,000, about $20,400 - but the batteries, electronics, and storage businesses give BYD revenue streams Tesla does not have. It is not all up and to the right. BYD's 2025 revenue grew only 3.46%, its slowest in six years, net profit fell 18.97% - its first yearly profit drop in four years - blamed on a fierce domestic price war that squeezed margins. Overseas is now the profitability lever: exports passed the 1 million mark for the first time, hitting 1.05 million, a 145% jump, and overseas operations rose to 38.65% of revenue. If you want to track BYD as the conglomerate it actually is, read past the vehicle delivery numbers. Its 2025 annual report is filed on the Shenzhen exchange under 002594.SZ and on HKEX under 01211.HK, where the segment breakdowns show handset revenue and the rest. Watch the energy storage shipments, since that is where BYD just overtook Tesla. And keep an eye on U.S. legislation banning Chinese vehicle software from 2027 and Chinese hardware from 2030, on top of existing 100 percent tariffs on Chinese EVs - the regulatory wall that will decide how much of this empire ever reaches American roads. artigo.texto: A single project in Paducah just put a spotlight on how huge AI energy and data needs could reshape listed digital infrastructure stocks. A planned US$100b American Energy Hub ties Brookfield Asset Management, NextEra Energy and other data center linked players to long-duration power and compute demand that few investors are modeling yet. This article walks through three stocks exposed to that news and explains why their stories now deserve closer attention. The three stocks in this article are a small sample, and the full screen surfaced 20 more listed digital infrastructure and yield-oriented data center owners with similarly interesting stories that are not covered here. To identify and analyze the highest conviction ideas for your own watchlist, head straight to the Listed Digital Infrastructure & Yield-Oriented Data Center Owners screener. Equinix is the clearest expression of this screener's theme. It is a pure data center and interconnection REIT where AI traffic, high power density and long-term colocation deals all converge in a single, scaled digital infrastructure platform. Equinix runs a global network of colocation and interconnection facilities, generating about US$9.9b from designing, building and operating its IBX data centers, and carries a market value of roughly US$100.6b. "Control of roughly 3 GW of designed power, with about 600 MW under some form of development and an expected 1 GW under production by early next year, positions Equinix to convert power constrained market demand into incremental rental revenue and cash flow over time." The real swing factor is how one pressure on future build returns shapes the balance between higher demand, project costs and eventual cash flow. That trade off between power, capital and future cash generation is exactly what the full narrative for Equinix unpacks, including how Equinix's AI build cycle could be accelerating. Iron Mountain taps into the same Listed Digital Infrastructure & Yield-Oriented Data Center Owners theme as Equinix, but from a different angle, pairing long-standing physical records storage with newer colocation sites that link directly to AI and cloud demand. Iron Mountain helps more than 240,000 customers manage and secure physical and digital information, while building out data centers that fit the screener's yield-oriented digital infrastructure angle. Most revenue still comes from the Global RIM Business at about US$5.5b, with around US$1.1b from Corporate and Other and close to US$1.0b from the Global Data Center Business. The stock carries a market value near US$34.1b. "Iron Mountain is transitioning from a legacy storage-focused REIT toward a broader information infrastructure platform with digital and data center exposure. If this is successful they could see new pillars of significant revenue." What really matters for investors is how one unseen pressure on funding and returns shapes that shift from storage workhorse to full digital infrastructure platform. That hidden pressure on funding and returns is exactly what the full narrative for Iron Mountain pulls apart, revealing how Iron Mountain's AI push could be accelerating faster than investors expect. Digital Realty Trust is one of the clearest plays on the Listed Digital Infrastructure & Yield-Oriented Data Center Owners theme, running a global PlatformDIGITAL network of data centers, colocation sites and interconnection hubs that together generated about US$6.8b from commercial REIT activities on a business now valued around US$67.3b. Where Equinix and Iron Mountain show different ways into AI ready infrastructure, Digital Realty Trust pulls the theme together by pairing large scale data centers with dense interconnection that can support AI, cloud and high performance computing tenants. "Digital Realty's record signed but not yet commenced lease backlog of about US$1.9b, plus a further US$410m of hyperscale leases signed in July, points to a large pipeline of contracted revenue that has not yet flowed through earnings and could support future core FFO per share." What happens to future returns depends heavily on how one funding pressure shapes the pace and profitability of Digital Realty Trust's build out. That funding question is exactly what the full narrative for Digital Realty Trust unpacks, revealing how accelerating AI demand could reshape returns and re-rate Digital Realty Trust's role in global infrastructure. A novidade é um micro data center desenvolvido para atender às necessidades de empresas que buscam otimizar os ambientes tecnológicos. O lançamento reúne os principais sistemas necessários à operação de uma infraestrutura de tecnologia da informação (TI), incluindo energia, climatização, monitoramento e segurança. artigo.texto: Netbox Labs Faz Parceria com a NVIDIA e a Grafana Labs e Anuncia Novas Adições à Plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura NetBox para Agregar a Camada de Inteligência para Data Centers de IA e Criação de Infraestrutura Corporativa AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 14 de outubro de 2026 CABO CANAVERAL, Flórida, Oct. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Centro Espacial Kennedy — A NetBox Labs, empresa criadora do NetBox, o sistema de registro para redes e datacenters, anunciou hoje parcerias com a NVIDIA e a Grafana Labs, além de uma série de novos recursos da plataforma, na primeira conferência NetBox Evolve. Juntos, esses anúncios ampliam a posição do NetBox como a camada de inteligência central para a infraestrutura tecnológica mundial. - A NVIDIA agora está integrada ao NetBox como uma fonte de verdade nativa do NVIDIA Configuration Manager (NVCM), o componente de orquestração de rede do NVIDIA DSX OS. Com a aceleração da implementação da infraestrutura de IA, essa parceria coloca o NetBox no centro de como a infraestrutura de IA é projetada, provisionada e operada. - A Grafana Labs e a NetBox Labs lançaram um plugin oficial do NetBox no catálogo da Grafana. Ele leva o contexto da infraestrutura em tempo real para os dashboards e alertas da Grafana, viabilizando que as equipes de rede e de data centers atribuam significado aos seus dados. - A Plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura da NetBox Labs foi ampliada com novos produtos e recursos. O NetBox Designs se junta ao NetBox Visual Explorer e ao NetBox Asset Lifecycle para acelerar o design e o planejamento, a aquisição e o gerenciamento de implementações de data centers e redes. Além disso, novos agentes e recursos de operações de IA ajudam todas as equipes a automatizar sua infraestrutura com base no contexto independente de fornecedores do NetBox. Por fim, uma grande variedade de novas integrações e novos dashboards para o NetBox Analytics ajudam as equipes a inserir mais dados no NetBox e a entender rapidamente sua infraestrutura. Seja para as equipes criarem redes e infraestruturas corporativas no setor de varejo, saúde, serviços financeiros ou implementarem um data center de IA com velocidade e escala gigantescas, a configuração, a observabilidade e a automação dependem de um registro confiável de qual infraestrutura deve existir e como ela deve operar. Esse registro é o NetBox, disse Kris Beevers, CEO e cofundador da NetBox Labs. O NetBox é usado por empresas como Arm, CoreWeave, Kaiser Permanente e J.P. Morgan Chase para criar, operar e expandir suas redes e infraestruturas. Estamos observando um crescimento enorme, com mais de 90% das principais neonuvens usando o NetBox para projetar e escalar seus datacenters de IA, e esperamos que o NetBox alimente mais de 100 GW de capacidade de datacenters de IA até 2030. O NetBox se torna nativo do NVIDIA DSX OS A NVIDIA fez uma parceria com a NetBox Labs para tornar o NetBox uma fonte nativa de referência para o NVCM, de modo que a configuração de rede no DSX OS venha diretamente do sistema de registro que as equipes de infraestrutura de IA já usam. Isso coloca o NetBox no centro do design, do provisionamento e da operação das implementações de IA em grande escala da atualidade. O NetBox fornece os dados centrais que impulsionam a automação da configuração em todas as malhas de cluster nativas da NVIDIA. Leia mais sobre a Parceria NetBox Labs NVIDIA aqui. Contexto do NetBox em todos os dashboards da Grafana Labs A infraestrutura está produzindo cada vez mais telemetria. Mas a telemetria só mostra o que a infraestrutura está fazendo, não o que ela é: a qual dispositivo uma interface pertence, onde ela está localizada, qual função ela desempenha, quem é o proprietário dela e se ela deveria existir. Atualmente as equipes preenchem essa lacuna manualmente, com scripts ou suposições frágeis. Com a nova parceria da NetBox Labs com a Grafana Labs, o NetBox registra como a infraestrutura deve ser e a Grafana mostra o que ela está realmente fazendo. O plugin gratuito e de código aberto do NetBox, desenvolvido em colaboração com a Grafana Labs e publicado no catálogo da Grafana, transfere o contexto do NetBox em tempo real (local, função, tenant, rack, proprietário, ciclo de vida) para os dashboards e alertas da Grafana. Ele não exige alterações no pipeline, evita rótulos desatualizados e não adiciona nenhum custo de métrica. Separadamente, a plataforma Orb de código aberto da NetBox Labs agora oferece aos usuários da Grafana Cloud uma nova fonte de fluxo de rede e telemetria de pacotes. A observabilidade das redes e da infraestrutura são casos de uso populares em toda a comunidade da Grafana, e o contexto é o que separa uma parede de métricas das respostas e ações, disse Ash Mazhari, VP de Desenvolvimento Corporativo da Grafana Labs. O NetBox é o sistema de registro em que as equipes já confiam. Com a fonte de dados do NetBox em nosso catálogo e a Orb fornecendo telemetria de rede para a Grafana Cloud, nossos usuários passam a ter um entendimento mais profundo da sua infraestrutura e dos dados de rede. Leia mais sobre a Parceria entre a NetBox Labs e a Grafana Labs aqui. Novos recursos da plataforma NetBox Labs para pessoas e agentes de IA Além das parcerias, a NetBox Labs também anunciou várias novas adições à plataforma de Inteligência de Infraestrutura da NetBox Labs. - Agora em versão de pré-visualização pública, o NetBox Designs oferece modelos reutilizáveis para um projeto de infraestrutura rápido. As equipes definem um local, um rack ou um plano de IP uma vez e, em seguida, podem repetir o processo para implantações em grande escala. O NetBox Asset Lifecycle então acompanha os objetos planejados ao longo da lista de materiais, do pedido de compra, do envio e da instalação. - O NetBox Analytics ganhou vários dashboards prontos para uso esta semana para ajudar as equipes a entender seus complexos ambientes de infraestrutura. artigo.texto: In recent weeks, Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton have adopted increasingly tough rhetoric against data centers, promising to crack down on hundreds of facilities that failed to disclose required information about their water use over the past five years. But the law that Texas political leaders are invoking carries a maximum fine of just $500 — a potentially negligible penalty that’s just a blip for large companies. Data centers use millions of gallons of water a year to run their facilities and cool their servers. Under state law, facilities that fail to complete required water-use surveys can be charged with a Class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to a $500 fine, and barred from certain state funding and environmental permits. But some experts say those consequences have significant limitations, raising questions about whether the state has the tools to force compliance from an industry expanding rapidly across Texas. State officials don’t know whether misdemeanor penalties have been issued against data centers, and the facilities aren’t eligible for state funding. Increasing fines for Class C misdemeanors in the Water Code would require state legislation. Lawmakers do not convene in Austin for the 2027 legislative session until January. “The governor is like, ‘Let’s enforce the laws on the books that weren’t being enforced.’ That’s not much in the way of incentive,” said Kathryn Guerra, who leads a watchdog campaign at the environmental nonprofit Public Citizen. “If those are the laws that we already have and nobody’s enforcing them, the data centers know.” Abbott’s office defended its enforcement crackdown by saying that the water board, along with other agencies including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and the Public Utility Commission of Texas, will work together. “No other state agency will approve data centers until the Public Utility Commission, ERCOT, and the Water Development Board have the information they need to make informed decisions,” said Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary. Mahaleris added that the governor has recommended that data centers pay for their own electric infrastructure, use less water-intensive cooling technologies and add power generation to the state’s power grid. Cameron Poursoltan, the director of energy policy at Texas for the Data Center Coalition, said the organization, which represents many data center operators, supports annual water reporting because state and regional planners need accurate data to build a water plan that meets the needs of all Texans. The state already requires large water users, including data centers, to complete annual water use surveys. The Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state’s water planning process and financing water projects, uses responses to assess the current demand and to plan for water needs 50 years into the future. But data centers have largely ignored the surveys. Or some argue they haven’t received them. Last year, 329 data centers were surveyed. Only about 30% responded. One lawmaker described the response rate as “pretty pathetic” at a legislative hearing this summer, despite the requirement being written into state law. Some data center operators have defended the low response rate, saying they have not received a survey. “Data centers take water stewardship extremely seriously,” Poursoltan said. He added that the organization has worked with TWDB to resolve “significant contact information and data discrepancies that contributed to the TWDB Water Use Survey’s initial lower response rate.” Tracking data centers in Texas The survey has long been the state’s only way to track how much water the rapidly expanding data center industry uses. Another effort to collect the information by the PUC this year has been voluntary and also had a low response rate. Now, amid growing scrutiny of data centers and their demands on Texas’ dwindling water supply, Abbott and Paxton are asking state agencies to enforce the existing law. The enforcement push comes as both Republicans face competitive elections and opposition to data center development grows. A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released in August found that 57% of Texas voters opposed building a data center in their community. Republicans remained closely divided, with 45% supporting while 43% opposed local data center construction. Meanwhile, 75% of registered Texas Democrats oppose data centers. The water board, which collects the surveys to help plan the state’s water needs, has historically had little ability to enforce the requirement. Abbott has directed the agency to notify local prosecutors about noncompliant facilities, while Paxton has launched an investigation. But the board says it has no authority to prosecute violations itself, and state officials don’t know if fines have been issued against data centers. The state’s next steps could reveal how much leverage officials actually have. The water board is required to update Abbott’s office by Oct. 14 on the progress of its enforcement efforts. “We will continue working with state leaders to ensure our industry’s growth in Texas is responsible, transparent, and responsive to the communities where our members operate,” Poursoltan said in an email. What enforcement looks like Abbott has directed the water board to notify county and district attorneys about facilities that fail to comply, leaving local officials to determine whether to pursue criminal cases. Historically, the board relied on local law enforcement to ask for the list of noncompliant water users. Experts say this would put the onus on law enforcement to identify a crime, without knowing about the crime. artigo.texto: Por muito tempo, o senso comum tratou os data centers como meros galpões técnicos: edifícios reforçados projetados para abrigar servidores. Hoje, essa definição não apenas se tornou obsoleta, como representa um risco para quem deseja competir na economia global. O setor passa por uma transformação profunda e acelerada, migrando da categoria de ativo imobiliário para o patamar de infraestrutura estratégica nacional, impulsionado pela demanda de processamento gerada pela inteligência artificial. Nesse novo cenário, a América Latina ganha relevância no tabuleiro global, e o Brasil desponta na linha de frente dessa corrida, sustentado por vantagens competitivas únicas. Ao lado de Brasil e Argentina, o México compõe a vanguarda latino-americana na atração de capitais para infraestrutura digital. Contudo, a concorrência entre os maiores mercados da região não se resume a uma escolha de quem é "melhor", mas a objetivos estratégicos distintos. O México desfruta da integração direta com a economia norte-americana, capturando a onda de reshoring e funcionando quase como uma extensão operacional dos Estados Unidos. O Brasil, por sua vez, oferece um conjunto diferente de fundamentos: detém o maior mercado consumidor da região, ampla disponibilidade territorial para expansão contínua e, acima de tudo, uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável — atributo decisivo para empresas globais com metas rigorosas de descarbonização. Enquanto a escolha pelo México atende à lógica da proximidade com a América do Norte, a aposta no Brasil consolida a criação de um hub desenhado para abastecer o mercado doméstico e irradiar serviços para quase toda a América do Sul. Embora o fluxo mais visível de aportes no Brasil continue capitaneado por operadores globais, hyperscalers norte-americanos e fundos internacionais de private equity, o capital chinês acompanha os movimentos. A atratividade é direta: a China se consolidou como uma das maiores potências em consumo e desenvolvimento de IA, além de liderar a fabricação de equipamentos críticos para data centers. Para as corporações asiáticas, posicionar-se em mercados com grande potencial de expansão, segurança energética e apetite digital é um desdobramento natural dos negócios. Integração de quatro pilares O perfil dos investidores e a dinâmica dos projetos mudaram nos últimos cinco anos. O modelo em que bastava aportar capital e erguer paredes o mais rápido possível deu lugar a uma abordagem sofisticada e interdisciplinar. Hoje, o sucesso de um empreendimento depende da integração de quatro pilares: acesso garantido à energia de longo prazo, mitigando riscos de abastecimento; capacidade de execução técnica, cumprindo cronogramas rigorosos; excelência operacional contínua, assegurando disponibilidade crítica ininterrupta; e relacionamento comercial robusto e conformidade regulatória. Essa evolução reflete uma prática já madura nos Estados Unidos – onde consultorias especializadas atuam há mais de uma década – e que ganhou tração no Brasil nos últimos seis anos. O suporte a esses projetos passou a exigir uma atuação ponta a ponta (end-to-end), abrangendo desde a formulação da estratégia de entrada (como criação de joint ventures, aquisições de empresas ou projetos greenfield e brownfield) até modelagem financeira, due diligence, governança corporativa e assessoria regulatória. Essa visão holística assegura que as premissas desenhadas no papel se sustentem quando a operação estiver sob carga máxima. O efeito multiplicador na economia real Enxergar o data center apenas como tecnologia é deixar valor na mesa. Trata-se de um catalisador de encadeamento produtivo raro. Na fase de implantação, o setor mobiliza pesadamente a engenharia, a construção civil especializada e fabricantes de equipamentos de alta complexidade, como transformadores, sistemas elétricos dedicados, automação e soluções térmicas de refrigeração. Já na fase operacional, desdobra-se em contratos de longo prazo com geradoras de energia, empresas de telecomunicações, segurança cibernética e serviços gerenciados, além de demandar mão de obra técnica altamente qualificada. O impacto mais transformador, entretanto, é indireto. Ao expandir a infraestrutura digital de um país, destravam-se gargalos para toda a economia: bancos ganham robustez para acelerar algoritmos de IA, parques industriais ampliam a automação, a saúde avança na telemedicina e no processamento de dados genômicos, universidades aceleram pesquisas complexas e startups ganham musculatura para escalar operações. Soberania digital e a corrida contra o gargalo da IA A expansão dessa malha computacional transcendeu as planilhas econômicas para se tornar questão geopolítica. A soberania digital, ou seja, a capacidade de um país armazenar, processar e salvaguardar dados críticos dentro de suas fronteiras, passou a ditar o equilíbrio global de forças. Na era da IA, armazenar dados não basta; é imperativo ter capacidade computacional para convertê-los em produtividade, inovação e riqueza. Historicamente posicionado apenas como consumidor de tecnologia, o Brasil tem diante de si a oportunidade de se firmar como hospedeiro de infraestrutura crítica global, espelhando a relevância que certas nações conquistaram no passado como polos logísticos ou financeiros internacionais. *Este artigo é uma adaptação de entrevista publicada no The Shift.

artigo.texto: HPQ Silicon Signs Cell Evaluation Agreement with Aptera Motors for HPQ ENDURA+ High-Capacity Battery Cells - Agreement advances HPQ ENDURA+ 21700 cells into application-level evaluation with U.S . solar electric vehicle developer MONTREAL , Oct. 15, 2026 /CNW/ -- HPQ Silicon Inc. ("HPQ" or the "Company") (TSX-V: HPQ) (OTCQB: HPQFF) (FRA: O08), a technology company specializing in advanced materials innovation and the development of next-generation processes, is pleased to announce that HPQ Silicon, through its HPQ ENDURA+ battery initiative, together with its French technology partner Novacium SAS ("Novacium"), has signed a Cell Evaluation and Confidentiality Agreement with Aptera Motors Corp. ("Aptera") (NASDAQ: SEV), a Nasdaq-listed U.S. solar mobility company advancing ultra-efficient transportation. Under the agreement, Aptera will evaluate HPQ ENDURA+ high-capacity 21700 lithium-ion cells based on Novacium's silicon-based anode materials and related cell technology. The evaluation will include laboratory testing. The agreement represents an important step in HPQ's North American battery commercialization strategy, moving HPQ ENDURA+ cells from technology development and internal validation into application-level evaluation. Advancing HPQ ENDURA+ Toward Commercial Applications Aptera is developing a solar electric vehicle designed around ultra-high efficiency, aerodynamics and integrated solar generation. The company has recently reported several milestones, including receiving an EPA Certificate of Conformity for its 2026 Launch Edition and announcing a manufacturing partnership with Launch Design. For HPQ, the evaluation provides an opportunity for ENDURA+ cells to be assessed in an application where energy density and overall system efficiency are important engineering considerations. "This agreement represents exactly the kind of progression we have been working toward with HPQ ENDURA+," said Bernard Tourillon, President and CEO of HPQ Silicon. "We have focused on moving our technology from advanced materials to high-performance cells, and ultimately into application-level evaluation, where its performance can be assessed in an EV application. We are excited to begin this process and see where the results may lead." From Cell Development to External Evaluation Novacium has been advancing silicon-based anode materials and related cell technologies designed to increase the energy-storage capabilities of conventional lithium-ion battery formats. HPQ holds applicable commercial rights relating to Novacium technology in North America and participates in the commercial and industrial follow-up of potential future deployment. "Moving into evaluation with Aptera is an important next step for our cell technology," said Jed Kraiem, Chief Operating Officer of Novacium SAS. "Our development work has been focused on translating the performance of our silicon-based materials into practical, high-capacity cells. Having those cells evaluated provides valuable application-level feedback, and we look forward to supporting Aptera's technical team throughout the process." The evaluation also marks another step in HPQ's strategy of building a North American commercialization pathway for HPQ ENDURA+, advancing from technical development into application-level evaluation as a first step toward validation for EV applications. The initial evaluation does not constitute a commercial supply commitment. If the results support continued discussions, the parties may separately consider subsequent technical, qualification and commercial steps. About HPQ Silicon HPQ Silicon Inc. is a Quebec-based TSX Venture Exchange industrial issuer (TSX-V: HPQ) focused on innovation in advanced materials and critical process development. HPQ holds a strategic 36.8% equity interest in Novacium, its research, development and commercialization partner. Together, HPQ and Novacium are developing next-generation silicon-based anode materials (Gen3 and Gen4) for batteries, pursuing commercialization of ENDURA+ lithium-ion cells, and developing innovative technologies for clean hydrogen production and energy recovery from waste materials. HPQ holds the exclusive rights to commercialize these technologies in North America. HPQ is also pursuing proprietary technologies to become a low-cost, zero-CO₂ producer of fumed silica with technical support from PyroGenesis Inc. Together, these initiatives position HPQ to capture growth opportunities in the energy storage, clean hydrogen, and advanced materials markets essential to achieving global net-zero goals. For more information, please visit HPQ Silicon web site. About Novacium SAS Novacium is a French deep-tech company based in Solaize, specializing in developing silicon-based anode materials for lithium-ion batteries using a proprietary process. The company also designs custom battery cells and packs for demanding applications, particularly in the defence, aerospace and portable energy sectors. artigo.texto: BOTETOURT CO., Va. – A coalition of environmental groups is asking the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to release updated documents, reopen public comment and hold a public hearing on Google’s proposed data center campus in Botetourt County. In an Oct. 9 letter drafted by Appalachian Mountain Advocates and EAST, the Environmental Accountability and Strategy Team, on behalf of 19 other organizations, the coalition raised concerns about potential impacts to streams, wetlands and water quality. The groups argue that additional environmental information submitted after the Corps’ original public comment period ended April 9 should be made available for public review before the agency makes a permit decision. The coalition is requesting at least 30 days for additional public comments and a hearing in Botetourt County. EAST member Sylvia Powell said a public hearing would give residents another opportunity to voice their concerns about the proposed development. “My hope, of course, is that people wake up and they realize that it’s the people who have the power. It is not one business that came here and decided that it wanted to construct a data center,” Powell said. The letter points to a mitigation plan and revised stream-impact figures submitted after the original comment period closed. The Corps’ original public notice listed 6,715 linear feet of stream impacts. In a June message to Google, Virginia Department of Environmental Quality officials flagged inconsistencies in the reported totals. “The impacts to the site have not been verified as figures and summaries provide inconsistent numbers throughout the submittal,” the DEQ message stated. The coalition also questioned whether the project’s stream maps account for streams and areas that were previously protected. An EAST member identified streams and potential groundwater contamination as primary concerns, citing the possibility that pollution could flow into rivers that support protected species. “I would say that at the site scale, the streams are the main concern to me, the streams and the groundwater potentially getting polluted, which would flow down to rivers that have protected species,” Powell said. The letter also references an email from a DEQ representative to an environmental scientist with the Timmons Group concerning records of protected areas associated with a Virginia Water Protection permit. “As we know, there are different plats of the preservation areas from 98-0159 VWP Permit and the document of record should be recorded in the Botetourt County Clerk’s Office,” the email stated. The coalition is asking the Corps to review that document and clarify which streams and preservation areas must be protected. The request does not establish that the project violates environmental protections. Instead, the groups are seeking additional review and public input before the Corps decides whether to issue the requested permit. 10 News reached out to the Army Corps of Engineers for comment on the letter and the status of the hearing request but had not received a response at the time of publication. The coalition asked the Corps to respond to its request by Oct. 30.

artigo.texto: Rapid City surveyed citizens in a town hall to get to the bottom of the ongoing data center debate. The results were clear – most believe data centers are at best necessary evils, at worst drains on natural resources which should be banned from city limits. Though no public comment session was held at Wednesday’s event, over 220 residents had their anonymous surveys shared over the course of the night. The answer was overwhelming, though not universal, in opposition to data centers. The results of this survey, which will be published online to take for the coming weeks, will be used to inform policy on the allowances for data centers in the states second largest city. Jeff Shelton is a Democrat running for the District 32 Senate seat. Though not the crux of his campaign, he wants strict controls on data center development in the state. He said this isn’t surprising. “I think that we got some very clear responses that what we don’t want is any large-scale data centers," Shelton said. "Even on the smaller side on things that aren’t covered by (SB)135, I saw some strong opposition there.” Shelton refers to Senate Bill 135, otherwise known as the data center bill of rights, which passed last session. Data center opposition is bipartisan in nature, and Shelton said the bill needs more fine tuning. “A mistake that was made with Senate Bill 135 that I hope to address if I’m elected in the Senate, is to have more comprehensive definitions to make sure that when we say ‘data center,’ we mean a drain on our resources and something meaningfully harmful to our communities," Shelton said. "I think if we’re not careful we really run the risk of missing the mark.” That is what Rapid City is hoping to hash out specifically with municipal policy. This builds off the platform of SB135, hoping to fill in the gaps Shelton refers to with specifics relating to size and resource consumption of the data center. Jessica Olson is the city planning manager. “They also gave the city the ability to limit, prohibit, or other ways regulate data centers," Olson said. "That is what’s we’re talking about doing today, for ten megawatts or greater.” Below is the handout given to survey takers with details on scope and size of data centers in question and their status under currently drafted policy.

Eni (ENI IM) CEO says the Emissions Trading System should be suspended until there is a solution to the global geopolitical events influencing the market Unidentified explosions reportedly heard within the Sulaymaniyah province of Iraq Fed's Bowman (Voter) says not seeing urgency on further action on rates On the Newsquawk feed at , 20 minutes before this page. Context Calls from European energy and industrial executives to suspend or reform the Emissions Trading System recur whenever allowance prices or geopolitical shocks squeeze margins, and they have historically been advocacy rather than imminent policy: the ETS is EU legislation, and changes require the Commission, Parliament, and Council, a sequence that runs to months or years rather than sessions. The relevant distinction is between rhetoric that moves EUA prices intraday, which commentary from a single CEO of a covered entity occasionally does on light volume, and the structural triggers that have actually repriced the market, namely Commission proposals, auction supply decisions, and stability reserve mechanics. Eni's chief executive has form on energy policy intervention, and integrated oil majors sit on both sides of the carbon market as compliance buyers and as beneficiaries of gas-for-coal switching economics that a higher carbon price supports, which tempers how much weight the street puts on the ask. What tends to matter next is whether the call is echoed by member state governments, particularly those with heavy industrial lobbies, since capitals, not companies, carry votes in the Council. For the equity itself, the read-through runs through European gas and refining margin sentiment rather than any direct ETS exposure repricing on one quote. artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center 14 de outubro de 2026, às 03:42 SAN JOSE, Califórnia, 14 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), anunciou hoje um portfólio expandido de sistemas, racks e trocadores de calor de porta traseira (RDHx) certificados como Open Compute Project Accepted(TM). Com o suporte do DCBBS, o portfólio de soluções pode ser incorporado em implantações completas de ponta a ponta, em escala de rack e cluster. “O boom da IA redefine a forma como os data centers são projetados, construídos e implementados, e a Supermicro lidera essa transformação com o DCBBS”, disse Charles Liang, presidente e CEO da Supermicro. “Ao integrar computação, redes, energia, refrigeração avançada, software e serviços em soluções validadas em escala de rack, ajudamos os clientes a simplificar a complexidade e acelerar o caminho da inovação até a produção. O DCBBS possibilita que os clientes reduzam o TTM e o TTO ao oferecer infraestrutura essencial de IA de forma mais rápida e eficiente.” As soluções OCP da Supermicro já estão disponíveis; clique aqui para saber mais. Ao aproveitar as melhores práticas da comunidade OCP e o design e serviços do DCBBS, os operadores de data centers podem aumentar a densidade de computação e a eficiência energética para cargas de trabalho de IA e HPC com base em uma infraestrutura aberta e validada em escala de rack — desde sistemas e barras de distribuição até o resfriamento em nível de rack e de data centers — para implementar soluções de alta densidade de forma mais eficiente e acelerar o tempo de lançamento no mercado (TTM) e o tempo de operação (TTO). “Os clientes precisam de uma infraestrutura aberta e flexível que possa ser dimensionada de acordo com as demandas em rápida evolução da IA, ao mesmo tempo que se adapte à realidade de seus data centers”, disse Dirk Van Slyke, vice-presidente de Marketing da OCP. “Ao reunir sistemas, racks, energia e refrigeração aceitos pelo OCP em soluções validadas em escala de rack, a Supermicro ajuda os clientes a simplificar a integração, maximizar a capacidade e a eficiência das instalações e acelerar a implantação da infraestrutura de IA de produção.” Os racks ORv3 e ORW substituem as fontes de alimentação e os cabos individuais por servidor por uma barra de distribuição CC centralizada de 48 V, permitindo que os clientes otimizem seus sistemas de CPU e GPU para racks de computação de maior densidade. Essa densidade é ainda mais reforçada pelo sistema de resfriamento líquido DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip da Supermicro, que remove o calor de forma mais eficiente de CPUs, GPUs e outros componentes críticos, enquanto o calor residual pode ser removido do rack por meio de unidades de resfriamento ORv3 RDHx especialmente desenvolvidas, sem a necessidade de adaptações adicionais nos sistemas de ar-condicionado do data center. As unidades RDHx da Supermicro podem ser montadas na parte traseira de racks ORv3 e ORW, removendo o calor residual do ar de exaustão dos servidores antes que ele entre na sala do data center. O portfólio abrange capacidades de refrigeração de 10 kW a 120 kW, oferecendo aos operadores uma maneira prática de aumentar a densidade de racks tanto em novas instalações de IA quanto em data centers existentes. Os modelos alimentados por corrente contínua conectam-se à barra de distribuição do rack para reduzir a quantidade de cabos, enquanto os designs incluem ventiladores redundantes N+1 para garantir o tempo de atividade e um sistema anticondensação inteligente para evitar danos causados pela umidade a outros componentes dentro do rack. Os operadores podem monitorar e gerenciar todo o portfólio de componentes DCBBS, por meio do SuperCloud Composer®, utilizando protocolos padrão do setor. Além disso, os softwares da Supermicro, como o SuperCloud Director, o SuperCloud Automation Assistant e o SuperCloud Developer Console, possibilitam que as empresas gerenciem e operacionalizem todos os aspectos das modernas fábricas de IA, centros de dados corporativos e infraestrutura NeoCloud, por meio de uma solução unificada de controle de software. Como parte do portfólio do DCBBS, a Supermicro também oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções de rede para IA, que variam de switches Ethernet 800G e 1.6T com refrigeração a ar ou líquida, incluindo plataformas Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) de última geração baseadas no silício de comutação Broadcom Tomahawk 6, otimizadas para racks EIA ou ORv3. O sistema operacional de rede SONiC Advanced da Supermicro Enterprise oferece aos clientes a flexibilidade de selecionar a arquitetura de rede que melhor atenda às suas necessidades de desempenho, energia, escalabilidade e implantação, à medida que a IA e os ambientes de data center de grande escala continuam a evoluir. A linha Supermicro DCBBS também incluirá sistemas de switches NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics, os primeiros switches Ethernet coembalados com SerDes de 200 Gb/s. Baseada no ASIC Ethernet NVIDIA Spectrum-6 de 102,4 Tb/s, a tecnologia Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics oferece eficiência energética 5 vezes superior, MTBI 10 vezes maior, tempo de atividade 5 vezes mais longo para aplicações de IA e tempo de implementação 1,3 vezes mais rápido, em comparação com redes baseadas em transceptores plugáveis. A tecnologia Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics já está em produção. Visão geral do portfólio: o amplo portfólio de soluções da Supermicro incorpora muitos padrões baseados na comunidade, o que permite que data centers mais rápidos e otimizados sejam colocados em operação mais rapidamente. Estas soluções incluem: Solução 1 OU FlexTwi

artigo.texto: No último mês, em conversa com o líder de uma indústria intensiva em energia, ele se mostrou surpreso porque vinha conversando com outros líderes de setores relevantes da economia real e encontrava, na maioria deles, pouco conhecimento e nenhuma ação sobre a precificação de carbono em andamento no Brasil. O assunto já tem lei, tem cronograma e terá consequência direta no caixa de quem estiver no rol de regulados. Mesmo assim, ainda está longe da pauta de nossas lideranças. Pouco depois, a cena foi diferente, mas dizia o mesmo. Em uma conversa sobre carbono e questões de competitividade, uma liderança de inovação de um grupo multinacional pontuou: “o Brasil tem que fazer isso direito”, ao que eu respondi: “Quem é o Brasil?” Pergunto a você que lê esta coluna e atua em um setor da economia real: quem é o Brasil que deve agir proativamente para que nosso framework regulatório de precificação de carbono seja redigido com adequação técnica, visão prática para assegurar que seja exequível, cronograma compatível e incentivos econômico-financeiros apropriados? Quem é o Brasil que deve agir proativamente para materializar nossa vantagem comparativa (em termos de disponibilidade de capital natural e de matriz elétrica) em competitiva para prosperarmos econômica e socialmente neste novo cenário de mundo em 2026? Na minha opinião, o “Brasil” somos nós, a economia real que emprega, emite gases de efeito estufa, depende de água, de solo, de clima estável, gera PIB. Nossos reguladores escrevem as normas, mas a eficácia delas será diretamente proporcional a quanto a economia real conseguirá (ou quererá) colocar em prática. Conteúdo técnico, ritmo, viabilidade prática e incentivos devem ser resultado de trabalho colaborativo de alta qualidade entre reguladores e regulados. Evolução reativa: a falta do foresight estratégico Amy Webb, futurista e CEO do Future Today Strategy Group, publicou uma reflexão que descreve com precisão o que vejo na agenda da liderança brasileira quando os temas são clima e natureza. Os CEOs descrevem a própria empresa como “adaptativa”, evoluindo de forma reativa: a empresa só muda depois que a pressão chega e a seleção natural faz o resto. Não há foresight estratégico. O argumento central dela me interessa por uma razão prática. Quem enxerga uma restrição se formando cedo, nos sinais fracos, nos rascunhos regulatórios, nos movimentos de concorrentes e de financiadores, ganha algo raro: a possibilidade de contribuir para essa inovação e de escolher entre várias saídas. Quem espera a pressão chegar, no caso, a regulamentação de carbono ser publicada, tem que cumprir (ou se aventurar no judiciário brasileiro). Interessante também é a lista de desculpas que ela ouve, como “esperar para ver qual padrão vence, achar que o conselho jamais aprovaria, ter prontidão para implementar ou ter feito um piloto”. Quando o tema é clima e natureza, com frequência ouço variações dessas frases em conversas com lideranças. Sinais evidentes A precificação de carbono está quase passando do ponto de precisar de foresight estratégico para se materializar como pressão instalada. O mundo já precificou ou está precificando carbono. Mecanismo de ajuste de carbono na fronteira da União Europeia, o CBAM, começou a produzir plenos efeitos desde janeiro deste ano. Já a lei antidesmatamento está prevista para entrar em vigor a partir de 1º de janeiro de 2027. Fundos de pensão, a exemplo do NBIM e do Nest, demandam a incorporação da avaliação de riscos e oportunidades de clima e natureza nas decisões de alocação de capital. No Brasil, nossos bancos estão sujeitos a regulação de clima e natureza desde 2021, com implementação gradual e atualizações, não apenas para refinar dados e quantificá-los, mas também para incorporar diretrizes de reporte financeiro de sustentabilidade e clima padronizadas globalmente. As seguradoras estão no mesmo caminho, com regulação para gerenciamento de riscos e oportunidades de clima e natureza desde 2022 e recente consulta para atualização visando harmonização do disclosure com referidos padrões globais. Especificamente para a regulamentação do mercado de carbono aplicável às indústrias, temos cronograma previsto em lei, que demanda conclusão em dezembro de 2026, e cronograma do Executivo que vem sendo cumprido. Por que sair da evolução reativa Na lógica da Amy Webb, a empresa que se diz adaptativa tem uma única tentativa diante do ambiente e o ambiente decide o resultado. O foresight estratégico permite rodar essa extinção como simulação, antes de vivê-la no resultado da companhia. Para a economia real brasileira, a janela dessa simulação é agora, porque as regras de precificação de carbono ainda estão sendo escritas. Na minha perspectiva, a precificação de carbono altera a estrutura de custos, o acesso a capital, a relação com a cadeia de valor (clientes e fornecedores) e a competitividade na exportação. Quem avalia antecipadamente esses efeitos decide estratégia, investimento, contrato e portfólio com várias opções à mesa. Quem cruza os braços e aguarda a regulamentação, escolhe entre compliance ou litígio. O ciclo de investimento (capex) de uma indústria intensiva em energia é longo, uma decisão de investimento tomada hoje carrega o custo de carbono de décadas. Isso importa a dois públicos: a economia real que compõe o setor regulado e todos aqueles que compõem a cadeia de valor dos regulados. O custo do carbono, uma vez precificado no regulado, impactará a cadeia nos contratos, preços e critérios de compra e venda. A mesma lógica vale para a natureza: a lei antidesmatamento da Europa, citada acima, tende a chegar à cadeia dos exportadores brasileiros. Sair da inércia exige líderes capazes de enxergar o valor do foresight como ferramenta de gestão, com rotina, métrica e responsabilidade. Aplicando essa realidade para nossa regulamentação de carbono em andamento, isso significa entender: inventário de emissões, intensidade por produto e qualidade do dado; cenários de preço, aborda

artigo.texto: Benson, James battle over data centers, economy in Michigan gubernatorial debate Michigan gubernatorial candidates Jocelyn Benson and John James laid out competing plans for the state's future during a debate Thursday night, clashing over affordability, taxes, data centers, education and health care. Benson, who currently serves as the Secretary of State, and James, a U.S. congressman, are competing to succeed term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Both candidates said they want to make Michigan more affordable, but they offered different approaches to how that will unfold. James focused on lowering energy costs and suspending Michigan's state gas tax, adding that he supports suspending it immediately. He also called for cutting the state income tax and argued that Michigan needs a more accountable government. Benson emphasized lowering health care costs, including prescription drug prices. She also called for protections against what she described as profit-driven increases in utility rates. She also added that she's open to reducing the state's gas tax. Benson criticized James over his position on the conflict abroad, while James said Iran should not have nuclear weapons and called for the war to end. The candidates also clashed over how Michigan should handle new data center development, including concerns about electricity costs, water use, pollution, and local control. Benson said her family has not profited from data centers and pointed to her publicly disclosed personal finances on the Michigan Secretary of State's website. Her remarks came after James challenged her position on a development in Saline Township. Benson supports a moratorium on new data center development until safeguards are in place to protect water resources, limit increases in electricity costs and give local communities a voice. She also accused James of purchasing stock in companies involved in data center development. James also called for a moratorium, saying the state needs a plan to protect communities before approving new projects. His five-point proposal includes giving local communities more control, preventing electricity bills from increasing, protecting water, preventing pollution and prioritizing previously developed brownfield sites over productive farmland. Both say they want to ease the financial pressures facing Michigan families, but their proposals differ on taxes, health care, energy costs and the state's approach to data center development. Thursday's debate marks 19 days until election day, Nov. 3.

artigo.texto: The California Energy Commission will revise and recirculate its environmental review of a proposed 300-megawatt battery energy storage project near Vacaville after determining that significant new information requires another round of public review. The announcement is a development in the state’s review of the proposed Corby Battery Energy Storage System, which drew more than five hours of public comment at a Sept. 1 hearing in Vacaville. Local officials and residents urged the commission to reject the project, citing concerns about fire safety, groundwater contamination, agricultural land and the facility’s proximity to future development. In an Oct. 7 update to the Solano County Board of Supervisors, Deputy County Counsel Holly E. Tokar said the commission determined that the project’s Staff Assessment/Draft Environmental Impact Report requires “significant new information” and will be recirculated at a future date for another 60-day public comment period. Tokar said the county’s comments may have contributed to the commission’s determination and told the Board the continued review is good news. “In my view, this is the best-case scenario at this stage in the process,” she wrote. “We will now wait to see what changes the CEC makes to its DEIR, recommendation, and proposed conditions of approval, and plan to submit another set of comments once the next iteration of the Draft EIR is released.” Officials will also monitor proposed regulatory changes to the state’s permitting process for energy storage projects, Tokar said. The commission has scheduled a remote workshop for Nov. 2 to discuss proposed changes to the process established under Assembly Bill 205. Written comments on the proposed regulatory changes are due Nov. 10. The next version of the Corby project’s environmental review, along with any revised recommendations and proposed approval conditions, will help determine how the state proceeds with the application. The commission has not announced a new timeline for its decision on the project. The proposed project would occupy approximately 40 acres of unincorporated land near Kilkenny and Byrnes roads, about 250 feet southeast of Vacaville’s jurisdictional boundary and roughly five miles northeast of downtown. The facility would be capable of storing up to 1,200 megawatt-hours of electricity. Plans include battery units, a project substation, inverters, fencing, a sound barrier, roads, drainage facilities, and other infrastructure. At the Sept. 1 hearing, Vacaville Mayor John Carli and other local officials urged the commission to reject the project at the proposed location, citing agricultural land preservation and the city’s plans for future residential and commercial growth. Local officials emphasized that they support battery energy storage as a technology but oppose placing a large-scale facility on the Corby site. Solano County Supervisor Mitch Mashburn pointed to the county’s battery energy storage ordinance and Measure T, the voter-approved orderly growth regulation, arguing that state permitting authority does not erase the importance of local land-use policies. Residents also raised concerns about lithium-ion battery fires, potential groundwater contamination, noise, risks to nearby homes and the facility’s proximity to future development. Some questioned the environmental report’s analysis of potential impacts on groundwater resources used by nearby communities and agricultural operations.

artigo.texto: To keep up with artificial intelligence, Illinois needs batteries big enough to keep its air conditioners running on hot summer nights and to replenish its electrical grid during winter storms lasting for days. The state took a step in this direction Monday when Richardson Electronics said it would expand production of commercial-scale storage batteries at its factory in La Fox, a suburb west of Chicago. Richardson, a diversified manufacturer of power products, expects to sell batteries worldwide. But company officials say they’ll deploy many of their batteries in Illinois because of the state’s hefty tax incentives for renewable power and for batteries that make solar and wind less intermittent. When layered on top of each other, Illinois and federal tax incentives add up to almost the entire cost of one of Richardson’s storage batteries, said Scott DuBois, director of the company’s storage operations. The battery, which the company plans to build at its La Fox site next summer, would be able to store 5 megawatts of power and will cost about $3 million. It will be the largest battery ever connected to the grid by an Illinois company, Richardson officials said. Without more batteries, Illinois will be even more reliant on dirty, expensive electricity imports from other states and more likely to delay the natural gas power plant closures it’s planned for years to clean the air. “We are depending on out-of-state resources to essentially keep the lights on,” said Matthew Tomc, vice president of regulatory policy and energy supply for Ameren, which serves customers in downstate Illinois. “There are many states building new generation, but it’s not built yet. So there are reliability issues first and foremost,” Tomc said. “And it raises the risk that you have price spikes seasonally, namely in the summer, right when you’re trying to meet those capacity requirements.” Tomc’s not alone in sounding the alarm. PJM Interconnection, the regional grid that includes northern Illinois, 12 other states and the District of Columbia, could face 13 days of service interruptions a year by 2030 in a worst-case scenario, Pennsylvania regulators said last month. PJM’s longstanding goal has been to have just one day of service interruptions every 10 years. Prices already are climbing. Commonwealth Edison customers in northern Illinois pay an average residential bill of $141 per month, according to Heatmap News and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. That’s up just 4% since 2021, partly because PJM imposed price caps last year. Ameren customers downstate pay an average of $224, up 51% in five years. The downstate area is part of the Midwest Independent System Operator grid or MISO, which also serves 14 other states from Mississippi to North Dakota as well as Manitoba. To blunt further increases, Richardson and its supplier Gotion, a Chinese-owned company with a $2 billion factory in Manteno, Illinois, start with 4,500 battery cells, each about the size of a college textbook. For their biggest batteries, they will then stack, weld and seal the battery cells, cooling equipment and electronic controls inside a metal box resembling a 20-foot shipping container. DuBois wouldn’t give a precise estimate for how big Richardson’s battery business will get. But he said he expects exponential growth. Gil Quinones, ComEd’s chief executive, is thinking big, too. “If the majority of our residential, commercial and industrial customers put in batteries, that’s going to be a big win for the state,” Quinones said. “It could increase the capacity utilization for the grid we’ve already paid for, and have a chance to really put downward pressure on prices for everybody,” Quinones said. Because Richardson sees itself as an engineering specialist rather than a high-volume manufacturer, it will focus on customized storage systems for so-called microgrids. These are clusters of solar and wind operators that can either supply electricity directly to nearby users or buy and sell power as a group into the regional grid. One of the company’s first orders, for example, came from a microgrid serving seven remote communities in Alaska. Illinois needs more batteries to unlock the full potential of its growing wind and solar capabilities, according to consultants to the Illinois Power Agency and other state regulators in a report last month. Illinois will need 50 gigawatts of installed solar and wind capacity by 2050 to get close to its goal of using only non-carbon sources to generate electricity by then, the agencies said. But regional grid operators still regard wind and solar as too intermittent. As a result, the state will be able to count only about 6 gigawatts of its renewable output as the baseload power electricity grids need to operate around the clock. With additional batteries, Illinois could make its solar panels more productive and reliable by, for example, storing the power they generate during the day and then pumping it into the grid or nearby homes and businesses after the sun goes down. In addition to more batteries, the Ameren service area downstate will need 9 gigawatts of out-of-state imports by 2045, according to the Sept. 24 consultant report to the IPA. That’s more than half the Ameren area’s total requirement of 16 gigawatts of round-the-clock power in 2045. The ComEd service area will need 4 gigawatts of out-of-state imports, or about 13% of its baseload requirement. The imports will include power produced by new natural gas plants that Illinois ratepayers will help build in other states. Illinois can’t build these plants because of the state’s clean air rules. artigo.texto: Agility Robotics Selects Nyobolt as its Ultra-Fast Charging Battery Technology Partner for Digit 5 Nyobolt's Battery Technology Enables Digit 5 to Work More Than 20 Hours in a 24-hour Day SALEM, Ore. and CAMBRIDGE, United Kingdom, Oct. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Agility Robotics, a leading humanoid robotics and physical AI company, today announced that Nyobolt, a pioneer of high-power, ultra-fast charging solutions, is the technology provider to Agility. The technology powers one of Digit® 5's most significant upgrades: a fast recharge battery system that enables Digit to work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day. Agility recently unveiled Digit 5 as its first humanoid robot designed for cooperatively safe work at scale, allowing it to work in close proximity to people. As part of its upgrades, Digit 5 will feature a new battery system that delivers 90-minutes of runtime and charges in just 9 minutes, achieving a 10:1 run-to-charge ratio, up from Digit 4's 2:1 ratio. This rapid charge capability is designed to keep Digit working, enabling more than two shifts in a single day and helping customers get more from each robot. "For our customers, Digit's uptime is the business case," said Daniel Diez, Chief Business Officer of Agility Robotics. "Digit 5 will deliver more than 20 hours of productive work in a 24-hour day, more than two full shifts. That's the kind of gain that materially improves the value customers get from Digit and the economics of deploying a humanoid robot fleet. Nyobolt's ultra-fast charging technology gets us there, and it's one of the pieces that makes Digit 5 ready for full-scale operation." Nyobolt's unique high-power battery technology is built for demanding industrial conditions, combining fast charging, exceptional cycle life, and reduced system weight. By removing the power bottleneck that has historically constrained autonomous robot fleet economics, the system addresses a key constraint on robot utilization: downtime. The result is a compelling potential advantage for Digit 5 customers, who can target longer operating windows, more productive shifts and more demanding task sequences. Combined with Agility's experience deploying humanoid robots in real commercial environments, this battery performance is designed to strengthen Digit's value proposition for warehouse, distribution and manufacturing operations. "Nyobolt's technology was chosen because Digit 5 will need more power from a smaller, lighter pack, in environments where reliability isn't optional," said Sai Shivareddy, Co-founder and CEO at Nyobolt. "Agility set an exceptionally high bar for what a battery has to withstand in live warehouse and manufacturing environments, and this partnership shows what's possible when ultra-fast charging is engineered for the toughest conditions in physical AI." Early access to Digit 5 equipped with Nyobolt's battery technology is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with increasing availability over the following six to nine months for manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators. Agility is preparing to become a public company through its previously announced business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI (Nasdaq: CCXI) ("Churchill XI"). The business combination is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, after which the combined company will operate as Agility Robotics and is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "AGLT." artigo.texto: From pressures facing Iowa farmers to the costs of major industrial projects, Iowa’s U.S. Senate candidates outlined their priorities and challenged each other’s records in their second and last debate Tuesday night. Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, faced off in their second debate for U.S. Senate hosted by WHO-13 in Des Moines. The candidates continued to highlight hot button issues, discussing the importance of agriculture and economic developments throughout the state. The debate also covered immigration enforcement, rural healthcare, and Social Security with the candidates offering differing approaches to border security, access to care, and retirement benefits. Questions about transgender athletes in women’s sports and congressional stock ownership prompted further exchanges, alongside criticism of each other’s voting records and personal finances. On agriculture and economic development, the candidates debated how to expand markets for Iowa farmers and attract investment while protecting taxpayers from the costs and risks of major projects. Agriculture continues to be a top priority The candidates offered differing views on tariffs and farmland ownership, with both emphasizing the need to support Iowa farmers. Turek criticized the administration’s tariffs and said they have hurt farmers by limiting markets and increasing costs. He supports targeted tariffs to protect American manufacturing but opposed those he said burden agriculture and small businesses. “Our farmers rely on open markets and free trade more than any other group,” he said. He also called for year-round E-15 sales, mandatory out-of-origin labeling, and a federal right-to-repair law allowing farmers to repair their equipment. He urged Congress to pass a farm bill before adjourning. Hinson defended tariffs as a tool to counter unfair trade practices while acknowledging farmers’ uncertainty. She said she has raised their concerns directly with President Donald Trump and pointed to agricultural exports and trade negotiations as signs of progress. “Nobody loves tariffs, but what I like even less is an unlevel playing field for Americans and for our farmers,” she said. Hinson emphasized preventing foreign adversaries from purchasing agricultural land, particularly near sensitive military sites. Turek agreed restrictions on foreign ownership were important but said large corporations posed the greater concern, pointing to pressures facing small family farms. Data centers, industrial projects raise economic questions Both candidates opposed a federal moratorium on new data centers but differed on how to oversee the projects and who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support them. Turek demanded no further tax breaks for multinational tech firms and suggested requiring closed-loop water circuits that reuse water to reduce data centers’ consumption of local water supplies. “We should be doing what we can to protect Iowa and to protect the tax rates here,” he said. He opposed using taxpayer funds for the reopening of the Duane Arnold nuclear plant — a facility near Palo, northwest of Cedar Rapids, that shut down in 2020 — if most energy is diverted to Google. Hinson, on the other hand, maintained that data center regulation should occur at the local level rather than through a federal moratorium and supports reopening Duane Arnold to help meet rising electricity demand. “It is really critical that we have enough energy production in this country to handle the necessary needs of whether it’s a data center or another big energy consumer,” she said. “We want to reinvigorate American manufacturing in this country.” Questions about taxpayer protections extended to the proposed steel plant in southeast Iowa, with both candidates saying Iowans should not bear infrastructure costs if the project falls through. Turek said he supported the $15 billion Masabi Metallics steel plant’s job potential but questions the risks associated with a $770 million federal loan given the company’s history of bankruptcy. He argued companies should cover their own infrastructure. “There’s no upfront state money,” he said. “The incentives are only there if they provide the actual jobs and metrics achieved.” Hinson said she views the plant as critical for national security and the domestic steel supply chain, though she agrees taxpayers should not be held liable if the project fails or is scaled back. “We need definite accountability measures built in,” Hinson said. “And I think what’s important about the policies we’ve put into place is that they are going to supercharge potential future investments just like this one.”

artigo.texto: In a situation with parallels to the community debate in Beacon Falls, residents of Cromwell are balking at an apparent plan for a large-scale data center in their town. Homeowners lined up at a recent zoning board hearing to promote the idea of a one-year moratorium against data centers in Cromwell, and others have organized an online petition drive opposing the possibility of a massive center next to the town’s middle school. Even though no formal zoning application has been put forward, residents are concerned that a Long Island-based energy services entrepreneur is already advertising a data center it would build off Geer Street in Cromwell. “The proposal would put 1.2 million square feet of data center space (roughly the size of the Westfarms Mall) in the middle of a small suburban neighborhood adjoining schools and parks,” said Jake Dressler, whose law firm has an office a few miles from the site. “The idea of having a data center isn’t shocking, but the sheer size and location of this proposal — right next to kids, schools and parks — has residents dumbfounded,” Dressler told The Courant. A newly formed group calling itself Stop Cromwell CT Data Center posted an even more emphatic message on Reddit, drawing 108 replies. Concern about data centers has grown across the state in recent months. “This is a quiet safe neighborhood full of homes and families,” the Cromwell group wrote. “The construction alone will completely upend the only quiet, middle class part of town for years to come.” “The Cromwell zoning commission and town have quietly voted to fast track an immense data center on Geer Street directly next to a brand new middle school and park,” the group wrote. “Cromwell residents found out about the plan and overwhelmingly spoke at a recent town meeting against it, but the town has voted to move forward in spite of this.” But Mayor James Demetriades noted that nobody has formally proposed a data center at the roughly 160-acre site along Geer Street. “There is currently no application submitted to the town on the property for a data center,” Demetriades said Tuesday. “Once an application is submitted it would go through the public hearing process” with the zoning and wetlands boards. The website for Global Common acknowledges that the company hasn’t sought zoning approval yet, but makes clear that it intends to in early 2027 — and that it will need a site plan approval but no zoning permit. “Global Common LLC is developing a data center campus powered by fuel cells supplied by natural gas from three Enbridge interstate pipelines that run in a single ROW directly across the project site,” the company said. “The site is a 159-acre assemblage zoned for data centers ‘by right,’ midway between NY and Boston. “Phase 1 will provide about 40 megawatts of IT power within 18–21 months of equipment deposit. Grid power is expected to be available for office needs and auxiliary loads if required. Full build-out of up to 300-plus megawatts IT can be delivered within 26–32 months from equipment deposits or may be phased in over several years.” The situation is similar to Beacon Falls, where an large landowner has been advertising a 100-megawatt data center to be built soon — but still has sought no state or local permits. Global Common’s site says of the Cromwell plan: “The project has not yet filed for site plan approval. The project would eliminate an existing sand-and-gravel trucking operation that currently uses a residential portion of Geer Street and preserve open space along Geer Street. The project will only occupy approximately a third of the total site area after full build out, thus minimizing aesthetic impacts.” Neighbors feel very differently. “It is distressing to imagine how the introduction of a data center could irrevocably change our environment, health, and property values,” according to sponsors of the change.org petition opposing the center. It is becoming increasingly clear from other communities that data centers pose threats to the health and wellbeing of the surrounding residents.” In a 5-2 vote, the Republican-dominated planning and zoning commission last month rejected the proposed moratorium. Opponents said they are discussing whether to try again.

artigo.texto: LOGAN, Utah — Before a crowd here at Utah State University on Tuesday night, Republican Congressman Blake Moore and Democratic challenger Peter Crosby debated a number of big issues facing the newly-formed Second Congressional District. It was a collegial, policy-focused debate where they presented their views for northern Utah. Both were quizzed on data centers, a particularly hot topic in the district, where celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary's plans for a massive data center have sparked significant public protest. Both candidates agreed local control is best. "Data centers are a part of our immediate future, right? There's no question. We're all using cellphones. We're all, you know, doing some type of AI utilization and whatnot, but the issue is, we cannot have this kind of situation take over the way that it did and that people have to be brought along," Moore said, pointing to what was being done on a congressional level. "There's good, strong legislation that should have passed in the Senate, but it didn't, to make sure electricity costs don't go up for residents and the Department of Defense is doing a unique thing where they're going to start to use more of their resources and their land in a more productive way, which is a good change that's happening." Crosby said he had been involved in some of the pushback on data centers. "I think as we talk about the future of data centers in Utah specifically, we have to acknowledge that local control is oftentimes being ignored because external pressure coming from the top down is forcing a decision against the will of local residents," he said. "That's inappropriate. I am all for a future where local communities decide whether or not that kind of infrastructure is appropriate for them, and what we have seen in Box Elder is a direct counter to that reality." The two expressed a desire to save the Great Salt Lake, but offered differing viewpoints on water policy. "I don't want the federal government making water policy for the state of Utah," declared Crosby. "I think that's a bad road to head down. The state of Utah has to decide: Are we a state that grows to 10 million people? Are we a state that decides to fully invest in Silicon Slopes? Are we a state that decides to maintain local resiliency in agriculture? We can't have all three." But Moore said he has already been passing legislation to help the lake, though he acknowledged President Trump's pledge of a billion dollars for the lake is unlikely to get through Congress. "We were able to do bite-size projects to help funding the support from different elements of the of the lake that the state is actually leading a lot of the effort and then of course you're seeing the White House now get involved, so it's nice to be able to see a throughput," he said. Crosby was critical of Moore's votes on President Trump's Big, Beautiful Bill. Moore defended his work to mitigate tariffs, even noting that he had removed some of the harsher impacts on a major northern Utah employer. "There is a lot of pain with this and every time that Procter and Gamble has reached out to our office, we've gone and actually successfully been able to mitigate their issues," Moore said. "If I may say, Procter and Gamble, that's great, but none of the small business owners seem to receive the same attention," Crosby countered in a rebuttal. But the candidates both pledged ongoing support for Hill Air Force Base and bolstering northern Utah's aerospace industry. They also supported agriculture, a major industry in the area.
