artigo.texto: Energia hidroelétrica. A “arma-secreta” portuguesa para armazenamento Como podemos tirar maior proveito dos recursos naturais em Portugal para aumentar a capacidade de armazenamento da nossa rede elétrica? A transição energética depende do armazenamento e esta realidade tornou-se mais evidente nos últimos anos. Hoje, as redes modernas e de maior eletrificação, como as redes portuguesa e ibérica, enfrentam desafios relacionados com a interoperabilidade, a flexibilidade, maiores consumos energéticos e maior complexidade dos sistemas, que exigem soluções inovadoras. Estas soluções podem também residir no armazenamento. O conceito de armazenamento de energia abrange diferentes tecnologias, algumas mais maduras e outras mais inovadoras, sistemas híbridos e controlos digitais que nos permitem deslocar a procura e a oferta de energia e controlá-las de acordo com as necessidades. Um dos tipos de armazenamento, complexo em termos de maturidade, aplicação histórica e efeitos na rede, é a energia hidroelétrica e a bombagem. “Energia hidroelétrica” não é a primeira palavra que se associaria ao armazenamento. Quanto à produção, a energia hidroelétrica é a tecnologia de produção de energia renovável mais difundida e madura, fornecendo um sexto da eletricidade global atual, mais do que todas as outras fontes renováveis combinadas, de acordo com a IEA. Esta disponibilidade e maturidade resultaram também no desenvolvimento do seu verdadeiro potencial para o armazenamento de energia: a bombagem hídrica, ou Pumped-Storage Hydropower. Esta tecnologia de bombagem hídrica representou, em 2020, 95% de toda a capacidade de armazenamento de energia instalada a nível global (International Hydropower Association, 2023). A União Europeia reconheceu a importância das tecnologias de armazenamento por bombagem para a mitigação das alterações climáticas e para o futuro dos sistemas energéticos, no relatório “Hydropower and pumped storage hydropower in the EU” (Joint Research Centre, 2025). Em Portugal, é evidente a predominância da energia hidroelétrica como fonte de energia, com uma contribuição no mix energético de 30%. A Estratégia Nacional de Armazenamento de Energia, recentemente lançada, visa atingir 10,5 GW total de armazenamento de energia em 2040, incluindo baterias e bombagem. Portugal dispõe atualmente de uma capacidade de de 3,6 gigawatts (GW) apenas em sistemas hidroelétricos de armazenamento por bombagem, que o governo pretende quase duplicar para 5,6 GW em 2040, confirmando o protagonismo que deve ser atribuído a esta tecnologia em termos de potencial de armazenamento e mecanismos de proteção da rede. Atualmente, Portugal já dispõe de várias centrais hidroelétricas com bombagem que contribuem para a rede nacional. As centrais de Alqueva, Alto Lindoso, Frades II e, mais recentemente, o complexo de Gouvães, no Tâmega, não só trouxeram mais energia limpa para a rede, como também estão a contribuir significativamente para o seu equilíbrio e para o aumento da utilização de outras energias renováveis. Só o complexo hidroelétrico do Tâmega contribuiu para aumentar a capacidade de armazenamento da rede portuguesa em mais de 40 milhões de kWh, o equivalente ao consumo de energia de 11 milhões de pessoas durante 24 horas (Iberdrola, 2026). A barragem de Alqueva acrescenta mais 10 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento ao sistema. Esta barragem participou no projeto de inovação XFLEX Hydro, financiado pela UE, no âmbito do qual se testaram soluções operacionais inovadoras. Este projeto permitiu uma melhor compreensão das capacidades das centrais hidroelétricas nacionais para proporcionar flexibilidade energética à rede portuguesa, comprovando que são capazes de prestar serviços como inércia sintética e aumentando as suas capacidades para fornecer outros serviços de frequência, serviços de Black Start e Controlo de Tensão. Todos estes serviços são cruciais em redes dominadas por energias renováveis, uma vez que permitem equilibrar a rede de forma a prevenir eventos como o Apagão na Península Ibérica de 2025. A utilização de sistemas de armazenamento por bombagem permite assim proteger a integridade da rede. A utilização das tecnologias de armazenamento com hidroelétricas em benefício da rede já não está limitada pelos desenvolvimentos tecnológicos, dependendo sim de mudanças políticas e regulamentares. É agora necessário analisar a regulamentação das redes em toda a Europa e em Portugal e eliminar as barreiras regulamentares existentes. As mesmas barreiras regulatórias aplicam-se à falta de remuneração de serviços de sistema específicos ou a criação de mercados que garantam a prestação de serviços auxiliares a custos mais baixos, o que incentivaria o investimento em novos sistemas de armazenamento flexíveis. Ao mesmo tempo, existe um grande número de centrais hidrelétricas envelhecidas que não estão a atingir o seu pleno potencial. A participação em projetos de inovação e o aumento dos recursos do meio académico para implementar novas tecnologias podem trazer benefícios para a modernização do portfólio energético. Através de estratégias nacionais como a portuguesa, é possível observar como a energia hidroelétrica e, em particular, as soluções de armazenamento por bombagem, têm tido e continuarão a ter um papel fundamental na eletrificação, flexibilização e modernização das redes. Tendo em conta os recursos naturais a que o país tem acesso, faz todo o sentido recorrer a eles e utilizá-los de forma respeitosa, de modo a permitir o objetivo global de mitigar as alterações climáticas e proteger esses próprios recursos naturais. Por meio deste canal pretendemos trazer conteúdos ligados ao ESG e Energia de forma descomplicada para a sociedade, na voz de mulheres, de gerações diferentes, que detêm expertise técnica na área. artigo.texto: Projeto da Mombak prevê restaurar 7,2 mil hectares e gerar créditos de carbono; operação anterior eleva a R$ 360 milhões o financiamento do banco à empresa restauração de áreas degradadas na Amazônia é uma necessidade ambiental, mas, quando uma operação privada destinada a recuperar florestas também abre caminho para a geração e comercialização de créditos de carbono, o dinheiro público exige uma conta completa: quanto custa, quais resultados entrega e quem fica com os ganhos econômicos. O Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) aprovou financiamento de R$ 200 milhões para a Mombak, empresa especializada em projetos de remoção de carbono. O empreendimento prevê restaurar 7,2 mil hectares, principalmente no Pará, com investimento total estimado em R$ 457 milhões e prazo de financiamento de 25 anos. Segundo o banco, o projeto poderá remover mais de 4,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente ao longo de 50 anos, com potencial de gerar até 4,7 milhões de créditos de remoção de carbono. Esses ativos poderão ser negociados no mercado voluntário e, futuramente, em mercados regulados. A operação foi anunciada pelo BNDES em 21 de setembro. O financiamento representa aproximadamente 44% do investimento previsto. Em uma conta direta, equivale a cerca de R$ 27,8 mil por hectare em recursos financiados pelo banco. Considerado o investimento total, o custo projetado chega a R$ 63,5 mil por hectare. Os números, isoladamente, não demonstram desperdício nem irregularidade. A restauração florestal envolve preparo do solo, aquisição de sementes e mudas, plantio, manejo, manutenção e monitoramento. O que eles justificam é uma pergunta objetiva sobre as condições financeiras e os resultados esperados de uma operação dessa dimensão. O projeto não se limita à recomposição da vegetação nativa. A captura de carbono prevista poderá dar origem a créditos comercializáveis, criando uma fonte potencial de receita para o empreendimento. É um modelo econômico que pode contribuir para a recuperação de áreas degradadas e para o enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Mas a combinação de financiamento público de longo prazo com receitas futuras provenientes de ativos ambientais também exige transparência sobre a distribuição dos riscos e dos benefícios. Quais são os juros e as demais condições contratuais do financiamento? Que garantias foram exigidas? Quem será titular dos créditos gerados e como se dará sua comercialização? Se a captura de carbono ficar abaixo das projeções ou os preços dos créditos caírem, quem absorverá os prejuízos? São questões que não pressupõem qualquer irregularidade. Constituem, porém, parte necessária da avaliação de um empreendimento apoiado por uma política pública. O financiamento de R$ 200 milhões não é o primeiro concedido pelo BNDES à Mombak. Em agosto de 2024, o banco anunciou uma operação de R$ 160 milhões para projetos de restauração de 13 mil hectares na Amazônia. Naquela primeira operação, os recursos foram divididos entre R$ 80 milhões do Fundo Clima e R$ 80 milhões da linha BNDES Finem. Portanto, não se deve confundir o valor total do financiamento com a parcela proveniente especificamente do Fundo Clima. Com a nova operação, os financiamentos aprovados para a empresa somam R$ 360 milhões, enquanto os dois projetos preveem recuperar aproximadamente 20,2 mil hectares. Segundo o BNDES, até junho de 2026, 9,4 mil hectares do primeiro empreendimento já haviam sido implantados. O dado permite avançar na apuração. Quais resultados ambientais já podem ser medidos? Quanto foi efetivamente desembolsado e qual é o cronograma dos recursos restantes? Que indicadores de sobrevivência das árvores, recuperação da biodiversidade e remoção de carbono estão sendo utilizados para avaliar o projeto anterior? E de que maneira esses resultados foram considerados na aprovação do novo financiamento? A previsão divulgada pelo banco é de até 440 empregos diretos e 65 indiretos durante a implantação do novo projeto. Depois dessa fase, a estimativa é manter aproximadamente 50 postos de trabalho, entre diretos e indiretos. A diferença entre o emprego temporário e o permanente não invalida o empreendimento. Projetos de restauração podem produzir benefícios ambientais duradouros sem depender de uma grande estrutura permanente de pessoal. Ainda assim, é pertinente conhecer a parcela dos investimentos que permanecerá na economia paraense, a participação de fornecedores locais e as oportunidades abertas aos moradores das áreas abrangidas. A recuperação da floresta pode gerar benefícios muito além da captura de carbono, mas esses resultados precisam ser identificados e acompanhados. Também importa saber onde estão as áreas contempladas, quais são as condições dos contratos com os proprietários e como serão monitorados os resultados ambientais ao longo das décadas previstas para a operação. A Amazônia precisa de floresta em pé. Precisa igualmente de ciência, saneamento, infraestrutura, regularização fundiária, fiscalização, bioeconomia e geração de renda para quem vive no território. O desafio é impedir que a valorização econômica do carbono se descole dos interesses ambientais e sociais da região que o produz. Restaurar florestas com financiamento público pode ser uma política acertada. Mas o resultado não deve ser medido apenas pelo número de hectares recuperados ou de toneladas de CO₂ que se espera retirar da atmosfera. É preciso saber quanto custará a recuperação, quais benefícios serão comprovados, como os riscos serão distribuídos e quem ficará com a receita gerada pelos créditos de carbono. •Os rumores chegaram ao fim no sábado, 10. A prefeita de Marituba, Patrícia Alencar (foto), anunciou nas redes sociais que está grávida de uma menina, fruto do relacionamento com o prefeito de Mãe do Rio, Bruno Rabelo. Agora é esperar a chegada da pequena - e desejar saúde à futura mamãe e à bebê. •Deputados que andavam de olho na área da saúde do Estado podem tirar o cavalinho da chuva.

artigo.texto: "BUMDs need to start identifying carbon units or activities that can be properly maintained and developed as a basis to drive regional revenue," Jumhur told reporters in Jakarta on Tuesday. He made the statement after delivering his opening remarks at a technical briefing for regional leaders on Carbon Pricing Implementation and Climate-Resilient Low-Carbon Development. Jumhur said that regional enterprises can turn carbon trading into a reliable revenue source while maintaining strict land management standards, ensuring that regional carbon potential remains well-preserved in the process. He then pointed to mangrove restoration as an example, noting that mangroves can absorb around 3,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare annually. Based on an estimated carbon offset rate of US$50 to US$60 per ton, the carbon value from a hectare of mangroves could reach around US$150,000. Beyond local revenue potential, Jumhur stressed that regional governments must ensure the financial benefits of carbon trading reach local communities, in line with the central government's expectations. According to Jumhur, the need to build local capacity around carbon pricing governance is also important, so that regional leaders can accurately understand carbon market mechanisms and opportunities. Clear communication between central and local governments is essential, he added, to ensure that carbon market development yields maximum benefits for the public. He expressed hope that, with BUMD involvement, regional environmental potential can be developed into economic activities that boost local revenue while benefiting communities. artigo.texto: The debate over data centers has become one of the major issues in the race for New York's 17th Congressional District, with both campaigns trading accusations over facilities in Rockland County. Speaking Wednesday in front of the JPMorgan Chase data center in Orangeburg, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler said he had no involvement in the approval of data centers in Orangetown. Orangetown Supervisor Teresa Kenny, who previously served as the town attorney, said local officials have exclusive authority over zoning decisions. "The reality is, the only entity with jurisdiction over local zoning is the town of Orangetown. Decisions are made by a building inspector, which then went on to the planning board, and they had to go through a rigorous process and they ultimately received approval from the town of Orangetown," Kenny said. The comments came in response to criticism from Democratic congressional candidate Cait Conley, who raised the issue during a News 12 debate last month. "On Mike Lawler's watch there have been five data centers built in Rockland County," Conley said during the debate. Lawler on Wednesday sought to connect Conley to former Democratic Orangetown Supervisor Andy Stewart, whose administration approved the facilities, while also questioning Conley's stance on the issue. "She has no consistent position on anything. My view hasn't changed, the people who live next to these things should decide," Lawler said. Lawler showed that two were approved before he was deputy town supervisor from 2018-2020 and he was not on the town boards that would approve of these projects. Maddy Rosen, with the Conley campaign, pushed back on Lawler's comments, issuing a statement that read in part, “Mike Lawler himself bragged about his role overseeing these data centers during his time as Deputy Town Supervisor and making Rockland County 'the destination for data centers.'" Adding, "Mike Lawler is the biggest champion of data centers the Hudson Valley has ever seen." The Conley campaign pointed to Lawler's opposition to data center moratoriums as an example. Data centers have become a hot-button issue in the battleground race for New York's 17th Congressional District. Former New York state Sen. David Carlucci said the topic has emerged as a major campaign issue. "Every campaign year we have the topic of the year, right? This year it has been data centers. They've developed into the boogeyman of 2026," Carlucci said. Carlucci said voters want more information about how future developments could affect their communities. "I think voters want to know and understand what can be done to make sure that their quality of life is not denigrated while we continue to build the data centers," Carlucci said. News 12's September debate between the two congressional candidates is available on the network's website. Separately, current Republican state Sen. Bill Weber also criticized his opponent, Mayor Joe Rand, during Wednesday's press conference. Andy Stewart currently serves as Nyack's village administrator under Mayor Rand. Rand told News 12 that he supports legislation to temporarily halt the construction of new data centers and add protections for local communities. Election Day is Nov. 3.

artigo.texto: Unlocking the Green Story Behind Containment Sealed containment material delivers real, measurable carbon savings in data centers—so why isn't anyone reporting it? October 14, 2026 The growth of AI-driven power and cooling demands is putting data center operators under much harsher scrutiny when it comes to environmental impact. Sustainability mandates mean more questions are being asked of operators’ carbon footprints, PUE gradings, and long-term net-zero commitments. While ambitious green roadmaps, solar power purchase agreements, and liquid cooling systems all check the carbon-reduction box, one of the simplest sustainability wins is already happening in many data halls. Yet the material used to seal and fully enclose either horizontal or vertical containment, a product already installed and doing its job, barely gets mentioned. A Sealed Story, Left Untold Hot aisle and cold aisle containment is standard practice in modern data centers. The containment roof panel for cold aisle containment and vertical panel for hot aisle containment, and the material used, is often treated as a minor detail within a much larger cooling strategy. There is often one detail that goes unaddressed: openings above the cold aisle containment due to a lack of roof system, and openings above the hot aisle due to containment not going up to the plenum ceiling, and it's been driving up cooling costs since the day the facility opened. It's not an oversight or a design flaw. It's a direct byproduct of adhering to fire code. Sprinkler heads are engineered for the widest possible dispersal pattern to maximize coverage in a fire event and fully sealing or enclosing the top of the cold aisle with a roof system or with vertical panels above the hot aisle and up to the plenum ceiling can take the facility out of compliance with the fire code. That leaves facility operators with two options: - To leave the roof system off of cold aisle containment or to leave at least 24” of containment off the top of the vertical hot aisle containment up to the plenum ceiling, preserving the sprinkler's coverage pattern at the cost of a fully sealed containment system; or - Install sprinkler heads in every single aisle, which solves the dispersal problem but comes with a catch — a layout that made sense at commissioning rarely stays fixed for the life of the facility, and a sprinkler system built around a specific aisle plan doesn't adapt easily when that plan changes. Most facilities take the first option. It's simpler, cheaper, and satisfies fire code, but it also means that either the cold or hot aisle containment system is not fully sealed and contained, allowing the hot air to rise, drift across the gap, and mix back into the cold aisle. This design undoes some of the benefits that the containment system just performed, and the HVAC system compensates by working even harder. This is a constant, low-grade condition and rarely gets flagged as an issue. Instead, it shows up as elevated energy costs and lower cooling efficiency, spread across the operational life of the facility in a way that's easy to normalize and tough to trace back to its origin. However, closing the openings outright isn't as simple as adding a horizontal roof or vertical panels for the physical containment seal. Doing that just reintroduces the original problem of fire code compliance. If the suppression system can't detect a fire fast enough because the containment is fully sealed, it becomes a real hazard. Why DAB Panels Are the Overlooked Asset DAB panels solve a problem that has limited containment for years. Traditional roof panels can obstruct sprinkler coverage, force relocation of sprinkler heads, or get rejected outright by the local Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ). DAB panels are currently the only approved product that seals the horizontal gap over the cold aisle without triggering those concerns. The same is true with hot aisle vertical panels up to the plenum ceiling. DAB panels that are made from an EPA-certified, plant-based cellulose composite provide a continuous seal across the top of a contained aisle. Cooling equipment runs closer to design conditions instead of continuously compensating for leaked airflow, and panels can be easily cut, configured and fitted on-site around cable trays, pipes, and other overhead obstructions, ideal for both new builds and retrofits. Paired with a purpose-built passive airflow flap, a small mechanism fitted with a melting fuse plug, DAB panels keep the containment seal closed and intact under normal operating conditions, letting the HVAC system run at full efficiency. If a fire starts and aisle temperature rises, the fuse plugs melt, the flap opens, and hot air is immediately released upward for cold aisle containment and outward for hot aisle containment to the sprinkler activation system. The sprinklers dissolve the DAB panels within 30 seconds, removing the risk of any falling-object hazard that might restrict egress, so response time stays fast and AHJs stay satisfied. This is a design that fire protection engineers have reviewed and signed off on directly. A fully sealed cold or hot aisle, paired with airflow flaps where needed, meets fire code requirements without compromising fire suppression response times. Why the Disconnect Exists DAB panels are being adopted because they solve a fire-safety-versus-efficiency conflict that had nothing to do with ESG reporting. They weren't adopted because someone was chasing a carbon number. That's why the sustainability benefit has gone unclaimed. It's a side effect of a sound engineering decision. Containment sealing is typically a facilities and procurement decision, evaluated on cooling performance, installation cost, and code compliance, not on its contribution to a corporate carbon disclosure. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA A Comerc Energia projeta um salto no segmento de baterias no Brasil após a realização do primeiro leilão para atendimento ao sistema elétrico, marcado para dezembro. À Agência iNFRA, a CEO da empresa, Clarissa Sadock, destaca que usos de baterias elétricas como junto a indústrias, ao agronegócio e sistemas isolados devem ganhar escala. Esse efeito positivo resultaria numa redução dos preços e dos custos de financiamento para baterias. “O leilão reduz o custo da bateria. Quanto mais a indústria cresce, o preço cai. A gente vê na indústria de placas solares como o crescimento fez o preço cair”, diz a CEO. Dentre os usos possíveis de baterias que devem ganhar escala, segundo Clarissa, está o das plantas eletrointensivas, como datacenters, que precisam de energia firme. Ela ainda lembra das usinas que sofrem com o curtailment – cortes de geração obrigatórios – e dos sistemas de geração distribuída, que poderão apostar mais no armazenamento com um barateamento da tecnologia. “O leilão é importante para a matriz energética brasileira e ele abre uma porta importante para a indústria de baterias. Ao trazermos grandes fornecedores para o Brasil, uma legislação mais clara sobre o uso da bateria, viabilizar financiamento entendendo mais sobre o setor de bateria, isso destrava e abre portas para os investimentos em outras funcionalidades”, afirma. Controlada desde 2025 pela Vibra, a Comerc completa 25 anos em 2026 e já atua com baterias há pelo menos oito anos. Neste ano, comprou a totalidade da MicroPower, empresa focada em sistemas de armazenamento da qual já era acionista. Através desse braço, o grupo já fornece baterias para indústrias e clientes do agro, e vê espaço para crescimento. Competitividade A Comerc cadastrou projetos para o primeiro leilão, segundo a CEO, e vê no certame “oportunidade de negócio”. Tudo dependerá, ela explica, do nível de competição do certame, que tem cerca de 300 GW (gigawatts) cadastrados. “Nós temos bons projetos cadastrados e o nosso sucesso no leilão vai depender da competitividade e da gente conseguir viabilizar financeiramente esses projetos. Vamos ver como é que vai ser esse nível de competição. A gente não vai fazer nenhuma maluquice aqui”, diz. Clarissa Sadock ainda defende a realização do certame na data prevista, mas com todas as regras esclarecidas até lá para garantir a segurança. “A gente entende que é muito importante que o leilão ocorra, ele é importante para a matriz energética brasileira, ele complementa muito bem as fontes que a gente já tem, e abre uma porta importante para a indústria.” Abertura de mercado Outra oportunidade de crescimento no radar da empresa é com a abertura do mercado livre de energia para a baixa tensão. Um desafio na visão da executiva da Comerc é o fato de que esse perfil de consumidor conhece menos e não tem o nível de profundidade técnica do setor de energia, o que exigirá adaptações na forma de se comunicar e vender. “Isso faz com que a gente precise apresentar produtos e soluções simples. É um mercado novo, temos que aprender junto com a abertura de mercado qual vai ser essa necessidade do cliente. A gente tem que trazer soluções que estimule ele a consumir da melhor forma possível, para que ele tenha o desconto, mas que seja uma linguagem mais simples”, comenta. A CEO destaca que a empresa já tem experiência com esse tipo de cliente por causa da atuação no segmento de geração distribuída, que têm tickets menores e necessidade de uma comunicação mais simples. Por outro lado, isso demanda investimentos em sistemas e produtos diferenciados e mais capilaridade. Apesar da competição com o mercado livre, Clarissa afirma que o mercado de GD deve continuar em evidência no país e seguirá sendo uma aposta da companhia, que tem hoje 430 MWp (megawatt-pico) em painéis solares distribuídos e 200 mil clientes. “A gente percebe que vários competidores estão com dificuldades nesse mercado. Mas a gente acredita que esse segmento deve se consolidar nos próximos anos. E a Comerc, como um player que tem tido muito sucesso na geração distribuída, quer estar nesse mercado buscando oportunidades e crescimento”, diz. Crise Quanto à crise no segmento de comercialização de energia, a executiva da Comerc defende um novo modelo do setor elétrico para que a liquidez e competitividade do mercado volte ao normal. Ela culpou pelo cenário atual os preços elevados da energia no país e a alta volatilidade, o que tem afetado várias comercializadoras. Clarissa aponta que os preços altos são causados em grande parte pelo nível de aversão ao risco na operação do sistema. “Isso acabou ficando muito restritivo e a gente entende que ele está muito mais alto do que ele precisava ser. E o nível de aversão ao risco tão elevado tem dois componentes. O primeiro é que a energia está mais cara entre 30% e 44% do que precisaria estar. E o segundo fator é que está também muito mais sensível para qualquer mudança no mercado, com alta volatilidade”, diz. Ela ponderou ainda sobre o impacto que esse cenário tem no consumidor do mercado livre: “Esse cenário todo gera uma redução relevante da liquidez do mercado que é muito ruim para os nossos clientes, porque eles estão com menos oportunidades na mão para poder fazer suas contratações de energia. Então ele tem um preço de energia mais alto e ele tem menos competitividade no mercado”.

artigo.texto: Data centers’ net benefit to Ohio could shrink sharply, report finds COLUMBUS, Ohio (WTAP) - Data centers have delivered a net benefit of about $62 billion to Ohio since 2013, according to a new analysis from Scioto Analysis, a Columbus-based public policy firm. Scioto Analysis Principal Rob Moore said much of that benefit comes from employment, with data centers creating about 96,000 jobs over that 13-year period. “It’s not just the 50 jobs or whatever that are inside a data center, it’s also the infrastructure that’s built around it,” Moore said. “So the people who have to come and do maintenance on the data center, not just the construction at the start, but the ongoing work that needs to be done to keep a data center going.” The report projects that from 2027 through 2034, that net benefit could shrink dramatically. “From 2027 until 2034, if all the new data centers that are planned are built, that net benefit would only be $2.4 billion,” Moore said. Moore said the decline is caused by the fact that the benefits data centers provide in employment are front-loaded. “Counties that have a new data center, they end up having an increase in employment that is sustained as time goes on,” Moore said. “But when you build the second or third data center, you get fewer and fewer economic benefits that come from that. But the energy costs still keep on going up.” If every planned project is built, Ohio data centers will go from 178 to 270 by 2028. The report estimates higher electricity prices will cost ratepayers $16 billion. Data centers can reduce that figure by producing their power behind the meter, generating their own electricity instead of drawing from the same power grid as residential customers. But Moore said the costs aren’t limited to power bills. “The 16 billion number that we estimated for the increased electricity costs, that’s what people are kind of fixating on and sometimes missing the 41 billion dollars that comes in public health costs that are associated with all this energy that’s needed,” Moore said. The $41 billion figure comes from air pollutants from high-emissions electricity generation, including nitrogen oxide, sulfur dioxide and fine particulate matter, which are linked to asthma, heart attacks and strokes. “These are local emissions that decrease air quality in Ohio and end up killing people,” Moore said. Going behind the meter alone won’t eliminate those pollutants if data centers use high-emission technology. “That’s still something that’s going to be spewing particulate matter, nitrous oxide and sulfur dioxide into the air, which is going to impact public health,” Moore said. Taking employment, emissions and other factors into account, the report compares several policy options to the status quo, which has a projected $2.4 billion net benefit from 2027 through 2034. Stopping data center construction completely would have a net benefit of about $35 billion, as would requiring new data centers to generate their power behind the meter, with 90% using natural gas. Requiring new data centers to generate their power on-site with 90% of it from renewables produces the largest benefit, at $43 billion. Moore said the biggest takeaway for Ohioans from the analysis is that how data centers generate their electricity matters — whether they are plugged into the grid or behind the meter, and whether they are using renewable energy or high-emission technology. artigo.texto: The fight over data centers is only partly about data centers. The buildings stand in for AI, and AI stands in for something older, which is the trust Americans once gave the technology companies without asking for proof. That trust used to be assumed. Now it has to be inferred from what the companies do, and the inference is fraying. This essay argues that the opposition to data centers is best read as the public’s answer to that longer history, given at the one place where these companies have to ask permission. The signal What needs explaining is how quickly and how widely opinion has turned. In the summer of 2025 voters were evenly split on having a data center built near them, and a year later three in four were opposed [1]. Seven in ten Americans now oppose one in their own area, including clear majorities of Democrats, independents, and Republicans [2]. In Ohio the Republican and Democratic nominees for governor both want to pause new projects [3]. Americans agree on very little right now, so when people who disagree about nearly everything else agree on this, the agreement is a signal, and the question is what it is a signal of. The two usual answers do not go far enough. One holds that the complaints about water, electricity, and noise are exaggerated [4], and some of them may be. The effect on household bills so far looks small in most places, though prices have jumped on the mid-Atlantic grid, partly because of data center demand [5][6]. The other answer holds that the opposition is manufactured by foreign adversaries. Some of the online activity is, but what has been documented is small and its effect has been overstated [7]. Both questions are worth settling on the facts. Neither one explains how three in four voters came to the same view in a year. The first stand-in A better explanation begins with what kind of thing a data center is. AI is hard to see, even for people who use it every day, and a data center is the one part of it that sits in a particular place, where it can be seen, measured, and voted on. Others have already said that the buildings have become a stand-in for AI itself [8][9][10], and the evidence gives them some support. Only 8 percent of opponents know of a data center anywhere near them [8]. Americans are more opposed to a data center in their area than to a nuclear plant [2]. When opponents explain themselves in their own words, about one in eight talk about AI taking jobs, and a similar share say they dislike or distrust AI [2]. Neither has anything to do with a building down the road. That reading is only part of the truth. Most opponents still name water, power, land, and bills, and one pollster who looked at the reasons people give concluded that the idea “isn’t exactly right” [11]. But it points in the right direction, because people are bringing more to the building than the building itself explains. The second stand-in This essay goes one step further. If the buildings stand in for AI, then AI stands in for distrust of the companies that build it, and that distrust is much older than AI. Others have pointed toward this as well [9][12], and an earlier essay argued that the change people fear from AI began years ago, with the smartphone and social media [13]. What this essay adds is an account of what happened to the trust. It helps to separate two kinds. Assumed trust is given in advance, before anyone checks. Inferred trust is worked out from what a person can observe: what a company did last time, whether it fixed what went wrong, and whether anyone outside the company can verify what it says. A forthcoming book, Governance, Bureaucracy, and Organization, draws the same line about competence in organizations [14], and it carries over to trust. For years the technology companies enjoyed the first kind. In 2015 seven in ten Americans thought these companies were good for the country, and by 2019 only half did [15]. Confidence in them has since fallen to the lowest level since Gallup began asking in 2020 [16]. Each party has taken its turn, Republicans first and Democrats now [16][17], for different reasons and in the same direction. So AI did not arrive to a public ready to assume the best. Half a year after ChatGPT appeared, more than eight in ten Americans, in both parties, already said they did not trust the companies developing AI to do it responsibly [18]. The puzzle is that almost everyone kept using the products while the trust drained away. Nine in ten adults now own a smartphone [19], and nearly half of teenagers say social media is bad for people their age [20]. One experiment shows how both can be true. College students put a real value on their own access to TikTok, and yet on average they were willing to pay to have it switched off for everyone on campus, themselves included [21]. They used it because everyone else did. Albert Hirschman observed that a person unhappy with an organization can leave or can speak up [22]. With phones and social media most people could do neither, because leaving meant losing touch with family, school, and work, and there was never a meeting to speak at. These products arrived one phone at a time, and nobody held a vote. So people stayed, but they stopped taking the companies’ good faith for granted and began judging them by what they could see. That is the move from assumed trust to inferred trust, and it explains how use could keep rising while trust kept falling. The same pattern is already visible with AI, where about half of adults now use chatbots and most have little confidence that the companies will handle the technology responsibly [23]. The inference is fraying Inferred trust depends on evidence, and the evidence the public has been given this year is poor. On March 4, seven companies signed a pledge at the White House to pay for the power their data centers need [24]. Two of them were Meta and Google. artigo.texto: Residents and local officials in Kenosha County are pushing back on a utility-scale standalone battery project being proposed in the town of Wheatland. Robin Energy Storage, a subsidiary of Danish investment firm Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, filed an application with state regulators late last month seeking approval for a 200-megawatt battery energy storage system, or BESS. While Kenosha County is already home to the Paris Solar and Battery Park, this storage project wouldn’t be charged up by a specific generation resource. Instead, it would draw power from the grid at periods of low demand and discharge that energy back onto the grid at times of high demand. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “It’s not connected to a data center, a solar farm, wind turbines or anything — it’s connected to the overall grid, and it just provides stability,” said Scott McPherson, a spokesperson for Robin Energy Storage. “It can provide energy when it’s needed under peak demands. It would be storing energy when there’s excess capacity.” While the company argues the project could help boost reliability for Wisconsin’s energy grid, residents have raised potential safety concerns as well as concerns about the loss of rural character in the community. Wheatland Town Board Supervisor Kyle Madsen said the town’s planning commission voted against the proposal before the developer filed its application with the state Public Service Commission. He said he’s against the battery project because he feels there are too many unknowns. “We’re not against making progress or anything like that,” Madsen said. “It’s just, what’s the best fit for our town? And we do not believe, at this point in time, that these standalone battery storage facilities should move forward within our town.” County leaders say developer is trying ‘sidestep’ locals At the county level, officials have framed the company’s application with the PSC as an effort to “sidestep” a countywide moratorium on battery energy storage systems. Kenosha County Executive Samantha Kerkman said the county established zoning requirements for battery storage systems in 2024 after learning of a potential battery storage proposal. The county passed an initial moratorium while it was working on those regulations. This May, the county passed another moratorium, citing “potential health and safety issues” and “changes in technology and circumstances” around battery systems. Kerkman said she believes counties have a role to play when it comes to regulating utility-scale battery projects. “The Public Service Commission does have the right to regulate BESS systems that are attached to large-scale solar projects,” she said. “I believe state statute does give them that authority. But for the standalone BESS systems, there’s no statutes with regards to the PSC’s authority to regulate those.” Under state law, electric generation facilities with a capacity of 100 megawatts or more generally require siting approval from the state Public Service Commission rather than local governments. That applies to natural gas power plants and large-scale solar and wind projects. PSC staff believe a standalone battery project of 100 megawatts or more would generally be subject to the same requirement, but it will ultimately be up to the commission itself to review the facts and make a determination, according to an agency spokesperson. “The Commission carefully reviews all applications it receives and will render a decision in accordance with the applicable law and Commission’s authority,” the spokesperson said via email. McPherson, the spokesperson for Robin Energy Storage, said the company was not trying to sidestep local governments. He said they filed their application after the PSC released new rules this year giving developers more clarity in applying for standalone battery projects at the state level. “We were working at the local level all the way. The state came up with their rules. Now we’re going to the state,” he said. “Pretty cut and dried.” Safety concerns fuel debate Aside from disagreements over regulatory authority, Kerkman said the county’s experience with the existing storage facility in Paris has raised concerns about another battery proposal in the county. She said maintenance alarms have been going off “on a very regular basis” at the battery facility in Paris since around May, requiring first responders to show up to make sure it’s just a maintenance alarm. We Energies is the majority owner of the Paris battery project. Spokesperson Brendan Conway said in an email that the utility is working with first responders to address “alarm notification issues” at the Paris site. He said the company appreciates “their partnership as we resolve the matter.” Conway said the batteries in Paris are “providing energy to the grid regularly, including supporting customers during periods of peak electricity demand.” While standalone battery proposals are relatively new in Wisconsin, Ciaran Gallagher, energy and air manager at the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, said the technology is the same as the technology used in the battery systems paired with solar farms. She said that risks of fires or explosions tied to utility-scale battery storage have generally decreased as the technology has become more widely adopted. “There have been some fires at batteries in the United States, but that risk is pretty low, especially as the technology has developed and the fire safety measures around it have developed,” Gallagher said. “I think all energy systems come with some element of risk.” A new report from the national nonprofit Electric Power Research Institute shows the failure rate for BESS systems dropped by 98 percent from 2018 to 2025. artigo.texto: The domestic carbon market, which began operating on June 29, marks an important step in Vietnam's green transition while highlighting the need for stronger financial mechanisms to support its development, he said at a workshop on credit policy and carbon markets in Hanoi on October 14. The event was organised by VIR in coordination with the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) at VIR's headquarters. “If the carbon exchange is the market’s infrastructure, credit policy, the banking system and capital markets are the driving forces behind the green transition,” Hoanh said. Credit policy plays a leading role in directing financial resources towards emissions reduction, helping businesses and individuals invest in greener activities and linking sustainable development objectives with the flow of capital throughout the economy. The green transition ultimately requires tangible investments in cleaner technologies, energy efficiency, changes to production processes, low-emission agriculture, forest protection and development, waste treatment, renewable energy and more sustainable supply chains. "To bring these projects to fruition, Vietnam needs a financial system capable of identifying, pricing, allocating and managing green capital," said Hoanh. Vietnam’s carbon market framework was established under the 2020 Law on Environmental Protection and subsequently developed through a series of legal documents. The latest regulations include Decree No.29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange and Decree No.112/2026/ND-CP on international exchanges of greenhouse gas emission reduction outcomes and carbon credits. Vietnam has also gained experience in monetising verified emissions reductions on international markets. In 2024, the country received its first $51.5 million payment from the World Bank for 10.3 million tonnes of verified emission reductions under the North Central Region Emission Reductions Programme. The launch of allowance trading on 29 June 2026 introduced a new way of recognising the economic value of emissions reductions. However, the establishment of a trading platform alone will not ensure the market's long-term success. "A sustainable carbon market also requires liquidity, reliable data, verification mechanisms, confidence among buyers and sellers, and a strong financial ecosystem to support market participants," Hoanh said. He highlighted several questions that policymakers, financial institutions and businesses need to address, including how to remove regulatory and financial bottlenecks, channel green capital towards the right projects, and enable banks to assess both the opportunities and risks associated with green investments. Businesses must also be able to demonstrate the effectiveness of their transition efforts and access bank lending along with medium- and long-term financing from capital markets. Meanwhile, carbon value needs to become an increasingly reliable factor in financial decision-making. These challenges were among the reasons VIR organised the workshop, bringing together policymakers, banks, businesses, experts and other stakeholders to exchange views and identify practical solutions. "The carbon market would create a new economic driver when businesses could see the financial benefits of emissions reductions, banks and capital market institutions could manage green capital effectively, investors could identify value, and producers received commensurate benefits," said Hoanh. He expressed his hope that discussions at the workshop would lead to concrete policy proposals, practical cooperation initiatives, and models that could be implemented in practice. The event forms part of broader efforts to connect Vietnam’s carbon market development with credit policy and capital mobilisation, helping ensure that the country’s green transition is supported by the financial resources needed to deliver measurable results. The workshop featured presentations by the SBV, the Asian Development Bank, and Agribank, followed by a discussion with representatives from regulatory authorities, capital markets, banks, businesses, and consulting organisations. Key topics included expanding green capital flows, improving businesses' access to finance, developing the carbon market, and strengthening the links between emissions reduction value and financial decision-making.

artigo.texto: A auxiliar de saúde Jessica Kivell, mãe e moradora de West Memphis, no Arkansas, pediu à Comissão de Serviço Público do Arkansas os registros públicos sobre quem pagaria por um data center do Google na região. Em vez de respostas, ela recebeu o título de ré numa ação judicial movida pela utilidade elétrica Entergy Arkansas, responsável por construir a usina solar que abasteceria o projeto, publicada pelo site The Intercept nesta terça-feira, 13 de outubro de 2026. Os documentos obtidos por Kivell indicavam que o Google cobriria apenas um terço do custo da nova usina solar, contrariando a promessa de que os consumidores de energia não arcariam com a conta. Ela compartilhou os registros com o jornal Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, que os publicou. A Entergy Arkansas então processou Kivell, o Democrat-Gazette, o repórter do jornal e o Arkansas Times, que afirmou nem ter tido acesso aos documentos. A empresa alegou que a comissão errou ao liberar os registros, que eles conteriam segredos comerciais e que os réus deveriam ser impedidos de discuti-los, com retirada do que já havia sido publicado. A utilidade também contestou os cálculos do jornal sobre a divisão de custos com o Google. A coluna é assinada por Seth Stern, diretor de defesa da Freedom of the Press Foundation, que classifica o caso como uma ação estratégica contra a participação pública, o chamado SLAPP, um processo cujo objetivo é silenciar críticos pelo custo da defesa. Pelo menos quatro decisões da Suprema Corte dos EUA rejeitam censura prévia que tente recolher registros liberados pelo governo, mesmo por engano. No caso Florida Star contra BJF, envolvendo a publicação do nome de uma vítima de estupro, o tribunal considerou inconstitucional punir veículos por divulgar informação que o próprio governo havia liberado. A corte já chamou a censura prévia à imprensa de a mais grave de todas as violações à Primeira Emenda. O juiz federal Lee Rudofsky negou o pedido de ordem de mordaça de emergência da Entergy, que em seguida desistiu da ação. O processo, porém, já havia custado dinheiro, tempo e sono aos réus. Kivell, que correu ao tribunal ainda com o uniforme de trabalho para a audiência, chegou a chorar no corredor do fórum. Como o caso tramitou na Justiça federal, os réus não puderam recuperar as despesas advocatícias. O Arkansas é um dos 40 estados americanos com lei antisslapp, mas a proteção não alcançou o caso, e a coluna defende uma lei federal contra processos destinados a calar a liberdade de expressão.

artigo.texto: Leilão de 6 GHz pode financiar data centers fora dos grandes mercados Proposta em consulta prevê compromissos de infraestrutura digital para acompanhar a expansão da capacidade das redes móveis A proposta do leilão da faixa de 6 GHz prevê a possibilidade de destinar parte dos compromissos associados às autorizações de espectro à implantação de infraestrutura de processamento de dados em localidades com menor atratividade econômica. A medida foi detalhada por Leonardo Tostes, assessor do Conselho Diretor da Anatel, durante o 22º Wireless Mundi, realizado pelo Tele.Síntese nesta quinta-feira, 15, em São Paulo. Segundo Tostes, o objetivo é evitar que o aumento da capacidade de transmissão das futuras redes móveis não seja acompanhado por investimentos suficientes em processamento de dados. O assessor explicou que a proposta considera data centers de pequeno e médio porte, especialmente em regiões onde a expansão da infraestrutura digital não ocorreria necessariamente por iniciativa do mercado. A obrigação ainda está em discussão na consulta pública do futuro edital de 6 GHz. Capacidade de processamento acompanha evolução das redes Tostes afirmou que a política de espectro precisa considerar outros componentes da infraestrutura digital além das redes de acesso. Segundo ele, não basta disponibilizar frequências capazes de transportar volumes maiores de dados se a infraestrutura de processamento não acompanhar essa evolução. O assessor explicou que a proposta busca antecipar uma possível insuficiência de capacidade em determinadas localidades. A preocupação está relacionada à evolução das redes móveis e à expectativa de aumento da demanda por processamento de informações. O compromisso foi apresentado como uma alternativa para direcionar investimentos a regiões nas quais o mercado não desenvolveria espontaneamente a infraestrutura necessária. Tostes ressaltou que a intenção não é financiar data centers que já seriam implantados por razões comerciais. Critérios de localização ainda precisam ser definidos Questionado sobre a identificação das localidades que poderiam receber os investimentos, o assessor reconheceu que a proposta apresenta diferenças em relação às obrigações tradicionais de cobertura. Nos leilões de frequências móveis, a agência pode identificar áreas sem atendimento e estabelecer compromissos de implantação de redes. No caso dos data centers, entretanto, a definição das localidades envolve a avaliação de uma demanda futura por processamento. Tostes explicou que a proposta busca antecipar uma lacuna que poderá se tornar mais relevante com a evolução das tecnologias móveis. O assessor não apresentou uma relação de municípios, metas quantitativas ou estimativas de investimento para os possíveis compromissos. Também não informou critérios definitivos para determinar quais localidades receberiam a infraestrutura. Compromissos deverão evitar investimentos já previstos Outro ponto discutido durante o painel foi a necessidade de impedir que os recursos associados ao leilão sejam utilizados para financiar projetos que já seriam executados pelas empresas. Segundo Tostes, a proposta precisa estabelecer condições para que os investimentos representem uma ampliação efetiva da infraestrutura disponível. O assessor mencionou a preocupação com a autonomia da infraestrutura em relação à empresa vencedora da licitação. A discussão envolve a forma de execução dos compromissos e sua relação com a operação das redes móveis. Tostes destacou que os parâmetros ainda poderão ser aperfeiçoados com as contribuições recebidas durante a consulta pública. Setor debate condições econômicas do leilão Luiz Henrique Barbosa, presidente executivo da TelComp, defendeu que os compromissos dos futuros leilões sejam compatíveis com a capacidade de investimento das prestadoras. Segundo ele, os certames devem priorizar a expansão da infraestrutura e evitar exigências que antecipem investimentos sem condições de retorno econômico. Barbosa também argumentou que a distribuição geográfica dos blocos de espectro precisa refletir a demanda efetiva de cada mercado. Na avaliação do executivo, a combinação de obrigações e custos das autorizações influencia a participação das empresas nas licitações. Tostes afirmou que a Anatel pretende utilizar a consulta pública para discutir o desenho dos blocos e dos compromissos antes da realização do certame. O assessor explicou que a previsão de leilão em 2028 não implica implantação imediata de toda a infraestrutura. As obrigações poderão ser escalonadas, conforme as condições estabelecidas no edital definitivo. A inclusão de data centers representa uma proposta regulatória ainda sujeita a alterações. A Anatel não anunciou, durante o painel, valores, localidades ou metas definitivas para esses investimentos.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter. Cindy O’Neil understands the boom-and-bust cycles of industry. Her husband spent years working in Carbon County’s namesake coal mines. In this pocket of central Utah, energy and the economy have long been intrinsically linked, at great sacrifice to county residents. “We’ve had the coal. We’ve dealt, the whole community, with black lung,” O’Neil said. “The explosions, the fires, and all the things that came along with it.” But a new industry and type of energy production is about to move near her rural home. And she says it has her and her neighbors even more worried than they were about the dangers that came from their long history with coal. “It’s all descending, these data centers,” said O’Neil, who tracks mysterious new projects in the works and shares updates on Facebook community pages. “They’re setting these things within a couple of miles of homes.” Her latest updates involve a lot of chatter about Valar Atomics, a nuclear startup. The company plans to build a mega-complex of 456 small modular reactors — a still largely untested and unproven technology in the United States — on the vast tracts of Bureau of Land Management land in the county. The project will store radioactive waste, according to a report from National Public Radio, and power an array of industrial activities, including data centers. “Project Beehive” has support from the state of Utah, and will include a square mile of state-owned trust lands. Another data center complex planned for the county, Altigen Energy’s “Jurassic Spark,” will cover hundreds of acres and include a massive natural gas plant. It’s an abrupt shift. Carbon County’s coal mines produced nearly 10 million tons of coal in 2006. But a shift to cheaper energy sources, like renewables and natural gas, along with depleted supplies in the coal seams, sank the region’s main economic engine in just a few decades. Since 2023, not a single pound of coal has been mined in Carbon County. “They say everything’s left us, and if we don’t grab these table scraps we’re not going to get anything,” said O’Neil. “I don’t think our county has to take the table scraps.” None of Carbon County’s new data center plans call for coal. The Utah Trust Lands Administration recently agreed to lease a square mile of its state-owned land for up to 100 years to Valar Atomics. The nuclear startup intends to use that lease to run some of its small modular reactors, process its uranium TRISO-fuel to feed the reactors, build water desalination, manufacture steel, refine critical minerals — and support data centers. The Valar site is expected to generate $35 million in lease rents over 50 years, according to information the Trust Lands Administration staff presented to its board last month. Revenue collected from the project benefits Utah schools. (The state agency declined to comment on the Valar project.) During that September board meeting, three Carbon County residents who are employed or expected to be employed by Valar spoke in favor of the project. All three of the Carbon County commissioners also voiced their support. “[We] realize that this topic is a hot button now, along with data centers,” said Larry Jensen, one of the commissioners. “It’s important that you understand that the Carbon County commissioners are committed to allowing these things to move forward. Even with the pushback — we realize that there are a few in our community who will push back — but the silent majority are the ones that we really represent.” Cheryl Lupo, a longtime resident of the county, balked at that assertion. She is running for a seat on the county commission this year. As an unaffiliated candidate, she had to collect 300 signatures to land on the ballot. She said the opinions she heard during that process were overwhelmingly opposed to data centers and nuclear plants. “People are up in arms,” Lupo said. “Torches and pitchforks. Because they’re not being heard.” Gov. Spencer Cox (R), U.S. Sen. John Curtis (R), and other high-ranking Utah officials welcomed Valar to the state earlier this year, allowing it to test its “Ward250” microreactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab in neighboring Emery County. Valar announced it had achieved “self-sustaining criticality” in June — a process where atoms split and maintain a steady fission chain reaction without being fed more neutrons. The company has plans to power a 30-megawatt nuclear-powered AI data center in Emery County, too, in partnership with the computer-chip giant Nvidia. Small modular reactors have yet to be deployed for commercial use in the United States. During the recent Trust Lands Administration meeting, Mike Nelson, the board’s chair, seemed to acknowledge that the deal with Valar came with some unknowns. “We weren’t always sure what to ask about,” Nelson said, while offering praise for the nuclear startup, “and probably still aren’t sure of everything to ask about because this is a first, right?” Utah has a troubled history with nuclear testing. Lupo’s mother was 38 years old when she died, and Lupo believes the cause was downwind effects from radioactive weapons testing in nearby Nevada during the 1950s. Her mother lived in Carbon County at the time. She believes the fallout caused her grandfather’s death, too. “I will never, ever be a proponent of nuclear,” Lupo said. Even before the proposal to build Valar’s complex started causing a stir, rumors swirled about the possibility of another data center campus in Carbon County. Altigen, a company that builds natural gas power plants for data centers, has selected an area east of Wellington for its 1,200-acre “Jurassic Spark” project — nearly double the size of the Valar campus, according to meeting minutes from the local Community Economic Development Board. artigo.texto: Para esclarecer esses benefícios e sua aplicação prática, um repórter do jornal Agricultura e Meio Ambiente entrevistou o Dr. Vu Duy Hoang, Vice-Diretor do Centro de Agricultura Ecológica e Formação Profissional e membro do Grupo de Pesquisa em Tecnologia de Cultivo Sustentável de Culturas da Academia de Agricultura do Vietnã. Muitos agricultores estão acostumados a manter seus arrozais inundados. Por que a irrigação alternada com períodos de seca e alagamento pode reduzir as emissões e, ao mesmo tempo, garantir a produtividade? Quando os arrozais são constantemente inundados, o solo fica em estado anaeróbico, criando condições favoráveis para a proliferação de microrganismos produtores de metano. A irrigação alternada com períodos de seca (AWD, na sigla em inglês) promove aeração do solo, interrompendo a formação de metano (CH₄) e reduzindo as emissões. É importante ressaltar que AWD não significa períodos prolongados de seca, mas sim a alternância entre períodos de irrigação e períodos em que o nível da água está abaixo da superfície segura do arrozal. A regulação da irrigação deve ser adaptada a cada fase de crescimento, evitando a escassez de água durante períodos sensíveis, como o espigamento e a floração. Em um estudo sobre arroz semeado diretamente em três localidades de Ninh Binh, em 2025, os campos com irrigação alternada (AWD) alcançaram rendimentos de 6,58 toneladas/ha na safra de primavera e 6,17 toneladas/ha na safra de verão, em comparação com 6,28 e 5,53 toneladas/ha em campos inundados regularmente. Os resultados mostram que a redução das emissões de CH₄ pode ser acompanhada pela manutenção dos rendimentos quando as técnicas adequadas são aplicadas. A pesquisa dele mostra que a época de cultivo tem uma taxa de redução de emissões menor do que a primavera, mas a quantidade de emissões reduzidas é maior. Ele pode explicar esse ponto interessante? É necessário considerar tanto a taxa de redução quanto a quantidade real de emissões reduzidas. Na safra de 2025, temperaturas mais altas, maior pluviosidade e um período de consórcio de culturas mais curto podem promover a decomposição da matéria orgânica, resultando em maiores emissões de CH₄ em campos regularmente inundados em comparação com a safra de primavera. Como as emissões iniciais eram maiores, mesmo com uma taxa de redução menor, a quantidade de emissões reduzidas pelo sistema de irrigação por alagamento alternado (AWD) ainda foi maior. Convertendo para equivalente de CO₂, a redução atingiu aproximadamente 3,41 toneladas/ha/safra na safra de primavera e cerca de 4,25 toneladas/ha/safra na safra de outono. Isso demonstra que, ao avaliar a eficácia da redução de emissões ou o potencial de créditos de carbono, é necessário basear a avaliação na quantidade real de redução para cada safra e região de produção, e não apenas na porcentagem. Segundo ele, antes de receberem receitas com a venda de créditos de carbono, que benefícios claros os produtores de arroz poderiam obter que justificassem uma mudança em suas práticas agrícolas? O benefício mais evidente é a redução de custos, mantendo a produtividade. Através de estudos e modelos em diversas províncias do norte, o número de ciclos de irrigação pode ser reduzido em média de 2 a 3 vezes por cultura, diminuindo assim os custos com mão de obra e bombeamento de água. Quando aplicada adequadamente, a irrigação alternada (AWD) também promove melhor desenvolvimento radicular, plantas mais fortes, solo mais firme e facilita a mecanização. Em alguns modelos, os agricultores também relataram menor incidência de pragas e doenças e redução no número de aplicações de pesticidas. Alguns de nossos estudos mostraram que a produtividade pode ser de aproximadamente 6 a 20% maior do que no tratamento controle, dependendo da variedade e da localização. Portanto, os benefícios imediatos devem ser observados na eficiência no campo: custos reduzidos, uso eficiente da água e produtividade mantida. A geração de renda com créditos de carbono é um benefício potencial. Senhor, se quisermos implementar isso em larga escala, quais são as condições mais importantes para garantir que os agricultores possam implementá-lo com sucesso? Este método pode ser aplicado em muitas regiões, desde que as condições sejam adequadas, mas o fator mais importante é a capacidade de regular a água de forma proativa. Áreas com produção concentrada, sistemas de irrigação adequados e o envolvimento de unidades de gestão de recursos hídricos e cooperativas terão mais facilidade em implementá-lo em larga escala. Se as famílias desejarem retirar água, mas o sistema continuar a fornecer água da maneira antiga, será muito difícil implementar o procedimento correto. Portanto, é necessária a coordenação entre os produtores de arroz, as cooperativas, as unidades de irrigação e as autoridades locais para que se chegue a um acordo sobre um cronograma de fornecimento e retirada de água de acordo com cada fase de crescimento. Além disso, é necessário ajudar as pessoas a compreenderem corretamente a irrigação alternada, sabendo quando deixar os campos secarem e quando irrigar novamente. Para expandir essa prática, são necessários não apenas bons procedimentos técnicos, mas também uma gestão hídrica sincronizada, uma organização de produção adequada e o consenso da população. Por meio de pesquisas realizadas em diversas regiões produtoras de arroz que utilizam o método de irrigação alternada (molhado e seco), os repórteres descobriram que os agricultores esperam um melhor acesso ao mercado e renda adicional proveniente de créditos de carbono. Na sua opinião, o que precisa ser feito para transformar essa expectativa em um benefício concreto? O Vietnã implementou um procedimento piloto de MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) para arroz de alta qualidade e baixa emissão no Delta do Mekong; o Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP também fornece uma base legal para o intercâmbio internacional de resultados de redução de emissões e créditos de carbono. artigo.texto: (Bloomberg) -- ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a deal that would secure vital components for TikTok's owner while helping the Taiwanese chipmaker compete with Qualcomm Inc. Most Read from Bloomberg - Stocks Fall on Inflation Woes as Chip Rout Deepens: Markets Wrap - Apple Unveils $299 HomeView Hub as Part of New Smart Home Push - Epic Games Delays Disney Project, Asks Developers to Use More AI - CoreWeave's Big Dream Crashes Into Reality as Yields Top 15% - CoreWeave's Bonds Turn Distressed, Drawing 'Yikes' From Musk The Chinese social media company is in advanced talks with MediaTek over the supply of bespoke chips that will help run ByteDance data centers, people familiar with the matter said. The Taiwanese firm will provide an unspecified amount of Application Specific Integrated Circuits, or chips customized to work with a clients' platform, the people said, asking to remain anonymous to talk about a private arrangement. If the deal goes through, ByteDance may become MediaTek's second major customer for such ASICs, after Alphabet Inc.'s Google. ByteDance is ramping up hardware spending to fuel a bet on AI as its next growth engine. But like Chinese rivals Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and Tencent Holdings Ltd., it's barred from the most cutting-edge AI chips from the likes of Nvidia Corp. Local players such as Huawei Technologies Co. can't meet all demand. China's biggest private firm is thus exploring alternatives including partnerships with chip designers — something that's allowed under current US export curbs so long as the AI computing power a Chinese firm is seeking doesn't exceed a certain threshold. ByteDance struck a similar deal with Qualcomm earlier this year to procure millions of AI chips, Bloomberg News reported. For MediaTek, a large-scale contract win would boost its efforts to diversify away from mobile phones and compete with Qualcomm and Broadcom Inc. in data centers, an arena it's less familiar with. The Taiwanese firm expects its AI chip sales to reach about $2 billion this year and is targeting 15% of the $80 billion market next year. Nvidia announced a deal to invest $3.5 billion in the Hsinchu-based chipmaker in September, propelling those ambitions. ByteDance didn't have immediate comment, while MediaTek representatives declined to comment. MediaTek has emerged as a key beneficiary of a push by technology companies to design custom semiconductors for AI applications, using its expertise in mobile processors to participate in the data center infrastructure rush. With a market value of around $210 billion, it's Taiwan's biggest firm after Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

artigo.texto: Econergy Ltd, a leading European renewable energy independent power producer, has connected its 40 MW/120 MWh Dalmarnock battery energy storage system (BESS) in Glasgow, Scotland, to the UK grid. It is Econergy's second connected BESS in the UK, after the 50 MW/100 MWh Swangate project connected in 2024. Full commercial operation is expected by December 2026, providing flexibility to the regional electricity system, storing, and dispatching power in response to market conditions. Dalmarnock is supported by a project financing agreement with Santander UK plc for approximately £21 million. Econergy has also entered into a 10-year floor agreement with EDF, providing a minimum annual revenue, together with an additional revenue-sharing mechanism. Dalmarnock is part of Econergy's ~2.2 GW storage-led UK portfolio. Four further UK projects are under construction: Immingham (80 MW/240 MWh, financed on the same Santander and EDF structure, with grid connection expected in 2027) and a portfolio of three projects totalling 160 MW/500 MWh, expected to connect in 2027 – 2028. Joshua Murphy, Director of Energy Storage at Econergy, commented: “We are delighted to have connected Dalmarnock to the grid. We finalised the development, financed and delivered the project, and are now bringing it into operation. With a three-hour duration, the system is designed to absorb surplus renewable generation and discharge during peak demand. We have chosen EDF to optimise the asset and our agreement with them provides a 10-year revenue floor while preserving exposure to upside through revenue sharing. I’m excited to start seeing the first commercial operation of this asset after a successful project delivery!” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: Consumer Liaison Group explores growing role of energy storage The third 2026 meeting of the Consumer Liaison Group (CLG) centered on batteries, energy storage, and the future of the electric grid, examining how storage technologies are evolving, the role they can play in supporting grid operations and reliability, and their potential to help meet New England’s changing energy needs. A video recording and summary of the Sept. 24 meeting in Portland, Maine, are available online. Drew Landry, CLG Coordinating Committee member and Maine’s deputy public advocate, began the meeting with opening remarks and provided an overview of the group as well as the critical roles of ISO New England. He introduced the topics of discussion and described innovations in battery technology. Heather Sanborn, Maine’s public advocate, discussed electrification during her keynote address, noting that demand growth from heat pumps and electric vehicles (EVs) has largely been offset by declining industrial consumption. She highlighted findings from the ISO’s 2050 Transmission Study, describing how it showed the potential cost savings of reducing peak demand. The audience followed up with questions on load growth trends, EV charging timing, stakeholder coordination, solar incentives, and utility data transparency. The first panel discussion was moderated by Cole Cochrane, policy affairs lead at Powertown and a Coordinating Committee member, and featured Greg Geller, Stack Energy Consulting; Kelly Kaufmann, ReVision Energy; Jessica Robertson, New Leaf Energy; and Elio Torres, Powertown. The panelists examined how market reforms, incentive programs, and interconnection processes affect energy storage development. They emphasized the need for better alignment between wholesale markets and retail programs, more predictable revenue streams, and reduced barriers to battery deployment. Audience questions focused on the impact of FERC Order No. 2222 and market complexity on storage participation. The ISO’s Eric Johnson, executive director of External Affairs, and Ruben Flores-Marzan, policy advisor for environmental and community affairs, provided a regional grid update covering market, planning, and policy developments. Highlights included consumer engagement opportunities and community outreach activities, growing battery participation on the system, market trends, transmission planning initiatives, and large load integration efforts. Audience questions focused on battery visibility in ISO-NE tools and maintaining a safe, affordable resource mix. The final panel discussion, moderated by Landry, featured George Baker, Gridworks Consulting; Ian Burnes, Efficiency Maine Trust; Al McBride, ISO New England; and Ethan Tremblay, Maine Department of Energy Resources. They discussed the growing role of energy storage in New England, highlighting state initiatives, battery participation in ISO-NE markets, and the reliability and operational benefits storage can provide. Audience questions focused on battery deployment, interconnection challenges, and opportunities for greater participation in wholesale markets. The next CLG meeting, scheduled for Dec. 2 in Boston, will include the biennial election of the Coordinating Committee. - Categories - Events - Tags - consumer liaison group

artigo.texto: 'People are big mad in Texas': Hinojosa challenges Abbott's data center policies DALLAS - Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for Texas governor, discussed her stance on data centers during a press conference in Dallas on Tuesday. What they're saying: Hinojosa said she believes Texans should "have a seat at the table" when it comes to deciding whether there are data centers in their communities, and called for lawmakers to pass legislation putting more protections in place. She also took aim at her opponent, Gov. Greg Abbott’s attitude toward AI data center development by criticizing the rapid expansion in the state and blaming it on tax breaks and other incentives. "There's no protections for people to have a seat at the table to decide if and how they come into their communities. There is no protection for water or electricity costs," Hinojosa said. "We are left to fend for ourselves under Greg Abbott, and people are big mad in Texas about the data centers." Abbott pauses data center permits, calls for more regulations The other side: Abbott, who previously welcomed the artificial intelligence industry, appears to have shifted his stance. The governor ordered a pause on some data center approvals in August, and a month earlier said he wants to ban data center development in rural Texas neighborhoods. "We must prohibit them from building AI data centers in rural Texas neighborhoods, and we must eliminate the tax break they are getting," Abbott said during a campaign stop in Bullard. "They must be responsible for funding their own projects here in Texas." Hinojosa echoed a need for a moratorium, but said she believes her opponent's pause on data center development is "in name only." "I could issue a moratorium, but it would be in place until laws are passed to accomplish those things," Hinojosa said, referring to her calls for more guardrails and stricter protections. Abbott's office has previously emphasized his willingness to work with lawmakers, pointing to a letter the governor sent to the Public Utilities Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas in June. The letter laid out some of his ideas, which included having the legislature repeal sales tax exemptions. Data centers remain a major topic of debate in Texas Big picture view: Data centers have been a major topic of debate in the state, which has seen hundreds spring up in recent years. The concerns of local leaders and residents mainly center around noise, light and water pollution. A resident of the Joppa community who spoke Tuesday also shared concerns with locals being included in discussions, saying she did not know a data center was being built in her neighborhood until it was already there. "We do not want one," she said. "However, it is now up and running, and we are faced with the challenge of having the data center less than 0.3 miles, 1,500 feet -- not 15 miles, but 1,500 feet – from our community." The Source: The information in this article comes from a press conference held by Democratic gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa in Dallas, as well as previous reporting on data centers.
