artigo.texto: PowerCo × Gotion: Volkswagen’s LFP Battery Push Builds European Independence Three Joint Ventures Span Cells, Cathode Material and Cross-Regional Supply €1.6 Billion Investment Fills Critical Technology Gap Restructuring and Profit Targets Frame Broader Group Renewal Volkswagen Group and its battery subsidiary PowerCo have formed a landmark partnership with Gotion High-Tech to establish Europe’s first large-scale production of lithium‑iron‑phosphate (LFP) batteries, a chemistry poised to dominate affordable electric vehicles but currently manufactured almost entirely outside the continent. The agreement creates three joint ventures across Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, combining Volkswagen’s platform and vehicle scale with Gotion’s proven LFP manufacturing expertise. Announced against a backdrop of sweeping restructuring across the Group, the move underscores a dual imperative: to secure supply chains for the next generation of accessible EVs and to restore profitability amid intense global competition. The LFP Opportunity and the Gap LFP batteries are central to affordable electric mobility: they use no nickel or cobalt, offer exceptional longevity and safety, and deliver compelling cost advantages. Yet Europe has no meaningful domestic LFP production capacity, even as demand is projected to surge from roughly 10% of the market today to between 40% and 60% by 2030. Closing that gap is not merely about supply — it is about who controls the technology, the manufacturing infrastructure, and the value chain. Thomas Schmall, Volkswagen Group Board Member for Technology and PowerCo Supervisory Board Chairman, described the partnership as “a major breakthrough” that makes Volkswagen the first European automaker to cover the entire battery value chain from development and cathode processing through to cell production. Three Sites, Complementary Roles Each facility is designed with a distinct strategic purpose and ownership structure: - Valencia, Spain — The flagship hub. PowerCo holds a 51% majority stake in the gigafactory currently under construction, which will be reoriented to produce PowerCo’s Unified Cell in LFP format. Gotion invests approximately €1.1 billion for its 49% share, reflecting the site’s centrality to Volkswagen’s volume plans. Because the plant is still being built, it can be engineered for LFP from the ground up rather than retrofitted, a decisive advantage in speed and efficiency. - Šurany, Slovakia — Gotion holds a 51% majority here, converting an existing cell plant to supply LFP batteries for both electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems (ESS). Serving two markets from one line provides operational flexibility as EV adoption rates evolve, giving the facility a second, more stable revenue stream. PowerCo contributes around €470 million across this and the Kenitra site combined for its 49% stakes. - Kenitra, Morocco — Upstream security. Gotion holds 51% in a new facility producing LFP cathode active material, diversifying supply sources and expanding the regional value chain beyond cell assembly alone. All three ventures will operate under joint management, combining PowerCo’s cell design and platform integration strengths with Gotion’s manufacturing process expertise. Frank Blome, CEO of PowerCo, emphasised the partnership’s resilience: “It strengthens the resilience of our value chain, accelerates industrialization and combines PowerCo’s capabilities with the strengths of a long-standing partner.” Broader Restructuring Frames the Push The battery initiative advances alongside a comprehensive Group-wide efficiency drive unveiled by CEO Oliver Blume at the June 2026 annual general meeting. Volkswagen targets annual net savings exceeding €6 billion by 2030, including roughly 50,000 job reductions across the Group, 35,000 at Volkswagen AG alone, with over 28,000 departures already agreed through collective bargaining. Factory costs in Germany fell by more than 20% in 2025, and the Group aims to lift operating return on sales from 3.3% in the first quarter of 2026 to between 8% and 10% by decade’s end. Pressures are intense: first-quarter profit dropped 28.4% to €1.56 billion, revenue fell 2.5%, and US tariffs alone cost an estimated $4 billion annually. In this context, LFP leadership is not just a technology play; it is a pathway to lower vehicle costs and restored margins. Strategic Alignment and Shared Evolution Concurrent with the joint ventures, Volkswagen is selling down a 5.3% equity stake in Gotion to optimise capital structure while retaining full board representation and voting rights, a financial recalibration that leaves the strategic partnership intact. Gotion Chairman Li Zhen characterised the relationship as transcending typical supplier-customer ties: “Six years of close collaboration have built deep mutual trust… together we are accelerating our global strategic cooperation.” Realising the ambition will depend on execution at scale. LFP manufacturing differs materially from nickel-rich chemistries, requiring new materials, electrode processing, and pack design. Running dual-product lines in Šurany adds further operational complexity. As the Group acknowledged, covering the value chain on paper is one thing; delivering consistent yield, ramp-up speed, and quality cell by cell is where the claim will be proven. The PowerCo–Gotion alliance answers a defining question for European automotive: who will build the batteries that power mass-market electrification? By combining European industrial ambition with proven LFP expertise, Volkswagen is positioning itself to lead the transition while strengthening supply chain independence. Success will not be measured in announcements, but in affordable vehicles rolling off production lines powered by cells made on the continent and in the resilience of a partnership built to last. artigo.texto: Leader Energy breaks ground on 100-MW battery project in Malaysia It is scheduled for commissioning in 2027 under Malaysia’s MyBeST programme. Malaysia-based Leader Energy Group Berhad has begun construction of a 100-megawatt (MW)/400-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system (BESS) in Pajam, Negeri Sembilan. The facility is scheduled for commissioning in 2027 under Malaysia’s Battery Energy Storage System bidding programme (MyBeST). It is expected to improve flexibility in Peninsular Malaysia’s electricity grid, supporting renewable energy integration and helping manage changes in electricity supply and demand. Administered by Malaysia’s Energy Commission, MyBeST comprises four grid-connected BESS projects, each with a capacity of 100MW/400MWh. Together, the projects represent 400 MW of power capacity and 1,600 MWh of energy storage capacity. The programme supports Malaysia’s goals of reducing reliance on fossil-fuel peaking plants, lowering electricity system costs over time and achieving the National Energy Transition Roadmap’s target of 70% renewable energy capacity by 2050. Leader Energy’s project forms part of this national effort to develop energy storage infrastructure alongside renewable generation. “As Malaysia’s renewable energy capacity grows, the electricity system needs greater flexibility to manage when power is available and when it is needed,” said Dato’ Sean H’ng, Executive Deputy Chairman and Group CEO of Leader Energy. “Storage helps meet that need.”

artigo.texto: In the American psyche, data centers have become so reviled that big tech can’t even pay residents life changing money to welcome the facilities into their backyards. That’s not an exaggeration: voters in the former coal-mining community of Hazle Township, Pennsylvania are mobilizing en masse against a massive Amazon Web Services facility that would come along with a $10,000 direct cash dividend to every resident. That’s according to reporting by PennLive, which notes that nearly 17 percent of the township’s residents live below the federal poverty line. Despite the possibility of a $10,000 payout, residents are organizing to reject both the data center campus itself — named “Project Hazelnut” by the developer NorthPoint Development — and a lengthy stretch of power lines meant to supply power to the facility. As PennLive observes, the $10,000 scheme is an unusual attempt by a data center developer to smooth over opposition in a section of the country which is overwhelmingly opposed to the facilities. “We think it’s creative. We’ve not seen (anything like) this,” executive director of the Pennsylvania Ethics Commission Mary Fox told PennLive of the strategy. Yet residents of Hazle Township aren’t swayed by the prospect of fast cash, viewing it as a payoff, and a weak one at that. “It’s like bribery,” as local resident Brian Malloy told PennLive. “Our property values are going to drop. Dramatically,” said Ed Negra, a homeowner and small business owner who characterized the $10,000 as a drop in the bucket compared to the cost of allowing Project Hazelnut to go forward. “If that’s not a bribe, I don’t know what is.” The matter is far from settled, though it doesn’t help that both state and local officials are acting shifty. Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, for example, has previously characterized the project as a “technology campus,” using an executive order to fast-track the process by which developers can erect data center facilities across Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, PennLive reports that Hazle Township supervisor Anthony Griguoli has struggled to present a united front with NorthPoint Development, even as his office works to engineer a zoning ordinance which would allow Project Hazelnut to plow forward. When residents cornered Griguoli at a town meeting in August about the $10,000 bribes, he shrugged that “that’s what they’re saying they want to do,” adding that “I don’t even know if that’s legit, that it’s going to happen.” More on data centers: This Graph of Data Center Spending Compared to All Other Construction Will Give You Chills

artigo.texto: Mount Pleasant finalizes 2-year data center development pause MOUNT PLEASANT, S.C. (WCSC) — Mount Pleasant is officially pausing any possible data center development. Mount Pleasant town leaders finalized a moratorium, buying time to figure out where these facilities belong and where they don’t. The originally proposed moratorium was for 120 days, but the council extended that pause to two years, giving the town time to study where and how data centers could fit into the community. “We are starting to feel the pressure, predominantly upstate, but we’re certainly starting to feel it in the region,” Michelle Reed, the town of Mount Pleasant’s director of planning, land use and neighborhoods, said. Across the country, towns and cities are working on ways to manage data center development. Mount Pleasant’s code allows data centers in some commercial and industrial zones. “They were actually permitted in area-wide business two, light industrial and our economic development properties. We don’t have a lot of light industrial, but we have a lot of AB2 properties. Most of them are not vacant, but that doesn’t mean we wouldn’t lose a use and perhaps a data center could come in,” Reed said. “It gives us time to study the issue and to make sure that we’re protecting our residents and protecting our natural resources,” Daniel Brownstein, a member of Mount Pleasant Town Council, said. Power usage, water and noise are all major concerns that the town is looking to address. “There are environmental impacts that we want to look at as well, and make sure we have the proper locations for them, proper buffering, those sorts of things if we were to have one come to the town,” Reed said. Those are concerns that environmental groups also want at the forefront of the conversation. “Recent analysis from the Sierra Club is warning that the data centers under development right now could reverse 15 years of climate progress in just three years,” Taylor Allred, State Energy and Climate Program director at the Coastal Conservation League, said. “Pivoting away from evaporative cooling technology that uses a lot of water toward more closed-loop systems that use less water. And that’s generally a good thing, but there are some concerns that need to be addressed with those systems. For one thing, they tend to use more energy. And the power plants that produce that energy use water too. Not to mention air pollution and other issues. Potentially, some of the coolants used in some of these closed-loop systems could be hazardous. So, making sure that containment and spill avoidance is properly accounted for is really important too.” But not every data center looks like the massive campuses being built by big tech companies. This moratorium applies to facilities of at least one megawatt, and the town says it’s working to avoid unintended consequences for local businesses. “The video game developer that just needs some of their data, but they don’t need a huge system; they have to get it from somewhere. And so, that’s what we’ve been helping do. Smaller scale, up to 1 MW of compute can actually fit in a 20-ft by 8-ft container and take up less than half an acre of space. The sound is no more than a commercial air conditioning unit and it doesn’t use any more water than like a regular garden at your house,” Andrew Harris, a local business owner and resident in Mount Pleasant, said. “There are a lot of industries and businesses, commercial centers, strip malls, parking lots of a Target where those owners of those properties are interested in somehow figuring out a way to increase income. We install the canopy solar that feeds EV charging, but that canopy solar also can feed these data compute centers, which allows that landowner or business owners to actually get a little bit more income based on selling that kind of compute versus a corner of their parking lot that otherwise was sitting vacant.” The town will study suitable locations and development conditions, then recommend changes to its zoning code and comprehensive plan. If a data center development is proposed, the town says it should go through a public approval process. “The people of South Carolina deserve to have a seat at the table with respect to the future of data center development in our state,” Allred said. “The real work begins with making sure that we’re limiting it and making sure that if there were a data center to come to town, that there would be a public process for it to go through rather than our current zoning code which would just allow it by right without a public process,” Brownstein said. Rules around data center development are expected to be taken up in the State House. Environmentalists say that will be a key test: whether statewide standards could be enough for Mount Pleasant, or whether the town will need stronger protections of its own. For now, this creates a temporary pause on accepting, processing or approving applications, permits or other requests related to data centers in Mount Pleasant. Copyright 2026 WCSC. artigo.texto: It’s not just your electricity bill that could be going up — it sounds like the massive boom in AI data centers is making practically everything more expensive. As the Washington Post reports, officials at the Federal Reserve are starting to sing a different tune after blaming president Donald Trump’s tariff war on rising prices, admitting that the explosion in “AI-related investments” is contributing to inflationary pressures. That’s on top of Trump’s Iran war already sending the price of oil soaring. Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee told Semafor that AI-tied inflation is “jumping out of its lane.” “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said. “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” In economics, overheating occurs when aggregate demand outpaces productive capacity, leading to demand-side inflation, higher prices, and eventually reduced demand and consumption. In the worst case scenario, overheating can even trigger a recession. “It takes a long time for overheated demand to get going, and once it’s going, it’s hard to get rid of that,” Goolsbee added. While the prices for groceries have yet to be directly impacted, economists are wondering whether it’s only a matter of time. Worse yet, whether raising the interest rate, which makes borrowing more expensive and lowers consumer spending, will be able to meaningfully address rising inflation, is also starting to look less like a certain bet. The Fed raised interest rates in September, the first time in three years, as inflation proves tough to beat. Futures markets expect yet another increase later this month, according to Reuters. Meanwhile, the tens of billions of dollars being spent on AI data centers are starting to mask some fundamental problems plaguing the US economy, triggering fears over what it could look like if the AI bubble were to burst. Sectors that have already seen instant knock-on effects from the construction boom have been consumer electronics becoming practically unaffordable, as well as a major shortage in skilled labor available for housing projects. According to Goolsbee, “it’s clear what the Fed has to do” if inflation “remains persistent:” continue raising rates. But as tech companies show no signs of slowing down their extreme levels of spending, that lever may end up driving up the cost of investment — a reality that would make things tougher for AI companies as well. artigo.texto: As Georgia becomes one of the fastest-growing markets for data centers, voters are approaching their ballots wondering where candidates stand on their development — especially southeast Georgians who soon will see a hyperscale OpenAI data center built in their "backyard." One of the most significant races for data center development is the state Public Service Commission, which has five seats, and is the regulatory body for Georgia Power and other state utilities. While the PSC doesn't decide where data centers are built, it does make decisions on how much energy power companies serve these facilities and for how much. In August, PSC members reviewed and approved the large load contract for Georgia Power to serve electricity to the future OpenAI data center in Effingham County. Two seats are up for election in November. Republican Joshua Tolbert and Democrat Shelia Edwards are competing for the District 5 seat, while Democratic incumbent Peter Hubbard and Republican former PSC member Fitz Johnson are facing off — again — for District 3. District 5: Tolbert vs. Edwards Tolbert, who has an engineering background in building power plants, said he believes Georgia should welcome businesses that want to invest in the state from factories to data centers. However, he said local communities should be able to decide whether they want data centers and where they should be located. He criticized the lack of transparency with Effingham County's OpenAI announcement. "Number two, if they do decide they want a data center, that should not come on the financial backs of the local members of the community," Tolbert said. "That is where the PSC comes in." The PSC should be ensuring that data center development does not shift costs onto residential customers or other communities, he said. Tolbert also said there is a difference between the direct cost of electricity and less obvious costs associated with serving massive new loads. "It's very easy to make sure the data centers pay for the electricity they use," he said. "The part that's more challenging is adding infrastructure, whether it's transmission lines or pipelines or purchasing fuel reservations. How are those costs being allocated? How are they being paid for?" Tolbert was also critical of the PSC's 2025 decision to approve roughly 10 gigawatts of new generation. He said he objected because much of the projected demand was speculative at the time. "If the forecast is wrong, who's paying for that," he said When approaching large load contracts as a PSC commissioner, Tolbert said he would scrutinize the contract's collateral, termination provisions and payments to determine whether the data center is paying more than the incremental cost of serving it. He also supports considering solar and other generation technologies as part of Georgia's energy mix, but said power companies must evaluate resources according to the particular needs of the grid rather than selecting technologies in advance. Edwards has a background in Cobb County politics and working in the Kennedy Space Center's Space Shuttle Program. She ran for the Georgia PSC in 2022, but her race was taken off the ballot because of a voting-rights lawsuit that was ongoing at the time. Edwards is back and when it comes to data centers, she said both the state and local governments have offered too many incentives to data center companies, causing development to move too quickly. "They should have to pay their own way," she said. "You kick women and children off of welfare, but you allow these companies to come into our state and get corporate welfare." Edwards also criticized the state for a lack of regulations for things such as data center's water usage, noise pollution and ensuring ratepayers are protected from paying for increased energy demand. She also called for greater transparency around large-load contracts. When it comes to approaching these contracts, Edwards said she would push for fewer redactions and an end to nondisclosure agreements. She said Georgia residents should be able to see what they are paying for and how major projects, like OpenAI's, affect utility costs. She said she also wants contracts to include clearer plans for water use and community benefits as well as protections for ratepayers, ensuring data center companies are paying for needed infrastructure and not receiving abatements or incentives. Edwards said she would like to push for utility companies powering data centers to look into more renewable energy resources, including solar. She said she also worries about strains on power grids, particularly in severe storm-prone south Georgia. Edwards said she also questions the long-term risk of building large amounts of infrastructure around an industry that is expanding rapidly but remains relatively new. "If that bubble bursts," she asked, "who's left holding the bill?" District 3: Hubbard vs. Johnson Hubbard is a former renewable-energy developer and energy analyst and has been vocal about his belief that Georgia needs a more comprehensive state policy for data centers. Hubbard said Georgia has provided substantial incentives to data centers while also allowing them to access electricity under favorable large-load arrangements, thus "rolling out the red carpet," for them. When approaching large load contracts, Hubbard said he would push for additional safeguards, including financial protections if projects terminate early. He also supports provisions allowing data centers to reduce electricity consumption during periods of grid stress. Hubbard was one of the commissioners to review the OpenAI contract and got the review period extended because he believed such a significant contract deserved more scrutiny. The commissioner said another major concern is how the electricity needed to power new data centers is generated. artigo.texto: Dear Gov. Gregg Abbott I’m sure you are aware that in every statewide election, the Texas hill country counties cast 80% of their votes for the Republican candidates running for statewide offices. The huge Republican numbers cast by voters in the conservative rural counties offset the Democrat vote totals in the large Democrat controlled Texas cities. However this year, those of us that call the Texas hill country home, are having a hard time trying to decide how to vote for Governor. For most of our lives, conservative hill country voters have voted for Republican candidates. This year however we have a real problem Governor. Those of us that live here don’t want Lithium Battery Energy Storage Systems built in our communities and you, a republican, are allowing their construction. Our concerns with the planned BESS facilities are many: • The construction site in Harper is within 300 yards of a school campus containing 600+ students and teachers with potential fires sending plumes of toxic smoke into the school campus. • The construction site is within 100 feet of the headwaters of the Pedernales River with potential contamination of the Pedernales waterway a real possibility. • Potential for thermal runaway fires containing toxic gas release. Thermal runaway can lead to explosions and fires within seconds. • Residual ash thermal runaway fire contains toxic materials, strong winds can blow this toxic ash far and wide and cause soil and water contamination. • Battery storage fires at a facility in California have shown that lithium gas can potentially kill/harm nearby outdoor pets and livestock. • A pressure wave from a blast can damage nearby homes and has been known to send shrapnel over a 1/2 mile away. • HVFD’s total inability to fight a Bess fire because of lack of proper equipment and training in thermal runaway fires. • Nearby property values are expected to drop 10 to 30% or more depending on how close your property is in relation to the BESS facility. Governor, not only are you willing to let these facilities be built in our communities but you are also giving the developer incentives by making low interest rate loans available from the $10 Billion Texas Energy Fund. How do we vote for you this November, when you are the one trying to shove these BESS facilities down our throats. I don’t understand how you can be in favor of subsidizing a toxic BESS facility that will be built within a few feet of the headwaters of the Pedernales River, the same Pedernales River that empties into Lake Travis, the lake that supplies drinking water to the city of Austin. So Governor, perhaps you can come to Fredericksburg or Kerrville sometime before November 3 and tell the thousands of Republican voters that live here in the hill country why we should vote for you again. We don’t want these Battery Energy Storage Systems built here. If you need backup power for the Texas Electric Grid, offer loan incentives to natural gas power plants only - not lithium battery systems. We need answers before the Nov 3 election Governor.

artigo.texto: Projeto da Mombak prevê restaurar 7,2 mil hectares e gerar créditos de carbono; operação anterior eleva a R$ 360 milhões o financiamento do banco à empresa restauração de áreas degradadas na Amazônia é uma necessidade ambiental, mas, quando uma operação privada destinada a recuperar florestas também abre caminho para a geração e comercialização de créditos de carbono, o dinheiro público exige uma conta completa: quanto custa, quais resultados entrega e quem fica com os ganhos econômicos. O Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) aprovou financiamento de R$ 200 milhões para a Mombak, empresa especializada em projetos de remoção de carbono. O empreendimento prevê restaurar 7,2 mil hectares, principalmente no Pará, com investimento total estimado em R$ 457 milhões e prazo de financiamento de 25 anos. Segundo o banco, o projeto poderá remover mais de 4,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente ao longo de 50 anos, com potencial de gerar até 4,7 milhões de créditos de remoção de carbono. Esses ativos poderão ser negociados no mercado voluntário e, futuramente, em mercados regulados. A operação foi anunciada pelo BNDES em 21 de setembro. O financiamento representa aproximadamente 44% do investimento previsto. Em uma conta direta, equivale a cerca de R$ 27,8 mil por hectare em recursos financiados pelo banco. Considerado o investimento total, o custo projetado chega a R$ 63,5 mil por hectare. Os números, isoladamente, não demonstram desperdício nem irregularidade. A restauração florestal envolve preparo do solo, aquisição de sementes e mudas, plantio, manejo, manutenção e monitoramento. O que eles justificam é uma pergunta objetiva sobre as condições financeiras e os resultados esperados de uma operação dessa dimensão. O projeto não se limita à recomposição da vegetação nativa. A captura de carbono prevista poderá dar origem a créditos comercializáveis, criando uma fonte potencial de receita para o empreendimento. É um modelo econômico que pode contribuir para a recuperação de áreas degradadas e para o enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Mas a combinação de financiamento público de longo prazo com receitas futuras provenientes de ativos ambientais também exige transparência sobre a distribuição dos riscos e dos benefícios. Quais são os juros e as demais condições contratuais do financiamento? Que garantias foram exigidas? Quem será titular dos créditos gerados e como se dará sua comercialização? Se a captura de carbono ficar abaixo das projeções ou os preços dos créditos caírem, quem absorverá os prejuízos? São questões que não pressupõem qualquer irregularidade. Constituem, porém, parte necessária da avaliação de um empreendimento apoiado por uma política pública. O financiamento de R$ 200 milhões não é o primeiro concedido pelo BNDES à Mombak. Em agosto de 2024, o banco anunciou uma operação de R$ 160 milhões para projetos de restauração de 13 mil hectares na Amazônia. Naquela primeira operação, os recursos foram divididos entre R$ 80 milhões do Fundo Clima e R$ 80 milhões da linha BNDES Finem. Portanto, não se deve confundir o valor total do financiamento com a parcela proveniente especificamente do Fundo Clima. Com a nova operação, os financiamentos aprovados para a empresa somam R$ 360 milhões, enquanto os dois projetos preveem recuperar aproximadamente 20,2 mil hectares. Segundo o BNDES, até junho de 2026, 9,4 mil hectares do primeiro empreendimento já haviam sido implantados. O dado permite avançar na apuração. Quais resultados ambientais já podem ser medidos? Quanto foi efetivamente desembolsado e qual é o cronograma dos recursos restantes? Que indicadores de sobrevivência das árvores, recuperação da biodiversidade e remoção de carbono estão sendo utilizados para avaliar o projeto anterior? E de que maneira esses resultados foram considerados na aprovação do novo financiamento? A previsão divulgada pelo banco é de até 440 empregos diretos e 65 indiretos durante a implantação do novo projeto. Depois dessa fase, a estimativa é manter aproximadamente 50 postos de trabalho, entre diretos e indiretos. A diferença entre o emprego temporário e o permanente não invalida o empreendimento. Projetos de restauração podem produzir benefícios ambientais duradouros sem depender de uma grande estrutura permanente de pessoal. Ainda assim, é pertinente conhecer a parcela dos investimentos que permanecerá na economia paraense, a participação de fornecedores locais e as oportunidades abertas aos moradores das áreas abrangidas. A recuperação da floresta pode gerar benefícios muito além da captura de carbono, mas esses resultados precisam ser identificados e acompanhados. Também importa saber onde estão as áreas contempladas, quais são as condições dos contratos com os proprietários e como serão monitorados os resultados ambientais ao longo das décadas previstas para a operação. A Amazônia precisa de floresta em pé. Precisa igualmente de ciência, saneamento, infraestrutura, regularização fundiária, fiscalização, bioeconomia e geração de renda para quem vive no território. O desafio é impedir que a valorização econômica do carbono se descole dos interesses ambientais e sociais da região que o produz. Restaurar florestas com financiamento público pode ser uma política acertada. Mas o resultado não deve ser medido apenas pelo número de hectares recuperados ou de toneladas de CO₂ que se espera retirar da atmosfera. É preciso saber quanto custará a recuperação, quais benefícios serão comprovados, como os riscos serão distribuídos e quem ficará com a receita gerada pelos créditos de carbono. •Os rumores chegaram ao fim no sábado, 10. A prefeita de Marituba, Patrícia Alencar (foto), anunciou nas redes sociais que está grávida de uma menina, fruto do relacionamento com o prefeito de Mãe do Rio, Bruno Rabelo. Agora é esperar a chegada da pequena - e desejar saúde à futura mamãe e à bebê. •Deputados que andavam de olho na área da saúde do Estado podem tirar o cavalinho da chuva.

artigo.texto: Shelby Co. Commissioner holds data center moratorium meeting MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - A Shelby County commissioner spent time Thursday breaking down the data center moratorium to her constituents. Commissioner Henri Brooks and the Memphis Community Against Pollution held a town hall about the temporary ban on new data center developments. The event was held at First Baptist Church on Broad. Shelby County commissioners narrowly advanced a proposed temporary moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas outside the city limits Monday. Commissioner Brooks said the vote was important even if there are no data centers planned in that area. “Even though there are no data centers, we still need to move forward, be proactive, get ahead of these developers, so that they’ll know the rules that we’re gonna play by,” Commissioner Brooks said. The Greater Memphis Chamber has come out against the moratorium, saying Memphis is uniquely positioned to lead the nation in responsible digital infrastructure growth and the moratorium will hurt the advantageous place Memphis has right now. artigo.texto: Silicon has long been the dream anode material for lithium-ion batteries. Its theoretical capacity of 4,200 milliampere-hours per gram is nearly ten times that of the graphite used in virtually every commercial cell, and unlocking it would transform the energy density of everything from electric vehicles to grid storage. The problem is that silicon has also been a nightmare: it swells by more than 300 percent during lithiation, cracks into powder, and grows an ever-thickening solid electrolyte interface that consumes electrolyte and drains performance cycle after cycle. A research team from D. Y. Patil Education Society in Kolhapur, the Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology in Pune, and Chonnam National University in Gwangju now reports a strikingly simple answer, built from three humble ingredients: hierarchically porous spherical cluster silicon nanoparticles, carbonized sucrose powder, and activated charcoal. The composite anode, assembled in a standard CR2032 3-volt half-cell, delivered a specific capacity of 3,412.44 milliampere-hours per gram at a rate of 0.56 C, with an energy density of 204.74 watt-hours per kilogram. The initial capacity of the half-cell, 3,103.42 milliampere-hours per gram, declined to 1,674.53 milliampere-hours per gram after 200 cycles at 2.57 C. Those numbers may not sound like a complete victory, but in the silicon anode field, where pristine silicon electrodes often collapse within a few dozen cycles, the retention of more than half the initial capacity over 200 cycles at a demanding rate is a meaningful achievement. The team attributes the resilience to a dual charge-storage mechanism that blends faradaic bulk reactions with pseudocapacitive surface processes. The structural analysis reveals why the material behaves the way it does. X-ray diffraction showed sharp crystalline silicon peaks at 28.91, 47.76, 56.69, 69.69, and 76.97 degrees, corresponding to the (111), (220), (311), (400), and (331) planes, alongside a broad amorphous silicon dioxide hump near 14 degrees. Using the Scherrer equation, the team calculated an average crystallite size of 96.75 nanometers, closely matching the roughly 100-nanometer particle size supplied by the manufacturer. The amorphous silicon dioxide layer, far from being a defect, acts as a passivation shell that protects the crystalline core from further oxidation and helps absorb the mechanical strain of repeated lithium insertion and extraction. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed the surface chemistry. Broad silanol bands between 3,300 and 3,500 inverse centimeters, together with Si-O-Si asymmetric stretching vibrations at 1,192.31, 1,084.17, and 885.56 inverse centimeters, revealed a hydrated, siloxane-rich surface. The team notes that these silanol groups enhance wettability, improving electrolyte penetration and lithium-ion diffusion during cycling. Notably, the absence of carbon-hydrogen stretching peaks in the 2,852 to 2,924 inverse centimeter region indicated high material purity with minimal organic contamination, while residual Si-H stretching modes at 1,868 and 2,258 inverse centimeters pointed to some surface hydride bonds. Brunauer-Emmett-Teller and Barrett-Joyner-Halenda analysis painted a picture of a mesoporous architecture with a specific surface area of 61.89 square meters per gram and an average pore diameter of 38.50 nanometers. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy showed porous spherical clusters formed by aggregated particles ranging from 50 to 200 nanometers. Raman spectroscopy found a sharp first-order silicon-silicon vibration peak at 523 inverse centimeters, confirming a highly ordered crystalline lattice with minimal defects and low residual stress. Perhaps most strikingly, a water contact angle measurement showed the electrode surface to be superhydrophilic, with droplets spreading completely at a zero-degree angle, ensuring uniform electrolyte contact across the entire coating. Cyclic voltammetry between 0.0 and 3.0 volts at scan rates from 20 to 200 millivolts per second revealed redox peaks near 1.5 and 1.0 volts corresponding to lithium insertion and deinsertion. The absence of a distinct intercalation peak between 1.0 and 0.5 volts suggested that lithium storage in this voltage window proceeds through surface-dominated faradaic processes rather than classical bulk intercalation. When the team measured stability at 200 millivolts per second across 700 cycles, the voltammetric profiles barely changed, indicating sustained redox activity and preserved electrochemical performance over long-term operation. The charge-storage kinetics were dissected using a power-law relation between peak current and scan rate. The analysis showed that the anode stores the majority of its charge through diffusion-controlled bulk redox reactions, with a capacitive contribution of 37.79 percent at 200 millivolts per second. As the scan rate decreased, the diffusion-controlled contribution increased, driving higher specific capacity. The team suggests that the increased film thickness of the coated electrode allows deeper penetration of the LiPF6 electrolyte, promoting bulk redox activity throughout the active material rather than confining reactions to the surface. Galvanostatic charge-discharge measurements across a wide range of C-rates, from 0.56 C all the way to 2,155.69 C, showed discharge plateaus associated with electrolyte decomposition and solid electrolyte interface formation at all current densities. The lithium-silicon alloy phases evolved systematically during cycling: Li15Si4 formed in the initial stage, transitioning to Li21Si5 as capacity declined, and later to Li13Si4. artigo.texto: The European Union Emissions Trading System: What Can We Learn from the Proposed Changes to One of the World’s Longest-Running Carbon Pricing Policies? This issue brief dives into key proposed changes to the European Union Emissions Trading System and their implications for several industrial products. Introduction On July 17, 2026, the European Commission published a proposal to revise the EU emissions trading system (ETS). ETS revisions tend to happen roughly every five years to account for changes in the European Union’s overall climate policy and the global economy. Earlier this year, the European Union confirmed its climate target for 2040 of reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 90 percent relative to 1990. In this issue brief, we review some of the key proposed changes to the ETS design, especially as related to allowance allocation and other design elements that are relevant to industrial product regulation. 1. Allowance Supply: More Supply and a More Flexible Supply As a cap-and-trade system, the EU ETS shrinks the allowance supply each year by a fixed amount—the linear reduction factor. Under the current trajectory, no new allowances would be issued after 2039. Under the proposed new trajectory, the cap is lowered more gradually, especially after 2036, so that it will not reach zero until 2048. For reference, in 2025, total ETS emissions were 1,009 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, a 51.8 percent reduction compared to 2005 (the ETS launch year). Figure 1 shows the development of the ETS allowance supply and emissions covered by the system since 2013. Figure 1. EU Emissions Trading System Allowance Supply and Emissions by Sector, 2013–2025 The European Union proposes to create room for additional ETS supply through the purchase of 260 million international carbon credits (funded by selling ETS allowances). This would increase domestic emissions in exchange for more international reductions, but only if the credits can be procured in the desired quantity and quality. If not, the ETS cap will still be reduced commensurately. Another source of additional supply is permanent carbon removals. The European Union proposes that companies under the ETS can also buy units certified under its carbon removal certification mechanism and use these for compliance. Because permanent carbon removal is costly, likely exceeding the ETS allowance price, it is unclear if the volumes of removals will be significant. 2. Allowances Allocated for Free: More Conditionality, More Benchmarks? Free allocation in energy-intensive industries in the EU ETS has been justified as a compensation mechanism against the risk of carbon leakage risk. With protecting industrial competitiveness as a goal, making free allocation conditional (e.g., on low-carbon investment) has been resisted. This may be changing, as the commission suggests making it conditional on companies submitting transition plans for their facilities that align with the European Union’s climate neutrality goals. Twenty percent of free allowances may face even stricter rules, as operators will need to prove that they invested the value in actual decarbonization of their facilities. Unlike with the other allowances, this 20 percent would not be allocated ex ante but several years later, after verification of the investments. Although conditionalities like this may be heavily contested during the upcoming legislative process, the proposal reflects a core challenge in free-allocation design. It carries a high opportunity cost in foregone auction revenue that could be used to finance green industrial policy. Shifting free allocation from a compensatory logic to directly supporting low-carbon investments can be a way to bridge a period when allocation mostly benefits conventional, higher-emitting producers to one where it benefits lower-carbon producers as a decarbonization coinvestment mechanism. Figure 2. Free Allocation and Verified Emissions in the EU Emissions Trading System The European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism also fits here, as it will gradually replace free allowances. However, the proposal suggests a more gradual phaseout of free allowances to sectors included in the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), so the effective price for CBAM certificates will not reflect the full ETS price for a few years longer (until 2038), as the price is adjusted for the share of free allocation (see Figure 3). The full CBAM payment obligation depends on not just this CBAM factor but the emissions embedded in imported goods. If actual emissions data cannot be verified, default values apply as a fallback approach, which act as an intensity benchmark. Figure 3. Current and Proposed Phase-In of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism 3. Benchmarks: Technical Allocation Rules Can Affect Decarbonization Incentives A more technical change to free allocation concerns benchmarks. These are set at the product level and should ensure that free allocation volumes are “benchmarked” to the 10 percent most efficient EU installations for a given product. However, some industrial facilities yield many different products (e.g., refineries or the chemicals industry). In these cases, input-based fallback benchmarks are used that relate more to generic industrial processes (heat and fuel consumption, expressed as GHG emissions per terajoule of input) than to products (expressed in output terms as tons of GHG per ton of product). Examining the evolution of ETS benchmarks can provide insight into policy design choices that also are relevant when considering product carbon intensity standards—a topic that Resources for the Future will work on over the coming year. Heat and fuel benchmarks in the EU ETS are based on a baseline (2007–2008) performance and have been ratcheting since then. The lower the value, the fewer free allowances per unit of product. artigo.texto: Ampotech and Buskowitz Energy Collaborate to Deliver Integrated Energy Solutions Combining Energy Efficiency, Solar and Battery Storage SINGAPORE, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ampotech and Buskowitz Energy are collaborating to help commercial and industrial customers in the Philippines unlock greater energy savings and sustainability through an integrated approach combining energy efficiency, rooftop solar, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and AI-powered energy management. The collaboration combines Buskowitz Energy's solar development, engineering, EPC, PPA and battery storage capabilities while Ampotech provides energy efficiency solutions and its AmpoCloud AI-powered energy management platform, enabling customers to integrate and manage multiple energy assets through a unified platform. Combining renewable generation with energy efficiency Under the collaboration, Ampotech identifies commercial and industrial projects where customers can benefit from a combination of energy efficiency measures, rooftop solar PV and/or BESS. Buskowitz provides the renewable energy and energy storage infrastructure, while Ampotech supports the efficiency side and provides the digital intelligence layer through AmpoCloud. This integrated approach is designed to help customers move beyond generating renewable energy alone by also improving how energy is measured, managed and optimized across their facilities. Buskowitz Energy has extensive experience in commercial and industrial solar deployment in the Philippines, with capabilities spanning project development, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), power purchase agreements (PPAs), and operations and maintenance (O&M). Over 3 MWp of projects currently in development Ampotech and Buskowitz are currently working together on 3.3 MWp of solar projects as part of Ampotech's engagement with PEZA locator companies in the Philippines. The collaboration is intended to support businesses operating within economic zones as they look for practical ways to manage rising energy costs, increase renewable energy adoption and improve operational efficiency. Ampotech has been actively working with PEZA and its locator companies to demonstrate how digital energy solutions can support energy efficiency, ESG data management and the integration of distributed energy resources such as solar PV and BESS. Exploring AI-powered management of existing solar assets Beyond new projects, Ampotech and Buskowitz are also discussing a separate Proof of Concept (POC) to deploy Ampotech's distributed energy resource management application across Buskowitz's existing solar portfolio. "Solar is an important part of the energy transition, but maximizing the value of a facility's energy system requires visibility and optimization across on-site generation, storage, and demand," - William Temple, CEO and Co-Founder of Ampotech. "Our collaboration with Buskowitz allows us to combine renewable energy deployment with energy efficiency and AI-driven energy management, helping businesses take a more integrated approach to reducing energy costs and improving sustainability." The proposed POC would explore how centralized digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can provide greater visibility across distributed solar assets and support more efficient asset management. This initiative builds on Buskowitz's established commercial and industrial solar portfolio and its experience in asset monitoring, performance reporting, technical support, and ongoing operations and maintenance. "As our solar portfolio continues to grow, we see opportunities to leverage technology and data to improve how we monitor and manage our assets. Through this collaboration, we look forward to exploring how AI-powered analytics can complement our existing capabilities and support more efficient operations as we continue delivering reliable renewable energy solutions to our customers" — James Buskowitz, CEO, Buskowitz Energy Toward smarter, integrated energy systems The collaboration reflects a broader shift in how commercial and industrial facilities approach energy management. Rather than treating solar generation, battery storage and energy efficiency as separate initiatives, Ampotech and Buskowitz are exploring an integrated model in which these assets can work together as part of a smarter energy system. Through the collaboration, the companies will continue to identify suitable projects, develop integrated energy solutions and explore opportunities to apply digital intelligence across existing and new renewable energy assets. About Ampotech Ampotech provides intelligence driven energy solutions for commercial and industrial clients in Asia Pacific. With over 10 years of experience developing, deploying, and maintaining AI-enabled internet of things and energy asset solutions in the real estate and renewable energy sector, Ampotech is at the forefront of the transition to an AI-native energy sector. For more information visit our website. About Buskowitz Energy Buskowitz Energy is an energy infrastructure company with deep solar expertise. It develops, finances, builds, operates and supplies energy for Philippine businesses under contracts of 20 to 25 years. Founded in 2016, it has delivered more than 300 installations and is financed by international lenders and by institutional infrastructure investors. Website: www.ampotech.com SOURCE Ampotech

artigo.texto: BYD Atto 3 Gets New Atlantis Gray Colour Option in India BYD has replaced Surf Blue with Atlantis Gray on the Atto 3, which continues to offer two battery options, up to 521km of claimed range, and the same equipment list. BYD has introduced a new colour option for the Atto 3 electric SUV in India, with Atlantis Gray replacing the previously available Surf Blue. The change is limited to the exterior colour palette, with no reported updates to the SUV's features, battery packs, or performance. The Atto 3 continues to be offered in multiple variants. Also Read: BYD Denza India Entry Confirmed; Here's What to Expect BYD Atto 3: What's Changed? With Surf Blue discontinued, the BYD Atto 3 is now available in four colours: Atlantis Gray, Cosmos Black, Ski White and Harbour Grey. The SUV retains its existing design, including full-LED lighting, chrome and black exterior elements, a panoramic sunroof and either 17-inch or 18-inch wheels, depending on the variant. BYD Atto 3: Battery The electric SUV is available with 49.92kWh and 60.48kWh battery packs. Both use an electric motor that develops 201bhp and 300Nm of torque. The smaller battery offers an ARAI-certified range of 468km, while the larger unit has a claimed range of 521km. BYD claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 7.3 seconds. For charging, the smaller battery supports DC fast charging at up to 70kW, while the larger pack supports up to 80kW. The cabin features a 12.8-inch rotating touchscreen, wireless smartphone connectivity, wireless charging and a six-speaker audio system. Other equipment includes a powered tailgate, a 360-degree camera, an NFC key card, tyre pressure monitoring and auto-hold. The front seats are electrically adjustable, with six-way adjustment for the driver and four-way adjustment for the front passenger. Safety equipment comprises seven airbags, Level 2 advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and disc brakes on all four wheels, with ventilated discs at the front. The BYD Atto 3 is priced from Rs 24.99 lakh to Rs 34.49 lakh (ex-showroom), depending on the variant. The new colour has not brought a price increase, and the SUV's existing specifications remain unchanged.

artigo.texto: A Resolução CTCP/SBCE nº 5, assinada em 14 de outubro de 2026 e publicada em edição extra do Diário Oficial da União em 15 de outubro, instituiu o Grupo de Trabalho Temático sobre Aspectos de Competitividade do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (GTT Competitividade). O ato é da presidência do Comitê Técnico Consultivo Permanente do SBCE (CTCP/SBCE), com base em deliberação do Plenário de 28 de setembro de 2026. O grupo tem o objetivo de subsidiar tecnicamente o Comitê nas competências previstas no art. 9º, inciso IV, da Lei 15.042/2024 e no art. 2º, inciso II, alínea "e", do Decreto 12.768/2025. O GTT poderá analisar e propor recomendações sobre riscos regulatórios e de competitividade dos setores regulados e de suas cadeias produtivas; risco de deslocamento de produção e emissões para jurisdições sem precificação de carbono equivalente; e impactos econômicos sobre produção, preço, emprego, investimento, produtividade e comércio. A lista inclui ainda indicadores de competitividade, medidas de equalização de custos de carbono frente a bens importados, interoperabilidade com outros mercados de carbono, custos e rotas de descarbonização, alternativas de destinação das receitas do SBCE e o impacto de mecanismos de ajuste de carbono na fronteira adotados por outros países. A coordenação caberá à Subsecretaria de Regulação e Metodologias da Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, que convoca reuniões, define o plano de trabalho e encaminha ao Plenário do CTCP/SBCE os relatórios e recomendações. A Secretaria-Executiva do CTCP/SBCE dará apoio técnico e administrativo. Integrarão o grupo os órgãos e entidades do CTCP/SBCE que manifestarem interesse, cada um com um representante titular e um suplente, com conhecimento técnico ou experiência em temas como mercados de carbono, competitividade industrial e comércio exterior. As indicações devem ser enviadas à Secretaria-Executiva em 10 dias a partir da publicação, por formulário eletrônico a ser disponibilizado.

artigo.texto: AI companies can soften support for statewide data center moratoriums like New Yorkâs by committing to pay for related electricity costs and lessen local environmental impacts, according to a new poll from major firms in both parties. The research was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research â run by Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio and Biden pollster John Anzalone, respectively â on behalf of the American Infrastructure Alliance, a coalition of AI companies, private equity firms, and labor unions advocating for âresponsibleâ data center development. Fifty-eight percent of those polled nationwide said they oppose building data centers in their state, according to results shared first with Semafor. But 54% said they would actually support data center construction if companies pledged to cover electricity costs, protect consumers from higher utility bills, and safeguard surrounding environmental resources; 31% still opposed data center construction outright. The poll also found that seven in 10 voters worry that outright moratoriums on AI data centers could lead to China having more control over infrastructure that houses US information. Meanwhile, 64% said theyâre concerned that bans will lead to jobs, investment, and economic growth going to other states instead.

artigo.texto: - Supermicro expands its Open Compute Project portfolio with integrated AI racks, networking, power and cooling - Standardized 21-inch rack designs aim to simplify deployment of increasingly power-hungry AI systems - The move reflects growing demand for preintegrated infrastructure as server manufacturers compete to deliver complete AI clusters Supermicro is expanding its portfolio of open-standard AI infrastructure, betting that preintegrated racks, cooling systems and networking will help data center operators bring increasingly complex AI installations online faster. The company announced the expansion at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose this week, adding OCP-accepted systems, racks and rear-door heat exchangers to its Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) portfolio. The objective is to deliver more of the infrastructure required for AI computing as a validated system, rather than leaving customers to integrate servers, networking, power distribution and cooling separately. That’s an increasingly important proposition as AI infrastructure moves beyond individual servers toward entire racks and clusters, with growing demands on power delivery and heat removal. Supermicro’s expanded portfolio includes OCP Open Rack version 3 (ORv3) and Open Rack Wide (ORW) designs, centralized 48-volt DC power distribution, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, rear-door heat exchangers and management software. The ORv3 architecture uses wider, 21-inch equipment bays rather than the conventional 19-inch mounting format common in enterprise data centers. It also replaces individual server power supplies and associated cabling with centralized rack-level power distribution. Supermicro is supporting both open-rack and conventional EIA rack designs, allowing customers to select architectures appropriate to their existing facilities. Cooling becomes part of the system Power and cooling are central to the announcement. As GPUs and CPUs become more powerful, the amount of heat generated by densely packed computing equipment is becoming a major constraint on AI data center design. Supermicro’s expanded portfolio includes direct-to-chip liquid cooling and rear-door heat exchangers designed to remove residual heat from server exhaust before it enters the data hall. The company said its rear-door heat exchangers provide cooling capacities ranging from 10 kW to 120 kW, while a separate in-rack coolant distribution unit supports up to 250 kW of cooling capacity. The approach could help operators increase rack density without relying entirely on conventional room-level air conditioning, although actual performance will depend on the configuration and the facility’s cooling infrastructure. Emilio Guerrero, a Supermicro product manager speaking at the OCP event, described the shift toward more efficient power delivery and cooling. “It is a new way to deliver power more efficiently to the servers,” Guerrero said, adding that the design could support 97% heat capture. From server supplier to infrastructure integrator The announcement also reflects a broader change in the competitive position of server manufacturers. Increasingly, customers are buying complete, prevalidated computing environments rather than assembling individual components themselves. ABI Research identified this shift in its assessment of leading AI server suppliers, naming Supermicro, Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Cisco as its five highest-ranked vendors. The research firm highlighted the growing importance of modularity, integrated cooling and deployment services alongside conventional server performance. It also identified openness as an increasingly important consideration, with organizations such as OCP helping establish hardware standards that can simplify upgrades and reduce dependence on proprietary designs. For Supermicro, supporting OCP specifications offers a way to combine hardware from multiple semiconductor suppliers within standardized rack-scale architectures. The company’s portfolio includes systems built around processors and accelerators from Nvidia, AMD and Intel, alongside high-performance Ethernet networking and liquid-cooling infrastructure. But open hardware standards do not necessarily eliminate vendor dependency. Operators must still consider compatibility across management software, networking, accelerators and cooling systems when selecting integrated platforms. Supermicro is also expanding its management software portfolio, including tools for monitoring and automating infrastructure across AI factories, enterprise data centers and cloud environments. That creates an interesting competitive tension: customers want the flexibility associated with open standards, while suppliers increasingly differentiate themselves through their ability to integrate and manage the complete infrastructure stack. For data center operators, the attraction is straightforward. The faster a validated AI cluster can be installed, powered, cooled and connected, the sooner it can begin delivering computing capacity. Whether standardized rack-scale infrastructure can materially reduce deployment times and costs across different facilities remains an important question. Supermicro has outlined the engineering approach but has not provided comparative deployment data in its announcement. For an industry pouring enormous amounts of capital into AI computing, that distinction is worth watching. artigo.texto: - AI workloads are pushing data centers beyond siloed management of facilities and IT resources - Operators increasingly need orchestration layers that can coordinate infrastructure in real time, not just monitor it - The payoff could be better capacity utilization, fewer performance bottlenecks and tighter control over cost and reliability Data centers have historically operated as a collection of little kingdoms, with facilities teams managing power and cooling while IT teams wrangled servers and networks. But the rise of AI and high-performance computing is making this model harder to sustain. Rather than optimizing for their own distinct metrics, data center systems increasingly need to be orchestrated together. What we’re talking about here isn’t too different from the idea of co-design between hardware and software that you might be familiar with. As GPU clusters push rack densities higher and workloads fluctuate faster, factors like compute placement, power availability, cooling capacity and even network behavior have become critical to squeezing the most out of constrained compute and power resources. That shift is creating demand for a new kind of control layer, PADO AI, Hammerhead AI and Texas Instruments told Fierce. The risk if data center operators can’t rise to the task? “Performance breaks first, followed by cost control,” PADO AI’s CEO Wannie Park said. “Poor coordination rarely causes immediate catastrophic physical failure. Instead, it triggers a domino effect across the stack,” with cascading effects hitting performance, cost controls, reliability, cooling efficiency and then network capacity, he said. “We are moving rapidly toward a software-defined control plane where compute, networking, power and cooling operate as a single, holistic optimization domain.” What does a data center orchestration layer look like? At its core, orchestration means moving beyond visibility into active coordination. Data center operators already have plenty of telemetry coming from servers, GPUs, switches, power systems and cooling equipment. The harder problem is turning those siloed feeds into a control layer that can decide, in real time, how to place workloads, adjust cooling, avoid simultaneous power peaks and make fuller use of the capacity already inside the facility. As Hammerhead AI CEO Rahul Kar explained, the goal is not simply to optimize cooling, compute or power independently, but to co-optimize them. Today, there isn’t “one large system or large system of systems that is trying to bring everything together for a common outcome,” Kar said. “If you can coordinate, orchestrate across all these different silos and bring data and controls together, you can squeeze out not only more power, but also more compute from both newer infrastructure as well as the existing infrastructure.” For instance, he added, you could use machine learning and AI to forecast when peak power utilization might happen within a data center and then use an orchestration system to control cooling, compute and anything else behind the meter as a means of managing through that peak. But coordination depends on physical infrastructure that can measure and control what is happening inside the facility. Karthik Vasanth, VP and GM for Texas Instruments’ Data Converter Business Unit, said the company is looking at data center power and cooling “in a holistic manner,” from power efficiency and telemetry to temperature sensors, leak detection and pump controls. "It has to be coordinated, because it is now a complete system solution," he said. "You cannot just say, 'I have the power, but…I don't know how to do the cooling or monitor the cooling.'" To make a coordinated system work, Park said time-synchronized telemetry is needed across four key layers of data center infrastructure: compute (servers and chips), connectivity (switches and network), thermal management (cooling systems) and electrical (power distribution systems). What roles do humans and AI have in data center orchestration? Of course, all of this data would be too much for a human to sift through and react to in real-time. So, AI and automation have a role to play here. “Automation and AI should act as the high-speed nervous system of modern data centers—handling sub-second telemetry, predictive adjustments, and real-time co-optimization across compute, power and cooling,” Park said. But that doesn’t mean humans disappear from the loop. Park said people still play a crucial role in setting strategy, governing risk, establishing policies across different infrastructure domains and stepping in when unusual failure scenarios arise. Humans are also needed to define the guardrails and weigh trade-offs that AI systems may not be able to fully measure or resolve on their own.

artigo.texto: Standalone data centers, including large-scale facilities used to power artificial intelligence, are prohibited under St. Petersburg’s existing zoning regulations, according to a new memorandum from the city’s planning director. In an Oct. 9 memo to Mayor Ken Welch, Planning Director Derek Kilborn clarified how the facilities are classified under the city’s land development code. He concluded that data centers are neither permitted uses nor eligible for special exceptions. The determination comes as local governments across Pinellas County consider how to regulate the rapidly expanding industry amid concerns about electricity consumption, water resources and land availability. St. Petersburg’s zoning code contains a matrix identifying permitted land uses. Data centers are not included, and city regulations presume that uses not specifically listed are prohibited. Kilborn also examined whether data centers could qualify as similar to other permitted uses, including utility infrastructure, but found no sufficient justification. “For these reasons, Data Centers generally, and Large-Scale Data Centers explicitly, remain prohibited as a permitted, principal (P) or Special Exception (SE) use in the City of St. Petersburg,” Kilborn wrote. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Senate Bill 484, which recognizes the infrastructure and environmental challenges of large utility users, like data centers, last May. However, DeSantis preserved local authority over land use regulation in the same bill, which took effect July 1. Under the new law, a large-scale data center is defined as a facility with an anticipated monthly peak electrical demand of at least 50 megawatts at a single location. St. Petersburg’s determination applies to standalone data centers regardless of whether they meet that threshold. The memo follows similar actions elsewhere in Pinellas County. Pinellas Park approved a one-year moratorium on data center development in August. Additionally, in September, county commissioners adopted a resolution restricting large standalone facilities in unincorporated areas. Unlike those actions, St. Petersburg’s memorandum simply clarifies that standalone data centers are already prohibited under existing regulations, and presumably no further action is needed to overhaul the law. It was not indicated whether the city has received any recent data center development proposals, or whether officials are considering changes to the zoning code.

artigo.texto: Impact Carbon Appoints Christopher Morgan Zink CEO to Drive Carbon Market Growth - Leadership Transition: Christopher Morgan Zink takes over as CEO, bringing nearly two decades of experience in international carbon finance and compliance markets. - Climate and Development Impact: Impact Carbon’s programmes reach more than 1.2 million households with efficient cooking solutions and 24 million students with safe drinking water. - Carbon Market Expansion: The company is positioning for growth as demand shifts towards high-integrity carbon credits, Article 6 mechanisms and compliance markets. Impact Carbon has appointed Christopher Morgan Zink as Chief Executive Officer, effective September 30, strengthening its leadership as international carbon markets move towards stricter integrity standards and expanding compliance demand. Zink joins from Conservation International, where he served as Vice President and led the organisation’s global carbon finance activities. His appointment comes as governments and corporate buyers increasingly seek verified emissions reductions with measurable development benefits. The leadership transition places an experienced carbon finance executive at the helm of a company operating across Uganda, Nigeria and Kenya. Leadership Change Positions Impact Carbon for Expansion Zink brings nearly two decades of experience spanning conservation finance, government policy and commercial carbon markets. Before joining Conservation International, he spent 15 years working in climate and carbon finance with the Swedish government and Dutch energy trading company Eneco. His experience covers both public and private carbon financing mechanisms, providing expertise as international markets adapt to new regulatory frameworks. Impact Carbon’s founders, Evan Haigler and Tim Neville, will remain closely involved in the business. Zink will assume responsibility for day-to-day operations and strategic execution. Announcing his appointment, Zink said: “I just started as CEO of Impact Carbon. Impact Carbon is one of the longest-running carbon project developers in the market. Nearly twenty years of taking energy-efficient cooking and safe drinking water to scale, now across Uganda, Nigeria and Kenya, through every phase of the carbon market. The scale is real: well over a million households cooking on efficient stoves, and 24 million students with safe water at school. I’m still wrapping my head around these numbers.” Carbon Finance Supports Millions Across Africa Impact Carbon has spent nearly two decades developing carbon programmes that combine emissions reductions with measurable social benefits. Its energy-efficient cooking initiatives have reached more than 1.2 million households, primarily in Uganda and Nigeria. These programmes use carbon finance to support access to improved cooking technologies, potentially reducing fuel consumption and associated emissions. The company also develops and manages carbon programmes supporting Impact Water, a major provider of school-based safe drinking water. Impact Water currently serves more than 24 million students across 60,000 schools in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda. By supporting safe drinking water access, these programmes can reduce reliance on boiling water, which often requires biomass fuels. The approach connects carbon finance with broader development priorities, including public health, education and access to cleaner energy. Article 6 and Compliance Markets Shape Growth Strategy Impact Carbon has historically structured its projects with compliance markets in mind, using voluntary carbon markets to support programme development. Its experience spans the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), South Korea’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), and emerging opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The company is also targeting demand associated with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). RELATED ARTICLE: Climate Impact Partners Certifies Lob’s Carbon Neutral Offering Article 6 enables international cooperation on emissions reductions, including transfers of mitigation outcomes between countries under agreed accounting requirements. For project developers, these mechanisms create potential access to new buyers while increasing expectations around verification, authorisation and environmental integrity. Zink described the company’s growth ambitions: “The company is in a growth phase, and the market is moving in the direction I have long believed it should: towards higher-quality units, Article 6 and compliance demand. I believe in the long-term fundamentals of carbon finance as a way to pay for things that work for climate and people, in the places that need them most. That is what Impact Carbon does.” African Carbon Markets Enter a New Phase Zink’s initial engagements include visits to Impact Carbon’s operations and partners in Kenya and Uganda. He is also scheduled to speak at the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali before travelling to Nigeria. His appointment comes amid growing scrutiny of carbon credit quality, particularly around additionality, emissions accounting and the durability of project benefits. For investors and corporate buyers, Impact Carbon’s strategy reflects the increasing importance of connecting verified climate outcomes with established delivery systems. Its expansion will depend on maintaining programme integrity while navigating evolving compliance requirements and buyer expectations. Across Africa, the broader challenge remains translating carbon market demand into reliable financing for climate and development projects. Impact Carbon’s leadership transition places that challenge at the centre of its next phase of growth. artigo.texto: Guilford County commissioners hear public input on proposed data centers Guilford County, N.C. — Guilford County commissioners heard from residents Tuesday evening as they consider whether to temporarily pause new data center projects and craft rules for future development. During the public hearing, community members urged county leaders to take time to study the potential impacts of data centers and to build trust with residents. One speaker told commissioners, “You have the opportunity to build strong trust with the people you represent.” Commissioners have been discussing the possibility of imposing a 180-day moratorium on data centers, which would temporarily halt new projects from moving forward. But several residents argued that six months would not be enough time for the county to gather information and develop protections, calling instead for a 32-month moratorium. “Give your board time to learn all you can about data centers and to use that knowledge to put into place strong policies that protect our community from air, water and noise pollution,” one speaker said. Another resident echoed concerns about the timeline, saying, “When I look at these things, it's clear that you will need more than six months to seriously address these things and protect the health and safety of the residents of Guilford County.” Not everyone at the meeting supported a longer pause. Some speakers said they want the county to remain competitive for future projects. “I don't want to see us sit on the sidelines and someone else scores the touchdown and we say 'man, we could've had that data center,'” one speaker said. No decision was made Tuesday evening. One commissioner cautioned against a one-size-fits-all approach, saying, “Data centers as defined is not one size fits all and I think we have to be careful when we craft legislation, rules, ordinances and those types of things on data centers.” The board voted unanimously to delay any decision on a moratorium until its next meeting on Nov. 5.
