artigo.texto: HiTHIUM Reaches 200GWh Cumulative Shipments Milestone at Chongqing Base HiTHIUM, a global energy storage technology company, marked a cumulative shipment milestone of 200GWh during a ceremony held on October 15, 2026 at its Chongqing manufacturing base, according to a company press release. The press release, issued on October 16, 2026, stated that the company's cumulative shipments moved from surpassing 100GWh in August 2025 to 200GWh, a gain of another 100GWh in roughly a year. The company said shipments began at the end of 2021 and that it has built three core strengths: cost leadership, service quality, and safety and reliability. Its global ranking rose from fifth in 2023 to third in 2024, then to a position among the top two globally in 2025 and the first half of 2026, according to the release. HiTHIUM attributed the advance to capabilities across long-duration energy storage, end-to-end integration, manufacturing supported by its lighthouse factory, and global delivery and service. Leadership Comments on the Milestone Jason Wang, co-founder and chief executive, described the 200GWh level as a new starting point for the company's global development, according to the release. He indicated that HiTHIUM aims to become a leading global energy storage brand through technology innovation, integrated development, and international expansion. The Chongqing manufacturing base, described in the release as the world's first energy storage battery lighthouse factory, serves as a strategic hub that deepens supply-chain collaboration and supports large-scale product delivery, Wang said. Wang also commented that competition in the energy storage industry is no longer defined by individual products but by integrated capabilities across the entire value chain. He said the company will continue to strengthen its competitiveness in three areas: innovation, systems, and responsibility. Three Focus Areas On innovation, the release said HiTHIUM remains focused on energy storage and its long-duration strategy, accelerating global deployment of its first kAh-class integrated long-duration energy storage solution and building full-scenario solutions spanning cells to the grid. On systems, the company is implementing a globalization strategy led by its Xiamen headquarters and supported by the Chongqing manufacturing base and overseas localization, with the aim of driving end-to-end integration across technology, products, supply chain, and delivery. On responsibility, the release said HiTHIUM is committed to the long term by promoting value-chain collaboration through localized operations, fostering new quality productive forces, and contributing to sustainable development for its business, the industry, and local communities. Wang characterized the milestone as a matter of scaling end-to-end capabilities rather than growth alone, according to the release. The company said it will advance long-duration energy storage technology, upgrade its lighthouse factory smart manufacturing system, strengthen global delivery, and pursue the next 100GWh in support of the global green energy transition. - 1. artigo.texto: India's Battery Storage Capacity Projected to Climb Sharply Through 2032 India's annual battery storage installations are expected to roughly double each year through the 2032 fiscal year, according to a report by Nuvama cited by Indian media, as the renewable energy buildout pulls in more investment for battery energy storage systems. The Nuvama analysis places total BESS capacity in India at 302 gigawatt-hours by 2032, compared with 6.3 GWh at present, a trajectory the analysts describe as a compound annual growth rate of 91% over the period. The Central Electricity Authority offers a more conservative view, estimating BESS installations of 236 GWh by FY32 and 1,840 GWh by 2047. The India Energy Storage Alliance said last month that rising renewable capacity will require more battery storage to support growth and give the grid greater flexibility. Discussions at the IESA Chennai Connect 2026 indicated that India would need about 888 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2035-36 to serve growing electricity demand and to integrate renewable power reliably. Ashok Jhunjhunwala, an Institute Professor at IIT Madras, described energy storage as one of the defining technologies of India's energy transition, adding that renewable energy must remain central while being backed by storage to create a stronger, more reliable and increasingly affordable power system. India has recognized the need to scale up battery storage installations substantially to keep pace with rapid renewable energy growth. Authorities plan to introduce a regulation from July 1, 2027 that would require developers of solar and wind projects to install battery storage at project sites, a step aimed at better managing renewable output and reducing curtailments. Even with a major solar and wind installation boom in recent years, India has struggled to fully use those capacities because output has often been curtailed when battery storage is unavailable. - 1. artigo.texto: Albany considers battery storage system to address electricity surplus “For me, this is all about ratepayers. Will this keep our rates low? That’s my biggest concern on a project like this.” ALBANY – In the novel “Catch-22,” it is a persistent point of confusion as to how mess officer Milo Minderbinder can buy eggs for seven cents and sell them for four cents and still make a profit. That question of how the city of Albany is making money by purchasing electricity for 7 cents per kilowatt and selling it for 4 cents is not, by contrast, confusing. The answer is that it is not. The 2025 estimated loss by Albany Utilities based on that equation came out to about $2 million, according to Mayor Bo Dorough, who also chairs the Albany Utility Board. That’s because the city has to sell excess power at times for a lower rate than it is paying. To reduce those losses, the Albany City Commission is considering a battery energy storage system (BESS) that would allow the storing of electricity that could be sold during peak use times at a profit. Earlier this month, the commission heard from representatives of three solar energy companies. Now commissioners are looking for another source to crunch the numbers to determine whether the concept could be beneficial. The two options presented include one featuring a single site on the city’s grid, and the second would place batteries at two sites. During times when energy use is low in Albany, the batteries would store the excess energy purchased. The stored energy would be held in a battery to sell at a better price. The average price per kilowatt for customers is 15 cents in the state, Dorough said. Pete Marte, CEO of Hannah Solar, one of the representatives who spoke at an Oct. 1 commission meeting, estimated that the city could sell excess electricity at perhaps an average of 9.5 cents per kilowatt. Sales during peak hours during the summer could net more than that amount. “People try to sell into the super–peak marketplace,” Marte said. “That is really the question: Where is the electricity going and how am I going to sell it? Is there a market out there? There really is.” Of the two options presented to commissioners, the first would total about $45 million, and the second option would be more than double that amount. The first option would recoup and estimated 18% of the city’s losses, while the more expensive option would recoup about 53%, Marte said. The city could initially install one of the systems and later add another if it makes sense. A key issue for the city is that it suffered a decline in population and cannot escape a long-term deal with the Municipal Electrical Authority of Georgia, Dorough said during a telephone interview. “We’ve got a contract with MEAG to purchase a specific amount of electricity,” he said “In most months we don’t consume as much energy as we’re contractually obligated to purchase. We’re obviously in a predicament because we have to sell it within a short window.” Although battery storage is used by commercial entities, no other municipalities are in the electricity storage business, the mayor said. The Dougherty County Commission in October 2025 approved an ordinance that allowed and regulates battery storage systems, clearing the way for projects at the solar installation on Highway 133 and a site located near the former Georgia Power Co. plant on Old Georgia Highway 3. The novelty of a city getting into the business is one reason commissioners have urged that the city take its time and enlist an independent party to give an opinion. One advantage that Albany has is that federal funds would cover half of construction costs, Dorough said. Without that incentive, the project would not make economic sense. “Without the 50%, we wouldn’t be talking about it,” Commissioner Chad Warbington said. Having an excess of electricity has an advantage in that the situation reduces the city’s chances of having blackouts, the commissioner said. A long-term contract to sell electricity could be a benefit to residents in helping to keep customers’ rates as low as possible. “It’s pretty complicated,” Warbington said. “You’ve got to evaluate it. For me, this is all about ratepayers. Will this keep our rates low? That’s my biggest concern on a project like this.”

artigo.texto: The Sioux County Board of Supervisors advanced proposed data center regulations on another 4–1 vote Tuesday, October 13, following public questions about enforcement, electricity costs, agricultural impacts, and protections for neighboring properties. Supervisor Dan Altena again cast the lone opposing vote, matching the board’s September 29 decision. The amendment to County Ordinance No. 1, the county’s zoning ordinance, now moves to a third and final reading October 27 at 9 a.m. County Zoning Director Shane Walter said the proposed language had not changed between the first and second readings. He explained that the county already has a conditional-use process for industrial projects but developed additional requirements to address the particular demands of data centers. Oversight, Utilities, and Neighbor Protections Questions during Tuesday’s hearing included who would verify compliance and whether penalties would be substantial enough to discourage violations. Walter said independent studies would be required before a facility could open, with periodic reviews afterward. The county zoning director would ultimately be responsible for ensuring that oversight occurs. He said a separate fine schedule would be established, although the amounts had not yet been determined. The discussion also addressed the potential to shut down an operation that failed to comply with required agreements. On electricity, Walter pointed to the proposed 25-megawatt limit and argued that using existing, underutilized infrastructure at the former Bison project site near Hull could help spread costs among more users. He also said applicants would be responsible for necessary infrastructure improvements. “So they have to enter an agreement with the provider to do that, so that that cost is borne entirely by the applicant and not consumers,” Walter said. Other protections discussed included closed-loop cooling, setbacks, and noise limits measured at neighboring homes rather than at the data center itself. Walter said technology improvements could reduce resource demands over time. The proposal also includes a community betterment fund. Walter said the initial contribution amount and the structure of subsequent payments would be determined later. Altena Cites Residents’ Reservations Altena acknowledged the work that had gone into the proposed rules and Path One’s efforts to explain its plans through public meetings. However, he said residents who had contacted him remained uneasy about bringing a data center to the county. “I think people are still scared and worried and would like to take some time and let somebody else try it first before we do is what I’m hearing,” Altena said. He later emphasized that he recognizes the value of technology in agriculture and law enforcement. His concern, he said, was residents’ reluctance to be among the first nearby communities to host such a facility—not opposition to using data. Altena also pushed back on any suggestion that Sioux County would lose access to data services without a local center. Agriculture and the Facility’s Lifespan Students from MOC-Floyd Valley’s FFA attended as part of their preparation for an agricultural issues contest. Their questions prompted discussion about how data processing relates to farming and how the proposed rules would protect agricultural resources. Supervisor Craig Hoftyzer said he was speaking about data centers generally, rather than the specific local proposal. He pointed to precision spraying technology that identifies individual weeds instead of treating an entire field. “So instead of broadcasting chemicals over an entire field, you’re using probably seventy to eighty percent less chemicals,” Hoftyzer said. He also described combine technology that uses cameras and satellite imagery to anticipate changing crop conditions. “And the combine is automatically adjusting settings, RPMs, and ground speed to be most efficient. And the operator is not even doing that,” Hoftyzer said. Walter said the county’s approach seeks to balance agricultural preservation with industries that support the local economy. Questions about decommissioning also led to a discussion of how long a data center could operate. After Walter offered a tentative estimate of 10 to 20 years, Path One representative Gyles Uhlenhopp said the building itself could have a significantly longer life than the equipment inside it. “There’ll be a process where we have to upgrade on the inside for a variety of reasons, but that doesn’t mean that we’ll tear down the facility. That means you make an upgrade and you move from there,” Uhlenhopp said. Uhlenhopp also said smaller data centers have existed throughout the internet’s history, distinguishing them from the much larger facilities receiving national attention. Final Reading Scheduled October 27 Walter said changes could still be made before final approval, but revised language would need to return to the Planning and Zoning Commission for review and a recommendation to supervisors. Tuesday’s vote advanced the zoning amendment; it did not approve a specific data center application. Walter said Path One is interested in submitting an application if the ordinance is approved. The third and final reading is scheduled for October 27 at 9 a.m. If approved at that reading, the amendment would take effect upon publication. The proposed ordinance is available for the public to review at siouxcounty.org. Sioux County’s data center moratorium for its unincorporated parts remains in effect.

artigo.texto: - Michigan’s data center boom has brought with it some exaggerated claims from supporters and critics - Bridge spoke with experts to get their take on everything from economic benefits to local control - Among the takeaways, data centers indeed pose environmental concerns, but they aren’t raising electricity rates — at least not yet Few issues are as controversial today as data centers, which polls show are overwhelmingly opposed by Michigan residents. Amid the debates, there are plenty of exaggerated claims from both opponents and supporters. Bridge spoke with some of the leading experts in the field to separate fact from fiction. Despite assurances from state leaders that Michigan is a fitting destination to build warehouse-scale server farms across hundreds of acres, projects have been met with considerable pushback from a public worried about everything from their potential environmental impact to the unpredictable nature of artificial intelligence itself. Claim: Data centers are a new thing for Michigan What the experts say: No, but their scale is much, much bigger. “A data center is the most fantastic economic development opportunity in the last 150 years,” said business leader and former US ambassador John Rakolta Jr. before the Detroit Policy Conference this year. His company, Walbridge, is leading construction of one of the state’s largest projects: Oracle’s 1.4-gigawatt data center complex in the farmlands of Saline Township. It’s also a partner in the proposed 282-acre Google data center in Van Buren Township. Data centers have been in Michigan for decades — tucked inside office parks, university buildings and industrial parks. They’ve generally gone unnoticed as they’ve powered our email, streaming services and websites. By some estimates, there are upward of 70 commercial data centers operating in Michigan powering our digital information ecosystem. Rakolta was referring to a new class of “hyperscale” data centers that are far bigger, more powerful and more expensive. Tech companies like Meta and Amazon plan to spend trillions of dollars on AI infrastructure through 2030 with thousands of projects underway, saying the technology will usher in a new era of cost savings, increased productivity and domestic industrial development. A new generation While a standard data center facility used for cloud computing may draw around 50 megawatts of energy, the increasingly sophisticated AI systems powering large language models and neural networks require magnitudes more power. Related: - Where Michigan governor candidates stand on data centers, the environment - Survey: Michigan local leaders sour on data centers, want more regulations - Ypsilanti Township eyes moratorium on power transmission to slow U-M data center “The technology is turning data centers into a new class of industrial infrastructure,” said Hengguang Li, director of the Institute for AI and Data Science at Wayne State University. “It’s nothing like the data centers we built 30 years ago.” Near Grand Rapids, Switch, a Las Vegas company, operates what is likely Michigan’s biggest functioning data center. Appearing as a modern pyramid jutting up from the freeway, the sprawling data center in Gaines Township has expanded for AI in recent years, with a planned electrical capacity of 237 megawatts. With the growth of AI, the US and Michigan are promoting data center development to buoy the economy. In 2024, the Michigan Legislature exempted qualifying data centers from Michigan’s 6% sales and use tax. We do not need certainty that a data center will locate here to recognize our responsibility to prepare. We should establish clear expectations before an application arrives. Reading is open for business. But the people who already call this city home must come first. That is the purpose of this legislation and my commitment to my constituents. artigo.texto: Changan And CATL Are Developing Solid-State Batteries With Nearly 1,000 Miles Of Range Electric vehicles capable of traveling nearly 1,000 miles on a single charge could eventually become a reality if Chinese automaker Changan achieves its latest battery ambitions. The company is expanding its partnership with battery giant CATL while continuing development of next-generation solid-state technology. Changan has outlined plans for batteries capable of delivering over 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) of driving range, which is much farther than the range offered by most electric vehicles currently on sale. The technology promises improvements in energy density, charging performance, and battery durability. However, the impressive figures are just manufacturer targets, not independently verified results from production vehicles. The announcement also includes a major expansion of battery manufacturing capacity in China. Together, Changan and CATL are preparing to strengthen their supply chain while developing technologies that could shape future electric vehicles. Solid-State Batteries Could Deliver 932 Miles Of Range According to Libattery, Changan is continuing development of its Golden Bell solid-state battery technology, first announced in 2023. The automaker is targeting an energy density of up to 400 Wh/kg, potentially enabling electric vehicles to travel over 1,500 kilometers on a full charge. Changan also claims its battery technology could deliver improved safety through AI-assisted monitoring. The company has previously suggested a 70 percent safety improvement compared with conventional liquid-electrolyte batteries, although the precise testing conditions are unclear. Durability is another major focus, with Changan targeting a lifespan exceeding 5,000 charging cycles. Its Golden Bell battery technology also includes a claimed 30-to-80-percent charging time of just nine minutes using 6C fast charging. Changan And CATL Expand Battery Production The two companies plan to establish a combined battery production capacity of 75 GWh through their joint venture. Their collaboration also extends to sodium-ion batteries, battery swapping, and solid-state technology. A new 25 GWh manufacturing facility is planned for the Sichuan-Chongqing region, with production expected to begin during the second half of 2027. The project involves an investment of approximately 5.5 billion yuan ($770 million) and is expected to create around 2,500 jobs. The facility will supply batteries to Changan's electric vehicle brands, including Avatr, Deepal, and Nevo. Full production capacity is expected to be reached within three years of operations beginning. Production Could Begin In 2027 Changan previously outlined plans to begin testing its all-solid-state batteries in vehicles during 2026. The automaker is targeting a gradual transition toward commercial production starting in 2027. Achieving those goals will depend on overcoming the manufacturing and durability challenges associated with solid-state batteries. For now, the nearly 1,000-mile range represents an ambitious projection rather than a capability available to customers. If Changan succeeds, the technology could significantly reduce the frequency of charging stops and help make long-distance electric driving far more convenient. artigo.texto: Protesters call for oversight of data centers, Flock cameras at Michigan Capitol LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Dorr Township resident Rachel McGrady-Hawley joined protesters on the Capitol steps Wednesday calling for more oversight before data center projects move forward. McGrady-Hawley said her life turned upside down after learning about a data center development proposed across the street from her home. “And my focus went from guiding my child through her senior year, from trying to stop this data center campus from going in across the street from my home. And that’s what my life has been like since,” McGrady-Hawley said. Residents oppose neighborhood data centers “We just don’t feel like it’s a good fit for our community, we don’t believe that data centers belong in neighborhoods,” McGrady-Hawley said. Marjorie Steele with the Economic Development Responsibility Alliance of Michigan said the issue has united people from all walks of life. “Michiganders as a whole across the political aisles are tired of being ignored. They are tired of having projects that they don’t want forced on them, and they are tired of their politicians telling them that there’s nothing they can do,” Steele said. Supporters of data center developments claim they create local jobs and boost the local economy and tax revenue. Surveillance concerns raised Attendees also spoke out against the use of Flock cameras and other automated surveillance methods. “I haven’t met a single Michigander who is in favor of this kind of AI-automated surveillance,” Steele said. Law enforcement officials have said the cameras make a difference in solving serious crimes. Attendees said regardless of who represents them at the Capitol, communities will continue to speak up at the local level. “These issues that we’re all battling, they’re non-partisan, they’re about all of us. And it turns out we Michiganders have a lot more in common, you know, than we have different,” Steele said. Candidates weigh in The protest was hosted by Libertarian candidate for Michigan’s governor, Anthony Hudson. Hudson said he invited the other candidates, Jocelyn Benson and John James, to participate, but they did not attend. Both Benson and James shared their stances on data centers in a recent debate, in which they called for guardrails and protections for local communities. artigo.texto: Mount Airy commissioners discuss data center ordinance updates Mount Airy commissioners held a meeting to address updates to city ordinances for data centers, aiming to protect residents and businesses as the city considers future applications. Mount Airy commissioners discuss data center ordinance updates Mount Airy commissioners held a meeting to address updates to city ordinances for data centers, aiming to protect residents and businesses as the city considers future applications. Mount Airy commissioners met Thursday night to discuss updates to city ordinances regarding data centers, focusing on measures to protect residents and businesses as the city refines its approach during a moratorium. The city already has one data center, and officials noted there have been no complaints about its operation. "As far as I know, we've never had a complaint about data centers, no sir, not that I'm aware of," one official said. While data centers are not new to Mount Airy, city leaders are working to update ordinances on the topic, which has been gaining national attention. "It really is about putting the groundwork in place in case we have an application for a new one or the one that's here asks to expand," another official said. The city is currently under a moratorium after requesting a 90-day extension following an initial 60-day vote to refine its statutes on data centers. "Currently, we don't have anything in place to protect us, so any data center could currently come and say, 'I want to move there and set up house,'" one official said. Some residents voiced concerns about the proximity of data centers to residential areas. "I see a problem with that, and I'm offering a solution that it be a 1,000-foot linear feet restriction," one resident said. Others raised questions about the potential strain on infrastructure. "How are the residents going to be protected and businesses from what could be potentially high volume of water with pressure and an aging system, and who pays for that?" another resident asked. Mayor Jon Cawley acknowledged the importance of the discussion. "We will take this matter up hopefully for a decision at our next meeting," Cawley said. Other commissioners emphasized the need to evaluate each application individually. "I would like to just make sure that each project will be a case-by-case," one commissioner said. The mayor said he looks forward to continued discussions, updates, and a decision in two weeks. Related Coverage: Keep up with the latest news and weather by downloading the WXII app here. artigo.texto: Green credit partners with the carbon market, unlocking capital flows for businesses. (Chinhphu.vn) - Green credit provides capital for businesses to transform their technology, while the carbon market opens up opportunities to generate revenue from emission reductions. According to Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh, these two tools can complement each other, enhancing the efficiency of mobilizing and utilizing green capital. The carbon market opens up additional resources for green transition. Speaking at the workshop "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) Nguyen Ngoc Canh emphasized that fulfilling the COP26 commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 requires significant resources for technological innovation, energy transition, and greenhouse gas emission reduction. Besides the state budget, capital and monetary markets, the carbon market plays a crucial role in mobilizing resources, transforming emission reduction results into economic value, and encouraging businesses to proactively transition to green. Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange, along with the pilot phase in 2025-2026, with a scale of over 511 million tons of CO₂ equivalent across three sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement, creates the legal basis for the development of the carbon market. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, green credit and the carbon market have a complementary relationship. Green credit provides capital for businesses to invest in clean technologies, save energy, and reduce emissions. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market can help businesses generate revenue from emission reductions, improve cash flow, and enhance debt repayment capacity, thereby contributing to improving the quality of bank credit. For green capital to be effective, the issue is not just about funding projects identified as green, but also about measuring and verifying the results of energy savings, emission reduction, and environmental protection. Measuring, reporting, and evaluating emission reduction results, as well as trading in carbon quotas and credits, will provide additional data for credit institutions to assess capital efficiency, monitor projects, and manage risks. Connecting green credit with the carbon market will help unlock resources for businesses to transform their technology, reduce emissions, and move towards sustainable growth. According to Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh, since the start of green credit implementation in 2017, this activity has expanded both in terms of credit scale and the level of participation of credit institutions. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit is expected to reach over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. In the context of growing capital demand for green transformation, the carbon market is expected to open up additional financial resources, reducing pressure on bank credit. According to the Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, during the period 2017-2025, green credit is expected to grow by an average of over 20% per year, with expansion in both scale and the number of participating credit institutions. Capital flows are primarily concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation, accounting for over 31%; green energy accounts for nearly 28%. Notably, outstanding loans assessed for environmental and social risks reached over 6.2 trillion VND, accounting for over 31.33% of the total outstanding loans in the entire economy. However, the capital needs for green transition remain enormous. According to Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, Vietnam estimates it needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment for climate change adaptation, resilience enhancement, and emission reduction by 2040, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Specifically for the electricity sector, the estimated investment needed for developing power sources and grids during the 2026-2030 period, according to the revised Power Development Plan VIII, is approximately 136 billion USD. According to Mr. Giap, the carbon market creates economic incentives for emission reduction, while credit provides capital for businesses to invest. Both tools are only effective when the project has a viable cash flow, the ability to repay debt, and verifiable emission reduction results. Revenue from carbon credits can come from selling credits, energy savings, or reduced quota purchase costs. However, banks need to assess the likelihood of credit approval, output, selling price, verification costs, and timing of collection before including this revenue source in their debt repayment plan. At the workshop, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank , stated that Agribank's green credit outstanding reached nearly 30,000 billion VND by the end of March 2026. Developing a measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system, standardizing data, and reducing verification costs for small businesses and cooperatives are also crucial conditions for expanding their market access. artigo.texto: Ricardo Alban cita investimentos de WEG, Moura e BYD e pede regras que estimulem a indústria brasileira sem elevar custos O presidente da Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), Ricardo Alban, defendeu nesta quinta-feira (15) a ampliação da participação de empresas brasileiras no mercado de armazenamento de energia. Durante encontro com empresários e autoridades em Salvador, ele afirmou que o governo deve avaliar a possibilidade de aumentar as exigências de conteúdo local no leilão de sistemas de armazenamento por baterias. “Por que não aumentar o conteúdo local, se entendermos que nós estamos capacitados a isso?”, questionou Alban. O dirigente citou empresas que atuam ou investem no segmento, como WEG, Moura e BYD, para argumentar que o país tem condições de ampliar a participação da indústria nacional na cadeia de fornecimento desses equipamentos. Alban também mencionou a Windey, fabricante chinesa que anunciou uma fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em Camaçari, na Região Metropolitana de Salvador. Na avaliação do presidente da CNI, a política industrial deve aproveitar a capacidade produtiva já instalada no país e estimular novos investimentos, desde que as exigências não comprometam a competitividade dos projetos. Conteúdo local Os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, permitem guardar eletricidade para utilizá-la posteriormente. A tecnologia pode contribuir para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico e para a integração de fontes renováveis, como a solar e a eólica. A discussão sobre conteúdo local envolve a definição de quanto dos equipamentos, componentes e serviços utilizados nos projetos deverá ser produzido ou fornecido no Brasil. Alban defendeu que o governo dialogue com as empresas do setor antes de definir as regras, de modo a avaliar a capacidade da indústria nacional e as condições necessárias para ampliar sua participação. A proposta busca conciliar o estímulo à produção brasileira com a manutenção de custos competitivos para os empreendimentos.

artigo.texto: A Green Credit estabelece parcerias com o mercado de carbono, desbloqueando fluxos de capital para empresas. (Chinhphu.vn) - O crédito verde fornece capital para que as empresas transformem sua tecnologia, enquanto o mercado de carbono abre oportunidades para gerar receita com a redução de emissões. De acordo com o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, essas duas ferramentas podem se complementar, aumentando a eficiência na mobilização e utilização do capital verde. O mercado de carbono abre recursos adicionais para a transição verde. Em seu discurso no workshop "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", realizado em 14 de outubro, o vice-governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã (SBV), Nguyen Ngoc Canh, enfatizou que o cumprimento do compromisso da COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050 exige recursos significativos para inovação tecnológica, transição energética e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Além do orçamento estatal, dos mercados de capitais e monetários, o mercado de carbono desempenha um papel crucial na mobilização de recursos, na transformação dos resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico e no incentivo às empresas para uma transição proativa para energias verdes. O Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP sobre a troca de carbono no mercado interno, juntamente com a fase piloto em 2025-2026, com uma escala superior a 511 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente em três setores: energia térmica, ferro e aço e cimento, cria a base legal para o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono. Segundo o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh, o crédito verde e o mercado de carbono têm uma relação complementar. O crédito verde fornece capital para que as empresas invistam em tecnologias limpas, economizem energia e reduzam as emissões. Por outro lado, um mercado de carbono eficiente pode ajudar as empresas a gerar receita com a redução de emissões, melhorar o fluxo de caixa e aumentar a capacidade de pagamento de dívidas, contribuindo assim para a melhoria da qualidade do crédito bancário. Para que o capital verde seja eficaz, a questão não se resume apenas a financiar projetos identificados como verdes, mas também a medir e verificar os resultados em termos de economia de energia, redução de emissões e proteção ambiental. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados da redução de emissões, bem como a negociação de cotas e créditos de carbono, fornecerão dados adicionais para que as instituições de crédito avaliem a eficiência do capital, monitorem projetos e gerenciem riscos. Conectar o crédito verde ao mercado de carbono ajudará a desbloquear recursos para que as empresas transformem sua tecnologia, reduzam as emissões e avancem rumo ao crescimento sustentável. Você também pode gostar O crédito verde ultrapassou 856 trilhões de VND. Segundo o vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh, desde o início da implementação do crédito verde em 2017, essa atividade se expandiu tanto em termos de escala de crédito quanto no nível de participação das instituições de crédito. Até o final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde deverá ultrapassar 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. No contexto da crescente demanda de capital para a transformação verde, espera-se que o mercado de carbono disponibilize recursos financeiros adicionais, reduzindo a pressão sobre o crédito bancário. Segundo o vice-governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã, durante o período de 2017 a 2025, o crédito verde deverá crescer em média mais de 20% ao ano, com expansão tanto em escala quanto no número de instituições de crédito participantes. Os fluxos de capital concentram-se principalmente na agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade, representando mais de 31%; a energia verde representa quase 28%. Notavelmente, os empréstimos pendentes avaliados quanto aos riscos ambientais e sociais atingiram mais de 6,2 trilhões de VND, representando mais de 31,33% do total de empréstimos pendentes em toda a economia. No entanto, as necessidades de capital para a transição verde continuam enormes. De acordo com Bui Minh Giap, economista-chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (ADB) no Vietnã, o país estima que precisa de aproximadamente US$ 368 bilhões em investimentos adicionais para adaptação às mudanças climáticas, aumento da resiliência e redução de emissões até 2040, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Especificamente para o setor elétrico, o investimento estimado necessário para o desenvolvimento de fontes de energia e redes durante o período de 2026 a 2030, de acordo com o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado, é de aproximadamente 136 bilhões de dólares. Segundo o Sr. Giap, o mercado de carbono cria incentivos econômicos para a redução de emissões, enquanto o crédito fornece capital para que as empresas invistam. Ambas as ferramentas só são eficazes quando o projeto apresenta fluxo de caixa viável, capacidade de pagamento da dívida e resultados verificáveis de redução de emissões. A receita proveniente de créditos de carbono pode advir da venda de créditos, da economia de energia ou da redução dos custos de aquisição de cotas. No entanto, os bancos precisam avaliar a probabilidade de aprovação do crédito, a produção, o preço de venda, os custos de verificação e o cronograma de recebimento antes de incluir essa fonte de receita em seu plano de pagamento de dívidas. No workshop, a Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank , afirmou que o saldo de crédito verde do Agribank atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND até o final de março de 2026. artigo.texto: Washington County, VA approves zoning ordinance for battery storage facilities Washington County, Virginia, is clamping down on where large-scale battery storage facilities can be built. On Tuesday night, the Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a new zoning ordinance that takes effect immediately. The law restricts utility-scale battery facilities—the kind often used by data centers—strictly to manufacturing zones. Officials say the rule ensures these facilities stay close to existing power lines and substations to keep taxpayer costs down. It also guarantees that no project can start without explicit local approval. Moving forward, any developer looking to build a battery storage site in Washington County must first secure a special exception vote from the board.

artigo.texto: Schrödinger Research Published in Nature Reveals New Insights into Lithium-Ion Battery Chemistry New study uncovers multi-lithium ion clustering in common battery electrolytes, paving the way for improved battery performance and design NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- Schrödinger, Inc. (Nasdaq: SDGR) today announced the publication of new research in Nature that reveals critical insights into the atomic-scale structure of lithium-ion battery (LIB) electrolytes. In a joint study with researchers from Columbia University and the New York Structural Biology Center, the team discovered new insights that challenge long-held assumptions of the fundamental chemistry of lithium-ion batteries, including multi-lithium ion complexes that may play an important role in electrolyte behavior and battery function. These new mechanistic insights into electrolyte behavior have the potential to transform battery development from empirical trial-and-error toward predictive design to high-throughput, rational, computationally-driven design for higher-capacity, faster-charging, and longer-lasting batteries. The research, which leveraged Schrödinger’s physics-powered computational platform, addresses a long-standing bottleneck in energy storage design. LIB electrolytes are crucial for battery performance, influencing properties such as conductivity, viscosity, salt dissociation, and electrochemical stability. LIB electrolytes also drive the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, which is the critical protective film on the battery anode that dictates battery lifespan and safety. However, a detailed atomic-level understanding of how electrolyte structure impacts these properties had remained limited. Utilizing Schrödinger’s advanced machine learning force field technology, the team simulated LIB electrolytes at unprecedented accuracy and scale. These simulations showed that lithium ions frequently form clusters coordinated by ethylene carbonate solvent molecules without the presence of anions, a fundamental structural phenomenon previously unrecognized. “Simulating complex battery systems has historically forced scientists to choose between quantum precision and large-scale simulation. Our machine learning force field technology eliminates that trade-off,” stated Mat Halls, senior vice president, materials science, of Schrödinger. “Predicting these multi-lithium complexes and validating them experimentally demonstrates that our platform can detect previously inaccessible chemical phenomena to accelerate materials discovery.” “Using Schrödinger’s proprietary, advanced machine learning force fields, we discovered lithium ions in batteries actually group together into clusters in the absence of anions, and that these clusters are what drive the creation of the protective film on the battery's surface,” stated Richard Friesner, co-founder and member of the Board of Directors at Schrödinger, and William P. Schweitzer Professor of Chemistry at Columbia University. “Predicting this unexpected chemistry computationally and confirming it experimentally demonstrates that Schrödinger’s physics-powered platform can accurately model the hidden atomic details of batteries. Furthermore, these results suggest that many, if not most, complex chemical systems are now amenable to predictive physics-based simulation using machine learning force fields to atomic resolution.” Key Findings: - Multi-Lithium Ion Clustering: In standard battery electrolytes, up to 40% of lithium ions group together into multi-ion clusters, with clustering becoming even more prevalent at higher salt concentrations. This finding upends the long-held assumption that lithium ions remain predominantly isolated in solution. - Accurate Experimental Validation: The machine learning force field simulations demonstrate strong agreement with a wide range of condensed-phase experimental data, including NMR spectra, electrolyte density, viscosity, ionic conductivity, and diffusion coefficients, confirming the physical reality of the predicted multi-lithium clusters. - Electrochemical Implications: Quantum chemical calculations indicate that these multi-lithium clusters have uniquely facile reduction potentials, suggesting they are key intermediates in the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, which is critical for battery longevity and safety. - Foundation for Rational Electrolyte Design : The insights gained provide a fundamental understanding that can guide the rational design of next-generation electrolytes with enhanced performance, stability, and charge rates. This research is ongoing and is supported by funding from Gates Ventures. About Schrödinger Schrödinger is transforming molecular discovery with its computational platform, which enables the discovery of novel, highly optimized molecules for drug development and materials design. Schrödinger’s software platform is built on more than 30 years of R&D investment and is licensed by biotechnology, pharmaceutical and industrial companies, and academic institutions around the world. Schrödinger also leverages the platform to advance a portfolio of collaborative and proprietary programs. To learn more, visit www.schrodinger.com, follow us on LinkedIn. artigo.texto: 156 Texas data centers warned to comply with water use reporting requirements AUSTIN, Texas - The Texas attorney general’s office has sent letters to 156 data center developments across the state urging them to comply with water use reporting requirements. What we know: Attorney General Ken Paxton said data centers are required by law to respond to the Texas Water Development Board’s water use survey, and many have not done so. His office announced the letters were being sent out on Thursday, but did not provide any further details regarding what the letters said. What they're saying: "Data center developers must follow the law and respect the Texans and communities affected by their operations," Paxton said in a news release. Dig deeper: Data centers in over 30 counties will be receiving letters. They include: Bexar, Brazos, Cameron, Collin, Dallas, Denton, Ector, El Paso, Glasscock, Harris, Hidalgo, Hood, Lubbock, Maverick, McLennan, Midland, Montgomery, Nacogdoches, Nueces, Pecos, Potter, Randall, Sherman, Tarrant, Tom Green, Travis, Victoria, Waller, Ward, Webb, Wichita, Williamson. State audit looks at data centers' impact on natural resources The backstory: This comes as a statewide audit is being conducted to determine what impact data centers could have on Texas' power grid and natural resources. Gov. Gregg Abbott in August instructed state energy regulators to halt approvals for new data center projects until the audit is completed. Information on water use is required to be disclosed as a part of the audit. The governor also ordered the state’s water development board to start penalizing major water users like data centers that are not in compliance with reporting requirements. What's next: Failing to comply could make certain data center developments ineligible for permits and renewals, and could result in fines, according to officials. The Source: The information in this article comes from a press release from the Texas attorney general's office and previous Fox Local reporting.

artigo.texto: Rivian and Redwood Materials Expand Partnership to Span the Lifecycle of the Battery Redwood will now recycle Rivian’s battery scrap and end-of-life packs as well as provide energy storage for its manufacturing plant IRVINE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- American automaker Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) and energy technology company Redwood Materials today announced a major expansion of their partnership, establishing Redwood as one of Rivian's key partners to enabling end-to-end energy solutions—recycling Rivian’s production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, as well as providing stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. Through the partnership, Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack to determine whether to repurpose it for energy storage—deployed directly at Rivian's manufacturing facilities or at other locations—or to recycle it. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian's manufacturing operations. This new scope of the partnership builds on the existing work, announced in April 2026, that is deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker's manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois. “Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition," said RJ Scaringe, Rivian Founder and CEO. "By partnering with JB and the Redwood team, we're turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.” "Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials," said JB Straubel, Redwood Materials Founder and CEO. "Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.” When EV batteries reach the end of their useful lives in vehicles, they often still have substantial useful energy capacity for second-life applications, such as stationary storage. Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease stress on the grid during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for the user, as well as the grid at large. During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, these packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with Rivian—and other—EV battery packs, Redwood's proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving. Once batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or where scrap is generated during manufacturing, they can be recycled. Redwood's advanced process is capable of recycling and recovering critical minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper at rates exceeding 95 percent, encouraging the development of a circular, domestic supply chain for battery materials in the United States. This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power. As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem—recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors. Rivian’s work with Redwood is a model for that approach: one partnership spanning the full lifecycle of a battery, built to move faster than the grid alone can. About Rivian Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) is an American automotive technology company that develops and manufactures category-defining electric vehicles as well as vertically integrated technologies and services. Through innovation across its electrical architecture, end-to-end software, autonomous driving platform, artificial intelligence and propulsion, the company creates vehicles that excel at work and play while accelerating the global transition to zero-emission transportation and energy. Rivian vehicles are manufactured in the United States and are sold directly to consumer and commercial customers. Whether taking families on new adventures or electrifying fleets at scale, Rivian vehicles all share a common goal—preserving the natural world for generations to come. Learn more about the company, products, and careers at www.rivian.com. About Redwood Materials Redwood Materials is building the U.S. stockpile of critical materials and deploying large-scale energy storage. Founded by JB Straubel, the company produces lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, and cathode active material at scale in the U.S., manufactures key components for advanced batteries, and deploys energy storage systems that power data centers and the nation’s grid. Redwood is expanding domestic capacity for next-generation energy storage and strengthening U.S. energy dominance. Learn more at www.redwoodmaterials.com. artigo.texto: Federal regulators on Friday rejected PJM’s plan for curtailing large loads that failed to procure their own capacity, finding it would intrude into state authority and unfairly single out new large loads. Regulators did approve PJM’s proposed large load registry, a centralized database to be managed by the grid operator which will track all current and prospective loads of 50 megawatts or more. PJM’s proposed “Interim Resource Adequacy Service,” part of its broader framework for shielding consumers from the cost of serving data centers, would have curtailed data centers and other large loads that don’t bring their own new capacity, and assigned the responsibility for curtailing them to states. Notably, it would have curtailed those loads at the earliest stages of emergency grid conditions, before customers enrolled in voluntary demand response. For the tech companies and aggregators already signing a flurry of these so-called bring-your-own-capacity deals in the region, the rejection is certainly a setback, said Mary Yang, former regulatory counsel for PJM and chief operating officer at 804 Advisory. But it’s not necessarily a dealbreaker for BYOC, she added. Many of those deals were already in limbo, she added, ready and waiting to close, but not yet signed because companies were waiting for more clarity on how exactly BYOC rules would work. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s ruling, though not unexpected, gives them no relief. Now, Yang added, the uncertainty “is going to keep dragging,” in part because PJM is juggling a number of competing priorities, and re-writing IRAS rules isn’t likely to be the top one. “It does slow down the development of these more innovative bilateral mechanisms to solve some of these problems,” Yang added. “There’s a point at which it becomes challenging to wait longer. We are seeing anecdotally a lot of people saying ‘Okay, PJM needs to sort itself out, let’s go to a different region that’s got more certainty.” But aggregators — including those like Voltus who are pushing distributed energy resources for BYOC deals — aren’t particularly worried about the ruling, in large part because most stakeholders expect states to implement IRAS regimes of their own. The real regulatory momentum in PJM is in the hands of states, Yang added. And now, with the approval of PJM’s large load registry, states will have the data they need to shape their own standards. An expected setback Last week’s ruling was largely anticipated, particularly because FERC had already instructed PJM to rework its plan for securing new supply to meet load growth, including via a centralized, one-time auction. For distributed resource aggregators looking to sign bring-your-own-distributed-capacity deals with hyperscalers, the delay in the backstop auction was generally seen as positive, because it provides more time for inking those agreements. But the rejection of IRAS is more complicated, and more consequential for other parts of the country, where grid operators are watching closely to see how PJM’s attempt at curtailment plays out. In another potential setback for aggregators, FERC also rejected the grid operator’s proposed rules for BYOC deals, which would have allowed large loads to avoid IRAS curtailment. FERC highlighted as problematic several elements that aggregators had applauded as expanding potential participation. For example, PJM proposed locking in resource capacity accreditation values for 10 years, which FERC said would give those resources preferential treatment — and in the long run, would risk counting capacity they can’t actually provide, and shifting costs onto existing ratepayers. PJM’s plan would also have allowed distributed capacity to be delivered anywhere in the market, rather than within the specific, constrained zone where a large load is located. That approach, FERC said, doesn’t take into account transmission constraints between the data center and the distributed resources, and could “exacerbate the resource adequacy shortfall.” That said, it isn’t clear from FERC’s ruling whether the commission is rejecting those features outright, or seeking stronger justification for them, Yang explained. A future design for IRAS could still preserve similar benefits in a different form. For generators, the ruling’s impact will largely depend on the details of a specific deal, Yang said. In some cases, signing a bilateral deal as soon as possible may become more attractive given the ongoing uncertainty over the central procurement auction. But other generators considering bilateral agreements might see the delays as useful wiggle room to see whether it will make sense for them to instead get in on the central auction. Looking ahead IRAS drew pushback from stakeholders including merchant generators, state utility regulators, and the AI companies themselves. Supporters of the plan, including Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, argued that targeting non-capacity-backed large loads for curtailment would prevent the financial and operational strain of interconnecting data centers from being shifted onto everyday consumers. For data centers, their biggest problem with PJM’s approach had to do with curtailment authority, Yang said. In its plan, PJM assigned the responsibility of enforcement to states and utilities, meaning those entities and not the grid operator would ultimately decide which large loads get curtailed when, and by how much. The concern among data centers was that even if they do bring new capacity, they could still be asked to curtail. artigo.texto: Lexington extended its temporary ban on data center construction. Mercer County rejected regulations that would allow hyperscale data centers. And a Carroll County ethics board is looking into dealings surrounding a proposed hyperscale data center. As local governments in Kentucky are weighing and making decisions on potential hyperscale data centers, some Kentuckians came to Frankfort to tell state lawmakers that they need to do more to regulate large data centers — not put that burden on local governments. Just a few months away from when state lawmakers meet again in Frankfort, catch up on the latest data center news in this round-up as reported by the Lantern and other news outlets from around Kentucky. Kentuckians tell state lawmakers to act More than 60 people from across the state, ranging from Pike County to Daviess County, came to a committee room earlier this month to lay out a number of concerns they have about hyperscale data center proposals and their potential impacts on electricity ratepayers, rural land and the state’s natural resources. The gathering was for a “listening session” on data centers organized by Rep. Adam Moore, D-Lexington, who is preparing legislation on data center regulations for when the GOP-controlled state legislature meets again next year. Rep. Josh Bray, R-Mount Vernon, the vice-chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, is also preparing legislation on data centers. A few of those speakers told the state lawmakers at the meeting that local governments shouldn’t be expected to regulate data centers on their own. “Finally, stop expecting local officials without specialized technical, legal, environmental, or utility expertise to negotiate billion-dollar industrial development deals on equal footing with the wealthiest companies on Earth,” said Diane Floyd of Mercer County. Local government decisions Meanwhile, local governments including Mercer County have been hearing public commentary and taking votes on whether to regulate hyperscale data centers or allow them at all. The Mercer County Fiscal Court through a unanimous voice vote in late September rejected proposed regulations that would have allowed the placement of hyperscale data centers next to a coal-fired power plant. Opponents of the regulations argued the land near the power plant was also relatively close to Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, a historic site preserving structures of the Kentucky Shakers religious community. In Kentucky’s second-largest city of Lexington, the city council voted to move forward with potential data center regulations and also a temporary ban, or moratorium, on data center construction in the city through October 2027, according to public radio station WEKU. In Carroll County, Kentucky Public Radio reported in late September that frustrated community members have filed local ethics complaints arguing that several city council members for the Carroll County seat of Carrollton should have abstained from votes to sign land deals with a prospective hyperscale data center because of conflicts of interest. Carroll County is home to two proposed large data centers, one of them by Poe Companies and PowerHouse Data Centers, which is also building a hyperscale data center in West Louisville. Other communities, including the Christian County seat of Hopkinsville, are moving forward with proposed data center regulations, or, in the case of the Scott County seat of Georgetown, looking at an outright ban on hyperscale data centers.

artigo.texto: Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle Establish OCP Working Group to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security - New Open Compute Project (OCP) working group: Companies form a new working group to standardize on a silicon-based and attested secure integrated hardware security module (HSM) solution for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure. - Strengthening cloud security: Secure key caching and attestation cryptographic key lifecycle management at the server level will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads. - Open technical specification: Initial draft of technical specification to be released at OCP Global Summit in October 2026 , paving the way for broad industry adoption of in-server security for data centers. SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 2026-- Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), Microsoft Corporation and Oracle today announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure. To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads. Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party. “An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security,” said Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell. “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry.” “As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important,” said Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure. “Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security.” “An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle. “This effort aims to establish a common foundation for adoption across the industry.” About OCP and the New Security Working Group The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative community focused on redesigning hardware technology to efficiently support the growing demands of compute infrastructure. As founding members of the new OCP working group, Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle will collaborate with the broader OCP community to publish a joint technical specification, with an initial draft targeted for release around the 2026 OCP Global Summit and version 1.0 to follow. The companies plan to demonstrate the new technology in their exhibit booths and during Security Track presentations at the OCP Global Summit (October 12-15) at the San Jose Convention Center in San Jose, California. Organizations interested in participating in the security working group are encouraged to join through the Open Compute Project. Trusted by the world’s leading technology companies for over 30 years, we move, store, process and secure the world’s data with semiconductor solutions designed for our customers’ current needs and future ambitions. Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better. artigo.texto: Keysight Expands Active and Passive 1.6T Copper Interconnect Validation for Scale-Out Data Centers Validating digital-layer error performance is the next step for high-speed interconnects after completing optical and electrical layer compliance testing SANTA ROSA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 14, 2026-- Keysight Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: KEYS) today announced the Functional Interconnect Test Solutions (FITS)-16CH digital-layer error performance validation system, expanding Keysight’s FITS portfolio for optical, active copper, and passive copper interconnects. With 16 transmit and 16 receive channels, FITS-16CH has twice the channel density of FITS-8CH, and is designed to validate complete interconnect assemblies across research and development, product design, manufacturing, and pre- and post-production AI and network infrastructure deployments. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261014439659/en/ With 16 transmit and 16 receive channels, Keysight’s FITS-16CH enables digital-layer error performance validation of 1.6T optical and copper interconnects. As interconnect speeds increase, testing only the physical-layer does not provide a complete view of system-level error performance. FITS-16CH combines bit error ratio (BER) and forward error correction (FEC) measurements at the digital layer to evaluate how complete interconnect assemblies perform under real-world conditions. The platform enables 106G and 212G lane-rate validation for today’s 800G interconnects and emerging 1.6T technologies. FITS-16CH supports validation across a broad range of optical and electrical interconnects. These include full-retimed optics (FRO), active optical cables (AOCs), linear-retimed optics (LRO), linear pluggable optics (LPO), active copper cables (ACCs), active electrical cables (AECs), passive direct attach cables (DACs), and high-speed copper flyover cables used in networking and high-performance computing equipment. The platform also supports development and manufacturing workflows for silicon chips, networking equipment, and interconnect products, as well as performance benchmarking for data center operators. Key capabilities include: - Higher channel density for complete-assembly validation: With 16 transmit and 16 receive channels, FITS-16CH is designed to test fully assembled interconnects using two Module Compliance Boards (MCBs) with independent channel groups and MCB controls, enabling teams to validate interconnect performance on more lanes simultaneously, ensuring a high degree of system-level qualification. - Broad interconnect support and insertion-loss capability: A large insertion-loss budget supports signals across lossy channels and customer fixtures, enabling validation of a broad range of optical and copper interconnects, including active copper and high-speed copper flyover cables. - Automated lane tuning: The FITS Windows 11 graphical user interface integrates FITS-16CH with the Keysight DCA-X to automatically calculate optimal transmit finite impulse response (FIR) tap settings and open the electrical eye. The automated process can reduce tuning time to a few minutes compared with manual tuning that can take hours, days, or even weeks. - Flexible integration and automation: FITS-16CH can integrate as a transmitter or receiver with Keysight data communications analyzers (DCAs), high-performance bit error ratio testers (BERTs), and UXR real-time oscilloscopes. The platform supports automated validation workflows with Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (SCPI) API support, automatic real-time charts and data tables, pass/fail flagging, and PDF and .csv report generation. The solution reduces validation complexity by using the common FITS software framework, providing a familiar environment across the FITS portfolio. Ameet Suri, Vice President of Product, Credo Technologies, said: “The tighter margins at 1.6T make it essential to evaluate active electrical cable performance at the system level, not in isolation for each link. Keysight's solutions give Credo a practical way to test our AEC cables during development and qualification, so issues surface sooner and designs reach production with greater assurance.” Ram Periakaruppan, Vice President and General Manager, Network Test & Security Solutions, Keysight, said: "As interconnect speeds increase, manufacturers need to validate more lanes simultaneously on many types of interconnects without adding unnecessary complexity to their labs. FITS-16CH expands our functional interconnect validation portfolio with the capacity, flexibility, and automation needed to help engineers move from product development and qualification to mass production with greater confidence." Resources About Keysight Technologies Keysight (NYSE: KEYS) serves technology innovators as a mission-critical design enablement partner for the world’s most complex engineering challenges. By connecting market-leading design, emulation, and test solutions across the full life cycle, Keysight helps engineering teams accelerate innovation, reduce risk, and bring new technologies to market faster. Customers across AI infrastructure, communications, industrial automation, aerospace and defense, automotive, semiconductor, and general electronics rely on Keysight to bridge virtual design and physical reality, enabling confident decisions earlier. Learn more at www.keysight.com. artigo.texto: Adani Enterprises, Jabil Sign MoU for 50:50 Data Center Hardware Joint Venture - The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) sets out a proposed joint venture (JV) between Jabil and Adani for building a multi-gigawatt AI infrastructure platform in India — spanning AI racks, servers, networking, power and cooling systems. - The proposed JV aims to serve India’s accelerating data center demand, with industry forecasts projecting capacity of 5–8 GW by 2030 and more than $50 billion in planned hyperscaler spending across data center, cloud and AI ecosystems. - The companies estimate the global market opportunity at more than $3 trillion over the next seven years, as investment in AI compute infrastructure continues to surge. - Once established, the JV would serve the world’s leading AI ecosystem players — from hyperscalers and neoclouds to data center operators and enterprises — with infrastructure Made-in-India forIndia and for the world. NEW DELHI, India & ST. PETERSBURG, Fla.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 2026-- Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), the flagship company of the Adani Group, and Jabil Inc. (NYSE: JBL), a global engineering, supply chain and manufacturing company, have signed a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) setting out the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble artificial intelligence (AI) and data center equipment in India. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261013719250/en/ Mr. Gautam Adani, Chairman, Adani Group (left), and Mr. Mike Dastoor, CEO, Jabil (right). The companies have signed a non-binding MoU setting out the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble artificial intelligence and data center equipment in India. The proposed joint venture remains subject to execution of definitive agreements and satisfaction of applicable approvals and customary conditions. The MoU follows the June 2026 announcement of Adani Group and Jabil’s intent to establish a strategic alliance to develop an AI and data center infrastructure manufacturing ecosystem in India. Mr. Gautam Adani, Chairman, Adani Group, said: “The AI revolution will demand far more than just breakthroughs in algorithms. It will require an entire new industrial architecture where energy, hyperscale infrastructure, advanced computing and precision manufacturing converge to power the intelligence economy.” “At Adani, our vision is to expand up the AI value chain evolving from powering and hosting AI infrastructure to engineering and manufacturing the critical systems that will define the next generation of computing.” “Our proposed joint venture with Jabil marks a strategic step towards this future, combining Jabil’s world-class engineering and manufacturing capabilities with Adani’s integrated strengths in energy, infrastructure and data centers to help build the physical backbone of the global AI economy.” Mr. Mike Dastoor, Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Jabil Inc., said: “The signing of this MoU is the next step forward in our shared efforts to establish a scaled AI infrastructure manufacturing platform in India, a market we believe will become increasingly important for both domestic and global AI infrastructure demand. Integrating Jabil’s 60 years of engineering and manufacturing expertise with Adani’s significant infrastructure and energy capabilities, we can bring our rack-level data center solutions to more hyperscalers in India and around the world. We look forward to building on the work we started together in June.” Manufacturing AI Hardware in India The joint venture would manufacture and assemble AI racks, servers, storage and networking equipment used in data centers. The racks would house high-performance computing systems for AI applications and other digital services. The portfolio would also include equipment required to power and cool these systems, including power distribution units, liquid-cooling systems and transformers. The venture is expected to have multi-gigawatt AI rack manufacturing capacity, supporting computing systems with a combined power capacity of several gigawatts. It would also provide installation and commissioning services. India’s Data Center Opportunity India’s data center capacity is projected to reach 5–8 gigawatts (GW) by 2030, driven by AI adoption, cloud expansion and data localization. The venture would provide a manufacturing base in India to serve domestic demand and support exports. The companies estimate the global market opportunity at more than $3 trillion over the next seven years, driven by investment in AI computing. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, provides a framework for personal data protection. This legal safeguard, complemented by the Union Budget 2026 tax holiday for data centers until 2047, is expected to support investment in domestic data infrastructure. The venture is aligned with Adani Group’s $100 billion commitment to develop 5 GW of green-energy-powered, hyperscale AI-ready data centers by 2035. The proposed venture would add hardware manufacturing to the Group’s presence across infrastructure, energy, logistics and data centers. For Jabil, which reported $36 billion in revenue in fiscal year 2026, the venture would expand its engineering and manufacturing footprint in India’s data center market. The company has also expanded its data center capabilities through the acquisition of Hanley Energy Group, which provides critical power and energy management solutions, and Mikros Technologies, which specializes in liquid-cooling solutions for high-performance computing systems.
