artigo.texto: Agência reguladora prepara os primeiros leilões brasileiros dedicados a grandes sistemas de armazenamento de eletricidade, com contratos de 15 anos, fornecimento previsto para 2028 e disputas programadas para 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) prevê publicar em 29 de outubro de 2026 os editais dos primeiros leilões brasileiros dedicados à contratação de grandes sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. As disputas estão programadas para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro e representam uma nova etapa na modernização do sistema elétrico nacional. O cronograma foi apresentado durante um workshop promovido pela Aneel e pela Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE), em 14 de outubro. Segundo o Canal Solar, Ivo Sechi Nazareno, responsável pela área de leilões da agência, informou que os documentos deverão ser analisados pela diretoria colegiada em 27 de outubro, com publicação prevista para dois dias depois. A iniciativa pretende contratar sistemas capazes de armazenar eletricidade e disponibilizar potência quando o sistema elétrico precisar. - China perde mais de 40 mil empregos em cinco fabricantes de painéis solares, mesmo com instalações recordes no mundo, após excesso de produção derrubar preços e margens de lucro - Aeroporto na Nova Zelândia inaugura usina solar de 150 MW com 300 mil painéis, investimento de NZ$ 273 milhões e energia suficiente para abastecer 36 mil residências por ano - DAH Solar apresenta solução modular de 1,5 kW e 2 kW para instalações de até 7,5 kW no Brasil, com controle da energia enviada à rede e possibilidade de integração com baterias - Empresa chinesa inicia construção de usina solar de 70,8 MW na Bahia, prevê gerar 144 milhões de kWh por ano e destina eletricidade ao Metrô de São Paulo a partir de 2027 A tecnologia ganha importância diante do crescimento das fontes solar e eólica no Brasil, cuja produção varia conforme as condições climáticas. Brasil terá dois leilões de baterias em dezembro, com contratos previstos para 15 anos Os certames são denominados Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na Forma de Potência (LRCAP) e serão realizados pela Aneel em parceria com a CCEE. Segundo informações oficiais da agência, as disputas estão previstas para 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026, em ambiente eletrônico. Os projetos participantes deverão oferecer sistemas autônomos de armazenamento de eletricidade em baterias, conhecidos internacionalmente pela sigla BESS. Os dois leilões terão regras específicas. Uma das modalidades prevê exigências relacionadas ao conteúdo nacional dos equipamentos, enquanto a outra possui condições distintas de participação. Os contratos deverão ter duração de 15 anos, com início do fornecimento de potência previsto para agosto de 2028. Esse prazo é importante porque os vencedores precisarão desenvolver, construir, conectar e colocar os sistemas em condições de operação antes do início das obrigações contratuais. Os editais definitivos ainda dependem de aprovação pela diretoria da Aneel. Por isso, as condições apresentadas até agora podem sofrer ajustes. Como as baterias poderão ajudar a aproveitar a energia solar e eólica produzida no Brasil? Diferentemente de uma usina solar ou eólica, um sistema de armazenamento não produz eletricidade a partir de uma fonte primária. Sua função é receber energia, armazená-la e devolvê-la posteriormente à rede, conforme a necessidade operacional. Na prática, as baterias podem ser carregadas durante períodos de maior disponibilidade de eletricidade e descarregadas quando o sistema precisar de potência adicional. Esse recurso pode ajudar a administrar as oscilações da geração renovável e reduzir a necessidade de manter determinadas fontes convencionais disponíveis exclusivamente para atender aos horários de maior consumo. O benefício, entretanto, depende da duração do armazenamento, da localização dos equipamentos, das condições de operação e das regras de contratação. Os leilões de dezembro não significam que toda a energia solar ou eólica atualmente desperdiçada no Brasil passará a ser armazenada. A contratação será voltada à disponibilidade de potência, um serviço específico para a segurança e a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico. Quem poderá participar dos leilões e quais serão os próximos prazos? A programação apresentada pela Aneel prevê participação de empresas brasileiras e estrangeiras, individualmente ou reunidas em consórcios, desde que atendam aos requisitos dos editais. Os projetos também deverão observar regras de cadastramento, habilitação técnica e apresentação de garantias financeiras. De acordo com o calendário divulgado, o registro das propostas está previsto para novembro, enquanto a homologação dos resultados deverá ocorrer em 2027. A agência já realizou consultas públicas e audiência para discutir as condições dos contratos. Um dos principais pontos de debate envolve a distribuição dos custos da contratação entre os agentes do setor elétrico, assunto que também provocou discussões sobre possíveis medidas judiciais. Apesar das divergências, a Aneel informou que continua trabalhando com as datas previstas para dezembro, sem considerar, neste momento, o adiamento das disputas. A etapa mais próxima será a análise dos editais em 27 de outubro. Se o cronograma for mantido, o Brasil deverá conhecer em dezembro os vencedores de seus primeiros leilões específicos para baterias de grande porte, com início de suprimento planejado para 2028. Até lá, a publicação das regras definitivas será fundamental para que investidores e fornecedores conheçam as exigências técnicas, financeiras e operacionais dos projetos.

artigo.texto: O novo "reduto" da China em sua ambição de construir o maior centro de dados do mundo. A área parece uma miragem de alta tecnologia. Fileiras de enormes centros de dados, tanto recém-concluídos quanto em construção, erguem-se em meio a planícies onduladas e campos de girassóis e sorgo. Os edifícios ostentam os nomes de algumas das maiores empresas de tecnologia da China , desde a gigante de hardware Huawei e a plataforma de mídia social Kuaishou até a provedora de serviços VNET. Todas estão concentradas em uma área constantemente movimentada por atividades de construção e operação. Esta é Ulanqab, uma cidade na Região Autônoma da Mongólia Interior, na China, localizada na orla do Deserto de Gobi. Ela está se tornando rapidamente um dos polos de dados que impulsionam o poderoso boom da inteligência artificial (IA) na China, posicionando o país como o único rival verdadeiramente formidável dos EUA em sua ambição de domínio tecnológico. Quase 90 data centers estão planejados para serem construídos nesta cidade com menos de 2 milhões de habitantes. Ulanqab possui um número crescente de centros de dados de IA e big data, demonstrando as vantagens que a China está ganhando na corrida para desenvolver tecnologias que podem moldar o século XXI. As estruturas gigantescas aqui foram construídas em ritmo acelerado. Grande parte do Parque Industrial de Big Data de Bayin, densamente construído, foi formada em apenas dois anos. Isso demonstra a capacidade de construção rápida da China. Ventos fortes, sol intenso e vastos espaços abertos proporcionam à região acesso a energia verde barata e abundantes recursos de terra. Ulanqab faz parte da visão de Pequim de expandir rapidamente sua infraestrutura de dados. Essa é uma prioridade fundamental para o governo chinês, que vê a IA como um motor de crescimento crucial para sua economia em desaceleração, em meio a uma população em declínio. “A China abriu os braços para a IA”, disse o presidente chinês Xi Jinping em uma conferência global sobre inteligência artificial em Xangai, em julho passado. Ele mencionou iniciativas para integrar a IA em diversas áreas, da saúde aos eletrodomésticos, e elogiou os esforços para integrar a IA na indústria como um dos destaques da modernização da China. Segundo estatísticas oficiais, mais de 700 milhões de pessoas na China utilizam atualmente IA. O plano de integrar a IA na manufatura, na indústria e no cotidiano também exige enorme poder computacional. No mês passado, a China anunciou um plano de US$ 560 bilhões para expandir rapidamente sua infraestrutura de informação nos próximos cinco anos. Empresas privadas de tecnologia também estão aumentando seus investimentos em infraestrutura de IA, embora ainda estejam muito atrás de suas contrapartes do Vale do Silício, nos EUA. Segundo a empresa de pesquisa Rhodium Group, o investimento total de empresas chinesas listadas na bolsa nesse setor dobrará este ano, chegando a aproximadamente US$ 139 bilhões. No entanto, esse valor ainda representa menos de um quinto dos US$ 800 bilhões investidos em data centers de IA por empresas americanas. As empresas chinesas também enfrentam outro desafio sério: o fornecimento limitado de hardware de ponta para equipar data centers. As proibições de exportação dos EUA restringem o acesso aos melhores chips de IA, como alguns modelos da Nvidia e da AMD, enquanto a China também limita as importações de alguns chips de desempenho inferior. Os fabricantes nacionais de chips estão correndo para alcançar a concorrência, mas a tecnologia ainda está atrás da dos EUA, e o fornecimento dos modelos mais avançados continua escasso. "Considerando o custo total de construção de um centro de dados, os chips são o fator mais importante, e a China simplesmente não tem chips suficientes", disse Nick Corvino, pesquisador da Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Você também pode gostar No entanto, o que a China não tem em termos de chips e capital de investimento pode ser compensado por outra vantagem: eletricidade abundante e acessível, grande parte da qual é energia verde. Fontes de energia em excesso Enquanto os centros de dados com alto consumo de energia pressionam a rede elétrica dos EUA, a China adicionou capacidade de geração de energia entre 2022 e 2025 equivalente à capacidade total de todas as fontes de energia industrial dos EUA até o final de 2025. A China também possui mais energia verde do que necessita. O excedente de energia verde que o país desperdiçará nos primeiros seis meses de 2026 é suficiente para abastecer todo o México por um ano. A China quer aproveitar esse excedente de energia para alimentar centros de dados, localizados principalmente em áreas rurais do oeste, onde há muita luz solar, vento e vastas extensões de terra. Essa estratégia também impulsiona o setor de tecnologia verde da China, conhecido como "Dados no Oriente, Computação no Ocidente". De acordo com uma estratégia implementada pela primeira vez em 2022, a China planejou oito centros nacionais de computação, incluindo vários no oeste do país, além de 10 clusters nacionais de data centers. O mais recente plano quinquenal de desenvolvimento econômico do país reforça ainda mais essa orientação para a conectividade, prevendo o desenvolvimento coordenado da infraestrutura de computação com energia limpa. A disponibilidade abundante de energia também pode ajudar a China a compensar as limitações de desempenho de seus chips nacionais. Fabricantes de chips chineses, como a Huawei, estão combinando múltiplos clusters de chips para criar poder computacional equivalente ao de tecnologias mais avançadas. Segundo analistas, essa solução pode ser eficiente para algumas tarefas, mas consome significativamente mais energia. No entanto, especialistas argumentam que, mesmo com energia abundante, a visão de Pequim ainda apresenta limitações. artigo.texto: - The companies are developing the new module because their customers are asking for it - Customers want to embrace more powerful technology for AI workloads with something they’re familiar with - The new modules will increase bandwidth density from 200 Gbps-per-lane to 400 Gbps-per-lane. OCP GLOBAL SUMMIT, SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA — Cisco and Nvidia this week unveiled plans to develop an ultra-dense small form factor pluggable (USFP) optic module for AI data centers. The USFP is capable of 400 Gbps-per-lane and is expected to deliver 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of 200 Gbps-per-lane optics. The companies are developing the USFP because their hyperscaler and neocloud customers are asking for it. The customers want to extend their use of octal small form factor (OSFP) modules but scale from 200 Gbps-per-lane to 400 Gbps-per-lane. With USFP, they can embrace next-generation optical technology for AI workloads without overhauling their data center infrastructure. Fierce asked Will Eatherton, Cisco SVP of Engineering, to break down all this information for us. He said pluggable modules are used in AI data centers to connect servers — which house the GPUs — to the switches. The modules “have the fiber optic pigtail coming out of them, and these plug into both servers as well as into the switches, and then the optic runs between, and that's how you connect up your cluster of hundreds of thousands to millions of GPUs,” he said. The current OSFP technology is topping out, and data centers need an upgrade for the future. In terms of the increase in “lanes,” this refers to the tiny copper pathways that carry electrical signals between the chip and the optical module. Eatherton said others are working on different solutions to increase bandwidth for pluggable optic modules in data centers. For instance, Arista and Broadcom are working on a solution called XPO that involves liquid cooling going to the module. And co-packaged optics (CPO) is another alternative. But Eatherton said Cisco has gotten feedback from its customers that what they really want is something that's like the old thing, but in the next generation. For their USFP, Cisco and Nvidia will work with a variety of vendors. “These modules will have massive engineering,” said Eatherton. “You have an ecosystem. So, what we're announcing is we have simulated and tested and are ready for this module to move into the next stage. And Cisco and Nvidia will champion it.” They will work with connector vendors and then go through a process of forming an open standard. And that’s why they announced the new product at the Open Compute Project (OCP) event, because OCP is all about open technologies that aren't proprietary or locked in. Interestingly, even though Cisco and Nvidia are working together, and Arista and Broadcom are working on the competing standard XPO, Eatherton said that ultimately, everyone will probably support both standards just to cover their bases in terms of providing customers whichever product they want. Although Cisco and Nvidia are not giving specifics about roadmaps or timelines for their USFP, Eatherton said everything is moving so fast it will take a matter of months, not years. Its target market for OSFP are the AI hyperscalers, neoclouds, telcos around the world that are creating sovereign AI clouds, and even high end-enterprises. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – Residents gathered at Northwest Vista College on Tuesday to voice concerns about data center development in San Antonio and discuss what regulations city leaders should consider as they prepare to update the city’s land development rules. The town hall, hosted by District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan, the Greater Edwards Aquifer Alliance and Public Citizen, focused on issues including water use, electricity demand, noise, zoning and the effects of data centers on nearby neighborhoods. The meeting also gave residents an opportunity to learn about the city’s process for updating its Unified Development Code and share feedback on proposed data center regulations. The city’s Development Services Department is drafting regulations for data centers, with City Council expected to vote on the rules in the near future. Randy Sipe said residents need more notice about proposed projects before permits are approved and construction begins. “When you first notice them, it’s too late to do anything because I’ve been to some meetings before and unfortunately the permits are done and over,” Sipe said. “So once they break ground, there is no stopping them.” Luis Leon said he is concerned about how data center development could affect future generations, particularly access to water and electricity costs. “I’m concerned about the future of my descendants,” Leon said. “I want to know that they’re going to be OK, that they’re going to have water and the cost of electricity.” Residents also discussed where data centers should be allowed, how noise should be controlled and what requirements developers should meet. Potential policy changes discussed at the meeting included establishing a clear, updated definition of a data center, revisiting zoning qualifications, strengthening site plan requirements and updating fire and building codes. Galvan said San Antonio has just under 30 data centers within city limits, with 18 or 19 located in District 6. “A little under 30 data centers here in San Antonio city limits, with 18-19 of them here in District 6,” Galvan said. “We’ve seen them grow over time with rapid development over the last 15 years.” Galvan said the city and its residents need to understand how local policies could affect future projects and the communities where they are built. “It’s incumbent on us to make sure we’re understanding what’s going on and how local policies can help impact some of the developments here so our communities aren’t left behind,” he said. Organizers said the town hall was intended to bring more residents, particularly those on the far West Side and in District 6, into discussions about data center development. Annalisa Peace, executive director of the Greater Edwards Aquifer Alliance, said she hopes the city’s development code will be updated to address the growth of large-scale data centers. “We hope that the City will be amending the UDC to accommodate new hyperscale data centers with regulations that best serve the citizens of San Antonio,” Peace said. No official decisions were made at Tuesday’s citizen town hall. The feedback comes as the city works to develop regulations for data centers and prepares for further City Council consideration of updates to the Unified Development Code. Read also:

artigo.texto: Colorado can help lead data center construction — in space | PODIUM Across Colorado, proposals for new data centers are running into fierce opposition. Residents are worried about noise, water use, health risks and high electricity costs. Six municipalities, including Denver, have imposed bans, caps or moratoriums while they figure out how these massive facilities could affect their communities. Local officials cannot ignore voters’ concerns. But the response to new data centers can’t simply be “no” because there’s too much at stake. Abundant computing power is critical to U.S. medical and scientific progress, military and intelligence capabilities and economic growth. Recommended Stories So it’s exciting Colorado may soon have an opportunity to play a key role in developing another option: moving some of that computing infrastructure off the ground and into space. In June, Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper joined Texas U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz in introducing the NEW HORIZON Act, which would direct the Department of Defense to establish a pilot program to test orbital data centers and space-based cloud computing. Currently in early-stage development by well-known companies like Google, SpaceX and Amazon — as well as new entrants like Starcloud and Sophia Space — orbital data centers would put computing, storage and networking equipment aboard state-of-the-art platforms in low-Earth orbit. Then, instead of sending data collected by satellites back to Earth, the orbital facilities would process and store much of that data in space. Sen. Hickenlooper’s proposed program would start small, testing whether orbital computing can quickly, safely and reliably process satellite imagery, national-security information, weather observations and other data already being generated in space, while also assessing key cybersecurity and compatibility issues. But there’s much bigger potential here. If powerful computing systems work reliably in space, we may be able to move into orbit some of the intensive computing now performed in massive ground-based data centers. That would allow us to expand America’s computing capacity without putting so much pressure on local power grids, water supplies and communities. Colorado is an obvious place to start making this happen. Aerospace is one of our defining industries, and we’re also home to important military installations, research universities, federal laboratories and innovative startups. As Sen. Hickenlooper put it, “Space innovation and military preparedness are Colorado’s bread and butter.” It won’t be easy. Launching equipment into space is expensive — and incredibly complex. Computers in orbit have to withstand intense radiation, and keeping powerful processors cool is a serious engineering challenge. Space-based data facilities would also mean more orbital congestion, debris and collision risks. And when something breaks, sending someone up to fix it is a lot harder than calling a technician to a building in Denver or Colorado Springs. But those aren’t reasons to walk away. Rather, as many tech-industry leaders have argued, they’re reasons to start innovating and experimenting with new technologies, including the power systems, cybersecurity, heat management and radiation-resistant hardware that could make commercial orbital data centers possible. Colorado can demonstrate leadership quickly. State agencies, universities, aerospace employers, federal installations and startups can pursue research funding, host demonstrations, train workers and ensure Colorado companies are competing to participate in NEW HORIZON pilot programs. Orbital data certainly won’t arrive soon enough to resolve today’s thorny local disputes. But decisions we make today could determine where the new orbital computing industry takes root in the years to come. Colorado can get there early — creating jobs, developing new national security technology and giving future policymakers another way to meet America’s growing demand for computing power. The fights over data centers happening across Colorado highlight why this idea is worth pursuing. Communities shouldn’t have to choose between protecting their residents and resources and building the infrastructure America needs to power the next generation of innovation. Colorado has the scientific talent, national-security expertise and industrial capabilities to help find another way: up. Kyle Shannon of Denver is chief executive of Storyvine and founder of AI Salon. Dave Cavossa of Washington, DC., is president of the Commercial Space Federation.

artigo.texto: Vikram Solar Subsidiary Plans 7.5 GWh BESS Assembly Plant in Tamil Nadu VSL PowerHive plans to expand from battery storage system assembly into cell manufacturing, building towards an integrated domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem. October 13, 2026. By News Bureau VSL PowerHive, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vikram Solar, has announced plans to establish a 7.5 GWh per annum Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly plant at Oragadam, near Chennai, Tamil Nadu. The facility is designed to scale up to 15 GWh in later phases and will anchor PowerHive's broader roadmap to build 30 GWh of total battery manufacturing capacity by 2030. Spread across approximately 1.65 lakh sq. ft., the facility is slated for inauguration in January 2027, with commercial operations expected to begin in April 2027. The development comes at a time when energy storage has moved to the centre of India's clean energy agenda. As solar and wind capacity grows, storage has become critical to keeping the grid stable, shifting renewable power to evening peaks and enabling round-the-clock clean energy. The Central Electricity Authority projects that India will need about 47 GW /236 GWh of energy storage by 2031-32. Meeting this need at scale will require a strong domestic manufacturing base and reduced reliance on imported systems. Complementing that, PowerHive's ambitions extend well beyond assembly. The company will move into cell manufacturing with a 7.5 GWh programme from 2028, a key step towards building a fully integrated battery manufacturing ecosystem in India, from cell to system. Backing this roadmap, PowerHive is developing indigenous battery technologies and has already initiated multiple patent filings to strengthen its technology ownership and reduce reliance on imported know-how. Once operational, the plant will assemble Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP)-based energy storage systems for utility-scale and Commercial and Industrial (C&I) applications. The portfolio will include 5.016 MWh and 6.25 MWh liquid-cooled BESS containers, PowerHive's P261 battery cabinets, utility-scale energy storage systems and renewable energy-integrated storage solutions, all to be manufactured in India under the Make in India initiative. Gyanesh Chaudhary, Chairman and Managing Director, Vikram Solar, said, "Storage is the bridge between India's renewable ambition and round-the-clock clean power. As the country scales up solar and wind, the ability to store that energy reliably will define the next phase of the transition and that capability must be built in India. The new plant is a decisive step in that direction and extends Vikram Solar's role in the clean energy value chain from generating power to storing it." Arun Mittal, CEO, VSL PowerHive, said, "Energy storage is what makes renewable power dependable, and demand for it in India is rising faster than ever. With this development, we are setting out to build world-class battery manufacturing capability in the country, starting with 7.5 GWh of assembly and progressing to cells and an integrated ecosystem. Our aim is to give utilities, developers and industries a future-ready, domestically built storage partner for the decades ahead." Through the upcoming facility, PowerHive plans to create skilled jobs, develop local talent in advanced storage solutions and strengthen the local industrial ecosystem, supporting Tamil Nadu in building a thriving clean-tech industry. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Testing results show that the toxic plume in the vicinity of the Cove Hollow Road battery energy storage system, or BESS, has not seeped into private wells in a significant capacity — but the groundwater has shown readings that are orders of magnitude higher than drinking water standards. Officials at various levels of government, who have been wading through the multifaceted fallout from the contamination, are now turning their focus to cleanup. Suffolk County Department of Health Services found readings of the contaminant, PFPrA, at maximum levels of 25.1 million and 9.4 million parts per trillion in the area just south of the BESS plant — a number that is exponentially higher than the screening level of 3,000 parts per trillion set by state agencies. But the data varied heavily based on location and depth. Previous stories in The Press used the parts per billion measurement, which is used by state agencies, but here the numbers are recorded in parts per trillion, which is the preferred measurement at the county level. One part per trillion, for reference, is equal to one drop in 20 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The results have allowed the Suffolk County Department of Health Services to map the approximate extent and location of the toxic plume, which was confirmed to have reached public Suffolk County Water Authority wells earlier this year. The public wells, roughly a quarter mile from the BESS plant, represent the plume’s furthest reach south, as PFPrA had marginal readings at the testing wells on Buckskill Road — immediately south of the water authority’s wellfield. Detection of the PFPrA has been linked to a May 2023 fire at the BESS plant. The gaseous fire suppressant installed at the BESS facility, NOVEC 1230, can break down into PFPrA when mixed with water. Around 5,000 pounds of the fire suppressant, in conjunction with 1 million gallons of water, were used in the hands-off firefighting operation — and were subsequently funnelled into the ground. Tests were done at various intervals and depths in the groundwater and do not represent the levels of the contaminant in the drinking water in the neighborhood — in either the public wells, which have been taken offline or reduced to emergency use, or the private wells. The Suffolk County Department of Health Services did three rounds of outreach to homeowners on private wells in the area — in June, July and August. Of the 24 homes reached out to, just 13 were sampled. The remainder either declined to be sampled, did not have anyone answer the door or were vacant. No properties exceeded the state’s 3,000 parts per trillion screening level for PFPrA, while the highest reading came in at 606 parts per trillion. Of the 13 wells sampled, 12 did have a hit — though these were all below the state’s screening level. But another contaminant, PFOS, was also discovered in the vicinity of the Cove Hollow Road neighborhood — albeit at levels substantially lower than PFPrA. The State Department of Environmental Conservation does not yet know the source of this so-called “forever chemical.” The results were presented at a public forum led by Suffolk County officials, at which were also representatives from East Hampton Town, East Hampton Village, state health agencies and the DEC. “What is needed now is not what the county does; it’s what the DEC does,” Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine said. “They will put together a remediation plan, and that’s going to be significant because you want to be able to remediate the damage that has been done.” There are any number of outstanding question marks lingering as to why the BESS plant was equipped both with a sprinkler fire suppression system and a gaseous substance that was apparently known to be incompatible with water — but eyes and ears stayed, mostly, on the future and the impending cleanup. NextEra Energy, the operators of the BESS facility, did not return a request for comment on what information was consulted regarding the fire suppression system prior to the plant’s construction a decade ago. “Our focus now is going to be on cleanup and continued testing and safeguards in place before we reopen this facility,” East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen said. “I know we have concerns from our local school board. I met with them. I know the supervisor met with them, and they’re very concerned about evacuations. So we need to address all of this, and I think it’s a good time now to do a full environmental review.” East Hampton Town Planning Board materials from May 2017, when the facility was working through reviews, detail that the plant would be equipped with a gaseous fire suppression system “backed up by a water suppression (sprinkler) system.” The system was described as an automatic dual suppression system. This issue has been the focus of East Hampton Village Fire and EMS Administrator Gerry Turza, who was at the scene of the May 2023 incident and who has since been left with a raised eyebrow over the disposal of the contaminated water used to fight the fire. “We’re still not getting answers,” Turza said. “Our job is to protect you guys, protect the public, protect our responders. We’re still not getting the right information. There are papers out from 2008 to 2009 that said that NOVEC is incompatible with water — the DEC alluded to this at a Town Board meeting about a month ago.” Both of NextEra’s BESS plants, located in East Hampton and Montauk, were shut down earlier this month as attorneys from the county and the town geared up for litigation as they continued to negotiate with the company. The NOVEC 1230 is expected to be removed from the plants and disposed of away from East Hampton Town. The DEC did conduct analysis after the May 2023 fire, but those efforts focused predominantly on metals in the soil — and none were found. artigo.texto: Os data centers entraram de vez no planejamento energético do país. O Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2036 (PDE 2036), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) para o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), já trata os centros de dados como uma das grandes cargas que terão peso na expansão da geração e, principalmente, da rede de transmissão nos próximos dez anos. A mudança é importante porque tira os data centers do campo restrito da política digital e dos incentivos fiscais. Para atrair essa indústria, não basta oferecer benefícios tributários ou energia renovável. É preciso garantir que haverá eletricidade e capacidade de transmissão onde os empreendimentos quiserem se instalar. No PDE, data centers aparecem ao lado de projetos de produção de hidrogênio e de outros grandes consumidores de eletricidade. Juntos, esses novos empreendimentos podem representar cerca de 3,7 gigawatts (GW) de carga em 2036. O número não é uma estimativa exclusiva para data centers, mas dá a dimensão do impacto que essas novas atividades começam a ter no planejamento do sistema elétrico. Os centros de dados, isoladamente, já aparecem como um dos principais motores do aumento do consumo. A EPE estima crescimento médio de 13,7% ao ano até 2036 na eletricidade usada por essa atividade. Dentro do setor de comércio e serviços, eles são apontados como o principal vetor de expansão da demanda. Essa pressão ajuda a explicar por que o consumo comercial deverá crescer cerca de 6% ao ano, acima de outras classes. A expansão da infraestrutura digital, especialmente dos data centers, é apontada pelo próprio planejamento como uma das razões para esse avanço. O movimento também pesa nas contas gerais do setor elétrico. A participação da eletricidade no consumo final de energia do país deverá subir de 20% em 2026 para 23,3% em 2036. Entre os motivos estão a eletrificação da economia, a mobilidade elétrica, mudanças na estrutura produtiva e a expansão dos data centers. Nova geografia Embora os grandes centros consumidores do Sudeste, Centro-Oeste e Sul continuem atraindo boa parte desses empreendimentos, o planejamento chama atenção para o Nordeste. A região reúne três vantagens importantes para os centros de dados: grande oferta de energia renovável, pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos internacionais de fibra óptica e a possibilidade de usar esses investimentos como instrumento de desenvolvimento regional. A preocupação já chegou ao planejamento da transmissão. A EPE cita entre os trabalhos recentes o Estudo Prospectivo para Inserção de Cargas Eletrointensivas na Região Nordeste, realizado em 2026. Ao mesmo tempo, estudos para São Paulo analisam reforços da rede necessários para atender ao crescimento das grandes cargas. Esse é provavelmente o sinal mais concreto de que os data centers deixaram de ser apenas uma expectativa de investimento. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética já precisa considerar onde essas cargas poderão aparecer e o que será necessário fazer na rede para conectá-las. Construir uma nova linha de transmissão nem sempre é a primeira saída, principalmente nos grandes centros urbanos. Por isso, o PDE também considera tecnologias que permitem aumentar a capacidade das linhas existentes e controlar melhor o fluxo de eletricidade. São soluções que podem aliviar gargalos e, em alguns casos, adiar obras maiores. A lógica é relativamente simples. Um grande data center pode consumir continuamente uma quantidade de eletricidade comparável à de uma cidade. Se vários empreendimentos tentarem se instalar na mesma região, não basta haver geração disponível no país. A rede precisa conseguir transportar essa energia até cada instalação com a segurança exigida por uma atividade que praticamente não pode ficar sem eletricidade. Pressão da IA A inteligência artificial aumenta essa incerteza. Por enquanto, a EPE considera que os data centers ligados à Rede Básica apresentam consumo relativamente constante ao longo do dia. Isso facilita o planejamento porque eles aumentam a carga, mas não provocam necessariamente grandes oscilações entre determinados horários. O próprio PDE, porém, alerta que esse comportamento pode mudar com o crescimento de centros de dados voltados ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial. Se esses empreendimentos ganharem participação relevante, será necessário acompanhar melhor como e quando consomem energia. A EPE reconhece que precisará de mais dados para fazer esse planejamento. O problema não é apenas brasileiro. O Caderno de Contexto do PDE mostra que a expansão mundial dos data centers e da inteligência artificial já pressiona a demanda por geração, transmissão e equipamentos elétricos. A EPE cita, por exemplo, o aumento das encomendas de turbinas a gás e prazos de entrega que podem chegar a cinco anos. Nesse cenário, o Brasil considera sua matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável uma vantagem para disputar esses investimentos. Mas existe uma ressalva. Como data centers precisam de fornecimento contínuo e extremamente confiável, a instalação de geração própria próxima aos empreendimentos pode aumentar o uso de gás natural. O documento aponta o biometano como uma alternativa renovável para parte dessa necessidade. O PDE 2036 não chega a constituir um plano nacional específico para data centers. Não há no documento uma relação fechada de empreendimentos, locais de instalação, capacidade elétrica reservada para cada projeto ou cronograma de conexões. E nem seria essa exatamente a função do plano. O PDE é indicativo: procura mostrar para onde o consumo e a oferta de energia podem caminhar e quais investimentos poderão ser necessários, sem determinar o que empresas privadas deverão fazer. A novidade é outra. Pela primeira vez, a expansão dos centros de dados aparece de forma clara como uma variável do planejamento da infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. O governo já trabalha com seu impacto sobre o consumo, estuda onde essas grandes cargas poderão se concentrar e começa a avaliar

artigo.texto: Back in my corporate days, I started every new project with one rule: you can't control what you don't measure. Twenty years in energy added a second half to it. You can't sell what you can't prove. In the power business, nobody ever asked me to take my own word for anything. The meter did the talking instead. It sat at a defined point, recorded continuously, and both sides of every contract trusted it. Today I develop AI data centers and keep running into the opposite problem. Operators measure everything, from GPU utilization and node uptime to power draw and temperature at the rack, yet almost none of it counts outside their own control room. It's their own data, collected their own way and shown when they choose to show it, so enterprise customers and capacity buyers end up taking the operator's word for what a facility actually delivered. Hyperscalers get past that on brand and scale. Mid-market operators cannot, and as I see it, that's one of the biggest commercial handicaps they carry. It has nothing to do with how well they run their sites. The market has noticed. Buyers now use independent assessments of AI cloud operators to decide where their workloads go. The money side has noticed too. CoreWeave's $8.5 billion facility, secured against its infrastructure and a contract with a strong customer, has a fixed-rate tranche priced at around 5.9%, while its own unsecured five-year bonds sit close to 10%. Part of that gap is the hardware pledged behind the deal, but the rest, as I read it, is a contract that gave lenders something to rely on beyond the company's own word. Lenders will finance what they can check. With no record of your own, you borrow against someone else's name or pay a few hundred basis points more, and deals take longer either way. The dashboard was never built to answer this Here's a distinction I keep coming back to. A dashboard answers the operator's question: "How is my facility performing?" The person across the table is asking something else: "Can I rely on this when I sign a contract?" Running the first instrument harder won't answer the second. In my experience, three things separate a record somebody else can rely on from good monitoring. The readings need to be collected in a way the other side recognizes, at a defined point and interval, just like the meter. The record needs to be continuous, bad quarters included, because a history with the worst months taken out isn't really a history. And it has to stay blind to what customers are actually computing, the way a meter sees kilowatt-hours but not what you use them for. What I'd start writing down today You don't need new instrumentation for any of this, just a decision about what to keep and the discipline to keep it. Building uptime isn't the best place to start, because a building can be up while half the chips inside it are failing. I'd track how many contracted GPU hours actually turned into usable work after failures, restarts, and degraded links. The industry calls this goodput, and it's what a customer is really paying for. I'd keep the incident history beside it: what failed, how often, and how fast it was replaced. How an incident was resolved is something an outsider can check. Then there's how a site behaves when power gets tight, and that's the one I'd pay most attention to, because the grid side has made up its mind. This May, after incidents in which a gigawatt or more of computing load dropped off the grid unexpectedly, NERC, North America's grid reliability body, issued a rare top-level alert. It told grid operators to tighten how large computing loads are studied, tested, and connected. Load behavior now has to be measured to a standard, rather than described by the operator. Finally, I'd write the methodology down: what's measured, where, how often, who may check it, how long it's kept. That costs almost nothing and gets skipped most. A two-year record can't be built backwards, which is why I'd start now. A power plant with a certified generation and dispatch history talks to the market very differently from one showing its own charts, because a stranger can act on it without knowing or liking the operator. The meter is coming Every mature infrastructure industry eventually got its meter. Electricity has certified metering, and telecom carriers that compete every day still settle with each other against a shared record. AI infrastructure is young and still runs mostly on trust and brand, and I don't think that phase lasts. When a neutral way to record what a facility delivered arrives, I expect it to favor the operators who kept honest, continuous records all along, and that's where a mid-market operator can actually win against a hyperscaler. You don't win in infrastructure by promising the most. The winner is the one who can prove what they've already delivered. artigo.texto: Egypt to Host Rosatom-Teletech Energy Storage Assembly Facility of 500 MWh per Year Rosatom and Egypt's Teletech sign an agreement to set up local assembly capacity for lithium-ion storage systems, with staff training and a gradual ramp-up of production. The Energy Storage Business Unit of Rosatom's Fuel Division and Egyptian technology company Telecom and Technology Co. (Teletech) have signed an agreement to establish local assembly facilities in Egypt. The agreement also provides for personnel training and a gradual expansion of production capacity. According to the two partners, the planned facilities would have a potential production capacity of 500 MWh per year. Battery storage is the subject of other recent announcements, such as Turbo Energy bringing 62.5 MWh of energy storage online across three Spanish industrial sites, or Nala Renewables starting construction of a 125 MW/250 MWh project in Finland. An agreement concluded on the sidelines of Egypt Energy 2026 The agreement was concluded in connection with the Egypt Energy 2026 Exhibition and Conference. Rosatom and Teletech took part in a session there titled "Powering Resilience: The Future of Energy Storage Systems." The session addressed the growing role of energy storage technologies. Discussions on localized production and the product portfolio continued on the sidelines of the conference. A signing ceremony followed the session. Murad Aslanov, Director of Rosatom's Country Office in Egypt, represented the Energy Storage Business Unit. Teletech's Chief Technology Officer represented the Egyptian company. Lithium-ion solutions across the full technological cycle During the session, Rosatom presented its capabilities in lithium-ion energy storage systems. The company says it develops solutions across the full technological cycle, from the development and production of electrodes, cells, battery management systems (BMS) and modules to finished traction batteries and stationary energy storage systems. The applications cited include integrating storage with renewable energy sources, improving the reliability of electricity supply, compensating for fluctuating loads and deploying lithium-ion systems in autonomous power systems. The cooperation is expected to serve as a platform for deployment in the electric power industry, telecommunications, data centers, oil and gas, and other industrial applications. Localization and import-reduction objectives According to Murad Aslanov, building local capacity for energy storage systems can support grid stability as renewable energy expands, reduce dependence on imported technologies and external supply chains, and develop domestic technical expertise. He says the collaboration supports Egypt's 2030 vision. Teletech's Chief Technology Officer states that the partnership combines lithium-ion storage technology with local implementation capabilities and will help strengthen supply chain flexibility. Both parties link the assembly facility to Egypt's Sustainable Clean Energy Plan 2030, which prioritizes diversification of the national energy mix, greater integration of renewable energy sources and the localization of advanced energy technologies. Under the agreement, local assembly of battery energy storage systems (BESS) is expected to help reduce dependence on imported technologies. It is also expected to support grid stability and strengthen domestic technical capabilities. Rosatom adds that the local presence will expand its ability to bring Russian technological solutions to international markets, while adapting its portfolio to the requirements of local energy infrastructure. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: Decision 2026 | Nearly $100 million in data center money on the line on Mason County ballots MASON COUNTY, W.Va. (WSAZ) - As Mason County voters head to the polls for the 2026 general election as early as next Wednesday, they will see a familiar tax levy on their ballot, for the Mason County Board of Education. The levy asks for the same percentage of property tax as is currently being taxed, and is projected to bring in nearly $10 million if passed. And according to state Treasurer Larry Pack, the two new data centers currently being developed in the county could bring in an additional $90 million for the county’s schools - but only if the levy is passed in November. “If [the levy] is defeated, then the Board of Education will lose the regular amount - the $9 million - and they will also lose the $90 million,” Pack told WSAZ. Pack explained any money county school boards would get from data centers are contingent on their tax levies. “The only money the Board of Education can get, any Board of Education can get, with respect to these data centers, is if they have an excess levy in the county,” Pack explained. “If the excess levy goes away, then the Board of Education does not get any of the money, with respect to the data centers.” And if the levy fails, Pack said the data center developers would get to keep the $90 million. “The data center will pay $90 million less in taxes if the levy fails,” he told WSAZ. “So basically, it’s a reduction in taxes to the data center, so the data centers will gain the $90 million.” Pack said this is due to how H.B. 2014, the West Virginia law meant to incentivize data centers and microgrids coming to the state, is structured. He explained under the current bill, all of that money goes to the state and county commissions, but not county Boards of Education. “I think it definitely needs to be addressed, without a doubt,” Pack told WSAZ, calling for legislators to amend H.B. 2014 surrounding this issue. WSAZ asked Pack if he agreed with those who argue that all the money should go to the county and locality level, rather than the state. “If the county could tell us how they’re going to do it,” he responded. “I think those are the discussions we’ve got to see. I think if you take that money back to the state and you put $100 million in a $5 billion sack, I think it would be really easy for that $100 million to get lost ... I think the locals may have a good argument, but we need more information.” Mason County Superintendent Melissa Farmer and members of the county school board were unavailable for comment. They told WSAZ they plan to meet with Pack Friday to get more information about the issue. Copyright 2026 WSAZ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Na manhã de 14 de outubro de 2026, o jornal Finanças e Investimentos, em colaboração com o Banco Central do Vietnã, organizou o seminário "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde", com foco na discussão das relações entre a política de crédito, o mercado de carbono e o mercado de capitais, buscando, assim, soluções para desbloquear recursos financeiros para o processo de transição verde. Em seu discurso de abertura no workshop, o Vice-Governador do Banco Estatal do Vietnã, Nguyen Ngoc Canh, elogiou a iniciativa do jornal Finanças e Investimentos de organizar o workshop "Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono : Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde". Este é um fórum prático para que agências de gestão, instituições de crédito, empresas e especialistas participem e troquem ideias sobre um tema cada vez mais importante para a transformação verde da economia : a mobilização e a utilização eficaz de capital para esse processo. Em cumprimento ao compromisso assumido pelo Vietnã na COP26 de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050, o Partido, o Estado e o Governo emitiram diversas políticas e diretrizes importantes para promover o crescimento verde, a transição energética e o desenvolvimento de uma economia de baixo carbono . Essa transição exige recursos significativos para investimentos em inovação tecnológica, transformação dos métodos de produção, uso eficiente de energia e redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Nesse contexto, além dos recursos do orçamento estatal e da mobilização dos mercados de capitais e monetários, é necessário desenvolver simultaneamente outros mecanismos de mercado para mobilizar mais recursos e criar incentivos econômicos para que as empresas reduzam proativamente as emissões, incluindo o mercado de carbono . Por meio do estabelecimento de cotas, da mensuração dos resultados da redução de emissões e da formação de preços de transação para cotas e créditos de carbono , o mercado de carbono cria um mecanismo para converter os resultados da redução de emissões em valor econômico. Isso proporciona às empresas motivação e recursos adicionais para continuarem investindo no processo de transição verde, em vez de dependerem principalmente do crédito bancário. Em 29 de janeiro de 2026, o Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 29/2026/ND-CP, que regulamenta a bolsa de carbono nacional, criando um arcabouço legal para a organização e operação do mercado e da negociação de cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa e créditos de carbono . O mercado piloto está sendo inicialmente estabelecido com uma escala superior a 511 milhões de toneladas de CO2, equivalente às quotas de emissão atribuídas às instalações nos três principais setores emissores: energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento, durante o período de 2025-2026. A fase piloto terá duração até o final de 2028, antes de entrar na fase de operação obrigatória completa a partir de 2029. Neste mercado, os bancos comerciais participam como bancos liquidadores; durante a fase piloto, o BIDV é o único banco liquidador do mercado. O vice-governador Nguyen Ngoc Canh afirmou que, da perspectiva do setor bancário, é necessário reconhecer claramente o papel do crédito verde e do mercado de carbono no processo de transição verde. Em primeiro lugar, o crédito verde fornece capital para investimento e inovação tecnológica, criando recursos para o desenvolvimento de indústrias/setores verdes, resultando, assim, na redução das emissões. As reduções de emissões provenientes de projetos financiados por bancos criarão a base e as commodities para o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono . Por outro lado, um mercado de carbono que funcione de forma eficiente apoiará as empresas, fornecendo-lhes receitas estáveis e fluxo de caixa provenientes da redução de emissões, o que sustentará suas atividades de produção e negócios, melhorará a qualidade de seu crédito bancário e lhes permitirá comprar créditos de carbono para atender aos rigorosos padrões das atividades de importação e exportação. Para atividades de crédito verde, é importante não apenas que os fundos desembolsados para um projeto sejam identificados como verdes, mas também que os resultados de economia de energia, redução de emissões e proteção ambiental alcançados pelo tomador do empréstimo sejam verificados. A mensuração, o relato e a avaliação dos resultados de redução de emissões, bem como a negociação de cotas e créditos no mercado de carbono , podem fornecer informações adicionais para monitorar os resultados ambientais de um projeto. Isso ajuda as instituições de crédito a avaliar a eficácia da utilização do capital e aprimorar a gestão e a supervisão dos fluxos de capital verde. Segundo o Vice-Governador, na realidade, ao longo dos últimos anos, o setor bancário tem implementado proativamente diversas soluções para promover o crédito verde, direcionando fluxos de capital para indústrias e setores que trazem benefícios ambientais e reduzem as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. O Banco Central do Vietnã aperfeiçoou gradualmente o arcabouço político, emitiu orientações e diretrizes sobre crédito verde, gestão de riscos ambientais e sociais, e incentivou as instituições de crédito a desenvolverem estratégias, processos internos e produtos de crédito adequados às metas de crescimento verde. Embora outros canais de mobilização de capital verde estejam se desenvolvendo, o crédito verde continua a desempenhar um papel crucial como um importante recurso para o desenvolvimento de indústrias/setores verdes e para apoiar a transição do modelo de crescimento para uma economia de baixo carbono . Desde os primeiros anos de implementação do crédito verde (2017) até o presente, as atividades de crédito verde expandiram-se tanto em termos de escala de crédito quanto no nível de participação das instituições de crédito. No final de junho de 2026, o saldo de crédito verde atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025

artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência de PL sobre divisão de custos de baterias Votação do mérito deve ficar para depois das eleições; projeto impacta leilões de dezembro A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o regime de urgência do projeto de lei 3.716 de 2026, que altera a divisão dos custos de contratação de baterias no setor elétrico. A proposta enfrenta divergências entre agentes do setor, e ainda não há prazo para a votação no Legislativo. A aprovação do texto pode afetar os primeiros leilões de armazenamento de energia em larga escala no Brasil, marcados para dezembro. Com a aprovação da urgência, o projeto passa a tramitar de forma acelerada e pode ser votado diretamente no plenário da Câmara, sem precisar passar pelas comissões temáticas. O texto ainda precisa ser analisado pelos deputados e, se aprovado, seguirá para o Senado. A expectativa do setor é que a votação do mérito do projeto só aconteça depois das eleições. Os leilões estão marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, com contratos de 15 anos e início do fornecimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Em setembro, o diretor da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Gentil Nogueira, afirmou que uma alteração na legislação às vésperas dos leilões poderia levar ao adiamento das disputas por até 30 dias, para permitir a adaptação das regras. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o PL 3.716 de 2026 propõe revogar um dispositivo da lei 15.269 de 2025 que determina que os custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade por baterias sejam pagos exclusivamente pelas empresas geradoras de energia. Com a mudança, as despesas passariam a seguir a regra geral da reserva de capacidade e seriam divididas entre os usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo consumidores e autoprodutores. A proposta é apoiada por associações ligadas à geração de energia solar e eólica, além de produtores independentes e empresas de armazenamento. As entidades argumentam que as baterias beneficiam todo o sistema elétrico ao armazenar eletricidade para utilização nos horários de maior demanda. Por isso, defendem que o custo seja distribuído de maneira proporcional entre os beneficiários. Manutenção da regra atual Do outro lado, as distribuidoras defendem a manutenção da regra atual. A Abradee (Associação Brasileira de Distribuidores de Energia Elétrica) argumenta que a expansão das fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, contribuiu para a necessidade de contratar baterias. Na avaliação da entidade, os geradores devem arcar com os custos, uma vez que os consumidores já financiam a expansão dessas fontes por meio de subsídios incluídos nas tarifas de energia. Em nota, a Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) classificou a aprovação da urgência como um “avanço” para ampliar a segurança jurídica dos leilões. A entidade defende a mudança na divisão dos custos, mas afirma que a discussão no Congresso não deve comprometer o calendário dos leilões. Eis a íntegra (PDF – 166 kB). A associação alerta que um eventual adiamento pode comprometer a entrada dos sistemas de armazenamento em operação em 2028 e aumentar o risco de deficit de potência e de apagões em períodos críticos de atendimento. Durante uma audiência pública que inaugurou as contribuições dos agentes do setor para o edital do leilão, o adiamento foi discutido. Beneficiados pelo PL em discussão no Congresso temem que o certame seja realizado antes da eventual aprovação da lei. A Aneel, até o momento, tem assegurado que manterá o cronograma, salvo se a lei for alterada durante os 30 dias que antecedem o leilão. Nesse caso, poderá adiar em até 30 dias a realização do certame para que empresas possam adaptar suas propostas.

artigo.texto: Eskom has launched a process to select a strategic partner to help deliver the 1.5GW Tubatse pumped-storage scheme, a landmark project in Limpopo set to become South Africa’s largest energy-storage programme. As a flagship development in Eskom Green, an unbundled renewable energy subsidiary of the state power utility, the project will provide the long-duration energy storage needed to integrate increasing volumes of renewable energy into the national grid, strengthen energy security and support South Africa’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon electricity system. “As South Africa advances its energy transition, long-duration storage will be essential to maintaining a reliable and resilient power system. Tubatse will provide the flexibility needed to integrate increasing volumes of renewable energy while strengthening grid stability and security of supply,” Eskom group CEO Dan Marokane said in a statement on Tuesday. Last week, electricity & energy minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa said the government would prioritise the procurement of 4,600MW of battery energy storage systems and 5,000MW of gas-to-power under its integrated resource plan unveiled last year. The combined allocation of 9,600MW responds to the electricity system’s immediate requirements for storage, flexibility and dispatchable supply amid increasing curtailment, which occurs when available generation cannot be accommodated due to network constraints or operating conditions, including periods when supply exceeds demand. South Africa plans to build 14,000km of new high-voltage transmission lines over the next decade, at an estimated cost of R440bn, to connect new wind, solar, battery storage and gas generation projects to the national grid while strengthening the network to support changing electricity flows. The just-launched request-for-qualification process for Tubatse is the first stage of a competitive exercise to identify a partner with the financial strength, technical expertise, development experience and long-term commitment required to advance the scheme, Eskom said on Tuesday. The proposed facility will provide about 21 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage through four reversible pump-turbine units. A gigawatt-hour is a unit of total energy equal to 1-billion watt-hours (Wh) delivered or consumed over an hour. Able to generate at full output for up to 14 hours, the scheme will help balance the power system, support greater renewable energy integration and enhance grid reliability. Eskom Green is targeting up to 6GW by 2030, with plans to expand its clean energy portfolio to 21GW by 2035 and up to 32GW by 2040, including 5GW of hydro and pumped storage. “Tubatse is … a cornerstone of Eskom Green’s ambition to develop the infrastructure required for a modern, low-carbon electricity system. By combining Eskom’s development experience with private-sector expertise and investment, we aim to unlock the full potential of this project while supporting economic growth, localisation and skills development,” Eskom group executive for renewables Rivoningo Mnisi said. Tubatse will store surplus electricity when demand is low and release it during peak demand, when wind and solar output drops, or when the grid is under strain. This will help reduce wasted renewable energy, make better use of existing generation and strengthen security of supply. The project has been classified as one of the top 12 national priority projects by Infrastructure South Africa and forms part of the country’s just transition programme towards cleaner renewable energies. Tubatse builds on more than two decades of Eskom’s experience in operating and maintaining pumped storage schemes and conventional hydropower plants, including the delivery of the 1,332MW Ingula pumped storage scheme commissioned in 2017. The power utility currently operates 2,732MW of pumped storage capacity across Drakensberg, Palmiet and Ingula, as well as 661MW of conventional hydroelectric capacity, primarily at Gariep and Vanderkloof. The required land has been secured, environmental authorisation has been granted for the scheme, and key technical studies and access-road designs have reached an advanced stage, Eskom said. Grid connection studies have also advanced, and the department of water & sanitation has confirmed water availability from De Hoop Dam. “Together, these milestones distinguish Tubatse from an early-stage concept and provide prospective partners with the opportunity to invest in an advanced development platform where critical enabling work is either complete or well progressed,” the utility said. artigo.texto: Madison County planning commission votes against battery energy storage facility Madison County’s Planning Commission has given a unanimous unfavorable recommendation for zoning changes to allow a proposed battery energy storage facility. IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports. Audio Transcript Developers with Jupiter Power want to build two battery energy storage system facilities in the county. Battery storage facilities hold surplus energy from a local power grid in large lithium batteries until it’s needed in times of peak power use. These kinds of facilities do not generate any power on their own. As part of hours of deliberation, Nat Drucker with Jupiter Power addressed several concerns from residents – like capping the number of total batteries, draining water to an independent system, and taking precautions against fire. “We hope that all of this shows and demonstrates that we are absolutely willing to work with people.” Drucker said. “And we’re working to do this better, and to provide this very important piece of infrastructure that is going to help keep this county, and this part of Indiana, moving forward.” The rezoning was proposed last month with the planning commission, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions. Despite that new information, members of the public remained firmly against the battery storage facility. Former Madison County Council member Ben Gale was among them. “So the numbers we’re seeing up here, I don’t buy them,” he said. “I’ve been through the process before, I see how it works, and the promises made up front are never what ends up working.” Officials with Jupiter Power say neither project involves a large building. The sites instead feature “container-based” energy storage. After the unfavorable recommendation, the project will now move to the county commissioners to consider and vote on the rezoning request. If it were to be approved in Madison County, Jupiter Power says the first site, Liberty 1, would start construction in 2027 and be operational in 2028. Indiana Michigan Power has an agreement with Jupiter Power to purchase the battery storage facility upon its completion. The second site, Liberty 2, is significantly bigger, and has a longer development time. No long-term ownership of the site has been determined yet. Thomas Ouellette is our reporter and producer. Contact him at thomas.ouellette@bsu.edu.

artigo.texto: BYD Is a Battery Company That Happens to Build Cars Ask most people what BYD does and they will say electric cars. That is true, and it undersells the company by a wide margin. BYD is a Chinese multinational manufacturing conglomerate that builds rechargeable batteries, stationary energy storage, solar panels, semiconductors, forklifts, and entire monorail systems. The car business is the loudest part. It is not the whole company, and it was not even the first. BYD Company Ltd. operates across electronics, autos, renewable energy, and rail transit. That spread is not an accident of acquisition. It is the result of a battery maker deciding, over three decades, that it could build the things its batteries power, then the things that move those things, then the infrastructure they run on. To understand BYD you have to start before the cars existed. Wang Chuanfu founded BYD to make rechargeable batteries in February 1995, formally registered as Shenzhen BYD Battery Company Ltd. Before that he worked as a vice supervisor at Beijing's Nonferrous Research Institute. He saw an opening as Japanese companies shifted from NiCd toward higher-value nickel-metal hydride and lithium-ion chemistries, and he went after the segment they were leaving behind. The early strategy was labor, not automation. BYD built its business on manual labor rather than the capital-intensive, highly automated processes Japanese rivals used, and that approach, combined with in-house production of key machinery, cut its unit costs to roughly five or six times lower than Japanese competitors. It worked. BYD won an order from Sanyo in 1996 that marked its arrival in the global supply chain, and by July 2002 it had surpassed Sanyo to become the world's leading NiCd battery maker, accounting for 65% of global production. The car business came later. BYD Auto was established in 2003. For a battery company that had just won the NiCd crown, building cars was the logical place to put all those cells. BYD is well known for its Blade Battery, and one sits in every BYD EV. The headline feature is safety: it has passed the nail penetration test, and its compressive strength reaches 445 kN, the equivalent of a 45-ton truck. The warranty runs eight years or longer, covering 310,685 miles and in some cases up to 621,371 miles. BYD does not keep the batteries to itself. It functions as an OEM battery supplier, and FinDreams Battery, its subsidiary, ranked as the world's number-two EV battery producer in 2024, holding 17% of the EV battery market behind CATL. Its customers include rivals. The Toyota bZ3, a China-only sedan co-developed with BYD, runs a BYD Blade Battery underneath, and regulatory filings show Tesla has fitted BYD cells in the Model Y. BYD Energy Storage was founded in 2008 and specializes in energy storage solutions. According to its website, it has rolled out industrial and residential projects in 110 countries. The scale here is genuinely large and often overlooked in all the EV coverage. In 2025, BYD topped global Battery Energy Storage System shipments at more than 60 GWh, displacing Tesla — the first year it held the number one BESS position worldwide. That gave BYD a 13 percent global BESS market share, against Tesla's 10 percent, per Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Tesla shipped 46.7 GWh of storage that year. The grid-scale battery business, in other words, is now another market where BYD leads and Tesla follows. The most surprising corner of BYD is the one where it stopped being a parts supplier and became a civil engineering firm. SkyRail is an advanced monorail; its carriages ride on an elevated single beam that supports and guides them, and BYD built the entire system — vehicles, tracks, stations, and communication systems. The R&D project ran five years, mobilized more than 1,000 engineers, and cost over 600 million euro, with total SkyRail investment exceeding $1 billion. The pitch is cost. SkyRail runs about a fifth of what a subway costs to build, with construction taking as little as two years — one third the time a subway takes, helped by prefabricated track beams. It can move 10,000 to 30,000 passengers per hour in one direction. BYD positions it for cities worried about the financial burden of a subway. It has launched lines in Shenzhen and Sao Paulo, Brazil. The grand plan was bigger: an initial rollout across more than 200 Chinese cities was cut back sharply once Beijing moved to curb local government debt. The vertical integration shows up in the financials. BYD's net profit in 2025 was CNY 32.62 billion, roughly $4.72 billion, and it earned 1.25 times more net profit than Tesla while pulling in 1.23 times the revenue. It sold 2.81 times as many vehicles. That volume comes at a lower price per car — a domestic average selling price around CNY 141,000, about $20,400 — but the batteries, electronics, and storage businesses give BYD revenue streams Tesla does not have. It is not all up and to the right. BYD's 2025 revenue grew only 3.46%, its slowest in six years, net profit fell 18.97% — its first yearly profit drop in four years — blamed on a fierce domestic price war that squeezed margins. Overseas is now the profitability lever: exports passed the 1 million mark for the first time, hitting 1.05 million, a 145% jump, and overseas operations rose to 38.65% of revenue. If you want to track BYD as the conglomerate it actually is, read past the vehicle delivery numbers. Its 2025 annual report is filed on the Shenzhen exchange under 002594.SZ and on HKEX under 01211.HK, where the segment breakdowns show handset revenue and the rest. Watch the energy storage shipments, since that is where BYD just overtook Tesla. And keep an eye on U.S. legislation banning Chinese vehicle software from 2027 and Chinese hardware from 2030, on top of existing 100 percent tariffs on Chinese EVs — the regulatory wall that will decide how much of this empire ever reaches American roads. artigo.texto: On the morning of October 14, 2026, the Finance and Investment Newspaper, in collaboration with the State Bank of Vietnam, organized the seminar "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows," focusing on discussing the linkages between credit policy, the carbon market, and the capital market, thereby seeking solutions to unlock financial resources for the green transition process. In his keynote address at the workshop, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam Nguyen Ngoc Canh highly appreciated the initiative of the Finance and Investment Newspaper in organizing the workshop "Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows" today. This is a practical forum for management agencies, credit institutions, businesses, and experts to participate and exchange ideas on an issue that is becoming increasingly important for the green transformation of the economy : mobilizing and effectively utilizing capital for this process. In fulfillment of Vietnam's commitment at COP26 to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the Party, State, and Government have issued many important policies and guidelines to promote green growth, energy transition, and the development of a low -carbon economy. This transition requires significant resources for investment in technological innovation, transformation of production methods, efficient energy use, and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. In this context, in addition to resources from the state budget and mobilization from the capital and money markets, it is necessary to simultaneously develop other market mechanisms to mobilize more resources and create economic incentives for businesses to proactively reduce emissions, including the carbon market. Through the establishment of quotas, measurement of emission reduction results, and the formation of transaction prices for quotas and carbon credits, the carbon market creates a mechanism to convert emission reduction results into economic value. This provides businesses with additional motivation and resources to continue investing in the green transition process, instead of relying primarily on bank credit. On January 29, 2026, the Government issued Decree No. 29/2026/ND-CP regulating the domestic carbon exchange, creating a legal framework for organizing and operating the market and trading of greenhouse gas emission quotas and carbon credits. The pilot market is initially being established with a scale of over 511 million tons of CO2, equivalent to the emission quotas allocated to facilities in the three major emitting sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement, during the 2025-2026 period. The pilot phase will last until the end of 2028, before entering the full mandatory operation phase from 2029. In this market, commercial banks participate as settlement banks; during the pilot phase, BIDV is the sole settlement bank in the market. Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that, from the perspective of the banking sector, it is necessary to clearly recognize the role of green credit and the carbon market in the green transition process. First, green credit provides capital for investment and technological innovation, creating resources for the development of green industries/sectors, thereby resulting in reduced emissions. The emission reductions from projects funded by banks will create the basis and commodities for the development of the carbon market. Conversely, an efficiently functioning carbon market will support businesses by providing them with stable revenue and cash flow from emission reductions, which will support their production and business activities, improve their bank credit quality, and enable them to purchase carbon credits to meet the stringent standards of import and export activities. For green credit activities, it is important not only that the disbursed funds for a project are identified as green, but also that the results of energy savings, emission reduction, and environmental protection achieved by the borrower are verified. Measuring, reporting, and evaluating emission reduction results, as well as trading quotas and credits in the carbon market, can provide additional information to monitor the environmental outcomes of a project. This helps credit institutions assess the effectiveness of capital utilization and enhance the management and supervision of green capital flows. According to the Deputy Governor, in reality, over the past years, the banking sector has proactively implemented many solutions to promote green credit, directing capital flows into industries and sectors that bring environmental benefits and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The State Bank of Vietnam has gradually perfected the policy framework, issued orientations and guidelines on green credit, environmental and social risk management; and encouraged credit institutions to build strategies, internal processes, and develop credit products suitable for green growth goals. While other green capital mobilization channels are developing, green credit continues to play a crucial role as an important resource for developing green industries/sectors and supporting the transition of the growth model to a low -carbon economy. From the early years of green credit implementation (2017) to the present, green credit activities have expanded both in terms of credit scale and the level of participation of credit institutions. By the end of June 2026, outstanding green credit reached over VND 856 trillion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025, with an average growth rate of over 20% per year during the 2017-2025 period, mainly concentrated in agriculture , forestry, fisheries and biodiversity conservation (accounting for over 31%), and green energy (accounting for nearly 28%). artigo.texto: BYD Dolphin Mini 2027 já está nas lojas e marca atualiza carro em silêncio Outra novidade é o aerofólio traseiro, emprestado do Dolphin Surf, nome usado pelo modelo na Europa. A peça prolonga visualmente a linha do teto e foi projetada para ajudar a organizar o fluxo de ar na traseira. Sem aviso prévio, a BYD começou a distribuir a linha 2027 do Dolphin Mini para algumas concessionárias brasileiras. O hatch elétrico ganhou uma nova opção de pintura cinza metálico, além de mudanças nos pneus e no aerofólio traseiro. A configuração GS, topo de linha, já pode ser encomendada por R$ 119.990. As alterações, contudo, nem sequer aparecem no site da marca. A principal mudança técnica está nos pneus. O modelo deixa de utilizar os Hankook 175/55 R16 e passa a contar com os Pirelli Cinturato P6, na medida 185/55 R16. A largura aumenta em 10 mm, enquanto o perfil ligeiramente mais alto mantém as rodas de aro 16. Outra novidade é o aerofólio traseiro, emprestado do Dolphin Surf, nome usado pelo modelo na Europa. A peça prolonga visualmente a linha do teto e foi projetada para ajudar a organizar o fluxo de ar na traseira. A linha 2027 mantém os conjuntos mecânicos e as baterias da versão anterior. O Dolphin Mini GL utiliza uma bateria de 30,08 kWh e tem autonomia de 224 km pelo Inmetro. Já o GS conta com bateria de 38,88 kWh e alcance homologado de 280 km. A recarga em corrente contínua também varia conforme a versão: são até 30 kW no GL e 40 kW no GS. Em corrente alternada, a potência máxima permanece em 6,6 kW. BYD não quis comentar as mudanças A BYD foi procurada, por meio de assessoria de comunicação, para comentar as alterações na linha 2027, mas não respondeu até o fechamento da reportagem original.
