artigo.texto: Veja o resumo da notícia - O mercado de carbono no agronegócio brasileiro é visto como promissor, mas pode ser uma ilusão para a realidade econômica do setor. - A aventura do mercado de carbono revela-se pouco rentável para o produtor rural, devido aos altos custos de mensuração e taxas de intermediários. - A regra de adicionalidade impede que produtores pioneiros monetizem o estoque de carbono preservado, premiando apenas os retardatários. - Esquemas voluntários e fragmentados, com altos custos de transação, carecem de eficácia e falham em gerar valor real, segundo economistas. - O caminho viável para o campo envolve a valorização do carbono na cadeia de suprimentos, acesso a crédito verde e ganhos de produtividade. Para muitos o mercado de carbono representa a próxima grande safra do agronegócio brasileiro mas quando confrontada com a realidade econômica do setor pode ser uma grande ilusão. Para o produtor rural, essa aventura revela-se muitas vezes pouco rentável. Nos solos tropicais, onde o carbono possui dinâmica complexa e instável, a comprovação do sequestro exige amostragens físicas caras e auditorias rigorosas. Como o sequestro líquido anual no plantio direto costuma ser inferior a uma tonelada por hectare, os altos custos de mensuração e as taxas cobradas por intermediários devoram a margem financeira, deixando para a fazenda um retorno meramente residual. Soma-se a isso a perversidade da regra de adicionalidade, que exige que a prática mitigadora seja nova, impedindo que o produtor pioneiro monetize o estoque que preserva há décadas e premiando apenas o retardatário. Essa dispersão contratual ilustra os alertas de economistas como William Nordhaus (premio Novel de 2018) e Robert Stavins: esquemas voluntários, fragmentados e repletos de custos de transação carecem de eficácia e falham em gerar valor real. O caminho viável para o campo não passa pela especulação de papéis, mas sim pela valorização do carbono dentro da própria cadeia de suprimentos, pelo acesso a crédito verde e pelos ganhos diretos de produtividade e resiliência que um solo vivo naturalmente proporciona e mecanismos como RenovaBio.

artigo.texto: The Kremlin in Moscow is investigating how much financial loss Yandex -- which supports AI and search in Russia -- has incurred after last week's drone attack on three of its data centers. One of the data centers is used to train its AI models. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was too early to assess whether users had suffered financial losses from outages, Reuters reported. Asked by Reuters whether the government was considering a mechanism to compensate users, he said Yandex was "currently facing difficulties," adding that "the matter is being discussed by the government, but the company is taking urgent steps to address the consequences of the attack." Media reports in Russia are calling Yandex,Russia’s largest technology company." Last week it announced that two of its data centers were struck by drones. “Serious" damage was reported at all three locations. advertisement advertisement In a statement posted on Friday, Yandex said operations at its Sasovo facility were “completely halted,” while part of the infrastructure in Kaluga was “disabled.” The Vladimir facility was taken completely offline on Sunday, according to the company. "Data centers are the 'iron heart' of Yandex," according to a post on the company’s website translated into English from Russian. “Their operability is critical for services that have become part of people's everyday lives. Millions of users check traffic and build routes, listen to music, watch movies, order groceries, and get answers to questions. Our technologies help hundreds of thousands of companies run their businesses: taking orders, serving customers, and interacting with partners.” Following the attacks on the Sasovo and Kaluga facilities, a third Ukrainian drone strike hit Yandex's Vladimir data center on Sunday, Oct. 11, forcing a complete shutdown of operations at that site. The Sasovo data center is noted for housing two of Yandex's top supercomputers equipped with Nvidia A100 chips used to train its YandexGPT AI models. Chinese conglomerates represent one of the largest foreign ad segments on Yandex today that leverages search, video, and geotargeted navigation ads across Yandex Maps and Navigator, according to Google Gemini. These recent targeted drone strikes hit a company still trying to recover from a recent restructuring following a corporate split in 2024. Yandex is based in Russia. It has retained the brand’s name and continues to operate as Russia's leading search engine and AI lead. Its Dutch parent company rebranded as Nebius Group. Yandex still dominates domestic search with the most market share in the region, but it is currently battling infrastructure challenges after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted several of its data centers and supercomputers. In 2024, Yandex NV, the parent company of the Russian search engine at the time, agreed to sell its assets in Russia to a group of local investors for $5.2 billion in one of the largest corporate exits from Russia since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. Nebius Group, which now focuses on AI, found that its shares fell 2% on Tuesday -- opening at $200.50 versus a prior close of $210.06, while trading volume reached nearly 6.94 million shares, according to MarketBeat. The company does not sell advertising space or operate an advertising network. Unlike its predecessor Yandex, focused on digital advertising, Nebius has completely exited the consumer-facing ad-tech industry.

artigo.texto: Saudi Arabia’s ACWA is expanding its renewable energy, electricity storage and water desalination projects as the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and data centers drives up power demand and increases the need for reliable, efficient and competitively priced electricity. Omar al-Hassan, ACWA CEO in Saudi Arabia, told Asharq Al-Awsat that the accelerating expansion of AI and data centers was reshaping the energy sector’s requirements. The challenge is no longer limited to generating more electricity, he explained, but also involves ensuring a continuous supply, operational efficiency and competitive costs. ACWA is developing projects that combine renewable energy and storage with solutions to strengthen supply reliability, drawing on its experience in large-scale power and water projects. The company’s total power generation capacity stands at 98.2 gigawatts, while its desalination portfolio has a capacity of 9.7 million cubic meters per day. Al-Hassan also highlighted ACWA’s efforts to harness digital technologies and AI to improve the performance of its assets, going beyond meeting rising electricity demand to developing more efficient and reliable solutions. Storage supports renewable energy expansion As Saudi Arabia expands its solar and wind projects, electricity storage is becoming increasingly important, allowing power generated during periods of abundant supply to be stored for use when demand rises. Al-Hassan expects storage to play a growing role in the Kingdom’s energy system alongside generation facilities and transmission networks. In August 2026, ACWA signed three agreements with the Saudi Power Procurement Company, acting as the principal buyer, to develop battery energy storage projects in Haden, Muwayh and Al-Kahfah. The projects have a combined power capacity of 1,500 megawatts and an energy storage capacity of 6,000 megawatt-hours, under agreements spanning 15 years. Al-Hassan described the projects as evidence of opportunities in the Saudi market and the importance of storage in supporting renewable energy expansion. He expects storage to become an increasingly significant factor in planning new projects, depending on grid needs, individual project requirements and economic feasibility. Red Sea project demonstrates off-grid potential ACWA’s Red Sea project, which combines solar generation and battery storage, has demonstrated the feasibility of operating an integrated utilities system powered by renewable energy and storage without connecting to the national electricity grid. The project began commercial operations in September 2026 and includes a 340-megawatt solar power plant and a battery storage system with a capacity of 1,227 megawatt-hours. According to al-Hassan, the project underscores the importance of integrated planning from the outset, with generation and storage capacities designed to meet actual demand and ensure uninterrupted supplies. He emphasized that the success of renewable energy projects depends not only on generation capacity but also on the integration of system components and operational efficiency, while accounting for differences in site requirements, costs and operating conditions. Partnerships to advance desalination In the water sector, ACWA sees opportunities to advance desalination through greater use of renewable energy and more efficient technologies, helping reduce energy consumption and production costs while meeting growing demand. With a desalination portfolio capable of producing 9.7 million cubic meters of water per day, the company is focusing on improving plant efficiency, developing desalination technologies and reducing reliance on conventional energy sources wherever technically and economically feasible. In August 2026, ACWA signed a memorandum of understanding with Veolia to cooperate on improving desalination plant designs, equipment and operational performance. It also signed a joint development agreement with Indonesia’s PT Garam to establish a project combining seawater desalination with industrial salt production. The project would use shared infrastructure to meet water needs and support industrial activities. Al-Hassan identified further growth opportunities in increasing water production, improving the efficiency of existing plants, developing new technologies and expanding partnerships to provide reliable water supplies at competitive costs.

artigo.texto: Media gets first look at Project Jupiter AI data center in Santa Teresa Oracle and Stack Infrastructure offered a first glimpse of Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, highlighting its progress, technology, and workforce impact. Media gets first look at Project Jupiter AI data center in Santa Teresa Oracle and Stack Infrastructure offered a first glimpse of Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, highlighting its progress, technology, and workforce impact. Media crews were invited for the first time to tour Project Jupiter, a $165 billion AI data center under construction in Santa Teresa, which began building within the past year. The tour showcased several aspects of the roughly 1,400-acre campus, including energy solutions, construction progress, and workforce details. Oracle highlighted Bloom Energy's fuel cell technology, which uses natural gas to generate electricity without burning it. The company explained that this system will reduce air pollution and water usage. Visitors were also shown Building A, one of four planned data center buildings, and its cooling system. "It's a closed-loop cooling system, and so what that means is the project is not continuously consuming water for data center operations," Josh Timberlake, SVP of site strategy at Stack Infrastructure said. The equipment staging area was another stop on the tour, where materials and equipment are managed. Stack Infrastructure, the company developing and building the campus, shared workforce details, saying, "We have just about 4,400 construction workers working here full time. 1,200 of those are New Mexicans. Over 600 of those are from Doña Ana County." The tour concluded inside one of the data halls, where rows of server racks will eventually fill the space. Over the past year, Project Jupiter has faced community concerns regarding water use, air quality, and transparency. During a Q&A session, Oracle executives addressed these concerns, saying, "We're committed to New Mexico at this point. So we're making sure we do everything right. We're taking the feedback we need to adjust something. We keep adjusting till we get to making sure we come through on our New Mexico economic benefit." Oracle noted that this was the first time media had been allowed inside the construction site but assured it would not be the last. The company emphasized its commitment to keeping the community informed as construction progresses. Stack Infrastructure stated that the number of construction workers on-site is expected to grow to nearly 7,000, and hiring for permanent data center operations jobs has already begun.

artigo.texto: It’s a common myth that ostriches bury their heads in the sand when frightened or agitated. Ostriches actually don’t do that. But apparently, some local politicians do. Officials in the Columbia County city of Hudson last week proposed a six-month moratorium on battery energy storage systems — designed to store energy generated from solar arrays and wind turbines — after being approached by a couple of companies about the city’s codes. It turns out the city didn’t have an answer for the companies because it has nothing in its codes about the facilities. That leads to an obvious question: How does any community in New York — a state that seven years ago passed a major long-term initiative to battle climate change — go this long without taking some local initiative to regulate these systems? State law doesn’t require local governments to develop their own municipal regulations for the systems, but it should. These facilities can have major local impacts that might not be prioritized in state-level regulations, including the impact on local property values, rural character and quality of life. Local government officials can play a significant role in where such facilities are located and the conditions for approval. They should not only not be hiding from local regulations, they should be aggressively pursuing them. In fact, in an editorial on Wednesday, we supported the town of Duanesburg’s effort to assume authority from the state to manage large-scale energy projects — citing the town’s years of adapting its comprehensive plan, local zoning codes and local laws to address these projects. Hudson is in the opposite situation. The good news for Hudson and other communities that have similarly avoided addressing this growing issue is that the state has plenty of information and advice available for them. Hudson officials can start by checking out the website of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) website. Among a significant amount of information, the website features a 46-page “Battery Energy Storage System Guidebook for Local Governments.” The guidebook includes a model law to help local government officials adopt legislation and regulations and a model permit to help local officials establish requirements for electrical and structural plan review necessary for permitting. In addition, NYSERDA offers free technical assistance for planning and zoning board members, code officials, first responders and others. Sticking one’s head in the sand doesn’t make a problem go away. It just makes it more difficult to deal with. Fortunately, Hudson officials have time and access to state resources to help them. They should use the time afforded by the moratorium to get caught up.

artigo.texto: The Minneapolis City Planning Commission, a 10-member body of elected officials that advises the City Council on land use, advanced regulations on Oct. 13 that would rein in the size, noise and geographic reach of data centers within city limits. The commission’s move aimed to balance demands from many residents to limit data centers with the need for significant tax revenue that would flow to the city from the use of empty downtown buildings. The proposed regulations, developed within the city’s department of Community Planning and Economic Development (CPED), would restrict data center development to two zoning districts in downtown, including Nicollet Mall and the North Loop. Related: Five things to know as data centers spread across rural America Initially, CPED proposed allowing them to use up to 175,000 square feet of white space – the interior area that houses servers and other technology. But commissioners approved an amendment reducing that maximum to 50,000 square feet. Another amendment was passed to ensure city staff would be able to evaluate and approve data center proposals on a case-by-case basis. Under CPED’s recommendations, data centers could not be the sole occupant of a building or operate on its first or second floor. To limit noise pollution, the regulations would require servers to be located at least 20 feet inside a building and 100 feet from the walls of residential properties. Who would benefit? Dozens of residents in attendance called for stricter regulations or a complete ban on new data center developments, arguing Minneapolis leaders should focus on expanding infrastructure that directly serves the community. Stephen Johnson, who lives within one of the downtown districts designated under the proposed regulations for data center development, urged the commission to create a more robust approval process. “My question for the City Council and this planning commission is, ‘Who benefits?’” Johnson said. “Because it certainly isn’t us, your neighbors.” Data centers support internet services by collecting, storing and transmitting data through large rooms of computer servers. Minneapolis has eight of them in operation, but cloud-based computing and artificial intelligence are driving their rapid expansion across the county and state, said Jason Wittenberg, a manager in the city’s Community Planning and Economic Development department, during Tuesday’s meeting. Minneapolis’ zoning code does not specifically define data centers. Without new regulations, the facilities would continue to be classified as “communication exchanges,” he said, allowing them to operate in more than half of the city’s zoning districts without tailored regulations. Community Voices: The Pine Island blueprint: How Minnesota is setting the standard for data centers In May, the City Council approved a six month pause on the development of new data centers to give city staff time to study the facilities’ impacts and develop regulations. Barring an extension from the Council, the pause is set to expire on Nov. 21. Some residents, including Council member Aisha Chughtai (Ward 10), called for extending the pause to a year. Wittenberg, speaking for the CPED, said that about 30% of downtown building space is vacant and that data centers are taxed at a higher rate than residential buildings. In the face of a roughly $30 million budget shortfall in 2027, he said that even if they’re not an ideal land use, data centers could provide a needed economic boost. “The decline in our downtown tax base is a significant reason why we are in the current budget situation that we’re in,” he said. ‘Please don’t sell it out’ About 40 residents signed up to testify at Tuesday’s meeting. Since the May moratorium, Chughtai said community members have submitted more than 1,600 public comments. Speakers raised concerns about electricity and water consumption, noise and environmental impacts. Data centers use water to cool their systems and prevent servers from overheating. The amount of water used can vary significantly based on a facility’s size and cooling method. While the proposed rules would require developers to disclose anticipated water and electricity use, the city cannot directly regulate consumption. Minneapolis, which draws its water from the Mississippi River, has “tremendous capacity” to supply water to data centers, Wittenberg said, adding that the city currently distributes slightly more than half of its available daily capacity of 111 million gallons. Jane Nalezny, a student in Minneapolis Public Schools, called out the river’s importance to Indigenous communities, wildlife and people throughout the Twin Cities. Related: Minnesota GOP lawmakers grapple with data centers as Republican voters turn against the projects “It’s an amazing accomplishment that we have our water usage below capacity,” she said. “Just because we are able to, does not mean we should be taking more.” Data centers also require substantial amounts of electricity, prompting concern from downtown residents about strain on the electric grid, which is managed by Xcel Energy. Suzanne Murphy, Xcel Energy’s Minneapolis community relations manager said during Tuesday’s meeting that Xcel Energy can reliably serve the energy needs of data centers in downtown Minneapolis. Other residents said the city should focus on uses for buildings that promote a vibrant, welcoming downtown, like housing or business development.“Minneapolis has a lot of work yet to do to reimagine our downtown,” said resident Kate Derickson. “But please don’t sell it out to tech infrastructure,” Derickson said. The recommendations came from the city’s department of Community Planning and Economic Development (CPED), which manages urban planning. The proposals now head to the Minneapolis Business, Housing and Zoning Committee on Nov. 6 and then the Minneapolis City Council. artigo.texto: If Amendment 3 passes in November, it will not only annually take nearly $12 billion away from public safety, roads, parks and other government services, but it will also create a system where the majority of homeowners become a financial drag on the very local governments from which they expect and demand services. If government is supposed to “run like a business,” as we’ve heard so many times before, then the most logical business response would be to deprioritize any future expansion of a sector that creates costs with no financial recuperation while fast tracking sectors that can fill the financial holes for existing residents. Local governments are limited in the revenue they can raise to provide the services people expect. Property taxes are a big chunk of that revenue, which local governments also leverage as a required match to secure federal and state dollars for major projects like stormwater management, flood control, beach renourishment and even affordable housing projects. Often, every dollar cut from property taxes is really a double or even triple loss for major infrastructure projects. To complete these projects to create livable cities, local governments will have no choice but to try and replace most of the lost funds due to Amendment 3. Thus, Amendment 3 could easily usher in an era of mega data centers and other industrial projects that promise the property taxes needed to fill the hole left by homesteaded properties often contributing zero dollars to local services. Indeed, Florida TaxWatch is already pitching local governments and citizens to drop opposition to data centers on the grounds they could generate $1 billion in property tax revenue. Right now, with data center projects in heavy demand, there’s no doubt these could be some of the biggest projects available to fill that sudden property tax hole. As Amendment 3 forces a major shift of tax collections to non-homestead properties, local governments are also likely to raise the millage (“taxes per $1,000 of value”) to fill the $12 billion hole. This will increase taxes on local businesses and multi-family housing like apartments — and, of course, increase the rent for those living there. It will also increase taxes for those newer homeowners with higher assessed values. To keep current funding levels, Orange County millage would need to increase by 20% for property owners still paying taxes, while fire and police millage would need to increase by more than 23%. Bedroom communities like Belle Isle, Oakland, Ocoee and Winter Garden would need more than 40% increases. On the flip side, Amendment 3 will take nearly 50% of existing homeowners off the non-school tax rolls. Since homeowners have also been protected with a 3% annual cap via Save Our Homes, the current assessed value of many homes is below $250,000, even if the market value of that home has substantially increased well beyond that in the last decade. And once taxable value becomes $0, it doesn’t matter how much millage is increased because anything multiplied by $0 is still $0. As a result, Amendment 3 will make new single-family homes (or even owner-occupied condos) much, much less attractive for local government to zone or move along in the permitting process. And it’s inevitable that projects with higher value homes will get more attention. Projects proposing more affordable housing with smaller houses and smaller lots will be de-prioritized. Indeed, for population growth, the best avenue for local governments will be multi-family apartments that are not owner-occupied and will continue to pay the higher property tax rates. All of this is not to say that Florida doesn’t have property tax issues. We continue to punish new entrants into the market by resetting assessed values when the home changes hands, which results in newer homeowners paying vastly higher amounts than their neighbors simply because they bought their first home a few years later. If property taxes are supposed to reflect services, Florida needs to reform property taxes to bring about fairness among all similar homeowners. But wiping half of homeowners off the rolls — most of whom will be longtime homeowners — while leaving most newer homeowners holding the bag along with renters and businesses, is not the ticket to prosperity that some organizations seem to think it is. So unless someone wants to vastly increase the likelihood of a mega data center in their community while also reducing the chances their kids have of moving into a home they can afford, we should say no to Amendment 3 and demand a better ballot proposition built on fairness for all taxpayers and residents. Scott Randolph is Orange County’s Tax Collector.

artigo.texto: Data Centers Voters in Six States Will Decide Future of Data Center Construction September 24, 2026 | Kim Miller October 13, 2026 | Billy Culleton Key Takeaways: The sheer power demand from data centers has recently pushed state lawmakers to consider new policies that allow large energy users to access dedicated power sources without everyday ratepayers shouldering the cost. These arrangements, called "behind-the-meter" or "bring-your-own-power," share the same goal: addressing public concern over rising electricity costs while giving data center developers alternatives to lengthy utility interconnection queues. While utilities and large-load users have long negotiated power purchase agreements for generation, state policymakers are seeking to make behind-the-meter arrangements more common and easier to establish. This type of legislation saw more activity in 2025 than in 2026 but is likely to remain of interest to state lawmakers as more data centers connect to the grid. Last year, seven states enacted legislation allowing data centers to source their own energy. In May 2025, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt (R) signed SB 480, which exempts large users from being defined as public utilities if they provide their own electricity. The bill also allows data centers to contract with regulated and non-regulated utilities to house onsite generation. Ohio lawmakers followed suit by enacting a sweeping energy bill (HB 15) that removes barriers for large energy users to self-generate power, either directly or through a third party. In addition, the bill removed previous rules requiring self-generation sources to be located on a customer's premises. In Utah, lawmakers created a pathway for behind-the-meter generation by allowing large-load users to enter the competitive market if an agreement is not reached with the utility within 90 days. SB 132 allows data centers to source energy from the grid through a third-party supplier or from a source entirely separate from the grid. Texas, a state known for its energy production, also enacted a major bill in 2025 that addressed behind-the-meter options for data centers. SB 6, which broadly sets standards for how data centers can interconnect with the grid, allows large-load users to connect directly to an existing stand-alone generation source. The bill also requires utility regulators to direct data centers to source energy from backup generators during emergency power situations. Finally, New Hampshire lawmakers allowed off-grid power generation for large users, with the main caveat being that they have to be completely independent of the grid (HB 672). Bills that create this type of arrangement, called "consumer-regulated electricity" (or CRE) were also considered in Maryland (HB 1219 & SB 947), Illinois (HB 4163), New Jersey (A 5431), and New York (S 8037). However, none of these bills advanced out of their committee of origin. Behind-the-Meter Behind-the-meter refers to energy generation or storage systems that are located on the customer's side of the utility meter, allowing large users like data centers to generate or source their own electricity independently from the main utility grid. These arrangements can reduce reliance on the grid and help avoid passing costs onto other ratepayers. Consumer-Regulated Electricity (CRE) Consumer-regulated electricity (CRE) is a system where large energy users, such as data centers, operate their own private electricity networks or source power independently, rather than relying solely on traditional public utilities. This model allows for greater flexibility and can help large users avoid regulatory and cost structures imposed on standard utility customers. Some behind-the-meter bills explicitly make it possible for multiple large users to source off-grid power through microgrids. As part of their efforts to attract more data center development, West Virginia lawmakers created a microgrid program (HB 2014) that allows data centers to operate in certified microgrid districts. The law gives the state authority over local governments in regulating microgrids as part of its effort to attract data center users to West Virginia. In New Mexico, lawmakers enacted microgrid legislation that is more regulatory in nature. HB 93 allows customers to enter agreements with investor-owned utilities in the state for microgrid operation, including generation and distribution for onsite use. By the time legislative sessions kicked off in January 2026, data centers had become one of the most contentious issues facing lawmakers, especially at the local level, where moratoriums were being enacted. Because of this, the politics of enacting laws that speed up the process for data centers to connect to the grid became more challenging. New Jersey lawmakers enacted a pro-clean-energy measure (A 796) that directs the state's Board of Public Utilities to create energy rates that encourage large loads to bring their own generation and storage, as long as it comes from non-carbon-emitting sources. Additionally, lawmakers in Arizona (HB 4097) and Virginia (SB 751 & HB 1087) considered bills that provide pathways for large users to source behind-the-meter power. In Louisiana, a failed attempt (SB 490) to create a pathway for behind-the-meter power sourcing encouraged the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC) to open its rulemaking docket on private-use electrical networks. Meanwhile, proposals in Connecticut and Maryland made behind-the-meter generation a requirement to enter the market rather than an option that data centers could exercise. Maryland's SB 596 and HB 940 banned large-load customers from connecting to the grid unless 25% of their capacity is met by either backup storage or a demand-response program. Connecticut's HB 5469 requires load customers of 50 MW and above to receive 100% of their electricity from a colocated source or off-grid supplier. artigo.texto: Riverside’s proposed pause on new data centers is headed to the City Council — this time with a backup option if a temporary moratorium cannot secure enough votes. The council’s Land Use Committee voted Tuesday, Oct. 13, to advance two alternatives: a 45-day moratorium or a resolution affirming staff’s interpretation that data centers cannot move forward under the city’s existing zoning code. A moratorium requires support from six of the seven councilmembers, which prompted the second option. The discussion and public hearing are planned for 3 p.m. Nov. 10. Neither a new moratorium nor a permanent ban has been adopted. The action builds on the committee’s September recommendation for a temporary pause while officials develop a definition of data centers and consider permanent restrictions. That earlier recommendation called for 90 days; Tuesday’s discussion clarified that the state moratorium process begins with 45 days. The debate centers on how facilities housing large amounts of computing equipment could affect Riverside’s electricity supply, water resources and utility bills. Councilmember Sean Mill brought up these concerns at Tuesday’s meeting. “My greatest concerns are that we already lack the utility capacity to probably service many of our future endeavors here in the city until we get a second connection to the statewide power grid. And I don't think we can afford to have something like large scale data centers coming to Riverside,” he said. City Planner Laurel Reimer told the committee that Riverside has not received an application for a data center. Staff currently considers the facilities prohibited because they are not listed among the city’s permitted land uses. Data centers house servers, storage systems and networking equipment supporting services such as cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI). The staff report identifies potential concerns including electricity and water consumption, noise, air quality and effects on surrounding neighborhoods. Mill questioned whether Riverside could accommodate large data centers without shifting infrastructure costs onto residents and businesses. He pointed to the city’s reliance on a single connection to the statewide power grid and its pursuit of a second connection. Reimer said staff could not determine whether the city had sufficient electricity and water capacity without reviewing a specific proposal. Environmental review would examine a project’s impacts on those resources, she said. If Riverside eventually allows data centers, the city could establish standards requiring developers to study the impacts and pay for necessary improvements, Reimer said. She agreed that setting policy before an application arrives would help avoid uncertainty. “This is definitely the time to be working on creating those policies so that there is no ambiguity moving forward,” Reimer said. The committee revisited the issue partly because the council approved a separate AI strategy and policy working group on Sept. 15. Councilmembers Philip Falcone, Steven Robillard and Steve Hemenway serve on that group, which has up to 13 months to complete its work. Falcone, who also serves on the Land Use Committee, said the two efforts should have coordinated timelines. He supported preventing data center applications from advancing while the working group develops recommendations. “In the meantime, we just need to ensure that no data centers move forward or applications move forward in those 13 months because of that other work that’s happening,” Falcone said. Committee Chair Clarissa Cervantes initially suggested a one-year moratorium. A city attorney’s office representative explained that the state process begins with a 45-day moratorium, with extensions potentially bringing the total duration to two years. The attorney’s office said a moratorium would require findings of a current and immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare, along with support from six of the seven councilmembers. Riverside’s zoning code generally prohibits unlisted uses, but allows the community and economic development director or a designee to determine that a proposed use is similar to, and no more detrimental than, an allowed use. The proposed resolution would put the council’s position in writing: Under the code as it currently exists, staff would not issue permits for data centers and would notify the council if a proposal came forward. The committee directed staff to prepare both options for Nov. 10. Any extension of an adopted moratorium would require further council action. Falcone had been developing a citywide data center ban before a proposed veterans’ workforce-training partnership brought the issue into sharper focus this summer. He previously told the Gazette that the project accelerated his timeline. The original partnership with the Institute for Veterans & Emerging Technology Skills (iVETS) and StemWorx Inc. included a second phase exploring a data center operated by StemWorx and staffed by veterans. The council later approved the training agreement with the data center component removed. That vote authorized no construction, infrastructure or land-use changes, Community and Economic Development Director Miranda Evans said at the time. On Tuesday, Cervantes said Riverside should act proactively as other cities restrict data centers and developers boxed out of those areas look to Riverside instead. The proposed pause would give the city time to examine its infrastructure and consider what long-term rules should apply, she said.

artigo.texto: Last year, the Springdale Borough council gave the green light for a new massive data center to be built in the small town outside of Pittsburgh. But it's actually Allegheny County that will give the project final approval — and organizers say there's still an opportunity for the public to weigh in. The Springdale data center could draw as much power at one time as nearly 200,000 homes. It has gotten pushback from locals worried about noise, pollution, property values, and rising utility bills. Marty Garrigan has been organizing against the center with the group Save Allegheny Valley Environment (SAVE). He said it’s not too late to push back on the computing warehouse “Many people thought that this whole thing was a done deal when the borough voted in favor of it,” Garrigan said. “But the county has the final say here.” Springdale Borough Council voted to grant the project a conditional use permit in December. Several members of council said during the vote that they did not want the data center in the borough, but felt they had to approve the application to avoid a costly lawsuit. Allegheny County must approve the center’s land development plan before the project can move forward. The plan lays out the details of how the facility would be built, connected to utilities, and landscaped. County staff made 97 comments on the data center’s preliminary application, noting errors and unanswered questions. For example, the comments note that “no evidence has been provided” that conditions related to noise mitigation will be met. A virtual hearing is set for Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 6 p.m. An in-person hearing is scheduled for Oct. 28 at 6 p.m. at the Springdale borough building. Written comments will be accepted until Nov. 30. “This is an opportunity for us to increase public awareness and relay the dangers that this behemoth poses,” Garrigan said. Garrigan’s group plans to drive a billboard truck around the area for the next two weeks, to remind people that the center is “not a done deal.” SAVE is hosting an in-person gathering for the county’s virtual hearing at the Pittsburgh Shrine Center at 1877 Shriners Way in Harmar Township. Garrigan said volunteers can help people register to speak during the hearing. The group has also launched a fundraiser for possible legal and expert fees if the data center does get county approval and the fight moves to the courts. “We've had an estimate from an attorney who's fought these kinds of things before that would be $20,000 to continue on with the fight for an appeal to the county,” Garrigan said. “And that's just the first level of courts.” The data center, which has been dubbed “Springdale Dynamo” in a nod to the area’s industrial history, is financially backed by the New York-based hedge fund Davidson Kempner. A website for the project shows it could draw up to 240 megawatts of power, up from the company’s original proposal of 180 mw. Recent increases in electricity prices have been attributed to the projected growth of data centers and other heavy power users.

artigo.texto: Franklin County residents, groups sue to stop data center rezoning and projects FRANKLIN COUNTY, Mo. (First Alert 4) - Two organizations and neighboring landowners have filed separate but similar lawsuits challenging Franklin County’s data center regulations and the rezoning for data center projects approved on September 15. Pacific ROOT Coalition and Franklin County Rural Coalition, along with their attorneys, formally announced the lawsuits Wednesday. On September 15, the Franklin County Commission unanimously approved the rezoning for a data center project near Villa Ridge by Shaw Nature Reserve. The commission approved rezoning for a second project south of Pacific off Highway O in a 2-1 decision. Bill and Janet Hubbard live on a five-generation farm south of Pacific. Their front porch view looks onto the land where a data center is planned. “From where those power lines are, that’s where the buildings will start. There’s going to be 16 of them. The height of them, that entire hilltop will be leveled, and they will put buildings on them,” Bill Hubbard said. “For me, it’s preserving this country’s farmland. People nowadays want to know where their food is coming from. They don’t want it imported from anywhere else. So the best farmers in the world, and that produce the best products, reside here in America. And we can’t afford to keep losing those,” Julie Carr said. The Hubbards and their daughter, Julie Carr, are not named plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed against the project near their farm, but they said they welcome it. “It gives us hope that perhaps we will get this put on the back burner or put someplace else,” Bill Hubbard said. “Or stop it completely. One of the big issues for me in particular, as a retired educator, are our schools and our students. My grandson attends a local school, and it will be a mile from Crooked Creek,” Janet Hubbard said. “That there is hope that we’re not going to be devastated, that our entire community won’t be sacrificed for, for lack of a better word, carpetbaggers coming in from out of state, taking over the community, and potentially upping our electrical bills, lowering the water table so that our wells, definitely our springs, we were already told that the springs would be drying up if they do drill wells,” Bill Hubbard said. The Hubbards expressed multiple environmental and health concerns, along with what it could mean to residents and kids. “Right now we’re hearing the little hum of a fan for a blow-up Halloween decoration. If it’s a diesel generator, it’s going to be a whole different story. If it’s just the 16 buildings, it’s going to be louder than a vacuum cleaner. That’s what they say. It’s like, ‘oh, the decibel level compares to a vacuum cleaner.’ Okay, 16 vacuum cleaners running 24-7, seven days a week for the rest of your life,” Janet Hubbard said. “It’s on multiple levels where it can hit us in a way that’s not in our best interest or anyone else’s,” Bill Hubbard said. Zach McMichael, an attorney at Capes Sokol representing Pacific ROOT Coalition, said the lawsuit has been filed and a Franklin County judge issued a writ of certiorari. “We’re looking to get the zoning overturned. We’re also trying to make it so the county commission has to do this again the right way and give the residents of Franklin County a fair opportunity to be heard on their concerns and to actually weigh those concerns when they make a future decision,” McMichael said. Both lawsuits make similar arguments: that no studies were conducted to determine environmental and utility impacts, that the rezoning constitutes illegal spot zoning by changing the classification of the properties to differ from surrounding land, and that the approval process was flawed. “Our claims are both to the substance and the procedure. So, the substance, we believe this is illegal spot zoning. So, what the county commission has done is they’ve taken one single parcel to benefit one particular property owner and given them an A zoning and a C of W zoning. So, it’s spot zoning that doesn’t comport with the master plan. And it isn’t for the public welfare,” McMichael said. “We also think procedurally, they didn’t follow the steps that Missouri law requires. We think they put unreasonable restrictions on the residents and the citizens of Franklin County at these public hearings. And they didn’t give proper notice,” McMichael said. The attorneys on Wednesday said filing the lawsuits isn’t saying that the county acted illegally; that is for the court to decide, and this goes beyond the issue of data centers to making sure the correct process is followed. “Beltline picked up their party toys and they went to the county and they sold them a bill of goods. You will make millions of dollars in tax revenue. And I think that’s when the commissioners at the county level stopped listening. So it’s very, very troubling that our county commissioners, who should be representing us, seem to be working for the carpetbaggers,” Janet Hubbard said. McMichael said the case will likely be decided based on details specific to the proposed site. “This case in Franklin County and these zoning cases normally are very site-specific. artigo.texto: North American Electric Reliability Corp. stakeholders approved new reliability standards for AI data centers, crypto mining facilities and other computational loads — an important step toward finalization, the grid watchdog said Thursday. The standards now head to the NERC Board of Trustees for a vote, and, if adopted, will be filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for final approval. The proposed standards build on insights and research related to a Level 3 alert NERC issued in May after several incidents where data centers unexpectedly dropped load or oscillated demand rapidly, threatening the stability of regional grids. The alert included seven actions grid entities “must implement to address immediate risks posed by computational loads” while permanent rules are created, NERC said. The new standards aim to “establish requirements to support the reliable integration of large computational loads into the bulk power system,” the reliability organization said in a statement. Electricity demand is increasing after decades of stagnant growth, with data centers, in particular, driving load projections. Summer peak demand across the bulk power system is forecast to grow by 224 GW over the next 10 years, a 24% increase from 2025 peak demand, NERC said in January. “These loads are reshaping the demand profile and exposing reliability gaps in both operational and planning time horizons,” NERC said on its standards development project site. Multiple standards for computational loads were developed as part of NERC Project 2026-02, including requirements around interconnection studies and modeling; operational data and communications; and load protection coordination and disturbance monitoring. Among other requirements, the standards establish modeling data, verification, and reporting procedures “for development of planning horizon cases necessary to support analysis of the reliability of the interconnected transmission system.” They are designed to ensure transmission operators, balancing authorities and reliability coordinators have computational load site data needed “to plan, monitor, and assess the reliable operation” of the bulk power system, and to establish communication capabilities “with predefined communications protocols to ensure prompt action to prevent or mitigate occurrences that adversely impact the reliability of the Bulk Power System.” The standards would apply to computational loads greater than or equal to 50 MW, connected at voltage levels greater than or equal to 100 kV. NERC’s board is expected to consider the new standards in the fourth quarter, based on development timelines in the proposals.

artigo.texto: The issue was among those discussed at a seminar in Hanoi on October 14, co-hosted by Tai chinh – Dau tu (Finance and Investment) newspaper and the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV). Green credit lays groundwork for carbon market In his opening speech, Pham Van Hoanh, the newspaper’s Editor-in-Chief, said Vietnam is progressively finalising policies on green growth and its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. The domestic carbon market began a pilot on June 29, 2026, raising the need to deepen links among green credit, banking system and new financial instruments. SBV Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh said meeting the 2050 net-zero pledge will require enormous resources for technological innovation, production overhaul, energy efficiency and emissions cuts. Alongside the State budget and capital and monetary markets, the carbon market is an important mechanism to raise additional funds, he said. The Government issued Decree 29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange on January 29, setting the legal framework for the market and trading greenhouse gas emission allowances and carbon credits. The pilot market was launched with more than 511 million metric tonnes of CO₂ in allowances, allocated to facilities in three emissions-intensive sectors for 2025-2026, including thermal power, iron and steel, and cement. The pilot runs through the end of 2028, with full mandatory operation starting in 2029. Canh said green credit funds the projects, technologies and sectors that deliver emissions cuts, while the carbon market can turn those cuts into economic value. If it works well, the market can generate extra revenue and cash flow, improving credit quality and helping companies meet environmental standards for exports. Outstanding green credit across the banking system topped 856 trillion VND (32.9 billion USD) at the end of June 2026, up 9.87% from end-2025. From 2017 to 2025, green credit grew by more than 20% a year on average, focusing on agriculture, forestry, fisheries, biodiversity and green energy. Proposal to connect carbon value chain Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Agribank Training School and deputy head of its ESG team, said the issue isn’t whether banks directly trade carbon credits. What matters is how they finance the creation of emissions reductions, and when carbon value becomes reliable enough to factor into lending decisions. Agribank said financing needs emerge before any credits exist. Projects pass through preparation, investment, operation, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV), credit issuance, trading and settlement. That gap gives banks room to offer credit, bridge financing, cash flow management, guarantees and blended finance. The lender proposed drawing clear lines among emissions-reduction potential, registered projects, verified results, issued credits, carbon-credit sales contracts and proceeds already collected. Each carries a different level of certainty and can’t automatically be treated as the same source of debt repayment. Agribank identified five roles for banks in the carbon ecosystem, including financing emissions-reduction activities, linking stakeholders across the value chain, providing payment and cash-flow services, pooling climate finance, and supporting companies and individuals through the transition. As an immediate step, it proposed a framework for identifying emissions-reduction projects and a set of criteria for assessing carbon-related credit. It suggested piloting value chains where emissions can be clearly gauged, such as low-emission rice, livestock and biogas, sustainable forestry, waste treatment and biomass energy. Banks also need to build partner networks, train interdisciplinary staff and strengthen data and governance systems. Agribank plans to focus on data, capacity, partnerships and pilot models in 2026-2028, scale up in 2029-2032 as the domestic market becomes more stable, and study products based on carbon-related cash flows or receivables from 2033. To support market growth, Agribank recommended clarifying ownership, disposition rights and benefit-sharing for emissions-reduction results and carbon credits, and completing rules on receivables, collateral, accounting, taxation and foreign exchange. It also called for treating data and MRV systems as market infrastructure, cutting verification costs, developing supply and demand together, and applying blended finance and risk-sharing mechanisms. Canh said an effective carbon market lets companies convert emissions cuts into financial resources of their own, which could ease pressure on green credit. Rather than relying mainly on their own capital, State funding or bank loans to finance the transition, firms gain greater capacity to generate funds from their own emissions reductions./.VNA

artigo.texto: Trending Assemblyman Andrew Molitor is among the Republicans in the state Assembly members signing on to a letter asking the New York Power Authority for more transparency about power subsidies for data centers. Assemblyman Ed Ra, R-Garden City and Assembly minority leader, recently sent a letter to Justin Driscoll, president and CEO of the New York Power Authority, asking for more information about discounted electricity for data centers through NYPA’s ReCharge program. Ra said data centers in several areas of the state have received low-cost power from NYPA, but NYPA hasn’t disclosed the rates paid by those facilities or the dollar value of the discount. “This prevents the Legislature and New York taxpayers from evaluating the cost and effectiveness of a publicly controlled economic development benefit” Ra wrote in his letter. “We recognize that the use of financial incentives can be a useful tool in attracting new businesses and facilitating economic growth. In highly technical arrangements, sensitive information should be protected. However, given the growing public interest in New York’s energy policy, cost concerns and the future reliability of the grid, we encourage NYPA to provide greater clarity on the financial commitments made to data centers.” According to data analyzed by Reinvent Albany, the Rockland County Industrial Development Agency (IDA) and New York Power Authority (NYPA) committed at least $321 million in sales tax exemptions and power subsidies to five data center sites in Rockland County since 2013. In return for these generous handouts of taxpayer funds, the corporations building the data centers -- which are among the world's wealthiest and include Wall Street giants like JP Morgan -- will create or keep the equivalent of 298 full-time equivalent jobs. The average NY household is paying about nineteen times more for electricity than most data centers in Rockland County. According to data from NY State's energy agency, NYSERDA, residential customers paid $244 per megawatt-hour (MWh), and NYPA preferred power customers - including Rockland data centers - $12.88 per MWh. Legislation (A.10852/S.9182) was introduced in the Assembly in April, sponsored by Assemblywoman Anna Kelles, D-Ithaca, and Sen. Rachel May, D-Syracuse. It would no longer allow ReCharge NY allocations for data centers along with caps on other subsidies, require the state DEC be the lead agency for projects that meet certain electricity use standards and require a full environmental impact statement and consultation for projects near federally recognized Indian nations. The legislation has attracted several Democratic Party co-sponsors, but no Republican support. "As electricity demand grows and infrastructure investment becomes more expensive, the state must be more deliberate about how public subsidies are used. Incentives should support projects that deliver broad and durable economic value, not simply reward scale or energy consumption," Kelles and May wrote in their legislative justification. The lack of Republican support is, in part, because the minority party in both houses of the state Legislature has its own plan for electricity subsidies for data centers. Assemblyman Scott Gray, R-Watertown, has introduced legislation (A.11419) that would create a procedure for utilities and high-demand customers to negotiate electric service agreements by requiring those agreements to be negotiated on a case-by-case basis and then approved by the state Public Service Commission. They would be required to be structured so costs are paid by high-use customers rather than ordinary ratepayers. “To be clear, our conference has staunchly opposed misguided energy policies that have undermined New York’s energy sector,” Ra wrote. “The state’s rush toward an all-electric future has done more harm than good – for consumers, for businesses and for energy capacity. The debate about data centers and their impacts on communities should be part of any conversation on energy policy. However, what can’t be debated is that the amount of electricity being used by data centers is a growing concern for ratepayers and grid reliability. NYPA’s commitment to transparency should reflect the same level of concern.”

artigo.texto: To Avoid Criticizing Trump's Tariffs and War, Vivek Ramaswamy Takes on Data Centers Republicans who want to speak to voters' anger over higher prices without criticizing the president who's caused them are in a bind. When Vivek Ramaswamy ran for president in 2024, he liked to describe himself as a "national libertarian" whose worldview included skepticism of new Middle Eastern wars and support for free trade (provided it wasn't with China). In a midterm election season in which voters are increasingly angry about higher prices born of protectionist tariffs and high gas prices caused by a new Middle Eastern war, that would seemingly give Ramaswamy, now running for governor of Ohio, a straightforward story to tell about how he'd bring costs down. Unfortunately for the Republican gubernatorial candidate, the person responsible for the tariffs and the war is President Donald Trump, whose support he's counting on to get him over the finish line in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Amy Acton. The latest polls show Ramaswamy slightly ahead of Acton, with many voters still undecided. Other Republican midterm candidates, most prominently Mike Rogers in Michigan, are escaping this bind by criticizing the tariffs and the war without explicitly naming the president who's responsible for both. Ramaswamy has chosen a different tactic: Shift the conversation to other sources of voters' cost-of-living anxiety that can't be directly laid at Trump's feet. In the last weeks of this election campaign, Ramaswamy has focused like a laser on two proposals he says will deliver cost relief to Ohio voters. The first is his proposed rollback of homeowners' property taxes. The second is a moratorium on new data center construction. Like many Midwestern and Western states, Ohioans' property tax bills have shot up in recent years, driven by a pandemic-era spike in home values. That's in turn sparked a full-blown property tax revolt in the state. The Republican-controlled Legislature passed a raft of property tax relief measures in 2025. Activists are also collecting signatures to place a full abolition of taxes on real property on the statewide ballot next year. Ramaswamy hasn't endorsed full property tax abolition, but he is promising voters that he will roll back property tax assessments for homeowners to pre-pandemic levels. On the data centers, he has staked out a very restrictionist position. Ohio is currently one of the leading states for data center development. Pew Research counts 57 projects currently in the pipeline there, attracted by cheap land and a robust power grid. The state's data center boom has caused a backlash in rural communities, where voters have objected to data centers' consumption of land and electricity and the special tax incentives some projects have received. On the ballot in 10 Ohio localities this November are initiatives that would impose additional restrictions on data center development. Ramaswamy has proposed to go further with a statewide moratorium that will remain in effect until the Legislature passes laws that not only require data centers to cover the full costs of the power infrastructure they need, but also provide property tax rebates and free electricity to nearby homeowners. Local property tax cuts paired with local reductions in spending would, of course, be well in line with a small government worldview. But the residential property tax rollback Ramaswamy has proposed doesn't directly do that. Instead, it would reduce property tax revenues and then leave it up to localities to make up for the lost revenue somehow. That could result in spending cuts. It could also result in localities shifting tax burdens onto commercial properties, raising non-property taxes (like sales taxes), or relying on the state government for more of their revenues. In the former two scenarios, local tax regimes would become more hostile to growth, given that property taxes are considered one of the most "efficient" taxes. In the latter scenario, the link between people who pay taxes and the people who consume taxpayer-funded local services would become more distant. Neither is ideal. While some data centers in Ohio have received tax subsidies, Ramaswamy's proposed solution is to block new data centers until they're legally required to subsidize their neighbors with free electricity and other community benefits. All of that is to say that it's a shame to see Ramaswamy adopt increasingly non-libertarian positions to avoid making critiques of Trump's cost-increasing tariffs and Iran war that would align with his erstwhile "national libertarian" worldview. It's ironic, too, that, in trying to avoid making those critiques, Ramaswamy has wound up being more restrictionist on data centers than Trump himself. In an August Truth Social post, the president famously urged local communities to "let Data Reign" and welcome data center development. Those that did would become "rich and successful," he predicted. Those that didn't would remain "poor and backward." At a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, over the weekend for Ramaswamy and Republican Senate candidate John Husted, Trump reiterated his support for data centers, saying, "We want them. Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." Rather than criticize the president's statist interventions, Ramaswamy is talking up his own instead. Ohio will be poorer as a result.

artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo Ironicamente, é fácil para os americanos concordarem que a polarização política está aumentando. Uma distribuição bimodal do sentimento político — com uma lacuna cada vez maior entre os dois extremos — tem caracterizado o cenário político americano nas últimas décadas. Segundo pesquisadores da Universidade de Cambridge, “De 1988 a 2024, encontramos evidências claras de que a polarização aumentou, principalmente devido a um período de polarização crescente e contínua de 2008 a 2020… Os grupos de esquerda e de direita nos Estados Unidos se distanciaram ainda mais, embora ambos permaneçam internamente coesos e tenham tamanhos semelhantes”. Esses pesquisadores também descobriram que “a posição do grupo de esquerda se deslocou mais para a esquerda desde 1988 do que a do grupo de direita, o que está em consonância com a tendência geral da opinião pública americana de se deslocar para a esquerda e se tornar mais polarizada”. Esse período de quatro décadas de polarização deixou os americanos praticamente sem pontos de convergência. Os centros de dados são a exceção. Os americanos estão unidos quando se trata de desprezo e desconfiança em relação a essas instalações — tanto que Bernie Sanders e Steve Bannon se uniram recentemente para desacelerar o desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial (IA) e defender a adoção de regulamentações de segurança. Uma pesquisa da Gallup revelou que sete em cada dez americanos se opõem à construção de centros de dados voltados para a inteligência artificial em suas regiões O que teria unido americanos tão polarizados? Preocupações ambientais, queda na qualidade de vida local, aumento nas contas de energia e custos de construção estão entre os principais fatores que levam as pessoas a se oporem à construção de novos centros de dados. Por outro lado, a parcela relativamente pequena de americanos que apoia essas construções as enxerga como uma oportunidade de expansão econômica. O desprezo pelos centros de dados, no entanto, é um fenômeno relativamente recente. Instalações que abrigam sistemas computacionais, servidores e estruturas de armazenamento de dados existem há muitas décadas. Por exemplo, a IBM desenvolveu um dos primeiros centros de dados na década de 1960, como parte do programa Apollo, que levou o homem à Lua. Muitos escritórios e universidades também têm seus próprios centros de dados para operar redes internas e sistemas computacionais. Não são os centros de dados em si que estão provocando o pessimismo, mas a dimensão extraordinária, a escala e a velocidade de sua expansão, que alimentam o medo. A inteligência artificial exige um volume significativamente maior de recursos computacionais do que as formas tradicionais de computação. Sua ascensão provocou um aumento vertiginoso na construção e na expansão dos centros de dados. Os centros de dados de hiperescala diferem dos tradicionais principalmente pelo porte: o tipo de instalação necessário na era da IA pode abrigar mais de 5 mil servidores e ocupar milhões de pés quadrados. O maior centro de dados de hiperescala do mundo, localizado na região da Mongólia Interior, na China, tem uma área equivalente à de 165 campos de futebol americano. Essa instalação, com 994 mil metros quadrados, custou US$ 3 bilhões. Os centros de dados de hiperescala não se limitam à China. Mais da metade dos centros de dados do mundo está nos Estados Unidos. Atualmente, o maior centro de dados em operação no país é o Colossus 2, em Shelby, Tennessee. Essa instalação ocupa uma área de 40 hectares e tem capacidade de geração de energia de 1.085 MW. No entanto, ela deverá ser superada em breve por instalações significativamente maiores, como o New Era Lea Data Center, em Lea, Novo México, cuja capacidade de geração de energia está projetada em 7.000 MW. Construir e operar um centro de dados de hiperescala exige quantidades significativas de terra, eletricidade e água. A terra é necessária devido à enorme área — que pode variar de centenas a milhares de hectares — exigida para a construção de uma dessas instalações. Centros de dados desse porte também consomem quantidades extraordinárias de eletricidade para alimentar os servidores e a infraestrutura física. A Agência Internacional de Energia prevê que, dentro de 18 meses, entre 6,7% e 12% do consumo total de eletricidade dos Estados Unidos será destinado aos centros de dados. Por fim, essas instalações utilizam grandes volumes de água para resfriar os servidores. Embora seja difícil determinar exatamente quanta água os centros de dados consomem, é evidente que a IA e essas instalações demandam água tanto para o resfriamento local quanto para a geração de eletricidade em outros locais. Além disso, uma quantidade imensa de água é necessária para fabricar os microchips que equipam os centros de dados. O tamanho e a escala dos centros de dados têm alimentado o medo e a preocupação com a construção de novas instalações. No entanto, as questões relacionadas ao porte dessas estruturas estão sendo cada vez mais ofuscadas por preocupações com o sigilo e a velocidade da expansão. Muitos cidadãos americanos, de todo o espectro político, manifestam preocupação com a falta de transparência e o ritmo imprudente de expansão da infraestrutura de IA Essas preocupações são especialmente acentuadas nas comunidades que enfrentam a construção de centros de dados em seus próprios bairros. A política conhecida como “Not in My Backyard” (Não no Meu Quintal), ou NIMBY, existe muito antes da era da IA. Projetos de construção, como conjuntos habitacionais, parques eólicos e instalações de tratamento de resíduos, frequentemente provocam resistência popular. Embora possa parecer que os centros de dados sejam apenas a mais recente manifestação da política NIMBY, há diferenças importantes nessa situação. artigo.texto: NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Before Nashville's next large data center can power up, it will have to clear a new set of rules aimed at limiting the impact these facilities can have on surrounding communities. Metro Council approved new zoning regulations for data centers in July, creating five classifications based on factors including size and electrical load. The regulations prohibit the largest category, campus data centers, countywide. Councilmember Rollin Horton, a sponsor of the legislation, described Nashville's approach this way during an interview with NewsChannel 5: "Nashville has passed some of the strictest rules and regulations protecting all of Davidson County from the dangers of data centers." The regulations followed significant public debate over data center development in Nashville, particularly after plans emerged for a DC BLOX facility next to the Nashville Zoo. In July, more than 100 people spoke in opposition to data center development during Metro Council public hearings. Under Nashville's new framework, allowable data centers face different requirements depending on their size. Small data centers have a 100-foot separation requirement from specified sensitive uses, while medium facilities generally face a 500-foot requirement. Large facilities face a 2,640-foot, or half-mile, separation requirement. Sensitive uses identified by the framework include residences, schools, daycares, religious institutions, parks and zoos. A new Metro Data Center Impact Assessment & Policy Recommendations compared Nashville's regulations with policies being adopted or considered in other communities. It found Nashville's requirements for small and medium facilities generally align with other jurisdictions, but said the half-mile buffer for large facilities makes Nashville"somewhat of an outlier." "We set very strict distance requirements, especially compared to other cities," said Horton. "And so I think it's important not just that we look at how we can continue to improve our regulations, but make sure that there's no effort to water down or weaken them." The regulations include more than where facilities can be built. They require closed-loop cooling systems, establish daytime and nighttime noise limits, require 24-hour noise monitoring and require utilities to confirm they have capacity to serve a proposed project. New data centers must also provide renewable energy systems accounting for at least 15% of annual power use. Despite concluding that the city's framework provides a strong foundation for addressing many known risks, Metro's report identifies several issues officials say warrant further evaluation. Among them are vibration, increases in background noise and potential contaminants in wastewater discharged from cooling systems. Nashville currently limits data center noise at the property line to 65 decibels during the day and 55 decibels at night. But the report says the city could consider another safeguard limiting how much a facility can increase the existing background noise around it, even if it remains below those absolute limits. Vibration is another area Metro says needs further research. The new regulations do not establish a separate vibration limit or require a vibration impact assessment comparable to the required noise assessment. Metro also wants to further study wastewater from closed-loop cooling systems. The report says that discharge can potentially contain substances including heavy metals and PFAS and recommends determining whether existing contaminant standards adequately capture potential data center process-water impacts. The report does not say Nashville's water has been contaminated by data centers. "I think we have the strictest and most comprehensive rules in the entire country. That said, this is a very fast-evolving industry. So I think it's important that we continue to monitor how the industry develops and make sure that our rules and regulations stay one step ahead of the industry," said Horton. Perhaps one of the biggest questions is what happens when Nashville's framework encounters a new proposal. Metro's report says the city has yet to apply the new regulatory framework to a new data center proposal, meaning some challenges remain relatively unknown. The report recommends several changes to how Metro implements the rules, including required pre-application coordination, completeness reviews and phased approvals tied to utility milestones. It also recommends forming a working group involving Metro, Nashville Electric Service and the Tennessee Valley Authority to develop compliance procedures, coordinate enforcement and determine whether additional resources will be needed as applications, inspections and monitoring begin. O PL, de autoria de Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), altera a Lei nº 15.269/2025, que estabelece que o custo do armazenamento é arcado pelas geradoras de energia. A nova proposta estabelece a divisão dos valores com os consumidores. O pedido de urgência foi apresentado à Mesa, nesta terça, pelos deputados Danilo Forte (PP/CE), Evair Vieira de Melo (Republicanos/ES), Vitor Lippi (PSD/SP) e Isnaldo Bulhões Jr. (MDB/AL). Agora, o texto segue direto para plenário. O PL ainda não tinha sido distribuído para nenhuma comissão. A matéria é apoiada por diversas organizações do setor que esperam a mudança na divisão do rateio antes dos leilões de baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) defende que o avanço da proposta é importante para ampliar a segurança jurídica para os certames e que a legislação estabelece um tratamento desigual para o armazenamento. “A aprovação da urgência representa um avanço para que o Congresso discuta o tema com a celeridade necessária. Em paralelo precisamos olhar para o prazo dos leilões: o sistema elétrico necessita de potência adicional em 2028, e é plenamente possível corrigir a isonomia no rateio enquanto prossegue o cronograma”, disse o diretor-executivo da Absae, Fabio Lima, em nota. Já a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine) considera que a aprovação sinaliza uma sensibilidade do Congresso Nacional em relação à necessidade de debater o tema. “A tramitação célere é fundamental para o setor, tendo em vista que a matéria ainda será submetida à análise do Senado Federal”, afirmou a associação, em nota. O tema integra as prioridades da Agenda Legislativa de 2026 da Apine, que busca por soluções estruturais para os cortes de geração de energia (curtailment) .
