Quick Read Big tech’s giant data center proposals have touched raw nerves in several Minnesota towns, sparking firestorms of criticism aimed at local government leaders, some of whom signed non-disclosure agreements to keep project details secret until after elected officials approved the plans. Seeing how data centers have churned up local politics and spurred newcomers to run for office, some city administrators came together to seek help. The end result is a new toolkit developed by researchers at the University of Minnesota to help local government officials better understand and weigh the pros and cons of having Google, Meta or some other big tech company build a massive data center in their community. "The way we've been framing it is how do you proactively address a data center?” said Elise Harrington, a University of Minnesota public affairs professor who is the tool kit project lead. “How do you think about it before you have one?" It’s the culmination of a year of research by the University of Minnesota and the Freshwater Society, a water conservation nonprofit. It was developed to help city leaders separate facts from fiction and to guide what city codes they can enact to mitigate environmental impacts if big tech pitches in their city next. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Arming local leaders with facts Harrington and her group of researchers released the tool kit last Friday afternoon in Rochester, where dozens of city planners, administrators and elected officials from cities and towns across southeast Minnesota gathered for a workshop to learn about the tool kit and try it out. Al Roder, city administrator for the nearby town of Byron, is part of the reason this tool kit exists in the first place. He and some of his peers in other southeast Minnesota cities had been talking a couple of years ago about how they could prepare for the seemingly inevitable arrival of data center proposals. “We just started having a conversation about data centers and how do we answer all these questions with facts instead of emotions?” Roder said. “Because so much of what I hear is emotional arguments for or against. Where are the facts?” He had observed how these emotions had created deep rifts in cities like Pine Island, about 20 minutes away, after Google proposed its Project Skyway data center there, dividing residents into heated factions of those who support the data center and those who vehemently oppose it. Roder and his counterparts in nearby Stewartville and Lewiston wanted to get ahead of such controversies. If Google or some other big tech company came to Byron, Roder wanted to be armed with facts and have city rules preemptively laid out for prospective data centers. “These are rules that we decided before we were in the heat of battle,” Roder told MPR News. “These are the conditions that we would find acceptable for our community. It's easier to do that before somebody's knocking on the door.” So they reached out to the community development folks at the University of Minnesota Extension for help gathering facts they could use to guide these discussions. What does the tool kit include? The guide, which will be made available to the public Wednesday, includes sections on how data centers can impact energy and water usage, and how these impacts can be regulated at the local level to manage environmental impacts. It also includes guiding questions for city leaders to ask if they get an inquiry from big tech about a data center proposal as well as examples of how to address data centers in local code. That’s why Greg Krushke attended the workshop. He's the community development manager for the city of Owatonna, and he’s in the midst of modernizing the city’s zoning and subdivision code that was developed back in the 1980s. He hopes the tool kit will help inform how they write the code and what is included in it. He said it’s especially helpful to come together with peers at a workshop like this one to talk with one another and share experiences. "What are they learning from others, and how can we be able to apply some of this and be able to use it to help ourselves and our neighbors?" Krushke said. A regional approach Andi Sutton, executive director of the Southeast Regional Sustainable Development Partnership with University of Minnesota Extension, said she was thrilled that so many local government decision makers showed up for Friday’s workshop in Rochester. Local data center decisions are not made in a vacuum, and she hopes the workshop, which has convened leaders from across the region, will spark these conversations early since the environmental impacts of data centers don’t stop at city borders. That’s especially true in southeast Minnesota, which has a unique geologic landscape. It’s made of karst, a type of rock that’s very porous. “It means that the way that water moves through our region is different from other parts of Minnesota,” Sutton explained. “We have sensitive aquifers. We have water that’s in use for agricultural purposes, for ecosystem purposes. So what one community does with the water that they have will very quickly and inevitably have an effect on another community.” Sutton hopes this workshop jump starts these conversations and leads local planners to ask their neighbors questions as they weigh the pros and cons of data center proposals; questions like, “Who is my neighbor in terms of energy, water, infrastructure or roads?” “All of these questions get pushed to their limits by data centers as a development opportunity,” Sutton said. “We're so grateful that we're able to h

Dos 16 projetos apresentados nas assembleias estaduais em 2026, oito criam restrições ou ônus aos empreendimentos. As propostas favoráveis eram maioria no ano passado, segundo levantamento da Innova Assuntos Públicos obtido com exclusividade pelo Valor. O estudo mapeou 20 projetos de lei e de lei complementar sobre data centers em 11 assembleias legislativas entre 2025 e outubro de 2026. Em todo o ano de 2025 foram registradas quatro iniciativas, valor que saltou para 16 no acumulado deste ano até outubro. Dos 20 projetos, nove são restritivos, sete favoráveis, dois misturam incentivos e exigências e dois são considerados neutros. artigo.texto: However, there may be at least one issue where the board's 21 members can find consensus. "The county board is pretty unified in all things related to data centers right now — very cautious, very much in favor of having strong regulations, very much in favor of transparency," Farney said. In that vein, two items related to this topic will be discussed at tonight's committee-of-the-whole meeting: an ordinance prohibiting nondisclosure agreements and a resolution against property-tax incentives for hyperscale data-center developments. No final action will be taken during the meeting. "These are all commitments that we have made," said board member Emily Rodriguez, who chairs the data-center activities task force. "We are not interested in anything that dodges taxes, for example. That's something we all agree on on the data-center task force. We also all agree that nondisclosure agreements are bad governance and that folks should be embarrassed to sign them, and data centers should not ask that of local governments." The proposed ordinance against NDAs states that such agreements have "become an issue with other units of government in local and national news." If approved, the ordinance would prohibit county board members and county employees from entering into NDAs regarding county business — in any situation, not just instances where data-center developers are involved. As for the other piece of legislation, the proposed resolution would prohibit "the negotiation of tax-abatement agreements, payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements and other concessions for the development and construction of hyperscale data centers within Champaign County." "No data-center applications have yet been submitted to the county for rural Champaign County, but rumors and public outcry have prompted the need for a formal position," the resolution states. The two proposals come after the village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data center project in "a rural area west of Champaign" that falls within Mahomet's extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency. Farney, who wrote the resolution against tax incentives for hyperscale data centers, sent a draft to the board's policy and finance committee chairs on Oct. 5. "And like a half-hour later, somebody texted me the article that says, 'Hey, Mahomet's saying they're backing off,'" he said. "But I wanted to get that out there right away for the county to actually be able to do something immediately. We don't have to go through the same processes that we do for the zoning ordinance change in order to put a policy in effect for tax breaks for developments. And so I wanted to have something on record." When asked how payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements work, Farney said it's his understanding that data-center developers sometimes offer to make payments to communities while also entering into agreements for long-term property-tax abatements or reductions. Farney said that such agreements end up "being a benefit to the developer and not to the taxing bodies within the area as far as collecting the full value of property taxes." "Basically, what I'm saying is, if you want to build a data center here, then you're going to have to do it by our ordinances, which are going to be very stringent when the data-center task force gets done with their work," he told The News-Gazette. "You're also going to have to play by the rules that are in place for every other taxpayer in the county, as far as the county's portion of the tax bill goes. And so we're not going to give any incentives for data centers. If they can make it, they're gonna make it on their own." It's his hope that other governments and taxing bodies will enact similar policies and form a united front. Champaign County currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with "at least 10,000 square feet of processing area"; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county also created the data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. A previous statement from Leslie Farmer, Clean Cloud Energy's director of environmental and permitting, indicated that the company may still be considering the project, just not in partnership with Mahomet. "Clean Cloud Energy has decided not to seek annexation into the village of Mahomet following discussions with village leadership," she said. "We respect Champaign County's ongoing review of data-center regulations and will evaluate our project's development in accordance with the framework established by the county." Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Communications between the village and Clean Cloud Energy included multiple drafts of a proposed redevelopment and annexation agreement. Both Farney and Rodriguez said that if a municipality annexes an unincorporated area, that land would no longer be subject to the county's moratorium or zoning regulations on data centers. "I was very surprised to hear that Mahomet was in those discussions, knowing that the county was working on a data-center ordinance," Farney said. "... I knew immediately, 'OK, this is how the data-center developers are trying to do an end-around around the county and any other entities that are trying to regulate this.'" Rodriguez said that the situation in Mahomet resulted in "broken trust," making it important for the county to "codify" its position. artigo.texto: Salix council clarifies no data center moratorium in place, approves MOU with Google SALIX, Iowa (KTIV) - Conversations continue in Salix, Iowa, over 900 acres of annexed land and plans for a data center project. Wednesday night, the Salix City Council agenda included three items involving data centers. One stemmed from the council’s September meeting, when the council discussed a “Memorandum of Understanding” between the City of Salix and Google, which wants to build a data center on the 900 acres of annexed land. Under the MOU, Google would pay for any independent advisors the council hires to study the data center’s impact. The MOU states the cost couldn’t exceed $150,000 and Google must pay invoices within 30 days. But if the council imposes a moratorium, Google’s payments stop immediately. First up was a vote on moratorium clarification, followed by the memorandum of understanding and updates from Google. One agenda item included “affirming and clarifying that the city council has NOT adopted a moratorium prohibiting the construction or development of data centers in the City of Salix, Iowa.” This stems from confusion during a previous city council meeting over an action where Gene Monk motioned for a moratorium, but the mayor later said it did not impose one in Salix. That vote passed 3-2. “Towards the beginning of the meeting, there was a resolution where the council voted three to two to approve a resolution saying that there is no moratorium in place, and if there was one, accidentally created, it is officially rescinded. So there is no moratorium on data centers in Salix,” the mayor said. That vote means there is no rule or ordinance in place preventing the building of a data center. The council also voted 3-2 in favor of a memorandum of understanding, an agreement between Google and the City of Salix that would see the company reimbursing the city for the cost of any unbiased research into the impact of data centers. “We take a climate-conscious approach to cooling that balances energy and water efficiency. Based on our ongoing evaluations and our commitment to protecting local resources, Google will not source any cooling water from the Dakota Aquifer,” Google representatives said. Google representatives say studies they will undertake on the site include the project’s impact on water and wastewater, on threatened and endangered species, and the impact of traffic and noise. When asked after Wednesday’s meeting if, with a moratorium failing, there are now official plans for a data center, the mayor said it is still up in the air. “Still very much up in the air. The same six or seven families that own that land last year still own that land today. They have not sold the land to Mid-American or Google or anyone else. So until they sign on the dotted line and actually buy it, then no project can proceed,” the mayor said. Google also said it is in the works for Salix residents and the city council to tour one of its already existing data centers in Iowa. artigo.texto: ComEd, Richardson Electronics to construct Illinois’ largest BESS asset Electrical utility Commonwealth Edison (ComEd) and engineering firm Richardson Electronics have partnered for a massive project, zeroing in on the Land of Lincoln. The corporate duo plans to install the largest commercial battery energy storage system (BESS) asset in the state of Illinois, officials announced Oct. 12. The companies have joined up with state and industrial leaders to announce that Richardson has expanded its local BESS manufacturing plans to install the record-breaking project on ComEd’s grid. “For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” says ComEd president and CEO Gil Quiniones. “ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.” ComEd calls the project and the manufacturing bump “a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions,” as the U.S. strives for grid reliability. In addition to building the largest commercial BESS system in Illinois, Richardson is installing a 5 MWh research and development demonstration project, which will go through the ComEd interconnection process. “Richardson Electronics has a long history of solving complex power and energy challenges through innovation and U.S.-based manufacturing,” says Greg Peloquin, Richardson’s EVP and general manager of power and microwave technologies, and its green energy solution groups. “Our advanced energy storage solutions will help customers manage energy more efficiently while supporting a more reliable and resilient grid. We value ComEd’s collaboration in bringing this onsite demonstration project to life.” Constructing Illinois’ energy future Increasing battery storage capabilities is a cornerstone of Illinoisan energy policy in the mid-2020s, ComEd officials say. The Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA), one of a flurry of renewable-forward bills signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker, aims to bolster both solar and storage across the Prairie State. ComEd and Richardson’s collaborative effort is part of bringing CRGA’s vision for Illinois to life, officials say. “When Kane County Commissioner Rick Williams and I first met with Richardson to discuss this project, I was immediately intrigued by both the economic and energy benefits the project could bring to the area and the state,” says Illinois State Rep. Dan Ugaste. “Energy storage will be an important part of having affordable and reliable energy going forward. Seeing the value this project could bring, I was glad to help facilitate discussions with the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to bring this project to fruition.” The companies will also support the local community, says Illinois State Rep. Jeff Keicher. Richardson’s continued investment in its La Fox, Illinois manufacturing location serves as an example of “how Illinois businesses can lead the way in developing innovative energy solutions while creating good-paying jobs” at the local level, he says. “As Illinois works to strengthen the reliability and affordability of our electric grid, projects like this will play an important role in ensuring we meet our future needs, while strengthening our state’s position as an advanced manufacturing leader.” Battery projects across Illinois are also open to accessing ComEd’s Distributed Generation Rebate Program. With the program recently hitting the $350 million milestone, customers who install qualifying battery storage assets can receive a rebate of up to $300 per kWh of storage capacity.

artigo.texto: A heated debate is ongoing within the European Union regarding the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). In July, the European Commission presented a proposal to revise the scheme, and on 12 October this became the subject of political debates held by the Council of the EU. The Council has stated its aim to combine stronger climate ambitions with support for industrial competitiveness. This was reported by the Council of the European Union. The EU ETS is the bloc’s key climate policy instrument, which helps to reduce emissions and is the world’s first and largest carbon market. It requires companies to pay for their CO₂ emissions. Supporters of the EU ETS believe it encourages businesses to invest in the ‘green’ transition, whilst opponents see it as placing excessive financial pressure on them. "We must ensure that the EU Emissions Trading System is fit for the next decade. Our aim is to align our carbon market with our climate ambitions in a way that also ensures the competitiveness of our industry,” emphasised Dara O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, who currently holds the presidency of the Council of the EU. They added that the review of the EU ETS should align the carbon market with the EU’s climate target – to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 90 per cent by 2040. The ministerial discussions are focusing on the trajectory of the annual emissions cap after 2030, as well as the use of international carbon credits and carbon sequestration projects. The debate also assessed the proposed mechanisms for financing and allocating free allowances. Some politicians expressed the view that the EU ETS should be extended to cover aviation, shipping and the waste management sector. O’Brien noted that they would aim to reach agreements on the revision of the ETS by December 2026. At the same time, according to data from Politico, the three largest political groups in the European Parliament are set to oppose any watering down of the emissions trading scheme. It was previously reported that the European Parliament intends to make significant amendments to the European Commission’s proposal. In particular, the Member States wish to require 75 per cent of ETS revenues to be reinvested in the eco-modernisation of businesses A number of countries will call for the cancellation of the revocation of ‘excess’ quotas in the Market Stability Reserve. As a reminder, the European Commission presented its proposal to reform the EU carbon market on 17 July. It includes, in particular, an increase in funding for decarbonisation, an extension of the period for receiving free allowances, and a reduction in the level of allowances transferred to the market stability reserve. Work is continuing in Ukraine on the legislative framework for establishing a national emissions trading scheme. In addition to the draft bill from the Ministry of Economy – which was drawn up taking into account feedback from experts and stakeholders – there are three parliamentary proposals. A detailed comparison of these can be found in the article by EcoPolitika.

artigo.texto: Millington approves data center moratorium as county, Memphis weigh their own MILLINGTON, Tenn. (WMC) - Millington has approved its own data center moratorium as Shelby County and the City of Memphis weigh their own. Chris Thomas, executive director of the Millington Chamber of Commerce, confirms that the board of mayor and aldermen approved a six-month pause on development applications for non-grid power generation, accessory computing or industrial-scale computing facilities Monday. The moratorium took effect immediately and will expire April 12 unless extended. The pause gives the city time to reexamine its zoning ordinances without juggling proposals for developments that current land use regulations don’t address. “Whereas, non-grid power generation, accessory computing, and industrial-scale facilities are one of the fastest-growing land uses nationally and are not currently addressed as a distinct use in the Millington Zoning Ordinance, creating uncertainty for applicants and the city alike,” the resolution reads. In the next six months, city leaders plan to study, research, analyze and assess the impacts of any facilities of this kind, including their development, demographic trends, aesthetic qualities and burdens on the community. Applications the city has already accepted would be exempt from the development halt, but Thomas says that doesn’t apply, as Millington has yet to see a proposal for a data center. Shelby County is also considering its own data center moratorium for unincorporated parts of the county before any development applications are filed. It passed its first reading Monday by a 5-4 vote. The City of Memphis is also weighing a data center moratorium, but only after high-density computing facilities have already established a footprint in the municipality. The Memphis City Council is expected to make a final decision on its moratorium October 20. The council pushed the final vote back twice. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: Principais Pontos - As ações da Enerflex subiram 13% hoje após a empresa vencer um contrato para construir mais de um gigawatt de unidades de energia a gás natural para um data center norte-americano. - O contrato eleva o backlog de energia behind-the-meter da Enerflex para mais de 1,75 gigawatts, com entregas até 2028, e as estimativas de receita dos analistas foram definidas antes deste anúncio. - A Enerflex não divulgou o valor em dólares do contrato e está investindo cerca de US$ 100 milhões para expandir as instalações de Sistemas de Engenharia que irão construí-lo. - O CIBC elevou a recomendação da ação para Outperformer com um preço-alvo de US$ 35, e o relatório do terceiro trimestre será a próxima oportunidade para ver quanto vale o backlog em dólares. Enerflex (EFXT) As ações subiram 13% hoje após a empresa fechar um pedido de mais de um gigawatt de energia a gás para um único data center. Antes da abertura, a Enerflex anunciou que construirá unidades de energia a gás behind-the-meter para "um grande desenvolvimento de data center na América do Norte". Este novo contrato sozinho é mais que o dobro dos aproximadamente 450 megawatts anunciados em 1º de outubro. Somando esses e outros contratos, seu backlog de energia behind-the-meter agora ultrapassa 1,75 gigawatts, com entregas até 2028. O CEO Paul Mahoney atribuiu a demanda à IA e destacou o "sucesso da empresa em garantir mais de 1,75 gigawatts de backlog" (comunicado à imprensa). Às 10h, o CIBC elevou a recomendação da ação para Outperformer, de Neutral, com um preço-alvo de US$ 35. Gigawatts em um negócio de US$ 3,5 bilhões O backlog de Sistemas de Engenharia da Enerflex estava em US$ 1,5 bilhão no final de junho, acima dos US$ 1,1 bilhão no final de 2025, e a maior parte dos 1,75 gigawatts anunciados hoje foi contratada após esse período. A empresa não divulgou um valor em dólares para o novo contrato nem nomeou o cliente. O contrato chega a um negócio cuja receita tem se mantido estável, em US$ 3,52 bilhões em 2025, embora os analistas projetem US$ 4,37 bilhões até 2028... Essas estimativas são de 9 de outubro, antes do contrato de hoje. Com entregas ocorrendo até 2028, eu esperaria que os números de 2027 e 2028 sejam revisados para cima. Agora a Enerflex precisa construí-lo Para construir tudo em suas plantas norte-americanas, a Enerflex autorizou cerca de US$ 100 milhões para expandir suas instalações de Sistemas de Engenharia, e apenas US$ 15 milhões disso estão no guia de gastos de capital deste ano. A administração espera que isso aumente significativamente a capacidade de receita do negócio. É muito trabalho novo dependendo de um cronograma que se estende até 2028, então um atraso ou um custo excedente em um pedido na escala de gigawatts teria um impacto forte. A ação ainda não está esticada A Enerflex já negociava a 14x o lucro futuro no último fechamento, bem acima de sua média de cinco anos de 9,7x... Ao preço desta manhã, está próximo de 16x, ainda bem abaixo de seu pico de 23,8x em janeiro de 2022. E o preço-alvo de US$ 35 do CIBC está confortavelmente acima mesmo do preço de hoje. Eu posso ver a visão do mercado sobre a Enerflex mudando ainda mais a partir daqui. Por anos, o mercado precificou a empresa como uma fabricante de equipamentos a gás, e um pedido na escala de gigawatts é um forte sinal de que o negócio é algo mais do que isso. Os analistas também ainda não incorporaram o contrato em suas estimativas, o que deixa espaço para os números se ajustarem. Claro, ainda não sabemos quanto tudo isso vale em dólares. O relatório do terceiro trimestre da Enerflex é a primeira chance de descobrir. Então, quanto vale realmente a ação da Enerflex? artigo.texto: Growth through decarbonisation: Why the EU must stand firm on emissions trading EU Climate Week began in Brussels on 12 October. The EU itself should remember that the economy can grow while emissions fall. Technology Industries of Finland does not support erratic climate policy. We support a predictable investment environment, a strong and long-term emissions trading system, electrification and clean domestic energy. Climate action is still sometimes approached with caution on the grounds that it is too expensive. Europe’s own figures tell a different story: between 1990 and 2024, the EU’s GDP grew by more than 70 percent, while net greenhouse gas emissions fell by 40 percent. Since the launch of emissions trading in 2005, emissions in the sectors covered by the system have halved. The Commission wants to support the continuation of climate policy because it links climate policy more closely to competitiveness, affordable energy and reducing strategic dependencies. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen outlined the bigger picture in her State of the Union address in September: “The transition is complex, and we have to adapt our approach and learn along the way. But Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate goals.” The Commission has also consistently promoted the phase-out of Russian fossil energy imports, with transition periods. In Finland, security is understood broadly. Climate policy is also not seen as a separate cost item, but as part of building self-sufficiency and resilience. In Finland, the volatility of fossil fuel prices is visible in transport and logistics costs. In the marine industry and heavy transport, the transition to clean electricity and clean fuels is beginning. We need a major leap in electrification One of Finland’s strengths is that electricity is more than 95 percent emission-free and among the most competitive in Europe in terms of price. Growing electricity consumption creates demand, but networks are now starting to become a bottleneck. At the same time, the Confederation of Finnish Industries’ green investment data window, Fingrid’s assessments and the Finnish Wind Power Association’s own figures all point to strong readiness to unlock new production potential. In addition, Finland’s existing nuclear power capacity is being renewed, and readiness to produce electricity and heat with small modular reactors is being built in several locations. The Finnish economy needs a major leap in electrification, supported by hydrogen, clean fuels and other solutions. This electrification leap is the next growth step, and both society and companies must be brought on board. We cannot afford to stumble now. Emissions trading rewards the most efficient solutions Technology Industries of Finland has defended the EU Emissions Trading System as the cornerstone of climate policy because it is a market-based tool. In addition, it generates revenues that should be allocated to accelerating the transition in the sectors affected by emissions trading. It puts a price on emissions but leaves companies free to choose the means. Emissions are reduced where it makes the most sense and where it is most cost-effective. For the sake of the EU’s own competitiveness, this should not be distorted with state aid. Countries and companies that have invested early are now in a stronger position. Weakening emissions trading would punish frontrunners and would not eliminate regulation as it would simply be replaced by more detailed, less market-based and less efficient steering. Freedom from fossil fuels is also security policy Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels is both an economic and a security policy risk. Russia’s war of aggression has shown how energy can be used as an instrument of pressure and as a means to finance a war economy. Every unit of energy saved or produced cleanly in Europe reduces the need to transfer wealth outside the Union. According to Eurostat, the EU is moving in the right direction, but slowly. Energy import dependency has decreased: in 2022, net imports accounted for 63 percent of the EU’s energy, and in 2024 the figure was still 57 percent. Yet in 2025, oil, gas and solid fossil fuels worth EUR 337 billion were still imported into the EU. In other words, we remain heavily dependent on energy whose price is determined elsewhere. Fossil fuels are still needed in transport, heating and industry. But dependence — the obligation to buy — can be reduced especially through electrification, clean electricity production, a sufficient and smart grid, and energy efficiency. These are precisely the areas where Finland has solutions to offer. When carbon has a price, demand is created for clean technology. At the same time, the trade balance, security of supply and Europe’s own strategic autonomy are strengthened. Bringing the handprint into EU climate policy European solutions can also reduce emissions outside Europe. In Finland’s case, this export-driven carbon handprint is larger than the emissions of our emissions trading sector. There is therefore evidence of the positive impacts of technology exports. However, the EU has not yet strongly embraced the carbon handprint in its climate policy. Could the handprint be brought more firmly into the core of EU climate policy, alongside the carbon footprint? I am in Brussels for Climate Week — let’s discuss.

artigo.texto: Câmara aprova urgência do PL que faz rateio de custos de baterias elétricas Projeto ainda precisa passar pelo plenário, o que deve ficar para o período pós-eleitoral; setores argumentam que proposta traria maior segurança jurídica e previsibilidade para o setor elétrico A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou nesta terça-feira um requerimento de urgência para o projeto de lei que muda a proporção de rateio dos custos de baterias elétricas. O projeto em si, no entanto, deve ser votado no plenário da Câmara apenas após o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, marcado para 25 de outubro. Com a urgência aprovada, o texto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) se torna uma "prioridade" dos trabalhos legislativos. Na prática, o projeto altera uma revogação de uma lei de 2004, determinando que os custos das contratações de baterias sejam divididos entre os geradores e os consumidores de energia elétrica. Atualmente, uma regulamentação da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) determina a exclusividade para agentes do setor, o que produz, segundo o autor do projeto, "distorções na alocação de recursos". Ainda há a necessidade de negociar a tramitação da proposta junto ao governo federal para que vá de fato a voto. A proposta também depende de aprovação do Senado Federal para se tornar lei. Setores argumentam que a legislação atual cria um cenário de insegurança jurídica aos leilões de bateria que estão previstos para dezembro deste ano, além de acentuar a imprevisibilidade das tratativas do setor de energia. A proposta corrigiria "assimetrias" do modelo atual. As entidades Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica), Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica), Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) e Abiape (Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia) emitiram uma nota em apoio ao PL. “Todas as tecnologias e soluções que prestam serviços semelhantes aos usuários devem estar sujeitas ao mesmo regime jurídico, permitindo alocação e comparação justa dos custos. Por isso, as regras de custeio da reserva de capacidade devem ser as mesmas para todas as soluções eventualmente contratadas”, diz o comunicado. O principal ponto de convergência entre as entidades é de que a manutenção do modelo atual pode elevar o custo de energia para o consumidor, tendo em vista que os custos refletem diretamente no preço da energia que chega às casas brasileiras.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The global failure rate for lithium-ion battery energy storage systems, on a per-GWh basis, fell 98% from 2018 to 2025 and 50% from 2024 to 2025, the Electric Power Research Institute said in a new analysis of its BESS failure incident database. - Stationary energy storage systems’ annual failure rates range from 0.04% to 0.14%, according to the analysis. That is comparable to the 0.1% annual failure rate for oil-filled electrical transformers, EPRI said in the report, Risk Factors and Failure Statistics of Lithium-Ion BESS. - Safety reviews and, in some cases, retrofits can mitigate failure risk and improve reliability in older systems, which tend to fail at higher rates than newer systems built under stricter codes and design practices, EPRI said. Dive Insight: Ninety-three percent of the BESS safety incidents EPRI reviewed worldwide resulted in no injuries or fatalities, according to the report. In the United States, no reported injuries or fatalities have occurred as a result of BESS failures since April 2019, when an explosion at an Arizona Public Service facility seriously injured four firefighters. A post-incident report by Underwriters Laboratories, the global safety science organization known as UL, noted that the APS installation was commissioned before the initial release of NFPA 855, the safety standard that governs energy storage systems today. Lakshmi Srinivasan, a senior technical leader with EPRI’s energy storage program and a principal investigator on the report, told Utility Dive that battery systems deployed over the past five years appear significantly more reliable than earlier vintages. The trend continues today. “There are things we know in 2026 that were not necessarily understood in 2019 or 2020, when the older systems were being put in place,” Srinivasan said in an interview. The most dramatic BESS failure in the U.S. involved a utility-scale installation inside a 1950s-era turbine hall at a decommissioned thermal power plant near Santa Cruz, California, known as Moss Landing. In January 2025, thermal runaway in one of the units caused fire to spread throughout the indoor facility and ultimately destroyed most of the 300-MW battery array. Thick smoke emanated from the facility for days, but no injuries were reported and subsequent soil and water monitoring found no significant threats to human health or the environment. Experts later told Utility Dive the incident was a “learning opportunity” for the energy storage industry. Indoor BESS facilities fail at higher rates and sustain more damage on average than outdoor facilities, according to EPRI’s report. Propagation-prevention measures within battery units and fire walls or similar barriers between units can mitigate fire’s spread within indoor facilities, EPRI said. Vistra commissioned Moss Landing in 2020. BESS facilities commissioned before 2021 account for just 3% of global energy storage capacity, according to the report. It’s worthwhile for owners of those older facilities to run thorough risk assessments of them and take corrective action if warranted, Srinivasan said. For example, the 2019 incident in Arizona showed a need for older BESS facilities to address explosion risk, which represents “a different risk than fire and a bigger one from a personnel and equipment standpoint,” Srinavasan said. Explosion-mitigation retrofits range from what she called “a relatively low-difficulty change,” like installing flammable gas detectors inside battery enclosures, to more significant projects like installing new ventilation systems or making structural upgrades to direct pressure waves upward and away from first responders, Srinavasan said. Those last two types of projects generally require changes to battery unit envelopes, which could void the manufacturer’s warranty or interfere with other aspects of the system’s design, Srinavasan said. In some scenarios, it could make more sense to prematurely decommission an outdated, higher-risk system, she added. Although newer battery systems appear to be safer than early-vintage systems, local permitting remains challenging in some jurisdictions due to limitations in the NFPA 855 standard that lead most developers to apply for exemptions to allow for higher energy densities or other project modifications, Srinavasan said. To assist local authorities that may lack in-house expertise, New York added a requirement to its fire code — which took effect in January — that those authorities can make energy storage developers pay for independent technical reviews of exemption applications, she added. Correction: We have updated this story to remove a reference to a new NFPA standard expected this fall. NFPA 855 will remain the key standard for battery energy storage systems.

artigo.texto: DATA CENTERS NO NORDESTE: REGIÃO PODE ATRAIR 30% DOS INVESTIMENTOS ATÉ 2036 O Nordeste poderá concentrar cerca de 30% dos novos investimentos em grandes data centers no Brasil até 2036, além de ampliar a geração de energia eólica e solar e a produção de gás natural. As projeções constam no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2036), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), sob diretrizes do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). Divulgado para consulta pública em 8 de outubro, o documento aponta que a presença de pontos de chegada de cabos internacionais de fibra óptica, a disponibilidade de energia renovável e o potencial de desenvolvimento econômico regional estão entre os fatores que favorecem a instalação de centros de dados no Nordeste. Apesar dessas condições, a maior parcela dos novos investimentos deverá se concentrar no subsistema Sudeste/Centro-Oeste, com participação superior a 65%. O Sul deverá receber os 5% restantes, segundo as estimativas do plano. Consumo de energia dos data centers A expansão dos data centers está relacionada ao avanço da digitalização da economia, à demanda por armazenamento e processamento de informações e ao uso crescente de inteligência artificial. Nesse cenário, o PDE 2036 projeta que o consumo de eletricidade dessas instalações no Brasil alcance aproximadamente 30 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2036. Devido à dimensão dos empreendimentos previstos, o planejamento indica uma tendência de conexão direta dos novos centros de dados à rede básica de transmissão de energia elétrica. Demanda de eletricidade no Nordeste O crescimento das atividades de comércio e serviços deverá contribuir para a expansão da demanda por eletricidade no Nordeste. De acordo com o PDE 2036, a carga elétrica do subsistema deverá avançar, em média, 3,7% ao ano entre 2026 e 2036, a maior taxa projetada entre os subsistemas brasileiros. O índice supera a média estimada para o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), de 3,3% ao ano no mesmo período. Em termos absolutos, a carga global do Nordeste deverá passar de 14.209 megawatts médios (MW médios), em 2026, para 20.462 MW médios, em 2036. O indicador considera tanto o consumo final de eletricidade quanto as perdas registradas entre a geração e o fornecimento aos consumidores. O relatório também aponta uma mudança na composição do consumo nacional. A participação da classe comercial deverá aumentar de 19% para 24% entre 2026 e 2036, impulsionada, entre outros fatores, pela expansão dos data centers. No mesmo período, a parcela residencial deverá cair de 32% para 28%. Outra demanda considerada no planejamento está relacionada à produção de hidrogênio por eletrólise. Segundo o PDE, a implantação de projetos desse tipo deverá ganhar espaço no segundo quinquênio do horizonte analisado, devido ao prazo mais longo de maturação dos investimentos. Ainda assim, a participação dessas atividades deverá permanecer reduzida no período projetado. Expansão da transmissão A instalação de grandes consumidores de energia, como data centers e unidades de produção de hidrogênio, deverá exigir investimentos adicionais na infraestrutura de transmissão, segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. O PDE destaca estudos para a integração dessas novas cargas no Nordeste e recomenda a implantação do Bipolo Nordeste II, empreendimento destinado a ampliar a capacidade de transferência de eletricidade da região para os subsistemas Sudeste e Sul. De acordo com o planejamento, o projeto e as obras complementares deverão facilitar a conexão de novos empreendimentos de geração, consumo e armazenamento de energia. A infraestrutura também deverá contribuir para a estabilidade do sistema elétrico e para a redução de cortes de geração associados a restrições de confiabilidade da rede. *Informações do site Movimento Econômico. artigo.texto: Boulder City voters to forge city's path on data centers and infrastructure projects LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Boulder City voters are weighing two ballot questions ahead of the Nov. 3 general election that could shape the community’s future, from whether data centers can be built south of town to how much money the city can spend each year on infrastructure projects. The first of two ballot questions asks: “Should data center facilities be an approved land use within the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area outside of the Multi-species Habitat Conservation Easement?” The land is off of Highway 95 south of the main city. Approval would not guarantee a data center is built, but it would allow one to be located there. Some residents said they see potential benefits but also risks. “It is great to have data centers, but there are consequences,” said an anonymous Boulder City voter. The voter noted the area is already seeing development. “It is being used for solar and other things, including battery storage. So we have quite a lot going on,” the voter said. Tyson Ballard, a Boulder City resident, said he supports 'Yes' assuming companies follow through on promises to handle the project themselves. “If they do everything on their own like they say they could, then I am all for it,” Ballard said. Ballard said he believes data centers could bring hundreds of jobs to Boulder City, but he wants them built safely. UNLV history professor Michael Green said additional large-scale development could alter what draws residents to stay in Boulder City. “People will move to Boulder City looking for something different and realize, ‘I have found something different.’ I do not want to change it,” Green said. “It does not mean they do not improve the infrastructure or that sort of thing. But they are not going to want something like a data center that could turn the whole world topsy turvy.” The second ballot question asks whether Boulder City should be authorized to spend more from its Capital Improvement Fund each year. The question reads: “Shall the City of Boulder City be authorized to expend available funds from the Capital Improvement Fund in an amount up to 50% of the most recent audited fiscal year’s ending cash balance in the capital improvement fund each year in place of the previously authorized amount of $1,000,000.00 per year for capital improvement projects for the benefit of Boulder City residents and visitors?” If approved, the city would be allowed to have more money to spend on infrastructure improvements. If it fails, some improvements may have to wait. Green said Boulder City should continue to market its unique history, including Hoover Dam, its railroad role, art installations and its historic downtown. Ballard said he is voting yes on the funding question, arguing that improvements to historic districts and roads could help local businesses by supporting tourism. “[Tourists] stop, use our businesses. So I think it is good for people coming up here. You go downtown right now, it is packed. I think that is great for Boulder City,” Ballard said. Other residents said they are concerned about increased spending and the direction it could take the city. “Why increase tourism? We do not need more tourists,” said Marie, a Boulder City resident. Marie said she voted no, saying she worries a yes vote would open the city’s wallet too much and that projects would benefit construction companies rather than residents. “I voted no. They do not need more money to give their cronies jobs in this city,” she said. Environmental concerns also surfaced in the debate over both questions. “They need a blanket clause in it that says that they are responsible for any type of environmental impact that they might have,” said John “Two Hearts” Madrid, a Boulder City resident. Madrid said he cast no votes for both questions earlier Thursday, but would reconsider if the city and companies involved could be held legally responsible for potential environmental harm. “Mother Earth is going to go on forever, but what are we doing to pass that on to the next generation and the generations to come,” he said. The final day to vote is Tuesday, November 3.

artigo.texto: Tesla Major partner for wind farm integration projects According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Wind Energy Storage market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global wind energy storage market is entering a phase of accelerated expansion, driven by the rapid build-out of wind power capacity and the urgent need for grid flexibility. As wind penetration rises, the intermittency of generation becomes a critical operational challenge, making storage an essential enabler of reliable, dispatchable renewable power. This report analyzes the market from 2026 to 2035, covering lithium-ion, flow, mechanical, thermal, and hydrogen storage technologies deployed in onshore and offshore wind farms, grid-scale balancing, commercial and industrial settings, residential microgrids, and hybrid renewable systems. The market is shaped by declining battery costs, supportive policies, and evolving electricity market designs that reward flexibility. While utility-scale projects dominate, behind-the-meter and hybrid applications are gaining traction. The competitive landscape includes battery manufacturers, system integrators, power conversion specialists, and energy majors. Regional dynamics vary, with Asia-Pacific leading in deployment, North America and Europe advancing through policy and grid modernization, and emerging markets offering long-term potential. The forecast to 2035 anticipates a more technologically diverse and digitally integrated market, with storage becoming a standard component of wind energy projects worldwide. The baseline scenario for the world wind energy storage market from 2026 to 2035 assumes continued global wind capacity additions, supportive renewable policies, and further cost reductions in battery and power conversion technologies. Under this scenario, the market is projected to grow at a robust pace, with the market index reaching 245 by 2035 (2025=100), corresponding to a CAGR of 9.4%. This growth is underpinned by the increasing need to integrate variable wind generation into power systems, reduce curtailment, and provide essential grid services such as frequency regulation and peak shaving. Lithium-ion batteries will remain the dominant technology, but flow batteries, compressed air, and hydrogen storage will gain share in long-duration applications. Onshore wind farms will continue to account for the largest share of storage deployments, while offshore wind and grid-scale balancing segments grow faster. The commercial and industrial segment will expand as businesses seek to manage energy costs and sustainability targets. Regulatory frameworks, including capacity markets and storage mandates, will be critical in shaping adoption rates. Supply chain constraints for critical minerals and manufacturing capacity could pose risks, but ongoing diversification and recycling efforts are expected to mitigate these pressures. Overall, the market outlook is positive, with storage transitioning from an optional add-on to a fundamental component of wind energy projects. Onshore wind farms represent the largest end-use segment for wind energy storage, as developers seek to maximize the value of generated electricity and comply with grid requirements. Currently, storage is primarily deployed to smooth output fluctuations, shift energy to peak demand periods, and provide ancillary services. Through 2035, the segment will evolve as more onshore projects include storage by default, driven by declining battery costs and supportive policies. Demand-side indicators include the level of wind curtailment, peak-valley price spreads, and capacity market revenues. The integration of storage allows onshore wind farms to act more like conventional dispatchable plants, improving their competitiveness. As grid operators demand greater flexibility, storage becomes essential for new and repowered onshore wind projects, especially in regions with high renewable penetration. Current trend: Steady growth, with increasing co-location of storage to reduce curtailment and provide grid services.. Major trends: Co-location of batteries with onshore wind farms to reduce curtailment, Participation in capacity and ancillary service markets, Repowering of older wind farms with storage additions, Standardization of storage integration in project design, and Growth in hybrid projects combining wind, solar, and storage. Representative participants: NextEra Energy, Vestas, GE Vernova, Tesla, and Fluence. Offshore wind farms are increasingly paired with storage to address unique challenges such as long transmission distances, high capacity factors, and grid integration. Storage helps defer or avoid costly transmission upgrades, provides frequency support, and enables offshore wind to contribute to system reliability. Through 2035, the segment will expand significantly as offshore wind capacity grows, particularly in Europe and Asia-Pacific. Demand-side indicators include the scale of offshore wind auctions, transmission congestion, and the adoption of energy islands. Storage also supports the development of offshore hydrogen production, where excess wind energy is converted to hydrogen for storage and transport. The trend toward larger turbines and deeper waters further emphasizes the need for storage to manage variability and maximize output. Current trend: Rapid growth, driven by large-scale offshore projects and the need for transmission deferral and grid stability.. Major trends: Integration of storage with offshore wind to defer transmission investments, Development of offshore energy islands with centralized storage, Growth in offshore hydrogen production using wind electrolysis, Increasing size and capacity of offshore wind projects, and Policy support for offshore wind and storage co-location. Representative participants: Ørsted, Siemens Energy, Vattenfall, Equinor, and Sumitomo Electr

artigo.texto: Topeka City Council hears presentation on proposed data center, discusses sales taxes TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - Sales taxes and data centers were a few of the topics discussed at the Topeka City Council on Oct. 13. Council members heard a presentation from Metropolitan Topeka Airport Authority (MTAA) President Curtis Sneden on a proposed data center at Forbes Field. The proposed spot is by Southwest Topeka Boulevard and 77th Street. Many council members raised questions surrounding the transparency of the data center since MTAA has not disclosed who the developer is. “All developers have a different approach. They worry about their proprietary information, and that’s fair, but eventually, you can’t do it forever, you got to have an honest conversation with the community,” Spencer Duncan, Topeka Mayor, said. There is no contract with the county due to the moratorium in place. Council members also raised questions about how the data center might affect the airport and frequency and transmission waves, but MTAA said there shouldn’t be any interruption. Mayor Duncan emphasized the importance of not only meeting with council but talking with the community as well. “Starting with who you are is usually the best place,” Duncan said. “There’s a reason we walk up to people and introduce ourselves first, because that’s how you start to build trust. That, I think, was the biggest ask you heard tonight: it’s hard to have an honest conversation with people who we don’t know who you are.” The full presentation on the potential data center can be viewed here. Topeka City Council also continued discussions on potential sales taxes to fill projected budget gaps. Council is considering the following four tax question possibilities: - A half-cent sales tax that would raise about $20 million a year for city services like fire, police and public works - A one-tenth of a cent sales tax that would generate about $4 million a year for affordable housing and homeless services - Renew a current half-cent sales tax for infrastructure, which expires in 2029 - It would keep collecting with no tax increase - Create an independent City Auditor Office that reports directly to the City Council to review spending and performance. Council must make a decision by next week for any of these possible questions to appear on ballots in March 2027. “We will make some decision next week because we have pressing deadlines, election deadlines,” Duncan said. “What I think will happen is, personally, I don’t think we’re ready to send anything at this time to the public without some more public conversations. We might consider something as it relates to housing and homelessness issues.” More about the sales taxes the city is considering can be found here. The city also discussed Fiscal Year (FY) Goals in 2026 along with plans for 2027 through 2030. What’s been accomplished and what the city is still aiming to do can be found here. Copyright 2026 WIBW. artigo.texto: - Stratos data center's water permit application is expected to be filed soon. - The application includes detailed hydrological studies and water recycling plans. - Utah Division of Water Rights hasn't received the application as of Wednesday. SALT LAKE CITY — A self-imposed timeline for the Stratos data center in Box Elder County has come and gone with few new details about the project. Despite the project receiving approval from Utah's Military Installation Development Authority and the Box Elder County Commission, little information has been made public about factors that could have a major impact, including how much water the data center will use. It's information Utahns have been waiting on for months. When KSL Investigators spoke with developer Kevin O'Leary on July 1, he said details about water demand would be included in a water permit application expected to be publicly available by the end of August. "All that stuff is going to be put forward in the August proposal in terms of what the water demand is going to be," O'Leary said when asked for details. "I'd rather just wait until the design and the application's put forward." With that timeline having come and gone, KSL Investigators reached out to ask about the status of the application. In an emailed statement this week, Paul Palandjian, the chief executive officer of O'Leary Digital and co-founder of the business along with Kevin O'Leary, wrote: "To be clear, the water permit application isn't delayed. The timing Kevin shared in July was an estimate based on early input from our consultants. As the work progressed, we chose to go further than a standard application requires." Palandjian said the application will include detailed hydrological studies and engineering analysis for water treatment and recycling. "That is a significant body of work," he wrote. "We believe it's the right approach for Utah, and it gives regulators and the community a more complete picture." As for when the application will be filed, Palandjian said on Tuesday that it is complete, in final review, and will be submitted "shortly." The Utah Division of Water Rights told KSL it had not received the application as of Wednesday. The KSL Investigators will continue following the project and report on the contents of the application once it becomes public.

artigo.texto: A Câmara dos Deputados pode votar na tarde desta terça-feira, 13 de outubro, o requerimento de urgência do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3.716/2026, que altera o rateio dos custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS). A proposta busca transferir aos consumidores o custeio atualmente atribuído aos geradores e tem o apoio de seis associações do setor elétrico, que defendem a mudança para garantir isonomia entre as tecnologias contratadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade. Caso a urgência seja aprovada, o projeto poderá ser analisado diretamente pelo plenário, sem precisar concluir a tramitação nas comissões. O PL 3.716/2026 revoga um dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004, incluído pela Lei 15.269/2025, que determina que os custos das contratações de reserva de capacidade com baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Em nota conjunta divulgada em 7 de outubro, seis associações do setor elétrico defenderam a aprovação urgente do projeto. As entidades argumentam que o modelo atual cria uma diferença de tratamento entre as baterias e outras tecnologias que prestam serviços de reserva de capacidade, cujos custos são distribuídos entre os usuários finais de energia elétrica. O posicionamento é assinado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica), Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape), Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv), Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) e Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). As entidades alertam que a atribuição dos custos exclusivamente aos geradores pode encarecer a energia elétrica para os consumidores e reduzir a competitividade da indústria brasileira. Modelo de custeio das baterias Na avaliação das associações, a reserva de capacidade tem como objetivo garantir a segurança do suprimento de energia elétrica, assegurando potência e flexibilidade para a operação confiável do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Esses atributos podem ser fornecidos por diferentes tecnologias, que, segundo as entidades, devem receber tratamento equivalente. Atualmente, os custos da reserva de capacidade são distribuídos entre os usuários finais, conforme os parâmetros legais previstos no artigo 3º-A da Lei nº 10.848/2004. No entanto, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias recebem tratamento diferente, com os custos atribuídos exclusivamente aos geradores, conforme determinou a Lei n° 15.269/2025. Para as entidades, essa regra cria um descompasso entre a natureza sistêmica do serviço prestado, a distribuição de seus benefícios e a responsabilidade pelo pagamento dos custos. Baterias podem gerar economia de R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano As associações argumentam que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, inclusive os baseados em baterias, podem contribuir para reduzir outros encargos pagos pelos consumidores ao otimizar a operação do parque gerador. Como exemplo, a nota cita um estudo da Volt Robotics segundo o qual os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias podem reduzir a variação do Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças (PLD) e o acionamento de usinas termelétricas, gerando uma economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano para os consumidores. O documento também destaca que atribuir legalmente os custos aos geradores não impede que eles sejam repassados aos consumidores finais. No mercado regulado, as entidades mencionam o reconhecimento, pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), da inclusão integral e automática desses custos nas tarifas de energia. No mercado livre, o impacto pode ocorrer por meio de renegociações ou reajustes de preços. Já na autoprodução de energia, os custos podem ser incorporados aos preços de bens e serviços, afetando a competitividade da indústria brasileira. As associações acrescentam que o pagamento do encargo pelo segmento de geração pode elevar os custos para os consumidores devido ao repasse dos valores, acrescidos de tributos e despesas administrativas. Data centers e hidrogênio verde entram no debate A nota também relaciona a expansão da eletrificação da economia à necessidade de discutir a responsabilidade pelo custeio da reserva de capacidade. Segundo as entidades, novas cargas, como veículos elétricos, data centers e projetos industriais eletrointensivos, incluindo parques produtores de hidrogênio verde, influenciam a demanda máxima de energia e o déficit de capacidade do sistema. Na avaliação das associações, esses consumidores também podem contribuir para reduzir o déficit de capacidade caso recebam sinais econômicos adequados para ajustar sua demanda. Por isso, as entidades defendem que as baterias sejam tratadas em igualdade com as demais soluções de capacidade, considerando os atributos de potência e flexibilidade. O objetivo, segundo a nota, é permitir a contratação da tecnologia mais eficiente para cada cenário e reduzir os custos finais com transparência.

artigo.texto: AbraCloud pede regulamentação acelerada do Redata para destravar investimentos em 2026 Associação propõe comprovação gradual de exigências, publicação de normas em etapas e financiamento do BNDES para expansão de infraestrutura A Associação Brasileira de Infraestrutura e Serviços Cloud (AbraCloud) defende que o governo federal adote um procedimento acelerado de habilitação ao Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), permitindo que empresas iniciem investimentos ainda em 2026, mesmo antes da conclusão de todas as etapas de comprovação dos compromissos previstos no programa. A proposta integra uma carta aberta encaminhada ao Poder Executivo, em setembro, na qual a associação apresenta três medidas para a implementação do regime: criação de um mecanismo transitório de habilitação, regulamentação em etapas e desenvolvimento de instrumentos de financiamento compatíveis com a expansão recorrente da capacidade computacional instalada no país. Assinado pelo presidente da AbraCloud, Roberto Bertó, o documento argumenta que a tributação de equipamentos importados e o custo do capital dificultam a competição entre empresas brasileiras de infraestrutura digital e fornecedores internacionais. Segundo a associação, a demora na implementação do Redata pode postergar investimentos em equipamentos de processamento, especialmente unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs), utilizadas em aplicações de inteligência artificial. Habilitação com comprovação em três e seis meses A primeira proposta é a criação do chamado Redata Fast Track, um mecanismo transitório que permitiria às empresas comprovar parte das obrigações em momentos posteriores à habilitação. Pelo modelo sugerido, a empresa demonstraria inicialmente o atendimento às condições legais necessárias para ingressar no regime e assumiria formalmente os compromissos exigidos. Determinados documentos e comprovações poderiam ser apresentados progressivamente, em marcos de três e seis meses, sob fiscalização. A associação ressalta que o mecanismo não representaria dispensa das obrigações legais nem autorização para descumprimento dos compromissos. Exigências anuais, operacionais ou vinculadas à efetiva utilização da infraestrutura continuariam sujeitas aos prazos correspondentes. A proposta busca evitar que procedimentos documentais impeçam o início de aquisições e instalações de equipamentos durante o período de regulamentação. Na avaliação da AbraCloud, o desenho administrativo poderá determinar se os efeitos do regime serão percebidos imediatamente ou apenas depois de alguns trimestres. Regulamentação poderia avançar em etapas A segunda proposta prevê a publicação gradual dos atos necessários à implementação do Redata. Nesse modelo, as normas indispensáveis para habilitar empresas e permitir o início das aquisições seriam editadas primeiro, sem depender da conclusão de todas as regulamentações complementares. A associação argumenta que o mercado de infraestrutura computacional está em formação e poderá exigir ajustes regulatórios conforme novos desafios de implementação sejam identificados. O objetivo é permitir que as primeiras operações ocorram enquanto o governo desenvolve regras adicionais para situações que não precisam estar resolvidas no momento da habilitação. A carta foi elaborada após a aprovação legislativa do regime, mas antes da sanção e da regulamentação mencionadas no próprio documento. BNDES é apontado como fonte de financiamento A terceira frente trata do financiamento da expansão da capacidade de processamento instalada no Brasil. A AbraCloud diferencia os investimentos em instalações físicas e infraestrutura elétrica dos desembolsos necessários para aquisição de GPUs. Segundo a carta, a ampliação da capacidade computacional pode exigir novas rodadas de investimento em intervalos de poucos meses, conforme a utilização dos equipamentos existentes aumenta. Esse ritmo, na avaliação da associação, demanda instrumentos financeiros diferentes dos modelos tradicionais de financiamento de infraestrutura. O documento propõe que o Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e outras instituições avaliem mecanismos de crédito compatíveis com ciclos recorrentes de expansão. Também sugere que as GPUs instaladas sejam consideradas na estruturação de garantias, levando em conta seu valor econômico e sua capacidade produtiva ao longo dos anos. A proposta não apresenta valores de financiamento, taxas de juros ou estimativas de recursos necessários. Processamento local é associado à autonomia tecnológica A carta relaciona a implementação do Redata à capacidade de empresas brasileiras operarem infraestrutura computacional no território nacional. O documento defende a instalação de GPUs e o desenvolvimento de capacidade local para treinamento e operação de modelos de inteligência artificial, reduzindo a dependência de processamento realizado no exterior. A AbraCloud também sustenta que o domínio técnico necessário para operar, modificar e manter essa infraestrutura deve integrar a estratégia de autonomia tecnológica. A associação afirma que a maior parte da inteligência artificial comercial consumida por brasileiros ainda é processada fora do país, mas não apresenta dados quantitativos para essa afirmação. O documento sugere que os ministérios acompanhem a evolução da capacidade de processamento instalada nacionalmente após a implementação do regime. As três propostas constituem recomendações da AbraCloud ao Poder Executivo. A carta não informa compromissos assumidos pelo governo nem decisões sobre a adoção do procedimento acelerado, da regulamentação em etapas ou dos mecanismos de financiamento. *Com assessoria de imprensa

artigo.texto: Wapakoneta shares information about potential data center development WAPAKONETA, Ohio (WLIO) - Wapakoneta officials are sharing information about early discussions regarding a potential data center development in the city’s industrial park. In a Facebook post, city officials said they have had early discussions with Colocation Technology Services, which is looking to locate a smaller data center in Wapakoneta. Officials emphasized that the city has NOT entered into negotiations with the developer. In 2024, Wapakoneta City Council designated data centers as a “conditional use,” requiring additional city review and approval before one could be established. The city also conducted a study with AEP to determine whether the power needs of a data center could be met. According to city officials, the study found that the necessary power could be supplied without additional infrastructure. “So, we have that information, which makes it somewhat possible from that standpoint. So, now we’re just kind of in the process of gathering, you know, what information that they have, you know, what kind of stuff they’re bringing, and, you know, I talked about it a little bit in the posting, but the they’re using a closed loop, and what does that look like, and how much water does that use, and you know, what is the wastewater situation look like. So, there’s just a lot of questions right now that we have out there. There’s some some answers that they’ve given, more that I think they plan to give. They’ve been very open about being, you know, transparent and providing whatever information that they can,” says Tyler Price, Wapakoneta Safety Services Director. The Wapakoneta Area Economic Development Group has also been in discussions with the developers about holding informational meetings for the public, both online and in person. However, no dates have been finalized. Facebook Post of the City of Wapakoneta City Administration would like to provide an update about the potential development of a data center in our community and where it currently stands. To start, the City has not entered into negotiations with the developer, Colocation Technology Services (CTS), approved any part of the project, or made any commitments to the development. CTS has also not submitted requests for annexation, conditional use approval, or other project-related approvals. All of the known information comes from discussions with WAEDC and preliminary questions the city has asked WAEDC and CTS. For a little context, The Wapakoneta Area Economic Development Council (WAEDC), a separate entity from the city, works with businesses interested in locating or expanding in our community. Over the past few years, WAEDC has received several inquiries about potential data center projects. Recognizing this growing interest, City Council passed legislation in 2024 making data centers a “conditional use,” requiring additional review and approval before one could locate here. City Administration also made it clear to WAEDC that any potential data center project should be discussed openly, allowing residents to learn about the proposal, ask questions, and share concerns before decisions are made. WAEDC agreed with this approach and with evaluating each project on its own merits. CTS approached WAEDC about the possibility of developing a smaller sized data center in the industrial park. During early conversations between WAEDC and CTS, they also agreed to open and transparent discussions with the public, as that was made clear to them when they submitted their request. The City has been aware of this potential project for a few months. However, much of that time was spent exploring preliminary questions and waiting for responses about electric service and whether existing infrastructure could support a facility requiring 50 megawatts of power. We believed it was important to determine whether the project was even feasible before considering a more detailed proposal. As part of that work, the City requested an initial feasibility study with American Electric Power (AEP). The results indicated that the facility could be served without improvements to AEP’s existing infrastructure. The proposed arrangement would establish a new connection directly to an AEP electric line rather than supplying power through the City’s existing electric distribution system. Based on our utility structure, CTS would also be considered a Delivery Service Customer, meaning it would purchase electricity through separate contracts with American Municipal Power (AMP), independent of the City’s existing power supply contracts. This arrangement applies to large electric customers with demands exceeding 10 megawatts and would keep the facility’s power purchasing separate from that of the City’s other customers. Regarding water usage, CTS has indicated it would use a closed-loop cooling system requiring approximately 5,000 to 10,000 gallons per day. For comparison, the EPA estimates an average person uses about 80 gallons daily. While this may sound significant, the City’s water treatment plant is designed to handle millions of gallons per day, currently treats more than a million gallons daily, and already serves customers with substantially higher water demands. Based on the estimates provided, this facility’s water usage would be well within the capacity of our existing system and is not expected to present a concern. CTS has also indicated that wastewater would primarily come from normal restroom use. Water from its cooling system would not be discharged into the City’s sewer system but would instead be periodically removed and properly disposed of off-site. The proposed location is within an existing industrial park, where CTS anticipates noise levels similar to other industrial operations. artigo.texto: O Ministério Público Federal (MPF) oficializou nesta quinta-feira (15) um acompanhamento estratégico sobre a implantação de um projeto de créditos de carbono na Reserva Extrativista Cazumbá-Iracema, no interior do Acre. A medida visa garantir que as comunidades tradicionais sejam ouvidas e que seus direitos sejam respeitados durante todo o processo de negociação. Por meio da Portaria nº 54/2026, assinada pelo procurador da República Luidgi Merlo Paiva dos Santos, o MPF criou um procedimento administrativo válido por 12 meses para monitorar o diálogo entre a população da reserva e a empresa Joias Ecológicas da Amazônia Desenvolvimento de Projetos Ltda. A iniciativa centra-se no princípio da consulta livre, prévia e informada, assegurando que os moradores da região tenham a palavra final sobre projetos que possam afetar seus territórios e modos de vida. Segundo a empresa, que formalizou o interesse por meio do Ofício nº 004/2026, já foram realizadas reuniões informativas nas comunidades, a convite da Associação dos Seringueiros do Seringal Cazumbá (ASSC). O próximo passo será uma assembleia comunitária, também com a presença convidada do MPF, para apresentação dos resultados dessa etapa inicial. A atuação do MPF está alinhada com a Convenção nº 169 da OIT, que garante o direito à consulta prévia dos povos interessados. Além disso, o processo segue a Lei nº 15.042/2024 — o novo marco regulatório do mercado de carbono — que traz avanços importantes: -Titularidade dos créditos: comunidades extrativistas são reconhecidas como detentoras originárias dos créditos gerados em seus territórios -Consentimento obrigatório: nenhum projeto pode avançar sem consulta e consentimento das comunidades -Repartição de benefícios: pelo menos 70% dos créditos de projetos REDD+ devem ficar com as comunidades -Indenização prevista: contratos devem prever compensação por eventuais danos coletivos -Custos do processo: todas as despesas com a consulta são de responsabilidade da empresa interessada A legislação permite o desenvolvimento de iniciativas desse tipo em unidades de conservação de uso sustentável, desde que compatíveis com seus planos de manejo. O acompanhamento do MPF garante que o diálogo ocorra de forma transparente, com respeito às tradições e aos direitos de quem vive e protege a floresta.
