artigo.texto: Americans who live near data centers—specifically, within a mile or so—have become more likely than others to vote for Democrats this cycle, a new YouGov/Economist survey suggests. Since May alone, the share of people living near data centers who plan to vote Democratic has risen from 54 percent to 61 percent, according to the poll, released October 12. Nationwide, voter preferences have shifted too, but by a much smaller margin: from 53 percent to 55 percent. Over the past year, developers have secured land leases and begun construction on new “hyperscale” data centers at a dizzying rate—often operating too fast to, or simply choosing not to, involve nearby communities much in the zoning process. This dynamic is mostly playing out in rural and suburban areas, where, across the political spectrum, nobody seems to want to play host to a neighborhood data center. It’s easy to see why. Data centers need significant space, energy and water to operate, and they don’t provide many jobs relative to the investment they require. And they’re often unpleasant neighbors: their cooling systems can be noisy, and a growing number include onsite gas turbines that belch black smoke into the air. Town councils and zoning commissions across the country are unsurprisingly finding themselves the sites of anti-data-center protest. Data Center Opposition Report, a recently launched website tracking opposition to data center development across the country, counts at least 268 local opposition groups across 37 states, which it says are organizing more than 300,000 people. Planned data center projects worth more than $260 billion have already been canceled in 2026, per the climate outlet Heatmap. And politicians are paying attention: candidates from both parties are incorporating anti-data-center populism into their campaign promises. Donald Trump has bucked that trend, stating that towns that say no to data centers will be “backwards and poor,” and that Americans should let data centers “reign.” This, it seems, has not been enough to convince those communities, most of which historically lean Republican. 75 percent of data centers under construction, and 80 percent of data centers in the planning stage, are in red states, according to data shared with CBS by Cleanview Research, a company tracking data center development. Some Republicans are flipping on data centers. One Alabama gubernatorial hopeful who called data center fears “bullcrap” in July, for example, is now running on a strict regulatory platform. But the GOP overall has not been able to produce coherent messaging on data centers as a quality of life issue. The new poll is one of several to suggest that upcoming midterm election results may reflect that. As Ohio anti–data center activist Nick Owens recently told News 5 Cleveland, “The only way they’re going to wake up, whether it’s either party, is on November 3. People who are silent to the data center issue will find out, but frankly, both parties are complicit.”

artigo.texto: TRENTON, Ohio — Signs calling for voters to approve Issue 17, a data center ban in Trenton, were scattered across the parking lot of Edgewood Middle School Thursday as Amazon Web Services representatives welcomed people inside for an open house. The auditorium was lined with Amazon displays all about data centers, and the plan for an 18-building, 600-acre data center proposal along Wayne Madison Road just outside of Trenton featured prominently around the room. AWS Economic Development Manager John Werkman said the company had flown experts in from all over the country to talk with people living in this region, hear their concerns, and provide education where necessary. "We were able to build data centers for a long time without anybody kind of knowing or saying anything about it, right? We're in a different paradigm now. We understand that. Our company's leadership understands that, which is why we're changing," Werkman said. WATCH: We ask Amazon reps your questions at data center open house Werkman acknowledged the effort to ban data centers in Trenton and, when we asked what he thought of the animosity people feel, told us part of their mission was to show how their projects are different than developments from other tech companies. "I attribute that to a lot of fear and a lot of misunderstanding," he said. Amy Hubert walked into the auditorium wearing a bright white shirt with "ISSUE 17 VOTE YES" emblazoned across the front. Knowing she was advocating for a data center ban, we asked why she came to the open house. "I came to hear what AWS had to say," Hubert said. She told us she is a hard no on data centers over concerns about power consumption, land use, water use, potential contamination, and more. She said, for example, if someone could prove to her that water use was lower than she expected, it would go a long way to swaying her opinion. So, we talked to AWS Director of Power and Water Brandon Oyer. "We're only using water for about 3% of the year in this area," he said. "97% of the year, we're only going to use air. We'll take giant fans and we'll blow them across the servers to cool the servers," he said. Like many in the crowd, Hubert wasn't quick to take Oyer's answer at face value. "Ohio has bipolar weather, so 80s are nothing in November, even. There's going to be days that it's extremely hot, especially during summer months. So, 3%? I find that hard to believe," she said. Oyer referenced a Northern Indiana data center using water 2% to 3% of the year in a sustainability article from Amazon in June 2026. Hubert told us she would be checking meteorological data to see if the comparisons are appropriate. Werkman said the data center open house was part of an increased transparency push at Amazon, including turning away from making government officials they work with in the early stages of data center projects sign non-disclosure agreements. "We really are trying to be more transparent about what we're doing and at the same time allowing the folks that we work with locally to actually talk about what we're talking about," he said. Voters will go to the polls to either pass or reject the data center ban on Nov. 3.

artigo.texto: The Louisiana Tax Commissionâs approval of a motion establishing average economic lives for data center equipment and infrastructure marks a step toward statewide property tax valuation guidelines for this type of technology. The test of good policy is whether the guidelines reasonably reflect equipment value, giving taxpayers and local governments a predictable basis for assessments while accounting for advances in technology. The motion, approved at the LTCâs Sept. 23 tentative adoption proceeding, establishes three equipment categories with different average economic lives. Economic life refers to how long equipment is expected to remain economically useful, rather than simply how long it can operate. The motion would divide data center equipment into: - Computer, networking, and storage equipment and electronic controls, with a five-year average economic life - Power, cooling, and fixtures, with a 12-year life - Electrical infrastructure, with a 15-year life The LTC also approved a notation recognizing data centers as a new property category beginning in 2027 and stating that the provisions should apply until sufficient additional operational or market data becomes available to support revisions. Before the motion was approved, the Louisiana Association of Business and Industry and Advantous Consulting proposed three-year economic lives for servers, networking equipment, and storage systems, and eight-year lives for power and climate-control infrastructure. The proposal emphasized how advances in technology can reduce equipment value and how the economic life of supporting infrastructure may depend on the computer equipment it serves. They also proposed applying percent-good factors without cost indices. Percent-good factors estimate the percentage of equipmentâs value remaining as it ages. Cost indices adjust acquisition costs for changes in price levels. Separately, the West Feliciana Parish assessor requested that the LTC staff work with the Louisianaâs Assessorsâ Association to develop data center guidelines. The LTC subsequently asked industry representatives and assessors to form a working group to collaborate on a proposal for the Sept. 23 tentative adoption hearing. LAA filed a rebuttal to put its position in the record while the working group was being organized. It opposed LABIâs broad equipment categories and shorter economic lives, recommending more detailed classifications with lives ranging from five to 25 years. LAA also opposed eliminating cost indices and questioned reducing equipment value based on anticipated advances in technology. The approved motionâs five-year life for computer, networking, and storage equipment is consistent with LAAâs recommendation, but the motion uses different classifications and lives for supporting infrastructure. The proposal, rebuttal, and subsequent approval of the motion from the LTC illustrate the challenges of valuing data center equipment and infrastructure and, more broadly, property affected by rapidly evolving technology. The selected economic lives affect equipment valuations and property tax burdens. Longer lives generally result in higher valuations for equipment of the same age and cost and, all else equal, higher property tax burdens than shorter lives. These lives guide valuation rather than require equipment to be written down to zero. Existing LTC rules also allow a different economic life or other valuation adjustments when supported by evidence. Determining economic life can be challenging because itâs hard to discern how long property remains economically useful, rather than simply how long it can operate. For example, servers and artificial intelligence accelerators may remain operational, but newer technology may make them less competitive and reduce their market value. Supporting infrastructure presents additional challenges. Power and cooling systems may remain operational for many years, but their economic usefulness can depend on the technology they support. Changes in computing requirements or facility design may require substantial modifications or limit alternative uses. However, systems that can support newer computing equipment without substantial modifications may remain useful beyond the life of the original servers. Economic lives are also only one component of valuation. The disagreement over cost indices concerns whether adjusting acquisition costs for price changes accurately reflects equipment value when newer technology may reduce that value. Existing LTC rules generally apply both cost indices and percent-good factors: Acquisition costs are adjusted for price changes, then reduced to account for depreciation. The rules also allow separate adjustments for obsolescence, or losses in value caused by factors such as outdated technology or changes in economic conditions, when supported by evidence. The approved data center motion doesnât include the proposed exclusion of cost indices. The data center schedule would extend an existing valuation practice to a new equipment category. Louisiana already publishes economic lives and valuation factors for numerous categories of business personal property. Other states, such as Alabama, also use depreciation schedules for business equipment. A statewide schedule can be sound tax policy if its classifications and economic lives reasonably reflect market value. Consistent guidelines can improve predictability, help reduce valuation disputes, and account for losses in value as technology advances. But lives that are too long can overstate value and increase taxpayersâ burdens, while those that are too short can undervalue equipment and reduce the local tax base. Revisiting the guidelines as more data becomes available would help address both risks. artigo.texto: BYD Atto 8 Electric SUV Revealed at Paris Motor Show, Claims 653km Range The flagship SUV gets a 115kWh Blade battery and BYD's Flash Charging technology, which can charge the battery from 10 to 97% in nine minutes. BYD has revealed the all-electric Atto 8 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, adding a battery-powered option to its international flagship SUV range. The seven-seat model introduces the company's Flash Charging technology in Europe and will be offered in rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive versions. Sales are scheduled to begin in European markets in the first quarter of 2027, while BYD has not confirmed plans for an India launch at this stage. Also Read: BYD Atto 3 Gets New Atlantis Gray Colour Option in India BYD Atto 8: Battery & Range The Atto 8 uses a 115kWh second-generation Blade battery. The Design RWD variant has a claimed WLTP range of up to 653km, while the Excellence AWD version offers a range of up to 602km. The rear-wheel-drive model uses a single electric motor mounted on the rear axle, producing 456bhp and 365Nm of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in a claimed 8 seconds. The Excellence AWD gets an additional electric motor on the front axle. Its combined output stands at 753bhp and 775Nm of torque, allowing it to complete the 0-100 km/h sprint in 4.6 seconds. BYD Atto 8: Flash Charging The electric SUV is the first BYD model in Europe to feature the company's Flash Charging technology. According to BYD, the system can charge the battery from 10 to 70% in 5 minutes and from 10 to 97% in 9 minutes. The company also claims that charging from 20 to 97% takes 12 minutes in temperatures as low as -30 degrees Celsius. However, these charging speeds require compatible high-output chargers. BYD plans to install 3,000 Flash Charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027. This charging network is expected to support the rollout of the technology alongside the Atto 8 and other compatible models. BYD Atto 8: Design The Atto 8 features slim LED daytime running lights integrated with its matrix LED headlamps. At the rear, the tail-lamps have an infinity-knot design, with an illuminated BYD logo positioned between them. The roof-mounted spoiler and sculpted body panels complete the exterior design. The SUV offers seating for seven occupants. The first two rows get heated, ventilated, and massage functions, while the cabin focuses on comfort and space for passengers. BYD will introduce the Atto 8 in European markets in the first quarter of 2027. It will sit at the top of the company's SUV range and be available with rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive configurations. The Atto 8 is already available internationally as a plug-in hybrid in certain markets, and the Paris Motor Show appearance marks the debut of its all-electric version. BYD has yet to announce its prices for Europe.

artigo.texto: Changan and CATL target 75 GWh while Golden Bell solid-state batteries remain in validation Changan and CATL are continuing to expand joint battery production toward 75 GWh a year. An additional 25 GWh plant is due to start operating in the second half of 2027 and reach design output within the following three years. At the same time, the companies are cooperating on next-generation battery technologies. The claimed range of more than 1,500 km, however, still refers to Changan’s developing solid-state technology rather than a production EV. Changan reconfirmed these directions on October 12 through the Shenzhen Stock Exchange investor-interaction platform. The total 75 GWh capacity had already appeared in the manufacturer’s 2025 annual report. Changan and CATL also signed a five-year memorandum in January 2026 to deepen strategic cooperation, so the latest statement develops an existing program rather than announcing a sudden new project. The expansion is tied to the CATL-Changan joint venture established in 2023. The new production project adds another 25 GWh a year and is expected to require about 5.5 billion yuan of investment. The site will cover about 1,000 mu, or roughly 667,000 square metres. Its batteries are intended for Avatr, Deepal and Nevo EVs. Once full capacity is reached, annual output value is expected to be around 10 billion yuan. A separate track is Changan’s solid-state battery program. The company aims to raise cell energy density to 400 Wh/kg and says this could potentially enable more than 1,500 km of EV range. The specific vehicle, battery size and test cycle have not been disclosed. Changan’s annual report also says a 400 Wh/kg solid-state prototype cell was validated with Talent New Energy, so that figure should not be directly attributed to the CATL joint venture. Within the Golden Bell battery family, Changan has also cited a life of more than 5,000 cycles, little noticeable performance degradation over as much as 600,000 km, and 6C charging that can raise state of charge from 30% to 80% in about nine minutes. Available material does not establish that all of those figures belong to the same 400 Wh/kg solid-state cell. Vehicle validation of Changan solid-state batteries is scheduled for 2026, with gradual series introduction from 2027. The current figures should therefore be treated as targets for a developing technology rather than the final specification of a battery already in mass production. At the same time, Changan and CATL’s sodium-ion cooperation has already reached the production-vehicle stage. In February 2026 the partners presented what they described as the first mass-production passenger car using CATL Naxtra batteries. CATL quotes energy density of up to 175 Wh/kg, more than 400 km of range and strong low-temperature performance for the technology. The two tracks should therefore not be conflated. The CATL-Changan expansion to 75 GWh has defined industrial projects and timelines, while the 400 Wh/kg solid-state technology is still moving through validation and preparation for series use. The 75 GWh joint-production figure does not mean all of that capacity will be devoted to solid-state batteries. artigo.texto: Slovenia’s Velenje coal mine is one of the sites within international project GeoSolar for exploring the possibility of converting coal mines into underground thermal energy storage facilities. The idea is to store solar energy collected during the summer in mines and use it for district heating in winter. An increasing number of coal mines in Europe are reaching the end of their operational lives. In this context, the issues of just transition and sustainably reusing the mining infrastructure are becoming increasingly important. The Velenje coal mine, the last one in Slovenia, is also shutting down in the coming years. It is operated by state-owned firm Premogovnik Velenje. The mine supplies lignite to coal power plant Termoelektrarna Šoštanj (TEŠ), currently the main district heating source in the Šalek valley, where preparations are underway to switch to alternative energy sources. How coal mines could store thermal energy The GeoSolar project could offer a solution for giving coal mines a new lease of life. European coal mines contain millions of cubic meters of mine water, with temperatures ranging from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. Such a level is insufficient for direct use in district heating, but coal mines are often located near cities and towns with high seasonal heat demand, making them suitable for repurposing. The project envisages installing solar thermal systems on rehabilitated mining land to heat mine water to temperatures of 70 to 90 degrees Celsius during the summer. In winter, the hot water would be pumped to the surface and used for district heating. The cooled water would then be returned to the underground system to continue the cycle. Feasibility of the solution is being assessed in Slovenia and Poland The feasibility of applying this solution is being assessed at coal mines Velenje in Slovenia and Bolesław Śmiały in Poland. The project is coordinated by the Utrecht University and involves other partners from the Netherlands, Slovenia and Poland. It began in 2025 and is scheduled to run for 42 months. It is co-funded by the European Union’s Research Fund for Coal and Steel (RFCS). Project partners met in Velenje on October 5 to present their findings so far on the feasibility of the proposed solutions and agree on criteria for further research. In the next phase, they will develop more detailed models and compare the solutions based on the characteristics of the two mines.

artigo.texto: By — Jessica Hill, Associated Press Jessica Hill, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ai-data-centers-are-coming-for-federal-land-and-roiling-nevada-governors-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AI data centers are coming for federal land and roiling Nevada governor's race Politics Oct 13, 2026 2:20 PM EDT BOULDER CITY, Nev. (AP) — Janelle Sorenson loves the clear night skies in Boulder City, less than an hour's drive from the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. It's a small, quiet town, and she thinks an artificial intelligence data center would ruin the community and scar the desert landscape. So over the summer, she joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country. But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off. "Not only did we not get to decide anything or have a say," Sorenson said, "we were just really kept in the dark." The Townsite data center was the first in the country to be approved on federal public land, though construction is stalled after a judge ruled that the government couldn't use an old environmental review from when the project was intended to be a solar farm. Tech companies are eager for vast tracts to build data centers that can be as large as 70 football fields, and Townsite could set a precedent for similar projects on federal property with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. President Donald Trump has been a steadfast supporter of the artificial intelligence industry, which he views as a source of economic growth and part of a global competition with China. However, data centers have been unpopular in many communities as voters worry about higher electricity bills, declining water supplies and other impacts. In Nevada, where 80% of the land is owned by the federal government, Townsite and other projects have become a dominant issue in the battleground state's closely watched governor's race. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, one of his party's most vulnerable incumbents, doesn't outright oppose building data centers on public lands, as long as they have community support. He recently signed an agreement with Trump's Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands. Democratic nominee Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, has pledged to oppose data centers on public lands, saying affordable housing should be the priority. Both say the projects, whether on public or private land, must follow state rules, such as requiring data centers to cover their own energy costs and protecting water supplies, or they would lose eligibility for state tax abatements. Voters across the political spectrum unite against data centers Sorenson, the Boulder City resident, considers herself to be liberal, but she said her conservative neighbors are on the same page as she is. "We're all aligned on this," she said. Autumn McGrath-Shook, who lives in the same town, said she recently left the Republican Party and registered with the Green Party over data centers, though she still identifies as conservative. Worried about the environmental impact on wildlife, she joined forces with "these crazy libs" to oppose the project. Data centers have quickly become a "catalyzing issue" in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. Some state leaders who were previously supportive of data centers have rushed to respond. For example, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center approvals until audits are completed, and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order removing data center proposals from a fast-track permitting process and requiring them to receive local approval before seeking state approval. READ MORE: Data center controversies have transformed midterms. Here's where different groups stand In August, Ford announced his plan to pause new tax abatements for data centers while an audit is conducted to see if the projects have fulfilled promises about producing tax revenue and economic benefits. In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on data centers and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools. The two have successfully "muddied the waters" on their data center positions, Damore said. Lombardo criticized Ford for co-sponsoring 2015 legislation that created the state's tax abatement program for data centers, a measure that received bipartisan support. Ford criticized Lombardo for giving more than $200 million in tax breaks to data centers, which is connected to the legislation that Ford co-sponsored. Ford told The Associated Press that he would use "every tool" at his disposal to prevent data centers from skirting state guardrails, including withholding tax abatements and pursuing litigation. Lombardo, whose campaign declined to make him available for an interview, has a similar pitch. His office said he would not hesitate to confront the federal government to advocate for Nevadans. But that's not good enough for McGrath-Shook, who is on the fence in the governor's race. She thinks Ford is soft on crime, but she views Lombardo as more pro-data centers. "I would much rather vote for Lombardo than Aaron Ford in a normal world," she said. "But with the looming data centers, it really changes the landscape — and literally." artigo.texto: A Corning começou a produzir, este ano, cabos e conectores ópticos para data centers no Brasil, por meio de parceiros qualificados no estado de São Paulo. A operação busca reduzir os prazos de entrega, que chegavam a aproximadamente 40 dias quando os produtos dependiam de importações. A empresa também prepara a oferta de cabos com 288 fibras ópticas para atender às necessidades de conexão interna dos centros de dados. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Vertiv reforça equipe no Brasil para atender expansão de data centers A movimentação ocorre no momento em que o mercado é impulsionado pela expansão dos data centers e pela necessidade de infraestrutura para aplicações de inteligência artificial (IA). Para a Corning, o crescimento desse segmento abre oportunidades para soluções com maior densidade de fibras, capazes de acomodar um número crescente de conexões em espaços limitados. “Na verdade, não é uma aposta. É concreto. Todos os operadores já estão construindo data centers. Estão com projetos em andamento e planos de expandir mais ainda, com outros data centers por vir”, diz Antônio Augusto B. Macedo, gerente de produto de Data Center para a América Latina na Corning Segundo ele, a produção local atende à demanda atual do mercado brasileiro, concentrada principalmente em cabos de até 144 fibras. A companhia não informou o volume fabricado no país nem apresentou dados sobre a capacidade produtiva. Produção local reduz prazos de entrega Até recentemente, o fornecimento dos produtos dependia de importações, com prazos de entrega que chegavam a cerca de 40 dias. Com a estruturação da produção local em 2026, a Corning passou a contar com parceiros no estado de São Paulo para fabricar cabos e conectores ópticos de acordo com os padrões de qualidade da companhia. “Até o ano passado, mais ou menos, a gente tinha tudo a importar, em prazo de 40 dias. Agora, a gente tem uma questão de produção local”, diz o executivo. A fabricação por meio de parceiros qualificados permite à empresa atender às necessidades do mercado brasileiro sem depender exclusivamente do fornecimento externo. Macedo, no entanto, não detalhou a capacidade instalada da operação, os volumes produzidos ou as metas de crescimento para o mercado local. A oferta atual está concentrada em cabos de até 144 fibras ópticas, utilizados principalmente nas conexões internas dos data centers. A empresa prepara a produção para atender também à demanda por cabos de 288 fibras, acompanhando a necessidade de maior densidade nas instalações. Nas conexões externas, que interligam diferentes data centers, a quantidade de fibras pode ser ainda maior. Macedo cita cabos com 864, 1.728 e até 3.456 fibras, conforme a aplicação. Data centers de IA exigem mais conexões ópticas A expansão da inteligência artificial está mudando os requisitos de conectividade dos data centers. Segundo Macedo, instalações destinadas a essas aplicações podem demandar até dez vezes mais fibras do que centros de dados convencionais. O executivo cita a evolução do número de fibras que chegam a um rack: de aproximadamente 100 em configurações anteriores para quase 10 mil em determinados modelos atuais. Em projeções para os próximos dois anos, esse número poderá alcançar 64 mil fibras por rack, dependendo do modelo. O aumento da densidade exige soluções que acomodem mais conexões no mesmo espaço físico. Isso envolve o desenvolvimento de cabos e conectores menores e de tecnologias capazes de ampliar a capacidade de transmissão. Uma das soluções apresentadas pela Corning é a fibra multicore, que reúne quatro núcleos de transmissão em uma mesma fibra. De acordo com Macedo, a tecnologia permite quadruplicar a capacidade de transmissão por fibra em comparação com uma fibra convencional de núcleo único, utilizando cabos e conectores existentes. O lançamento comercial estava previsto para o fim de 2026. Na entrevista, o executivo afirmou que a empresa já havia firmado contratos com alguns clientes, mas ainda não tinha lançado oficialmente a tecnologia. Os primeiros usuários esperados são operadores que constroem grandes data centers voltados à inteligência artificial. No Brasil, a adoção dependerá da evolução dos projetos e dos requisitos de densidade de cada instalação. A Corning não informou se a fibra multicore será fabricada localmente. A produção brasileira mencionada pelo executivo refere-se a cabos e conectores ópticos, enquanto a nova tecnologia ainda estava em fase anterior ao lançamento comercial. Redata pode estimular novos investimentos A Corning avalia que o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) poderá estimular novos projetos no Brasil. Macedo ressalta, porém, que a demanda por infraestrutura não depende exclusivamente da iniciativa governamental e já é sustentada pela digitalização da economia. “Internet banking, redes sociais, streaming de vídeo e games requerem transmissão de dados. Por conta disso, os data centers precisam estar próximos dos consumidores”, afirma. Na avaliação do executivo, a redução de custos tributários poderá tornar o país mais atrativo para empresas interessadas em construir centros de dados. Entre as possibilidades está a instalação de estruturas destinadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, que concentram grande capacidade de processamento. Macedo diferencia esses ambientes dos data centers voltados a aplicações que exigem baixa latência. No treinamento de modelos de IA, explica, as instalações podem ser construídas em locais nos quais a disponibilidade e o custo da energia sejam fatores determinantes. O executivo considera que o Brasil reúne condições para receber esses projetos, embora avalie que os data centers de inteligência artificial previstos para o país ainda não devam alcançar imediatamente a escala de algumas instalações em construção nos Estados Unidos. artigo.texto: NIL elabora modelo de contrato de financiamento para apoiar projetos de redução de emissões Natural Investment Lab desenvolve modelo de contrato para facilitar financiamento de projetos de carbono no Brasil Apontada como um dos principais entraves para que projetos de reflorestamento e de Redução das Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal (Redd+) consigam acessar linhas de financiamento, a modelagem dos contratos passará a ter um padrão, que está em desenvolvimento pelo Natural Investment Lab (NIL). A minuta desse contrato modelo foi apresentada publicamente durante a Semana do Clima que aconteceu recentemente em Nova York e, para elaborá-la, o NIL conversou com 25 importantes instituições. Entre elas, Itaú BBA, Regia Capital, Systemica, Petrobras e Regreen. No próximo passo, o rascunho do contrato modelo será colocado em audiência pública e deve ganhar destaque durante a COP31, que acontecerá entre os dias 9 e 20 de novembro na Turquia. A meta é concluir o trabalho até o final deste ano. O NIL aposta no processo de amadurecimento desse mercado, que já vem durando mais de 20 anos e que deverá elevar o carbono ao status de commodity, com possibilidade de ser negociado internacionalmente "A ideia é preparar os desenvolvedores dos projetos de produção de carbono para que consigam lidar com todas as exigências com as quais vão se deparar quando tentarem acessar recursos", explica Fabiana Philipi, gerente de projetos da Climate Venture, organização que lidera o NIL. Ela pondera, no entanto, que o documento de referência poderá ajudar os outros players desse mercado, como os compradores e financiadores do mercado de carbono. Segundo Philipi, as propostas de produção de carbono bem elaboradas têm forte demanda e o objetivo é ajudar desenvolvedores de todos os portes, desde empresas já consagradas como Re.Green e Mombak, até aquelas que estão dando os primeiros passos. As maiores compradoras dos créditos de carbono brasileiros, atualmente, são as big techs, principalmente a Microsoft. A minuta apresentada em Nova York refere-se a contratos offtake - compra mínima garantida - que são acordos jurídicos firmados entre comprador e vendedor de uma mercadoria, antes dela entrar em produção. O documento apresenta cláusulas referentes à estrutura comercial, como preço, pagamento e financiamento, garantias, recebíveis e financiadores, ciclo de vida dos créditos, entrega e titularidade, falha de entrega, entre outros O NIL é um laboratório de investimentos criado a partir de uma iniciativa que reúne o Banco do Brasil, o Instituto Itaúsa, o Instituto Clima e Sociedade (iCS) e a internacional Gfanz. O seu objetivo é atrair e estruturar financiamentos, além de promover inovação financeira, para ampliar a chamada economia de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN).

artigo.texto: Drones ucranianos atingem maior centro de dados da Rússia em meio à corrida por IA Instalação do Sberbank pode abrigar o supercomputador mais potente do país; ataques anteriores atingiram estruturas de concorrente Drones ucranianos atingiram nesta quarta-feira, 14, o maior centro de dados da Rússia, pertencente ao banco estatal Sberbank. O ataque ocorre em meio à disputa de Moscou para reduzir a distância tecnológica em relação aos Estados Unidos e à China no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial (IA). Na semana passada, outras três ofensivas tiveram como alvo centros de dados da Yandex, uma das principais empresas de tecnologia russas. O primeiro vice-presidente executivo do Sberbank, Alexander Vedyakhin, confirmou o ataque à instalação localizada em Balakovo, mas afirmou que os serviços da instituição continuavam funcionando normalmente. Segundo a agência estatal russa RIA Novosti, o complexo deverá abrigar o maior supercomputador do país, com previsão de entrar em operação em 2027. Na quarta-feira, o presidente Vladimir Putin realizou uma reunião não anunciada com autoridades sobre segurança da informação, da qual participou o presidente-executivo do Sberbank, German Gref. O Kremlin negou, porém, que o encontro estivesse relacionado aos ataques. Os supercomputadores são essenciais para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial, e eventuais danos às instalações podem comprometer o avanço do setor russo. Nem o Sberbank nem a Yandex informaram se os equipamentos foram afetados pelas ofensivas. Corrida tecnológica O Sberbank e a Yandex são os principais desenvolvedores de inteligência artificial da Rússia. No mercado doméstico, as empresas disputam espaço com seus respectivos modelos, GigaChat e YandexGPT. Apesar dos investimentos, estimativas do próprio Sberbank indicam que as companhias estão até nove meses atrás das líderes americanas e chinesas. Parte da defasagem é atribuída às sanções ocidentais, que dificultam o acesso russo a componentes avançados. Em setembro, Gref apontou a escassez de unidades modernas de processamento gráfico, conhecidas como GPUs, como um dos principais obstáculos ao desenvolvimento da tecnologia no país. O Sberbank negocia a compra de chips de fabricantes chineses para contornar as restrições, mas enfrenta outro entrave: a dependência de tecnologias da americana Nvidia. Sua plataforma CUDA, usada para programar e operar chips em tarefas de inteligência artificial, tornou-se um padrão do setor. Segundo o especialista em tecnologia da informação Mikhail Klimarev, as sanções também dificultam a reposição de equipamentos danificados. Os componentes ainda chegam à Rússia por rotas indiretas, mas a aquisição é mais cara e depende de intermediários dispostos a correr riscos para contornar as restrições comerciais. A Ucrânia afirma que suas ofensivas respondem aos ataques russos contra infraestruturas ucranianas. Desde o início da guerra, os dois países têm mirado instalações de energia, refinarias, portos e empresas de comércio eletrônico do adversário. Diante da ameaça, o Ministério do Desenvolvimento Digital da Rússia informou nesta semana que negocia com os militares medidas para reforçar a segurança dos centros de dados. Parlamentares também defenderam a transferência de equipamentos para instalações subterrâneas. A proposta ganhou apoio de Valery Yermakov, vice-presidente da estatal Rostelecom, outra grande operadora russa de centros de dados. Em uma conferência em Moscou, ele defendeu a criação de uma espécie de “cofre de dados para o apocalipse”, capaz de proteger equipamentos essenciais contra ataques.

artigo.texto: Richardson Electronics works with ComEd on battery energy storage system Richardson Electronics is partnering with ComEd to expand manufacturing of battery energy storage systems in Illinois and install its first onsite battery energy storage system demonstration project. Richardson, based in La Fox, is building the largest commercial battery storage system in Illinois. As part of this, Richardson is installing a 5-MWh research and development demonstration project, supported through the ComEd interconnection process. The planned expansion will help scale the development and distribution of these products. “For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” ComEd President and CEO Gil Quiniones said. “ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.” This initiative is a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions that strengthen grid reliability, support renewable energy integration, and store energy for use during periods of high demand. “Richardson Electronics has a long history of solving complex power and energy challenges through innovation and U.S.-based manufacturing,” Greg Peloquin, executive vice president and general manager of Power & Microwave Technologies and Green Energy Solutions groups, said. “Our advanced energy storage solutions will help customers manage energy more efficiently while supporting a more reliable and resilient grid. We value ComEd’s collaboration in bringing this onsite demonstration project to life.” The project is supported by the Reimagining Energy and Vehicles in Illinois, or REV Illinois, program. REV is helping Richardson Electronics strengthen its La Fox operations, advance energy technology manufacturing and support continued economic growth in Illinois. “As demand for reliable and affordable energy increases, Illinois has an opportunity not only to deploy new technologies, but to manufacture them,” Illinois Economic Development Corporation President and CEO Christy George said. “Richardson Electronics’ expansion demonstrates how Illinois’ manufacturing expertise can drive growth in emerging industries like battery storage while helping strengthen the energy infrastructure that supports our economy.” Battery energy storage systems can charge when electricity is available and discharge when it is needed. This helps customers manage energy use and supports a more flexible electric system. ComEd is supporting the project through its customer interconnection process and engineering studies. The company’s work includes helping prepare the site for the demonstration system and guiding Richardson through any potential system upgrade needs. Projects like these are also eligible to apply for ComEd’s Distributed Generation Rebate Program, which recently hit a $350 million milestone. ComEd is a unit of Chicago-based Exelon Corporation. ComEd provides power to more than 4.2 million customers across northern Illinois.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Grécia propõe regra para novos data centers usarem 60% de energia renovável Publicado 15/10/2026 • 10:00 | Atualizado há 20 horas KEY POINTS Foto: Unsplash A Grécia busca limitar o impacto dos novos data centers sobre a rede elétrica. Uma proposta do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Energia prevê que essas instalações obtenham pelo menos 60% da eletricidade consumida por ano de fontes renováveis. O governo também pretende exigir mais garantias financeiras das empresas e cobrar dos investidores os custos das conexões à rede. As medidas fazem parte de um projeto de lei que busca organizar a expansão do setor no país. Mesmo com o avanço dos data centers, diversos países correm para evitar que a infraestrutura se torne um problema elétrico. Leia também: Capital Sustentável: Choque da energia freia economia global enquanto IA sustenta investimentos, avalia Carlo Pereira De acordo com a proposta do governo grego, os novos data centers precisarão atingir a meta de 60% de energia renovável no consumo anual de eletricidade. A regra busca estabelecer critérios para a expansão dessas instalações, que demandam grandes quantidades de energia. O projeto também prevê que as empresas arquem com os custos de conexão à rede elétrica e das obras necessárias para reforçar o sistema quando essas mudanças envolverem diretamente a instalação dos data centers. De acordo com a Enerdata, o governo pretende exigir uma garantia financeira de 200 mil euros (R$ 1,1 milhão) por megawatt de capacidade planejada. A medida busca frear empresas que reservam espaço na rede elétrica sem apresentar projetos avançados. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A proposta também estabelece critérios mais rigorosos de investimento e preparação ambiental antes da emissão da autorização final para conexão à rede. A discussão acontece em meio ao aumento do interesse pelo setor. Leia também: Alemanha prepara leilão de energia eólica offshore com capacidade de 4 GW O projeto do governo da Grécia também prevê a criação de um Fundo de Descarbonização das Ilhas, com 2,3 bilhões de euros (R$ 13 bilhões) para apoiar iniciativas que reduzam o uso de petróleo na geração de eletricidade nas ilhas gregas. Entre os investimentos previstos estão projetos de energia renovável e sistemas de armazenamento de eletricidade. A iniciativa busca diminuir a dependência dos combustíveis fósseis nessas regiões. Além disso, o governo grego abriu uma consulta pública sobre o projeto, que envolve a geração de energia para data centers, até 24 de outubro de 2026. artigo.texto: Democrat Jamie Davis and Republican U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, the two candidates vying for Louisiana’s open U.S. Senate seat, are taking different approaches to addressing heightened public concerns about AI and the data centers that power the technology. Davis, whose odds of winning the heavily Republican state in November are slim, has sought to draw a sharp contrast on the issue by releasing an aggressive, detailed agenda to regulate AI companies that includes a moratorium on new data centers. Letlow, whose trades in tech company stock have drawn scrutiny, has been less specific – but she says her approach would balance economic development with protecting the public and ensuring residents don’t have to pay for data centers’ power needs. In a statement, Davis said he would support liability for AI companies that deploy dangerous technologies and fight to ensure AI isn’t used in autonomous weapons systems. He also said he would back legislation mandating safety reviews of AI models before their release and requiring those models to include “kill switches” in case they need to be shut down. “‘Self-policing’ by these massive AI companies isn’t going to cut it,” Davis said. “Congress has to step in.” Letlow’s campaign did not answer specific questions about whether Letlow would support requiring AI models to have kill switches, liability for AI companies or limiting the use of AI in autonomous weapons. Instead, the campaign released a general statement about Letlow’s stance on AI. “When it comes to artificial intelligence, Julia believes we must protect Americans, safeguard our national security, and ensure the United States remains the global leader in technological innovation,” the statement said. “She supports a thoughtful approach that addresses legitimate risks without imposing unnecessary regulations that put American businesses and workers at a disadvantage.” Letlow’s campaign also noted the congresswoman supports a bill that would require state utility regulators to consider adopting a standard under which data centers would pay the full cost of the power they need to operate. “Julia believes Louisiana has an opportunity to lead in the development of new technologies that bring investment, create good-paying jobs, and strengthen our economy,” her campaign said. “At the same time, that growth must be done responsibly, with transparency, community input, and protections to ensure Louisiana families and small businesses aren't left footing the bill for new infrastructure.” A growing national issue The Louisiana race is an example of how AI and data centers are shaping mid-term elections across the country, which will determine which party controls Congress. Nationally, Democrats have been pressing Republicans on the issue, and polls show data centers are unpopular among members of both parties. Fears of AI-driven cyberattacks and recent high-profile instances of AI models breaking out of their controls have also caused alarm. President Donald Trump, who has a close relationship with tech titans like Mark Zuckerberg, has opposed mandatory restrictions on the technology, arguing such limitations would hinder the U.S. in the AI race against China. Some AI founders have celebrated Trump’s approach, which they expect will increase profits. But in recent months, tech leaders have also called for an AI development slowdown amid concerns that AI could break out of human controls and wreak havoc on power grids, financial institutions and transportation systems. Researchers and experts say that possibility is becoming stronger; last month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned rogue AI bots could take over the internet within a year. Skeptics say that even when AI agents have gone rogue, they have been following goals set by humans. In Louisiana, AI is a salient issue as Meta seeks to expand its massive data center project in Richland Parish, which is known as Hyperion. The project is controversial: critics worry household customers could end up paying for Meta’s power needs, and landowners have complained that Entergy, the power company that would fuel Hyperion, is using expropriation laws to seize land for transmission lines, among other concerns. Proponents of the project, including Letlow and state leaders like Gov. Jeff Landry, say that Meta’s data center and other large-scale developments mark a sea change for Louisiana’s economy that will create jobs and bring more community investment to the state. Letlow addresses Meta NDA, stock trade In 2024, Letlow signed a non-disclosure agreement with Laidley LLC, a Meta business, as Meta was working on plans for Hyperion; according to a public financial disclosure, she purchased Meta stock in the months that followed, before news of the project became public. As Congress grapples with allegations of insider trading against its members, Letlow has received backlash over her stock trades, which WNNO reported on in August. And in February, when she was fighting to win the Republican primary, she faced criticism from Sen. Bill Cassidy, her opponent, for failing to disclose her stock trades on time. In a statement, Letlow’s campaign said that Letlow “does not direct, execute, approve, or have prior knowledge of any individual trades.” “These transactions were made independently by a third-party investment firm exercising discretionary authority over a managed account, without Congresswoman Letlow’s input or involvement,” the statement said. Previously, Letlow expressed support for legislation that would ban members of Congress from purchasing new stock but that would not prevent them from trading existing stock. The statement from Letlow’s campaign also defended her decision to sign an NDA with Meta. “The NDA was utilized to understand the investment’s potential to have a profound impact on Northeast Louisiana,” it said. “Such agreements are common in economic development discussions, with the ultimate goal of securing new investments and creating jobs for

artigo.texto: Rep. Jay Dean, Fantasha Allen share thoughts on data centers in Texas House District 7 race Hear where the candidates stand on data centers, school vouchers, and other topics. LONGVIEW, Texas (KLTV) - The contest for who will represent Texas House District 7 pits incumbent state Rep. Jay Dean (R-Longview) against Democratic nominee Fantasha Allen. Dean is running for a sixth term. “This train has sort of left the station,” Dean said, referring to data center construction. “Those companies did a terrible job of getting out front in their public relations to explain and make sure people understood exactly what they are and what they are not.” “I like the idea of the power that they need, that they build their own power plants,” Dean added. Allen said data center constructions should be up to local citizens. “If the people in that county do not want the data centers there, they shouldn’t be there,” Allen said. “I do see a lot of people say that when a data center is built by them, they’re losing water and their electricity bill is going up,” added Allen. “I won’t want that for East Texas because most of us here are already living paycheck-to-paycheck.” The district includes Gregg, Harrison, and Marion counties. artigo.texto: FREMONT, Calif., Oct. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enovix Corporation ("Enovix" or the "Company," Nasdaq: ENVX), a developer and manufacturer of advanced lithium-ion batteries, today announced a purchase order from a multinational provider of dual-use drone systems. The initial order is for 100,000 battery units, with deliveries scheduled in the first half of 2027 as the customer scales its use of Enovix cells manufactured at the Company’s TAA-compliant, military-qualified facility in South Korea. Following successful initial deployment, the customer is expected to place follow-on orders for the program in the second half of 2027 and beyond. "Drone makers need high-performance batteries from a qualified, non-Chinese source now, and this order shows Enovix can deliver,” said Steve Bakos, Chief Revenue Officer and General Manager of Enovix. "It confirms that our technology performs in demanding applications and that our TAA-compliant, in-house manufacturing has real value to customers who need a secure source of supply.” The order moves one opportunity from the approximately $216 million drone, defense and industrial pipeline Enovix reported on October 12, 2026 into backlog, and is among the Q4’26 purchase orders referenced in that release. The Company expects additional pipeline opportunities to convert into purchase orders in the coming quarters. About Enovix Enovix develops and manufactures advanced lithium-ion batteries, including proprietary silicon-anode architectures for smartphones, smart eyewear, defense, industrial and emerging edge-AI applications. Its proprietary silicon-anode battery architecture enables higher energy density and performance in space-constrained devices while maintaining safety and reliability, supporting commercialization across consumer and industrial markets. Enovix is headquartered in Silicon Valley with facilities in India, South Korea and Malaysia, serving customers globally. For more information visit https://enovix.com and follow us on LinkedIn. artigo.texto: - Michigan’s second hyperscale data center is poised to be built after a metro Detroit township’s vote Wednesday night - Google expects the 1-gigawatt data center in Van Buren Township to start drawing power by late 2027 - Boosters call the facility a welcome addition, while neighbors say they’re already being affected by construction noise and dust Local officials on Wednesday approved the final site plan for Google’s proposed data center near the Detroit Metro Airport, paving the way for construction of Michigan’s second hyperscale facility. The Van Buren Township Planning Commission’s 5-1 vote followed nearly an hour of public comment from fans and foes of the development, capping a local approval process that began last year. Google has also secured electricity for the data center through a 20-year contract with DTE Energy that state utility regulators approved on Oct. 1. In August, state environmental regulators approved wetland permits for the project. Several commission members lauded Google’s willingness to work with the township to limit noise emanating from the facility’s vast computing warehouses and take other steps to alleviate community concerns. “If a data center is coming to Van Buren Township, I personally would want Google,” Commissioner Medina Atchinson said ahead of the vote. RELATED: - Google inks deal with DTE Energy for another southeast Michigan data center - Data center moratoriums pile up in Michigan. No one knows if they’ll work - Fact check: John James, Jocelyn Benson debate data centers, tariffs, more - Survey: Michigan local leaders sour on data centers, want more regulations But residents living near the facility railed against the project, saying early construction activities are already lowering their quality of life. “Crews are behind our homes from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m, six to seven days a week,” said Ashley Shukait, who lives in a subdivision adjacent to the data center property. “Dust has been coming into our homes since August and only getting worse. Children with asthma and people on oxygen can’t go in their backyards now. Our houses shake.” Google officials say they expect the development dubbed Project Cannoli will begin drawing electricity by late 2027. Here’s what to know: Land, energy, water use Sandwiched between interstates 94 and 275 to the north and south and Haggerty and Hannan roads to the west and east, the property just west of the Detroit airport has long been zoned for industrial use. That gave development company Pannatoni an easier path to local approval. Site plans call for six buildings, parking lots, a substation and equipment yards spread across 150 of the site’s 282 acres, with the remainder left as open space. Detroit-based construction giant Walbridge, the lead contractor on Oracle and OpenAI’s Stargate data center in Washtenaw County’s Saline Township, is set to build the Google site, too. The facility’s 1-gigawatt of energy demand amounts to the energy equivalent of 750,000 homes. It’s expected to start drawing power by December 2027 and ramp up to 1 GW within a year. Earlier this month, the Michigan Public Service Commission approved special contracts for DTE Energy to power the facility, concluding that the arrangement would not raise residential customers’ rates and may instead save them money. The contract commits Google to pay for the build-out of 480-megawatts of energy storage, 1.6 GW of renewable energy and 300 MW of other power capacity. Google says no new fossil fuel energy plants would be built or expanded to serve the facility. In a measure designed to insulate other customers from the prospect of a popped AI “bubble,” the contract also requires Google to pay for no less than 80% of the power it claims to need (even if actual demand is less) and imposes steep penalties for prematurely terminating the contract. On the water side, the facility will draw up to 3.6 million gallons per day from the Great Lakes Water Authority, which has 706 million gallons per day of surplus capacity in its system. The authority draws its water from Lake Huron and the Detroit River. Tax breaks, revenue Google is expected to take advantage of a 2024 law that exempts qualifying data centers from Michigan’s 6% sales and use tax — a perk likely worth millions if not tens of millions annually. Township and Wayne County officials have also agreed to charge the facility half-price on local taxes, worth an estimated $125 million over 12 years. In exchange, Google will separately pay the township $15.4 million for local infrastructure projects and guarantee at least 51 full-time jobs at the data center, among other vows. Pannatoni Data Centers President Adam Kramer called the project “an incredible generational investment from one of the best companies in the world into this community.” Where else are data centers planned? In addition to the Saline Township and Van Buren Township facilities, developers have floated dozens of proposals in communities across the state — some more seriously than others. DTE and Consumers, which have monopoly control over the power sector in most of the state, report being in advanced talks with multiple developers representing a combined 3-plus-gigawatts of power. Projects where land has been secured include Microsoft’s proposed data centers in west Michigan’s Gaines and Lowell townships and Project Flex, a facility intended for tech giant Anthropic in Oakland County’s Lyon Township. While tax breaks and available space on Michigan’s grid have created a data center prospecting rush in Michigan, experts expect demand to slow once the first few projects come online. “We’re not going to have like a dozen hyperscale data centers,” said Eric Dennis, research associate at Citizens Research Council of Michigan who has studied the state’s data center rush. “We’ll probably have, if they get approved, five or six.” What does the public think? artigo.texto: Iniciativa prevê compensação de cerca de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano com créditos certificados de parques eólicos A Azul Conecta, responsável pela operação regional da Azul, firmou parceria com a Auren Energia para compensar as emissões de carbono associadas ao consumo de combustível de todos os voos realizados pela companhia ao longo de 2026. A iniciativa integra o programa voluntário Conecta NetZero e prevê o uso de créditos de carbono certificados, sem custo adicional para os passageiros. A compensação será feita com créditos gerados pelos complexos eólicos Ventos do Piauí I e Ventos do Araripe III, que integram o portfólio de geração de energia renovável da Auren. O volume estimado de emissões a ser compensado é de 10 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) por ano. Os créditos possuem certificação do Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), administrado pela Verra, e passaram por processos independentes de validação e verificação. Também tiveram sua elegibilidade reconhecida para a fase piloto do CORSIA, mecanismo da Organização da Aviação Civil Internacional (ICAO) voltado à compensação de emissões da aviação internacional. Após a utilização, as unidades serão aposentadas no registro da Verra em nome da Azul Conecta, impedindo seu uso em novas compensações. A iniciativa integra a estratégia de descarbonização da Azul, que inclui renovação e modernização da frota e medidas de eficiência operacional. Entre 2019 e 2025, a companhia reduziu em cerca de 20% sua intensidade de carbono, indicador que relaciona as emissões de CO₂ ao volume transportado. A empresa também possui metas climáticas validadas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), alinhadas à trajetória de aquecimento global de 1,5°C. “A sustentabilidade é um dos pilares da estratégia da Azul e o Conecta NetZero representa mais um avanço concreto em nossa jornada de descarbonização. Ao compensar integralmente as emissões associadas ao consumo de combustível dos voos da Azul Conecta por meio de créditos certificados, reforçamos nosso compromisso de combinar eficiência operacional, inovação e responsabilidade ambiental”, afirma César Grandolfo, diretor de Relações Institucionais, Tributárias e de Sustentabilidade da Azul. Para a Auren, a parceria amplia as possibilidades de aplicação dos créditos gerados por seus ativos de energia renovável. “A parceria mostra como a geração de energia renovável pode contribuir também para a descarbonização de outros setores da economia. Ao levar créditos de carbono gerados a partir dos nossos ativos eólicos para uma iniciativa voltada ao setor aéreo, mostramos como nosso portfólio pode apoiar diferentes empresas em suas estratégias climáticas”, afirma João Guillaumon, vice-presidente de Clientes e Comercialização da Auren Energia. Mercado de créditos de carbono Cada crédito de carbono corresponde a uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e) que deixou de ser emitida ou foi removida da atmosfera. Esses instrumentos podem ser utilizados por empresas para compensar emissões associadas às suas operações, desde que observados os critérios de certificação e integridade ambiental. A Auren já comercializou mais de 7 milhões de créditos de carbono para clientes em mais de 20 países. Segundo a empresa, seu portfólio registra mais de 1,2 milhão de toneladas de CO₂ evitadas e certificadas por ano, com créditos provenientes de projetos de geração de energia renovável e de preservação de florestas nativas. artigo.texto: BlackRock CEO Pushes Back on Growing AI Data Center Fears A lot of Americans are worried about what the AI data center boom could mean for electricity, water and local infrastructure. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink thinks that debate is focused on the wrong risk. There are a lot of rumors and fear about data centers. Most of it is on misinformation. Most of it is wrong, Fink told CNBC, arguing that concerns around water use are often overstated. He pointed to golf courses as an example, saying they use more water than data centers. His bigger argument is economic. Fink warned that slowing or freezing data center construction could hurt the U.S. far beyond the technology sector because so much investment is now tied to AI infrastructure. Data centers are not the problem. They're creating more new jobs than ever before in terms of workers, he said. Fink sees a capital problem behind the AI boom The scale of the buildout is starting to change the financing side of the economy too. Fink said this is the first time in his roughly 50-year career that he has seen what he described as genuine shortages of capital. Part of the pressure comes from the federal government. Our government is demanding more and more credit. The bond auctions are getting larger and larger and larger, he said, pointing to U.S. national debt rising from roughly $8 trillion in 2000 to $40 trillion today. At the same time, AI companies need enormous amounts of money for data centers, GPUs and power infrastructure. BlackRock is trying to solve part of that problem by developing ways to securitize GPUs and other chip assets. The idea is to help smaller companies access compute even when they do not have strong credit ratings. Democratize compute; that is the only way it's going to happen, Fink said. BlackRock is working with hyperscalers and chip companies to study how long GPUs retain useful value. If those assets can receive credible residual-value estimates and ratings, they could eventually support a financing market resembling asset-backed securities. The next AI debate may be about financing, not chips That is the part of Fink's argument that stands out most. The AI boom has usually been framed as a shortage of GPUs, power and data-center capacity. Fink is adding another constraint: capital itself. If trillions of dollars are needed for AI infrastructure while government borrowing is simultaneously absorbing more credit, financing costs could become a much bigger part of the technology story. BlackRock has a clear financial interest in that evolution. Its third-quarter results showed assets under management reaching a record $55 trillion, with $205 billion in new client inflows. The company could benefit if GPUs and other AI infrastructure become a new institutional asset class. For investors, the next things to watch are data center financing costs, GPU-backed debt structures, hyperscaler capital spending and whether regulators or local governments begin placing meaningful limits on new projects.

artigo.texto: Vereadora quer esclarecimentos sobre consumo de energia e água, licenciamento ambiental e impactos do empreendimento BEL1, anunciado com investimento de R$ 250 milhões. Foto:reprodução A Câmara Municipal de Belém aprovou por unanimidade o pedido da vereadora Marinor Brito (PSOL) para a realização de uma sessão especial sobre a implantação do data center BEL1, previsto para a área portuária de Miramar, no bairro do Barreiro. O objetivo é ampliar a transparência sobre o projeto e discutir seus possíveis impactos na infraestrutura da cidade, especialmente no fornecimento de energia elétrica e no abastecimento de água. “Belém precisa saber o que está sendo planejado para a cidade. Um empreendimento desse porte não pode avançar sem transparência, sem informações acessíveis e sem que a população conheça seus possíveis impactos. Queremos respostas sobre o consumo de energia e água, o licenciamento ambiental e as medidas para proteger as comunidades próximas”, afirma Marinor Brito. A iniciativa ganha relevância diante da resposta oficial encaminhada pela Prefeitura de Belém ao Requerimento nº 729/2026, também apresentado pela vereadora. Em ofício de 29 de setembro, a Chefia de Gabinete do Prefeito informou que não havia processo administrativo de licenciamento ambiental instaurado na Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente (SEMMA). Por esse motivo, não existiam estudos técnicos em análise nem registros de consultas ou audiências públicas relacionadas a eventual procedimento de licenciamento na secretaria. A Prefeitura informou ainda que buscaria esclarecimentos sobre qual esfera de governo — municipal, estadual ou federal — será responsável pelo licenciamento ambiental do empreendimento. Consumo de energia e água preocupa O BEL1, da empresa Elea Data Centers, tem investimento anunciado de R$ 250 milhões, demanda inicial estimada em 7,5 megawatts (MW) e possibilidade de expansão para até 100 MW. O requerimento destaca que essa capacidade energética pode representar uma demanda expressiva de infraestrutura. Também cobra informações sobre o consumo de água, os sistemas de refrigeração, a geração de calor, os ruídos e os possíveis efeitos sobre as comunidades do entorno. “A sessão especial será uma oportunidade para reunir a empresa, os órgãos públicos, especialistas e a sociedade. Precisamos de dados concretos para avaliar os impactos e discutir medidas de prevenção e mitigação. Desenvolvimento não pode significar falta de informação para quem vive na cidade”, ressalta a vereadora. O requerimento também menciona a proximidade da Ilha das Onças, localizada a cerca de 4,5 quilômetros da área indicada para o projeto. A distância, por si só, não determina a ocorrência ou a extensão de impactos, o que reforça a necessidade de estudos técnicos. Com a aprovação unânime, a proposta de Marinor busca abrir espaço para o debate público sobre as condições de implantação do empreendimento, garantindo transparência, participação popular e acesso às informações necessárias para que Belém conheça os possíveis efeitos do projeto.

artigo.texto: AI data centers are coming for federal land. They’re roiling the Nevada governor’s race - Click here to listen to this article - Share via - A proposed AI data center near Boulder City was moved to federal land after residents defeated it locally; a judge later halted construction over the project’s environmental review. - With more than a dozen similar projects in the works, Nevada’s vast federal holdings could become a proving ground for data centers and a tinderbox over public-land protections. - The issue is reshaping the governor’s race, as Republican Joe Lombardo and Democrat Aaron Ford spar over development, tax breaks and safeguards for electricity bills and water supplies. BOULDER CITY, Nev. — Janelle Sorenson loves the clear night skies in Boulder City, less than an hour’s drive from the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. It’s a small, quiet town, and she thinks an artificial intelligence data center would ruin the community and scar the desert landscape. So over the summer, she joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country. But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off. “Not only did we not get to decide anything or have a say,” Sorenson said, “we were just really kept in the dark.” The Townsite data center was the first in the country to be approved on federal public land, though construction is stalled after a judge ruled that the government couldn’t use an old environmental review from when the project was intended to be a solar farm. Tech companies are eager for vast tracts to build data centers that can be as large as 70 football fields, and Townsite could set a precedent for similar projects on federal property with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. President Trump has been a steadfast supporter of the AI industry, which he views as a source of economic growth and part of a global competition with China. However, data centers have been unpopular in many communities as voters worry about higher electricity bills, declining water supplies and other effects. In Nevada, where 80% of the land is owned by the federal government, Townsite and other projects have become a dominant issue in the battleground state’s closely watched governor’s race. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, one of his party’s most vulnerable incumbents, doesn’t outright oppose building data centers on public lands, as long as they have community support. He recently signed an agreement with Trump’s Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands. Democratic nominee Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, has pledged to oppose data centers on public lands, saying affordable housing should be the priority. Both say the projects, whether on public or private land, must follow state rules, such as requiring data centers to cover their own energy costs and protecting water supplies, or they would lose eligibility for state tax abatements. Voters across the political spectrum unite against data centers Sorenson, the Boulder City resident, considers herself a liberal, but she said her conservative neighbors are on the same page as she is. “We’re all aligned on this,” she said. Autumn McGrath-Shook, who lives in the same town, said she recently left the GOP and registered with the Green Party over data centers, though she still identifies as conservative. Worried about the environmental impact on wildlife, she joined forces with “these crazy libs” to oppose the project. Data centers have quickly become a “catalyzing issue” in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. Some state leaders who were previously supportive of data centers have rushed to respond. For example, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center approvals until audits are completed, and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order removing data center proposals from a fast-track permitting process and requiring them to receive local approval before seeking state approval. In August, Ford announced his plan to pause new tax abatements for data centers while an audit is conducted to see whether the projects have fulfilled promises about producing tax revenue and economic benefits. In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on them and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools. The two have successfully “muddied the waters” on their data center positions, Damore said. Lombardo criticized Ford for co-sponsoring 2015 legislation that created the state’s tax abatement program for the facilities, a measure that received bipartisan support. Ford criticized Lombardo for giving more than $200 million in tax breaks to data centers, which is connected to the legislation that Ford co-sponsored. Ford told the Associated Press that he would use “every tool” at his disposal to prevent data centers from skirting state guardrails, including withholding tax abatements and pursuing litigation. Lombardo, whose campaign declined to make him available for an interview, has a similar pitch. His office said he would not hesitate to confront the federal government to advocate for Nevadans. But that’s not good enough for McGrath-Shook, who is on the fence in the governor’s race. artigo.texto: More than 40 University of Michigan staff, students and Ypsilanti community members gathered in the Trotter Multicultural Center Monday evening for a data center teach-in by Stop the Data Center, an advocacy organization against the the University’s planned Ypsilanti Township data center in collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory. Ypsilanti Township residents organized a presentation arguing the data center is another expression of the military-industrial-academic complex, which they said only serves to advance the United States’ hegemony while ignoring local communities. The presentation then shifted to discussing new ideas to secure their collective goal: ending the development of the research computing center. At the event, assistant information professor Justine Zhang said residents opposing the center are worried about toxic chemicals and the other potential consequences of proximity to data centers. “(The project is) proceeding in spite of opposition from people in Ypsilanti and beyond, who do not want a project that will extract land, water and capacity from the community while extending the infrastructure of U.S. imperialism,” Zhang said. “Our task is to collectively analyze and strategize around these developments, so we act in solidarity with our friends, coworkers, neighbors and comrades to the data center.” Ypsilanti Township resident Robin Wylie, the School of Public Health Epidemiology staff member, said he was concerned about a recent letter from Los Alamos handed out to the community during a September town hall. The letter claimed the proposed site was only a research computing facility that would allow scientists from Los Alamos to work more closely with U-M faculty and students to explore fields like brain cancer surgery outcomes, extreme weather predicting and various other scientific and engineering challenges. “Even at the town hall meetings, we keep asking, ‘What are we going to get out of this?’” Wylie said. “They don’t have an answer for us. We’re not — Ypsilanti is not — benefiting at all from this.” Wylie also said the statement highlighted the benefits the project could provide to the University, but it did not explain how the center would affect local communities. In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Wylie expressed concerns about his community’s safety given the health complications the project may cause. “Toxic chemicals will probably be used in the cooling system, and they can leak in the data center,” Wylie said. “They’ve been known to cause serious health problems. I don’t know how they’re going to prevent that from happening. How are they going to? It’s right next to a river.” University librarian Craig Smith said he worries the project is fully in the power of the University’s Board of Regents, instead of the local community. Smith also questioned why the University is providing nearly $850 million in funds, despite Los Alamos having greater access to the facility. “In our group, we were reflecting on the fact that Los Alamos is going to have 90% access to this data center, and U-M is going to have 10%,” Smith said. “Why are we doing this? We’re paying $800 million for this thing, and we’re getting 10% out of it.” LSA freshman Katrina Hunter told the Daily she was concerned that the majority of the student population remains unaware of the University’s affiliation with Los Alamos for the data center project. She said she believes more students would get involved in anti-data center activism if they were made aware. “I think getting a collective body of students aware of it, and then we can maybe move on to protesting, handing out flyers, talking to students, getting people outside petitioning or talking to town offices, calling up and going to board meetings,” Hunter said. “We can get more involved. Once we go to board meetings we can talk to officials and try to push our way into getting the students and community of Ypsilanti involved.” Daily News Contributor Elise Maurer can be reached at elisemau@umich.edu.
