artigo.texto: ComEd and Richardson Electronics, Ltd. joined state and industry leaders to announce Richardson Electronics’ expanded manufacturing of locally produced battery energy storage systems and plans to install its first onsite battery energy storage system demonstration project. This initiative is a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions that strengthen grid reliability, support renewable energy integration, and store energy for use during periods of high demand while helping ease supply-related energy costs. “For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” said ComEd President and CEO Gil Quiniones. “ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.” Richardson, a legacy manufacturer based in La Fox, is currently building the largest commercial battery storage system in Illinois. Its planned operational expansion will help scale the development and distribution of these products. Richardson is installing a 5-MWh research and development demonstration project, supported through the ComEd interconnection process. “Richardson Electronics has a long history of solving complex power and energy challenges through innovation and U.S.-based manufacturing,” said Greg Peloquin, Executive Vice President and General Manager of Power & Microwave Technologies and Green Energy Solutions groups. “Our advanced energy storage solutions will help customers manage energy more efficiently while supporting a more reliable and resilient grid. We value ComEd’s collaboration in bringing this onsite demonstration project to life.” The initiative is also supported by the Reimagining Energy and Vehicles in Illinois, or REV Illinois, program, which is helping Richardson Electronics strengthen its La Fox operations, advance energy technology manufacturing and support continued economic growth in Illinois. “As demand for reliable and affordable energy increases, Illinois has an opportunity not only to deploy new technologies, but to manufacture them,” said Illinois Economic Development Corporation President and CEO Christy George. “Richardson Electronics’ expansion demonstrates how Illinois’ manufacturing expertise can drive growth in emerging industries like battery storage while helping strengthen the energy infrastructure that supports our economy.” Increasing battery energy storage is a key component of Illinois’ recently enacted Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA), which seeks to strengthen grid reliability and help address forecasted energy supply shortfalls. By storing electricity for use during periods of peak demand, battery storage can support a more resilient grid, integrate additional clean energy resources, and help ensure Illinois has the energy capacity needed to power future economic growth. “Safe, reliable and affordable energy is critical to the success of Illinois’ manufacturing sector and will require new generation, transmission investment and new technologies such as battery storage,” said Mark Denzler, President & CEO of the Illinois Manufacturers’ Association. “Richardson Electronics and ComEd’s announcement of a next-generation 5 MWh commercial battery storage system is a great example of manufacturing innovation and ingenuity that will help drive growth and economic development in Illinois.” Battery energy storage systems can charge when electricity is available and discharge when it is needed, helping customers manage energy use and support a more flexible electric system. Depending on how they are configured, batteries can also provide backup capabilities, reduce demand during peak periods, and support the integration of renewable energy resources. “When Kane County Commissioner Rick Williams and I first met with Richardson to discuss this project, I was immediately intrigued by both the economic and energy benefits the project could bring to the area and the state,” said State Representative Dan Ugaste (65th District). “Energy storage will be an important part of having affordable and reliable energy going forward. Seeing the value this project could bring, I was glad to help facilitate discussions with the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to bring this project to fruition.” ComEd is supporting the project through its customer interconnection process and engineering studies. The company’s work includes helping prepare the site for the demonstration system and guiding Richardson through any potential system upgrade needs. This work will help to safely and reliably connect the demonstration system while maintaining service for surrounding customers. Projects like these are also eligible to apply for ComEd’s Distributed Generation Rebate Program, which recently hit a $350 million milestone. artigo.texto: Data centers were on tap for both the Pulaski County Quorum Court and the Little Rock Board of Directors on Tuesday night, with the city’s measure going forward for a vote next week and the county’s legislation pulled for further study. Little Rock City Director Kathy Webb tried and failed to get an 18-month moratorium passed in August – it tied on a 4-4 vote – and now has come back with a six-month pause, which was brought up at Tuesday night’s agenda meeting. There was little discussion and no vote taken. Webb said she had talked to her constituents, some of whom thought a year and a half was too long and others who thought six months wasn’t long enough. Her proposal allows for another six-month delay if more time is needed to study a data center proposal. Asked if she thinks she has the votes this time around, Webb said she hopes so. “If we were in the Legislature, lawmakers have those kinds of conversations every day,” she said. “But we can’t do that on the board so I depend on the people I’m working with to have those conversations with other board members. I can say this, there will be several co-sponsors this time.” Google has proposed a 100-megawatt, $1 billion data center that would be located on 380 acres in the Port of Little Rock area. The Board of Directors passed an ordinance in June outlining data center regulations, but it has been criticized for not going far enough. About a block and a half away from City Hall, at the county’s administration building, the Quorum Court’s own agenda was getting underway, but a proposed piece of legislation was pulled before it could be considered and placed on the full Quorum Court’s agenda. The proposed ordinance was written by Justice of the Peace Douglas House, who said he had taken his proposal off the agenda after talking with members of the county’s planning staff who had questions about some of the particulars. House, who was appointed by Gov. Sarah Sanders, is serving until the end of the year and took the place left vacated by Phil Stowers, who resigned in June. He said he has worked on the ordinance as an alternative to one proposed by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood. Blackwood’s ordinance was passed last month on an 11-4 vote and sets out detailed conditions under which large industrial projects, like data centers, can operate. After that vote, County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed the measure because, among other objections, he thinks the county will be sued if the ordinance passes. House’s ordinance includes some of the same topics as Blackwood’s measure, but makes an exception for a large data center project being pushed by AVAIO Digital. That project, located near Wrightsville, is estimated to be worth $21 billion and need 1 gigawatt of electricity to operate. House said he also thinks the county will be sued if the Avaio project is included in any legislation that slows the construction process that is now underway. “I am 99.9% sure that will happen,” House said after the meeting. House said if the Quorum Court overrides Hyde’s veto, thereby confirming the passage of Blackwood’s ordinance — nine votes are needed — he will toss his proposal in the trash, noting that his time on the Quorum Court will end soon after. If the justices of the peace fail to override the veto, he said he will continue pursuing his proposal.

artigo.texto: Editor’s note: We are publishing a series of fact-checks of advertisements in the Pennsylvania 8th Congressional District race between incumbent Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Dallas Twp. and Democratic challenger, Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. The election is key for both major parties’ hopes of holding a House majority the next two years. The 30-second ad is paid for by Paige For PA, Cognetti’s official campaign committee. It was approved by the candidate. The scene opens with two men sitting in Adirondack chairs in a front yard outside a home. One is reading a copy of The Times-Tribune, the other a recent edition of The Citizens’ Voice. “You see this?” one man asks. “Bresnahan wants data centers all over NEPA.” It kicks off a discussion between the two men centered on Bresnahan’s views and actions on data centers. The other man complains about already-high energy costs, while the original commenter adds that data centers “use more juice than 100,000 Sheetz (gas stations).” He goes on to say that Bresnahan gave data centers a $20 billion tax break, adding that he also “bought stock in a data center company.” “Rob Bresnahan is making more money, and we’re stuck with the bill,” he says. Cognetti appears, sitting atop a fallen tree, announcing she approves the ad. She’d say more, she concludes, “but I think these guys got it covered.” Key claim Rob Bresnahan supports data center construction throughout the region and encourages them with tax breaks. Is it factual? The dialogue hits on several points scrutinizing Bresnahan’s early support for data center development in Northeast Pennsylvania. Claims that Bresnahan desires data centers be built “all over” the region is at the very least a stretch. In June, Bresnahan introduced the Local Control Protection Act in the House. He said the bill would put data center development in the hands of local communities by putting limits on a corporation’s right to sue over local zoning decisions that deny applications to build them. The bill was sent to committee in June and has not been acted upon since. “We should never let billion-dollar corporations supersede the voices of those who live in the community,” Bresnahan said in a statement introducing the bill. However, it also is true that Bresnahan expressed support for area data center development in the past. In April 2025, Bresnahan said data centers could be “catalysts for economic growth and technological innovation” throughout the region. “I look forward to these investments and encourage companies to look to Northeastern Pennsylvania as a home for economic and technological advancements,” he said then. After a joint venture between PPL Corporation and Blackstone, a leading private equity firm, to invest $25 billion in data center development in Pennsylvania was announced in July 2025, Bresnahan pointed to potential benefits in NEPA, saying the region was full of “untapped power” and was “more than ready for new growth, investments and opportunities.” It is not true that Bresnahan voted in favor of a $20 billion tax break targeted solely to data center developers. Yet, critics argue the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, for which Bresnahan was a yes vote, included language that created broader capital expensing and depreciation rules allowing companies to write off equipment costs sooner than is deemed necessary based on useful life and is especially lucrative for companies that build AI infrastructure. A study by the nonprofit Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, for example, found that five big tech giants — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle — combined to claim more than $26 billion in depreciation tax breaks in 2025. Bresnahan indeed owns stock in data center companies. According to financial disclosures filed in August, Bresnahan owns between $19,005 and $110,000 worth of stock in four companies with direct ties to the data center industry. His portfolio also includes investments worth between $804,024 and $2.04 million in companies that supply chips, networking equipment, semiconductor manufacturing tools and software that aid the development of the AI industry and data centers.

artigo.texto: African countries must strengthen cooperation, attract investment and ensure communities receive fair returns to turn the continent’s carbon market potential into climate and economic benefits, experts have said. The call came at the opening of the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 in Kigali on Wednesday, October 14. The two-day summit brought together around 600 policymakers, investors, project developers, corporate buyers and climate finance stakeholders. Co-organised by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment and the African Development Bank, the summit aims to strengthen African carbon markets and turn climate ambitions into investment-ready projects. ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda’s carbon credit deal with Singapore, Kuwait Rwanda’s Minister for Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said Africa had reached a turning point in deciding how carbon markets operate and whom they benefit. “You are here because, like us, you believe that Africa’s carbon markets must be shaped by African priorities and that they must now deliver,” she told delegates. Despite progress in regulations and agreements, she said, slowing voluntary markets, concerns over credit integrity and a widening climate finance gap demanded renewed efforts. “These are not reasons to retreat. They are reasons to reset—and then build better,” Arakwiye said. From policy to investment Carbon markets generate credits from projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. When properly regulated, they can attract private investment into renewable energy, forest conservation, clean cooking and sustainable agriculture. However, Arakwiye said current market activity did not adequately reflect Africa’s development priorities. Forestry, land-use initiatives and improved cookstoves account for a significant share of African credits, while agriculture has generated barely one per cent of credits issued on voluntary markets over two decades. “The smallholder farmer, who has the most to gain and much to offer, is still standing largely outside this market,” she said. She called for greater investment in renewable energy, electric mobility, waste management, industrial decarbonisation and landscape restoration. Strengthening Africa’s bargaining power Dr Fatmata Lovetta Sesay, UNDP Resident Representative in Rwanda, said African countries needed stronger negotiating capacity despite progress in establishing carbon market regulations and institutions. Following a summit session on readiness to implement Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, she called for clear registration criteria, functional carbon registries, monitoring systems and project pipelines aligned with national priorities. “Africa is not lacking the legal framework that is required to govern how we operate in the carbon markets,” she said. “Africa is not lacking the opportunities that exist on the continent and several other places for this trading to happen.” She urged countries to negotiate from a position of strength and called for continental discussions to improve bargaining power and ensure African countries receive fair value for their climate assets. “This is not a race that is a sprint for countries in Africa. It's a marathon,” she said, noting that countries were progressing at different speeds. Ensuring communities benefit Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa, said carbon markets must channel benefits to communities whose land and conservation efforts make projects possible. He called for stronger community rights and transparent benefit-sharing, early-stage project financing and partnerships based on measurable results. “A registry tracks a credit. It does not settle a land dispute,” he said, stressing the need for community consent and enforceable benefit-sharing arrangements. Gomera urged development banks to finance project preparation, while buyers should offer longer-term purchase agreements and advance funding. “Trust is market infrastructure, not sentiment,” he said. He also stressed the need to recognise the benefits of landscapes, from food production and water regulation to biodiversity and carbon storage, while preventing emissions reductions from being counted or sold twice. Rwanda seeks to diversify carbon credit projects beyond cookstoves Rwanda launched its National Carbon Market Framework in December 2023 to establish rules for developing, authorising, trading and monitoring credits, Arakwiye said. In May 2025, Rwanda and Singapore signed an implementation agreement under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, providing a pathway for authorised carbon credit transfers. Singapore committed to cancelling two per cent of correspondingly adjusted credits at first issuance and directing five per cent of the value of authorised credits towards adaptation measures in Rwanda. Rwanda has registered 29 carbon market projects across forestry, agriculture, land conservation, electric mobility, waste management and renewable energy. However, improved cookstove projects account for around 87 per cent of the country’s issued credits. The government has generated about $1.5 million (Rwf2.2 billion) from carbon credit sales. artigo.texto: Supermicro expande seu portfólio de projetos de computação aberta integrada para acelerar as implantações de data centers de IA em escala de rack AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 14 de outubro de 2026 - O portfólio integrado baseado no Open Compute Project (OCP) abrange sistemas de IA/HPC em escala de rack, racks ORv3 e ORW, alimentação de 48V CC, redes e soluções de refrigeração líquida para viabilizar a computação de maior densidade em data centers existentes e novos - O portfólio abrange desde a infraestrutura até operações inteligentes, incluindo fluidos de resfriamento DCBBS, CDUs integradas ao rack (in-rack), switches e o pacote de software de gerenciamento de sistemas da Supermicro para a gestão da infraestrutura - O Supermicro DCBBS reúne essas tecnologias baseadas em OCP em soluções integradas em escala de rack, simplificando e acelerando a implementação de recursos de computação, energia, rede e refrigeração para reduzir o tempo de entrada em operação (TTO). SAN JOSE, Califórnia, 14 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), anunciou hoje um portfólio expandido de sistemas, racks e trocadores de calor de porta traseira (RDHx) certificados como Open Compute Project Accepted(TM). Com o suporte do DCBBS, o portfólio de soluções pode ser incorporado em implantações completas de ponta a ponta, em escala de rack e cluster. “O boom da IA redefine a forma como os data centers são projetados, construídos e implementados, e a Supermicro lidera essa transformação com o DCBBS”, disse Charles Liang, presidente e CEO da Supermicro. “Ao integrar computação, redes, energia, refrigeração avançada, software e serviços em soluções validadas em escala de rack, ajudamos os clientes a simplificar a complexidade e acelerar o caminho da inovação até a produção. O DCBBS possibilita que os clientes reduzam o TTM e o TTO ao oferecer infraestrutura essencial de IA de forma mais rápida e eficiente.” As soluções OCP da Supermicro já estão disponíveis; clique aqui para saber mais. Ao aproveitar as melhores práticas da comunidade OCP e o design e serviços do DCBBS, os operadores de data centers podem aumentar a densidade de computação e a eficiência energética para cargas de trabalho de IA e HPC com base em uma infraestrutura aberta e validada em escala de rack — desde sistemas e barras de distribuição até o resfriamento em nível de rack e de data centers — para implementar soluções de alta densidade de forma mais eficiente e acelerar o tempo de lançamento no mercado (TTM) e o tempo de operação (TTO). “Os clientes precisam de uma infraestrutura aberta e flexível que possa ser dimensionada de acordo com as demandas em rápida evolução da IA, ao mesmo tempo que se adapte à realidade de seus data centers”, disse Dirk Van Slyke, vice-presidente de Marketing da OCP. “Ao reunir sistemas, racks, energia e refrigeração aceitos pelo OCP em soluções validadas em escala de rack, a Supermicro ajuda os clientes a simplificar a integração, maximizar a capacidade e a eficiência das instalações e acelerar a implantação da infraestrutura de IA de produção.” Os racks ORv3 e ORW substituem as fontes de alimentação e os cabos individuais por servidor por uma barra de distribuição CC centralizada de 48 V, permitindo que os clientes otimizem seus sistemas de CPU e GPU para racks de computação de maior densidade. Essa densidade é ainda mais reforçada pelo sistema de resfriamento líquido DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip da Supermicro, que remove o calor de forma mais eficiente de CPUs, GPUs e outros componentes críticos, enquanto o calor residual pode ser removido do rack por meio de unidades de resfriamento ORv3 RDHx especialmente desenvolvidas, sem a necessidade de adaptações adicionais nos sistemas de ar-condicionado do data center. As unidades RDHx da Supermicro podem ser montadas na parte traseira de racks ORv3 e ORW, removendo o calor residual do ar de exaustão dos servidores antes que ele entre na sala do data center. O portfólio abrange capacidades de refrigeração de 10 kW a 120 kW, oferecendo aos operadores uma maneira prática de aumentar a densidade de racks tanto em novas instalações de IA quanto em data centers existentes. Os modelos alimentados por corrente contínua conectam-se à barra de distribuição do rack para reduzir a quantidade de cabos, enquanto os designs incluem ventiladores redundantes N+1 para garantir o tempo de atividade e um sistema anticondensação inteligente para evitar danos causados pela umidade a outros componentes dentro do rack. Os operadores podem monitorar e gerenciar todo o portfólio de componentes DCBBS, por meio do SuperCloud Composer®, utilizando protocolos padrão do setor. Além disso, os softwares da Supermicro, como o SuperCloud Director, o SuperCloud Automation Assistant e o SuperCloud Developer Console, possibilitam que as empresas gerenciem e operacionalizem todos os aspectos das modernas fábricas de IA, centros de dados corporativos e infraestrutura NeoCloud, por meio de uma solução unificada de controle de software. Como parte do portfólio do DCBBS, a Supermicro também oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções de rede para IA, que variam de switches Ethernet 800G e 1.6T com refrigeração a ar ou líquida, incluindo plataformas Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) de última geração baseadas no silício de comutação Broadcom Tomahawk 6, otimizadas para racks EIA ou ORv3. artigo.texto: Hanoi (VNA) - Vietnam is moving to link green credit with its carbon market, a step expected to free up additional funding for the green transition and give banks a firmer basis to assess and manage capital flows to emissions-reduction projects. The issue was among those discussed at a seminar in Hanoi on October 14, co-hosted by Tai chinh – Dau tu (Finance and Investment) newspaper and the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV). Green credit lays groundwork for carbon market In his opening speech, Pham Van Hoanh, the newspaper’s Editor-in-Chief, said Vietnam is progressively finalising policies on green growth and its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. The domestic carbon market began a pilot on June 29, 2026, raising the need to deepen links among green credit, banking system and new financial instruments. SBV Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh said meeting the 2050 net-zero pledge will require enormous resources for technological innovation, production overhaul, energy efficiency and emissions cuts. Alongside the State budget and capital and monetary markets, the carbon market is an important mechanism to raise additional funds, he said. The Government issued Decree 29/2026/ND-CP on the domestic carbon exchange on January 29, setting the legal framework for the market and trading greenhouse gas emission allowances and carbon credits. The pilot market was launched with more than 511 million metric tonnes of CO₂ in allowances, allocated to facilities in three emissions-intensive sectors for 2025-2026, including thermal power, iron and steel, and cement. The pilot runs through the end of 2028, with full mandatory operation starting in 2029. Canh said green credit funds the projects, technologies and sectors that deliver emissions cuts, while the carbon market can turn those cuts into economic value. If it works well, the market can generate extra revenue and cash flow, improving credit quality and helping companies meet environmental standards for exports. Outstanding green credit across the banking system topped 856 trillion VND (32.9 billion USD) at the end of June 2026, up 9.87% from end-2025. From 2017 to 2025, green credit grew by more than 20% a year on average, focusing on agriculture, forestry, fisheries, biodiversity and green energy. Proposal to connect carbon value chain Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Agribank Training School and deputy head of its ESG team, said the issue isn’t whether banks directly trade carbon credits. What matters is how they finance the creation of emissions reductions, and when carbon value becomes reliable enough to factor into lending decisions. Agribank said financing needs emerge before any credits exist. Projects pass through preparation, investment, operation, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV), credit issuance, trading and settlement. That gap gives banks room to offer credit, bridge financing, cash flow management, guarantees and blended finance. The lender proposed drawing clear lines among emissions-reduction potential, registered projects, verified results, issued credits, carbon-credit sales contracts and proceeds already collected. Each carries a different level of certainty and can’t automatically be treated as the same source of debt repayment. Agribank identified five roles for banks in the carbon ecosystem, including financing emissions-reduction activities, linking stakeholders across the value chain, providing payment and cash-flow services, pooling climate finance, and supporting companies and individuals through the transition. As an immediate step, it proposed a framework for identifying emissions-reduction projects and a set of criteria for assessing carbon-related credit. It suggested piloting value chains where emissions can be clearly gauged, such as low-emission rice, livestock and biogas, sustainable forestry, waste treatment and biomass energy. Banks also need to build partner networks, train interdisciplinary staff and strengthen data and governance systems. Agribank plans to focus on data, capacity, partnerships and pilot models in 2026-2028, scale up in 2029-2032 as the domestic market becomes more stable, and study products based on carbon-related cash flows or receivables from 2033. To support market growth, Agribank recommended clarifying ownership, disposition rights and benefit-sharing for emissions-reduction results and carbon credits, and completing rules on receivables, collateral, accounting, taxation and foreign exchange. It also called for treating data and MRV systems as market infrastructure, cutting verification costs, developing supply and demand together, and applying blended finance and risk-sharing mechanisms. Canh said an effective carbon market lets companies convert emissions cuts into financial resources of their own, which could ease pressure on green credit. Rather than relying mainly on their own capital, State funding or bank loans to finance the transition, firms gain greater capacity to generate funds from their own emissions reductions./.

artigo.texto: Fundo para provedores de internet: proximidade com data centers (thinkstock) Editor de Invest Publicado em 15 de outubro de 2026 às 05h00. O provedor de internet de uma cidade do interior paulista tem uma receita relativamente previsível, já que milhares de clientes pagam a mensalidade todo mês. O que costuma faltar é crédito para crescer. É nesse espaço que a Möbius Capital e a Desenvolve SP querem atuar com um fundo de R$ 70 milhões dedicado a provedores regionais de internet e a data centers de pequeno porte no estado. O veículo é um FIDC (Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios), estrutura que investe em valores que as empresas têm a receber. Na prática, o fundo poderá adiantar ao provedor o dinheiro das mensalidades pagas por seus clientes, sejam pessoas físicas ou empresas. Também poderá financiar a compra de equipamentos e operações de expansão, incluindo a compra ou a fusão de empresas. Esse último ponto conversa com o momento do setor. O mercado de provedores regionais passa por um movimento de consolidação, em que empresas maiores compram concorrentes menores, e esse tipo de operação depende de capital. A Desenvolve SP é a agência de fomento do governo do Estado de São Paulo. Funciona como um banco público estadual, que empresta dinheiro a empresas paulistas, sobretudo pequenas e médias, para estimular a economia do estado. Além do crédito direto, a agência também investe em fundos administrados por gestoras privadas, selecionadas por meio de chamadas públicas. Foi assim que a Möbius chegou ao negócio. A gestora apresentou a proposta na chamada da Desenvolve SP para FIDCs e FIPs, passou por análise de elegibilidade, apresentação presencial e due diligence, e teve o investimento aprovado pelo comitê da agência. A Desenvolve SP subscreveu R$ 50 milhões em cotas seniores, que têm prioridade para receber os pagamentos. A Möbius ficou com R$ 20 milhões em cotas subordinadas, que só recebem depois das seniores e são as primeiras a absorver eventuais calotes. Se alguma operação der errado, o prejuízo bate antes no bolso da gestora. "Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores", afirma Ricardo Brito, diretor-presidente da Desenvolve SP, em comunicado. O termo blended finance se refere à combinação de dinheiro público e privado num mesmo investimento. A aposta é que cidades do interior com baixa penetração de internet ganhem conectividade e acesso mais próximo a data centers, o que tende a ajudar empresas locais a ganhar produtividade. A Möbius atua há cerca de cinco anos com infraestrutura digital. "Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias", diz Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da gestora. A Möbius foi fundada por ex-executivos do Credit Suisse e reúne cerca de R$ 1 bilhão entre capital comprometido e investido. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no A vantagem brasileira na corrida pelos data centers Publicado 14/10/2026 • 12:00 | Atualizado há 20 horas Foto: Divulgação/Ascenty A inteligência artificial parece existir na nuvem, mas sua infraestrutura é profundamente física. Por trás de cada modelo ou agente inteligente existem servidores, chips, redes, sistemas de refrigeração e instalações que funcionam 24 horas por dia. A nuvem, afinal, tem endereço, ocupa terreno, consome energia e precisa ser resfriada. Estamos entrando em uma transformação mais profunda: inteligência deixa de ser apenas uma capacidade humana e passa a existir também como infraestrutura disponível em escala. Carros poderão dirigir sem motorista, fábricas operar com crescente autonomia e agentes de IA comprar, contratar e negociar. Governos poderão antecipar congestionamentos, fraudes e falhas de infraestrutura. É a capacidade de produzir, decidir e antecipar multiplicada por milhões de máquinas. Mas inteligência em escala exige energia em escala. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia, os data centers consumiram cerca de 485 TWh de eletricidade em 2025 e poderão chegar a 950 TWh em 2030, ligeiramente mais que todo o consumo atual do Japão. A revolução aparentemente imaterial da IA encontrou um limite concreto: eletricidade. Isso começa a mudar a geografia da economia digital. Conectividade, segurança e talentos continuam importantes, mas uma nova pergunta entrou na mesa: onde está a energia? Servidores podem ser instalados rapidamente; redes de transmissão e geração levam anos. A infraestrutura digital começa a correr mais rápido do que a energética que precisa sustentá-la. Há ainda a água. Sistemas de refrigeração podem demandar volumes relevantes. A questão não é ser a favor ou contra data centers, mas quais queremos, onde instalá-los e com que padrões de eficiência. Reúso de água, refrigeração eficiente e energia de baixo carbono podem transformar restrição ambiental em vantagem competitiva. É aqui que o Brasil ganha relevância. Em 2025, 86,8% da matriz elétrica brasileira foi renovável; eólica e solar responderam juntas por 26,4% da geração. Poucos grandes mercados combinam escala territorial e econômica com uma matriz dessa natureza. Na economia da IA, um ativo que durante décadas enxergamos principalmente como ambiental passa a ser também tecnológico. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A dimensão do movimento já aparece nos números. Em junho de 2026, o Ministério de Minas e Energia informou 38 GW em pedidos de acesso relacionados a data centers, dos quais 7,1 GW estavam associados a cerca de R$ 159 bilhões em investimentos previstos. Os 38 GW superam em mais de duas vezes e meia a capacidade instalada de Itaipu. São grandezas distintas, mas revelam a pressão potencial sobre o sistema. O Redata, aprovado pela Câmara em fevereiro, prevê benefícios tributários e contrapartidas. Mas a questão decisiva será menos quantos servidores atrairemos e mais quanto valor permanecerá no país. Um data center isolado é infraestrutura. Ligado a energia, telecomunicações, software, universidades, fornecedores e talentos, pode integrar um ecossistema de inovação. Estados e municípios disputarão esses investimentos como no passado disputaram montadoras e siderúrgicas. Os vencedores dificilmente serão os que oferecerem apenas o maior incentivo fiscal, mas os que conseguirem combinar energia, água, conectividade, licenciamento, qualificação profissional e integração com a economia regional. A próxima fronteira da inteligência artificial será definida tanto pelos algoritmos quanto pela infraestrutura capaz de executá-los. O Brasil pode transformar energia de baixo carbono, eficiência ambiental e escala territorial em uma razão para esses investimentos virem para cá. Na economia da IA, sustentabilidade não precisa ser o preço que se paga pelo desenvolvimento. Pode ser uma de suas vantagens competitivas. artigo.texto: Iowa residents raise health and environmental concerns over data center expansion Advocacy groups and residents are raising concerns about the potential health and environmental impacts of Iowa's expanding data center industry, which relies on increased fossil fuel use. Brian Campbell, executive director of Physicians for Social Responsibility, spoke during a briefing hosted by The Sierra Club, addressing the potential risks for communities near these facilities. "We know that these fossil fuel-combusting electricity-generating plants lead to and increase toxic air pollution," Campbell said. "These exacerbate the incidence of asthma, heart attacks, cognitive decline, certain cancers, adverse birth outcomes and premature death." Earlier this week, residents in Woodward learned about a proposed 600-acre data center. Many expressed concerns about the project's timeline and its potential environmental impact. The Sierra Club Iowa Chapter has stated that it seeks to provide more information about such projects to help Iowans better understand their implications.

artigo.texto: Badland Batteries has officially opened a new 80,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility in Fargo, North Dakota, expanding domestic production capabilities for unmanned aircraft systems, defense platforms, robotics and other autonomous technologies. The Badland Batteries manufacturing facility, which celebrated its grand opening on October 8, 2026, represents an investment in rebuilding the U.S. battery supply chain and reducing dependence on overseas manufacturers for critical energy storage technologies. The facility combines automated and operator-controlled manufacturing equipment to produce lithium-ion pouch cells, with the capacity to manufacture more than 15,000 battery cells per day as production scales. Badland Batteries Manufacturing Facility Opens in North Dakota The new Fargo facility is designed to manufacture lithium-ion pouch battery cells for defense, aerospace and autonomous systems applications. The 80,000-square-foot plant incorporates a combination of automated manufacturing processes and equipment operated by personnel. According to Badland Batteries, the facility is intended to support domestic battery production while providing greater control over materials, manufacturing quality and supply chain traceability. “Opening this facility marks an important step forward in building a secure and resilient battery supply chain here in the United States,” said Terri Zimmerman, CEO of Badland Batteries and Packet Digital. “Simply put, we believe that America should build its own batteries, and this facility represents years of work towards that goal and demonstrates our unwavering commitment to supporting our nation’s defense.” New Facility Targets Drone and Autonomous Systems Batteries The manufacturing operation is focused on producing battery cells for technologies that require reliable and domestically sourced power systems. Target applications include: - Unmanned aircraft systems - Military and defense platforms - Autonomous vehicles - Robotics - Aerospace technologies - Commercial autonomous systems Battery technology is a critical component of electric unmanned aircraft, affecting flight endurance, payload capacity and operational reliability. Badland Batteries is positioning its domestic production capabilities to support growing demand from U.S. defense and commercial customers. “These battery cells will help power today’s and tomorrow’s cutting-edge autonomous and UAS systems, which are critical to our nation’s security,” Zimmerman said. Domestic Battery Supply Chain Reduces Foreign Dependence According to Badland Batteries, more than 80% of batteries and critical materials used in autonomous systems are manufactured overseas. The company identifies this dependence as a significant supply chain vulnerability for U.S. defense and advanced technology programs. Badland Batteries describes its Fargo operation as the first UAS-specific battery manufacturing facility designed to control the complete manufacturing process, beginning with raw material sourcing and qualification. The company plans to use domestic or allied-sourced raw materials with full traceability. This approach is intended to strengthen supply chain security while giving customers greater visibility into the origins and production of critical battery components. Integrated Battery Cell and Pack Manufacturing The new facility will handle lithium-ion pouch cell production, beginning with raw material sourcing and in-house material qualification. Once cells are manufactured, they can be transported to Badland Batteries’ existing manufacturing and assembly facility located approximately one mile away. That second facility provides the capability to assemble completed cells into customer-ready battery packs. The combined operations create a manufacturing workflow covering: - Raw material sourcing - Material qualification - Lithium-ion cell production - Battery cell manufacturing - Battery pack assembly - Customer-ready power systems The company said this integrated approach is intended to provide a reliable domestic source of batteries for UAS and other autonomous platforms. Production Capacity Exceeds 15,000 Battery Cells Per Day Badland Batteries said the new facility has the ability to produce more than 15,000 lithium-ion battery cells per day. The company also designed the manufacturing operation with the flexibility to increase production as demand grows. The announced figure represents the facility’s production capacity rather than a confirmed current daily output. Actual production volumes, battery cell specifications and customer delivery schedules were not disclosed in the announcement. The manufacturing capacity is intended to support growing demand for domestically produced energy storage technologies across defense, aerospace and autonomous systems markets. Federal Investment Supports North Dakota Battery Industry The facility opening brought together federal, state, local, industry and military representatives. U.S. Senator John Hoeven highlighted the importance of domestic battery manufacturing for national security and economic competitiveness. “Building a strong domestic battery ecosystem is critical to our nation’s economic competitiveness and national security,” Hoeven said. “That’s why we’ve worked over the last six years to secure more than $50 million in federal funding to advance these efforts in North Dakota.” Hoeven said the Badland Batteries investment supports efforts to expand American manufacturing, create skilled employment opportunities and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The announcement does not specify how much of the referenced federal funding was awarded directly to Badland Batteries. artigo.texto: CONNEAUT, Ohio — The debate over data centers is reaching the ballot box in Conneaut, where voters will decide in November whether to ban data center developments larger than 25 megawatts. A group of residents gathered enough signatures to place a charter amendment on the ballot. Read the charter amendment here: Among those who rallied the signatures are Julia Barton and Susan Ferritto, who understand the allure for businesses to come to Conneaut. “Our infrastructure is absolutely the most attractive, maybe in the state,” Ferritto said. “We’ve got the lake, the rail, the highways.” At Northridge by Octagon Acres, Julia Barton and her family grow blueberries, strawberries and chestnuts. Barton said concerns about protecting the area's natural resources are part of why she is paying close attention to the data center debate. Watch the story here: “If we don’t protect the natural resources, the soil, the land, the water, the air that sustains us, then we won’t be able to eat,” Barton said. Growth Partnership for Ashtabula County, the area's economic development organization, says on its website that a developer is conducting a feasibility study at a Conneaut industrial park. The organization also identifies two other sites that are being explored as potential locations for data centers. The effort comes despite Conneaut City Manager Nick Sanford saying the city has never received a formal proposal from a data center company. “We don’t have a proposal for a data center, we never have, it’s just been due diligence,” Sanford said. Two months ago, the city declined to impose a one-year moratorium on data centers. “It has become a critically hot-button issue,” Sanford said. “A charter amendment, I don’t believe, has ever happened in the city’s history." Supporters of the ballot measure say they want the community to determine what kinds of development it accepts rather than waiting until a project is formally proposed. “We do not have to take the first thing that comes to us for revenue, for jobs, for the growth in our community,” Ferritto said. “Communities should have a say with what happens where they live,” Barton said. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Clay LePard is the Ashtabula, Geauga and Portage counties reporter at News 5 Cleveland. artigo.texto: As data center rumors swirl, Livingston Parish President meets with battery storage company NextEra has fueled data center speculation with battery storage facility planned for parish LIVINGSTON PARISH, La. — Livingston Parish President Randy Delatte said he met with representatives from NextEra Energy as the company explores building a battery storage facility in the parish. The energy capacity of the proposed facility has fueled speculation of a possible data center development in the parish. Delatte said NextEra officials are in the parish meeting with government and business leaders. The company has filed with MISO, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator that oversees the power grid in 15 states including Louisiana, and is exploring several sites statewide. “We will be monitoring their progress in Livingston and will keep you informed,” Delatte said. No project has been finalized. Permitting records describe NextEra’s proposed 500-megawatt facility as intended to power an unnamed commercial development. That language has fueled speculation about a possible data center tied to a 690-acre site off Buddy Ellis Road, which was rezoned from residential to industrial in November 2025. Livingston Parish’s Economic Development Council (LEDC) told WAFB that plot of land is not a part of the properties it has been marketing to the state for possible large industrial developments. Delatte has previously said a facility of that size could support a data center. “I would wanna say, without starting a rumor, it would need that much power to power a data plant and more,” Delatte said. “I wanna approach this the right way, but if NextEra comes down here, then that’s smoke; where there’s smoke, there’s fire.” Delatte said he has not signed any non-disclosure agreements related to the project, citing transparency. Councilman Ricky Goff has said he did sign a confidentiality agreement tied to the rezoned site on Buddy Ellis Road. Residents near Buddy Ellis Road have raised concerns about water use, noise and property values. Delatte said any tenant would need parish approval and vowed no project will move forward with an adverse impact on residents. What is MISO and why does the filing matter? MISO — the Midcontinent Independent System Operator — manages the power grid across 15 states, including Louisiana. Energy companies like NextEra must file with MISO to connect large projects to the grid and study impacts on reliability. A MISO filing does not mean a project is approved or finalized. It is an early step in the permitting process that signals where the company is exploring development. NextEra is exploring multiple sites statewide, according to Delatte. artigo.texto: A falta de definição sobre a aplicação de incentivos tributários aos projetos de armazenamento de energia pode elevar os custos de financiamento e comprometer a competitividade dos leilões de baterias previstos para dezembro de 2026. O alerta é da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), que defende o esclarecimento das regras do Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento da Infraestrutura (Reidi) antes dos certames, para evitar que os custos adicionais sejam repassados aos consumidores por meio dos encargos setoriais. Em ofício encaminhado em 13 de outubro ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) e ao Ministério da Fazenda, a associação pediu ajustes no Decreto nº 6.144/2007 para viabilizar o acesso dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia (SAE) ao regime especial. A Lei nº 15.269/2025 incluiu esses empreendimentos no Reidi e estabeleceu um limite de R$ 1 bilhão por exercício para a renúncia fiscal, condicionado à previsão na Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA). A regulamentação, porém, ainda não foi atualizada. Os leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) para armazenamento estão previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Para a Absae, a definição antecipada das regras tributárias é necessária para que os participantes considerem o benefício na formação dos preços dos lances. A entidade também defende que os editais esclareçam como o Reidi será aplicado aos projetos, já que a aprovação pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) está prevista para até 27 de outubro. Se não houver tempo para concluir os ajustes regulatórios até essa data, a associação considera que a publicação do decreto antes dos leilões ainda poderá oferecer mais segurança aos investidores, já que, sem uma definição, os participantes podem adotar premissas tributárias diferentes, incluir margens de segurança nos cálculos ou exigir maior remuneração para investir nos projetos. Essa incerteza, segundo a entidade, pode prejudicar a comparação entre as propostas e a eficiência econômica dos certames. Impacto financeiro de R$ 36,4 milhões em projetos de 2 GW Para demonstrar os possíveis efeitos da ausência do benefício, a associação considerou um investimento de R$ 5 mil/kW, com base no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE) 2035, e uma contratação hipotética de 2 GW. Nesse cenário, o investimento total seria de R$ 10 bilhões. Considerando, apenas para fins ilustrativos, uma alíquota de referência de 9,21% para a CBS em 2027, a Absae estima que o tributo poderia representar cerca de R$ 921 milhões sobre essa base. O valor efetivamente sujeito à tributação e elegível ao Reidi dependerá da composição dos investimentos de cada projeto. A associação também adotou um prazo aproximado de 105 dias para a recuperação dos valores e uma taxa Selic de 13,75% ao ano. Com essas premissas, estimou um custo financeiro de aproximadamente R$ 36,4 milhões durante o período. A Absae ressalta que os valores são ilustrativos e que o impacto decorre da necessidade de antecipar recursos enquanto os créditos tributários não são recuperados. Mesmo com o ressarcimento posterior, o custo de financiar esse intervalo pode afetar a rentabilidade e a estrutura econômica dos empreendimentos. Incentivo reduz necessidade de financiamento dos projetos Com base nesse contexto, a Absae pede esclarecimentos sobre a aplicação do benefício diante da exceção prevista na Lei Complementar nº 224/2025 para incentivos sujeitos a limite quantitativo global e a habilitação ou autorização administrativa prévia. Outro pedido é o reconhecimento de que a exclusão da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS) e do Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS) da formação da receita fixa prevista nos editais não afasta nem torna desnecessária a aplicação do Reidi. O enquadramento no regime permite suspender a incidência de PIS/Pasep e Cofins sobre a aquisição de bens e a contratação de serviços destinados à implantação de projetos de infraestrutura. Entretanto, a partir de 1º de janeiro de 2027, está prevista a extinção dessas contribuições e a introdução da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS) e do Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS), conforme a Emenda Constitucional nº 132/2023 e a Lei Complementar nº 214/2025, posteriormente alterada pela Lei Complementar nº 227/2026. A Absae argumenta que a exclusão da CBS e do IBS da formação da receita fixa dos contratos não elimina a importância do Reidi. Pelas minutas dos editais, a receita fixa deverá contemplar os custos necessários à implantação e à prestação do serviço de armazenamento, com exceção desses dois tributos. A regra busca evitar que a incerteza sobre suas alíquotas afete os preços dos lances. O ponto central, segundo a associação, é o intervalo entre o pagamento dos tributos e a recuperação dos valores. Sem o Reidi, os investidores podem precisar utilizar recursos próprios ou contratar financiamento para pagar os tributos incidentes sobre os investimentos e aguardar a posterior recuperação por meio de créditos, compensação ou ressarcimento. Esse intervalo é especialmente relevante para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, que exigem investimentos elevados antes do início da receita fixa contratada. A aquisição de baterias, inversores, sistemas de conversão e outros equipamentos ocorre durante a implantação, enquanto os pagamentos previstos nos contratos começam posteriormente. Por isso, a entidade avalia que a possibilidade de recuperar créditos tributários não elimina o custo financeiro da antecipação dos recursos. A aplicação do Reidi reduziria a necessidade de capital de giro e poderia favorecer a competitividade dos projetos. artigo.texto: Imagine que você liga para o seu mecânico e fala: “o carro não pegou hoje de manhã, deve ser a bateria”. Em vez de concordar, ele responde com uma pergunta: “como você usa o carro durante a semana?”. Você estranha. Afinal, o que o seu trajeto até o trabalho tem a ver com um carro que não liga? Tem tudo a ver, e é isso que vamos traduzir hoje. Olá, queridos e queridas! Segunda-feira, 7h40, você gira a chave (ou aperta o botão) e o carro faz um “rrr... rrr...” sem vontade, ou nem isso. O painel acende fraco, o rádio reinicia, e vem o veredicto de sempre: “a bateria morreu do nada”. Mas ontem estava tudo certo, não estava? Bateria quase nunca morre do nada. Leia também - Troca de óleo a cada 10 mil km é regra ou é lenda? - Tudo sobre a gasolina E35: separando fato de boato antes que você acredite em qualquer coisa O que costuma acontecer é que ela vinha avisando e ninguém traduziu. E, em muitos casos, ela nem é a culpada: é só a vítima. Para entender isso, é preciso saber o que ela faz. A bateria não guarda eletricidade; ela guarda energia química, uma reação entre os componentes internos que se converte em energia elétrica na hora que o carro pede. Na partida, ela entrega muita corrente em poucos segundos para o motor de arranque. Mas o trabalho não acaba aí: com o motor desligado, é ela que mantém alarme, memórias e módulos vivos, e com o motor ligado ela ajuda a estabilizar a tensão do sistema elétrico. Quem a recarrega é o alternador. Pense na bateria como a caixa d’água da casa e no alternador como a bomba que a enche. Se a caixa estiver furada, você enche e ela esvazia. Se a bomba estiver fraca, a caixa nunca enche direito. Trocar a caixa d’água quando o problema é a bomba só garante uma caixa nova que nunca enche. E quanto tempo dura uma bateria? Não existe prazo universal, e desconfie de quem prometeu um. Trajetos curtos e frequentes não dão tempo de o carro repor a energia gasta na partida, então a conta nunca fecha. Carro parado por semanas vai se descarregando sozinho. O calor castiga a estrutura interna, e o frio exige mais dela na hora da partida. Um carro cheio de demanda elétrica (multimídia, câmeras, acessórios instalados depois) pede mais da bateria do que um carro simples. Dois veículos iguais, com donos e rotinas diferentes, podem ter vidas de bateria bem diferentes. É por isso que o mecânico perguntou do seu trajeto. Os avisos costumam aparecer antes da falha. Partida mais lenta que o normal, principalmente de manhã ou depois de alguns dias parado. Carro que “acorda cansado” depois de um período sem uso. Luzes que enfraquecem na partida, vidros mais lentos, multimídia reiniciando sozinho. Em carros com Start-Stop, o sistema deixar de atuar ou atuar de um jeito estranho também pode ser sinal, já que ele depende de condições da bateria para funcionar. Mas atenção: sintoma não é diagnóstico. Cada um desses sinais pode ter outra origem, e quem fecha a conta é o teste, não o palpite. Aliás, uma frase que ouço muito na oficina é “medi com o multímetro e a tensão está boa”. Medir só a tensão é como medir a temperatura de uma pessoa e concluir que ela está em forma para correr uma maratona. A tensão em repouso mostra quanto de carga a bateria tem naquele momento, mas não mostra se ela aguenta o esforço da partida. Uma bateria desgastada pode marcar uma tensão aceitável parada e não sustentar a corrente quando é exigida. O que revela a condição real é um teste apropriado, com equipamento próprio. E o teste não termina nela: é preciso avaliar o sistema de carga, ou seja, se o alternador está carregando como deveria com o motor funcionando. Outro engano comum é achar que bateria é tudo igual. Não é. A convencional é a mais simples e atende carros sem muita exigência. A EFB é uma evolução desse conceito, pensada para suportar melhor o ciclo de muitas partidas e paradas, comum em carros com Start-Stop mais básico. A AGM tem outra construção interna, é mais robusta em ciclos de carga e descarga e costuma ser exigida em carros com sistemas mais exigentes. Qual delas o seu carro precisa depende do projeto, e o lugar para descobrir é o manual do proprietário e a especificação do fabricante. Trocar por uma tecnologia inferior à exigida, só para economizar, é uma aposta bem ruim. E mesmo dentro da tecnologia certa, duas baterias de 60 Ah não são necessariamente iguais. O Ah indica a capacidade, ou seja, quanta energia ela armazena. Mas existem ainda a corrente de partida a frio (CCA), as dimensões, a posição dos pólos e as exigências do fabricante. É como dois tênis número 40: o número é o mesmo, mas um é de corrida e o outro é de passeio. Há ainda um detalhe que pouca gente conta: em alguns veículos, principalmente os com gerenciamento eletrônico de energia, a troca pode exigir registro da nova bateria ou algum procedimento específico. Isso não vale para todo carro, e é justamente por isso que vale perguntar antes de sair da oficina: “o meu exige algo depois da troca?”. Já a chupeta, quando bate à pressa, parece a solução óbvia. Mas improvisar pode gerar faísca, inversão de polaridade e danos a módulos eletrônicos. Muitos manuais trazem orientações próprias ou até pontos específicos para partida auxiliar. Se for fazer, faça como o fabricante prevê. E se você trocou a bateria e, meses depois, o problema voltou? Antes de culpar a bateria nova, vale investigar o resto. O alternador está carregando bem? Existe alguma fuga de corrente, algo consumindo energia com o carro desligado? E o seu jeito de usar o carro combina com a bateria que foi escolhida? Voltando à ligação para o mecânico: a pergunta dele sobre o seu trajeto não era conversa fiada, era o início do diagnóstico. Ele queria saber se a bateria está ruim, se ela é a certa para o seu carro e se o sistema que a mantém carregada está funcionando. São exatamente as três perguntas que você deve levar para a oficina. E no fim das contas, quem faz essas perguntas deixa de ser refém daquela frase “troca que resolve”. Pergunte antes de pagar.

artigo.texto: A transmissão de energia e a geração hidrelétrica estão entre os segmentos do setor elétrico brasileiro com maiores riscos acumulados associados às mudanças climáticas, segundo estudo da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Enquanto as hidrelétricas estão mais expostas à redução das chuvas e ao prolongamento das secas, a infraestrutura de transmissão enfrenta ameaças relacionadas a temporais, ventos extremos e aumento das temperaturas. Para reduzir essas vulnerabilidades, a EPE propõe reforçar as linhas de transmissão, ampliar o armazenamento de energia e incorporar projeções climáticas ao planejamento de novos empreendimentos. As recomendações integram o Roadmap para Fortalecimento da Resiliência do Setor Elétrico Brasileiro em Resposta às Mudanças Climáticas, publicado nesta quarta-feira, 14 de outubro. O documento apresenta seis estratégias de adaptação, que abrangem desde investimentos em infraestrutura até mudanças nos procedimentos operacionais e na gestão da demanda. Segundo a EPE, os riscos mais relevantes estão associados ao aumento das temperaturas extremas e ondas de calor, à intensificação de chuvas extremas e à maior frequência e duração das secas. Esses fenômenos podem reduzir a disponibilidade de água para geração hidrelétrica, danificar instalações de transmissão e elevar o consumo de eletricidade, especialmente para refrigeração. No cenário intermediário analisado pelo estudo, esses impactos já apresentam classificações de risco alto no curto prazo, entre 2021 e 2040, para determinados segmentos do sistema elétrico. A EPE destaca que os efeitos podem ocorrer simultaneamente. Ondas de calor, por exemplo, podem elevar a demanda por eletricidade em períodos de menor disponibilidade hídrica, pressionando o atendimento ao consumo. As temperaturas elevadas também podem reduzir a capacidade de transmissão de energia, agravando o desequilíbrio entre oferta e demanda. Secas, chuvas e ventos extremos Para as hidrelétricas, os principais fatores de risco são a redução das precipitações médias, o aumento da frequência e duração das secas e a ocorrência de chuvas extremas. A menor disponibilidade hídrica pode comprometer a produção de energia e a gestão dos reservatórios. Já episódios de precipitação intensa podem exigir vertimentos e medidas de controle de cheias, além de provocar assoreamento e danos às instalações. No caso da transmissão, os riscos estão principalmente associados a ventos severos, descargas atmosféricas e chuvas extremas, capazes de danificar estruturas e interromper o transporte de energia. O estudo também identifica impactos do aumento das temperaturas sobre a eficiência dos equipamentos e a capacidade de transmissão. Para o período de 2041 a 2060, no cenário intermediário, os danos à infraestrutura de transmissão decorrentes de chuvas e ventos extremos são classificados como risco alto. A redução da disponibilidade hídrica para geração e o aumento da demanda também aparecem nessa categoria. Reforço da rede e ampliação do armazenamento Entre as medidas propostas para enfrentar esses riscos, a EPE recomenda reforçar as infraestruturas existentes, utilizar equipamentos e materiais mais resistentes às condições climáticas futuras e ampliar redundâncias para reduzir a vulnerabilidade de ativos estratégicos. O documento também defende a expansão e o reforço da rede de transmissão para preservar a continuidade do fornecimento diante dos impactos climáticos. Outra frente é a ampliação da flexibilidade e da capacidade de armazenamento de energia, apontada como instrumento para fortalecer a segurança do suprimento e reduzir os efeitos da variabilidade climática. A EPE recomenda ainda promover a diversificação e a complementaridade da matriz elétrica, considerando as diferenças regionais e sazonais de disponibilidade dos recursos energéticos. O objetivo é reduzir a dependência de fontes sujeitas às mesmas condições climáticas e ampliar a capacidade de resposta do sistema em situações adversas. O roadmap também propõe fomentar a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento de novas tecnologias e materiais voltados à resiliência das instalações elétricas. Novos projetos devem considerar mudanças no clima Uma das principais recomendações é incorporar de forma sistemática os riscos climáticos aos estudos de planejamento e às decisões de investimento no setor elétrico. A EPE defende que a localização e o dimensionamento de novos empreendimentos considerem as condições climáticas futuras, de modo a antecipar vulnerabilidades e orientar a escolha das soluções de infraestrutura. O documento também recomenda reavaliar as premissas e os critérios utilizados no planejamento da expansão, além de desenvolver metodologias específicas para avaliar a resiliência climática dos ativos. A proposta representa uma mudança na abordagem tradicional de planejamento, ao considerar não apenas as condições históricas de temperatura, precipitação e disponibilidade de recursos, mas também possíveis alterações dessas variáveis ao longo da vida útil dos empreendimentos. A EPE ressalta, contudo, que as projeções climáticas estão sujeitas a incertezas e que as decisões precisam ser robustas diante de diferentes cenários, sem perder a capacidade de adaptação à medida que novas informações se tornem disponíveis. Resposta da demanda e redes inteligentes O estudo também propõe ampliar os mecanismos de resposta da demanda para reduzir a pressão sobre o sistema elétrico durante períodos críticos. Entre as medidas estão programas estruturados para redução ou deslocamento do consumo, além de mecanismos tarifários que reflitam as condições operativas e os custos do sistema, incluindo horários de ponta e situações de escassez. >>> ONS propõe prorrogar sandbox de resposta da demanda até 2030 e ampliar flexibilidade A EPE recomenda expandir a integração entre consumidores e o sistema elétrico por meio de redes inteligentes e infraestrutura de medição avançada, como smart grids e smart meters. artigo.texto: Taking the routers out of fiber networks will unlock de-centralized data center architectures. Orange and NTT show how - Summary: - The IOWN Global Forum hopes to make data centers tens of kilometers apart behave as one. At least with regard to latency. The upshot is that it might support smaller, distributed data centers better tuned to energy and data sovereignty requirements. Fiber optics has carried most long-distance network traffic for decades. But current networks face numerous speed bumps arising from routers that turn photons into electrons and back again. That’s an impediment for AI workloads that demand many more back-and-forth exchanges that depend on previous ones. Thus, a lot of the hyperscalers are planning to build super-data centers of sorts and raising all sorts of environmental, energy, and sovereignty concerns in the process. But what if you could smooth over the speed bumps and make a bunch of tiny data centers look like one? New sites could be situated right next to renewables or privacy-sensitive enterprise data. That’s the ambition of the Innovative Optical and Wireless Network (IOWN) Global Forum, which has been developing standards and testbeds for All-Photonic Networks (APNs). It was formed in 2020 by NTT, Sony and Intel and now counts more than 180 members. At its recent meeting in Amsterdam, members worked on a common set of requirements for designing and deploying APNs, which is to be released later this year. Eric Hardouin, Vice President of Networks and Infrastructure Research at Orange, says Orange joined in 2021 to help tame costs and reduce its carbon footprint. He says the original Forum vision was about using APN to increase data rates while reducing energy and latency. But then AI changed the importance of low latency. On top of that, local opposition and limited access to power are restricting where data centers can be built. Very fast links were a side effect of APNs rather than the goal. He says: To be honest, the use cases for extremely low latency were not so clear at the time for us. It was, I would say, a consequence of the all-photonic networks, but we weren’t sure about what would be the applications. Now, with the need to distribute computing across different nodes, the latency benefit is very clear. Multiple patterns Masahisa Kawashima, IOWN Technology Director at NTT and chair of the IOWN Global Forum’s Technology Working Group, sorts the work into three patterns: Scale-Across for joining data centers into larger clusters, Sync-Across for replication, and Reach-Across for connecting enterprise sites to AI data centers: Typically the industry is talking about Scale-Across use cases, which is to make the computing capacity bigger by connecting multiple data centers. On the other hand, Sync-Across is focusing on making the data infrastructure more resilient by connecting multiple data centers and enabling synchronous data replication across data centers. Another important concept is Reach-Across, which is about connecting computing infrastructure with customer places like enterprise R&D campus or industrial facilities, because now we are moving from developing AI to using AI. Reach-Across is trying to connect such enterprise campuses with AI data centers with high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnect, so that the data stored in user premises can be accessed from GPU computing nodes in the data centers without any performance degradation. The Forum has been running technical and financial tests of equipment and configurations for these patterns. For example, one Reach-Across demo trained an AI model on remote data with one to two percent duration overhead. They are also seeing some promising results with replicating operational databases, which met the targets set by the Forum’s financial services members. An earlier trial linked two AI data centers 40 kilometers apart to operate as one with only two percent duration overhead. Adding visibility and control APNs also need new affordances for visibility and control, since they remove the routers and switches, or packet-forwarding nodes, operators have used to troubleshoot problems. Kawashima explains: Network digital twin aims to digitalize the state of the optical transport system, so that we can identify the point of failure. And also, by developing a digital twin system, we can simulate the optical communication with DWDM [dense wavelength division multiplexing], and that will allow us to optimize the optical route and the transceiver parameters for reliable communication. Orange is helping build an open-source controller for these networks. Hardouin says: One of the pieces of work where we, Orange, are particularly involved is an open source optical network controller that allows us to control equipment from several vendors. And this is also one aspect of the work which is being done in the Global Forum to make sure that we can have this end-to-end Open APN with several vendors being involved, and all of this being controllable by the operator. Bolstering sovereignty with encrypted compute An obvious worry with de-centralized networks is that sensitive data can leave an enterprise’s estate. Thus, the Forum has tested ways to combine remote GPU access over APN with confidential computing, which keeps data encrypted even while a processor is working on it. Kawashima explains: With IOWN APN, we can have remote GPU processes run, retrieving enterprise data through fast storage access. But at the same time, enterprises are concerned about the data leakage risk that comes from the use of third parties’ GPU resources. So what we did is we combined a confidential computing technology with our design, meaning that the AI computing process that runs on GPU data centers will run with confidential computing technologies. artigo.texto: DETROIT (WXYZ) — Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Congressman John James squared off Thursday night in their second gubernatorial debate, clashing over a range of issues that included data centers, healthcare costs, energy prices and Michigan's economic future. WATCH the report here: The debate, held at WDIV studios in downtown Detroit, featured sharp exchanges as both candidates sought to draw contrasts with one another ahead of the election. James criticized Benson's record in statewide office, arguing Michigan needs a different approach to leadership. “Michigan has been on fire and she’s been in Lansing for eight years holding the can,” James said. “Maybe we should try something different.” Benson responded with attacks of her own, accusing James of putting personal interests ahead of Michigan residents. “My opponent is only in this for himself,” Benson said. “In just four short years in Congress, he’s become a multimillionaire.” One of the most heavily discussed topics of the night was the future of data centers in Michigan, a growing issue in communities weighing the potential economic benefits against concerns about water use, energy consumption and noise. Benson said Michigan should establish safeguards that protect local communities while allowing development. “We have to put guardrails in place to protect local voices,” Benson said, adding that data center companies should be responsible for their own energy demands and comply with community benefit agreements. James argued local residents should have the final say on whether projects move forward in their communities. “If you want a data center, fine. If you don’t want a data center, fine,” James said. “It should be up to you and not the powerful people in Lansing.” The candidates also outlined competing plans to address the rising cost of living. Benson pointed to proposals focused on reducing healthcare costs, expanding affordable childcare and increasing housing affordability. “My plan will actually ensure that we are working with you to drive down the cost of healthcare and invest in clean energy infrastructure to reduce the cost of energy,” she said. James emphasized lowering energy costs by rolling back regulations. “There’s no reason Indiana and Ohio should have double-digit lower energy rates than us,” James said. Other issues raised during the debate included gas prices, education and Michigan’s relationship with Canada. For some voters, however, the focus wasn't on the political attacks. “I’m going to have to find out which candidate has that kind of focus, not bashing the other politician, but just telling me what you’re going to do,” said Lakeisha Conley, an undecided voter. “I don’t care if they’re doing bad. Tell me you’re good.” Detroit resident Carolyn Preston said she wants Michigan’s next governor to be transparent and focused on serving residents. “Someone to be transparent and someone who is for the state of Michigan, not themselves,” Preston said. The debate marked another opportunity for voters to hear directly from the candidates as the race for Michigan governor continues to take shape.
