artigo.texto: Data Centers (KM Stock/Shutterstock) Publicado em 13 de outubro de 2026 às 21h10. A recente sanção da Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), colocou a infraestrutura digital brasileira no centro da agenda econômica no país. Mas, para além de criar um regime tributário para um setor específico, o Redata oferece a oportunidade de aproximar duas agendas que ainda são frequentemente tratadas de maneira separada: o aumento da capacidade de processamento de dados em território brasileiro e o fortalecimento de uma cadeia industrial para tornar essa expansão possível. Data centers são infraestruturas de engenharia de alta complexidade, cujos efeitos ultrapassam o setor de tecnologia, mobilizando verticais estratégicas como energia, construção civil, telecomunicações e serviços especializados. Dentro deles existem muito mais do que servidores de processamento: são utilizados sistemas elétricos, transformadores, painéis e equipamentos de distribuição, UPS, barramentos, sistemas de refrigeração de alta eficiência, automação, controle, cabos, estruturas metálicas e uma extensa cadeia de serviços especializados para instalação e manutenção desses equipamentos. Isso significa que cada novo megawatt de capacidade de data center no país representa também uma nova demanda para uma cadeia física e industrial - muito maior do que normalmente aparece quando se discute economia digital. Cada novo projeto impulsiona a procura por equipamentos, sistemas, engenharia e serviços, fomenta a criação de postos de trabalho e acelera a necessidade de habilidades verdes (green skills) e qualificações técnicas em pilares essenciais para sustentar o avanço da inteligência artificial (IA). Um estudo da FGV Projetos, utilizando a Matriz Insumo-Produto do IBGE, ajuda a dimensionar esse potencial. Para cada R$ 1 de demanda final associada ao setor de data centers é gerado R$ 1,45 em valor de produção na economia, considerando desdobramentos diretos e indiretos. Outro dado é ainda mais relevante para a discussão industrial: R$ 1,16 desse resultado ocorre por meio da ativação da cadeia de fornecedores. O mesmo encadeamento aparece na geração de empregos. Para cada R$ 1 milhão investido, a FGV estima cerca de 7,5 empregos diretos e indiretos, incluindo aqueles originados na cadeia de fornecedores. Esses números contribuem para tangibilizar o fato de que parcela expressiva do impacto econômico de um data center acontece do lado de fora e, quanto maior a participação de fornecedores instalados no país, maior tende a ser a parcela do investimento que permanece e se multiplica dentro da economia nacional. Da mesma forma, quanto maior e mais previsível for a demanda doméstica por data centers, maior será a possibilidade de ampliar a escala, a produtividade e a competitividade da nossa indústria, assegurando novas linhas de produção, investimentos em capacidade produtiva, desenvolvimento tecnológico e qualificação de fornecedores. Estamos falando, portanto, de uma relação de interdependência, na qual data centers competitivos necessitam de uma indústria forte e competitiva, e uma indústria apta a competir globalmente precisa de mercados que gerem escala e demanda tecnológica. Por isso, o debate sobre o desenvolvimento dos data centers no Brasil não pode correr o risco de ser limitado a uma escolha entre “incentivo ao investimento estrangeiro” ou “proteção da indústria nacional”. Essa é uma abordagem míope que apequena uma lógica de ecossistema a uma falsa dicotomia. O que a experiência internacional e a dinâmica dos mercados mostram é que é factível atrair capital, tecnologia e capacidade computacional e, ao mesmo tempo, tracionar nossa cadeia de fornecedores, engenharia, inovação e produção nacional. Isso não implica pressupor que todos os componentes necessários à infraestrutura digital devam ser manufaturados no país – aliás, nenhuma grande economia é autossuficiente na cadeia de infraestrutura digital. Com isso, o desafio de uma política industrial moderna é combinar o acesso competitivo às tecnologias que ainda não produzidas localmente com condições para que a indústria brasileira consolide sua participação à medida em que o mercado doméstico ganha escala. A primeira premissa para a concretização desse cenário, porém, é que novos projetos sejam viabilizados. É neste ponto que reside a importância da regulamentação do Redata e da aprovação do convênio nacional, no âmbito do Confaz, para reduzir o ICMS sobre alguns equipamentos específicos. Afinal, se a infraestrutura brasileira continuar mais cara do que a de mercados concorrentes – e atualmente o custo econômico para um data center no Brasil é 26,7% maior do que nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo – o país perde competitividade na disputa global por esses investimentos. Quando um projeto de infraestrutura digital é alocado em outro mercado, ele leva consigo a demanda que poderia alavancar a indústria local - sem mencionar as atividades econômicas habilitadas na cadeia downstream, que dependem de capacidade computacional, nuvem e IA. Por isso, desenvolvedores de data centers e fabricantes nacionais estão olhando para o mesmo horizonte. Ambos dependem de um ecossistema competitivo, capaz de atrair investimentos, estimular demanda, desenvolver tecnologia e incrementar a produção local. É nessa articulação entre políticas públicas, investimentos privados e indústria de alta eficiência que o tamanho da participação brasileira na nova economia global será definido. *Rafael Segrera é presidente da Schneider Electric para a América do Sul e líder do grupo de trabalho "Fostering Human and Social Development", da Sustainable Business COP (SB COP) *Luciano Fialho é vice-presidente Sênior de Desenvolvimento Corporativo, Energia e Imóveis da Scala Data Centers

artigo.texto: Open specs could cut AI data center hardware integration from a year to months As AI factories scale, hardware interoperability is becoming as important as raw performance. Accelerators, memory and storage now come from many different suppliers, and every mismatch between them slows deployment across the data center. Pressure is mounting as AI infrastructure bottlenecks shift attention from individual chips to entire systems. Open communities such as the Open Compute Project, or OCP, integrate separately developed technologies, from Peripheral Component Interconnect Express to Compute Express Link, or CXL, into complete systems that many suppliers can build, according to Siamak Tavallaei (pictured), senior principal engineer at Samsung Semiconductor, a unit of Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. “There are different companies skilled in different aspects of the problem. And you would like to, as an integrator, as an open industry … take advantage of all of that,” Tavallaei said. “Therefore, interoperability matters a lot.” Tavallaei spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at the AI Data Pipeline Forum, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why open specifications matter for hardware interoperability and how they can shorten the time it takes hyperscalers to adopt new designs. (* Disclosure below.) Why hardware interoperability depends on open integration Tavallaei’s work with OCP traces back to his time at Microsoft Corp.’s Azure cloud, where he co-led OCP’s server project. Large cloud operators kept asking suppliers to build the same hardware, but each supplier read the specification differently, so server fleets drifted apart, he explained. “Software was what Microsoft was doing well, but we wanted hardware to be common so a number of our suppliers could build the same thing,” Tavallaei said. A finished system handed to OCP as a monolithic contribution may never catch on, while one shaped in the open draws input from many companies, according to Tavallaei. That broader buy-in brings volume and more engineers working on the same problems. “If you were to work that with the community, different people will interject their own ideas, and at the end, story will be something that a number of different companies would like, and therefore adoption goes up,” Tavallaei said. “When adoption goes up, volume goes up.” Memory is the next proving ground. Samsung recently demonstrated CXL memory pooling with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. at the OCP summit, and Tavallaei is bringing the CXL specification into OCP’s Composable Memory Systems subproject. The bet is that hardware interoperability will sharply cut the time hyperscalers need to adopt new designs. “When a specific thing is built for, for example, one hyperscaler, a different hyperscaler trying to reintegrate that takes time, about nine months, 12 months of reintegrating,” Tavallaei said. “Whereas if things are crisply defined in a specification, when something is good and is recognized, integrating that into a new hyperscale data center might take three months or six months instead of a year or year and a half.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Data Pipeline Forum: (* Disclosure: ScaleFlux Inc. sponsored this segment of theCUBE. artigo.texto: A Corning começou a produzir, este ano, cabos e conectores ópticos para data centers no Brasil, por meio de parceiros qualificados no estado de São Paulo. A operação busca reduzir os prazos de entrega, que chegavam a aproximadamente 40 dias quando os produtos dependiam de importações. A empresa também prepara a oferta de cabos com 288 fibras ópticas para atender às necessidades de conexão interna dos centros de dados. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Vertiv reforça equipe no Brasil para atender expansão de data centers A movimentação ocorre no momento em que o mercado é impulsionado pela expansão dos data centers e pela necessidade de infraestrutura para aplicações de inteligência artificial (IA). Para a Corning, o crescimento desse segmento abre oportunidades para soluções com maior densidade de fibras, capazes de acomodar um número crescente de conexões em espaços limitados. “Na verdade, não é uma aposta. É concreto. Todos os operadores já estão construindo data centers. Estão com projetos em andamento e planos de expandir mais ainda, com outros data centers por vir”, diz Antônio Augusto B. Macedo, gerente de produto de Data Center para a América Latina na Corning Segundo ele, a produção local atende à demanda atual do mercado brasileiro, concentrada principalmente em cabos de até 144 fibras. A companhia não informou o volume fabricado no país nem apresentou dados sobre a capacidade produtiva. Produção local reduz prazos de entrega Até recentemente, o fornecimento dos produtos dependia de importações, com prazos de entrega que chegavam a cerca de 40 dias. Com a estruturação da produção local em 2026, a Corning passou a contar com parceiros no estado de São Paulo para fabricar cabos e conectores ópticos de acordo com os padrões de qualidade da companhia. “Até o ano passado, mais ou menos, a gente tinha tudo a importar, em prazo de 40 dias. Agora, a gente tem uma questão de produção local”, diz o executivo. A fabricação por meio de parceiros qualificados permite à empresa atender às necessidades do mercado brasileiro sem depender exclusivamente do fornecimento externo. Macedo, no entanto, não detalhou a capacidade instalada da operação, os volumes produzidos ou as metas de crescimento para o mercado local. A oferta atual está concentrada em cabos de até 144 fibras ópticas, utilizados principalmente nas conexões internas dos data centers. A empresa prepara a produção para atender também à demanda por cabos de 288 fibras, acompanhando a necessidade de maior densidade nas instalações. Nas conexões externas, que interligam diferentes data centers, a quantidade de fibras pode ser ainda maior. Macedo cita cabos com 864, 1.728 e até 3.456 fibras, conforme a aplicação. Data centers de IA exigem mais conexões ópticas A expansão da inteligência artificial está mudando os requisitos de conectividade dos data centers. Segundo Macedo, instalações destinadas a essas aplicações podem demandar até dez vezes mais fibras do que centros de dados convencionais. O executivo cita a evolução do número de fibras que chegam a um rack: de aproximadamente 100 em configurações anteriores para quase 10 mil em determinados modelos atuais. Em projeções para os próximos dois anos, esse número poderá alcançar 64 mil fibras por rack, dependendo do modelo. O aumento da densidade exige soluções que acomodem mais conexões no mesmo espaço físico. Isso envolve o desenvolvimento de cabos e conectores menores e de tecnologias capazes de ampliar a capacidade de transmissão. Uma das soluções apresentadas pela Corning é a fibra multicore, que reúne quatro núcleos de transmissão em uma mesma fibra. De acordo com Macedo, a tecnologia permite quadruplicar a capacidade de transmissão por fibra em comparação com uma fibra convencional de núcleo único, utilizando cabos e conectores existentes. O lançamento comercial estava previsto para o fim de 2026. Na entrevista, o executivo afirmou que a empresa já havia firmado contratos com alguns clientes, mas ainda não tinha lançado oficialmente a tecnologia. Os primeiros usuários esperados são operadores que constroem grandes data centers voltados à inteligência artificial. No Brasil, a adoção dependerá da evolução dos projetos e dos requisitos de densidade de cada instalação. A Corning não informou se a fibra multicore será fabricada localmente. A produção brasileira mencionada pelo executivo refere-se a cabos e conectores ópticos, enquanto a nova tecnologia ainda estava em fase anterior ao lançamento comercial. Redata pode estimular novos investimentos A Corning avalia que o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) poderá estimular novos projetos no Brasil. Macedo ressalta, porém, que a demanda por infraestrutura não depende exclusivamente da iniciativa governamental e já é sustentada pela digitalização da economia. “Internet banking, redes sociais, streaming de vídeo e games requerem transmissão de dados. Por conta disso, os data centers precisam estar próximos dos consumidores”, afirma. Na avaliação do executivo, a redução de custos tributários poderá tornar o país mais atrativo para empresas interessadas em construir centros de dados. Entre as possibilidades está a instalação de estruturas destinadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial, que concentram grande capacidade de processamento. Macedo diferencia esses ambientes dos data centers voltados a aplicações que exigem baixa latência. No treinamento de modelos de IA, explica, as instalações podem ser construídas em locais nos quais a disponibilidade e o custo da energia sejam fatores determinantes. O executivo considera que o Brasil reúne condições para receber esses projetos, embora avalie que os data centers de inteligência artificial previstos para o país ainda não devam alcançar imediatamente a escala de algumas instalações em construção nos Estados Unidos. artigo.texto: Um grupo de 32 entidades e nove frentes parlamentares pediu ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva que acelere a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em setembro. Em carta aberta, os signatários defendem que as regras permitam o uso de diferentes fontes de energia, incluindo gás natural e nuclear, no suprimento dos empreendimentos beneficiados. A Lei nº 15.504, sancionada em 15 de setembro de 2026, estabelece incentivos tributários para a instalação, modernização e ampliação de data centers no Brasil. Entre os benefícios estão a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins e Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) na aquisição de equipamentos e componentes, além do Imposto de Importação para produtos sem equivalente nacional. Para acessar os incentivos, os empreendimentos deverão atender à totalidade de sua demanda de eletricidade por meio de contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. A legislação, no entanto, deixou para a regulamentação a definição dos critérios de atendimento dessa exigência. Na carta, as entidades defendem uma abordagem tecnologicamente neutra no Redata, que considere hidrelétricas, solares, eólicas, biomassa, biogás, biometano, energia nuclear e gás natural. Segundo os signatários, as regras devem considerar a necessidade de fornecimento firme e contínuo de energia e evitar a transferência de custos associados aos data centers para os demais consumidores do sistema elétrico. O documento reconhece a existência de divergências técnicas no governo, mas propõe que o decreto seja publicado com os parâmetros essenciais do regime, deixando questões ainda não consensuadas para regulamentação posterior, inclusive mediante consulta pública. As entidades também pedem que a lista de equipamentos beneficiados pelos incentivos tributários não seja excessivamente restritiva e solicitam ao governo federal apoio para acelerar as discussões sobre o ICMS no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz). A regulamentação é cobrada cerca de um mês após a sanção da lei, que estabelece prazo até 31 de dezembro de 2026 para os benefícios fiscais relativos ao PIS/Pasep, à Cofins e ao IPI. Entre os signatários estão a Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas (Abraget), a Associação Brasileira de Energia Nuclear (Aben), a Associação Brasileira de Distribuidores de Energia Elétrica (Abradee), a Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado (Abegás), o Instituto Brasileiro de Petróleo, Gás e Biocombustíveis (IBP) e a Associação Brasileira dos Grandes Consumidores de Energia e Consumidores Livres (Abrace Energia).

artigo.texto: Amwins Global Risks (AGR), the specialist global risk division of Amwins, has broadened the scope of its Commercial & Industrial (C&I) insurance facility to include battery energy storage systems (BESS) and electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure. The expanded facility enables developers, owners and investors to insure multiple distributed energy assets across different locations under one insurance programme. AGR said the updated offering is intended to meet the needs of businesses developing portfolios of smaller energy infrastructure projects, which may be spread across several sites but form part of a larger investment. “The expansion is designed to support the growing deployment of distributed energy infrastructure, where individual assets may be relatively small, and geographically dispersed, but collectively represent increasingly substantial portfolios for developers, owners and investors,” commented Dr Tom Harries, Director at Amwins Global Risks. “By aggregating assets within a portfolio, AGR provides a consistent underwriting approach across multiple locations while assessing and managing accumulated natural catastrophe exposure at portfolio level.” The facility will provide insurance options for the construction of EV charging infrastructure in the United States, as well as cover for assets once they are operational. AGR said protection can include Delay in Start-Up (DSU) and Business Interruption (BI), addressing risks that may affect project completion or interrupt business activities. The structure also allows deductibles to be adjusted to reflect the size and risk profile of individual installations. According to AGR, this offers an alternative to insurance arrangements developed for utility-scale projects, under which deductibles may be less suited to smaller assets. AGR said the growth of distributed energy infrastructure has created insurance requirements that do not always fit established models. While traditional cover has often focused on individual projects or large-scale energy developments, battery storage facilities and EV charging networks can comprise numerous smaller installations operating across a broad geographical area. “Individual sites can be relatively small, but developers are increasingly building portfolios comprising numerous assets across multiple locations,”added Harries. “Bringing those assets together allows us to underwrite them efficiently at portfolio scale, while still recognising the individual risk characteristics of each site.” The expanded facility builds on AGR’s existing Community Solar offering, which provides portfolio-based insurance for commercial and community-scale solar installations. By adding battery storage and EV charging infrastructure, AGR is extending its approach to cover a broader range of distributed energy assets. Harries said the inclusion of these technologies will allow AGR to assess how a portfolio’s exposure to natural catastrophes changes as further projects are incorporated. The programme is intended to accommodate portfolio growth while taking account of the risk characteristics of individual sites. “The addition of BESS and EV charging infrastructure reflects the increasing convergence of distributed energy technologies,” said Harries. “It allows us to focus on monitoring how the portfolio’s natural catastrophe exposure changes as new projects are added and gives developers the freedom to concentrate on building out their portfolios, knowing their insurance programme can adapt and grow alongside them.”

artigo.texto: African countries must strengthen cooperation, attract investment and ensure communities receive fair returns to turn the continent’s carbon market potential into climate and economic benefits, experts have said. The call came at the opening of the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026 in Kigali on Wednesday, October 14. The two-day summit brought together around 600 policymakers, investors, project developers, corporate buyers and climate finance stakeholders. Co-organised by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment and the African Development Bank, the summit aims to strengthen African carbon markets and turn climate ambitions into investment-ready projects. ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda’s carbon credit deal with Singapore, Kuwait Rwanda’s Minister for Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said Africa had reached a turning point in deciding how carbon markets operate and whom they benefit. "You are here because, like us, you believe that Africa’s carbon markets must be shaped by African priorities and that they must now deliver,” she told delegates. Despite progress in regulations and agreements, she said, slowing voluntary markets, concerns over credit integrity and a widening climate finance gap demanded renewed efforts. "These are not reasons to retreat. They are reasons to reset—and then build better,” Arakwiye said. From policy to investment Carbon markets generate credits from projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. When properly regulated, they can attract private investment into renewable energy, forest conservation, clean cooking and sustainable agriculture. However, Arakwiye said current market activity did not adequately reflect Africa’s development priorities. Forestry, land-use initiatives and improved cookstoves account for a significant share of African credits, while agriculture has generated barely one per cent of credits issued on voluntary markets over two decades. "The smallholder farmer, who has the most to gain and much to offer, is still standing largely outside this market,” she said. She called for greater investment in renewable energy, electric mobility, waste management, industrial decarbonisation and landscape restoration. Strengthening Africa’s bargaining power Dr Fatmata Lovetta Sesay, UNDP Resident Representative in Rwanda, said African countries needed stronger negotiating capacity despite progress in establishing carbon market regulations and institutions. Following a summit session on readiness to implement Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, she called for clear registration criteria, functional carbon registries, monitoring systems and project pipelines aligned with national priorities. "Africa is not lacking the legal framework that is required to govern how we operate in the carbon markets,” she said. "Africa is not lacking the opportunities that exist on the continent and several other places for this trading to happen.” She urged countries to negotiate from a position of strength and called for continental discussions to improve bargaining power and ensure African countries receive fair value for their climate assets. "This is not a race that is a sprint for countries in Africa. It&039;s a marathon,” she said, noting that countries were progressing at different speeds. Ensuring communities benefit Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa, said carbon markets must channel benefits to communities whose land and conservation efforts make projects possible. He called for stronger community rights and transparent benefit-sharing, early-stage project financing and partnerships based on measurable results. "A registry tracks a credit. It does not settle a land dispute,” he said, stressing the need for community consent and enforceable benefit-sharing arrangements. Gomera urged development banks to finance project preparation, while buyers should offer longer-term purchase agreements and advance funding. "Trust is market infrastructure, not sentiment,” he said. He also stressed the need to recognise the benefits of landscapes, from food production and water regulation to biodiversity and carbon storage, while preventing emissions reductions from being counted or sold twice. Rwanda seeks to diversify carbon credit projects beyond cookstoves Rwanda launched its National Carbon Market Framework in December 2023 to establish rules for developing, authorising, trading and monitoring credits, Arakwiye said. In May 2025, Rwanda and Singapore signed an implementation agreement under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, providing a pathway for authorised carbon credit transfers. Singapore committed to cancelling two per cent of correspondingly adjusted credits at first issuance and directing five per cent of the value of authorised credits towards adaptation measures in Rwanda. Rwanda has registered 29 carbon market projects across forestry, agriculture, land conservation, electric mobility, waste management and renewable energy. However, improved cookstove projects account for around 87 per cent of the country’s issued credits. The government has generated about $1.5 million (Rwf2.2 billion) from carbon credit sales. She called for African-suited methodologies, project-preparation facilities and long-term demand from buyers willing to pay fair prices. Rwanda is also exploring whether carbon revenue could be channelled through the Rwanda Green Fund to prepare and pre-finance projects. artigo.texto: Cass County residents learn more about proposed Harmony Energy Park data center CASS COUNTY, N.D. (Valley News Live) - Cass County residents gathered in Wheatland Tuesday night to learn more about a proposed data center park, with a vote on a building moratorium just over a week away. The conversation on data centers continued as people gathered to learn about what is being called “Harmony Energy Park”. Harmony Energy Park is a proposed powered data park by Geronimo Power in Harmony Township. The property, set to be located off 32nd Street Southeast and 160th Avenue Southeast, would include two main data center buildings. Project details shared with residents Tuesday night, residents had a chance to learn about the 640-acre project, which would keep buildings at least a mile from any home. “We have noticed in our renewable energy business that the data center companies, the large tech companies have been our biggest customers for the past five or six years. When we saw what the power was going for when we were working with these different tech companies, we thought that we saw an opportunity to bring an even more big, and powerful economic opportunity,” said Blake Nixon, CEO and President of Geronimo Power. With Applied Digital building a data center in Harwood, Nixon said there are pros and cons. “When something new comes to town, change is concerning. Everybody wants to know what is this thing? Why? How is it going to impact me and my community? I think being able to see what a data center looks like is actually a really good thing because it’s just 10 miles away. I think it’s a little bit not good in the fact that, that’s a part of an industrial park and it looks like an industrial park. Which of course where we’re developing, is beautiful rural farmland,” Nixon said. Green space and community input About 80% of the space is expected to remain green space. “We’re asking the community to engage with us and tell us, ‘What do you want us to do with the other 80%? Do you want it to be trees? Grass?’ We can make it so you don’t see the data center if you don’t want to see the data center,” Nixon said. Some residents say data centers can have advantages and disadvantages. “I’m not against it coming in, it just needs to come in properly. Just like any other business, manufacturing elevator, you name it. Even farmers themselves on what they do on the land like I do. I should be cognizant of how I affect the community, too,” said Nathan Faleide, a Wheatland resident. For those who may be leaning toward not wanting a data center in the area, Nixon said: “We want to be a valued, added part of this community like we have been in the other places where we do business. We think the data center can be a big part of that story.” Moratorium vote and public forum Harmony Township has proposed a 24-month zoning moratorium on building solar and wind energy facilities as well as data centers. There is set to be a public hearing and proposed vote on October 22nd at 7 p.m. Residents will have another chance to weigh in on AI and data centers Wednesday. The Challey Institute is hosting a public forum from 5:30 to 7 p.m. in the Oceti Sakowin Ballroom at NDSU’s Memorial Union, looking at what data center growth could mean for North Dakota’s power grid, rates and local communities. The forum is free and open to anyone who wants to attend. More information can be found, here. Copyright 2026 KVLY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Datacenters em Pernambuco atestam qualidade e infra digital para negócios Certificações Tier III — divididas em Tier III Design (projeto) e Tier III Facility (instalação e operação) — representam rigor máximo internacional Clique aqui e escute a matéria À parte das controvérsias sobre geração de emprego e impactos socioecológicos, Pernambuco avança na consolidação de sua transformação digital e de novas demandas do ecossistema tecnológico, impulsionado pela expansão de infraestruturas de data centers de classe mundial no Estado. É importante reconhecer que, nesse novo cenário, o Estado já conta com empreendimentos de destaque que garantem certificações internacionais de qualidade máxima: os selos Tier III e Tier III Facility, concedidos pelo Uptime Institute. As certificações Tier III — divididas entre Tier III Design (projeto) e Tier III Facility (instalação e operação) — representam o rigor máximo em padrões internacionais de disponibilidade e tolerância a falhas. Na prática, um data center classificado como Tier III opera com sistemas totalmente redundantes (energia, climatização e infraestrutura de suporte). Isso significa que a instalação pode passar por manutenções preventivas ou corretivas sem que haja qualquer interrupção nos serviços hospedados, garantindo uma disponibilidade operacional contínua de 99,982% ao ano e máxima segurança para dados de missão crítica. Marcos tecnológicos em solo pernambucano Esse patamar de excelência é encabeçado pela Surfix Cloud & Data Center, localizada no bairro de Boa Viagem, que sagrou-se como o primeiro data center com certificação Tier III Facility de Pernambuco. A conquista atesta que toda a sua operação — englobando energia, climatização, governança e segurança — atende aos critérios mais rígidos do mercado global. Em paralelo, o Estado avança com investimentos estruturais, a exemplo da chegada da Atlantic Data Centers (nova empresa da Um Telecom baseada no Parqtel) com o projeto do data center Recife 1, cujo primeiro contrato foi firmado com a EVEO no último mês de setembro. O investimento fora do Sudeste Nesse ecossistema qualificado, a EVEO — reconhecida como a maior empresa de servidores dedicados e nuvem privada (private cloud) do Brasil — reforçou seu investimento fora do eixo Sudeste, fincando bandeira no Nordeste e escolhendo a capital pernambucana para expandir suas operações, para além da base em Fortaleza. O volume de novos negócios na região supera o registrado no mesmo período de 2025, e a base de clientes local cresceu 62% no último ano. Movida por uma expansão expressiva na região — com um avanço acumulado de 272% desde 2024 na sua base —, a EVEO identificou que as distâncias continentais do Nordeste tornavam inviável atender a todo o mercado apenas a partir de sua unidade em Fortaleza (CE). Com a nova operação no Recife, a empresa passa a cobrir os dois principais polos nordestinos, reduzindo drasticamente a latência e viabilizando projetos de altíssima complexidade voltados para Inteligência Artificial (IA) com clusters de GPU dedicada. Com esse movimento focado no Nordeste, a EVEO avança na meta global de R$ 500 milhões em receita até 2030, atestando que a descentralização da tecnologia de ponta para fora do Sudeste segue sendo viável.

artigo.texto: This year, voters will elect the first new District 72 state representative for the first time in nearly two decades. Longtime Republican state Rep. Ed Clere, who has held the seat since 2008, is not seeking reelection. He’s focusing instead on a 2027 bid for mayor of New Albany, as an independent. Democrat Michele Henry and Republican Darrell Neeley are hoping to fill the role. Both recognize Hoosiers’ financial challenges, and they agree the state has a role in regulating data centers. Neither has held public office, though Neeley ran unsuccessfully for New Albany City Council in 2023. Meet the candidates Henry is a civil rights and worker’s rights attorney. She said she didn’t plan to run, and hadn’t previously considered running for office. But she wants to see changes. “I think that our legislature truly has just forgotten why it exists, and that is to improve the quality of life in our state,” Henry said. “And we haven't been doing that for 20 years now, and it is time to elect people who want to do that.” She said Indiana ranks poorly in some areas, such as public education. “We should be at the top of those lists,” she said. “This is a great state, and District 72 is a fantastic community.” Neeley is an associate pastor in New Albany and served more than three decades in the U.S. Navy. He said he wasn’t seeking the spot but that a lot of people reached out to him when it opened up. He said he sees it as a way to continue his track record of serving people. “This was another aspect in helping people, and being there to support those that think they don't have a voice,” Neeley said. When people asked him about running, “I finally sat down, prayed about it, thought about it, and so here we are.” Big goals Both candidates say they’ve heard from residents about how much they’re struggling to make ends meet, and Henry said focusing on affordability would be a priority. “We know that the rate of foreclosure is at…the highest in Indiana of all the 50 states, and that is largely because people are struggling to afford housing,” she said, adding that the prices of gas, groceries and utilities are also up. One way to help alleviate this, she said, is by eliminating sales tax on utilities and necessary household items, including hygiene products. She also wants to see the state minimum wage raised from its current $7.25 to at least $15. “There's nobody in the United States who could live on $7.25 an hour in any community, and certainly not in Indiana and not in District 72,” she said. She also said leaders should be responsible when bringing in new companies. “If we are going to provide incentives for companies to come to Indiana and bring jobs, we need to make sure that those jobs are quality jobs: that they offer a a salary, an hourly rate, and benefits that allow people to buy a home, to raise a family if that's what they choose to do, to not have to have a second job,” Henry said. Neeley said he wants to continue the state’s economic growth through fiscal responsibility. During his Navy career, he managed $300 million budgets, he said. “I knew how to budget, knew how to use taxpayers' money,” Neeley said. “Because it's not the government's, it wasn't the Navy's. It's the people's money.” He said he also thinks most people just want to make sure their tax money is spent wisely. He noted that 2027 is a biannual budget year for Indiana, which is a “prime opportunity to address the cost of living.” He said legislators need to increase grants and remove barriers for child care, so working families can continue to work. He wants state and local leaders to address what he calls burdensome restrictions on housing, and to see the state’s Residential Housing Infrastructure Assistance Program continue. He said he supports property tax reform, especially when it “addresses our problematic assessment system” and targets relief for seniors and people with disabilities. Getting things done Henry said she hopes Republicans won’t be in the supermajority at the statehouse after the election, which she thinks could make it easier for Democrats to be more effective, rather than continuing what she calls Republicans’ “pro-corporation legislative activity.” “I think there is a very real chance that the Democrats do get out of the superminority this year,” she said. “And once that happens, we will obviously have a lot more play at the table. We'll be able to implement proposals… We'll be able to take action that actually helps people in our communities.” She said even if the partisan gap doesn’t change, she hopes the parties can work together “to actually implement real relief and pro-Hoosier legislation.” Neeley said it’s crucial to work together, and that it’s not beneficial to reject good ideas based on party labels. “These games have to stop,” he said, adding that whether constituents support him or not, “you still have a voice in this district and at the statehouse too. We have to work together, or we're not going to get anywhere.” Both candidates said they would like to continue in the spirit Clere served with for so long. “I have a tremendous amount of respect for Ed,” Henry said. “He’s a moderate person who actually does listen to his constituents.” That’s something she’d like to continue. She also wants to make sure people in the district are represented at the state level. “Southern Indiana folks feel a lot of the time like they aren't heard, that Indianapolis doesn't remember that we are part of the state and not part of, you know, Louisville,” she said. “And so I think it's important that we listen to what the needs are in our community and bring those to the statehouse and then work on solutions that work for our community.” Neeley noted Clere’s focus on health care and legislation for people with disabilities, which he’d like to carry on. “I plan on picking his brain,” Neeley said. artigo.texto: The No Data Centers SGV Coalition and the Puente Hills Community Preservation Association (PHCPA) will hold a community fundraising rally on Sunday, October 18, to raise $90,000 for PHCPA’s legal challenge to the Marici Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facility project and potential data center developments in the City of Industry. By News Desk The rally will take place from 10:00 am to 1:00 pm at Schabarum Regional Park, 17250 E. Colima Road in Rowland Heights, across from Puente Hills Mall and near the approved Marici project site. Funds will support litigation-related costs, including legal fees, court expenses, and expert analysis. A limited portion will go toward community outreach and operational expenses related to the effort. Organizers are urging residents to support responsible development, environmental protection, and transparent public decision-making. They cite concerns about potential effects on homes, schools, parks, natural resources, and quality of life. They are calling for thorough environmental review, disclosure of project impacts, and meaningful public participation. Recent industrial and battery-related fires—including the Lineage Logistics fire in Boyle Heights, the Moss Landing battery storage fire, and a battery fire at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne—have heightened community concerns about fire hazards, emergency preparedness, toxic smoke exposure, and evacuation planning. Residents can contribute to PHCPA’s legal fund at the rally or online at this link. PHCPA will also hold a Panda Express fundraiser on October 18, from 9:30 am to 10:00 pm, at the restaurant on Colima and Azusa. Supporters can also purchase a $16 digital voucher for a dozen Original Glazed doughnuts at participating Krispy Kreme locations in the United States. Each voucher raises $8 for PHCPA.

artigo.texto: Supermicro expande seu portfólio de projetos de computação aberta integrada para acelerar as implantações de data centers de IA em escala de rack - O portfólio integrado baseado no Open Compute Project (OCP) abrange sistemas de IA/HPC em escala de rack, racks ORv3 e ORW, alimentação de 48V CC, redes e soluções de refrigeração líquida para viabilizar a computação de maior densidade em data centers existentes e novos - O portfólio abrange desde a infraestrutura até operações inteligentes, incluindo fluidos de resfriamento DCBBS, CDUs integradas ao rack (in-rack), switches e o pacote de software de gerenciamento de sistemas da Supermicro para a gestão da infraestrutura - O Supermicro DCBBS reúne essas tecnologias baseadas em OCP em soluções integradas em escala de rack, simplificando e acelerando a implementação de recursos de computação, energia, rede e refrigeração para reduzir o tempo de entrada em operação (TTO). SAN JOSE, Califórnia, 14 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), uma provedora de soluções completas de TI para IA, empresas, armazenamento e 5G/Edge, com destaque para as soluções Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), anunciou hoje um portfólio expandido de sistemas, racks e trocadores de calor de porta traseira (RDHx) certificados como Open Compute Project Accepted™. Com o suporte do DCBBS, o portfólio de soluções pode ser incorporado em implantações completas de ponta a ponta, em escala de rack e cluster. "O boom da IA redefine a forma como os data centers são projetados, construídos e implementados, e a Supermicro lidera essa transformação com o DCBBS", disse Charles Liang, presidente e CEO da Supermicro. "Ao integrar computação, redes, energia, refrigeração avançada, software e serviços em soluções validadas em escala de rack, ajudamos os clientes a simplificar a complexidade e acelerar o caminho da inovação até a produção. O DCBBS possibilita que os clientes reduzam o TTM e o TTO ao oferecer infraestrutura essencial de IA de forma mais rápida e eficiente." As soluções OCP da Supermicro já estão disponíveis; clique aqui para saber mais. Ao aproveitar as melhores práticas da comunidade OCP e o design e serviços do DCBBS, os operadores de data centers podem aumentar a densidade de computação e a eficiência energética para cargas de trabalho de IA e HPC com base em uma infraestrutura aberta e validada em escala de rack — desde sistemas e barras de distribuição até o resfriamento em nível de rack e de data centers — para implementar soluções de alta densidade de forma mais eficiente e acelerar o tempo de lançamento no mercado (TTM) e o tempo de operação (TTO). "Os clientes precisam de uma infraestrutura aberta e flexível que possa ser dimensionada de acordo com as demandas em rápida evolução da IA, ao mesmo tempo que se adapte à realidade de seus data centers", disse Dirk Van Slyke, vice-presidente de Marketing da OCP. "Ao reunir sistemas, racks, energia e refrigeração aceitos pelo OCP em soluções validadas em escala de rack, a Supermicro ajuda os clientes a simplificar a integração, maximizar a capacidade e a eficiência das instalações e acelerar a implantação da infraestrutura de IA de produção." Os racks ORv3 e ORW substituem as fontes de alimentação e os cabos individuais por servidor por uma barra de distribuição CC centralizada de 48 V, permitindo que os clientes otimizem seus sistemas de CPU e GPU para racks de computação de maior densidade. Essa densidade é ainda mais reforçada pelo sistema de resfriamento líquido DLC-2 Direct-to-Chip da Supermicro, que remove o calor de forma mais eficiente de CPUs, GPUs e outros componentes críticos, enquanto o calor residual pode ser removido do rack por meio de unidades de resfriamento ORv3 RDHx especialmente desenvolvidas, sem a necessidade de adaptações adicionais nos sistemas de ar-condicionado do data center. As unidades RDHx da Supermicro podem ser montadas na parte traseira de racks ORv3 e ORW, removendo o calor residual do ar de exaustão dos servidores antes que ele entre na sala do data center. O portfólio abrange capacidades de refrigeração de 10 kW a 120 kW, oferecendo aos operadores uma maneira prática de aumentar a densidade de racks tanto em novas instalações de IA quanto em data centers existentes. Os modelos alimentados por corrente contínua conectam-se à barra de distribuição do rack para reduzir a quantidade de cabos, enquanto os designs incluem ventiladores redundantes N+1 para garantir o tempo de atividade e um sistema anticondensação inteligente para evitar danos causados pela umidade a outros componentes dentro do rack. Os operadores podem monitorar e gerenciar todo o portfólio de componentes DCBBS, por meio do SuperCloud Composer®, utilizando protocolos padrão do setor. Além disso, os softwares da Supermicro, como o SuperCloud Director, o SuperCloud Automation Assistant e o SuperCloud Developer Console, possibilitam que as empresas gerenciem e operacionalizem todos os aspectos das modernas fábricas de IA, centros de dados corporativos e infraestrutura NeoCloud, por meio de uma solução unificada de controle de software. Como parte do portfólio do DCBBS, a Supermicro também oferece um portfólio abrangente de soluções de rede para IA, que variam de switches Ethernet 800G e 1.6T com refrigeração a ar ou líquida, incluindo plataformas Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) de última geração baseadas no silício de comutação Broadcom Tomahawk 6, otimizadas para racks EIA ou ORv3. O sistema operacional de rede SONiC Advanced da Supermicro Enterprise oferece aos clientes a flexibilidade de selecionar a arquitetura de rede que melhor atenda às suas necessidades de desempenho, energia, escalabilidade e implantação, à medida que a IA e os ambientes de data center de grande escala continuam a evoluir. A linha Supermicro DCBBS também incluirá sistemas de switches NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics, os primeiros switches Ethernet coembalados com SerDes de 200 Gb/s. Baseada no ASIC Etherne

artigo.texto: The Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL) has issued an advisory outlining the procedure for enhancing the energy storage capacity of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects that have already received connectivity approval. The guidelines apply to developers seeking to increase storage capacity measured in megawatt-hours (MWh) without increasing the approved charging or discharging power capacity measured in megawatts (MW). Under the advisory, developers intending to enhance their BESS storage capacity while keeping the existing MW capacity unchanged must submit a formal application under Regulation 5.2 of the General Network Access (GNA) Regulations. Applicants are required to indicate nil additional MW capacity while clearly specifying the proposed increase in MWh storage capacity. CTUIL has also clarified the applicability of connectivity bank guarantees under Regulation 5.2(e) of the GNA Regulations. The existing requirements for Conn-BG1 and Conn-BG3 remain applicable. However, since Conn-BG3 is generally calculated at ₹2 lakh per MW and the proposed enhancement does not involve additional MW capacity, CTUIL will approach the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) to seek clarification on the requirement. Pending CERC’s clarification, CTUIL will not demand Conn-BG3 immediately for such applications. However, developers will remain obligated to submit the applicable bank guarantee in accordance with any future directions issued by the commission. Failure to comply with these directions could lead to cancellation of the approval for additional MWh capacity and encashment of Conn-BG1. To expedite the approval process, CTUIL will issue intimations reflecting the enhanced storage capacity once applicants fulfil all required regulatory compliances. Such applications will not require prior discussion in Central Monitoring and Evaluation of Transmission System (CMETS) meetings. Instead, the cases will be presented at subsequent meetings for information and noting. The advisory also reiterates that developers must comply with all applicable requirements relating to land acquisition, financial closure, the Scheduled Commercial Operation Date (SCOD), and other provisions under the GNA Regulations and prevailing guidelines. CTUIL has further confirmed that applications for MWh capacity enhancement submitted before the advisory’s issuance will also be processed under the newly established procedure. The guidelines provide a defined framework for developers seeking to increase storage duration without modifying their approved power capacity. artigo.texto: Trending Failing to regulate data centers could cost Ohioans billions of dollars in higher electricity cost and air pollution, according to a new analysis. The study by Columbus-based analytic firm Scioto Analysis estimates Ohioans would end up spending $16 billion more in electric bills and would suffer $41 billion in air pollution damage without regulations. The analysis estimates under current policies, data center growth could cost Ohio electricity customers $16 billion in higher utility costs between 2027 and 2034. Meanwhile, Ohio’s data center sales and use tax exemption cost the state an estimated $1.6 billion in revenue in 2025. "We are watching a financial crisis develop in real time, and the Ohio Statehouse is failing to respond,” said State Rep. Tristan Rader, D-Lakewood. “We have allowed some of the wealthiest corporations on Earth to receive billions in tax breaks while Ohio families face the prospect of billions more in electricity costs. At this point, our continued inaction isn’t just disappointing - it’s irresponsible.” Rader is working on legislation that he says would reconsider Ohio's "generous" tax exemptions for data centers and establish long-term financial commitments and safeguards protecting existing customers. "Ohio families should not be the venture capitalists for Silicon Valley’s expansion," the legislator said. "We don’t get a share of their profits, and we shouldn’t be handed their bills. The Statehouse needs to act before those bills come due.” According to the tracking group Data Center Map, Ohio has 240 data centers. Another study, by the Goldwater Institute, downplays the threat from data centers, "The bigger problem is an electricity system that hides scarcity from consumers until strain appears as congestion, reliability risks, or higher costs," the institute said. Higher prices would lead to higher efficiency, according to the Institute. "When millions of consumers face fixed prices, demand remains high precisely when the system is under the most pressure, the institute concluded.

artigo.texto: Amazon builds workforce pipeline alongside data center construction in Caddo, Bossier parishes Company outlines education programs, apprenticeships and tuition fund tied to new data centers SHREVEPORT, La. (KSLA) - Construction is progressing on Amazon data centers in Caddo and Bossier parishes, and the company says it is also focused on building a workforce to support the facilities. KSLA’s Marvin Andrade spoke one-on-one with Amazon Web Services Vice President of Economic Development Roger Wehner about the company’s workforce plans. Construction progress Progress is visible along Stateline Road in Caddo Parish and in Bossier Parish, about 40 minutes away. At the Resilient Parkway site in Shreveport, Amazon leaders said they are weeks away from breaking ground. Amazon said the first building is on track to go online by next summer. Education outreach Alongside construction, Amazon said one of its priorities is education. “Have you ever thought about being a fusion splicer or your really into hardware and computer do you want to be a data center technician? So that’s where we always start with educating the folks students, educators, and influencers on what those career opportunities are,” Wehner said. The company will host a program November 17 at Bossier Parish Schools’ Center for Technology and Innovative Learning, followed by sessions November 18 and 19 at North Louisiana Technical Community College. The goal is to show students the career paths a data center can open up before they apply for a job. Apprenticeship program Amazon plans to launch a four-week paid apprenticeship program designed to give students hands-on experience. “We kind of expose them to all the job skills in a data center everything from construction to operation, etc. We pay for that historically, we have had an 85% placement rate for the graduates,” Wehner said. Tuition fund Amazon said it wants to help cover community college costs for students by creating a new fund. “We’re going to create an endowment. We are going to use the current financial apparatus that already exists; we will invest in that, and then they will manage the funds back to the students when they apply,” Wehner said. Addressing skepticism Some residents remain skeptical about the data centers coming to the region. KSLA asked Wehner what he would say to critics. “We can talk and bring in folks from other communities and share them their experience of 20 years and just give us a fair opportunity to explain how we’re different and how we operate the way we do,” Wehner said. Educator workshop planned Amazon will hold an educator workshop December 3. The goal is to teach educators how to inform students about what future jobs at the data centers will look like. artigo.texto: RICHMOND, Va. — A state senator representing Virginia's data center alley in Loudoun County has filed a bill for the upcoming General Assembly session that would temporarily pause any new data centers from being approved in the Commonwealth. "The bill is really just a three year pause to take a look and stop more data centers being shoved down a pipe that is already overflowing," said State Sen. Russet Perry (D-Loudoun). If the bill becomes law as written, starting July 1 of next year local governments and state agencies would be banned from approving the necessary paperwork or applications that might be needed for new data centers The ban would be in place for three years. Perry said the aim is to prevent work from starting on new data centers, but notes there will be a discussion on which projects already in the approval process may have what is known as a vested right to continue. "I'm sure some in in the pipe that have already established legal protection and I don't think the state can lawfully do that," said Perry. "But certainly the state can say we are taking a pause until we can get our hands wrapped around this and that's really what we're looking at." Perry said the pause is needed to look at the impacts data centers are having on the state's resources and energy grid and what is sustainable. "Even today, the Department of Energy telling PJM, who...manages the grid up and down the East Coast, including in Virginia, saying, 'Hey, we're concerned about blackouts. We need you to bring everything up to speed so you can have extra power generation," said Perry. "So we have enough water, do we have enough power that can our grid possibly sustain these? What about all these massive transmission lines that are crisscrossing our state now, going through people's farms and and their homes." "I'm very happy to see that this is now becoming a bipartisan issue," said State Sen. Glen Sturtevant (R-Chesterfield) about Perry's bill. Sturtevant has been calling for an "indefinite" moratorium for months. "Virginia is the data center capital of the world. To the extent that new data centers need to be built, there are 49 other states where they can go. Virginia doesn't need to have them all," he added. "We need to get rid of the tax loophole that allows the big tech AI data center industry to not pay their taxes in Virginia. We need to address their impact on our water resources and our environmental resources." But Sturtevant added lawmakers do not have to wait until the 2027 General Assembly session to start in January to take up the moratorium and that it should be discussed at the end of the month when lawmakers are back in Richmond for a special session to take up judicial appointments. "We don't want to wait. We can't wait. Virginians' electric bills are too high to continue kicking this can down the road and pushing this off." Perry said special sessions are limited in scope and she has not gotten word that it will be expanded to allow for items other than judge appointments to be discussed. While Governor Abigail Spanberger has not accepted calls for a statewide moratorium, last month she signed an executive order that her office said was "the most comprehensive and aggressive data center accountability effort in the country." “Governor Spanberger last month laid out the nation’s most aggressive and comprehensive plan to hold data centers accountable. The Governor looks forward to implementing these nation-leading standards and working with lawmakers to protect the Commonwealth’s natural beauty, make energy more affordable for families, and listen to local communities across Virginia," a spokesperson added Thursday when asked about Perry's bill. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Data Center Coalition said the industry has brought over a billion dollars in local taxes and jobs to her home county and the bill would deny other counties the same opportunity. "Moratoriums and other anti-competitive policies send a signal that an area is closed for business, both for data centers and for other significant economic development projects. Local or state moratoriums could deprive communities of the opportunity to compete for investment and jobs, jeopardize multibillion projects that are in development, and force jurisdictions to relinquish significant long-term economic investment, high-wage jobs, and critical tax revenue to neighboring states,” said DCC's Director of Virginia Government Affairs Nicole Riley. Perry responded that while the industry does bring in tax revenue, it has to be balanced with other impacts. CBS 6 is committed to sharing community voices on this important topic. artigo.texto: Four Shreveport mayoral candidates address data centers, public safety and infrastructure at forum KSLA, Greater Shreveport Chamber of Commerce host forum at Centenary College SHREVEPORT, La. (KSLA) - Four of the seven candidates for Shreveport mayor took the stage Wednesday night to make their case to voters at a forum hosted by KSLA and the Greater Shreveport Chamber of Commerce. Arceneaux addresses data center concerns Incumbent Mayor Tom Arceneaux pointed to accomplishments during his time in office while also addressing concerns about data center projects. “Infrastructure is there for the data centers, will be paid for by the data centers, and will not be included in the residential rate base. So, I think that those actions have been sufficient to answer those particular questions. I also point out that all the sale of electricity also produces additional revenue to the city of Shreveport,” Arceneaux said. Gage-Watts proposes entertainment district Caddo Parish Commissioner Stormy Gage-Watts said she has her own plan for moving Shreveport forward. “I am in favor of a film and entertainment district here in Shreveport. I am open to do business with 50 Cent and any and all other public-private partnerships that will be positive and bring economic development to our area,” Gage-Watts said. Phelps calls for police pay review State Rep. Tammy Phelps focused on funding public safety and is calling for a review of police officer pay. “When we talk about recruiting, we talk about those salaries, I really would like to sit down and create a salary schedule and look at all the salaries, how we continue to move forward and how we continue to pay and raise the rates of our police department,” Phelps said. Young proposes water system audit Caddo Parish Commissioner John-Paul Young proposed an outside audit of Shreveport’s water system. “I propose to audit the system for the very first time, externally and forensically, so that we can weed out the fraud and recapture the waste to improve our system, and then put it under the management of a competent engineering firm,” Young said. Other candidates not included Three other candidates in the race — Chaunta Mero, Michael Williams and Sia Ravari — were not part of the forum based on criteria set by the chamber. artigo.texto: Future-Proofing Data Center Cooling: Designing for the Unknown Data center planners are being asked to make infrastructure decisions around workloads that can change in months. AI training, inference and traditional enterprise computing can place different demands on the same facility. Rack densities may rise unevenly, hardware roadmaps may shift, and the cooling strategy selected for one deployment may not fit the next. In that environment, future-proofing is less about choosing the winning technology and more about creating a mechanical system that can change without forcing the facility to start over. Design for a range, not a single design point A conventional design process begins with a target load, but that target ideally should be treated as part of a range. Depending on time of day, the usage may vary, requiring a varying range of cooling needs. The equipment must be able to provide necessary cooling at peak and off-peak times. Therefore, it's critical to have designed-in redundancy to maintain maximum uptime especially during peak usage. The system should account for mixed rack densities, partial buildouts and changing proportions of air- and liquid-cooled loads. A hall that supports high-density racks in one zone and lower-density equipment in another may need different supply temperatures, airflow rates and redundancy strategies at the same time. Zoning allows capacity to be directed where it is needed instead of requiring the entire room to operate for the most demanding rack. The roadmap should define day-one needs, staged additions and the physical constraints that could block growth. Space for piping, manifolds, heat exchangers, pumps, electrical distribution, controls and service access should be considered before those components are required. With capacity continuing to increase, it's important to design with that in mind. Liquid cooling does not mean water or to eliminate air The phrase “liquid cooling” can mislead important system differences. Liquid cooling is primarily tied to high-performance computing applications such as AI processing and machine learning. It's important to note that these cooling trends are not an industry wide change, but rather a modification to higher density applications where air cooling is no longer sufficient. Lower latency applications and general cloud storage will continue to be air cooled via fans. Liquid, in this case, describes how heat is transported, not necessarily tied to the water usage of the data center. Depending on the architecture, the above mentioned “liquid” may be treated water, a water-glycol mixture, a refrigerant or a dielectric fluid. Heat then moves through a coolant distribution unit, or CDU, and ultimately is rejected through dry, evaporative or hybrid equipment. Liquid cooling also does not make fans irrelevant. Direct-to-chip and immersion cooling remove heat directly from the source at the chip. Air cooling will still be required for the remaining 20-30% of the white and grey space, as heat is still produced by the remaining mechanical equipment. Rear-door heat exchangers, an air-assisted liquid cooling system, deliberately combine both media in this hybrid system. Future-proofing depends on reserving space, connections and control capacity for both air and liquid paths. That flexibility allows a facility to support higher-density or hybrid cooling without replacing the entire thermal system. The goal is not to predict which approach will dominate, but to make future transitions possible in manageable phases. Make retrofit readiness a design requirement A future-ready system should be evaluated by how it changes while the data center remains in operation. Can a new cooling zone be connected without shutting down an existing one? Can airflow be rebalanced as racks move? Can fans be replaced without reducing the required level of redundancy? Are operators able to see both air- and liquid-side performance through a coordinated control system? Can cooling capacity be increased in the existing footprint? These questions turn future retrofits from an impending construction concern into a present-day reliability requirement. Controls are especially important because installed capacity and actual demand rarely match perfectly. Temperature, pressure, flow and power data allow fans to respond to real loads rather than fixed calculations. They also give operators a baseline for identifying lost capacity, testing new configurations and verifying that a retrofit performs as intended. These critical systems can have zero downtime, even during a retrofit. It’s important to have real time and reliable controls for commissioning of these retrofit systems. Preserve choices No design can anticipate every processor, rack configuration or cooling medium that will arrive over the life of a facility. It can, however, preserve choices. A system designed around ranges, zones, modular increments, and coordinated controls can absorb change with less disruption. That is the practical meaning of future-proofing: not predicting the unknown but ensuring the next decision does not require undoing the last one. artigo.texto: Overview: A Former Navajo Nation President talks running for congress, data centers and water rights. Northern Arizona is confronting a collision of growth, drought and accelerating tech demand. Former Navajo president Jonathan Nez, now running for Arizona’s 2nd Congressional district as a Democrat, says the region’s political leadership hasn’t kept pace. Speaking to Native News Online, Nez outlines how data center proposals, shrinking Colorado River allocations and rising utility costs are reshaping daily life for Native and rural voters across the district – and how he hopes to address those issues if elected. Nez argues that transparency failures and rushed development have fueled public backlash from Tucson to Page, where residents ousted local officials over undisclosed data center negotiations. Nez ties those fights to broader questions of water security, tribal sovereignty and the future of clean energy in Indian Country. “Water is life,” Nez said. “We need to ensure water is available not just now, but for our children, grandchildren and seven generations and beyond.” This interview has been edited for clarity and length. What are your thoughts on the expansion of data centers in Indian Country and surrounding communities? Any type of economic development venture should start with local leaders being transparent with their constituents. I see time and time again, especially in Indian Country, where the public is not informed about what is going on, and the aftereffect is opposition to large-scale projects, including data centers. You have elected leaders who have good intentions for bringing in revenue and jobs, but we also have to be better stewards of the land and our resources. Data centers use a lot of water, they use a lot of energy, and there is a lot of noise from these types of facilities. Outside tribal nations, property values around these data centers lessen in value. As a person running for Congress right now, we have to have a better relationship with local leaders — and that means town leaders, city leaders, county leaders and state leaders. Technology is expanding throughout the world, and there is a need for data storage. That is why these data centers are being considered in places all across the country. But in the Southwest, we are in a drought, and water is life. I think in the Southwest, tribes are saying “no” to these data centers, and their neighbors outside tribal areas are also saying “no.” Here in Arizona, the city of Tucson in the southern part of the state has taken a position saying “no” to data centers. Recently, primary elections took place in the city of Page in northern Arizona, where local leaders, I believe, were not very transparent about what was going on. When the public found out that elected leaders were pursuing a data center, they came out in full force in opposition and even removed those council members from elected positions. So in the area, there’s a lot of pushback and opposition. The federal administration has announced that Arizona will face the largest cuts among states and tribes relying on the Colorado River amid the ongoing drought. What are you hearing from voters about water scarcity, and how are communities responding? They are upset that our current leaders, especially my opponent, are nowhere to be found and should be at the table during these water rights discussions. The federal government, as you said, made a decision to reduce water allocations from the Colorado River by 30%. That’s the largest of any state in the Upper and Lower Basins of the Colorado River. You probably have that data in front of you where it says large data centers can consume 1 million to 5 million gallons of water per day. That’s around 1.8 billion gallons per year. And that’s the concern. There’s a lot of growth in Arizona, people moving into the Southwest and into Congressional District 2 that I am running to represent. We need to make sure we get our fair share of water from tributaries that include the Colorado River and also protect our precious groundwater. There needs to be a serious discussion in the Southwest about conservation, especially when water levels are lessening. Two dams on the Colorado River right now — Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam — are at all-time lows since they were filling up. Those two dams create hydroelectricity, inexpensive power that goes to southern Arizona, California and Nevada. We’re at a point where the water that goes through the dam to spin the generators is almost below the intake valves. If that happens, they call it “dead pool,” meaning water will just sit there without going through the dam or downstream. That will increase utility rates. Electricity bills will only go up further. That’s the concern here in the Southwest. It all surrounds water security. As we say in Indian Country, water is life. We need to ensure water is available not just now, but for our children, grandchildren, and seven generations and beyond. How do you view the transition toward renewable energy in Indian Country, particularly as federal policies affect energy development and social services? As president and vice president of the Navajo Nation — the largest tribe in the country — we saw outside influence focused on shutting down coal-fired power plants in the Southwest, including the Navajo Generating Station. There were a lot of negotiations to keep that facility up because of the jobs and revenue coming in, alongside discussions of transitioning into renewable energy: natural gas, solar. But the powers that be decided it needed to be decommissioned. To this day, there is no more coal-fired power plant in that area. The coal used to fuel that station came from the Navajo Nation via Peabody Coal Company. When the plant went away, Peabody Coal had to close its doors. artigo.texto: Muita segurança, um edifício (quase) sem pessoas e que parece um organismo vivo, um apetite insaciável por energia elétrica, grandes clientes internacionais de tecnologia em fila de espera: fomos à Start Campus, em Sines, a linha da frente da nova economia da inteligência artificial. "Nunca tinha estado num data center?”, pergunta Luís Rodrigues, enquanto se ouve o som de uma porta de segurança a abrir e entramos num corredor longo sem janelas e com luz branca. Seguimos atrás do segurança que vai abrindo e fechando portas, parte do protocolo apertado. Para chegar ali passámos pelo controlo à entrada - com um grande portão automático de metal e uma cerca de arame farpado -, assinámos um acordo para não fazer imagens dos equipamentos no interior, vimos um vídeo de 10 minutos com as regras do centro e pusemos o telemóvel num saquinho de plástico para bloquear a câmara. “As pessoas que vêm pela primeira vez acham estranho, mas os clientes adoram ver tanta segurança”, diz o diretor operacional da Start Campus, que fica em Sines e é o maior centro de dados em construção na Europa. O segurança passa de novo o cartão - e entramos na linha da frente da economia mundial.

artigo.texto: OCP 2026: Agentic AI Drives the Data Center's Chip-to-Grid Transformation Key Highlights - OCP is extending its standards mission from servers and racks to the full AI infrastructure stack, encompassing silicon, cooling, power distribution, facilities and utility-grid integration. - AMD introduced its Helion agentic AI rack, while Arm and NVIDIA outlined new CPU architectures and infrastructure requirements for rapidly expanding autonomous workloads. - Meta detailed the engineering behind its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio, including fabric structures, new optical networking, open-source transport software and AI-optimized concrete. - Broadcom and NVIDIA presented advances in Ethernet networking and optical interconnects designed to overcome the growing physical constraints of accelerator clusters. - New OCP data center and grid-resilience specifications, along with NVIDIA's advances in dynamic power management, signal a shift toward treating the AI factory as a coordinated, grid-aware infrastructure system. Standing before thousands of engineers and technology executives at the opening of the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, Meta's Santosh Janardhan pointed to the enormous fabric structure surrounding the audience. It was, he explained, an example of the same construction technology Meta had begun deploying to accelerate its massive AI infrastructure buildout. At the company's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio, traditional assumptions about data center construction had given way to an urgent question: What if the next generation of AI infrastructure could be built in months rather than years, using engineered fabric structures instead of conventional concrete-and-steel buildings? "We are actually also training a model while we were building it," said Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure. The presentation offered a striking illustration of the larger message emerging from Monday's opening keynotes: The AI factory is becoming a fundamentally different kind of data center. Across presentations by AMD, Meta, Arm, Broadcom and NVIDIA, a common theme emerged. The rapid expansion of AI inference and autonomous agents is forcing new approaches to computing, networking, construction, power distribution and operations. At the same time, the diversity of silicon architectures and the enormous physical scale of deployments are making common infrastructure specifications increasingly important. The result is a significant expansion of OCP's original mission. Fifteen years after the organization began applying open-source principles to hardware design, the industry's next challenge is developing interoperable infrastructure across the entire data center, from processor architecture to the utility connection. OCP's New Mandate: From Chip to Grid OCP CEO George Tchaparian opened the summit by describing an organization whose scale increasingly reflects the industry's transformation. This year's event attracted approximately 15,000 attendees, with another 3,000 on a waitlist. Tchaparian said OCP expects membership to exceed 700 organizations by year-end, while technical contributions are growing approximately 30% annually. The organization has already announced that its 2027 Global Summit will move to San Francisco's Moscone Center to accommodate further growth. More consequential than the attendance figures, however, is the widening scope of OCP's work. Originally centered on open server designs, racks and supporting hardware, the organization's roadmap now encompasses facilities infrastructure, liquid cooling, power distribution, firmware, security, networking and the increasingly complex connections between data centers and utilities. Tchaparian characterized the emerging approach as "chip-to-grid" infrastructure. This reflects a fundamental engineering problem. As hyperscalers and AI infrastructure providers deploy increasingly specialized processors, the electrical, thermal and mechanical consequences of those design decisions extend well beyond individual servers. Higher accelerator densities require new cooling strategies. New power architectures affect rack configurations and electrical distribution. Faster networks alter equipment layouts and cable requirements. Different silicon designs can introduce entirely new facility-level constraints. The traditional process of designing computing equipment and adapting data centers to accommodate it is increasingly difficult to sustain at AI scale. OCP is therefore emphasizing what Tchaparian called co-optimized data centers: infrastructure in which silicon, racks, networking, cooling and power systems are developed with common interfaces and shared design objectives. The challenge is compounded by growing silicon diversity. Hyperscalers are developing custom accelerators alongside commercial GPUs and CPUs, increasing the risk of fragmented hardware ecosystems that require repeated engineering across otherwise similar facilities. OCP also intends to extend hyperscale-derived standards into what it calls the AI computing continuum, encompassing neocloud providers, colocation operators, enterprises and geographically distributed inference infrastructure. The objective is not to eliminate architectural differentiation. It is to reduce the amount of infrastructure that must be redesigned every time the underlying computing technology changes. Agentic AI Gives the CPU a New Mission One of the most consequential themes of the opening keynotes was the renewed importance of general-purpose computing. AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su described 2026 as the year of inference, estimating that inference now represents approximately 60% of the AI computing market. She pointed to an approximately 14-fold increase in agentic AI traffic during the year, reflecting the accelerating adoption of systems that do more than respond to individual prompts.
