artigo.texto: The AI Data Center Reckoning: Why Infrastructure Must Earn Its Social License Something fundamental is breaking in the data center world, and it's not just a technical problem. It's becoming a social and political one. October 13, 2026 The AI Data Center Reckoning: Why Infrastructure Must Earn Its Social License Something fundamental is breaking in the data center world, and it's not just a technical problem. It's becoming a social and political one. For decades, data centers operated quietly in the background of modern life. They were infrastructure in the truest sense: essential, reliable, and largely invisible. Communities welcomed them as economic engines that brought jobs and tax revenue without the noise, traffic, or pollution of traditional industry. Then AI arrived and changed everything. AI data centers consume vastly more power, not incrementally more, but orders of magnitude more. They can draw enormous volumes of water for cooling. They require utility infrastructure upgrades that strain local grids. And they're proliferating at a pace that's catching regulators, utilities, and communities off guard. The result is something the industry hasn't faced before: organized resistance. Local and national governments are imposing moratoriums. Utility commissions are questioning grid capacity. Environmental groups are raising alarms about water consumption and carbon emissions. Data centers are losing their social license to operate, and the industry needs solutions that address the root causes, not just the symptoms. Why Social License Demands Converged Architecture The social license crisis stems from a fundamental inefficiency in how data center infrastructure has traditionally been designed. Power, backup systems, and cooling are engineered independently and assembled only during construction. This siloed approach creates cascading inefficiencies that communities can see and feel. Power passes through multiple conversion stages, losing energy as heat at each step. Cooling systems respond slowly to load changes because they lack real-time visibility into compute demand. Energy storage sits idle until a utility outage occurs, providing no benefit during normal operation. The cumulative result is facilities that consume more power, use more water, and place greater strain on local infrastructure than necessary. When a community faces rising electricity rates or water restrictions while a data center down the road operates inefficiently, the backlash is predictable and justified. Incremental improvements won't solve this. The industry needs a fundamental rethinking of infrastructure design, and converged architecture provides a framework for doing exactly that. The Four-in-One Solution Converged architecture integrates power distribution, energy storage, and thermal management as a unified platform from the outset. Midea, working with Clou Electronics, has developed a four-in-one solution that demonstrates how this integration addresses the social license challenge directly. The system combines four critical components into a single coordinated architecture: - Power Supply Integration - Rather than treating power distribution as a separate system, the converged platform minimizes conversion stages, reducing energy loss and waste heat generation from the start. - Active Energy Storage - Instead of backup batteries that sit idle, the system uses energy storage to actively buffer demand spikes in real time. This reduces peak load on the grid, smoothing the facility's impact on local utility infrastructure and making it a better grid citizen. - Magnetic Levitation Cold Source - Traditional chillers rely on mechanical bearings that create friction and consume parasitic energy. Magnetic levitation technology eliminates physical contact in rotating components, using magnetic fields for suspension. This cuts energy consumption in the cooling plant itself while extending equipment life and reducing maintenance requirements. - Liquid-Cooled CDU - The liquid cooling distribution unit (CDU) is designed for higher-temperature operation and near-closed-loop water usage. By integrating with the magnetic levitation cold source and coordinating with real-time compute activity, the system dramatically reduces water consumption compared to conventional evaporative cooling approaches. The key differentiator is integration. These components aren't simply installed in the same facility; they're designed to work together from the ground up. The control systems coordinate across power, storage, and cooling. The thermal interfaces optimize heat transfer. The power buffering responds to actual compute demand, not ambient temperature changes. Magnetic CDU: The Efficiency Foundation As data centers face increasing demands from high-density computing and AI workloads, traditional cooling systems struggle to keep pace. Midea's Magnetic CDU offers a transformative approach to thermal management, combining exceptional energy efficiency with operational simplicity and reduced space requirements. The Magnetic CDU delivers outstanding energy performance that directly impacts operational costs. With a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.1 or lower, facilities can achieve substantial reductions in electricity consumption compared to conventional cooling systems. The unit's intelligent free cooling capabilities maximize the use of ambient conditions, further reducing energy costs while maintaining optimal operating temperatures for all equipment types. Designed for versatility, the system adapts to diverse cooling requirements with adjustable water temperatures, supporting everything from traditional servers to the latest high-performance computing chips. The unit seamlessly switches between cooling modes in seconds, ensuring stable temperatures even during sudden load changes—critical for preventing equipment stress and maintaining uptime. artigo.texto: More data centers headed to San Antonio. City Council will vote on data center regulations SAN ANTONIO - Tx — The debate over data centers popping up here in San Antonio and all throughout Texas has prompted calls of regulation from city leaders and the community. Tonight District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan hosted a town hall meeting to hear from the community before city council votes on two proposals to regulate data centers. Proposal 1 will automatically permit new data centers as long as they are within certain zoning districts that are at least 500 feet away from residential homes, schools, daycares, assisted living facilities, and hospitals. Proposal 1 would not require a vote from city council; however, Proposal 2 would require a city council vote. Proposal 2 would also give the community an opportunity to make public comments before the data center would be approved. Public commenters at Tuesday’s town hall meeting voiced their concerns. “After hearing what everyone said today it sounds like Proposal 2 needs to be implemented. We have three hospitals in this area. What’s going to happen to the ICU when the electricity goes out, and their generators are not enough?” Councilman Galvan says he is also advocating for data centers to only be allowed to use recycled water. The District 6 Councilman says he supports Proposal 2. “I think primarily what we should be looking towards is that every data center that comes to San Antonio goes before City Council for a full vote.” City Council will vote on the two proposals on Oct. 29.

The global thermal energy storage (TES) tanks market is undergoing a transformative phase, evolving from a niche component in district heating and concentrated solar power (CSP) to a cornerstone of the energy transition. This analysis, with a forecast horizon of 2026 to 2035, examines a market propelled by the urgent need to decarbonize heat, integrate variable renewables, and enhance grid flexibility. The market encompasses engineered vessels for sensible, latent, and thermochemical storage, serving applications from utility-scale power generation to commercial HVAC. Growth is underpinned by policy mandates, declining renewable costs, and the electrification of heat. However, expansion varies regionally, shaped by energy mixes and regulatory maturity. This report provides a comprehensive assessment of demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, competitive strategies, and price evolution, equipping stakeholders with the analytical foundation to navigate opportunities and risks in a rapidly evolving energy ecosystem. The baseline scenario for the thermal energy storage tanks market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust growth, driven by the global acceleration of renewable energy deployment and the imperative to decarbonize industrial and building heat. As solar and wind penetration increases, the value of thermal storage for shifting excess generation to peak demand periods rises, particularly in regions with ambitious net-zero targets. The market will see a shift from traditional CSP-dominated demand to broader applications, including industrial process heat, district energy, and data center cooling. Technological advancements in phase change materials and thermochemical storage will unlock new use cases, while cost reductions in tank fabrication and insulation improve project economics. Policy support, such as investment tax credits and renewable portfolio standards, will remain critical. However, supply chain constraints for specialty alloys and skilled labor may temper growth in some years. Overall, the market is expected to register a CAGR of 8.2% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 220 by 2035 (2025=100). Concentrated solar power (CSP) remains a primary end-use for thermal energy storage tanks, particularly molten salt tanks that enable dispatchable electricity generation. Currently, CSP plants in regions with high direct normal irradiance, such as Spain, the United States, and the Middle East, rely on TES to extend generation into peak demand hours. Through 2035, demand will be driven by new CSP capacity in emerging markets like Chile, South Africa, and China, where storage is essential for grid stability. The trend is toward larger storage capacities, with towers and parabolic troughs incorporating 10-15 hours of storage. Demand-side indicators include national renewable energy targets, auction results for CSP with storage, and the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) competitiveness. As molten salt technology matures, costs decline, but competition from PV-plus-battery systems poses a challenge. Nevertheless, CSP with TES offers long-duration storage and synchronous generation, ensuring a sustained market for specialized tanks. Current trend: Steady growth. Major trends: Increasing storage hours in new CSP projects, Adoption of advanced molten salt formulations, Hybridization with PV and thermal storage, and Growth in emerging markets with high solar irradiance. Representative participants: BrightSource Energy, Abengoa, Sener, SolarReserve, and Cobra Energía. District heating and cooling networks are increasingly integrating thermal energy storage tanks to balance supply and demand, improve efficiency, and incorporate renewable heat sources. In Europe, especially Scandinavia and the Baltic states, large stratified hot water tanks store heat from waste incineration, biomass, and solar thermal, while chilled water and ice storage tanks provide cooling in commercial districts. Through 2035, demand will grow as cities expand networks and retrofit existing systems to meet decarbonization goals. Key demand-side indicators include urban population growth, district energy network expansion, and the share of renewable heat. The shift toward low-temperature district heating and the use of surplus industrial heat will require advanced storage solutions. Additionally, the integration of heat pumps and solar thermal systems will drive demand for flexible storage. This segment is expected to see steady growth, supported by EU funding and national energy efficiency programs. Current trend: Accelerating. Major trends: Integration of solar thermal and waste heat into district networks, Expansion of low-temperature district heating, Retrofitting of existing networks with storage, and Growth in cooling demand in urban areas. Representative participants: Danfoss, Viessmann, Trane Technologies, and Baltimore Aircoil Company. Through 2035, demand will accelerate as companies face carbon pricing and seek to reduce fossil fuel dependence. artigo.texto: Acordo entre YOU.ON Energia e HyperStrong combina tecnologia chinesa com engenharia brasileira e busca espaço nos primeiros leilões de baterias de grande porte do país O Brasil está prestes a abrir uma nova frente no setor elétrico, e uma empresa nacional decidiu se unir a uma gigante chinesa para disputar esse mercado. A YOU.ON Energia e a HyperStrong firmaram um acordo para oferecer sistemas de armazenamento em baterias de grande porte, capazes de guardar eletricidade e fornecê-la à rede quando necessário. A parceria, anunciada em 6 de outubro de 2026, tem como principal objetivo participar das oportunidades comerciais relacionadas aos leilões de armazenamento previstos para dezembro. A iniciativa surge em um momento de expansão da energia solar e eólica, quando o país enfrenta novos desafios para equilibrar geração e consumo de eletricidade. Empresa brasileira aposta em tecnologia chinesa para entrar na disputa por baterias gigantes O acordo foi assinado no final de setembro entre a YOU.ON Energia e a HyperStrong International USA Corp., subsidiária do grupo chinês Beijing HyperStrong Technology. - Engie fecha acordo com indústria brasileira para usar energia de sete usinas solares no RN, com 340,5 MW e redução projetada de R$ 10 milhões por ano na conta de luz - Cemig abre edital de R$ 150 milhões para indústrias, condomínios e prefeituras em Minas Gerais; pela primeira vez, projetos podem incluir baterias para armazenar energia solar - Quatro usinas solares da Rio Alto na Paraíba têm desligamento comercial aprovado pela CCEE por multas não pagas; empresa invoca recuperação extrajudicial, mas pedido é rejeitado - Funai pede suspensão das licenças de duas hidrelétricas em Santa Catarina e abre disputa que envolve 20 usinas nos rios Chapecó e Chapecozinho, com potencial estimado em quase 550 MW Pela estratégia anunciada, a fabricante chinesa fornecerá os sistemas de armazenamento, conhecidos como BESS, enquanto a empresa brasileira ficará responsável pela engenharia, integração dos equipamentos, serviços técnicos e assistência local. Segundo informações divulgadas pela pv magazine Brasil, os equipamentos da HyperStrong deverão chegar ao país já montados e testados pela fabricante. A proposta é combinar a escala industrial chinesa com a experiência brasileira na implantação de sistemas elétricos, reduzindo riscos operacionais e oferecendo soluções competitivas aos investidores. Leilões de dezembro podem abrir caminho para uma nova indústria no Brasil A parceria foi estruturada especialmente para os dois leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para dezembro de 2026. De acordo com a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL), o primeiro certame está programado para 2 de dezembro e será destinado a sistemas que atendam às exigências de fabricação nacional. O segundo, previsto para 4 de dezembro, permitirá a participação de soluções que não cumpram esse requisito específico. Os projetos deverão oferecer potência mínima de 30 megawatts e capacidade de fornecimento durante quatro horas. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início do atendimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Mais de 6 mil projetos mostram o tamanho da corrida pelo armazenamento Os números divulgados pelo governo ajudam a dimensionar o interesse das empresas nesse mercado. Segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), foram cadastrados 6.091 projetos de armazenamento, somando 296.807 MW de potência para os leilões de 2026. O volume representa um recorde de cadastramentos para certames do setor elétrico brasileiro e demonstra o interesse dos investidores pelas oportunidades que poderão surgir. Entretanto, os números correspondem a projetos cadastrados, não a empreendimentos aprovados ou contratos garantidos. A capacidade efetivamente contratada dependerá das etapas de habilitação e dos resultados dos leilões. Gigante chinesa afirma ter mais de 400 projetos de baterias espalhados pelo mundo A HyperStrong chega à parceria com uma operação internacional consolidada. Fundada em 2011, a companhia abriu capital na Bolsa de Xangai em janeiro de 2025 e atua no desenvolvimento e na integração de sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Segundo dados apresentados pela própria fabricante, a empresa ultrapassou 400 projetos implementados e 70 gigawatts-hora (GWh) de capacidade acumulada instalada até agosto de 2026. A companhia também informa possuir capacidade anual de produção superior a 70 GWh, apoiada por cinco bases industriais na China. Apesar dessa estrutura, a parceria não inclui, até o momento, anúncio de construção de uma fábrica da HyperStrong no Brasil. Conteúdo nacional será um dos principais desafios da parceria Um dos aspectos mais importantes do acordo envolve as exigências brasileiras de conteúdo local. A YOU.ON já aparece na lista de fornecedores cadastrados pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), na categoria de empresa de engenharia. Contudo, o próprio BNDES esclarece que esse credenciamento inicial representa aproximadamente 15% do percurso necessário para a obtenção do código Finame de um sistema completo. A instituição exige a comprovação de processos produtivos realizados no Brasil, não sendo suficiente importar equipamentos e realizar apenas atividades comerciais. As empresas informaram que a solução conjunta envolverá dois componentes de conteúdo local, mas ainda não divulgaram quais serão esses itens nem o percentual de nacionalização previsto. Empresa brasileira já participou de projeto pioneiro de baterias em São Paulo A YOU.ON possui experiência em armazenamento de grande porte no Brasil. A companhia participou da implantação do sistema de baterias instalado na subestação de Registro, no litoral sul de São Paulo, empreendimento desenvolvido para a ISA Energia Brasil, antiga ISA CTEEP. O projeto possui potência de 30 MW e capacidade de fornecimento de 60 MWh durante duas horas, conforme os dados da transmissora. A instalação ajuda a atender os períodos de maior demanda elétri

artigo.texto: No Chile, a ENGIE inaugurou 160 contêineres de baterias em infraestrutura reservada à expansão térmica. O BESS Lile custou US$ 174 milhões, armazena 802 MWh e pode atender o equivalente a mais de 84 mil casas por até cinco horas. O que estava reservado para ampliar a geração térmica de um complexo industrial no norte do Chile agora abriga uma bateria de escala incomum: 160 contêineres, 40 equipamentos de suporte e capacidade de armazenar 802 MWh de eletricidade. A ENGIE Chile colocou o BESS Lile em operação comercial em Mejillones, na região de Antofagasta, após investir US$ 174 milhões. O empreendimento tem 142 MW de potência e pode devolver eletricidade ao sistema chileno por até cinco horas. Segundo a empresa, isso equivale ao consumo de mais de 84 mil residências durante esse intervalo. A autorização para operar comercialmente foi concedida pelo Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional em 25 de setembro de 2026; a companhia anunciou a conclusão da primeira etapa da reconversão do complexo em 8 de outubro. Um espaço planejado para aumentar a geração térmica recebeu 160 contêineres de baterias O BESS Lile reutiliza a subestação de interconexão, vias internas e áreas de um complexo que havia sido preparado para expansão de geração térmica. São instalações que já tinham acesso ao sistema elétrico, originalmente previstas para uma ampliação da geração a carvão. A antiga estrutura passou a ter outra finalidade sem que todo o complexo térmico fosse convertido de uma só vez. - Pesquisadores da USP usaram simulações de física quântica para investigar 22 espécies químicas e combater falhas em baterias de sódio que prometem formar camada protetora contra dendritos que reduzem a vida útil - Grécia inaugura parque de baterias de € 50 milhões e 200 MWh em Tessalônica, com armazenamento diário equivalente à recarga de 3 mil carros elétricos e reforço à rede elétrica - Peru conecta mais de 136 mil painéis solares no deserto de Nasca e forma complexo de 403,52 MW com dois parques eólicos, unindo sol e vento na mesma região de Ica - Estudo com 88 mil unidades consumidoras de energia solar por assinatura registrou inadimplência média de 17% e alerta para riscos da abertura do mercado livre no Brasil As baterias ficam distribuídas em 160 contêineres, acompanhados por 40 conjuntos elétricos de apoio. O parque funciona como sistema independente de armazenamento, conhecido como stand-alone: recebe eletricidade da rede e pode reinjetá-la quando o operador necessita. Ao contrário de uma usina, o equipamento não gera eletricidade: guarda a energia recebida e a devolve em horários determinados pela operação da rede. São 142 MW de potência, 802 MWh guardados e autonomia de até cinco horas A capacidade final divulgada em 2026 superou a previsão de 140 MW apresentada pela empresa um ano antes. Os 142 MW indicam a potência que o parque pode entregar ou receber. Os 802 MWh representam a quantidade de energia que seus módulos podem guardar. A relação entre potência e capacidade define por quanto tempo as baterias podem fornecer eletricidade. A empresa usa uma referência residencial para traduzir essa capacidade: eletricidade equivalente ao consumo de mais de 84 mil casas durante até cinco horas de fornecimento. Quando há muita produção solar durante o dia, baterias conectadas à rede podem absorver parte dessa energia e devolvê-la após o pôr do sol, quando a geração fotovoltaica diminui. Como o BESS Lile está conectado diretamente à rede, sua carga e descarga dependem da operação do sistema, e não de um parque solar exclusivo no local. O carvão começou a sair de Mejillones no fim de 2025, mas a transformação continua A mudança não começou com os contêineres. Depois de quase três décadas de operação, a ENGIE desligou em 31 de dezembro de 2025 as unidades a carvão CTM1 e CTM2, que tinham juntas 334 MW de capacidade instalada, segundo o relatório anual da companhia. O plano de descarbonização ainda prevê outros equipamentos e retiradas de unidades no mesmo conjunto industrial. Outra unidade da região, a Infraestrutura Energética Mejillones (IEM), está em processo de adaptação para funcionar com gás natural. Em outubro de 2026, a empresa dizia que essa instalação ainda aguardava a entrada em operação comercial após a conversão. A empresa mantém no plano de transformação o futuro encerramento de operações a carvão nas unidades Central Termoeléctrica Andina (CTA) e Central Termoeléctrica Hornitos (CTH). Potência de baterias no Chile saiu de 1,2 GW para 3,2 GW ao longo de 2025 O novo parque entra em uma rede que está mudando rapidamente. Um levantamento do Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional, divulgado em abril, mostrou que a potência de armazenamento em baterias no Chile passou de aproximadamente 1,2 GW para 3,2 GW ao longo de 2025. O mesmo relatório apontou participação conjunta recorde de 46,2% da geração solar e eólica em dezembro de 2025. O órgão também identificou gargalos e atrasos na infraestrutura de transmissão e apontou a necessidade de atualizar regras de operação e remuneração diante do crescimento das baterias. Antes de Lile, a ENGIE colocou mais 251 MW de baterias em operação em agosto Em 28 de agosto de 2026, a companhia informou a entrada em operação comercial de outros dois projetos: BESS Libélula, na região de Santiago, e BESS Los Loros, em Atacama. Juntos, eles adicionaram 251 MW de potência de armazenamento ao sistema chileno, com US$ 283 milhões investidos nessa parte dos empreendimentos. O BESS Libélula dispõe de 203 MW e 1.034 MWh, com 208 contêineres, e integra um projeto que também inclui geração solar. O Los Loros reúne 48 MW e 275,23 MWh junto a uma usina fotovoltaica existente. Lile é diferente: opera como armazenamento independente, dentro de um complexo de origem térmica. Com o início das operações em Mejillones, a ENGIE contabiliza cinco sistemas de baterias que começaram a operar comercialmente em 2026 e informa ter alcançado 803 MW de capacidade instalada nessa tecnologia no Chile. artigo.texto: About one-fifth of the 101 towns and villages in the Adirondack Park have passed moratoriums this year on building battery energy storage systems, and now bans are coming, according to local laws filed with the New York Department of State. The towns of Fort Ann, Gloversville and Forestport, which are all partially within the Adirondack Park, have banned battery systems. The town of St. Armand’s board had passed a ban this summer, but failed to evaluate the local law through the State Environmental Quality Review Act. Supervisor Davina Thurston said the town board is going through that process now and plans to pass the ban again. Twenty-one municipalities in the park have filed local laws since Jan. 1 delaying battery storage builds. The moratoriums range from six months to a year. Several are set to expire if they are not renewed. The state’s quest for more storage Battery energy storage systems are a way for the electric grid to store power for later use. Generally made up of lithium-ion batteries, the systems are intended to help the grid rely less on fossil fuel-using peaker plants, thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions. They may also increase the grid’s reliability and reduce the need for infrastructure upgrades. Large battery system fires in New York have spooked municipalities, even with the state’s updated fire code. The new fire code requires developers to fund a peer review of their projects, including inspections with the local permitting authority, to train local fire departments and to provide a battery fire expert on site within four hours of any fire. New York’s goal is to have 6 gigawatts of energy storage online by 2030, but the reality of that is looking grim. As of Aug. 31, the state’s total storage capacity was about 576 megawatts. New York has led a national, developer-tracked survey of moratoriums. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority has been sending representatives to Adirondack Park Agency and municipal meetings to help alleviate fire fears and answer questions. St. Armand’s ban Energy developer Carson Power had an initial proposal to install a 20-megawatt facility near the Mount Pisgah Ski Area in the town of St. Armand. In March, the town passed a one-year moratorium on battery storage builds. In June, the board decided to pass a ban without going through the State Environmental Quality Review Act. Thurston said the town’s attorney is assisting in getting the law reviewed under the act and is moving forward with an official ban. Jennifer Manierre, the director of clean energy and siting at NYSERDA, visited the town on Sept. 1 and spoke about batteries’ benefits and the safeguards the state now has in place to protect public health and the environment, meeting minutes show. Residents were still concerned about a potential battery fire, especially in the area of the proposed project. Thurston said she felt “the appropriate action is to move forward with a town-wide ban on battery energy storage systems,” according to meeting minutes. In an interview on Thursday, Thurston said the ban would prevent the Carson Power project from being built. She had invited Carson Power to the Sept. 1 meeting, but they declined, she added. Carson Power did not respond to Adirondack Explorer’s request for comment. Dannemora update In Dannemora, Supervisor Joey Varin remains openminded to battery energy storage. He’s attended classes and seminars related to the storage systems and fires. Varin has the beginnings of a proposal to put a battery energy storage system on the tailings pile of the former mining operation at Lyon Mountain. The developer examining the site is Brookfield Renewable Partners. The business is currently in talks with the utility company, New York State Electric and Gas, about potentially upgrading a nearby substation, Varin said. He is planning to host a public meeting about it around the beginning of next year once Brookfield has more information. He thinks the project is at an ideal site, outside of the hamlet in an old sand pit. “I’ve been asked by a number of people outside of our area to put a moratorium on,” Varin said. “I said no. … We’re just gathering more and more knowledge, educating ourselves the best way we can of understanding all we can about it. When the time comes, we’ll make sure our residents are totally educated on the process and start those general information sessions with our residents.” Moratorium progress and renewals In the town of Northampton, the Adirondack Park Agency (APA) permitted the first large-scale battery energy storage system in the park. It was a 10-megawatt, four-hour system, also proposed by Carson Power. In March, however, the town passed a one-year moratorium on battery system builds. The moratorium was on new projects. The Carson Power project did not appear to be covered. Concerned about battery storage facilities, Northampton resident Sara Will-White sued the town, the APA, Carson Power and the project site’s landowner. A Fulton County state supreme court justice issued a temporary restraining order, delaying the project, but has not yet issued a decision on the lawsuit. In Ticonderoga, a six-month moratorium passed in March is soon ending. Meeting minutes show the town is considering passing an additional six-month moratorium. The town of Indian Lake is in a similar position. It’s unclear from meeting minutes if the town is considering a renewal of its moratorium. Town Supervisor Brian Wells did not return Adirondack Explorer’s inquiry. The town of Hadley’s moratorium is on the cusp of ending, but meeting minutes show the board is working on a renewal.

artigo.texto: In ten months, India’s battery storage assembly industry has gone from a few containerised-system lines to a pipeline that, on company statements alone, adds up to about 180 GWh a year. Roughly 30-34 GWh is operating today. The rest is a mix of groundbreakings, state approvals and memoranda of understanding. Reliance’s upcoming 40 GWh (Long term-120 GWh) Jamnagar gigafactory, if counted, takes the total past 220 GWh. Set that against demand. CRISIL Ratings expects 45–50 GWh of storage to be commissioned across FY27 and FY28 combined, up from about 1 GWh at the end of FY26. That is roughly 25 GWh a year. Anyone who covered solar manufacturing in 2023 knows how this overcapacity arithmetic tends to end. The honest question is whether it ends the same way, and how soon. Thom Tillis criticized federal decisions to halt renewable energy projects and abruptly withdraw clean energy incentives Thursday, saying the country needs more electricity and businesses need certainty to build it. Speaking as North Carolina voters began casting early ballots in the midterm elections, the Republican senator also warned that his party faces “almost certain losses” and said poorly designed policies were giving opponents ammunition. Other WRAL Top Stories “When you make dumb policy, the ads write themselves,” Tillis said during the Making Energy Work conference in Cary. North Carolina is weighing how to meet growing electricity demand without leaving households paying for power plants and equipment built to serve data centers. A day before the conference, Attorney General Jeff Jackson and Gov. Josh Stein said Duke Energy’s proposed customer protections leave an important gap: Data centers would pay for equipment connecting them to the grid, but the proposal does not require them to cover new power plants needed to supply their electricity. Jackson said the proposal does not require large customers to pay for new power generation their demand makes necessary. Jackson also called for a separate customer rate class to better track the costs of serving data centers. “This is a massive step forward in making sure data centers pay their fair share — but we’re not done yet,” Jackson said in Wednesday’s announcement. U.S. Rep. Tim Moore, another North Carolina Republican who spoke at the conference, said companies building and profiting from data centers should bear the costs of serving them. “We want to make sure that the companies that are... building these and generating the profits... are responsible for the cost and that those don’t get passed on to the ratepayers,” Moore said. Duke announced the proposed agreement Oct. 7 with North Carolina Public Staff, a separate state agency representing utility customers, along with technology companies and other parties. The agreement requires approval from the North Carolina Utilities Commission. The proposal would require upfront payments for equipment built specifically for large customers, long-term contracts and minimum monthly bills even if customers use less electricity than expected. It also includes financial protections if customers leave early. Duke says the agreement would strengthen existing protections for other customers. “It’s simple — data centers will pay upfront for all costs to connect to the grid,” Duke Energy North Carolina President Kendal Bowman said. The distinction between paying to connect to the grid and paying for new power generation remains central to the debate. Matt Abele of the North Carolina Sustainable Energy Association, a clean energy advocacy organization, said questions remain about whether large customers will cover all the costs of upgrading the system to serve them. “Our belief is, as data centers come into the state of North Carolina, they need to be powered clean and they need to cover 100% of their costs,” Abele said. Producing enough electricity is another challenge. Tillis questioned federal decisions to stop renewable energy projects while demand grows. “Why are we canceling all these power purchase agreements for large-scale renewable projects and creating uncertainty there when we know we need every bit of it that can be generated?” Tillis said. Tillis pointed to a permitting deal under consideration in Congress as a way to speed up approval of energy projects. Tillis said the agreement has better-than-even odds of passing after the election, though political disagreements and year-end deadlines could get in the way. “The only reason I’d see it not getting done is people are just either the Democrats feel emboldened because maybe they’ve won the House, the Republicans feel annoyed because maybe they lost the House,” Tillis said. Abele said getting that agreement passed could help North Carolina bring more clean energy onto the grid. “Finding opportunities to expedite the permitting and bring those resources online … is going to be so imperative moving forward,” Abele said. Tillis called for a mix of energy sources, criticizing both an exclusively renewable approach and one dependent entirely on fossil fuels. Tillis also said renewable energy businesses should eventually operate without government subsidies. Tillis’ criticism centered on how abruptly the policy changes disrupted investments already underway. “It wasn’t even paying attention to the portfolio of businesses already out there,” Tillis said. Tillis said health care concerns were the primary reason for opposing President Donald Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, though energy policy was another concern. Moore said ending federal credits for home energy improvements was part of a broader effort to lower taxes. WRAL asked Moore how eliminating credits for insulation, heat pumps and rooftop solar fits with making energy more affordable. “There were some of these programs that are great programs to be able to have that we simply couldn’t have carveouts for if we were going to otherwise lower the rate,” Moore said. Moore said technologies such as solar and electric vehicles can still make financial sense without federal tax credits. The law ended the energy-efficient home improvement credit and the residential clean energy credit for new qualifying work after Dec. 31, 2025, according to the IRS. The residential credit previously covered 30% of qualifying solar and battery storage costs. Abele said rising electricity costs continue to make solar and battery storage attractive to homeowners despite the loss of federal incentives. artigo.texto: The most politically fascinating place in Virginia right now might be Amherst County, with Campbell County coming in second. Multiple forces are converging on both counties — and, admittedly, some others — that will require public officials there to make some decisions that most localities don’t have to. Many of these involve a subject that’s complicated, often misunderstood and usually politicized: energy. Let’s start with Amherst County. Many county taxpayers are still reeling from reassessments that are driving their tax bills higher. The board of supervisors reduced the tax rate but not by enough to hold tax bills the same. Just as the prices you and I pay at the store are going up, so, too, are the prices that governments must pay. That sticker shock from reassessments should make Amherst a prime candidate to hear options on how to hold down tax bills — and now it has some. Off-track betting Five years ago, Amherst voters were asked if they wanted to approve off-track betting for a Rosie’s Gaming Emporium. They said no, by a margin of 54.1% to 45.9%. Now Rosie’s is trying again. Will the post-assessment political landscape in Amherst produce a different result? We’ll see. (Pulaski County also has its own referendum on off-track betting.) A study by Mangum Economics commissioned by the Lynchburg Regional Business Alliance forecasts that such a facility would generate $1.9 million in tax revenue during its first year of operation — $1.6 million from the tax on pari-mutuel wagering, the rest through other taxes such as meals taxes and sales taxes and whatnot. That $1.6 million figure for tax revenue seems on track with what other Rosie’s outlets have generated in smaller communities. The three most comparable ones are in Collinsville (outside Martinsville), Vinton (outside Roanoke) and Emporia. Here’s what they generated last year: Collinsville: $254,636 Emporia: $1,574,946 Vinton: $3,478,266 Those localities were allowed to keep half that money; the rest was shared with New Kent County, home of the Colonial Downs racetrack. That law has now been changed to allow host localities to keep all the tax revenue. If Amherst were to reject off-track betting a second time, that would not be unprecedented: Manassas Park has voted it down three times, in 1996, 2004 and 2023. The off-track betting question might be simple compared to the other issues coming before Amherst. Data center There are possibly two data center projects that will soon come before Amherst County supervisors. Data centers have become politically unpopular, to put it mildly. However, they also generate enormous sums of tax revenues, which is why some localities prize them. Mecklenburg County’s Microsoft complex has generated so much revenue that the county has been able to build new schools — every school is now built in this century — and lower its real estate tax rate to the lowest in the state. Some may see this as a Faustian bargain: Amherst could generate lots of tax revenue (the exact amount is unclear) with a data center. Is Amherst so opposed to data centers that it’s willing to turn away millions in revenue? If Amherst says “no” to both a data center and to Rosie’s, then how does the county propose to generate new revenues? That’s not an argument to approve either if people don’t want them, but it is an argument that Amherst will need revenue options if taxpayers don’t like their bills going up. If Rosie’s and a data center aren’t those options, then what is? And then there’s this: Nuclear reactors Amherst and Campbell counties now find themselves in the middle of a nationwide debate over how we should generate electricity. Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s recent energy plan lays out some uncomfortable facts: Depending on which forecast you believe — low, moderate or high — Virginia will need to double, triple or quadruple the amount of power it produces. And yes, data centers are a big factor in what’s driving those energy demands. Under every option the governor’s plan lays out, Virginia needs more nuclear energy. The advantage of nuclear is that you can produce a lot of power in a small space — unlike, say, solar energy, which requires a lot of land to produce power only part of the time. The disadvantage is that nuclear has been expensive and time-consuming to build. And then there are those who are freaked out by the idea of splitting atoms. Nuclear development slowed to almost nothing after the Three Mile Island accident in Pennsylvania in 1979. It’s also been politically polarizing, with the right more receptive to it than the left. Now nuclear is seeing something of a renaissance with a push for small reactors that, in theory, can be built more quickly and cheaply. We’re also seeing a political realignment, with some on the left coming to see nuclear as the only realistic way to retire lots of carbon-belching energy facilities. There are now three proposals to build small nuclear reactors in Virginia: Dominion Energy and Amazon are exploring one that would go at Dominion’s existing North Anna nuclear station in Louisa County. That seems about as non-controversial as you can get. The place has two big reactors now and is authorized for a third anyway. (Disclosure: Dominion is one of our donors, but donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy. You can become a donor and test that proposition.) The other two reactor proposals are both in the Lynchburg area: Appalachian Power is looking at one at its Joshua Falls substation in Campbell County, and now a Charlotte, North Carolina-based energy company is pitching a facility that could involve multiple small reactors (sounds like two from the energy estimates) in Amherst County, almost directly across the James River from Joshua Falls. If there’s any place in Virginia that understands nuclear power — or, at least, isn’t automatically spooked by it — it should be the Lynchburg area. artigo.texto: Análise: Mercado de carbono expõe desafio brasileiro Enquanto a Europa amplia gradualmente a cobrança sobre emissões de produtos importados, o Brasil ainda define as regras de seu mercado regulado de carbono Exportar aço e alumínio para a União Europeia exigirá cada vez mais atenção às emissões de gases de efeito estufa geradas durante a fabricação desses produtos. Isso porque os europeus começaram a aplicar um mecanismo que atribui um custo à poluição associada às importações. Enquanto essa cobrança será ampliada gradualmente, o Brasil ainda regulamenta seu próprio mercado de carbono, criado por lei em 2024. A diferença entre os dois sistemas poderá se tornar especialmente importante em 2030, quando as regras europeias ficarão mais rigorosas. O CBAM (Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira) entrou em sua fase definitiva em janeiro de 2026. Pelo sistema, importadores europeus de produtos como aço e alumínio deverão adquirir certificados que representam as emissões de gases de efeito estufa associadas à fabricação dessas mercadorias. Cada certificado corresponde a uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). Embora não seja formalmente um imposto de importação, o CBAM estabelece uma cobrança sobre as emissões de gases de efeito estufa associadas à fabricação de determinados produtos vendidos à União Europeia. O pagamento será feito pelos importadores europeus, que comprarão das autoridades do bloco certificados cujo preço acompanha o mercado regulado de carbono europeu: € 82,32 por tonelada no terceiro trimestre de 2026. Não se trata de créditos do mercado voluntário. As compras começarão em fevereiro de 2027, referentes às importações realizadas em 2026. A cobrança sobre as importações aumentará gradualmente porque a União Europeia está reduzindo as permissões gratuitas de emissão de carbono concedidas às suas próprias indústrias. Essas permissões permitem que as empresas emitam determinada quantidade de gases de efeito estufa sem precisar comprar autorizações no mercado regulado. Em 2029, as indústrias europeias dos setores cobertos pelo CBAM ainda receberão gratuitamente 77,5% das permissões calculadas segundo os critérios do bloco, percentual que cairá para 51,5% em 2030. Isso significa que a redução do benefício, de 22,5% em 2029, chegará a 48,5% no ano seguinte. Essa mesma redução será considerada no cálculo da cobrança sobre os produtos importados, para que fabricantes europeus e estrangeiros estejam sujeitos a condições equivalentes de precificação do carbono. Isso não significa que o importador pagará sobre 48,5% das emissões de cada produto: o desconto é calculado sobre parâmetros de referência europeus, e não sobre as emissões reais. Quanto mais o produto emitir acima desses parâmetros, maior será a cobrança. O artigo 9º do CBAM permite reduzir a cobrança europeia quando o importador comprova que já houve pagamento pelas emissões de carbono no país onde a mercadoria foi produzida. No Brasil, porém, a Lei nº 15.042/2024 estabelece que, no primeiro ciclo do SBCE (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões), as empresas receberão gratuitamente cotas que autorizam a emissão de determinadas quantidades de gases de efeito estufa. Cada cota corresponde ao direito de emitir uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). Como essas autorizações serão inicialmente distribuídas sem cobrança, seu recebimento não representa um pagamento que possa ser descontado da obrigação europeia. Há uma consequência adicional. O artigo 11 da lei brasileira vincula o início da distribuição onerosa às fases de implementação do SBCE. A cobrança pelas cotas deverá ocorrer após o primeiro ciclo de alocação gratuita, na etapa de implementação plena. Assim, mesmo que o mercado comece a operar por volta de 2030, a possibilidade de reconhecer pagamentos brasileiros no CBAM não surgirá automaticamente. O SBCE ainda está em fase de regulamentação. Pela lei, empresas de setores abrangidos pelo sistema que emitam mais de 10 mil toneladas anuais de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e) deverão informar suas emissões ao governo. Acima de 25 mil toneladas, terão também de comprovar que possuem cotas ou certificados reconhecidos pelo mercado regulado em quantidade suficiente para cobrir suas emissões. Essa obrigação, entretanto, ainda não está em vigor. Consulta pública aberta pelo Ministério da Fazenda em julho propôs iniciar gradualmente o monitoramento das emissões em 2027, sem exigir, nessa etapa, a compra de cotas. A agenda inicial da Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono previa para junho a definição dos setores econômicos sujeitos à regulamentação e a criação da CAREG (Câmara de Assuntos Regulatórios). Esse órgão deverá reunir representantes das atividades reguladas para discutir as regras de funcionamento do mercado, incluindo a distribuição das cotas de emissão. Segundo a ata da reunião do comitê consultivo de 30 de junho, sua constituição ocorrerá somente depois da definição dos setores abrangidos. Isso significa que a demora na conclusão dessa primeira etapa também pode comprometer a formação da Câmara e o avanço das normas seguintes. O governo anunciou a intenção de concluir a regulamentação até dezembro de 2026, mas ainda precisa esclarecer a situação dessas entregas. A prioridade é definir os setores, constituir a CAREG e divulgar um calendário consistente para o primeiro Plano Nacional de Alocação. Também é necessário explicar como as cotas gratuitas serão substituídas gradualmente por mecanismos de precificação efetiva. A indústria precisa conhecer essa trajetória antes de comprometer recursos em instalações e tecnologias que permanecerão em operação muito além de 2030.

artigo.texto: SINEXCEL Completes Power Conversion System Shipment for 100 MW/400 MWh Chile Battery Storage Project SINEXCEL has completed the shipment of all power conversion systems for a 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage project in Chile, according to a company press release. The Shenzhen-listed firm said the delivery covers the full order of StellaON 1250K units for RelyEZ Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd. The project is a four-hour system located in the Atacama region. It is designed to charge when demand is lower and discharge during peak periods, a pattern intended to support grid flexibility and project returns. Delivery Timing and Project Execution SINEXCEL stated that it completed the full power conversion system order on schedule. The company said this helps RelyEZ Energy protect the timetable for transport, installation, commissioning, and grid connection. According to the release, large-scale overseas projects depend on production, inspection, and shipment schedules staying closely aligned with on-site construction. Coordinated delivery is described as reducing uncertainty and helping local teams plan subsequent stages, since delays in a single batch can narrow the construction window for a project of this scale. Equipment Specifications for Atacama Conditions The StellaON 1250K power conversion system is built for environments that can include high temperatures, dust, and sand. SINEXCEL reported a maximum efficiency of 99% and a rated-power efficiency of 98.5% for the unit. The system supports operation from minus 40 degrees Celsius to 60 degrees Celsius, maintains full power output at 55 degrees Celsius, and carries an IP65 protection rating. The company said maintaining rated output in high temperatures can reduce power derating and the need for additional capacity, while higher conversion efficiency limits energy losses across repeated charge-discharge cycles. Service Network and Company Scale Following shipment, the Chilean project moves into on-site installation and commissioning. SINEXCEL said it has a dedicated after-sales team in Latin America and seven service centres across the Americas. Technical requests can receive a response within 30 minutes, backed by round-the-clock support and a seven-day spare-parts guarantee. SINEXCEL reported that it has deployed more than 17 GW of energy storage capacity across over 5,000 projects and works with more than 600 partners in more than 60 countries and regions. The company said it will continue to expand its local operations across Latin America and provide customers with support throughout the project lifecycle. Founded in 2007, SINEXCEL describes itself as a pioneer in energy storage, electric vehicle charging, and power quality solutions. Its disclosed deployments include 17 GW of installed storage, 200,000 electric vehicle DC chargers, and nearly 20 million amperes of active harmonic filters. - 1. artigo.texto: MESA — Dozens of Valley residents shared concerns about data centers with Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes at a town hall in Mesa on Wednesday night. Mayes has called for a temporary moratorium on new data center approvals. “This really has to be dealt with at the statewide level, and that's why I have called for a moratorium for now, so that we can get our hands around the situation,” she told reporters after the town hall. Several speakers spoke out against a data center under construction in Ahwatukee. Menlo Digital is building a 1 million-square-foot hyperscale campus with an onsite power substation with 257 megawatts of power. “This is a very serious health concern for us,” said Kathy Monk, who lives a half mile away from the construction site. She said her family doctor told her people that close to the completed data center will face cardiac and pulmonary issues. “Do you know what he told me?” she told Mayes. “He said, ‘You need to move. You need to move.’ My doctor said that.” Do you have a concern in your community or a news tip? We want to hear from you! Connect with us: share@abc15.com Monk also said the high-pitch frequency emitted from the data center complex could harm people with hearing aids and pacemakers. “It’s toxic,” she said. Other data center opponents said such heavy industrial facilities shouldn’t be allowed in commercial areas located so close to residential areas. “We have talked to the city – our city councilman, the mayor – and it was really depressing, the answers that we got,” another opponent to the Ahwatukee data center said. The city of Phoenix updated its zoning ordinances in 2025 to address data centers, but the Menlo Digital project was approved in 2024, when the data centers were considered similar to an office use, the city told ABC15 in August. Mayes, whose office is investigating the project, said she is considering filing a nuisance lawsuit. She told reporters after the forum that she was concerned about hyperscaled AI data centers like the Menlo Digital campus being built in areas designed for lower-level commercial operations. “And then they are somehow flipping that into this gigantic industrial facility that can give off constant noise ... and possibly constant air pollution, if they're using diesel generators to power them at any time,” Mayes said. “And so there's a lot to be investigated here, I think, with regard to these data centers.” One person, Lisa Everett, spoke in favor of data centers, pointing to the tax dollars paid by the facilities and the number of construction jobs the projects would create. She said she was also concerned about misinformation on data centers. “I understand the frustration. I understand it’s new,” she said. “But I’m asking you, is this just a fashionable thing, to be against data centers? Are we really going to have honest conversations?” Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat like Mayes, has said the state should develop standards for data centers but does not support a moratorium. Mayes told ABC15 she will be talking with the governor about her proposal. “I'm going to lobby her. I'm going to advocate for my position,” she said. “I'm going to be working with legislators.” Hobbs said she hopes the Legislature will pass legislation addressing data centers next year. “And I think it'll be a bipartisan bill,” she said. “I think you're going to see Republicans and Democrats come together on this issue.” “If you like your tech and your phone and your computer and the stuff you can use that for, you probably think data centers are important,” he said during his debate with Mayes last month. Mayes said she plans to hold more town halls on data centers, including in Ahwatukee.

artigo.texto: MINNEAPOLIMEDIA NEWS | Xcel Energy Seeks Two-Year Minnesota Electricity Base-Rate Freeze Using Federal Battery Storage Tax Credits A newly filed proposal would hold electric base rates steady during 2027 and 2028, but the plan requires state regulatory approval and would not necessarily freeze every charge on customers' bills. ST. PAUL, MN (October 15, 2026). Xcel Energy has proposed an alternative to a conventional Minnesota electricity rate case, offering to freeze customer base rates for calendar years 2027 and 2028 in exchange for accelerated recognition of federal tax benefits associated with five battery storage projects. The proposal was submitted October 9 by Northern States Power Company, Xcel Energy's Minnesota utility subsidiary, to the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. Xcel disclosed the filing in a report to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The plan could provide a period of greater rate stability for Minnesota electricity customers, but its financial structure and long-term implications require regulatory review. The company has requested a commission decision by January 2027. If the proposal is not approved, Xcel expects to file a conventional electric rate case in early 2027. What the Company Is Proposing The proposal is called the Electric Customer Rate Stability Plan. According to the SEC filing, it contains three principal elements. First, customer base rates would remain frozen during 2027 and 2028. Second, Xcel would accelerate the recognition of federal investment tax credits related to five battery energy storage projects. Third, the company would continue certain existing regulatory adjustment mechanisms, including previously approved true-up and tracker arrangements. The third provision is particularly important. A base-rate freeze does not necessarily mean that every amount appearing on an electricity bill would remain unchanged. Customers may encounter charges or adjustments governed by mechanisms outside the base-rate component. The plan therefore should not be described as a guarantee that every customer's total monthly bill will remain identical for two years. Why Battery Storage Tax Credits Matter Federal investment tax credits can reduce the financial cost of qualifying energy projects. Battery storage systems are designed to store electricity for use at another time, helping utilities manage variations in supply and demand. Depending on their design and operation, storage projects can support reliability and help integrate electricity generated from variable sources. Xcel's proposal would recognize the financial benefits of certain federal tax credits earlier than originally scheduled. The company says those benefits could offset the additional revenue it would otherwise seek to recover from customers for necessary capital investments. The proposed arrangement is therefore based on the timing of tax benefits rather than a promise that utility operating expenses will stop increasing. What the Regulatory Commission Must Determine The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission must evaluate whether the proposed arrangement is consistent with applicable utility law and reasonable for customers. Regulators will need to examine the timing and value of the tax credits, the costs being offset and the consequences for future rate proceedings. One question is whether using benefits earlier reduces the amount available to offset costs later. Another is whether the proposed freeze adequately protects customers if other approved adjustment mechanisms continue changing charges. A third concerns the treatment of investments that Xcel makes during the two-year period. The company has indicated that the accelerated tax credits would help offset the revenue requirement associated with ongoing capital improvements. Regulators must assess whether the arrangement produces an appropriate balance between customer affordability and the utility's financial obligations. What It Could Mean for Households For households managing tight budgets, greater predictability in electricity base rates could be valuable. Electricity is an essential expense, and changes in utility costs affect residents regardless of whether they own or rent their homes. However, the exact savings from the proposal have not been independently established for a typical residential customer. Without a verified customer bill comparison, it would be misleading to assign a specific monthly or annual savings figure. The impact may also vary depending on customer usage, rate class and the components of a bill that remain subject to adjustment. Business and Community Implications Electricity costs also affect businesses, nonprofit organizations, schools and other institutions. A period of base-rate stability could help some organizations plan their operating expenses. For businesses with substantial electricity consumption, even modest changes in rates can affect budgets. But the proposal's effect on different customer classes must be evaluated through the regulatory filing. The public should not assume that every residential, commercial and industrial customer would receive an identical financial benefit. What Happens After 2028? The proposed freeze would apply to calendar years 2027 and 2028. It would not establish a permanent prohibition on future rate increases. The treatment of costs and tax benefits after the proposed period is therefore a central question. Regulators and consumer advocates must examine whether the plan provides a durable financial advantage or primarily changes the timing of rate recovery. That analysis requires access to the underlying financial calculations, not simply the headline promise of a freeze. artigo.texto: Enlight Renewable Energy (TASE: ENLT; NASDAQ: ENLT) and ENERTRAG SE announced yesterday the official start of construction work on the Bertikow battery storage project in Brandenburg, following the ground-breaking ceremony held on 13 October at the project site. The ceremony was attended by representatives from Enlight, ENERTRAG and 50Hertz, as well as politicians, partners and local residents. Bertikow is a large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) with a capacity of 200 MW and an energy storage capacity of around 840 MWh. It is a joint project between Enlight and ENERTRAG. The project is situated directly next to the Bertikow substation in the municipality of Uckerfelde; the land rights and grid connection have been secured. The transition from the development phase to the construction phase has been completed, and construction work is already underway. Commissioning is currently scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027, with commercial operation due to commence in the first half of 2028. Once it becomes operational, Bertikow is expected to participate in the German day-ahead and intraday energy markets, as well as in the balancing energy markets, and to help balance electricity supply and demand by providing flexibility. A seven-year off-take agreement has been signed with EDF Trading for part of the storage capacity. The agreement marks Enlight’s first BESS off-take transaction in Europe and signals the company’s entry into the German battery storage market. The facility is being optimised by Entrix. Osborne Clarke acted as legal advisers to Enlight and ENERTRAG in connection with the acquisition. Comments from the companies Marko Liposcak, Managing Director of Enlight Europe: “As renewable energy continues to expand across Europe, large-scale energy storage systems are becoming increasingly important for the flexibility and reliability of electricity grids. Bertikow is a prime example of how such projects can help meet these changing requirements, whilst further strengthening Enlight’s presence in the European energy storage market. Together with ENERTRAG, we are delighted to mark the start of construction and to take another important step towards the commissioning of this project.” Dr Gunar Hering, CEO of ENERTRAG: “Bertikow is proof that the energy transition works in practice. We store surplus electricity from renewable energy sources and feed it into the grid precisely when it is most urgently needed: in this way, we provide reliable green electricity round the clock and keep the value added within the region.” Stefan Schlüter, Head of the DACH Region at EDF Trading: “The expansion of battery storage across Europe is driving demand for increasingly sophisticated commercial solutions. This agreement combines revenue security with commercial flexibility and demonstrates how innovative procurement structures can support the roll-out of large-scale storage facilities. We look forward to working with Enlight, ENERTRAG and Entrix on the Bertikow project.” Constantin Nicklas, Chief Revenue Officer at Entrix: “There need not be a conflict of objectives between bankability and earnings potential. Together with ENERTRAG, Enlight and EDF Trading, we have created a structure that maximises the returns from Bertikow without compromising our partners’ risk profile or financing requirements.”

artigo.texto: Recently, the "Hydrogen Wind Series portable hydrogen power generation equipment" independently developed by Guangdong Huachen Hydrogen Energy Co., Ltd. is about to be officially released. As the first product in this series, the world's first 200W portable hydrogen power generation equipmentwas officially released at the "Five New" power equipment technology exhibition and new-type power system equipment upgrade technology conference during the 28th China (Shenzhen) International Hi-Tech Fair. Innovative hybrid energy architecture addresses mobile energy storage endurance pain points In scenarios such as emergency rescue, power repair, communication support, field operations, and outdoor mobile power consumption, energy supply is often constrained by multiple factors including fixed power grid coverage, equipment endurance, refueling efficiency, and transportation conditions. Especially in long-duration continuous operation environments, traditional mobile energy storage equipment mainly relies on increasing battery capacity to improve endurance, but the resulting increases in weight, volume, and charging time can also affect equipment mobility and usage efficiency. To address these needs, the Hydrogen Wind Series portable hydrogen power generation equipment is designed around the concept of "continuous power generation," using coordinated operation of multiple energy systems to build a mobile energy solution suitable for off-grid scenarios. The product adopts ahybrid energy architecture in which aluminum-based energy storage materials, hydrogen fuel cells, and lithium batteries work in coordination. Among them, aluminum-based energy storage materials handle energy storage functions, hydrogen fuel cells are responsible for energy conversion, and lithium batteries respond to equipment start-stop, instantaneous loads, and power fluctuations, achieving coordinated operation across energy storage, power generation conversion, and stable output. At the same time, the product adopts a modular refueling approach, enabling rapid refueling by replacing aluminum-based energy storage materials, and can flexibly configure energy reserves according to different mission durations and actual load requirements, enhancing continuous power generation capability while maintaining equipment portability. First 200W product released, covering diverse civilian and professional scenarios As the first product in the Hydrogen Wind Series, the world's first 200W portable hydrogen power generation equipment is primarily aimed at mobile application scenarios with high requirements for equipment portability, continuous power supply capability, and refueling flexibility. In the civilian sector, the product can serve outdoor travel, mobile office work, drone power supply, and other needs; in professional application fields, it can be further extended to emergency support, power and communication operations, and field operations, providing new power generation solutions for mobile electricity use in different environments. Starting with the 200W product, Guangdong Huachen Hydrogen Energy will continue to improve the Hydrogen Wind Series product lineup around different power levels and application needs, gradually forming a portable hydrogen power generation equipment portfolio covering multiple types of scenarios. Engineering validation continues to advance, safety assurance system refined Moving from laboratory technology to end-use products, engineering validation is a critical step in promoting product application. Currently, Hydrogen Wind Series products have undergone testing and validation around application scenarios such as emergency rescue, power repair, communication support, and field operations, with continuous optimization of system stability, safety, and environmental adaptability in complex environments. In terms of safety assurance, the product is equipped with an intelligent monitoring system that provides real-time monitoring of key parameters such as system operating status, temperature, and pressure, and enhances system operational reliability through multiple safety protection mechanisms. At the same time, to meet the demands of outdoor and complex environment applications, the product features targeted designs for wide-temperature-range operation, wind and sand resistance, and dust protection. Guangdong Huachen Hydrogen Energy Co., Ltd. is a hydrogen energy end-user industrialisation platform wholly established by Zhongyun Intelligent Technology (Guangzhou) Co., Ltd., primarily focused on high-end hydrogen energy end-use equipment R&D, scenario-based solutions, and industrialisation applications. The launch of the "Hydrogen Wind Series" portable hydrogen power generation equipment represents an important step for the company in advancing scenario-based, productised, and industrialised applications of hydrogen energy technology.

artigo.texto: CHARLOTTE, N.C., Oct. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Magnera today announced it has entered into a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Army Research Laboratory to evaluate and advance next-generation battery separator technologies, supporting evolving energy requirements across defense, critical infrastructure, and commercial applications. The collaboration will leverage Magnera's OmniSep™ platform, an advanced separator technology engineered to enhance battery performance, safety, and reliability in demanding operating environments. Designed with high ionic conductivity, superior electrolyte wettability, and enhanced thermal stability1, OmniSep™ supports the power, efficiency, and safety requirements of next-generation battery systems. The initiative aligns with the Department of War's growing emphasis on resilient energy, electrification, and assured power for distributed and contested operations. As the military deploys increasingly power-intensive capabilities, including autonomous systems, ISR platforms, electronic warfare, counter-UAS technologies, resilient communications, and directed energy systems, the need for safe, high-performance energy storage continues to grow. artigo.texto: World • the agreement reached overnight What European leaders have decided regarding the emissions trading market After a day of deadlock, the European Council has asked the Commission to reassess the impact of ETS2, the scheme that will charge for emissions from transport and heating from 2028. Italy did not secure a postponement. No agreement has been reached on the 2028–2034 EU budget. European Council in Brussels During the night between Thursday and Friday, the heads of state and government of the European Union member states, meeting in Brussels for the European Council, reached an agreement on the energy chapter, which had divided them throughout the day. The conclusions, adopted after a lengthy standoff, call on the European Commission to update its assessment of all the impacts of ETS2, particularly with regard to its structure and safeguard measures. It is a compromise between two groups of countries: on the one hand, Italy and the Visegrád Group countries; on the other, the Nordic countries. The ETS (Emissions Trading System) is the system through which the EU sets a price on carbon dioxide emissions. Companies in certain sectors must purchase allowances for every tonne of CO₂ they emit, and the price of these allowances is determined by the market: the idea is to make it more cost-effective to pollute less. The existing ETS covers industrial plants and power stations. ETS2 extends the same principle to fuels used in transport and in buildings, namely petrol, diesel and heating gas. It will come into force in 2028, and this is what worries some governments the most: unlike the first scheme, its costs are likely to fall directly on households and motorists. The row stemmed from the high energy prices of recent weeks. Alongside Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, as well as Greece and Cyprus, Italy was calling for changes to the system. According to Il Foglio’s account, the group aimed to postpone the entry into force of ETS2 from 2028 to 2030 and to introduce an assessment of the impact the ETS has had on European industry to date. Other accounts describe a more cautious stance: Italy did not wish to postpone ETS2 any further, knowing that it would lose that battle. Instead, the government was looking for a temporary ‘national exemption’, modelled on the one granted to Spain and Portugal in 2023 to keep electricity prices in check. Meanwhile, the prime ministers of Finland, Denmark and Sweden – Petteri Orpo, Mette Frederiksen and Ulf Kristersson – had written to the President of the European Council, António Costa, to oppose any weakening of the system. In their view, tampering with the ETS would have undermined the predictability on which investment decisions depend, and would have slowed down the decarbonisation of industry. The final text attempts to reconcile the two positions. In point 11 of the conclusions, the European Council reiterates the need to urgently ensure a well-functioning, transparent and predictable carbon market, to protect it from carbon leakage, to reduce price volatility and to mitigate its impact on electricity prices. The specific reference to ETS2 was included at the request of Italy and the Visegrád countries, but without an explicit reference to the postponement. At the same time, the text reaffirms the essential role of the ETS. In practice, Italy has secured a commitment from the Commission to re-examine the impact of ETS2, but not a postponement of its entry into force: the timetable remains as planned. The Commission must now present the new assessment, and any changes to the system will have to go through the normal European legislative process. The first day of the summit, however, ended without an agreement on the EU’s next multiannual budget, covering the period 2028–2034, and negotiations have been postponed until November. In their conclusions, the leaders did not commit to reaching an agreement by December, merely acknowledging that an agreement by 2026 would allow the necessary legislation to be approved in 2027 to ensure funding from the start of 2028. Meloni’s call for greater flexibility on public finances also remains unresolved, having received explicit support only from Greece. The European Council continues today to finalise discussions on Ukraine, defence and flexibility, with Meloni’s closing press conference. The first face-to-face meeting between Zelensky and the Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar is today’s top European political story: it marks the end of Orbán’s era of vetoes on Kyiv.

artigo.texto: PHOENIX — Arizona is one of the country's top destinations for data centers, and the largest projects have not yet been built. Do you have a concern in your community or a news tip? We want to hear from you! Connect with us: share@abc15.com According to the site US Data Center Map, there are 5,098 data centers across the country. Virginia and Texas each hold about 12% of those facilities. California, Ohio, Georgia and Arizona follow. Today, data centers nationwide draw about 49 gigawatts of power — three times Arizona's total power output. But the 1,600 more that are planned or under construction are far larger, projected to require 346 gigawatts — more than 20 times what Arizona produces. Arizona currently has 182 data centers. Of those, 107 are operating, 16 are under construction and 53 are planned. The facilities operating today are mostly small, combining for 1.8 gigawatts. But the planned facilities would add nine more gigawatts, pushing the state past 12 — roughly equal to what the entire state uses today. Most of Arizona's data centers are located on the edges of the Valley. In the far East Valley, four major campuses sit side by side: Meta, NTT, Apple and EdgeConneX. In south Chandler, a cluster of facilities is mostly owned by CyrusOne. In the West Valley, near Goodyear Airpark, Microsoft and Stream have facilities. The largest data centers yet to come are in Buckeye, where two campuses are each projected to exceed a gigawatt. The Greater Phoenix Economic Council estimates the industry has brought in 108,000 jobs over the past decade, added $11 billion to the state's economic output and driven half of its economic growth. The benefits are significant — and so is the power demand. The question is whether one outweighs the other. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.
